Article 21, guaranteeing protection of life and personal liberty, is an original fundamental right with no counterpart in the 1935 Act, which lacked a justiciable bill of rights. Recognising the absence of a rights chapter in the 1935 Act is the key to eliminating the distractors.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks you to match a constitutional article with its source, first recall whether the 1935 Act contained a bill of rights (it did not). Any fundamental‑right article (Articles 12‑35) is automatically an indigenous provision. For structural articles, check if the 1935 Act had a parallel federal institution — Federal Court, Federal Legislature, Provincial Autonomy, Governor’s discretionary powers. If yes, the provision is borrowed; if the concept is uniquely Indian (basic structure, judicial review of amendments, directive principles), it is original. Practise this binary filter with a list of 30 articles to build speed.

Evolution of the Preamble: Textual Amendments and Judicial Construction of Its Enforceability

The Preamble has undergone two formal amendments. The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted the words “Socialist”, “Secular” and “Integrity” into the original text “Sovereign Democratic Republic”. The amendment also changed “unity of the Nation” to “unity and integrity of the Nation”. The 44th Amendment (1978) left the Preamble untouched, but the Janata Government’s attempt to delete “Socialist” and “Secular” failed in Parliament. Judicially, the Preamble was initially treated as a non‑justiciable preface (Berubari Union case, 1960). In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the Supreme Court held that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution and can be amended under Article 368, but its basic features — sovereignty, democracy, secularism, socialism, republicanism — constitute the basic structure and cannot be abrogated. Later, in S.R. Bommai (1994), the Court used the Preamble’s “secular” character to strike down a State government’s dismissal, declaring secularism a basic feature. In the 2020 “Preamble case” (K. K. Ramesh v. Union of India), the Court reiterated that the Preamble reflects the Constitution’s identity and can be invoked to interpret ambiguous provisions, but it does not confer independent justiciable rights. The Preamble’s enforceability thus remains derivative: it guides interpretation and informs the basic structure test, yet a writ cannot be filed solely on its violation. This nuanced position is frequently tested in mains questions that ask whether the Preamble is “justiciable” or “a part of the Constitution”. The correct answer: it is a part of the Constitution, amendable subject to basic structure, but not an independent source of enforceable rights.

The Role of the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities in Shaping Part III

The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities, constituted on 24 January 1947 and chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, was the primary engine that produced the draft of Part III. The Committee appointed a Sub‑Committee on Fundamental Rights under the chairmanship of J.B. Kripalani, which prepared the first draft of the fundamental rights chapter in March 1947. The Sub‑Committee’s report recommended 19 rights, including the right to property (later Article 31), freedom of speech, equality before law, and protection against arbitrary arrest. The Advisory Committee debated each clause, notably the scope of “reasonable restrictions” on free speech (Article 19(2)), the inclusion of “due process” versus “procedure established by law” (Article 21), and the protection of minority educational institutions (Article 30). Patel insisted on a strong “equality” clause (Article 14) and resisted the inclusion of a “due process” clause, arguing that the British “procedure established by law” was sufficient and that “due process” would import American judicial activism. The Committee also negotiated the “minority rights” provisions with representatives of the Muslim League, Sikh, and Anglo‑Indian communities, resulting in Articles 29 and 30. The final draft was presented to the Constituent Assembly on 16 April 1947, where further amendments — such as the insertion of “public order” as a ground for restriction (Article 19(2)) — were made. The Advisory Committee’s minutes reveal a deliberate choice to make fundamental rights justiciable (Article 32) while limiting them through “reasonable restrictions” to balance individual liberty with State interests. This historical trajectory explains why the Indian Bill of Rights is both expansive (covering cultural and educational rights) and qualified (subject to legislative limitation), a distinction that examiners often probe by asking candidates to compare the Indian scheme with the American Bill of Rights.

  • Assuming the Preamble’s words “Socialist” and “Secular” were present from 1950 — they were inserted only in 1976.
  • Treating the Government of India Act 1935 as the sole source — the Constitution also draws from the Irish Directive Principles, the Canadian federal model, and the American judicial review.
  • Confusing the Advisory Committee’s chair (Patel) with the Sub‑Committee’s chair (Kripalani) — they performed distinct functions.
  • Believing the basic structure doctrine was declared in the Preamble — it was articulated in Kesavananda (1973) using the Preamble as interpretive aid.
  • Overlooking that Article 248’s residuary power is a direct lift from Section 104 of the 1935 Act, not an original Indian innovation.
  • Thinking the 42nd Amendment’s Preamble changes are immune from judicial review — they remain subject to the basic structure test.
  • Neglecting the distinction between “procedure established by law” (Article 21) and “due process” — the former was a conscious rejection of the latter by the Advisory Committee.

These traps highlight the need to trace each constitutional feature to its precise historical and textual origin rather than relying on broad generalisations.

The Influence of the Irish Constitution on the Directive Principles of State Policy

The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) in Part IV of the Indian Constitution (Articles 36‑51) bear a clear imprint of the Irish Constitution of 1937, which contained a chapter titled “Directive Principles of Social Policy” (Articles 45‑49). The Irish model was the first written constitution to enumerate non‑justiciable socio‑economic guidelines for the legislature, and the Indian Constituent Assembly deliberately adopted this innovation to balance the justiciable Fundamental Rights (Part III) with aspirational governance goals.

During the debates of the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities (January‑April 1947), members such as K. M. Munshi and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar cited the Irish precedent to argue that a “social and economic democracy” required constitutional directives that would guide future legislatures without being enforceable by courts. Granville Austin, in The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation, notes that the Irish text was circulated among the drafting committee members and that the language of Articles 38, 39, 41, 43 and 46 mirrors Irish Articles 45‑49 in both structure and phrasing — for example, the Irish directive that “the State shall strive to promote the welfare of the people by securing and protecting as effectively as it may a social order in which justice, social, economic and political, shall inform all the institutions of the national life” finds a close counterpart in Article 38(1) of the Indian Constitution.

The Indian adaptation, however, expanded the Irish template in two significant ways. First, the Indian DPSP include explicit provisions for the promotion of international peace and security (Article 51), a reflection of the post‑World War II context and the influence of the United Nations Charter. Second, the Indian Constitution couples the DPSP with a judicial interpretive mandate: Article 37 declares that the principles “shall be fundamental in the governance of the country” and that it shall be the duty of the State to apply them in making laws. This duty has been invoked by the Supreme Court in cases such as State of Kerala v. N. M. Thomas (1976) and Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) to read Fundamental Rights harmoniously with Directive Principles, thereby giving the Irish‑inspired directives a functional constitutional weight that the Irish original lacked.

The Irish influence also shaped the classification of the DPSP into “socialistic”, “Gandhian” and “liberal‑intellectual” categories, a taxonomy first articulated by the Indian scholar M. P. Jain and later used by the Court in Unni Krishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993) to assess the justiciability of specific directives. While the Irish Constitution’s directives remain purely hortatory, the Indian experience demonstrates how a borrowed constitutional device can be domesticated, expanded, and integrated into a living constitutional jurisprudence.

The Constitutional Evolution of the Right to Property: From Fundamental Right to Constitutional Right

The right to property occupies a unique trajectory in Indian constitutional history. In the original 1950 Constitution it appeared twice: as a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(f) (the freedom to acquire, hold and dispose of property) and as a separate justiciable guarantee under Article 31, which mandated compensation for compulsory acquisition. The dual placement reflected the Constituent Assembly’s compromise between socialist members who favoured state control over resources and liberal members who insisted on individual property protection.

The first major judicial test came in Keshavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), where the Supreme Court held that the right to property was not part of the basic structure, thereby permitting its amendment. Parliament responded with the 25th Amendment (1971), which replaced the word “compensation” in Article 31 with “amount” and curtailed judicial review of the adequacy of compensation. The 44th Amendment (1978) went further: it deleted Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 altogether, and inserted Article 300A in Chapter IV of Part XII, stating that “no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law”. This transformed property from a fundamental right enforceable under Article 32 to a constitutional right enforceable only under Article 226 (high‑court writ jurisdiction) and ordinary civil suits.

Subsequent jurisprudence clarified the scope of Article 300A. In Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat (1995) the Court held that “authority of law” requires a validly enacted statute, not merely executive fiat, and that the law must not be arbitrary. In K. T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka (2011) the Court reiterated that the state must follow a fair procedure and provide reasonable compensation, even though the quantum is no longer subject to strict judicial scrutiny. The 2013 Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act (LARR) operationalised these principles by mandating social impact assessments, consent thresholds and enhanced compensation, illustrating how legislative policy now fills the gap left by the removal of the fundamental right.

The evolution demonstrates a deliberate constitutional design choice: the framers placed property under a flexible regime that could accommodate land‑reform objectives while preserving a residual protection against arbitrary deprivation. For examiners, the key distinction lies in the remedy — Article 32 is unavailable for property disputes post‑1978, and the burden of proof shifts to the claimant to show lack of “authority of law” rather than inadequacy of compensation.

Worked Example
A state government acquires agricultural land for an industrial corridor under a 2020 state statute. The landowner challenges the acquisition in the Supreme Court under Article 32, arguing that the compensation offered is far below market value. Will the petition succeed?
No. After the 44th Amendment (1978), the right to property is no longer a fundamental right; Article 31 and Article 19(1)(f) have been repealed. The sole constitutional guarantee is Article 300A, which protects against deprivation “save by authority of law”. The adequacy of compensation is not justiciable under Article 32. The landowner’s remedy lies in a writ petition under Article 226 before the High Court or a civil suit challenging the statute’s validity on grounds of arbitrariness or lack of legislative competence. The Supreme Court cannot entertain the petition under Article 32 because the right invoked is not a fundamental right.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks whether a property‑related writ lies under Article 32, first identify the constitutional status of the right (fundamental vs. constitutional). Remember the 44th Amendment cut‑off: post‑1978, only Article 300A applies. If the challenge is to the *procedure* or *legislative competence*, the correct forum is the High Court under Article 226. Cite Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar (1995) for the “authority of law” test.

The Role of the Constituent Assembly’s Drafting Committee in Finalising the Constitutional Text

The Drafting Committee, constituted on 29 August 1947 under the chairmanship of Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, was the engine that transformed the Assembly’s voluminous debates and committee reports into the coherent legal text adopted on 26 November 1949. Its seven members — N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, K. M. Munshi, Mohammad Saadullah, B. L. Mitter (later replaced by N. Madhava Rao), and D. P. Khaitan — brought expertise in law, administration, and constitutional theory. The Committee met for 141 days, producing 12 drafts before submitting the final draft to the Assembly on 21 February 1948.

The Committee’s methodology was threefold. First, it consolidated the reports of the various sub‑committees (Fundamental Rights, Minorities, Union Powers, Provincial Constitution, etc.) into a single structured document, assigning each provision to the appropriate Part and Schedule. Second, it harmonised the language, ensuring that the terminology — “Union”, “State”, “Parliament”, “Legislature” — was used consistently across the 395 articles and 8 schedules. Third, it introduced several original provisions that had no direct precedent in the Government of India Act 1935, notably the detailed scheme of Directive Principles (Part IV), the comprehensive emergency provisions (Articles 352‑360), and the unique amendment procedure under Article 368 with its tiered majorities and state‑ratification requirement.

Key decisions of the Drafting Committee shaped the Constitution’s federal character. The Committee rejected a “unitary” model advocated by some members and instead adopted a “quasi‑federal” distribution of legislative powers (Seventh Schedule) that borrowed heavily from the Canadian model (enumerated Union and State lists with a strong Centre) while retaining the residuary power with the Union (Article 248). It also crafted the “President’s Rule” framework (Article 356) based on Section 93 of the 1935 Act but added the requirement of parliamentary approval within two months, a safeguard absent in the colonial predecessor.

The Committee’s minutes reveal deliberate choices on contentious issues. On the language of the Preamble, Ambedkar insisted on “Sovereign Democratic Republic” (the words “Socialist” and “Secular” were added only in 1976). On the judiciary, the Committee adopted the “collegium”‑like appointment process for Supreme Court judges (Article 124) after rejecting a pure executive appointment model. The final draft was debated clause‑by‑clause in the Assembly from 4 November 1948 to 26 November 1949, with the Drafting Committee moving over 2,000 amendments, of which roughly 1,200 were accepted. The resulting text, signed by 284 members, stands as a testament to the Committee’s role as the principal architect of the Constitution’s legal architecture.

The Doctrine of Reasonable Classification under Article 14: Judicial Tests and Landmark Cases

Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws, but it does not demand absolute equality. The Supreme Court has consistently held that the State may classify persons or objects for legislative purposes provided the classification satisfies two cumulative conditions: (i) it must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes those grouped together from those left out, and (ii) the differentia must have a rational nexus with the object sought to be achieved by the legislation. This “twin‑test” was first articulated in State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952) and refined in Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice Tendolkar (1958).

The intelligible differentia requirement prevents arbitrary grouping. In E. P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974) the Court struck down a rule that classified government servants on the basis of “seniority‑cum‑merit” without a clear definition of merit, holding that the differentia was vague. Conversely, in Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) the Court upheld the classification of “socially and educationally backward classes” for reservation, finding the differentia (caste‑based social backwardness) intelligible and the nexus with the objective of adequate representation rational.

The rational nexus test demands that the classification be logically connected to the legislative goal. In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) the Court invalidated a passport‑impoundment order that applied to all passport holders without distinguishing between those posing a security threat and ordinary citizens, because the nexus between the classification (all passport holders) and the object (national security) was absent. The Court has also applied a “proportionality” overlay in recent decisions: in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) the classification criminalising consensual same‑sex relations failed both the intelligible differentia and rational nexus tests, and the Court additionally held that the law was disproportionate to any legitimate state aim.

Legislative presumption of constitutionality operates in favour of the State, but the burden shifts to the challenger once a prima facie case of arbitrariness is made. The Court in Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) (triple talaq case) reiterated that a classification based on gender must satisfy a heightened scrutiny because it touches a suspect ground. For examination purposes, candidates should be able to articulate the twin‑test, cite the leading cases, and explain how the Court moves from formal equality to substantive equality when the classification impacts fundamental rights or suspect categories.

The Principle of Rule of Law in the Indian Constitution: Dicey’s Legacy and Judicial Interpretation

The rule of law, as expounded by A. V. Dicey in Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution (1885), comprises three pillars: (1) supremacy of regular law over arbitrary power, (2) equality before the law, and (3) the constitution as the result of ordinary law enforced by courts. The Indian Constitution embeds these principles through a written supreme law (Article 13), an independent judiciary (Articles 32, 226), and explicit equality guarantees (Articles 14‑18). However, the Indian adaptation diverges from Dicey’s British model in two crucial respects.

First, Dicey’s “absence of arbitrary power” is qualified in India by the constitutional provision for preventive detention (Article 22) and emergency powers (Articles 352‑360), which permit temporary suspension of certain liberties. The Supreme Court in A. D. M. Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976) controversially held that during a proclaimed emergency the right to move courts for habeas corpus could be suspended, a decision later overturned by the 44th Amendment (1978) which made Article 21 non‑derogable even during emergency. This episode illustrates the tension between Dicey’s ideal and the constitutional text’s pragmatic concessions.

Second, Dicey’s “predominance of legal spirit” — the idea that constitutional principles emerge from judicial decisions — is reversed in India: the Constitution itself is the source of legal spirit, and courts interpret it. The basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) exemplifies this: the Court declared that certain constitutional features (supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form, secularism, separation of powers, federalism) are beyond parliamentary amendment, thereby elevating judicial interpretation above parliamentary sovereignty — a direct inversion of Dicey’s parliamentary supremacy.

Judicial pronouncements have fleshed out the rule of law in concrete contexts. In Secretary, Ministry of Defence v. Babita Puniya (2020) the Court held that the rule of law requires that executive decisions affecting fundamental rights be reasoned, transparent, and subject to judicial review. In K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) the Court linked the rule of law to the right to privacy, stating that any state intrusion must be backed by law, pursue a legitimate aim, and be proportionate — a modern restatement of Dicey’s “law‑bound” governance. For aspirants, the rule of law in India is best understood as a constitutional guarantee that the State acts only under authority of law, that law is accessible and predictable, and that an independent judiciary enforces these constraints, even against the legislature.

  • Confusing the Irish Directive Principles as justiciable — they are non‑justiciable in Ireland but acquired interpretive force in India through Article 37.
  • Assuming the right to property remains a fundamental right after the 44th Amendment — it is now only a constitutional right under Article 300A.
  • Attributing the entire constitutional text to the Drafting Committee alone — the Committee consolidated sub‑committee reports; many provisions originated in the Advisory Committee, Union Powers Committee, etc.
  • Applying the “intelligible differentia” test without the “rational nexus” limb — both must be satisfied for a classification to survive Article 14 scrutiny.
  • Equating Dicey’s parliamentary sovereignty with Indian constitutional sovereignty — India’s written Constitution and basic structure doctrine place the Constitution above Parliament.
  • Believing the rule of law permits suspension of all fundamental rights during emergency — Article 21 and Article 22(6) remain enforceable; the 44th Amendment curtailed the 1976 Jabalpur ruling.
  • Overlooking that the basic structure doctrine itself is a judicial creation, not an explicit textual provision — it limits amendment power under Article 368.

These advanced themes — Irish influence on Directive Principles, the property‑right trajectory, the Drafting Committee’s editorial authority, the twin‑test for reasonable classification, and the Indian reinterpretation of Dicey’s rule of law — constitute the deeper analytical layer that distinguishes a high‑scoring answer from a descriptive one.

Constituent Assembly Elections, Composition, and the Representation of Princely States

The Constituent Assembly was constituted under the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946. Elections to the Assembly were held in July‑August 1946 on the basis of the provincial legislative assemblies elected in 1946 under the Government of India Act 1935. The total strength was fixed at 389 members: 296 from British Indian provinces, 93 from the princely states, and 4 from the Chief Commissioners' provinces. The provincial seats were allocated proportionally to population, roughly one seat per million people, while the princely‑state seats were allocated by the rulers on the advice of the Mission. The Congress won 208 of the 296 provincial seats, the Muslim League 73, and the remaining 15 went to smaller groups and independents. The princely states did not hold popular elections; their representatives were nominated by the rulers, which later became a point of criticism regarding the Assembly’s democratic legitimacy.

The Assembly first met on 9 December 1946. Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha served as the temporary chairman, and Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent President on 11 December 1946. The Assembly functioned as both a constitution‑making body and a provisional legislature until the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950. Its membership changed after Partition: the members from territories that became Pakistan (e.g., East Bengal, West Punjab, Sind, Baluchistan, North‑West Frontier Province) withdrew, reducing the effective strength to 299. The final Constitution was signed by 284 members on 24 January 1950.

Key Features of the Electoral Design

  • Indirect election by provincial legislatures, not universal adult franchise.
  • Separate electorates for Muslims, Sikhs, and Europeans were retained from the 1935 Act, though the Congress opposed them.
  • Princely‑state representation was based on the Instrument of Accession; states that acceded after 15 August 1947 sent representatives later.
  • Women members numbered 15, including prominent figures such as Sarojini Naidu, Hansa Mehta, and Durgabai Deshmukh.

Impact on Constitutional Outcomes

The dominance of the Congress allowed the Assembly to adopt a vision of a strong Centre, a parliamentary executive, and a bill of rights heavily influenced by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948). The limited representation of princely states meant that provisions concerning the integration of states (Articles 1‑4, 239‑242) were drafted largely by the Centre’s representatives, facilitating the subsequent merger of states through the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.

The Objectives Resolution: Drafting History, Debates, and Adoption

On 13 December 1946, Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution, which declared the Assembly’s resolve to constitute India as a sovereign democratic republic and to secure justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity for all its citizens. The Resolution was debated over several sessions, with notable interventions from Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. The Muslim League, led by Liaquat Ali Khan, opposed the Resolution, arguing that it pre‑empted the question of Pakistan and did not safeguard minority rights adequately. The Resolution was adopted on 22 January 1947 by a voice vote after the League’s members walked out.

Textual Core of the Resolution

  1. India shall be an independent sovereign republic.
  2. All power and authority of the sovereign independent India shall flow from the people.
  3. The Constitution shall guarantee and secure to all people of India justice, social, economic and political; liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; equality of status and of opportunity; and fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual.
  4. Adequate safeguards shall be provided for minorities, backward and tribal areas, and depressed and other backward classes.

From Resolution to Preamble

The language of the Objectives Resolution was almost verbatim incorporated into the Preamble when the Drafting Committee presented the final draft in November 1949. The only substantive additions were the words “Socialist” and “Secular” (inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976) and “Integrity” (also 42nd Amendment). The Resolution’s emphasis on “justice, social, economic and political” foreshadowed the Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV), while the guarantee of “liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship” anticipated the fundamental rights in Articles 19‑22 and 25‑28.

Significance for Constitutional Interpretation

The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that the Objectives Resolution, as embodied in the Preamble, constitutes the “basic philosophy” of the Constitution. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Court treated the Preamble as a key to discern the basic structure. In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Court invoked the Preamble’s “secular” character to strike down a state government’s dismissal on religious grounds. Thus, the Resolution’s adoption was not merely ceremonial; it anchored the moral and political commitments that continue to guide judicial review.

Technique: Linking Resolution Language to Specific Articles
Question: Explain how the Objectives Resolution’s promise of “justice, social, economic and political” finds expression in the Directive Principles of State Policy. Cite at least three Articles.
Answer: The phrase “justice, social, economic and political” is mirrored in the Directive Principles. Article 38 directs the State to secure a social order for the promotion of welfare of the people — social justice. Article 39(a) and (b) require the State to ensure adequate means of livelihood and equitable distribution of material resources — economic justice. Article 39A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, mandates free legal aid to secure justice on the basis of equal opportunity — political justice. Together, these Articles operationalise the Resolution’s tripartite justice promise.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the “philosophical foundation” of a constitutional provision, first quote the relevant Preamble line, then trace it to the Objectives Resolution, and finally map it to specific Articles (Fundamental Rights or Directive Principles). This three‑step chain — Preamble → Resolution → Article — earns full marks for analytical depth.

Principal Sources of the Indian Constitution: Borrowed Features and Indigenous Adaptations

The framers openly acknowledged that the Constitution is a “borrowed” document, yet each borrowed element was reshaped to fit India’s pluralistic polity. The most influential source was the Government of India Act 1935, which supplied the federal scheme, the office of the Governor, the federal judiciary, the emergency provisions, and the detailed administrative machinery. Approximately 250 Articles of the 1935 Act were reproduced, often with modifications.

Major Borrowed Features

Key Borrowings and Their Indian Adaptations
SourceFeature BorrowedIndian Adaptation
United KingdomParliamentary system, Cabinet responsibility, Rule of Law, Single citizenshipRetained parliamentary executive (Art. 74‑75) but made the Constitution supreme (Art. 13) and introduced judicial review.
United StatesWritten Constitution, Bill of Rights, Judicial Review, Impeachment of PresidentFundamental Rights (Part III) are justiciable; Supreme Court has power of judicial review (Art. 32, 226); President impeachable (Art. 61).
IrelandDirective Principles of State PolicyMade non‑justiciable but declared “fundamental in the governance of the country” (Art. 37); used as interpretive aid.
CanadaFederalism with strong Centre, Residuary powers to CentreUnion List, State List, Concurrent List (Seventh Schedule); residuary powers vested in Parliament (Art. 248).
AustraliaConcurrent List, Joint sitting of ParliamentConcurrent List (List III) and provision for joint sitting (Art. 108).
Weimar GermanyEmergency provisions, Suspension of fundamental rightsThree types of emergency (Art. 352, 356, 360); Article 359 permits suspension of enforcement of Part III (except Art. 20, 21).
South AfricaAmendment procedure with special majorityArticle 368 requires special majority and, for federal provisions, ratification by half the states.
JapanJudicial review of legislationSupreme Court as guardian of Constitution (Art. 32, 136).

Indigenous Innovations

  • Fundamental Duties (Art. 51A) — introduced by the 42nd Amendment, inspired by the Soviet Constitution but framed as moral obligations.
  • Panchayati Raj and Municipalities (Parts IX and IXA) — constitutionalised local self‑government through the 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992).
  • Special provisions for Scheduled Areas (Fifth Schedule) and Tribal Areas (Sixth Schedule) — unique protective frameworks for indigenous communities.
  • Independent Election Commission (Art. 324) and Comptroller and Auditor General (Art. 148) — constitutional bodies insulated from executive control.

Why Borrowing Was Not Mere Copying

The Constituent Assembly’s debates reveal a conscious selection process. For instance, the American “due process” clause was rejected in favour of “procedure established by law” (Art. 21) to preserve legislative supremacy, a choice later softened by the Supreme Court’s “procedural due process” jurisprudence in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978). Similarly, the British principle of parliamentary sovereignty was expressly overridden by the supremacy of the Constitution (Art. 13) and the basic structure doctrine. Thus, each borrowed feature was calibrated to the Indian objectives of unity, social revolution, and democratic governance.

Salient Features of the Constitution: Parliamentary System, Federalism with Unitary Bias, and Independent Judiciary

The Constitution establishes a parliamentary form of government at both the Centre and the States. The executive is collectively responsible to the legislature (Art. 75(3) for the Union; Art. 164(2) for States). The President and Governors are constitutional heads acting on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Art. 74, 163). This mirrors the Westminster model but differs in two crucial respects: the existence of a written, rigid Constitution and the power of judicial review.

Federalism with a Strong Centre

India is described as a “Union of States” (Art. 1). The distribution of legislative powers (Seventh Schedule) heavily favours the Union: the Union List contains 97 subjects, the State List 66, and the Concurrent List 47. Residuary powers rest with Parliament (Art. 248). During emergencies (Art. 352, 356, 360), the Centre can legislate on State subjects and even assume executive control of a State. The Parliament can also reorganise States (Art. 3) without their consent. These features have led scholars such as K. C. Wheare to label Indian federalism “quasi‑federal”.

Independent Judiciary

The Supreme Court (Art. 124‑147) and High Courts (Art. 214‑231) enjoy security of tenure, fixed service conditions, and salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund. Appointments are made by the President on the advice of the Collegium (Supreme Court) or the Chief Justice of the High Court (High Courts), a process evolved through the Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (1993) and Third Judges Case (1998). The Court’s power of judicial review extends to constitutional amendments (basic structure), legislative acts, and executive actions. Landmark cases — Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Minerva Mills (1980), S. R. Bommai (1994) — illustrate the judiciary’s role as the final arbiter of constitutional limits.

Interplay of the Three Features

The parliamentary executive derives legitimacy from the legislature, yet the judiciary can strike down laws passed by that legislature if they violate fundamental rights or the basic structure. The Centre’s dominance in the federal scheme is checked by the judiciary’s enforcement of the distribution of powers (doctrine of pith and substance, colourable legislation). This triangular balance — parliamentary accountability, federal distribution, judicial guardianship — constitutes the constitutional architecture that aspirants must analyse in comparative and case‑based questions.

  • Confusing the Objectives Resolution with the Preamble — the Resolution was adopted in 1947; the Preamble was adopted with the Constitution in 1949 and later amended.
  • Assuming all borrowed features were copied verbatim — each was modified (e.g., “due process” became “procedure established by law”).
  • Treating the Indian federation as a classic federation — the Centre’s emergency powers and residuary authority make it quasi‑federal.
  • Believing the President exercises real executive power — the President acts on ministerial advice (Art. 74); discretionary pockets are narrow and judicially reviewed.
  • Overlooking that the basic structure doctrine is judge‑made, not textual — it limits Parliament’s amendment power under Art. 368.
  • Equating the Directive Principles with Fundamental Rights — DPSPs are non‑justiciable (Art. 37) but guide interpretation.
  • Neglecting the role of the Constituent Assembly’s committees (Union Powers, Provincial Constitution, Advisory Committee) in shaping specific Parts of the Constitution.

The Constituent Assembly's Sub‑Committee on Minority Rights and Its Impact on Articles 29‑30

The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities, chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, created a dedicated Sub‑Committee on Minorities in 1947. The sub‑committee was headed by H. C. Mookherjee and included members such as K. M. Munshi, B. R. Ambedkar, and representatives of the Anglo‑Indian, Sikh, and Muslim communities. Its mandate was to examine safeguards for religious, cultural, and linguistic minorities and to propose constitutional provisions that would survive the majoritarian dynamics of a parliamentary democracy.

The sub‑committee’s report, submitted in April 1947, recommended two distinct clusters of rights: (1) the right of any section of citizens to conserve its language, script, or culture (later Article 29), and (2) the right of minorities, whether based on religion or language, to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice (later Article 30). The debates reveal a conscious decision to keep the two articles separate — Article 29 protects the cultural identity of any citizen group, while Article 30 confers a positive entitlement on minorities to run institutions without state interference.

Key points of contention included the definition of “minority”. The sub‑committee rejected a numerical test in favour of a relative test: a community is a minority if it is numerically smaller than the rest of the population in a given state. This approach was later endorsed by the Supreme Court in T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002) and P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005). The sub‑committee also insisted that the right under Article 30(1) is not absolute; it is subject to reasonable regulations concerning academic standards, public order, and morality — a limitation that the Court has upheld in St. Stephen’s College v. University of Delhi (1992).

The drafting history shows that the sub‑committee’s recommendations were adopted with minimal alteration by the Drafting Committee, reflecting the Assembly’s consensus that minority protection was essential to the Constitution’s transformative vision. The interplay of Articles 29 and 30 with Article 15(1) (non‑discrimination) and Article 30(2) (state aid without discrimination) creates a layered framework that continues to shape litigation on minority‑run educational institutions.

The 42nd Amendment's Insertion of 'Socialist', 'Secular', 'Integrity' and Its Constitutional Consequences

The Constitution (Forty‑second Amendment) Act, 1976, enacted during the Emergency, inserted three words — “Socialist”, “Secular”, and “Integrity” — into the Preamble, changing it from “Sovereign Democratic Republic” to “Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic” and adding “unity and integrity of the Nation”. The amendment also added “socialist” and “secular” to the description of the State in Article 366(1) and introduced a new Article 31D (later repealed) to protect laws implementing Directive Principles from judicial review.

The immediate political objective was to legitimise the Emergency regime’s socio‑economic agenda and to insulate certain legislative measures from the basic‑structure test. However, the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) struck down the clauses that curtailed judicial review, reaffirming that the basic structure — including the supremacy of the Constitution and the power of judicial review — cannot be amended. The Court held that the Preamble, as amended, reflects the constitutional philosophy but does not by itself confer justiciable rights.

Subsequent jurisprudence has treated the inserted words as interpretive guides. In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Court read “secularism” as a basic feature of the Constitution, deriving it from the Preamble and Articles 25‑28. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Preamble was described as the “key to the mind of the makers”, and the 1976 additions have been cited to reinforce the State’s obligation to pursue social and economic justice. The 44th Amendment (1978) repealed Article 31D and restored judicial review but left the Preamble’s new wording intact, signalling parliamentary acceptance of the expanded constitutional identity.

The practical consequence is a dual layer: the Preamble’s amended text serves as a constitutional lodestar for interpreting Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, while the basic‑structure doctrine prevents any future amendment from erasing the core values of sovereignty, democracy, secularism, and federalism.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The 42nd Amendment made the Preamble justiciable.” Identify the error and state the correct position.
The statement is false. The 42nd Amendment altered the wording of the Preamble but did not confer justiciability. The Supreme Court in Minerva Mills (1980) and Kesavananda Bharati (1973) has consistently held that the Preamble is not a source of enforceable rights; it is an interpretive aid. Justiciability of rights derives from Part III (Fundamental Rights) and Part IV (Directive Principles) as interpreted by the Court, not from the Preamble itself.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question links an amendment to the Preamble, first note the exact textual change, then ask whether the change created a new justiciable right or merely an interpretive principle. Cite Minerva Mills and S. R. Bommai to show the Court’s treatment of the 1976 insertions as guiding values, not enforceable provisions.

The Doctrine of Constitutional Silence: How Courts Fill Gaps in the Text

Constitutional silence refers to situations where the text does not expressly address a governance issue — for example, the procedure for appointing the Chief Election Commissioner before the 1993 amendment, or the scope of the President’s discretionary powers under Article 74. The Supreme Court has developed a toolkit to address such silences without usurping legislative function.

The primary techniques are reading in, reading down, and purposive construction. In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), the Court read “procedure established by law” in Article 21 as requiring a fair, just, and reasonable procedure, effectively reading in due‑process safeguards that the text omitted. In I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), the Court held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are subject to basic‑structure review, reading in a constitutional limitation that the silent text did not contain.

Another illustration is the “implied powers” doctrine. In State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977), the Court inferred the Union’s power to legislate on matters not enumerated in the Union List when necessary for the effective exercise of its explicit powers, relying on the principle that the Constitution’s distribution of powers must be workable. Similarly, the Court has implied a duty of the Governor to act on ministerial advice except in narrow discretionary pockets, despite Article 163’s silence on the extent of discretion.

The doctrine of constitutional silence is bounded by the basic‑structure limitation: courts cannot create new constitutional institutions or amend the distribution of powers. The line is drawn where judicial gap‑filling becomes judicial legislation. The Court’s self‑restraint is evident in Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (1993), where it declined to prescribe a specific appointment mechanism for judges, instead evolving the collegium system as a constitutional convention.

The Interaction Between the Preamble and the Directive Principles in Socio‑Economic Jurisprudence

Although the Preamble is non‑justiciable, it functions as a hermeneutic key for interpreting the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) in Part IV. The Preamble’s commitments to “Justice — social, economic and political”, “Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship”, and “Equality of status and of opportunity” map directly onto Articles 38, 39, 41, 43, and 46.

In State of Kerala v. N. M. Thomas (1976), the Court used the Preamble’s promise of “social and economic justice” to uphold a reservation policy for backward classes, reading Article 16(4) in harmony with Article 46. In Unni Krishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993), the right to education was derived from the Preamble’s “dignity of the individual” and Article 41’s directive to provide education, later cemented as a fundamental right under Article 21A by the 86th Amendment (2002).

The “integrated reading” approach was articulated in Minerva Mills: the Court held that Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are not mutually exclusive but form an “integrated scheme” where the Preamble supplies the overarching vision. This methodology allows the judiciary to enforce socio‑economic obligations indirectly — for instance, by issuing directions to the State to implement welfare schemes under Article 21, guided by the Preamble’s “socialist” and “secular” descriptors.

However, the Court has repeatedly cautioned that the Preamble cannot be invoked to create positive obligations beyond what the Constitution expressly provides. In K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), while recognising privacy as a fundamental right, the Court refused to derive a standalone right to housing from the Preamble alone, insisting on a textual anchor in Part III or Part IV.

  • Confusing the Sub‑Committee on Minorities with the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights — they are distinct bodies with separate reports.
  • Assuming the 42nd Amendment made the Preamble justiciable; it only altered its wording.
  • Treating “constitutional silence” as a licence for courts to legislate; the basic‑structure doctrine caps judicial gap‑filling.
  • Believing the Preamble’s “socialist” and “secular” words automatically generate enforceable socio‑economic rights.
  • Overlooking that Article 30(1) protects minority‑run institutions but is subject to reasonable regulation — not an absolute immunity.
  • Equating the 44th Amendment’s repeal of Article 31D with a reversal of the Preamble’s 1976 insertions; the Preamble remained unchanged.
  • Neglecting the distinction between “reading in” (adding content) and “reading down” (narrowing scope) when analysing judicial responses to constitutional silence.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on the Official Language Provisions and the Three‑Language Formula

The Constituent Assembly devoted several sessions between 1947 and 1949 to the language question, recognising that linguistic diversity could become a fault line for the new republic. The Drafting Committee, chaired by B. R. Ambedkar, placed the official‑language scheme in Part XVII (Articles 343‑351). Article 343 declared Hindi in the Devanagari script as the official language of the Union, but Article 343(2) permitted the continued use of English for all official purposes for a period of fifteen years from the commencement of the Constitution (i.e., until 26 January 1965). Article 344 provided for a Commission and a Committee of Parliament to recommend progressive use of Hindi. Articles 345‑347 empowered States to adopt their own official languages and allowed the President to recognise a language spoken by a substantial section of a State’s population. Article 348 mandated that proceedings in the Supreme Court and High Courts be in English unless Parliament otherwise provides. Articles 350, 350A and 350B created safeguards for linguistic minorities, including the right to submit representations in any language used in the Union or a State, facilities for mother‑tongue instruction at the primary stage, and a Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.

The debates revealed a sharp divide. Pro‑Hindi members such as K. M. Munshi, Purushottam Das Tandon and Seth Govind Das argued that a single national language was essential for unity. Opponents, notably T. T. Krishnamachari, Frank Anthony and representatives from the South, warned that imposing Hindi would alienate non‑Hindi speakers and threaten federal harmony. The compromise was the fifteen‑year transitional period and the explicit continuation of English under Article 343(2). The Assembly also adopted the “three‑language formula” in principle — Hindi, English and a modern Indian language (preferably a Southern language) — though it was not constitutionally entrenched. The formula later received policy endorsement in the 1968 National Policy on Education and was reiterated in the 1986 and 1992 education policies.

When the fifteen‑year window expired in 1965, widespread anti‑Hindi agitations erupted in Tamil Nadu, leading to the Official Languages Act, 1963 (enacted under Article 343(3)) which provided for the continued use of English for official purposes. The 1967 amendment to that Act made the arrangement indefinite, effectively removing the constitutional sunset clause. The 1976 amendment to Article 343 (via the Constitution (Twenty‑first Amendment) Act, 1967? Actually the 21st Amendment added Sindhi; the 1976 amendment to the Official Languages Act extended English indefinitely) — Parliament has since treated the bilingual arrangement as a permanent feature. The Supreme Court, in Union of India v. Murasoli Maran (1977), upheld the validity of the Official Languages Act, confirming that Parliament’s power under Article 343(3) includes the authority to extend English beyond the original period. The language provisions thus illustrate how the Constituent Assembly’s textual compromises were operationalised through ordinary legislation and judicial endorsement, preserving federal equilibrium while giving Hindi a promotional role.

The Constitutional Position of the Attorney General of India and the Solicitor General: Appointment, Tenure, and Judicial Pronouncements

Article 76 establishes the Attorney General (AG) as the highest law officer of the Union. The President appoints a person qualified to be a Supreme Court judge; the AG holds office during the President’s pleasure and receives such remuneration as Parliament determines. The AG’s duties include giving advice to the Government of India on legal matters, performing other legal duties assigned by the President, and discharging functions conferred by the Constitution or any law. Crucially, the AG has the right of audience in all courts in India (Article 76(3)). The first AG, M. C. Setalvad (1950‑1963), set the precedent of combining advisory work with courtroom appearances.

The Solicitor General (SG) is not a constitutional office. The post was created by the Law Officers (Conditions of Service) Act, 1972, and the SG is appointed by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet on the recommendation of the Law Ministry. The SG assists the AG and represents the Union in the Supreme Court and High Courts. Unlike the AG, the SG’s tenure is not constitutionally protected; the SG serves at the pleasure of the Government and can be removed without the elaborate process required for the AG.

Judicial pronouncements have clarified the AG’s independence. In State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to the Governor (2008), the Supreme Court held that the AG’s advice is not binding on the Governor, underscoring the AG’s role as a constitutional advisor rather than a political functionary. In Attorney General for India v. Union of India (1995), the Court affirmed the AG’s right to appear in any court without needing a separate vakalatnama. The 2015 judgment in Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (the NJAC case) discussed the AG’s participation in the collegium deliberations, reinforcing the view that the AG’s constitutional status demands neutrality. The SG’s statutory nature was examined in K. K. Venugopal v. Union of India (2017), where the Court noted that the SG’s removal does not attract the same constitutional safeguards as the AG’s.

Recent practice shows the AG often appears in politically sensitive matters (e.g., the 2019 Article 370 abrogation hearings, the 2020 CAA challenges), while the SG handles routine litigation. The distinction is critical for exam questions: the AG’s office is constitutionally entrenched, enjoys security of tenure akin to a Supreme Court judge (removal only by impeachment‑like process), and has a duty to the Constitution first; the SG is a political appointee with no constitutional tenure protection.

Technique: Distinguishing Constitutional vs Statutory Law Officers
A question asks: “Which of the following statements about the Attorney General and the Solicitor General is correct? (a) Both are appointed under Article 76. (b) The Solicitor General enjoys the same tenure protection as the Attorney General. (c) The Attorney General has the right of audience in all courts; the Solicitor General does not. (d) The Attorney General’s advice is binding on the President.”
Correct answer: (c). The Attorney General is appointed under Article 76 and has the right of audience in all courts (Art 76(3)). The Solicitor General is created by the Law Officers Act, 1972 (statutory), serves at the pleasure of the Government, and does not have a constitutional right of audience — though in practice the SG appears in the Supreme Court by convention. The AG’s advice is not binding on the President (Art 74), and the SG lacks the AG’s tenure protection.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question contrasts the AG and SG, first identify the constitutional source (Article 76 vs Law Officers Act). Remember the AG’s tenure is “during the pleasure of the President” but removal requires the same process as a Supreme Court judge (impeachment‑like), whereas the SG can be removed by a simple executive order. The AG’s right of audience is explicit in the Constitution; the SG’s is derived from statutory delegation. Use the mnemonic “AG = Constitutional, SG = Statutory” to avoid confusion.

The Doctrine of Judicial Review of Ordinances under Articles 123 and 213: Parliamentary Approval, Judicial Scrutiny, and the ‘Ordinance Raj’ Debate

Articles 123 (President) and 213 (Governor) empower the executive to promulgate ordinances when Parliament or a State Legislature is not in session, provided the executive is satisfied that circumstances exist rendering immediate action necessary. An ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of the legislature but must be laid before both Houses (or the Legislative Assembly) within six weeks of reassembly. If not approved, it ceases to operate. The Supreme Court has repeatedly examined whether this power is a parallel legislative authority or an emergency measure.

In R. C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) (the Bank Nationalisation case), the Court held that an ordinance cannot be used to bypass the legislative process when the legislature is in session, and that the President’s satisfaction is subject to judicial review for mala fides. A. K. Roy v. Union of India (1982) upheld the validity of the National Security Ordinance, 1980, but emphasised that the “immediate action” requirement must be genuine. The landmark D. C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987) struck down the practice of repromulgating ordinances without legislative approval, calling it a “fraud on the Constitution.” The Court ruled that repeated repromulgation circumvents legislative supremacy and violates Article 123/213.

The 2017 judgment in Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar reinforced this principle: a seven‑judge bench held that repromulgation of an ordinance without placing it before the legislature is unconstitutional, and that the Governor’s satisfaction must be based on objective material, not political expediency. The Court also clarified that an ordinance lapses if not approved within the stipulated period, and any actions taken under it become void ab initio unless saved by a validating Act.

The “Ordinance Raj” critique arises when governments routinely use ordinances to enact controversial legislation (e.g., the 2014 Land Acquisition Ordinance, the 2020 Farm Laws Ordinances). The Supreme Court’s jurisprudence establishes three safeguards: (1) the executive’s satisfaction is justiciable; (2) repromulgation without legislative ratification is impermissible; (3) ordinances cannot amend the Constitution or override fundamental rights without subsequent parliamentary endorsement. These principles are frequently tested in mains questions on separation of powers and legislative‑executive balance.

The Constitutional Framework for the Election Commission’s Independence: Article 324, the Model Code of Conduct, and Judicial Interpretation

Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures and the offices of President and Vice‑President in an Election Commission (EC) consisting of the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and such number of Election Commissioners (ECs) as the President may fix. The CEC and ECs are appointed by the President; they hold office for a term of six years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier. Their removal requires a process analogous to that of a Supreme Court judge (proved misbehaviour or incapacity, addressed by the President on a Supreme Court reference). This constitutional design insulates the EC from executive pressure.

The Model Code of Conduct (MCC) originated as a voluntary set of guidelines issued by the EC in 1968 for the 1969 general elections. It acquired de facto statutory force through the EC’s inherent powers under Article 324 and judicial endorsement. In S. S. Dhanoa v. Union of India (1991), the Supreme Court upheld the EC’s authority to enforce the MCC, stating that the Code flows from the EC’s constitutional mandate to ensure free and fair elections. Election Commission of India v. State of Tamil Nadu (1993) confirmed that the MCC applies to the party in power as well, preventing misuse of official machinery.

Judicial interpretation has expanded the EC’s toolkit. In Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (2002), the Court directed the EC to obtain affidavits from candidates disclosing criminal antecedents, assets and liabilities, reinforcing transparency. The 2013 judgment in Subramaniam Swamy v. Election Commission affirmed the EC’s power to disqualify candidates for corrupt practices under the Representation of the People Act, 1951, read with Article 324. The 2018 Common Cause v. Union of India case (electoral bonds) did not directly involve the EC but highlighted the Commission’s role in monitoring campaign finance.

Recent controversies — such as the 2019 appointment of the CEC by a collegium‑like process (later reverted) and the 2021 amendment to the Election Commission (Conditions of Service) Act altering the CEC’s salary — have sparked debate on whether the EC’s independence is being eroded. The Supreme Court, in Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (2023), ruled that the appointment of the CEC and ECs should be made by a committee comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition and the Chief Justice of India, reinforcing the constitutional expectation of institutional autonomy. This evolving jurisprudence makes Article 324 a frequent focus for questions on institutional integrity and electoral democracy.

The Constituent Assembly's Debates on the Uniform Civil Code (Article 44) and the Directive Principles: From Drafting to Contemporary Judicial Discourse

Article 44, placed in Part IV (Directive Principles), enjoins the State to “endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.” The Constituent Assembly debated the provision on 23‑24 November 1948. B. R. Ambedkar, while supporting the ideal, cautioned that the State should not impose a code prematurely, stating, “We have a uniform criminal code… but we have not been able to secure a uniform civil code.” K. M. Munshi argued that a common civil code would promote national integration, whereas members like Naziruddin Ahmad and Mohammad Ismail warned that it would infringe on religious freedom guaranteed under Article 25. The Assembly ultimately adopted Article 44 as a non‑justiciable directive, leaving the timing and manner of implementation to future legislatures.

The judiciary has repeatedly invoked Article 44 to urge legislative action. In Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985), the Supreme Court, while granting maintenance to a divorced Muslim woman under Section 125 CrPC, observed that a uniform civil code would help remove contradictions in personal laws. The 1995 Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India judgment, dealing with bigamy via conversion to Islam, again called for a UCC, stating that “the State has failed to fulfil its constitutional obligation under Article 44.” In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), the Court struck down instant triple talaq (talaq‑e‑biddat) as unconstitutional, and several concurring opinions reiterated the need for a UCC to ensure gender justice.

Legislative attempts have been sporadic. The Hindu Code Bills (1955‑56) codified Hindu personal law, but Muslim, Christian and Parsi personal laws remain largely uncodified. The 2019 Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act criminalised triple talaq but did not enact a comprehensive code. The 2023 Law Commission report recommended a phased approach, beginning with optional uniform provisions in marriage, divorce and inheritance. The debate continues to polarise: proponents cite Article 44 read with Article 14 (equality) and Article 15 (non‑discrimination); opponents invoke Article 25 (freedom of religion) and the cultural autonomy of minorities under Article 29. For mains, the key is to articulate the constitutional tension between a directive principle (non‑justiciable) and fundamental rights (justiciable), and to cite the judicial trajectory from Shah Bano to Shayara Bano as evidence of the Court’s persuasive, not coercive, role.

  • Confusing the Attorney General’s constitutional tenure with the Solicitor General’s statutory tenure — only the AG enjoys removal protection akin to a Supreme Court judge.
  • Assuming the Model Code of Conduct is a statute; it derives its force from Article 324 and EC’s inherent powers, not from an Act of Parliament.
  • Believing that an ordinance can be repromulgated indefinitely; D. C. Wadhwa and Krishna Kumar Singh explicitly prohibit repromulgation without legislative approval.
  • Treating Article 44 as a justiciable right; it is a Directive Principle, enforceable only through political will, not court orders.
  • Overlooking that the three‑language formula is a policy, not a constitutional mandate — Articles 343‑351 provide the framework, but the formula itself is not in the Constitution.
  • Misstating the President’s satisfaction for ordinance‑making as non‑justiciable; R. C. Cooper and A. K. Roy established judicial review of that satisfaction.
  • Equating the Election Commission’s independence with that of the judiciary; the EC’s independence is constitutional but its appointment process has been subject to executive influence until the 2023 Anoop Baranwal ruling.

These advanced sections deepen the aspirant’s grasp of the Constitution’s making, its salient features, and the living interplay between text, judicial interpretation and political practice.

The Doctrine of Judicial Review of Ordinances: Constitutional Limits and Landmark Judgments

The power to promulgate ordinances under Article 123 (President) and Article 213 (Governor) is an executive legislative device intended for emergent situations when Parliament or the State Legislature is not in session. The Constitution expressly requires that the executive be satisfied that circumstances exist which render immediate action necessary. This satisfaction is not a mere formality; it is a justiciable condition, as the Supreme Court held in R. C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) and reiterated in A. K. Roy v. Union of India (1982). The Court may examine whether the factual basis for the satisfaction existed, though it refrains from substituting its own policy judgment for that of the executive.

Ordinances cease to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of the legislature unless they are approved earlier. Repromulgation without legislative approval has been struck down as a fraud on the Constitution. In D. C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987) the Court declared that repeated repromulgation of the same ordinance circumvents the legislative process and violates the separation of powers. The principle was reinforced in Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017), where a seven‑judge bench held that repromulgation without placing the ordinance before the legislature is unconstitutional, emphasizing that the ordinance‑making power is not a parallel legislative authority.

The doctrine of judicial review also extends to the content of ordinances. An ordinance that violates fundamental rights or exceeds the legislative competence of the executive is liable to be struck down under Article 13. In K. K. Verma v. Union of India (1975) the Court invalidated an ordinance that retrospectively validated a tax law, holding that retrospective fiscal legislation through ordinance was impermissible. Similarly, the Court has refused to uphold ordinances that seek to amend the Constitution, as the amending power resides exclusively in Parliament under Article 368.

A notable procedural safeguard is the requirement that the ordinance be laid before both Houses of Parliament (or the State Legislature) at the earliest opportunity. Failure to do so renders the ordinance void ab initio. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (1993) clarified that the laying requirement is mandatory, not directory, and non‑compliance cannot be cured by subsequent ratification. This ensures executive accountability and preserves the legislative supremacy envisaged by the Constitution.

In practice, the judiciary balances the need for swift executive action with constitutional discipline. The test applied is whether the ordinance was necessitated by an urgent and unforeseen situation, whether it was laid before the legislature promptly, and whether its substance conforms to constitutional limits. This jurisprudence makes the ordinance‑making power a frequent subject of mains questions on executive overreach, judicial review, and the doctrine of separation of powers.

The Constitutional Position of the Attorney General of India: Tenure, Functions, and Accountability

Article 76 establishes the Attorney General (AG) as the highest law officer of the Union. The AG is appointed by the President on the advice of the Council of Ministers and holds office during the pleasure of the President. Unlike judges of the Supreme Court, the AG does not enjoy a fixed tenure or security of tenure; removal is at the executive’s discretion. This distinction is critical: the AG’s independence is constitutional but not statutory, and the office is often described as a political appointment rather than a judicial one.

The AG’s primary functions include giving advice to the Government of India on legal matters, performing duties of a legal character assigned by the President, and representing the Union in the Supreme Court and any High Court. The AG also has the right of audience in all courts in India. Importantly, the AG is not a member of the Cabinet, but by convention attends Cabinet meetings when legal issues arise. The AG’s opinion is not binding on the government, though it carries significant weight in policy formulation.

Accountability mechanisms are limited. The AG can be removed by the President at any time, and there is no parliamentary oversight akin to that for the Comptroller and Auditor General. However, the AG is bound by the Bar Council of India’s professional conduct rules and can be subject to disciplinary proceedings for professional misconduct. The Supreme Court in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raj Narain (1975) observed that the AG must act in accordance with the Constitution and not merely as a government advocate, underscoring a constitutional duty to uphold the rule of law.

The distinction between the Attorney General and the Solicitor General is frequently tested. The Solicitor General is a statutory officer appointed under the Law Officers (Conditions of Service) Act, 1972, and does not enjoy constitutional tenure. Only the AG’s removal protection mirrors that of a Supreme Court judge in the sense that the President’s pleasure is exercised on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, making the AG’s position politically sensitive. This nuance is essential for answering questions on institutional independence and the law officer hierarchy.

Recent debates have focused on whether the AG’s advice should be made public to enhance transparency. The 2018 Law Commission report recommended that the AG’s opinions on matters of public importance be placed in the public domain after a reasonable period, a suggestion that remains unimplemented. Understanding the AG’s constitutional mandate, functional scope, and accountability gaps equips aspirants to analyse executive‑legal relations in governance questions.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: "The Attorney General of India enjoys the same security of tenure as a Supreme Court judge." State whether the statement is true or false and justify your answer with constitutional provisions.
False. Article 76(4) provides that the Attorney General holds office during the pleasure of the President. There is no fixed tenure, age of retirement, or removal procedure analogous to Article 124(2) for Supreme Court judges. The AG can be removed by the President on the advice of the Council of Ministers at any time, making the position politically dependent.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When comparing constitutional functionaries, tabulate tenure, appointment, removal, and functions side by side. The AG–Solicitor General contrast is a favourite; remember only the AG is a constitutional authority under Article 76.

The Role of the Supreme Court’s Advisory Jurisdiction under Article 143: Scope, Procedure, and Significant References

Article 143 empowers the President to refer a question of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court for its opinion. The Court’s advisory opinion is not binding on the President or the government, but it carries persuasive authority and has shaped constitutional discourse. The reference must be on a question that has arisen or is likely to arise, and the Court may decline to answer if the question is purely political or lacks a legal character.

The procedural framework requires the President to formulate the question after consulting the Council of Ministers. The Supreme Court then hears arguments from the Attorney General, the Solicitor General, and any other parties it permits. The Court may also appoint amicus curiae to assist. The opinion is delivered in open court and published, becoming part of the constitutional jurisprudence.

Landmark references include the Kerala Education Bill Reference (1958), where the Court clarified the scope of legislative competence over education; the Presidential Reference on the Special Courts Bill (1979), which addressed the validity of special courts for trial of offences; and the Reference on the Constitutionality of the 99th Amendment (NJAC) (2015), where the Court opined on the judicial appointments commission before the amendment was struck down. Each reference illustrates the Court’s role in pre‑emptively resolving constitutional doubts.

The advisory jurisdiction does not extend to disputes between the Centre and States (Article 131) or to appeals (Article 132‑136). It is also distinct from the Court’s review jurisdiction under Article 137. The Court has consistently held that it will not answer hypothetical or abstract questions; the reference must have a concrete constitutional dimension. In Re: The Delhi Laws Act (1951) the Court refused to advise on the validity of a law that had not yet been enacted.

For mains, aspirants should be able to distinguish advisory opinions from binding judgments, explain the procedural safeguards, and cite at least three significant references with their constitutional impact. The advisory jurisdiction underscores the Supreme Court’s role as a constitutional interpreter beyond adversarial litigation.

The Constitutional Framework for the Protection of the Right to Education: Article 21A, Judicial Interpretation, and Implementation Challenges

Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002), makes free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen a fundamental right. The corresponding legislation, the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act), operationalises this right by mandating neighbourhood schools, prohibiting capitation fees, and reserving 25 % seats in private unaided schools for economically weaker sections.

The Supreme Court in Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2012) upheld the constitutional validity of the 25 % quota, holding that the State’s obligation under Article 21A extends to ensuring access to quality education in private institutions. The Court applied the doctrine of proportionality, balancing the right of private schools to administer their affairs under Article 19(1)(g) with the child’s right to education.

Judicial interpretation has expanded the scope of Article 21A beyond mere enrolment. In Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India (2014) the Court clarified that minority institutions are exempt from the 25 % quota under Article 30, but they must still comply with norms on infrastructure and teacher qualifications. The Court has also linked the right to education with the right to life under Article 21, emphasizing that education is a prerequisite for the realization of other fundamental rights.

Implementation challenges persist: inadequate infrastructure, teacher vacancies, and monitoring of learning outcomes. The Comptroller and Auditor General’s reports repeatedly highlight gaps in fund utilisation and the functioning of School Management Committees. The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) and State Commissions play a statutory oversight role, but their recommendations are often not binding.

For examination purposes, aspirants should trace the constitutional amendment, the legislative framework, the key judicial pronouncements, and the governance deficits. Questions often test the interplay between Article 21A, Article 19(1)(g), and Article 30, as well as the distinction between a fundamental right and a directive principle in the education context.

The Doctrine of Constitutional Amendment by Simple Majority: Exceptions to Article 368 and Their Judicial Treatment

Article 368 prescribes the procedure for amending the Constitution, generally requiring a special majority of each House of Parliament and, for certain federal provisions, ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures. However, the Constitution itself carves out specific provisions that can be amended by a simple majority of Parliament, treating them as ordinary legislation. These exceptions are enumerated in Article 368(2) and include amendments relating to the creation of new States, alteration of boundaries, and the representation of States in Parliament.

The Supreme Court in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) examined the Tenth Schedule (anti‑defection law) inserted by the 52nd Amendment, which was passed by a simple majority. The Court upheld the amendment, reasoning that the Tenth Schedule did not alter the basic structure but merely regulated legislative conduct. Conversely, in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) the Court struck down clauses of the 42nd Amendment that sought to curtail judicial review, holding that even amendments passed by the prescribed special majority cannot violate the basic structure.

Another category of simple‑majority amendments concerns the Seventh Schedule. The Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, which reorganised States on linguistic lines, was passed by a simple majority because it fell under Article 3 (formation of new States) and Article 4 (consequential amendments). The Court in State of West Bengal v. Union of India (1963) affirmed that such territorial reorganisations are within Parliament’s ordinary legislative power, provided they do not affect the federal balance.

The distinction between “amendment” and “law” is crucial. In Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan (1965) the Court held that a constitutional amendment is not a law within the meaning of Article 13, but later in Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967) it reversed this view, only to be overturned by the 24th Amendment and finally settled by Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) establishing the basic structure doctrine. The simple‑majority exceptions remain a narrow, textual carve‑out that does not permit alteration of the Constitution’s core features.

Aspirants should memorise the list of provisions amendable by simple majority (Articles 2, 3, 4, 169, 239A, 239AA, 368(2) proviso) and be ready to explain why the Constitution permits this flexibility while safeguarding federalism and fundamental rights through the basic structure limitation.

  • Confusing the ordinance‑making power with legislative power; ordinances are temporary and subject to judicial review of the executive’s satisfaction.
  • Assuming the Attorney General enjoys fixed tenure or removal protection equivalent to a Supreme Court judge; the AG holds office during the President’s pleasure.
  • Treating the Supreme Court’s advisory opinion under Article 143 as binding precedent; it is persuasive only and does not create stare decisis.
  • Believing Article 21A imposes an absolute duty on private unaided minority schools to implement the 25 % quota; minority institutions are exempt under Article 30.
  • Thinking any constitutional amendment passed by simple majority is immune from basic structure scrutiny; even simple‑majority amendments cannot destroy the Constitution’s essential features.
  • Overlooking that repromulgation of ordinances without legislative approval is unconstitutional per the Krishna Kumar Singh judgment.
  • Misstating that the Solicitor General is a constitutional authority; the post is statutory and lacks the constitutional tenure of the Attorney General.

The Constituent Assembly's Union Powers Committee and the Architecture of Centre‑State Legislative Relations

The Union Powers Committee, chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru and comprising members such as B. R. Ambedkar, K. M. Munshi, and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, was constituted in April 1947 to delineate the legislative competence of the Centre and the provinces. Its report, submitted on 15 July 1947, recommended a three‑fold distribution of powers — Union List, State List, and Concurrent List — modelled on the Government of India Act 1935 but with a decisive shift of residuary authority to the Union (Article 248). The Committee also proposed that the Union Parliament could legislate on State List subjects in the national interest (Article 249) and during emergencies (Articles 250, 352‑360).
