These recommendations were incorporated almost verbatim into the Seventh Schedule and Articles 245‑254 of the Constitution.

The Committee’s deliberations reveal a conscious design to prevent the fragmentation that plagued the pre‑independence provincial autonomy scheme. Nehru’s opening note stressed “a strong Centre capable of preserving unity and coordinating economic planning”. Ambedkar, while supporting a strong Centre, insisted on safeguards for linguistic and cultural diversity, leading to the inclusion of the Concurrent List as a negotiated space. The Committee’s minutes record a sharp debate on the extent of the Union’s power over industries; the final compromise placed “industries” in the Union List but left “regulation of mines and mineral development” to the States.

Judicial interpretation has repeatedly returned to the Committee’s intent. In State of West Bengal v. Union of India (1963), the Supreme Court held that the residuary power under Article 248 belongs exclusively to Parliament, citing the Committee’s report as evidence of the framers’ intention. In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Court referred to the Committee’s emphasis on “cooperative federalism” to limit the misuse of Article 356. The Committee’s work also underpins the doctrine of pith and substance: when a law’s true character falls within the Union List, incidental encroachment on the State List is permissible, a principle traced to the Committee’s recommendation that “the Centre should have the power to legislate on matters of national importance even if they touch State subjects”.

For examination purposes, aspirants should be able to (i) list the Committee’s key recommendations, (ii) link each recommendation to the specific constitutional articles, (iii) distinguish the Union Powers Committee from the Union Constitution Committee (which dealt with the structure of the Union executive), and (iv) cite at least two landmark cases where the Committee’s report was invoked. A frequent examiner twist is to ask whether the Committee recommended a “unitary” Constitution; the correct answer is that it recommended a federal Constitution with a strong Centre, not a unitary one.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on Emergency Provisions: Design, Safeguards, and Judicial Interpretation

The emergency provisions (Articles 352, 356, 360) were among the most contested parts of the Draft Constitution. The Drafting Committee, guided by B. R. Ambedkar, borrowed the framework from the Government of India Act 1935 but introduced critical safeguards: the requirement of a written Cabinet advice for proclaiming a national emergency (Article 352), a two‑month parliamentary approval period, and a provision for revocation by a simple majority of the Lok Sabha (Article 352(7)). The 44th Amendment (1978) tightened these safeguards further by mandating that the President act only on the written advice of the Council of Ministers and by reducing the period for parliamentary approval from two months to one month.

During the Assembly debates, members such as H. V. Kamat and K. T. Shah warned that the emergency clauses could become tools for authoritarianism. Ambedkar responded by emphasising that the Constitution’s “basic structure” — though not yet articulated — would prevent the suspension of fundamental rights beyond what was expressly permitted. The Assembly also debated the distinction between a “national emergency” (war, external aggression, armed rebellion) and “President’s rule” (failure of constitutional machinery in a State). The latter, under Article 356, was modelled on Section 93 of the 1935 Act but subjected to parliamentary oversight and judicial review.

Judicial interpretation has shaped the operational contours of these provisions. In Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court held that the power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 does not extend to destroying the basic structure, and that judicial review of a proclamation under Article 352 is permissible. In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Court laid down stringent guidelines for the imposition of President’s rule, requiring the Governor’s report to be based on objective material and subject to judicial scrutiny. The Court also ruled that a proclamation under Article 356 is not immune from review merely because it is a political question.

The 44th Amendment’s insertion of Article 352(1A) — requiring the President to act on the written advice of the Cabinet — was a direct response to the 1975‑77 Emergency, during which the Prime Minister’s oral advice was deemed sufficient. The Amendment also added Article 352(5), enabling the Lok Sabha to disapprove a proclamation by a simple majority, thereby restoring legislative control. Aspirants should note the chronological evolution: 1935 Act → Constituent Assembly debates → 1950 Constitution → 42nd Amendment (1976) expanding emergency powers → 44th Amendment (1978) curtailing them. A common examiner trap is to conflate the grounds for national emergency (Article 352) with those for President’s rule (Article 356); the former requires war, external aggression, or armed rebellion, while the latter is triggered by a breakdown of constitutional machinery in a State.

Examiner's Trap
A question asks: "Which of the following statements about the 44th Amendment's changes to Article 352 is incorrect? (a) It required the President to act on the written advice of the Cabinet. (b) It reduced the parliamentary approval period from two months to one month. (c) It made the proclamation immune from judicial review. (d) It enabled the Lok Sabha to disapprove a proclamation by a simple majority."
The incorrect statement is (c). The 44th Amendment did not make the proclamation immune from judicial review; on the contrary, the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills (1980) and S. R. Bommai (1994) affirmed that judicial review of emergency proclamations remains available. Options (a), (b), and (d) correctly describe the 44th Amendment's changes.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question lists multiple amendments to emergency provisions, create a quick mental table: 42nd Amendment (1976) — expanded grounds, suspended fundamental rights; 44th Amendment (1978) — written Cabinet advice, one‑month parliamentary approval, Lok Sabha disapproval, restored judicial review. This table eliminates confusion between the two amendments.

The Debate on the Uniform Civil Code in the Constituent Assembly and Its Constitutional Trajectory under Article 44

Article 44, placed in Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy), enjoins the State to “endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India”. The Constituent Assembly debated this provision on 23 November 1948 and again on 24 November 1948. Proponents — notably K. M. Munshi, B. R. Ambedkar, and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar — argued that a common civil code would promote national integration, gender justice, and legal certainty. Opponents, including Muslim members such as Mohammad Ismail and B. Pocker Bahadur, contended that personal laws were integral to religious freedom guaranteed under Article 25 and that a uniform code would violate minority rights.

Ambedkar’s speech highlighted the distinction between “religious practices” and “civil matters” such as marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption. He cited the Hindu Code Bills (later enacted as the Hindu Marriage Act 1955, Hindu Succession Act 1956, etc.) as a precedent for reform within a community. The Assembly ultimately adopted Article 44 without amendment, but the debates reveal a deliberate choice to keep it as a non‑justiciable directive rather than a justiciable fundamental right, reflecting the political compromise of the time.

Post‑independence judicial pronouncements have repeatedly invoked Article 44. In Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985), the Supreme Court held that a Muslim woman was entitled to maintenance under Section 125 CrPC, and observed that a uniform civil code would help remove contradictions in personal laws. In Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995), the Court urged the government to implement Article 44, stating that “the State cannot remain a mute spectator”. In John Vallamattom v. Union of India (2003), the Court struck down Section 118 of the Indian Succession Act as discriminatory but refrained from directing a uniform code, reiterating that Article 44 is a directive, not a mandate.

The 21st Law Commission (2018) released a consultation paper on “Reform of Family Law”, recommending a phased approach: first, codify and reform personal laws within each community; second, move towards a common code. The Supreme Court, in a 2023 observation, noted that the legislature, not the judiciary, is the appropriate forum for enacting a uniform civil code. For examinations, aspirants must distinguish between the justiciability of fundamental rights (Part III) and the non‑justiciability of directive principles (Part IV), while recognising that courts may use Article 44 as an interpretive aid. A frequent twist is to ask whether Article 44 can be enforced by a writ petition; the answer is no, but courts can issue directions to the legislature to consider legislation.

The Advisory Committee on Political Safeguards for Minorities: Shaping Articles 330‑342 and the Representation Framework

The Advisory Committee on Political Safeguards for Minorities, chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and with B. R. Ambedkar as a key member, was constituted in 1947 to devise mechanisms for adequate representation of Scheduled Castes (SCs), Scheduled Tribes (STs), and Anglo‑Indians in legislatures. Its report, submitted in August 1947, recommended reserved seats in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies (Articles 330 and 332), nomination of two Anglo‑Indian members to the Lok Sabha (Article 331), and similar nominations in State Assemblies (Article 333). The Committee explicitly rejected separate electorates, endorsing the Poona Pact’s principle of joint electorates with reserved seats.

The Committee’s deliberations were influenced by the 1932 Communal Award and the subsequent Poona Pact (1932), which had settled the issue of separate electorates for Depressed Classes. Patel argued that separate electorates would perpetuate communal divisions, while Ambedkar insisted on safeguards that would ensure effective political voice without segregating the electorate. The final constitutional scheme adopted a system of reserved constituencies where all voters participate, but only SC/ST candidates may contest.

Judicial interpretation has clarified the scope and limits of these safeguards. In Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992), the Supreme Court upheld the 50 % ceiling on reservations but distinguished between social and educational backwardness (OBCs) and the constitutional mandate for SC/ST reservations under Articles 330/332. In M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006), the Court held that the State must demonstrate “backwardness”, “inadequacy of representation”, and “overall administrative efficiency” before extending reservation in promotions for SC/STs, thereby introducing a judicial review standard for legislative reservations. The 104th Amendment (2020) extended the reservation of seats for SCs and STs in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies for another ten years, reflecting the continuing relevance of the Committee’s design.

For examination purposes, aspirants should be able to (i) trace the lineage from the Communal Award → Poona Pact → Advisory Committee Report → Articles 330‑342, (ii) differentiate between legislative reservation (Articles 330/332) and educational/employment reservation (Articles 15(4)/16(4)), (iii) cite the key judicial tests from Indra Sawhney and Nagaraj, and (iv) explain why the Anglo‑Indian nomination provisions (Articles 331/333) were discontinued by the 104th Amendment. A common trap is to conflate the “creamy layer” concept (applicable to OBCs) with SC/ST reservations; the Supreme Court has held that the creamy layer does not apply to SC/ST legislative reservations.

  • Confusing the Union Powers Committee’s recommendations with those of the Union Constitution Committee; the former dealt with legislative distribution, the latter with executive structure.
  • Assuming the 44th Amendment removed judicial review of emergency proclamations; it actually reinforced it.
  • Treating Article 44 as a justiciable fundamental right; it remains a non‑justiciable directive principle.
  • Equating the creamy layer exclusion for OBCs with SC/ST legislative reservations; the Supreme Court has expressly refused to extend the creamy layer to SC/ST seats under Articles 330/332.
  • Believing that the Advisory Committee on Political Safeguards recommended separate electorates; it endorsed joint electorates with reserved seats, following the Poona Pact.
  • Overlooking that the 42nd Amendment expanded emergency powers while the 44th Amendment curtailed them; the two amendments moved in opposite directions.

The Constituent Assembly’s Committee on the Union Judiciary and the Design of the Supreme Court

The Union Judiciary Committee was constituted in January 1947 under the chairmanship of Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, a senior member of the Drafting Committee and former Advocate‑General of Madras. Its membership included the Constitutional Adviser B. N. Rau, K. M. Munshi, and several legal luminaries such as M. C. Setalvad. The committee submitted its report on 21 March 1948 after examining the judicial structures of the United States, Canada, and the Federal Court of India established under the Government of India Act 1935.

The report recommended a Supreme Court of India consisting of a Chief Justice and not more than seven other judges, a ceiling later raised to thirty‑one by the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 2008. Appointment was to be made by the President after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, a formulation that the Supreme Court in Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (1993) interpreted as requiring the concurrence of the Chief Justice. Tenure was fixed at sixty‑five years, with removal only by an address of both Houses of Parliament on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity — mirroring the impeachment procedure for the President under Article 61.

Jurisdictional architecture drew heavily on the Federal Court’s original, appellate, and advisory functions. Original jurisdiction under Article 131 was confined to disputes between the Government of India and one or more States, or between States inter se. Appellate jurisdiction covered constitutional, civil, and criminal matters (Articles 132‑134), while advisory jurisdiction under Article 143 empowered the President to seek the Court’s opinion on questions of law or fact of public importance. The committee also entrenched judicial review in Article 13, declaring that any law inconsistent with fundamental rights shall be void to the extent of the inconsistency.

The Drafting Committee incorporated these recommendations almost verbatim into Articles 124‑147. Subsequent judicial pronouncements — notably the Third Judges Case (1998) and the National Judicial Appointments Commission judgment (2015) — have elaborated the “consultation” requirement into a collegium system, but the institutional blueprint remains the one sketched by the Union Judiciary Committee in 1948.

The Constituent Assembly’s Committee on the State Judiciary and the Architecture of High Courts

The State Judiciary Committee, chaired by K. M. Munshi, began its work in early 1947 and presented its report on 12 August 1948. Its mandate was to design a uniform high‑court structure for the provinces and the princely states that would accede to the Union. The committee recommended a High Court for each State, headed by a Chief Justice and such other judges as the President may appoint after consultation with the Governor of the State and the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned.

Age of retirement was initially fixed at sixty‑two years, later raised to sixty‑five by the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963, aligning it with the Supreme Court. The committee vested each High Court with superintendence over all subordinate courts within the State (Article 227) and original writ jurisdiction for the enforcement of fundamental rights and other legal rights (Article 226), a power broader than the Supreme Court’s Article 32 jurisdiction because it extends to “any other purpose”.

To ensure continuity, the committee provided that the existing Federal Court would become the Supreme Court of India, while the High Courts of the former provinces would continue as High Courts of the corresponding States. The report also addressed the integration of the judicial establishments of the princely states, recommending that their judges be absorbed subject to suitability determined by the Chief Justice of the relevant High Court.

These recommendations crystallised into Articles 214‑231. Judicial interpretation has since clarified the scope of superintendence (State of Rajasthan v. Union of India, 1977) and the limits of writ jurisdiction (L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, 1997). The abortive Ninety‑ninth Amendment (2014), which sought to replace the collegium with a National Judicial Appointments Commission, was struck down precisely because it altered the appointment mechanism the State Judiciary Committee had entrenched.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “Which Constituent Assembly committee recommended the creation of an independent Election Commission and who chaired it?”
The Committee on the Election Commission, constituted in 1948, recommended an independent Election Commission headed by a Chief Election Commissioner appointed by the President with security of tenure. The committee was chaired by K. M. Munshi, who also chaired the State Judiciary Committee. The recommendation was incorporated into Article 324.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the four key committee chairmen using the mnemonic “Alladi‑Munshi‑Munshi‑Ayyangar”: Union Judiciary (Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar), State Judiciary (K. M. Munshi), Election Commission (K. M. Munshi), Finance Commission (N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar). This prevents confusion between the Union Constitution Committee (Nehru) and the Union Judiciary Committee.

The Constituent Assembly’s Committee on the Election Commission and the Constitutionalisation of Electoral Democracy

The Committee on the Election Commission was formed in mid‑1948 under the chairmanship of K. M. Munshi, who brought his experience as a former Home Minister of Bombay and a member of the Drafting Committee. The committee submitted its report on 10 February 1949, advocating a permanent, independent body to supervise, direct, and control the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of all elections to Parliament and State Legislatures.

Its principal recommendations were: (1) a Chief Election Commissioner appointed by the President, removable only on the same grounds and in the same manner as a Supreme Court judge (Article 324(2)); (2) the possibility of additional Election Commissioners, also appointed by the President; (3) the Commission’s decisions to be made by majority vote, with the Chief Election Commissioner having a casting vote; (4) adult suffrage as the basis of elections to the House of the People and State Legislative Assemblies (Article 326); and (5) the bar on judicial interference in electoral matters except through an election petition (Article 329).

The Drafting Committee adopted these proposals into Articles 324‑329. The first Chief Election Commissioner, Sukumar Sen, assumed office in 1950 and conducted the inaugural general elections of 1951‑52. Landmark judicial decisions have reinforced the Commission’s autonomy: T. N. Seshan v. Union of India (1995) held that the Commission’s powers under Article 324 are plenary and not subject to executive control; Election Commission of India v. State of Tamil Nadu (1993) upheld the Model Code of Conduct as a legitimate exercise of the Commission’s supervisory authority.

The committee’s vision of an insulated electoral machinery has survived multiple amendment attempts, including the Forty‑second Amendment (1976) which briefly subjected the Commission to executive direction, a change reversed by the Forty‑third and Forty‑fourth Amendments (1977‑78). The constitutional entrenchment of the Election Commission remains a distinctive feature of India’s democratic architecture.

The Constituent Assembly’s Committee on the Finance Commission and the Institutionalisation of Fiscal Federalism

The Finance Commission Committee, chaired by N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar — a former Prime Minister of Jammu & Kashmir and a member of the Drafting Committee — commenced deliberations in late 1948 and reported on 30 March 1949. Its brief was to devise a mechanism for the equitable distribution of financial resources between the Union and the States, drawing on the experience of the Government of India Act 1935 and the Canadian model of federal finance.

The committee recommended the constitution of a Finance Commission every five years by the President (Article 280). The Commission’s duties were to recommend: (a) the distribution of net proceeds of taxes divisible between the Union and the States; (b) the principles governing grants‑in‑aid to States from the Consolidated Fund of India; (c) measures to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement the resources of Panchayats and Municipalities (later added by the Seventy‑third and Seventy‑fourth Amendments); and (d) any other matter referred by the President in the interests of sound finance.

The report also envisaged a Consolidated Fund for each State (Article 266) and a Contingency Fund (Article 267) to enable the executive to meet unforeseen expenditure. The first Finance Commission, chaired by K. C. Neogy, was constituted in 1951 and submitted its report in 1953, setting the template for vertical and horizontal devolution.

Judicial pronouncements have clarified that the Finance Commission’s recommendations are advisory; the President is not bound to accept them (State of West Bengal v. Union of India, 1994). However, the convention of accepting the recommendations has been scrupulously observed, lending the institution de facto binding force. The Goods and Services Tax Council (Article 279A), created by the One Hundred and First Amendment (2016), operates alongside the Finance Commission, together constituting the twin pillars of India’s fiscal federalism.

Parliamentary Sovereignty versus Constitutional Sovereignty: The Indian Model in Comparative Perspective

The United Kingdom exemplifies parliamentary sovereignty: Parliament can enact or repeal any law, and no court may invalidate an Act of Parliament. India, by contrast, adopts constitutional sovereignty. The Constitution is the supreme law (Article 13), and even Parliament’s constituent power under Article 368 is circumscribed by the basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973). This distinction explains why Indian courts can strike down constitutional amendments that violate the basic structure, whereas British courts historically could not.

Key differences are summarised below:

Parliamentary vs Constitutional Sovereignty
FeatureUnited Kingdom (Parliamentary Sovereignty)India (Constitutional Sovereignty)
Source of ultimate authorityParliament (statute + convention)Constitution (written, rigid amendment under Art. 368)
Judicial review of primary legislationNone (pre‑Factortame); limited to compatibility with EU law historicallyFull judicial review (Art. 13, 32, 226)
Amendment procedureOrdinary legislative majoritySpecial majority + State ratification for federal provisions
Basic structure limitationAbsentJudicially enforced (Kesavananda, Minerva Mills)

The Indian model also differs from the United States, where the Constitution is supreme but the amendment process (Article V) requires super‑majorities in Congress and ratification by three‑fourths of the States, with no judicial doctrine limiting the substantive content of amendments. In India, the basic structure doctrine operates as an unwritten substantive limit on the amendment power, a unique contribution of the Supreme Court to constitutional theory.

Historical episodes illustrate the tension: the Forty‑second Amendment (1976) attempted to curtail judicial review and extend Parliament’s amending power, but the Forty‑third and Forty‑fourth Amendments (1977‑78) restored the pre‑1976 position. Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) reaffirmed that the basic structure includes judicial review, the balance between fundamental rights and directive principles, and the federal distribution of powers. Thus, while Parliament enjoys wide legislative supremacy within its domain, it remains subordinate to the Constitution’s core identity.

  • Confusing the Union Judiciary Committee (Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar) with the Union Constitution Committee (Nehru).
  • Assuming the Election Commission was created by the Drafting Committee rather than a dedicated committee chaired by K. M. Munshi.
  • Believing the Finance Commission’s recommendations are legally binding on the President.
  • Thinking the State Judiciary Committee fixed the High Court retirement age at sixty‑five from the outset (it was sixty‑two until 1963).
  • Overlooking that the Union Judiciary Committee’s report preceded the finalisation of the Draft Constitution by several months.
  • Misattributing the basic structure doctrine to the Constituent Assembly debates instead of the Supreme Court’s 1973 judgment.
  • Assuming the Forty‑second Amendment permanently abolished judicial review of constitutional amendments.

These advanced sections equip aspirants with the granular institutional history that examiners frequently test in both direct and analytical questions.

Constituent Assembly Debates on Emergency Provisions and the Scope of Article 352

The Constituent Assembly devoted several sittings between July 1948 and October 1949 to the emergency provisions that would become Articles 352, 356 and 360 of the Constitution. The Union Constitution Committee, chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru, first placed a draft that vested the President with sweeping powers to proclaim a national emergency on the ground of war, external aggression or internal disturbance. The Drafting Committee, under B. R. Ambedkar, tightened the language by requiring that a proclamation under Article 352 be laid before each House of Parliament and cease to operate unless approved by a special majority within two months. Members such as K. T. Shah and H. V. Kamath argued that the phrase “internal disturbance” was too vague and could be used to suppress dissent; they proposed substituting “armed rebellion” – a change that was eventually adopted by the Forty‑fourth Amendment in 1978 but not in the original text. Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar defended the broad wording on the ground that the Union must possess the means to preserve the integrity of the State in a nascent republic. The Assembly also debated the safeguards for fundamental rights during an emergency. Ambedkar moved an amendment that Article 19 would be automatically suspended only when the emergency was proclaimed on the ground of war or external aggression, not on the ground of internal disturbance. The motion was negatived, and the final draft allowed Parliament to suspend the six freedoms under Article 19 for the duration of any emergency proclaimed under Article 352. The provision for President’s Rule under Article 356 was similarly contested. K. M. Munshi warned that the power to dismiss a State government should be exercised only on the report of the Governor and after parliamentary scrutiny. The Assembly accepted the requirement that every proclamation under Article 356 be approved by both Houses within two months, failing which it would lapse. Financial emergency under Article 360 attracted less debate; the Assembly accepted the Drafting Committee’s formulation that the President could issue directions to States to observe canons of financial propriety. The debates reveal a deliberate choice to concentrate emergency powers in the Union while embedding parliamentary oversight, a balance that has been tested repeatedly in subsequent judicial pronouncements such as S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) and Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980).

The Union Constitution Committee submitted its report on 21 July 1947, recommending a three‑tier emergency framework. The Drafting Committee’s report of 21 February 1948 refined the language and introduced the requirement of parliamentary approval. During the clause‑by‑clause discussion on 2 August 1949, Ambedkar moved that the President’s satisfaction under Article 352 be made justiciable; the Assembly rejected the motion, preferring to leave the satisfaction to the executive subject to parliamentary control. The final vote on Article 352 was recorded on 16 October 1949, with 207 members in favour and 12 dissenting. The dissentients, led by K. T. Shah, recorded their objection that the provision could be misused to stifle civil liberties. The Assembly’s decision to retain “internal disturbance” was later cited by the Supreme Court in State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) as a textual basis for the wide scope of emergency powers before the Forty‑fourth Amendment narrowed the ground to “armed rebellion”.

Constituent Assembly Deliberations on the Constitutional Amendment Procedure under Article 368

The amendment procedure was one of the most contested aspects of the constitutional design. The Union Constitution Committee’s initial draft, presented on 15 August 1947, proposed a simple majority for most amendments and a special majority only for provisions affecting the federal structure. The Drafting Committee, in its report of 21 February 1948, recommended a uniform special majority of two‑thirds of members present and voting in each House, coupled with ratification by the legislatures of not less than one‑half of the States for amendments touching the federal distribution of powers, the representation of States in Parliament, or the amendment procedure itself. B. R. Ambedkar argued that a rigid amendment process would protect the Constitution from transient political majorities, while K. M. Munshi cautioned that excessive rigidity could impede necessary reforms. The Assembly debated the threshold for the special majority on 3 September 1949. H. V. Kamath moved an amendment to require a three‑fourths majority, which was negatived. The final text of Article 368, adopted on 17 October 1949, provided for three categories: (a) amendment by simple majority for certain procedural matters such as the creation of new States; (b) amendment by special majority of Parliament for the bulk of the Constitution; and (c) amendment by special majority plus ratification by at least half the States for the “entrenched” federal provisions listed in the proviso. The Assembly also considered whether the power to amend fundamental rights should be expressly excluded. Ambedkar, supported by Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, maintained that the amendment power was plenary subject to the procedural requirements, a view that prevailed until the Supreme Court’s decision in Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967) and the subsequent Twenty‑fourth Amendment (1971) which inserted a new clause (4) in Article 368 declaring that nothing in Article 13 shall apply to amendments under Article 368. The debates show that the framers deliberately chose a graduated rigidity, balancing stability with flexibility, and left the substantive limits of the amendment power to judicial interpretation.

The Drafting Committee’s note of 10 March 1948 recorded that the Committee had examined the amendment formulas of the United States, Canada and Australia. The United States required a two‑thirds majority in Congress and ratification by three‑fourths of the States; Canada allowed Parliament to amend the Constitution unilaterally except for certain provincial matters; Australia required a referendum. The Indian formula was a hybrid: a special majority in Parliament plus State ratification only for a defined set of federal provisions. During the clause‑by‑clause discussion on 14 October 1949, K. T. Shah proposed that any amendment affecting fundamental rights should require a referendum; the motion was defeated by a voice vote. The final vote on Article 368 was taken on 17 October 1949, with 215 members voting in favour and 8 abstaining. The Assembly’s records show that the proviso listing the entrenched provisions was based on the report of the Sub‑Committee on Federal Structure chaired by Gopalaswami Ayyangar. This historical context is frequently tested in questions that ask candidates to identify the original categories of amendment and the subsequent judicial gloss that introduced the basic structure limitation.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “Which of the following statements about the original Article 368 is correct? (a) All amendments required ratification by half the States. (b) Amendments to fundamental rights could be made by simple majority. (c) The Constitution provided three distinct amendment categories with varying majorities and ratification requirements. (d) The President’s assent was not required for constitutional amendment bills.”
The correct answer is (c). The original Article 368, as adopted on 17 October 1949, created three categories: (i) amendment by simple majority for matters such as admission of new States; (ii) amendment by special majority of two‑thirds of members present and voting in each House for most provisions; and (iii) amendment by special majority plus ratification by legislatures of not less than one‑half of the States for the entrenched federal provisions listed in the proviso. Statement (a) is incorrect because only the third category required State ratification. Statement (b) is false; fundamental rights amendments fell under the special majority category. Statement (d) is false because Article 368 explicitly requires the President’s assent after the bill is passed by Parliament.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question lists multiple statements about Article 368, first identify the category each statement refers to. Remember the three‑tier structure: simple majority, special majority, special majority plus State ratification. The proviso’s list of entrenched provisions (federal distribution, representation of States, amendment procedure) is a frequent source of MCQ options. Memorise the list and the corresponding ratification requirement. Also note that the President’s assent is mandatory; there is no provision for a constitutional amendment to bypass the President.

Constituent Assembly Discussions on the Office of the President: Powers, Election, and Immunity

The design of the presidency emerged from prolonged deliberations in the Union Constitution Committee and the Drafting Committee. The Committee’s report of 21 July 1947 recommended an indirectly elected President chosen by an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament and the legislative assemblies of the States. The Drafting Committee, in its report of 21 February 1948, retained the indirect election but added a proportional representation formula to ensure that the value of each vote reflected the population of the State. K. T. Shah moved an amendment on 3 September 1949 advocating direct election by adult suffrage, arguing that a directly elected President would possess a popular mandate. The motion was defeated after Ambedkar explained that a directly elected President would conflict with the parliamentary system, where the real executive authority rests with the Council of Ministers responsible to the Lok Sabha. The Assembly fixed the term at five years (Article 56) and provided for re‑eligibility. The President’s executive powers were enumerated in Article 53, but the crucial Article 74, as originally drafted, stated that the President shall act in accordance with the advice of the Council of Ministers. During the clause‑by‑clause discussion on 13 October 1949, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar proposed that the President be given discretionary powers in the appointment of the Prime Minister when no party commands a clear majority. The Assembly accepted a limited discretion: the President may appoint the Prime Minister in such circumstances but must thereafter act on the advice of the Council of Ministers. Immunity from legal proceedings was granted under Article 361, which bars any criminal proceedings against the President during the term of office and requires a two‑month notice for civil suits. The impeachment procedure under Article 61 was modelled on the United States Constitution, requiring a charge by one House and investigation by the other, with a two‑thirds majority for removal. The final vote on the presidential provisions was recorded on 16 October 1949, with 210 members in favour and 15 dissenting. The dissentients, led by K. T. Shah, objected to the indirect election and the absence of a direct popular mandate.

The Assembly also debated the President’s legislative role. Article 85 empowers the President to summon, prorogue and dissolve Parliament, while Article 111 requires presidential assent for bills. The Drafting Committee initially gave the President an absolute veto, but Ambedkar moved to replace it with a suspensive veto: the President may return a bill (other than a money bill) for reconsideration, and if Parliament passes it again, the President must give assent. This amendment was adopted on 14 October 1949. The President’s ordinance‑making power under Article 123 was similarly constrained: an ordinance must be laid before Parliament and ceases to operate after six weeks unless approved. The Forty‑second Amendment (1976) made the advice of the Council of Ministers expressly binding on the President, a change that was partially reversed by the Forty‑fourth Amendment (1978) which restored the President’s right to require the Council of Ministers to reconsider its advice. The original debates thus established a ceremonial head of state with limited discretionary pockets, a design that has been interpreted by the Supreme Court in Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974) and Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006).

Constituent Assembly Deliberations on the Governor’s Role and the Doctrine of Pleasure

The office of the Governor was shaped by the Provincial Constitution Committee, chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, and later refined by the Drafting Committee. The Committee’s report of 10 August 1947 recommended that the Governor be appointed by the President and hold office during the pleasure of the President (Article 156). The Drafting Committee, in its report of 21 February 1948, retained the appointment mechanism but added that the Governor shall act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers except in matters where the Constitution expressly requires the Governor to act in his discretion (Article 163). During the clause‑by‑clause discussion on 5 September 1949, K. M. Munshi argued that the Governor should be an elected representative of the State to strengthen federalism; the motion was negatived after Ambedkar pointed out that an elected Governor would create a dual executive and undermine the parliamentary system at the State level. The Assembly accepted the doctrine of pleasure, meaning the Governor can be removed by the President at any time without assigning reasons. However, the Assembly also inserted a safeguard: the Governor’s salary and allowances shall not be diminished during his term (Article 158). The discretionary powers of the Governor were enumerated in the proviso to Article 163, which includes the appointment of the Chief Minister when no party has a clear majority, the dismissal of a ministry that has lost the confidence of the assembly, and the reservation of bills for the President’s consideration. The Assembly debated whether the Governor’s discretion should be subject to judicial review. Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar contended that the Governor’s satisfaction in discretionary matters is not justiciable, a view that prevailed until the Supreme Court’s decision in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) which held that the Governor’s report under Article 356 is subject to judicial scrutiny. The final vote on the Governor’s provisions was taken on 15 October 1949, with 208 members in favour and 10 dissenting. The dissentients, including K. T. Shah, objected to the President’s unchecked power of removal.

The Assembly also considered the Governor’s legislative role. Article 200 requires the Governor to assent to, withhold assent from, or reserve for the President’s consideration any bill passed by the State legislature. The Drafting Committee originally gave the Governor an absolute veto, but Ambedkar moved to replace it with a suspensive veto similar to the President’s, which was adopted on 14 October 1949. The Governor’s ordinance‑making power under Article 213 mirrors Article 123, with the same six‑week parliamentary approval requirement. The Forty‑second Amendment (1976) inserted a new clause (2) in Article 163 stating that the question whether any matter falls within the Governor’s discretion shall be decided by the Governor in his discretion and shall not be questioned in any court; this clause was omitted by the Forty‑fourth Amendment (1978), restoring the pre‑1976 position. The Sarkaria Commission (1988) later recommended that the Governor be appointed in consultation with the Chief Minister and that the doctrine of pleasure be exercised only on the advice of the Union Council of Ministers. These recommendations, though not constitutionally binding, have influenced subsequent practice. The original debates thus reveal a tension between the need for a Union representative in the States and the principle of State autonomy, a tension that continues to shape Centre‑State relations.

Constituent Assembly Debates on the Uniform Civil Code and Article 44

The inclusion of a uniform civil code as a directive principle was the outcome of intense deliberations in the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities, chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, and the Sub‑Committee on Fundamental Rights, chaired by J. B. Kripalani. The Advisory Committee’s interim report of 23 April 1947 recommended that the State shall endeavour to secure a uniform civil code for all citizens. The Sub‑Committee, in its report of 16 July 1947, debated whether the provision should be placed in the justiciable fundamental rights chapter or in the non‑justiciable directive principles. K. M. Munshi and B. R. Ambedkar argued for a justiciable right, contending that personal laws based on religion perpetuated gender inequality and undermined national integration. Maulana Abul Kalam Azad and Rajkumari Amrit Kaur opposed justiciability, warning that a compulsory uniform code would infringe on the religious freedom guaranteed under Article 25 and could alienate minority communities. The Advisory Committee ultimately voted to place the provision in the directive principles, and the Drafting Committee incorporated it as Article 44 in the chapter on Directive Principles of State Policy. The final text reads: “The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.”

The Constituent Assembly's Debate on Due Process versus Procedure Established by Law in Article 21

The wording of Article 21 — “No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law” — was the product of a sharp division in the Constituent Assembly between those who favoured the American “due process of law” standard and those who preferred the British “procedure established by law” formulation. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, speaking for the Drafting Committee on 6 December 1948, argued that “due process” would import a substantive judicial review of legislative policy, empowering courts to strike down laws on grounds of fairness, reasonableness or natural justice. He warned that such a clause would make the judiciary a “super‑legislature” and undermine parliamentary sovereignty. In contrast, K. M. Munshi, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar and H. V. Kamath contended that “procedure established by law” without any qualifier would permit the legislature to enact arbitrary, oppressive procedures, leaving citizens without effective protection. Munshi moved an amendment to insert “due process of law” but it was negatived by a vote of 115 to 84 on 13 December 1948. The Assembly finally adopted the phrase “procedure established by law” on 15 December 1948, with Ambedkar noting that the Constitution elsewhere (Articles 14, 19, 22) supplied the necessary safeguards against arbitrariness.

The narrow textual choice had immediate judicial consequences. In A. K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) the Supreme Court held that “procedure established by law” meant any procedure enacted by a competent legislature, irrespective of its fairness, and that Article 21 did not incorporate the principles of natural justice. This formalist reading persisted for nearly three decades. The turning point came in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), where a seven‑judge bench, led by Justice P. N. Bhagwati, read “procedure established by law” as requiring a “fair, just and reasonable” procedure, effectively importing due‑process standards through the interplay of Articles 14, 19 and 21. The Court held that the procedure must not be arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive, and must satisfy the test of reasonableness. Subsequent jurisprudence (Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi, 1981; Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation, 1985) expanded the right to life to include livelihood, health, shelter and a clean environment, all grounded in the broadened reading of Article 21. The evolution demonstrates how a deliberate textual compromise in the Assembly was later transformed by judicial interpretation into a robust due‑process guarantee.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on the Citizenship Provisions and the Impact of Partition

The citizenship clauses (Articles 5‑11) were drafted against the backdrop of the 1947 Partition, which displaced millions and created urgent questions about who belonged to the new Indian polity. The Advisory Committee on Citizenship, chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, submitted its report on 10 April 1947 recommending a single citizenship for the whole Union, rejecting the federal‑style dual citizenship proposed by some members. The Drafting Committee, however, had to accommodate the reality of mass migration. Article 5 conferred citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950) on every person who had domicile in the territory of India and who was born in India, or either of whose parents was born in India, or who had been ordinarily resident in India for not less than five years immediately preceding the commencement. Articles 6 and 7 addressed migrants from Pakistan: Article 6 granted citizenship to those who migrated before 19 July 1948 provided they had been ordinarily resident since migration; Article 7 dealt with those who migrated after that date, requiring a permit for resettlement and registration. Article 8 extended citizenship to persons of Indian origin residing outside India who registered with an Indian diplomatic mission. Article 9 stipulated that voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship would terminate Indian citizenship. Article 10 ensured continuity of citizenship subject to parliamentary law, and Article 11 empowered Parliament to regulate acquisition and termination of citizenship by law.

The debates reveal a tension between a generous, inclusive approach and the need for administrative control. K. T. Shah argued for automatic citizenship for all residents irrespective of domicile, while Dr. Ambedkar insisted on a domicile requirement to prevent “citizenship by mere presence”. The Partition‑driven cut‑off dates (19 July 1948) were a pragmatic compromise to stem the flow of refugees while honouring the commitment to those who had already crossed. The Citizenship Act, 1955, later codified the modes of acquisition (birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, incorporation of territory) and termination (renunciation, termination, deprivation). The 1986 amendment introduced the concept of “illegal migrant” and the 2003 amendment inserted provisions for Overseas Citizenship of India. The original Assembly design, therefore, laid a flexible framework that has been repeatedly reshaped by legislative response to demographic and geopolitical shifts.

Technique: Comparative Textual Analysis
Question: Explain how the Constituent Assembly's choice of "procedure established by law" in Article 21 differed from the American "due process of law" and how the Supreme Court later bridged the gap through judicial interpretation.
The Assembly deliberately rejected "due process of law" (Ambedkar, 6 Dec 1948) to avoid substantive judicial review of legislative policy, adopting instead the British phrase "procedure established by law". In A.K. Gopalan (1950) the Court gave a literal reading, holding that any legislatively enacted procedure satisfied Article 21. In Maneka Gandhi (1978) a seven‑judge bench reinterpreted the phrase to require a "fair, just and reasonable" procedure, reading Articles 14, 19 and 21 together. This judicial gloss effectively imported due‑process standards while retaining the original textual formulation.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the “original intent” versus “current interpretation”, structure the answer in two columns: (1) Constituent Assembly debates — cite the key speakers (Ambedkar, Munshi, Ayyar) and the vote outcome; (2) Landmark judgments — Gopalan (formalist), Maneka Gandhi (expansive), and later cases. This side‑by‑side format signals to the examiner that you grasp both historical design and doctrinal evolution.

The Constituent Assembly's Discussion on the Election of the President and Vice‑President: The Electoral College Design

The method of electing the President (Article 54) and Vice‑President (Article 66) was one of the few constitutional provisions where the Assembly explicitly rejected direct popular election in favour of an indirect electoral college. The Drafting Committee’s initial proposal, moved by Dr. Ambedkar on 10 September 1949, envisaged an electoral college consisting of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the Legislative Assemblies of the States (including the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the Union Territory of Puducherry after the 70th Amendment, 1992). The Vice‑President would be elected by members of both Houses of Parliament alone. The debate centred on three issues: (i) whether the President should be a ceremonial head or possess substantive executive authority; (ii) the risk of a directly elected President claiming a popular mandate that could clash with parliamentary responsibility; and (iii) the principle of federal balance — giving States a voice through their Legislative Assemblies. K. M. Munshi and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar supported the indirect model, arguing that a President elected by Parliament and State Assemblies would embody the federal character of the Union. H. V. Kamath and Prof. K. T. Shah advocated direct election, contending that it would enhance democratic legitimacy. The Assembly voted on 13 October 1949, adopting the indirect system by a majority of 158 to 73. The Presidential and Vice‑Presidential Elections Act, 1952, later detailed the single transferable vote system and the quota formula (total valid votes ÷ (number of seats + 1) + 1). The 1974 amendment (31st Amendment) extended the electoral college to include the Legislative Assembly of the newly created State of Sikkim. The design has endured, with the President remaining a constitutional head acting on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74), while the Vice‑President serves as ex‑officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

The Constituent Assembly's Debate on the Inclusion of Fundamental Duties: The Swaran Singh Committee and Article 51A

Fundamental Duties were absent from the original Constitution; they were introduced by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee (constituted in 1976 under the chairmanship of Sardar Swaran Singh). The Committee submitted its report in August 1976, proposing a set of ten duties to be inserted as Part IVA. The duties included respect for the Constitution, the national flag and the national anthem; cherishing the noble ideals of the freedom struggle; upholding sovereignty, unity and integrity; defending the country; promoting harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood; preserving the rich heritage of composite culture; protecting the natural environment; developing scientific temper and humanism; safeguarding public property; and striving towards excellence. The government accepted the recommendations with minor modifications and inserted Article 51A. The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 added an eleventh duty — “to provide opportunities for education to his child or, as the case may be, ward between the age of six and fourteen years” — aligning with the newly inserted Article 21A (Right to Education). The duties are non‑justiciable (Article 51A is not enforceable by courts), but the Supreme Court has used them as interpretive aids: in M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1983) the Court held that the duty to protect the environment (Article 51A(g)) reinforces the State’s obligation under Article 48A; in Ranganath Misra v. Union of India (1996) the Court referred to the duty to promote scientific temper while interpreting Article 51A(h). The inclusion of duties reflected a shift from a rights‑centric to a responsibilities‑centric constitutional philosophy, responding to the political climate of the Emergency period.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on the Special Status of Jammu and Kashmir: Article 370 and the Instrument of Accession

Article 370, placed in Part XXI (Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions), originated from the unique circumstances of Jammu and Kashmir’s accession to India. The Maharaja Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession on 26 October 1947, accepting Indian sovereignty over defence, external affairs and communications. The Constituent Assembly of India, recognising the conditional nature of the accession, empowered the President to specify, in consultation with the State Government, which other provisions of the Constitution would apply to the State. The original Presidential Order of 1950 (C.O. 10) extended only the provisions relating to the Union’s legislative jurisdiction over the three acceded subjects. The 1952 Delhi Agreement between Prime Minister Nehru and Sheikh Abdullah broadened the application to include citizenship, fundamental rights and the Supreme Court’s appellate jurisdiction. The Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 1954 (C.O. 48) further extended most constitutional provisions, albeit with modifications and exceptions, and recognised the State’s own Constitution (adopted 17 November 1956, effective 26 January 1957). Article 370(3) provided that the President could declare the article inoperative only on the recommendation of the State’s Constituent Assembly. After the State Constituent Assembly dissolved in 1957 without recommending abrogation, the provision acquired a de facto permanent character. The 2019 Presidential Order (C.O. 272) and the subsequent Parliamentary resolution (August 2019) effectively abrogated Article 370 by invoking the President’s power under Article 370(1) with the concurrence of the Governor (acting as the State Government under President’s Rule), and reorganised the State into two Union Territories. The Supreme Court, in a Constitution Bench judgment (2023), upheld the abrogation, holding that the President’s power under Article 370(1) could be exercised without the State Constituent Assembly’s recommendation once the Assembly ceased to exist. The trajectory from a negotiated, temporary arrangement to a contested constitutional amendment illustrates the interplay of constitutional text, political commitment and judicial interpretation.

  • Confusing the original textual choice in Article 21 (“procedure established by law”) with the later judicial importation of due‑process standards; always distinguish Assembly intent from Supreme Court evolution.
  • Assuming the citizenship cut‑off dates (19 July 1948) were arbitrary rather than a negotiated response to Partition‑driven migration flows.
  • Overlooking that the President’s electoral college includes State Legislative Assemblies, not just Parliament, and that the Vice‑President is elected solely by Parliament.
  • Treating Fundamental Duties as justiciable rights; they are expressly non‑justiciable and serve only as interpretive guides.
  • Believing Article 370 could be abrogated only by the Jammu and Kashmir Constituent Assembly; the 2019 abrogation relied on the President’s power under Article 370(1) after the Assembly’s dissolution.
  • Neglecting the role of the Swaran Singh Committee in shaping the duties; the 42nd Amendment did not originate the idea in the Assembly.
  • Failing to cite the specific Presidential Orders (1950, 1954, 2019) when discussing the evolution of Jammu and Kashmir’s constitutional status.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on Citizenship and the Partition‑Driven Cut‑Off Dates

The Citizenship provisions (Articles 5‑11) were among the most contested parts of the Constitution because they had to reconcile the massive population movements triggered by Partition with the principle of a single, uniform citizenship for the new Republic. The Assembly debated three distinct categories: persons domiciled in the territory of India on 26 January 1950 (Article 5), persons who migrated from Pakistan before 19 July 1948 (Article 6), and persons who migrated after that date but before the commencement of the Constitution (Article 7). The 19 July 1948 cut‑off was not arbitrary; it marked the date on which the Dominion of Pakistan enacted its own citizenship law, creating a legal asymmetry that the Assembly sought to address.

Key intervenors included B. R. Ambedkar, who defended the cut‑off as a pragmatic response to the “unprecedented migration” and warned against a “perpetual open door” that would undermine the sovereignty of the new state. Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar argued for a broader inclusion of post‑1948 migrants on humanitarian grounds, while K. M. Munshi emphasised the need for a clear, administrable rule to avoid endless litigation. The Assembly ultimately adopted the three‑tier scheme, leaving the detailed acquisition and termination of citizenship to Parliament, which enacted the Citizenship Act, 1955. The Act retained the 1948 cut‑off for migrants from Pakistan but introduced provisions for registration, naturalisation, and renunciation, thereby operationalising the constitutional framework.

The debates also touched on the status of persons of Indian origin residing abroad (Article 8) and the power of Parliament to regulate citizenship (Article 11). The Assembly rejected a proposal for a “commonwealth citizenship” model, affirming that Indian citizenship would be exclusive and non‑derivative. This decision has shaped subsequent jurisprudence, notably the Supreme Court’s ruling in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rehan (1975) that Parliament’s power under Article 11 is plenary but subject to the basic structure, and the 2003 amendment that introduced Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) without conferring full political rights.

The Uniform Civil Code Debate in the Constituent Assembly: Article 44 and Its Constitutional Trajectory

Article 44, placed in the Directive Principles of State Policy, enjoins the State to “endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.” The debate revealed a sharp divide between members who viewed a common code as essential for national integration and those who feared it would infringe on the religious autonomy guaranteed under Articles 25‑28. K. M. Munshi and B. R. Ambedkar argued that a uniform code would eliminate discriminatory personal laws, especially those affecting women’s rights in marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption. Ambedkar famously remarked that “the Constitution does not recognise the right of any community to have its own personal law” and that the State’s duty under Article 44 was a “mandate for social reform.”

Opposition came primarily from Muslim members such as Mohammad Ismail Khan and B. Pocker Bahadur, who contended that personal law was an integral part of religious practice protected by Article 25. They warned that a uniform code imposed by a Hindu‑majority legislature would amount to majoritarian imposition. The Assembly compromised by placing the provision in Part IV, making it non‑justiciable, while retaining the fundamental right to freedom of religion. The Hindu Code Bills (1955‑56) enacted shortly after independence partially fulfilled the directive for Hindus, but a comprehensive code covering all communities has never been legislated.

Judicial pronouncements have repeatedly highlighted the gap between the directive and reality. In Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985) the Supreme Court urged Parliament to enact a uniform civil code, observing that “the State has a duty to secure a uniform civil code.” The Court reiterated this in Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) and John Vallamattom v. Union of India (2003), each time stressing that Article 44 remains a “constitutional goal” rather than an enforceable right. The 2019‑2020 legislative proposals for a Uniform Civil Code have reignited the debate, but the constitutional position remains unchanged: the directive is aspirational, and any enactment must navigate the fundamental rights framework.

Application Question
A State legislature enacts a law governing marriage and divorce for all communities within the State, citing Article 44 as its constitutional mandate. A religious minority challenges the law, arguing it violates Article 25. How should the court resolve the conflict?
The court must recognise that Article 44 is a Directive Principle (non‑justiciable) while Article 25 guarantees freedom of religion (justiciable). The State may legislate on personal law under Entry 5 of the Concurrent List, but any law that substantially burdens a religious practice must satisfy the “essential religious practice” test and the reasonable‑restriction clause of Article 25(2). The court will examine whether the law targets a practice integral to the religion or merely regulates secular aspects (e.g., registration of marriages). If the law is neutral, generally applicable, and serves a compelling public interest (gender equality, national integration), it may be upheld; however, a blanket imposition without accommodation for essential practices is likely to be struck down as violating Article 25. The directive in Article 44 does not, by itself, confer legislative competence to override fundamental rights.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question pits a Directive Principle against a Fundamental Right, remember the hierarchy: Fundamental Rights prevail unless the law is a reasonable restriction under the specific article (e.g., Art. 25(2)). Cite the Shah Bano and Sarla Mudgal judgments to show the Court’s consistent stance that Article 44 is aspirational. Use the phrase “non‑justiciable directive” and “essential religious practice test” to score full marks.

The Doctrine of Territorial Nexus and Extra‑Territorial Operation of State Laws

Article 245(1) empowers Parliament to make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India, and State Legislatures to make laws for the whole or any part of the State. Article 245(2) clarifies that no law made by Parliament shall be deemed invalid on the ground that it has extra‑territorial operation. For State laws, however, the Constitution is silent on extra‑territorial reach, and the Supreme Court has developed the “territorial nexus” doctrine to test their validity. The principle requires a sufficient connection between the State and the subject‑matter of the legislation; a mere incidental effect outside the State is insufficient.

The leading case is State of Bombay v. R. M. D. Chamarbaugwala (1957), where the Court upheld a Bombay tax on lotteries sold outside the State because the lottery tickets were printed and the draws conducted in Bombay, establishing a real territorial link. In Wallace v. Income Tax Commissioner (1948), the Privy Council (pre‑Constitution) held that a State tax on income earned outside the State was invalid absent a nexus. Post‑independence, State of Bihar v. Charusila Dasi (1959) applied the test to a Bihar law taxing property situated outside Bihar but owned by a resident, finding the nexus in the owner’s domicile. The Court has consistently required that the “connection be real and not illusory” and that the legislation not be a colourable exercise of power.

The doctrine interacts with the distribution of legislative powers under the Seventh Schedule. A State law that purports to regulate a matter in the Union List (e.g., inter‑state trade) will be struck down for lack of competence, irrespective of nexus. Conversely, a State law on a State List subject (e.g., land revenue) may have extra‑territorial effect if the nexus is established. The test is also relevant for the validity of State laws on taxation of non‑residents, as seen in Tata Iron & Steel Co. v. State of Bihar (1958), where the Court upheld a tax on mineral rights because the mineral-bearing land was situated in Bihar.

The Doctrine of Occupied Field: Centre‑State Legislative Overlap and Judicial Tests

When both Parliament and a State Legislature enact laws on a subject in the Concurrent List, the “occupied field” doctrine determines whether the State law is repugnant to the Central law. The Supreme Court in State of West Bengal v. Union of India (1963) held that if a Central law “covers the entire field” of a Concurrent subject, the State law is impliedly repealed to the extent of the overlap, even without an explicit repugnancy clause. The test is whether the Central law intends to be exhaustive — i.e., whether it leaves no room for supplementary State legislation.

Subsequent cases refined the test. In Hoechst Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. State of Bihar (1983), the Court examined the Drugs (Control) Act, 1950 (Central) and a Bihar law on drug pricing, concluding that the Central Act did not occupy the entire field because it regulated quality and standards, not pricing. Therefore, the State law could operate concurrently. In M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India (1979), the Court held that the Central Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 occupied the field of corruption offences, rendering a State anti‑corruption law repugnant. The “occupied field” analysis thus requires a textual and purposive reading of the Central statute: does it provide a comprehensive code, or does it leave gaps for State supplementation?

The doctrine also interacts with Article 254(2), which permits a State law to prevail if it has been reserved for the President’s assent and receives it, even if repugnant to a Central law. However, the President’s assent does not cure a lack of legislative competence; the State law must still fall within the State List or Concurrent List. The Supreme Court in Gujarat University v. Krishna Ranganath Mudholkar (1963) clarified that the President’s assent under Article 254(2) is a political safeguard, not a judicial one, and the Court retains the power to examine whether the Central law truly occupies the field.

The Constitutional Position of the Vice‑President: Election, Role, and Judicial Interpretation

Articles 63‑71 establish the office of the Vice‑President of India. The Vice‑President is elected by an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament (Article 66), using the system of proportional representation by means of a single transferable vote. Unlike the President, the Vice‑President’s electoral college does not include State Legislative Assemblies. The Vice‑President serves a five‑year term, is eligible for re‑election, and can be removed by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a majority of its total membership and agreed to by the Lok Sabha (Article 67).

The Vice‑President’s primary constitutional function is to act as the ex‑officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 64). In this capacity, the Vice‑President presides over the House, maintains order, decides points of order, and exercises a casting vote in case of a tie (Article 100). The Vice‑President also assumes the duties of the President when the latter is unable to discharge functions due to absence, illness, or vacancy (Article 65). The office carries no executive powers independent of these roles.

Judicial interpretation has clarified several contentious issues. In K. K. Venugopal v. Union of India (1974), the Supreme Court held that disputes relating to the election of the Vice‑President are adjudicated by the Supreme Court under Article 71, and that the Court’s decision is final. The Court also ruled that the Vice‑President’s casting vote in the Rajya Sabha is a constitutional duty, not a discretionary political act, and must be exercised in accordance with parliamentary conventions. In R. C. Poudyal v. Union of India (1993), the Court examined the removal procedure and affirmed that the Rajya Sabha’s resolution must be passed by a majority of the total membership, not merely a majority of those present and voting, reinforcing the high threshold for removal.

The 1992 amendment (70th Amendment) did not alter the Vice‑President’s election or removal process but inserted Article 71(3) to clarify that the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction over election disputes extends to the Vice‑President. The office has occasionally been a focal point of political debate, especially when the ruling party lacks a majority in the Rajya Sabha, but the constitutional design insulates the Vice‑President from direct executive accountability, emphasising the role as a neutral presiding officer.

  • Confusing the citizenship cut‑off date (19 July 1948) with the commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950); the former determines migrant eligibility under Article 6, the latter is the date of constitutional commencement.
  • Treating Article 44 as a justiciable mandate; it is a Directive Principle and cannot be enforced by courts, though courts may urge legislative action.
  • Assuming any State law with extra‑territorial effect is automatically invalid; the territorial nexus test requires a real and substantial connection, not merely incidental impact.
  • Believing the “occupied field” doctrine applies only when a Central law expressly states it occupies the field; the Court infers occupation from the comprehensiveness of the Central statute.
  • Thinking the Vice‑President is elected by the same electoral college as the President; the Vice‑President’s college comprises only Parliament, not State Assemblies.
  • Overlooking that the Vice‑President’s casting vote in the Rajya Sabha is a constitutional obligation, not a discretionary political tool.
  • Neglecting the requirement that a State law repugnant to a Central law on a Concurrent subject can survive only with Presidential assent under Article 254(2), and even then it must be within State legislative competence.

The Constitutional Position of the Attorney General and Solicitor General: Articles 76 and 77

Article 76 establishes the office of the Attorney General for India as the highest law officer of the Union. The President appoints a person qualified to be a Supreme Court judge, and the Attorney General holds office during the pleasure of the President. The Constitution enumerates three core duties: (i) to give advice to the Government of India upon such legal matters as may be referred, (ii) to perform such other duties of a legal character as may be assigned, and (iii) to discharge the functions conferred by the Constitution or any law. The Attorney General has the right of audience in all courts in India and may participate in the proceedings of either House of Parliament without a vote.

Article 77, while primarily dealing with the conduct of business of the Government of India, implicitly reinforces the Attorney General’s role by requiring that all executive actions be expressed to be taken in the name of the President and that orders and instruments be authenticated in such manner as may be specified by rules made by the President. The Attorney General’s opinion is often sought before the President promulgates ordinances under Article 123, and the Attorney General represents the Union in the Supreme Court under Article 131 (original jurisdiction) and in appeals under Article 132‑134.

The Solicitor General of India, unlike the Attorney General, is not a constitutional office. The post was created by the Law Officers (Conditions of Service) Act, 1972, and the Solicitor General is appointed by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet. The Solicitor General assists the Attorney General and may be designated to appear in specific cases. In State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977), the Supreme Court clarified that the Attorney General’s advice is not binding on the President, but the President must act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers under Article 74(1). The Court in Attorney General for India v. Union of India (1995) held that the Attorney General’s right of audience is a constitutional privilege that cannot be curtailed by executive instructions.

Key distinctions for examination: the Attorney General is a constitutional authority with tenure during pleasure, while the Solicitor General serves at the pleasure of the government under statutory provisions. Both enjoy the right of audience, but only the Attorney General can participate in parliamentary proceedings. The Attorney General’s opinion is sought on constitutional questions such as the validity of ordinances, the scope of Article 356, and the interpretation of the basic structure doctrine.

The Doctrine of Legislative Competence and Residuary Powers under Article 248

Article 248 vests Parliament with exclusive power to make laws with respect to any matter not enumerated in the State List or the Concurrent List — the residuary legislative field. This provision mirrors the Canadian model where the federal legislature holds residuary authority, contrasting with the American model where states retain residuary powers. The distribution of legislative competence is primarily governed by Article 246 read with the Seventh Schedule. The doctrine of pith and substance determines the true character of a legislation when its incidental encroachment on another list is challenged.

In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), the Supreme Court upheld a State prohibition law, holding that the legislation’s pith and substance fell within the State List entry on “intoxicating liquors” despite incidental effects on inter‑state trade. Conversely, in Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon (1972), the Court struck down a Central law on the ground that its dominant purpose was to regulate a State subject, thereby violating the federal distribution. The residuary power has been invoked to sustain Central legislation on subjects such as cyber‑crime (Information Technology Act, 2000), space activities, and nuclear energy, none of which find explicit mention in the Seventh Schedule.

The interaction between Article 248 and Article 254 (repugnancy) is critical: a Central law enacted under residuary power prevails over any inconsistent State law, and the State law cannot be saved by Presidential assent under Article 254(2) because the Central law occupies the field by virtue of exclusive competence. The Supreme Court in K. K. Verma v. Union of India (1975) reiterated that the residuary clause cannot be used to circumvent the federal scheme by legislating on matters that are essentially State subjects under the guise of a “new” subject.

For exam purposes, remember: (1) Residuary power belongs exclusively to Parliament; (2) The pith and substance test applies to both Union and State laws; (3) A Central law under Article 248 is immune from Article 254(2) saving; (4) The Court examines the dominant purpose, not merely the label, to decide legislative competence.

Examiner's trap
A State enacts a law regulating “data protection” arguing it falls under “public health” in the State List. Parliament later passes a comprehensive Data Protection Act under its residuary power. The State claims its law survives under Article 254(2) because it received Presidential assent. Decide the validity of the State law.
The State law is invalid. Data protection is not enumerated in the State or Concurrent List; therefore it falls within the residuary field of Parliament under Article 248. A Central law enacted under residuary power occupies the field exclusively. Article 254(2) applies only to Concurrent List subjects; it cannot rescue a State law on a matter outside State competence. Presidential assent does not cure lack of legislative competence. Hence the State law must yield to the Central Data Protection Act.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes residuary power with repugnancy, first identify the legislative list of the subject. If the subject is not in any list, Parliament’s residuary power is exclusive and Article 254(2) is inapplicable. Use the pith and substance test only when the subject appears in more than one list.

The Constitutional Provisions for President's Rule under Article 356 and Judicial Review

Article 356 empowers the President to issue a Proclamation of President’s Rule in a State if the President is satisfied that a situation has arisen in which the government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution. The Proclamation must be laid before each House of Parliament and ceases to operate at the expiration of two months unless approved by both Houses. Once approved, it may continue for six months at a time, subject to a maximum of three years, with periodic parliamentary approval every six months. The 44th Amendment (1978) inserted the requirement that the Proclamation be based on “material facts” and not merely on the Governor’s report, and it mandated that the President’s satisfaction be subject to judicial review.

The landmark judgment in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) established that the President’s satisfaction under Article 356 is justiciable. The Court laid down guidelines: (i) the Proclamation must be based on objective material; (ii) the State Legislative Assembly cannot be dissolved before Parliament approves the Proclamation; (iii) the Centre must give the State a chance to prove its majority; (iv) the imposition of President’s Rule for political reasons is unconstitutional. The Court also held that the secular character of the Constitution is a basic feature, and a Proclamation that undermines secularism can be struck down.

In Rameshwar Prasad v.
