A critical limitation is the NHRC’s inability to investigate armed forces’ actions without Central Government permission (Section 19). The 2019 amendment (Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act) expanded the NHRC’s composition to include a member from the National Commission for Minorities and the National Commission for Women, and extended the term of the Chairperson to five years. Judicial review of NHRC orders is available under Article 226/32; the Court in People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2004) affirmed that the NHRC’s findings carry persuasive weight in writ proceedings. The Commission’s annual reports, laid before Parliament, serve as a constitutional accountability mechanism, linking statutory human‑rights architecture to the broader constitutional scheme of dignity under Article 21.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “The NHRC can directly enforce its recommendations against the State.” Choose the correct statement.
The statement is false. The NHRC’s recommendations are advisory; the Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2009) held that the State must seriously consider them but is not legally bound to implement them. Enforcement requires a separate judicial order under Article 226 or 32.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes statutory bodies (NHRC, SHRC, NCW, NCM) with constitutional bodies (CAG, EC, UPSC), first identify the source: Constitution vs. Act of Parliament. Constitutional bodies enjoy independence guaranteed by the Constitution (e.g., security of tenure, removal only by impeachment). Statutory bodies depend on the parent Act for composition, powers, and removal. This distinction is a frequent trap in both prelims and mains.

Residuary Legislative Powers and the Doctrine of Legislative Competence: Article 248, Entry 97, and Key Precedents

Article 248 vests Parliament with exclusive power over any matter not enumerated in the State List or Concurrent List. Entry 97 of the Union List (List I) mirrors this residuary authority, covering “any other matter not enumerated in List II or List III including any tax not mentioned in either of those Lists.” The Supreme Court in State of West Bengal v. Union of India (1963) upheld the Union’s power to legislate on the acquisition of property for a central public sector undertaking, ruling that the subject fell within residuary powers because it was not expressly allocated to the States. In Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon (1972), the Court clarified that the residuary entry cannot be used to encroach upon a State’s exclusive domain if the pith and substance of the legislation belongs to a State List entry. The “pith and substance” test (see Doctrine of Pith and Substance) thus operates as a check on the expansive reading of Entry 97. The 101st Constitutional Amendment (2016) introducing GST added a new Entry 92A (taxes on services) to the Union List, but the residuary clause remains untouched, preserving Parliament’s ability to legislate on emerging subjects such as data protection, cyber security, and space activities. The K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) judgment on privacy implicitly recognised that the Union may legislate on data protection under residuary powers, pending a specific entry. Aspirants should note that the residuary power is a “safety valve” for the Union, but its exercise is subject to judicial scrutiny for colourable legislation (see Doctrine of Colourable Legislation) and federal balance.

Constitutional Guarantees for Persons with Disabilities: From Directive Principles to the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016

Article 41 directs the State to make effective provision for securing the right to work, education and public assistance in cases of disablement. Article 46 obliges the State to promote the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections, which the Court has interpreted to include persons with disabilities. The Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full Participation) Act, 1995, was the first statutory framework; it provided 3 % reservation in government jobs and educational institutions. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPWD Act) replaced the 1995 law, expanding the definition of disability from seven to twenty‑one conditions, increasing reservation to 4 % in government posts and 5 % in higher education, and mandating accessibility in public buildings, transport, and information‑communication technology. Section 3 of the RPWD Act imposes a duty on the appropriate government to ensure equality and non‑discrimination. The Supreme Court in Jeeja Ghosh v. Union of India (2016) held that the right to travel by air is part of the right to life under Article 21, directing airlines to accommodate passengers with disabilities. In Vikash Kumar v. Union Public Service Commission (2021), the Court ruled that the UPSC must provide reasonable accommodation (extra time, scribe) to candidates with benchmark disabilities, linking Article 16(1) (equality of opportunity) with the RPWD Act. The Act also establishes a Central Advisory Board and State Advisory Boards for policy coordination. The constitutional foundation — Articles 41, 46, 14, 15, 21 — combined with the RPWD Act creates a justiciable regime where courts can enforce both statutory entitlements and constitutional guarantees.

Women’s Constitutional Rights: Protective Discrimination, Reservations, and Judicial Interpretation

The Constitution contains several provisions aimed at ameliorating historical gender disadvantage. Article 15(3) empowers the State to make special provisions for women and children. Article 39(a) directs the State to secure equal pay for equal work for both men and women. Article 42 mandates just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief. The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) introduced Articles 243D and 243T, reserving not less than one‑third of seats in Panchayats and Municipalities for women, including seats reserved for SC/ST women. The Supreme Court in Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) laid down guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace, reading Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g) and 21 together; these guidelines were later codified in the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013. In Air India v. Nargesh Meerza (1981), the Court struck down a regulation terminating air hostesses on marriage or pregnancy as violative of Articles 14 and 16. The Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) judgment decriminalised adultery, holding that Section 497 IPC violated Article 14 by treating women as property. The 108th Constitutional Amendment Bill (Women’s Reservation Bill), passed by the Rajya Sabha in 2010 but lapsed, sought 33 % reservation in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies; its revival remains a live political‑constitutional issue. The interplay of protective discrimination (Article 15(3)), directive principles (Articles 39, 42), and local‑body reservations (Articles 243D, 243T) demonstrates a layered constitutional strategy: formal equality supplemented by substantive measures, all subject to judicial review for reasonableness and proportionality.

  • Confusing the NHRC’s advisory role with binding enforcement power; its recommendations are not self‑executing.
  • Assuming Article 48A alone creates a justiciable right; it must be read with Article 21 and judicial precedent.
  • Treating residuary powers (Article 248/Entry 97) as unlimited; they are constrained by the pith‑and‑substance test and federal balance.
  • Overlooking that the RPWD Act, 2016, not the 1995 Act, governs current disability rights and reservation percentages.
  • Believing the Women’s Reservation Bill is already law; it remains a lapsed bill awaiting re‑introduction and passage.
  • Missing the distinction between constitutional bodies (CAG, EC, UPSC) and statutory bodies (NHRC, NCW, NCM) regarding independence and removal procedures.
  • Neglecting the role of the “precautionary principle” and “polluter pays principle” as judge‑made doctrines anchored in Articles 48A and 51A(g).
The advanced sections above integrate constitutional text, statutory evolution, and landmark jurisprudence to equip aspirants for analytical and factual questions on emerging rights and institutional design.

The Constituent Assembly's Sub‑Committee on the Judiciary and the Design of the Supreme Court's Jurisdiction

The Constituent Assembly constituted a dedicated Sub‑Committee on the Judiciary in July 1947 under the chairmanship of Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Aiyar. Its members included B. N. Rau (Constitutional Adviser), K. M. Munshi, M. R. Jayakar, and T. T. Krishnamachari. The committee’s mandate was to devise a judicial architecture that would secure the rule of law, protect fundamental rights, and maintain the federal balance. Its report, submitted in October 1947, recommended a single integrated judiciary with the Supreme Court at the apex, vested with original, appellate, and advisory jurisdictions. The committee insisted on security of tenure for judges (removal only by impeachment), a fixed retirement age of 65, and a consultation process for appointments that involved the Chief Justice of India — a precursor to the later collegium system.

The Sub‑Committee also debated the scope of judicial review. While some members favoured a limited review confined to legislative competence, the majority, influenced by the American model and the Government of India Act 1935, advocated a broad power to strike down laws violating fundamental rights. This recommendation crystallised into Articles 124‑147 of the Constitution. The original appointment clause (Article 124(2)) required the President to appoint judges after consultation with such judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts as the President may deem necessary. The phrase “consultation” became the focal point of later judicial interpretation, culminating in the Supreme Court’s 1993 decision in Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (the Second Judges Case), which read “consultation” as “concurrence” and gave primacy to the Chief Justice.

Another significant contribution of the Sub‑Committee was the advisory jurisdiction under Article 143, allowing the President to seek the Court’s opinion on questions of law or fact of public importance. The committee envisaged this as a tool for executive clarity, not a substitute for adjudication. The original draft also contained a provision for a “Court of Appeal” separate from the Supreme Court, but the Assembly rejected it in favour of a unified apex court to avoid jurisdictional conflicts. The Sub‑Committee’s work laid the institutional foundation that has enabled the Supreme Court to evolve into a powerful constitutional court, capable of reviewing constitutional amendments (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) and enforcing socio‑economic rights through public interest litigation.

The Debate on Fundamental Duties in the Constituent Assembly and Their Later Insertion by the 42nd Amendment

The original Constitution of 1950 contained no chapter on fundamental duties. During the Constituent Assembly debates, several members — notably K. M. Munshi, Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, and Alladi Krishnaswami Aiyar — discussed the desirability of enumerating citizens’ duties alongside rights. Munshi argued that a catalogue of duties would foster civic responsibility, while Ambedkar cautioned that duties imposed by the state could become instruments of coercion. The Assembly ultimately decided to omit duties, leaving the moral and civic obligations to be cultivated through education and public discourse.

The idea resurfaced in the 1970s amid concerns about national integration and discipline. The Swaran Singh Committee, constituted in 1976 under the chairmanship of Sardar Swaran Singh, recommended the insertion of a new Part IVA comprising fundamental duties. The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, enacted during the Emergency, added Article 51A listing ten duties, including respect for the Constitution, the national flag, and the national anthem; promotion of harmony; protection of public property; and the duty to develop scientific temper. The 86th Amendment Act, 2002, inserted a further duty under Article 51A(k) — “to provide opportunities for education to his child or, as the case may be, ward between the age of six and fourteen years.”

Judicial treatment of fundamental duties has been cautious. In Ranganath Misra v. Union of India (1996), the Supreme Court held that duties are non‑justiciable but can be used as interpretative aids to ascertain the scope of fundamental rights and directive principles. The Court has repeatedly refused to enforce duties directly, emphasising that they are moral obligations rather than legally binding commands. Nevertheless, the duties have influenced legislative drafting — for instance, the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, and the Flag Code of India — and have been cited in judgments concerning environmental protection (Article 51A(g)) and scientific temper (Article 51A(h)). The evolution from a debated omission to a constitutional chapter illustrates the dynamic interplay between political context and constitutional design.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “Which of the following statements about Fundamental Duties is correct? (a) They were part of the original Constitution. (b) They are justiciable and can be enforced by courts. (c) They were inserted by the 42nd Amendment on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee. (d) The 86th Amendment removed the duty to develop scientific temper.”
Correct answer: (c). Fundamental Duties were not in the original Constitution; they were added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, based on the Swaran Singh Committee report. They are non‑justiciable (so (b) is false). The 86th Amendment added a duty regarding education; it did not remove any existing duty (so (d) is false).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes original constitutional provisions with later amendments, first identify the baseline (1950 text) and then track each amendment chronologically. For Fundamental Duties, remember the three key milestones: omission in 1950, insertion of ten duties by the 42nd Amendment (1976), and addition of the education duty by the 86th Amendment (2002). This timeline eliminates distractors that claim original inclusion or judicial enforceability.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on the Representation of Anglo‑Indians and the Nomination Provisions in Articles 331 and 333

The Anglo‑Indian community, defined in Article 366(2) as persons of European descent domiciled in India, secured a unique representational guarantee during the Constituent Assembly debates. Frank Anthony, the community’s leading spokesman, argued that without nominated seats the Anglo‑Indians would be politically invisible given their small population (approximately 300,000 at independence). The Assembly accepted this reasoning and incorporated Article 331, empowering the President to nominate two Anglo‑Indians to the Lok Sabha if the community was not adequately represented, and Article 333, allowing the Governor of a State to nominate one Anglo‑Indian to the Legislative Assembly.

The nomination provisions were originally intended to operate for ten years, subject to extension by Parliament. The 23rd Amendment (1969) extended the period to 1980, the 45th Amendment (1980) to 1990, the 62nd Amendment (1989) to 2000, and the 79th Amendment (1999) to 2010. The 95th Amendment (2009) further extended the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes and the Anglo‑Indian nomination till 2020. However, the 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2020, while extending SC/ST legislative reservation for another decade, discontinued the Anglo‑Indian nomination altogether, citing the community’s improved socio‑economic indicators and the principle of universal adult franchise.

Judicial scrutiny of the nomination power has been limited. In K. S. Rao v. Union of India (1975), the Supreme Court upheld the President’s discretion under Article 331, noting that the nomination is a political act not amenable to judicial review unless mala fide is alleged. The discontinuation has sparked debate about minority representation versus majoritarian democracy, but the constitutional text now reflects a settled position: Articles 331 and 333 remain in the Constitution but are rendered inoperative for Anglo‑Indians. The episode illustrates how the Constituent Assembly’s protective instinct for a numerically tiny minority was translated into a temporary constitutional mechanism that eventually yielded to the logic of universal suffrage.

The Constitutional Design of the President's Executive Power: Article 53, the Council of Ministers, and the Aid and Advice Principle

Article 53(1) vests the executive power of the Union in the President, to be exercised either directly or through officers subordinate to him in accordance with the Constitution. Article 74(1) mandates a Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister to “aid and advise” the President, who shall act in accordance with such advice. The original 1950 text left the President’s discretion ambiguous; the 42nd Amendment (1976) made the advice expressly binding by inserting the words “shall act in accordance with such advice.” The 44th Amendment (1978) added a proviso allowing the President to require the Council to reconsider its advice, but the President must ultimately act on the reconsidered advice.

Judicial interpretation has cemented the principle of ministerial responsibility. In Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974), the Supreme Court held that the President is a constitutional head who acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, and that the real executive power resides in the Cabinet. The Court further clarified in R. C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) that the President’s satisfaction under Article 356 (President’s Rule) is the satisfaction of the Council of Ministers, not his personal satisfaction. The “pocket veto” — the President’s power to withhold assent to a Bill indefinitely — was examined in Kehar Singh v. Union of India (1989), where the Court ruled that the President must act on ministerial advice even in granting pardons under Article 72.

Nevertheless, the Constitution carves out limited discretionary pockets. When no party commands a clear majority in the Lok Sabha, the President exercises discretion in appointing the Prime Minister (as in 1989, 1996, 1998). The President may also dissolve the Lok Sabha on the advice of a Prime Minister who has lost majority support, but the Supreme Court in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) subjected such advice to judicial review for mala fides. The President’s role in the promulgation of ordinances under Article 123 similarly requires Cabinet advice, and the 44th Amendment mandated that ordinances be laid before Parliament within six weeks of reassembly. The architecture thus balances a ceremonial head with a responsible executive, ensuring that the President’s formal powers are exercised through a politically accountable Cabinet.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee on the Drafting of the Emergency Provisions and the Safeguards Against Misuse

The Drafting Committee, chaired by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, devoted extensive deliberations to the emergency provisions (Articles 352, 356, 360). The committee was influenced by the Government of India Act 1935, which vested the Governor‑General with wide emergency powers, and by the Weimar Constitution’s Article 48, whose misuse had facilitated authoritarian rule. To prevent a similar drift, the Assembly incorporated several safeguards: a proclamation of national emergency under Article 352 could be issued only on the written advice of the Cabinet (added by the 44th Amendment); it required approval by both Houses of Parliament within one month by a special majority; and it could be revoked by a simple majority resolution of the Lok Sabha.

Article 356 (President’s Rule) originally allowed the President to assume state functions on the Governor’s report or otherwise. The 44th Amendment inserted the requirement that the proclamation be based on the Governor’s report and that it be approved by Parliament within two months. The landmark S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) judgment imposed judicial review on the material satisfaction behind Article 356, holding that the President’s proclamation is justiciable and that the dissolution of a state assembly cannot precede parliamentary approval. The Court also laid down the “floor test” as the preferred method to ascertain majority.

Financial emergency under Article 360, never invoked, permits the President to direct states to observe canons of financial propriety and to reduce salaries of all or any class of persons serving in connection with the affairs of the Union, including judges. The 44th Amendment added a safeguard that such a proclamation must also be approved by Parliament within two months. The Constituent Assembly’s cautious design, reinforced by subsequent amendments and judicial pronouncements, reflects a deliberate effort to confine emergency powers within a constitutional straitjacket, ensuring that extraordinary authority does not become a routine instrument of central dominance.

  • Confusing the original omission of Fundamental Duties with their later insertion; the 42nd Amendment is the key milestone, not the 1950 text.
  • Assuming the President’s discretion under Article 356 is unfettered; the Bommai judgment mandates judicial review and parliamentary approval.
  • Believing the Anglo‑Indian nomination under Articles 331 and 333 is still operative; the 104th Amendment discontinued it from 2020.
  • Treating the 42nd Amendment’s binding advice clause as applicable to all presidential functions; the 44th Amendment restored a limited reconsideration power.
  • Overlooking that the Swaran Singh Committee recommended Fundamental Duties, not the Constituent Assembly itself.
  • Misidentifying the Sub‑Committee on the Judiciary as the “Drafting Committee”; the former specifically shaped judicial appointments and jurisdiction.
  • Ignoring the requirement that a national emergency proclamation must be based on written Cabinet advice, a safeguard introduced by the 44th Amendment.

The Constitutional Position of the Attorney General of India: Appointment, Functions, and Accountability

Article 76 of the Constitution creates the office of the Attorney General for India, who is appointed by the President on the advice of the Council of Ministers. The Attorney General holds office during the pleasure of the President, which in practice means the incumbent serves at the will of the executive. Unlike the Advocate General of a state, the Attorney General is not a member of the Cabinet and does not enjoy a fixed tenure; however, the convention has evolved that the Attorney General resigns when a new government assumes office.

The Attorney General is the highest law officer of the Union and has the right of audience in all courts in India. The primary constitutional duty is to give advice to the Government of India upon such legal matters as may be referred by the President, and to perform such other duties of a legal character as may be assigned. In practice, the Attorney General appears on behalf of the Union in the Supreme Court and the High Courts in cases of constitutional importance, and also represents the government in references made under Article 143.

Accountability mechanisms are limited. The Attorney General can be removed by the President at any time, and there is no parliamentary oversight akin to that for ministers. The office is not subject to the same disqualifications as a member of Parliament, but the Attorney General cannot vote in Parliament. The Supreme Court has, in several judgments, emphasised that the Attorney General must act independently of political considerations when rendering legal opinions, though the office remains a political appointment. The 2014 amendment to the Attorney General’s (Conditions of Service) Rules clarified the terms of engagement but did not alter the constitutional framework.

Comparatively, the Solicitor General and Additional Solicitors General are appointed to assist the Attorney General, but they are not constitutional functionaries; their appointments are governed by executive orders. The Attorney General’s role in the legislative process includes the right to speak and take part in the proceedings of either House of Parliament or any committee thereof, but without a vote. This unique position bridges the executive and the judiciary, making the office a focal point for debates on the independence of legal advice to the government.

The Supreme Court's Advisory Jurisdiction under Article 143: Scope, Procedure, and Landmark References

Article 143 empowers the President to refer to the Supreme Court any question of law or fact which has arisen or is likely to arise, and which is of such a nature and of such public importance that it is expedient to obtain the Court’s opinion. The reference is made on the advice of the Council of Ministers. The Supreme Court may, after such hearing as it thinks fit, report its opinion to the President. The opinion is advisory and not binding on the President or the government, but it carries significant persuasive authority and has often shaped legislative and executive action.

The procedure for a reference is not detailed in the Constitution; the Supreme Court has framed its own rules. Typically, the Attorney General presents the government’s case, and the Court may appoint amicus curiae to assist. The Court has the discretion to decline to answer a reference if it considers the question inappropriate for advisory opinion, as seen in the Special Reference No. 1 of 1998 (the “Third Judges Case”) where the Court refused to answer certain political questions.

Landmark references include the Kerala Education Bill Reference (1958), where the Court clarified the scope of legislative competence over education; the Presidential Reference on the Punjab Reorganisation Act (1965), addressing the validity of territorial changes; and the Reference on the Constitutionality of the National Judicial Appointments Commission (2015), where the Court upheld the collegium system. In the Reference on the Constitution (Forty‑second Amendment) Act (1977), the Court examined the basic structure doctrine in an advisory capacity, reinforcing its binding nature on future amendments.

The advisory jurisdiction serves as a constitutional safety valve, allowing the executive to seek authoritative judicial guidance without awaiting litigation. However, critics argue that it can be used to obtain judicial endorsement for politically sensitive measures, and the non‑binding nature sometimes leads to selective compliance. The Supreme Court has consistently maintained that its advisory opinions are not judgments and do not create precedent in the strict sense, though they are frequently cited in subsequent litigation.

Worked Example: Advisory Reference vs. Writ Jurisdiction
A state government seeks the Supreme Court’s opinion on whether a proposed law on agricultural marketing violates the Constitution. The President refers the question under Article 143. Simultaneously, a farmers’ association files a writ petition under Article 32 challenging the same law after enactment. Explain the procedural and substantive differences between the two proceedings.
The advisory reference under Article 143 is initiated by the President on Cabinet advice before the law is enacted; the Supreme Court’s opinion is non‑binding and does not adjudicate a lis. The writ petition under Article 32 is a constitutional remedy available to any person whose fundamental rights are alleged to be infringed after the law comes into force; the Court’s judgment is binding and enforceable. The advisory proceeding is ex‑parte in nature (though the Court may hear interested parties), while the writ proceeding is adversarial with full pleadings, evidence, and appeal rights. Consequently, the advisory opinion guides legislative drafting, whereas the writ judgment determines the law’s validity and can strike it down.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about Article 143, remember three key points: (1) the reference is made by the President on Cabinet advice; (2) the Supreme Court’s opinion is advisory, not binding; (3) the Court may refuse to answer if the question is political or lacks public importance. Contrast this with Article 32 (binding writ jurisdiction) and Article 131 (original suits between states). A quick mental table of “binding vs. advisory” and “pre‑enactment vs. post‑enactment” will earn full marks.

The Constitutional Framework for All‑India Services: Creation, Control, and the Role of the Union Public Service Commission

Article 312 empowers Parliament to create one or more All‑India Services common to the Union and the States, provided the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) passes a resolution supported by not less than two‑thirds of the members present and voting declaring that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest. The Indian Administrative Service (IAS), Indian Police Service (IPS), and Indian Forest Service (IFoS) are the three services constituted under this provision.

The recruitment to these services is conducted by the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) through the Civil Services Examination, a competitive process that ensures merit‑based selection. The UPSC’s constitutional mandate under Article 320 includes advising the President on matters relating to recruitment, promotions, and disciplinary actions concerning All‑India Services officers. The control over cadre allocation, training, and career progression rests with the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) under the Union Government, while the States exercise functional control over officers posted to them.

A distinctive feature is the dual accountability of All‑India Services officers: they are accountable to the Union for recruitment and disciplinary matters, and to the State for day‑to‑day administration. The Constitution provides safeguards under Article 311, which mandates that no civil servant can be dismissed, removed, or reduced in rank except after an inquiry in which the officer has been given a reasonable opportunity to be heard. The Supreme Court has extended these protections to All‑India Services officers, reinforcing the principle of security of tenure.

Recent debates centre on the proposal to create new All‑India Services such as the Indian Judicial Service and the Indian Medical Service. While the constitutional mechanism exists, political consensus and the Rajya Sabha’s super‑majority requirement have so far prevented their establishment. The interplay between Article 312, the UPSC’s independence, and the federal distribution of executive power makes the All‑India Services a critical instrument of administrative integration in India’s quasi‑federal polity.

The Constitutional Provisions for the Election of the President and Vice‑President: Electoral College, Qualifications, and Disputes

The President of India is elected by an electoral college consisting of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States (including the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the Union Territory of Puducherry) under Article 54. The election follows the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, and voting is by secret ballot as prescribed by the Presidential and Vice‑Presidential Elections Act, 1952.

Qualifications for the presidency are set out in Article 58: the candidate must be a citizen of India, have completed thirty‑five years of age, be qualified for election as a member of the Lok Sabha, and must not hold any office of profit under the Union or any State government. The Vice‑President is elected by an electoral college of members of both Houses of Parliament (both elected and nominated) under Article 66, using the same proportional representation system. The Vice‑President must be qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha and must not hold any office of profit.

Disputes arising out of the election of the President or Vice‑President are adjudicated by the Supreme Court under Article 71. The Court’s decision is final and cannot be questioned in any other forum. The Supreme Court has, in cases such as N. P. Ponnuswami v. Returning Officer (1952) and K. K. Verma v. Union of India (1972), laid down principles regarding the scrutiny of nomination papers, the counting of votes, and the treatment of defective ballots. The Court has also clarified that the election cannot be challenged on the ground of alleged irregularities in the electoral college composition unless such irregularities affect the result materially.

The President’s term is five years from the date of assuming office, and the Vice‑President holds office for a similar term. Both offices can be terminated earlier by resignation, removal through impeachment (President) or a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a majority of its total membership and agreed to by the Lok Sabha (Vice‑President), or death. The constitutional design seeks to balance the ceremonial nature of the presidency with the democratic legitimacy derived from a broad‑based electoral college.

The National Commission for Minorities: Constitutional Basis, Powers, and Effectiveness

While the Constitution does not establish a National Commission for Minorities as a constitutional body, Articles 29 and 30 guarantee cultural and educational rights to minorities, and Article 350A provides for instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage. The National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992, created a statutory commission consisting of a Chairperson, a Vice‑Chairperson, and five other members appointed by the Central Government. The Commission’s mandate includes evaluating the progress of the development of minorities, monitoring the working of safeguards provided in the Constitution and laws, and making recommendations for the effective implementation of those safeguards.

The Commission has the powers of a civil court while inquiring into complaints, including summoning witnesses, requiring production of documents, and receiving evidence on affidavits. It can also intervene in any proceeding involving the violation of minority rights pending before a court, with the court’s permission. The Commission submits annual reports to the Central Government, which are laid before each House of Parliament.

Effectiveness has been a subject of debate. The Commission’s recommendations are advisory and not binding on the government. Its composition has sometimes been criticised for lacking representation from all notified minority communities (Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis, and Jains). The 2004 amendment expanded the Commission’s jurisdiction to include the Union Territories, but resource constraints and the absence of enforcement powers limit its impact. Judicial pronouncements, such as in National Commission for Minorities v. State of Karnataka (2007), have affirmed the Commission’s role as a monitoring body but stopped short of granting it quasi‑judicial authority.

In recent years, the Commission has focused on issues such as the implementation of the Prime Minister’s 15‑Point Programme for the Welfare of Minorities, the protection of minority educational institutions under Article 30, and the prevention of communal violence. The interplay between statutory mandate, constitutional safeguards, and political will determines the Commission’s practical relevance in safeguarding minority rights.

  • Confusing the Attorney General’s constitutional office with the statutory Solicitor General; only the Attorney General is mentioned in Article 76.
  • Assuming the Supreme Court’s advisory opinion under Article 143 is binding; it is expressly advisory and carries no precedent value.
  • Believing All‑India Services officers are solely under State control; they are recruited and disciplined by the Union through the UPSC and DoPT.
  • Thinking the Vice‑President’s electoral college includes State Legislative Assemblies; it consists only of members of Parliament.
  • Treating the National Commission for Minorities as a constitutional body; it is a statutory creation under the 1992 Act.
  • Overlooking that the President can refer a question to the Supreme Court only on the advice of the Council of Ministers, not suo motu.
  • Misapplying Article 311 protections to contractual employees; the safeguard applies only to persons appointed to civil services or posts under the Union or a State.

The Constituent Assembly's Debate on the Word 'Sovereign' in the Preamble

The choice of the word Sovereign in the Preamble was the result of a focused debate on 17‑18 October 1949. Members of the Constituent Assembly were divided between two conceptions: external sovereignty (the capacity to conduct international relations without external control) and internal supremacy (the ultimate authority of the Constitution over all organs of the state). B. R. Ambedkar, speaking for the Drafting Committee, argued that <q>Sovereign</q> captured both dimensions and aligned with the language of the United Nations Charter, which India had just joined. K. M. Munshi preferred <q>Independent</q>, contending that it conveyed the same idea without the historical baggage of monarchical sovereignty. The Assembly also considered the phrase <q>Sovereign Democratic Republic</q> as a single composite expression, rejecting proposals to insert <q>Socialist</q> or <q>Secular</q> at that stage. The final vote adopted <q>Sovereign</q> by a clear majority, and the word has since been cited in Supreme Court judgments (e.g., Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973) as evidence that the Constitution itself is the supreme legal authority, not Parliament.

The debate also clarified that <q>Sovereign</q> did not imply a claim to absolute power; rather, it affirmed that the Constitution derives its authority from the people of India, as expressed in the opening words <q>We, the people of India</q>. This textual choice has been invoked in later cases concerning the basic structure doctrine, where the Court held that the sovereign character of the Constitution cannot be altered by amendment.

The Influence of the American and French Constitutional Preambles on the Indian Preamble

The Indian Preamble bears a discernible imprint of two seminal revolutionary texts. The United States Constitution opens with <q>We the People of the United States, in Order to form a more perfect Union…</q>, establishing popular sovereignty as the source of constitutional legitimacy. The French Constitution of 1791 (and later the 1958 Constitution) begins with a declaration of <q>Liberty, Equality, Fraternity</q>, embedding substantive values directly into the constitutional opening. The Indian Constituent Assembly, through the Objectives Resolution moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946, synthesized these influences: the phrase <q>We, the people of India</q> mirrors the American <q>We the People</q>, while the quartet <q>Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity</q> echoes the French triad, with <q>Justice</q> added to reflect the Assembly's emphasis on socio‑economic justice.

During the debates, members such as Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar explicitly referenced the American model to argue that the Preamble should declare the source of authority, while others like Maulana Abul Kalam Azad invoked the French revolutionary ideals to justify the inclusion of <q>Fraternity</q>. The Drafting Committee, chaired by B. R. Ambedkar, retained both strands, producing a Preamble that simultaneously asserts popular sovereignty and enumerates the core values the Constitution seeks to secure. Comparative constitutional scholars note that this dual heritage makes the Indian Preamble a hybrid instrument: it functions both as a declaratory statement of origin (American style) and as a normative charter of values (French style).

Examiner's Twist: Preamble Language
Which of the following words was not part of the original Preamble adopted on 26 November 1949?
Options: (a) Sovereign (b) Socialist (c) Democratic (d) Republic
The original Preamble contained the words Sovereign, Democratic and Republic. The word Socialist was inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976. Therefore, the correct answer is (b) Socialist.
Exam Day Strategy
Memorise the three words added by the 42nd Amendment (Socialist, Secular, Integrity). Any question asking for the “original” Preamble can be answered by eliminating these three. This single fact eliminates at least two distractors in most multiple‑choice questions.

The Preamble's Role in the Interpretation of the Constitution's Federal Character

Although the word <q>Federal</q> does not appear in the Preamble, the phrase <q>Union of States</q> has been pivotal in judicial construction of India's federal architecture. In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court held that the Preamble’s declaration of a <q>Union of States</q> signifies an indestructible union with a strong centre, but also recognises the distinct existence of the States as constitutional entities. The Court used the Preamble to reason that the distribution of legislative powers (Seventh Schedule) must be read in harmony with the federal principle implicit in the Preamble. Similarly, in State of West Bengal v. Union of India (1963), the Court observed that the Preamble’s reference to a <q>Union</q> does not diminish the States’ autonomy in their allotted spheres. The Preamble thus operates as an interpretive lens: when a statutory provision is ambiguous, courts may ask whether the interpretation preserves the <q>Union of States</q> character. This approach has been applied in disputes over Article 356 (President’s Rule) and in the GST Council’s decision‑making, where the Court has insisted that the federal balance reflected in the Preamble must guide the exercise of concurrent powers.

The Preamble's Reference to 'Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity' and Its Impact on Fundamental Rights Jurisprudence

The four ideals enumerated in the Preamble have been repeatedly invoked to expand the scope of Fundamental Rights. Justice (social, economic and political) underpins the Court’s reading of Article 21 as encompassing the right to livelihood, health and education (e.g., Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation, 1985). Liberty has been the doctrinal basis for the due‑process‑like protection in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), where the Court held that <q>personal liberty</q> under Article 21 cannot be curtailed by a procedure that is arbitrary, unfair or unreasonable. Equality informs the <q>reasonable classification</q> test under Article 14 and the prohibition of discrimination under Article 15; the Preamble’s promise of <q>equality of status and of opportunity</q> has been cited in Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) to justify reservations as a means of achieving substantive equality. Fraternity, though aspirational, has been used to interpret the duty to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood, notably in National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (2014), where the Court linked fraternity to the recognition of transgender rights. In each instance, the Preamble serves as a constitutional conscience that guides the Court in giving a purposive, expansive reading to the enumerated rights.

The Preamble's Role in the Interpretation of the Constitution's Republican Character

The word Republic in the Preamble signifies that the head of state is elected, not hereditary, and that public offices are open to all citizens on the basis of merit. This republican principle has shaped several constitutional outcomes. First, it underlies the abolition of privy purses and the derecognition of former rulers by the 26th Amendment (1971), which the Supreme Court upheld in H. H. Maharajadhiraja Madhav Rao v. Union of India (1971) as a necessary step to realise the republican ideal. Second, it informs the composition of the Electoral College for the President (Article 54), ensuring that the President derives authority from representatives of the people rather than from a monarchical lineage. Third, the republican character has been invoked in challenges to the nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha; the Court in Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006) held that the nomination process must not undermine the representative nature of the Upper House, a requirement flowing from the republican commitment to popular sovereignty. Finally, the Preamble’s republican declaration has been cited in debates on the death penalty, where the Court has emphasised that a republic committed to the dignity of the individual must subject capital punishment to the strictest scrutiny (e.g., Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, 1980). Thus, the single word <q>Republic</q> operates as a structural constraint on both legislative and executive action.

  • Confusing the original Preamble with the amended version; forgetting that the 42nd Amendment added Socialist, Secular and Integrity.
  • Assuming the Preamble is justiciable in the same way as Fundamental Rights; it is not independently enforceable.
  • Treating “Union of States” as a federal term equivalent to “Federal” in other constitutions.
  • Overlooking that the word “Socialist” was added in 1976 and does not reflect the original constitutional philosophy.
  • Misreading “Fraternity” as a legally enforceable duty rather than an aspirational goal.
  • Believing the Preamble can be amended by a simple majority; it requires the special majority under Article 368.
  • Ignoring the Constituent Assembly debates that show “Sovereign” was chosen over “Independent” for precise international law reasons.

The Constitutional Position of the Attorney General of India: Role, Tenure, and Accountability

The Attorney General for India is appointed under Article 76(1) by the President on the advice of the Council of Ministers. The office is a constitutional post, not a civil service position, and the Attorney General holds office during the pleasure of the President. Unlike the Advocate General of a State, the Attorney General does not have a fixed term; the Constitution does not prescribe a minimum age or qualification beyond being qualified to be a Judge of the Supreme Court. In practice, the appointee is a senior advocate of the Supreme Court with extensive experience in constitutional and administrative law.

The Attorney General’s primary duty is to give advice to the Government of India upon such legal matters as may be referred, and to perform such other duties of a legal character as may be assigned. The Attorney General has the right of audience in all courts in India, including the Supreme Court and High Courts, and may participate in the proceedings of either House of Parliament without a vote. The office is also the chief legal advisor to the Union Government, and the Attorney General’s opinions are often sought before the promulgation of ordinances, the introduction of bills, and the formulation of policy on matters with significant constitutional implications.

Accountability mechanisms are limited. The Attorney General can be removed by the President at any time, which in effect means removal on the advice of the Council of Ministers. There is no parliamentary impeachment process. However, the Supreme Court has held that the Attorney General must act independently and not merely as a mouthpiece of the executive. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raj Narain (1975), the Court observed that the Attorney General’s duty is to the Constitution and not to the government of the day. The Court has also ruled that the Attorney General cannot appear for private parties in cases where the Union of India is a party, reinforcing the principle of institutional integrity.

Recent controversies have centred on the perception of politicisation. The 2014 appointment of a former Solicitor General as Attorney General, and subsequent public statements on politically sensitive matters, sparked debate about the need for a statutory framework governing the office. The Law Commission’s 230th Report (2009) recommended a fixed tenure of three years and a transparent selection process involving a collegium comprising the Chief Justice of India, the Law Minister, and the Leader of the Opposition. No legislative action has followed, leaving the office governed solely by constitutional convention and executive discretion.

In comparative perspective, the United Kingdom’s Attorney General is a political appointee who sits in Cabinet, while the United States’ Attorney General heads the Department of Justice and is a member of the Cabinet. India’s model blends the advisory function with a quasi‑judicial aura, but the absence of statutory safeguards makes the office vulnerable to executive pressure. For UPSC aspirants, the key takeaway is that the Attorney General’s independence rests on constitutional morality rather than textual guarantee, and any reform would require an amendment to Article 76 or a dedicated statute.

The Doctrine of Legislative Privilege and Its Judicial Review: Articles 105 and 194

Articles 105 and 194 of the Constitution confer on Parliament and State Legislatures, respectively, powers, privileges, and immunities that are essentially those of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom as they stood on 26 January 1950, until defined by law. These privileges include freedom of speech in the House, immunity from court proceedings for anything said or any vote given, and the power to punish for contempt. The Constitution also empowers each House to regulate its own procedure and to determine matters of privilege.

The scope of legislative privilege has been a fertile ground for judicial interpretation. In Keshav Singh v. Speaker, Legislative Assembly (1965), the Supreme Court held that the power to punish for contempt is a judicial function and therefore subject to judicial review. The Court asserted that while the legislature is the sole judge of its privilege, the exercise of that power must not violate fundamental rights. This principle was reinforced in Raja Ram Pal v. Hon’ble Speaker, Lok Sabha (2007), where the Court examined the expulsion of members for alleged cash‑for‑questions and held that the decision is amenable to judicial review on grounds of mala fide, perversity, or violation of natural justice.

Freedom of speech under Article 105(1) is absolute within the House, but the Supreme Court in Tej Kiran Jain v. Sanjiva Reddy (1970) clarified that the immunity does not extend to publications outside the House. The Court distinguished between “speech in Parliament” and “speech about Parliament”, holding that the latter is not protected. Similarly, in State of Kerala v. K. Ajith (2021), the Court ruled that a legislator’s statement made in a press conference does not attract parliamentary privilege.

The power to punish for contempt has been narrowly construed. In P. V. Narasimha Rao v. State (CBI) (1998), the Court held that a legislator cannot claim immunity from criminal prosecution for bribery merely because the alleged act occurred in connection with parliamentary proceedings. The Court emphasised that privilege is a shield for legislative functioning, not a licence for criminal conduct. The 2003 amendment to the Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act and the subsequent Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006) judgment further limited the scope of privilege by subjecting disqualification decisions to judicial scrutiny.

State legislatures enjoy parallel privileges under Article 194. The Supreme Court in Special Reference No. 1 of 1964 (the “Keshav Singh” reference) affirmed that the High Courts have jurisdiction to review legislative privilege matters under Article 226. The Court also held that the power to punish for contempt is not absolute and must be exercised in accordance with the principles of natural justice. The 2018 judgment in K. K. Ramesh v. State of Tamil Nadu reiterated that legislative privilege cannot override the fundamental right to personal liberty under Article 21.

For examination purposes, aspirants should note the distinction between “privilege” (a collective right of the House) and “immunity” (an individual right of a member), the justiciability of privilege matters, and the evolving judicial trend towards greater accountability of legislatures. The interplay between Articles 105/194 and fundamental rights remains a live constitutional issue.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “The power of a State Legislative Assembly to punish for contempt is absolute and not subject to judicial review.” Identify the correct constitutional position and cite the leading case.
The statement is false. The Supreme Court in Keshav Singh v. Speaker, Legislative Assembly (1965) held that the power to punish for contempt is a judicial function and is subject to judicial review. The High Courts can examine whether the punishment violates fundamental rights or principles of natural justice. Therefore, legislative privilege is not absolute.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question on legislative privilege appears, first identify whether it concerns Parliament (Art. 105) or a State Legislature (Art. 194). Then recall the two‑step test: (1) Is the matter a “proceeding in the House”? (2) Does the exercise of privilege infringe a fundamental right or natural justice? Cite Keshav Singh for judicial review and Raja Ram Pal for expulsion cases. This framework covers 90 % of UPSC‑style questions.

The Constitutional Framework for the National Green Tribunal and Environmental Jurisprudence

The National Green Tribunal (NGT) was established under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, which came into force on 18 October 2010. The Act was enacted pursuant to the Supreme Court’s direction in M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1996) to create specialised environmental courts. The NGT is a statutory body, not a constitutional body, but its creation flows from the Directive Principle under Article 48A (protection and improvement of environment) and the fundamental duty under Article 51A(g). The Tribunal has original jurisdiction over substantial questions relating to environment, including enforcement of environmental laws listed in Schedule I of the Act, such as the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, and the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980.

The NGT comprises a Chairperson, judicial members, and expert members. The Chairperson must be a former Supreme Court judge or a former Chief Justice of a High Court. Judicial members are former High Court judges. Expert members possess qualifications in science, engineering, or environmental management. The Tribunal follows the principles of natural justice and is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, or the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. It can regulate its own procedure, allowing for expedited disposal of cases.

Landmark judgments have expanded the NGT’s reach. In Almitra H. Patel v. Union of India (2000), the Supreme Court recognised the principle of “polluter pays” and “precautionary principle” as part of Indian environmental law. The NGT applied these principles in Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) (though pre‑NGT, the principles were later adopted). In Goa Foundation v. Union of India (2014), the NGT ordered the closure of illegal mining leases in Goa, invoking the public trust doctrine. The Tribunal’s orders are enforceable as decrees of a civil court, and non‑compliance attracts penalties under Section 26 of the Act, including imprisonment up to three years and fine up to ten crore rupees.

The relationship between the NGT and High Courts has been delineated by the Supreme Court. In Union of India v. M. C. Mehta (2017), the Court held that the NGT’s jurisdiction is exclusive for matters under Schedule I, and High Courts cannot entertain writ petitions on the same subject matter unless a substantial question of constitutional interpretation arises. However, the Supreme Court retains appellate jurisdiction over NGT orders under Section 22 of the Act, and the High Courts retain supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 for procedural irregularities.

Critics point to the NGT’s limited territorial benches (initially five, later expanded) and the pendency of cases. The 2021 amendment to the Act increased the number of benches and allowed for video conferencing hearings. The Tribunal’s effectiveness hinges on the executive’s willingness to implement its orders, as seen in the delayed compliance with the Yamuna pollution directives. For aspirants, the NGT exemplifies the intersection of statutory innovation, Directive Principles, and judicial activism in environmental governance.

The Constitutional Position of the Vice‑President: Role as Chairman of Rajya Sabha and Acting President

The Vice‑President of India is elected by an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament under Article 66. The Vice‑President serves a five‑year term and is eligible for re‑election. The Constitution assigns two principal roles: ex‑officio Chairman of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) under Article 64, and Acting President when the office of the President falls vacant due to death, resignation, removal, or otherwise under Article 65.

As Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, the Vice‑President presides over its proceedings, maintains order, decides points of order, and certifies Money Bills under Article 110. The Chairman does not have a casting vote except in the case of a tie, where the Chairman may exercise a casting vote. The Vice‑President’s rulings on procedural matters are final and not subject to judicial review, as held in K. K. Ramesh v. State of Tamil Nadu (2018) regarding legislative privilege. However, the Supreme Court in Raja Ram Pal v. Hon’ble Speaker, Lok Sabha (2007) indicated that decisions affecting fundamental rights may be reviewed.

When acting as President, the Vice‑President assumes all powers and immunities of the President, including the power to promulgate ordinances (Article 123), grant pardons (Article 72), and appoint the Prime Minister. The Acting President’s tenure continues until a new President is elected, which must occur within six months of the vacancy. The first instance of a Vice‑President acting as President occurred in 1969 when Vice‑President V. V. Giri assumed office after President Zakir Husain’s death. Giri later resigned to contest the presidential election, establishing a precedent that the Acting President may resign to become a candidate.

The Vice‑President’s removal is governed by Article 67(b): a resolution passed by a majority of the Rajya Sabha and agreed to by the Lok Sabha. The process requires a 14‑day notice. No Vice‑President has been removed to date. The office has often been a stepping stone to the presidency; six of the fourteen Presidents have previously served as Vice‑President.

Constitutional debates in the Constituent Assembly reveal that the Vice‑President’s role was modelled on the American Vice‑Presidency but with a stronger legislative function. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar emphasised that the Vice‑President’s primary duty is to preside over the Rajya Sabha, ensuring the Upper House’s independence from the executive. The Vice‑President’s salary and allowances are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, guaranteeing financial independence.

For examination, key points include the dual constitutional role, the electoral college composition, the acting presidency provisions, the removal procedure, and the distinction between the Vice‑President’s legislative and executive functions. The interplay between Articles 64, 65, 66, and 67 is frequently tested in both preliminary and mains questions.

The Doctrine of Federalism and Inter‑State Water Disputes: Article 262 and the Inter‑State Water Disputes Act

Article 262 of the Constitution provides for the adjudication of disputes relating to waters of inter‑state rivers or river valleys. It empowers Parliament to enact a law for the adjudication of such disputes and to exclude the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and other courts in respect of those disputes. Pursuant to this, Parliament enacted the Inter‑State Water Disputes Act, 1956, which establishes a tribunal for each dispute referred by the Central Government. The tribunal’s decision is final and binding, and the Act bars the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 131, except for a limited review under Article 136 (special leave).

The first major tribunal was the Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal (1969), followed by the Godavari (1969), Narmada (1969), Cauvery (1990), and Ravi‑Beas (1986) tribunals. The Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal’s final award (2007) and the subsequent Supreme Court judgment in State of Karnataka v. State of Tamil Nadu (2018) illustrate the complex interplay between tribunal awards and judicial review. The Supreme Court held that while the tribunal’s award is binding, the Court can examine whether the tribunal acted within its jurisdiction, followed principles of natural justice, or committed an error apparent on the face of the record.

The 2002 amendment to the Inter‑State Water Disputes Act introduced a time‑limit for tribunal adjudication (three years, extendable by two) and provided for a single standing tribunal with multiple benches to reduce delays. The 2019 amendment further streamlined the process by mandating the Central Government to refer disputes within a year of receiving a request from a state, and by empowering the tribunal to issue interim orders. Despite these reforms, disputes such as the Mahanadi (Odisha‑Chhattisgarh) and the Mahadayi (Goa‑Karnataka‑Maharashtra) remain protracted.

Judicial interpretation has clarified the scope of Article 262. In State of Haryana v. State of Punjab (2002), the Supreme Court held that the exclusion of Supreme Court jurisdiction under Article 262 is not absolute; the Court retains the power to review tribunal awards for constitutional violations. In Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2000), the Court emphasised that the tribunal’s award must be consistent with the principles of equitable apportionment and the doctrine of prior appropriation, balanced against the needs of riparian states.

The constitutional design reflects a quasi‑federal approach: water is a State subject (Entry 17, State List), but inter‑state rivers fall under Union legislation (Entry 56, Union List). The Centre’s role in constituting tribunals and enforcing awards underscores the unitary bias in resource management. The recent proposal for a National Water Framework Bill seeks to create a permanent institutional mechanism, but it has not yet been enacted.

For aspirants, the critical takeaways are: (1) Article 262 and the 1956 Act constitute a self‑contained code for inter‑state water disputes; (2) tribunal awards are final but subject to limited judicial review; (3) the Centre’s power to refer disputes is discretionary but has been fettered by amendments; (4) the principle of equitable utilisation guides tribunal decisions; and (5) the tension between State autonomy over water and Union oversight remains a live federalism issue.

  • Confusing the Attorney General’s tenure with that of the Advocate General; the former holds office during the President’s pleasure, the latter during the Governor’s pleasure.
  • Assuming legislative privilege is absolute; the Supreme Court has consistently subjected it to judicial review for fundamental‑rights violations.
  • Treating the National Green Tribunal as a constitutional body; it is a statutory tribunal created under the NGT Act, 2010.
  • Believing the Vice‑President can vote in the Rajya Sabha on all matters; the Chairman votes only in case of a tie.
  • Thinking the Inter‑State Water Disputes Act completely ousts the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction; Article 136 review remains available.
  • Overlooking that the Vice‑President’s removal requires a Rajya Sabha majority and Lok Sabha agreement, not a simple parliamentary majority.
  • Misreading Article 262 as granting the Centre unlimited power to resolve water disputes; the tribunal’s award must respect equitable apportionment principles.

The Constituent Assembly's Debates on the Uniform Civil Code and Article 44

The Uniform Civil Code (UCC) was one of the most contested subjects in the Constituent Assembly. The debate centred on whether a common set of personal laws governing marriage, divorce, inheritance and adoption should replace the plurality of religious personal laws. The Objectives Resolution had promised a “secular” state, but the Assembly stopped short of making the UCC a justiciable right, placing it instead in Article 44 as a Directive Principle of State Policy.

Key Participants and Positions

  • B.R. Ambedkar argued that a UCC was essential for gender justice and national integration, but he accepted its placement in Part IV because the Muslim members feared immediate imposition would violate religious freedom under Article 25.
  • K.M. Munshi and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar supported a mandatory code, citing the need for a uniform legal framework in a modern republic.
  • Mohammad Ismail and B. Pocker Bahadur opposed a compulsory code, insisting that personal law was an integral part of religious practice protected by Article 25.

Compromise and Textual Outcome

The Assembly adopted a compromise: Article 44 reads, “The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.” The word “endeavour” makes the provision non‑justiciable, leaving the timing and manner of implementation to the legislature.

Post‑Constitutional Judicial Interpretation

  • Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985) – The Supreme Court held that a Muslim woman was entitled to maintenance under Section 125 CrPC, urging Parliament to enact a UCC.
  • Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) – The Court reiterated the need for a UCC to prevent fraudulent conversions for bigamy.
  • John Vallamattom v. Union of India (2003) – The Court struck down Section 118 of the Indian Succession Act as discriminatory, again highlighting the gap left by the absence of a UCC.

Contemporary Relevance

Successive Law Commissions (1974, 2003, 2018) have recommended a phased approach, beginning with optional uniform laws for marriage and divorce. The 2023 Law Commission report suggested a “gender‑just” UCC that respects cultural diversity while eliminating discriminatory practices. The debate remains a live constitutional issue, testing the balance between Article 25 (freedom of religion) and Article 44 (directive for uniformity).

The Constitutional Position of the Attorney General and Solicitor General: Appointment, Tenure, and Role in Governance

Article 76 establishes the Attorney General for India as the highest law officer of the Union. The President appoints a person qualified to be a Supreme Court judge. The Attorney General holds office during the pleasure of the President, receives such remuneration as Parliament may determine, and has the right of audience in all courts in India.

Functions and Limitations

  • Advises the Government of India on legal matters referred by the President.
  • Performs duties assigned by the President, including representing the Union in the Supreme Court and High Courts.
  • Cannot vote in Parliament but may speak and take part in proceedings of either House (Article 88).
  • Is not a member of the Cabinet; the post is non‑political, though in practice the appointee is usually a senior advocate aligned with the ruling party.

Solicitor General and Additional Solicitors General

The Solicitor General is not mentioned in the Constitution; the post is created by the Law Officers (Conditions of Service) Act, 1972. The Solicitor General assists the Attorney General and is appointed by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet. Additional Solicitors General are similarly appointed. Their tenure is also during the pleasure of the President, but they lack the constitutional standing of the Attorney General.

Key Judicial Pronouncements

  • State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to the Governor (2022) – The Supreme Court clarified that the Attorney General’s advice is not binding on the Governor; the Governor may seek independent legal opinion.
  • K. Veeraswami v. Union of India (1991) – Held that the Attorney General can be removed only by the President, but the pleasure doctrine is subject to judicial review for mala fide exercise.

Contemporary Issues

Recent controversies have arisen over the Attorney General’s participation in politically sensitive cases (e.g., the Rafale review, the Article 370 abrogation). Critics argue that the “pleasure” tenure compromises independence, while the government maintains that the post is inherently executive. The Law Commission’s 2020 report recommended a fixed tenure of three years to enhance autonomy, but no amendment has been enacted.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “The Attorney General of India can be removed only by impeachment.” Identify the error and state the correct constitutional position.
The statement is false. Article 76(1) provides that the Attorney General holds office during the pleasure of the President. There is no impeachment procedure; removal is effected by a presidential order. The pleasure doctrine is, however, subject to judicial review for arbitrariness or mala fide intent (K. Veeraswami v. Union of India).
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the distinction: Attorney General – constitutional (Art. 76), pleasure tenure, right of audience in all courts, can speak in Parliament. Solicitor General – statutory, assists AG, no constitutional mention. For MCQs, watch for “impeachment” or “fixed tenure” distractors.

The Doctrine of Legislative Privilege under Articles 105 and 194: Scope, Judicial Limits, and Contemporary Challenges

Articles 105 (Parliament) and 194 (State Legislatures) confer two core privileges: freedom of speech in the House and immunity from court proceedings for anything said or any vote given. Members also enjoy exemption from arrest in civil cases during the session and forty days before and after. These privileges are modelled on the British parliamentary tradition but are subject to the written Constitution.

Scope of Privilege

  • Freedom of Speech – Absolute within the House; no court can question a member’s speech or vote (Article 105(1)/194(1)).
  • Immunity from Legal Process – No civil or criminal proceedings for statements made in the House; extends to publication of reports, papers, votes or proceedings by authority of the House (Article 105(2)/194(2)).
  • Power to Punish Contempt – Each House can punish breach of privilege or contempt, including non‑members.

Judicial Limits

  • Keshav Singh v. Speaker, Legislative Assembly (1965) – The Supreme Court held that legislative privilege is not absolute; it is subject to fundamental rights. The Court can examine whether the House acted within its constitutional authority.
  • Raja Ram Pal v. Hon’ble Speaker, Lok Sabha (2007) – The Court affirmed judicial review of expulsion of members, ruling that the power to punish contempt cannot violate Article 21.
  • State of Kerala v. K. Ajith (2021) – The Supreme Court held that legislative privilege does not shield a member from criminal prosecution for bribery; the Prevention of Corruption Act prevails.

Contemporary Challenges

Recent disputes involve the conflict between legislative privilege and the right to information (RTI Act). In 2019, the Delhi High Court ruled that the Legislative Assembly’s secretariat is a “public authority” under RTI, rejecting a blanket privilege claim. The 2023 amendment to the Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act attempted to codify certain privileges, but the Supreme Court has yet to rule on its constitutionality. The tension between parliamentary autonomy and judicial oversight remains a fertile ground for examiner questions.

The Constitutional Framework for Environmental Protection: Articles 48A, 51A(g), and Judicial Activism

The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted Article 48A in Part IV (Directive Principles) and Article 51A(g) in Part IVA (Fundamental Duties). Article 48A directs the State to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard forests and wildlife. Article 51A(g) imposes a duty on every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife.

Judicial Expansion of Environmental Rights

  • M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) – The Supreme Court read Article 21 (right to life) to include the right to a wholesome environment, making environmental protection justiciable.
  • Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) – The Court recognised the “precautionary principle” and “polluter pays principle” as part of Indian environmental law.
  • Indian Council for Enviro‑Legal Action v. Union of India (1996) – Established the “public trust doctrine”, holding that the State holds natural resources in trust for the public.
  • Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991) – Affirmed that the right to clean water and air flows from Article 21.

Statutory Framework and Institutional Mechanisms

Parliament enacted the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, and the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974. The National Green Tribunal (NGT), established under the NGT Act, 2010, provides specialised adjudication. The Supreme Court has repeatedly directed the NGT to enforce the “polluter pays” principle and to monitor compliance with environmental clearances.

Recent Developments

  • 2020 Supreme Court order in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Air Pollution) – Directed the creation of a “Graded Response Action Plan” for Delhi‑NCR, linking Article 48A with emergency powers.
  • 2022 judgment in Conservation Action Trust v. Union of India – Held that the State’s duty under Article 48A includes preventing ecological degradation from infrastructure projects, requiring cumulative impact assessment.

Exam‑Relevant Takeaways

Article 48A is a Directive Principle (non‑justiciable per se) but has been elevated to a justiciable right through Article 21. Article 51A(g) is a Fundamental Duty, enforceable only through statutory mechanisms. The interplay of Directive Principles, Fundamental Duties, and judicial interpretation creates a “living” environmental jurisprudence that examiners test through case‑law matching and principle‑application questions.

  • Confusing the Attorney General’s constitutional tenure (pleasure of the President) with a fixed term or impeachment; the correct position is pleasure tenure subject to judicial review for mala fide removal.
  • Assuming legislative privilege under Articles 105/194 is absolute; the Supreme Court has subjected it to fundamental‑rights scrutiny (Keshav Singh, Raja Ram Pal).
  • Treating Article 48A as directly enforceable without invoking Article 21; the Directive Principle becomes justiciable only through the right to life.
  • Believing the Solicitor General is a constitutional authority; the post is statutory under the Law Officers Act, 1972.
  • Overlooking that the Uniform Civil Code remains a Directive Principle (Article 44) and not a Fundamental Right; judicial pronouncements urge but cannot compel legislation.
  • Misreading the “polluter pays” principle as a statutory rule only; it is a judicial principle derived from Article 21 and Article 48A.

The Constituent Assembly’s Deliberations on Citizenship and the Partition Legacy

The Constituent Assembly treated citizenship as a constitutional bridge between the newly independent state and the millions displaced by Partition. The Sub‑Committee on Citizenship, chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, submitted its report in July 1948 after examining the 1935 Government of India Act, the British Nationality Act 1948, and the emergent international law on statelessness. The Committee recommended a three‑tier scheme: citizenship by birth (Article 5), citizenship by descent (Article 6), and citizenship by registration or naturalisation (Articles 7‑11). The debates, held between 10 August and 12 August 1949, centred on the definition of “domicile” and the treatment of migrants from the newly created Pakistan. Article 6 granted citizenship to persons who migrated to India before 19 July 1948, while Article 7 extended it to those who returned after 1 March 1947 under a permit system. The Assembly rejected a proposal to make religion a criterion, affirming the secular character of the polity. The 1955 Citizenship Act gave statutory flesh to these provisions, introducing the concept of “illegal migrant” and empowering the Central Government to regulate naturalisation. The 1986 amendment (Act 31 of 1986) restricted birthright citizenship to children born to at least one Indian parent, a response to the Assam agitation. The 2003 amendment (Act 6 of 2004) created Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI), a novel category that stopped short of dual citizenship. The 2019 Citizenship (Amendment) Act (CAA) altered the 1955 Act by providing a fast‑track for non‑Muslim migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan, but left the constitutional Articles untouched. Judicial interpretation has repeatedly tested the constitutional limits: in State of Assam v. Union of India (1971) the Supreme Court upheld Section 6A of the 1955 Act as a valid exercise of Parliament’s power under Article 11; in Louis De Raedt v. Union of India (1991) the Court clarified that registration under Article 8 does not confer automatic citizenship if the applicant fails the “good character” test; and in Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India (2005) the Court struck down the Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act, 1983, for violating Article 14. These rulings illustrate how the original constitutional design, shaped by Partition’s exigencies, continues to mediate the tension between inclusive citizenship and border security.

The Debate on the Uniform Civil Code in the Constituent Assembly and Its Constitutional Trajectory

The Uniform Civil Code (UCC) entered the constitutional discourse as Article 35 of the Draft Constitution (later Article 44). On 23 November 1948 the Assembly debated the clause for three days. K.M. Munshi, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar and Hansa Mehta argued that a common civil code was essential for national integration and gender justice, urging its placement in the Fundamental Rights chapter. Muslim members — notably Mohammad Ismail, B. Pocker Sahib and Maulana Hasrat Mohani — contended that personal law was a matter of religious freedom protected by Article 25 and warned that a compulsory code would alienate minorities. The compromise, moved by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, placed the UCC in the Directive Principles of State Policy, making it a non‑justiciable goal. The Constitution thus recorded a “constitutional promise” rather than a mandate. Post‑independence jurisprudence has repeatedly invoked this promise. In Mohd. Ahmed Khan v.
