Shah Bano Begum (1985) the Supreme Court, while granting maintenance under Section 125 CrPC, observed that a UCC would “remove the discrimination against women” and urged Parliament to enact it. Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) held that a Hindu husband’s conversion to Islam for a second marriage did not dissolve the first marriage, reiterating the need for a UCC to prevent such misuse. John Vallamattom v. Union of India (2003) struck down Section 118 of the Indian Succession Act as violative of Article 14, again citing the Directive Principle. The 2017 Shayara Bano v. Union of India judgment, which declared instant triple talaq unconstitutional, referenced Article 44 as a constitutional nudge toward codified personal laws. Despite these judicial prods, Parliament has not enacted a comprehensive UCC; the 2023‑24 Law Commission report recommended a “gradual, consultative” approach. The constitutional trajectory thus shows a persistent tension between the aspirational Directive Principle and the pluralistic protection of religious autonomy under Articles 25‑28.

Technique
Explain how the Constituent Assembly’s citizenship provisions (Articles 5‑11) addressed the Partition migration crisis and how subsequent constitutional amendments and judicial decisions have modified the original scheme.
The Assembly created a three‑tier citizenship framework: Article 5 conferred citizenship on persons domiciled in India at commencement; Article 6 granted it to migrants from Pakistan who arrived before 19 July 1948; Article 7 covered those who returned after 1 March 1947 under a permit system. Articles 8‑11 empowered Parliament to regulate acquisition and termination of citizenship. The 1955 Citizenship Act operationalised these powers, introducing the concept of “illegal migrant”. The 1986 amendment (Act 31 of 1986) narrowed birthright citizenship to children with at least one Indian parent. The 2003 amendment (Act 6 of 2004) created Overseas Citizenship of India, a statutory category not envisaged in the Constitution. The 2019 CAA amended the 1955 Act to fast‑track non‑Muslim migrants from three neighbouring countries, leaving Articles 5‑11 unchanged. Judicially, State of Assam v. Union of India (1971) upheld Section 6A of the 1955 Act as a valid exercise of Article 11; Louis De Raedt v. Union of India (1991) clarified registration requirements under Article 8; Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India (2005) struck down the IMDT Act for violating Article 14. Together, these developments show a dynamic interplay between the constitutional text, parliamentary legislation, and judicial review.
Strategy
When a question links Partition, citizenship Articles and later amendments, first map the original constitutional scheme (Articles 5‑11), then list each statutory amendment chronologically, and finally note the key Supreme Court decisions that interpreted or limited those amendments. This three‑step structure ensures you cover the constitutional‑legislative‑judicial triangle that examiners favour.

The Emergence of the Doctrine of Constitutional Identity in Indian Jurisprudence

The doctrine of constitutional identity — the idea that certain core features of a constitution are immutable even under the formal amendment power — entered Indian law through the German Basic Law’s “eternity clause” (Article 79(3)) and was domesticated in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973). The thirteen‑judge bench held that Parliament’s amending power under Article 368 could not alter the “basic structure” of the Constitution, thereby establishing a judicially enforceable identity. The Court identified several identity markers: supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secularism, separation of powers, federalism, and the rule of law. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) reinforced this by declaring that judicial review itself is a basic feature, preventing Parliament from ousting the courts via amendment. S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) elevated secularism to an identity element, ruling that a state government’s dismissal on grounds of “secularism” must meet a stringent test. In NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018) the Court treated the federal balance and the democratic republican character as identity components that constrain the Lieutenant Governor’s powers. K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) extended identity to include the right to privacy, linking it to the Preamble’s promise of “liberty” and “dignity”. The doctrine has also been invoked to strike down constitutional amendments that sought to entrench political interests: the 39th Amendment (1975), which placed the Prime Minister’s election beyond judicial scrutiny, was invalidated in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) for violating the basic structure. More recently, the 99th Amendment (2014) establishing the National Judicial Appointments Commission was struck down in Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (2015) because it compromised judicial independence, an identity pillar. The doctrine thus functions as a constitutional “immune system”, preserving the founding vision against majoritarian erosion while allowing organic evolution within the identified core.

The Interaction between the Preamble and the Basic Structure Doctrine: Judicial Construction

The Preamble, though not legally enforceable in isolation, has become the interpretive lodestar for the basic structure doctrine. In Kesavananda Bharati the majority held that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution and reflects its “basic structure”. The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted the words “Socialist”, “Secular” and “Integrity” into the Preamble, signalling a political re‑definition of the Republic’s identity. The Supreme Court in S.R. Bommai used the Preamble’s “Secular” to articulate secularism as a basic feature, holding that any state action undermining religious neutrality violates the Constitution’s identity. In Minerva Mills the Court balanced the Directive Principles against Fundamental Rights by invoking the Preamble’s “Socialist” and “Democratic” aspirations, ruling that an amendment giving primacy to DPSPs over FRs destroyed the basic structure. K.S. Puttaswamy read “Liberty” and “Equality” from the Preamble into Article 21, expanding the right to privacy as a facet of constitutional identity. The 2018 Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India decision, which decriminalised consensual same‑sex relations, invoked the Preamble’s “Dignity” and “Fraternity” to strike down Section 377 IPC, illustrating how the Preamble’s aspirational language can animate substantive rights. Conversely, the Court has refused to treat the Preamble as a source of independent justiciable rights; in Union of India v. Sankalchand Himatlal Sheth (1977) it clarified that the Preamble cannot override express constitutional provisions. The interplay thus operates as a hermeneutic circle: the Preamble informs the content of the basic structure, while the basic structure doctrine safeguards the Preamble’s promises from majoritarian amendment.

The Influence of the United States Constitution on the Indian Bill of Rights and Judicial Review

The Indian Constitution’s Part III bears a visible imprint of the United States Bill of Rights, yet the borrowing was selective and adaptive. Article 14’s “equality before the law” mirrors the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause, but the Indian provision applies to “any person” and has been interpreted to encompass both negative and positive obligations. Article 19’s freedoms echo the First Amendment, yet the Indian text enumerates reasonable restrictions (public order, morality, sovereignty) that are absent in the US formulation. Article 21’s “procedure established by law” was deliberately chosen over the US “due process of law” to limit judicial activism; however, Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) imported substantive due process by reading “procedure” as “fair, just and reasonable”, effectively converging with the US standard. Judicial review itself derives from Marbury v. Madison (1803); Article 13 declares laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void, and Articles 32 and 226 empower the Supreme Court and High Courts to enforce rights. The US model of a written constitution with a supreme court capable of striking down legislation informed the Indian design, but the Indian system blends this with parliamentary sovereignty within constitutional limits. The “basic structure” doctrine, while indigenous, resonates with the US principle that certain constitutional fundamentals are beyond amendment — a concept the US Supreme Court has never formally articulated but which underlies its jurisprudence on unconstitutional constitutional amendments. Landmark Indian cases illustrate the dialogue: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) adopted a narrow, literal reading akin to early US “formalist” era; Maneka Gandhi shifted to a “living constitution” approach reminiscent of the US “incorporation” doctrine; Minerva Mills affirmed judicial review as a basic feature, echoing the US Supreme Court’s role as ultimate constitutional arbiter. Thus, the US influence is evident in the architecture of rights, the language of equality, and the institutionalisation of judicial review, yet Indian jurisprudence has forged a distinct path by embedding these borrowings within a parliamentary federal framework and a transformative constitutional vision.

  • Confusing the original citizenship scheme (Articles 5‑11) with the later statutory regime under the 1955 Act and its amendments; the Constitution only empowers Parliament, it does not prescribe the detailed criteria.
  • Assuming the Uniform Civil Code is a justiciable Fundamental Right; it remains a Directive Principle (Article 44) and courts can only urge, not compel, legislation.
  • Treating “constitutional identity” as synonymous with “basic structure” without recognising that identity is the theoretical foundation while basic structure is the judicial doctrine that enforces it.
  • Believing the Preamble can be directly enforced as a source of rights; the Supreme Court has consistently held it is interpretive, not independently justiciable.
  • Equating the US “due process” clause with Article 21’s “procedure established by law” before the Maneka Gandhi expansion; the two were distinct until 1978.
  • Overlooking that the 42nd Amendment’s insertion of “Socialist”, “Secular”, “Integrity” into the Preamble was a political act that later became a basic‑structure benchmark through judicial interpretation.
  • Ignoring the chronological sequence: Partition‑driven citizenship provisions → 1955 Act → 1986, 2003, 2019 amendments → judicial review; examiners often test this timeline.

Constitutional Supremacy versus Parliamentary Sovereignty in the Indian Framework

The Indian Constitution establishes constitutional supremacy as the governing principle, distinguishing it sharply from the British model of parliamentary sovereignty. Article 13 declares that any law inconsistent with the Fundamental Rights shall be void, and Articles 32 and 226 empower the Supreme Court and High Courts to enforce those rights. This judicial review mechanism makes the Constitution the highest legal authority; even an amendment passed by the requisite special majority under Article 368 can be struck down if it destroys the basic structure of the Constitution, as held in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973). In contrast, the United Kingdom’s Parliament can enact or repeal any law, and no court may invalidate primary legislation. The Indian Parliament enjoys supremacy only within the limits prescribed by the Constitution — its legislative competence is defined by the Union, State and Concurrent Lists, and its amendment power is circumscribed by the basic‑structure doctrine. The practical consequence is that Indian courts routinely examine the constitutional validity of statutes, executive orders, and even constitutional amendments, whereas British courts (prior to the Factortame litigation) could only interpret statutes for compatibility with European Community law. This supremacy also underpins the doctrine of constitutional morality, whereby courts interpret provisions in light of the Constitution’s transformative vision rather than mere majoritarian will.

  • Source of authority: Constitution (written, rigid amendment under Art. 368) vs. Parliament (unwritten conventions, ordinary legislation).
  • Judicial review: Explicit under Arts. 13, 32, 226; courts can invalidate laws and amendments.
  • Amendment rigidity: Special majority in both Houses plus, for federal provisions, ratification by half the States.
  • Basic‑structure limitation: Judicial innovation (Kesavananda) that certain core features — supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form, secularism, federalism, separation of powers — cannot be amended.

The interplay of these features creates a constitutional sovereignty model where the Constitution is the ultimate sovereign, not Parliament. This distinction is frequently tested in examinations through questions that ask whether India follows parliamentary sovereignty; the correct answer is that India follows constitutional sovereignty with parliamentary supremacy operating only within constitutional bounds.

The Constitutional Design of the Union Executive: President, Vice‑President, and Council of Ministers

The Union executive is structured around three constitutional offices — the President, the Vice‑President, and the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister — each defined by specific articles that balance ceremonial dignity with functional responsibility. The President is elected by an electoral college consisting of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the Legislative Assemblies of the States (Art. 54), serves a five‑year term (Art. 56), and can be removed only through impeachment for violation of the Constitution (Art. 61). Although the President is the formal head of state, executive power is exercised on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Art. 74), making the office largely ceremonial. The Vice‑President is elected by members of both Houses of Parliament (Art. 66) and serves as the ex‑officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, casting a vote only in case of a tie. The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Art. 75(3)); the Prime Minister is appointed by the President, and other ministers are appointed on the Prime Minister’s advice. The Constitution mandates that the Council of Ministers shall not exceed 15 % of the total strength of the Lok Sabha (91st Amendment, 2003). The President’s discretionary powers are narrowly confined — chiefly the power to refer a bill back for reconsideration (Art. 111), to grant pardons (Art. 72), and to appoint the Prime Minister when no party commands a clear majority. Judicial pronouncements such as Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974) and U.N.R. Rao v. Indira Gandhi (1971) have reinforced that the President acts on ministerial advice in all but these exceptional spheres. This design reflects the parliamentary system borrowed from the United Kingdom but embedded within a written constitution that subjects the executive to judicial review and constitutional limitations.

Examiner's Trap
A question states: "The President of India can dismiss the Prime Minister at will." Identify the error and explain the constitutional position.
The statement is false. Under Article 74 the President acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers. The Prime Minister holds office so long as he enjoys the confidence of the Lok Sabha. The President may dismiss the Prime Minister only when the government loses a vote of confidence or when the Lok Sabha is dissolved and a new Prime Minister must be appointed. The Supreme Court in Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974) held that the President’s satisfaction is the satisfaction of the Council of Ministers, not personal discretion.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about the President’s powers, first classify the power as either constitutional (expressly granted) or discretionary (exercised on ministerial advice). Remember the three genuine discretionary areas: referral of bills, pardoning power, and appointment of Prime Minister in a hung Parliament. This classification eliminates the majority of distractor options.

The Constitutional Scheme of Fundamental Duties under Article 51A: Enforceability and Judicial Interpretation

Fundamental Duties were inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee, and later expanded by the 86th Amendment (2002) to include the duty to provide opportunities for education to children between six and fourteen years. Article 51A enumerates eleven duties, ranging from respecting the Constitution, the national flag and the national anthem, to promoting harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood, protecting the natural environment, and developing scientific temper. Unlike Fundamental Rights, these duties are not directly enforceable by courts; Article 51A does not confer a justiciable right of action. However, the Supreme Court has repeatedly used them as interpretive aids. In M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) the Court invoked the duty to protect the environment (Art. 51A(g)) to widen the scope of Article 21. In Ranganath Misra v. Union of India (1996) the Court held that while duties are not legally enforceable, they serve as a moral compass for legislative and executive action. The 86th Amendment also added a corresponding right under Article 21A (free and compulsory education), illustrating how a duty can catalyse a justiciable right. The duties are addressed to citizens, not to the State, and therefore cannot be invoked against governmental inaction directly. Nevertheless, they have been cited in public interest litigation to reinforce the State’s obligation to create conditions that enable citizens to fulfil those duties. The non‑justiciability of Fundamental Duties remains a settled position; any attempt to make them legally binding would require a constitutional amendment.

The Role of the Rajya Sabha in Federal Legislation: Composition, Powers, and Judicial Precedents

The Rajya Sabha, or Council of States, embodies the federal character of the Indian Parliament. Its maximum strength is 250 members, of which 238 are elected by the Legislative Assemblies of the States and Union Territories through proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, and 12 are nominated by the President for expertise in literature, science, art, and social service (Art. 80). The House is not subject to dissolution; one‑third of its members retire every two years, ensuring continuity. In legislative matters, the Rajya Sabha enjoys co‑equal powers with the Lok Sabha except in respect of Money Bills (Art. 110), which can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha and where the Rajya Sabha’s recommendations are not binding. For Constitutional Amendment Bills under Article 368, the Rajya Sabha’s concurrence is mandatory; the special majority must be secured in both Houses. The Supreme Court has consistently upheld this requirement, holding that the Rajya Sabha’s role in amending the Constitution is not merely advisory but constitutive. In matters of ordinary legislation, a deadlock between the two Houses can be resolved by a joint sitting summoned by the President (Art. 108), but this mechanism does not apply to Money Bills or Constitutional Amendment Bills. The Rajya Sabha also exercises oversight through questions, debates, and committee work, and its Chairman (the Vice‑President) casts a deciding vote in case of a tie. The House’s composition reflects the principle of weighted representation, giving larger States more seats while guaranteeing a minimum presence for smaller States, thereby balancing federal equity with demographic reality.

The Constitutional Position of the Attorney General and the Solicitor General: Appointment, Tenure, and Functions

The Attorney General for India is the highest law officer of the Union, appointed by the President under Article 76(1). The appointee must be qualified to be a Judge of the Supreme Court and holds office during the pleasure of the President, meaning there is no fixed tenure and removal does not require parliamentary approval. The Attorney General has the right of audience in all courts in India, advises the Government of India on legal matters, and performs such duties as are assigned by the President. By convention, the Attorney General is a member of the Union Cabinet’s legal team but is not a member of Parliament; however, he may speak and take part in proceedings of either House without a vote (Art. 88). The Solicitor General of India, by contrast, is not a constitutional office; the position is created under the Law Officers (Conditions of Service) Act, 1972, and the appointee is appointed by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet. The Solicitor General assists the Attorney General and represents the Government in the Supreme Court and High Courts. Both officers are bound by the duty to give independent legal advice, and the Supreme Court has emphasised that the Attorney General’s opinion must not be influenced by political considerations (State of Punjab v. Union of India, 1975). The Attorney General’s tenure ends automatically when the Council of Ministers resigns or loses confidence, reflecting the principle that the law officer serves the executive of the day. This arrangement ensures continuity of legal expertise while maintaining accountability to the elected government.

  • Confusing the President’s ceremonial role with executive discretion; the President acts on ministerial advice except in three narrow areas.
  • Assuming Fundamental Duties are justiciable; they are moral obligations used only as interpretive tools.
  • Believing the Rajya Sabha can amend Money Bills; it can only make recommendations on them.
  • Treating the Solicitor General as a constitutional authority; the office is statutory, not constitutional.
  • Thinking the Attorney General has a fixed term; he holds office during the President’s pleasure.
  • Overlooking that the basic‑structure doctrine limits Parliament’s amendment power, not merely its ordinary legislation.
  • Misidentifying the electoral college for the President; it includes elected members of both Houses of Parliament and State Legislative Assemblies, not nominated members.

The Cabinet Mission Plan and the Constitutional Architecture of the Transfer of Power

The Cabinet Mission of March–June 1947, comprising Lord Pethick-Lawrence, Sir Stafford Cripps, and A. V. Alexander, remains the decisive constitutional blueprint that structured the Constituent Assembly and defined the terms of British withdrawal. Unlike the Cripps Mission of 1942, which offered dominion status after the war, the Cabinet Mission proposed a three-tier federal union with a weak centre controlling only defence, external affairs, and communications, while provinces and groups of provinces possessed residuary powers. The Mission's Statement of 16 May 1946 rejected the demand for a sovereign Pakistan, calculating that a truncated Pakistan would be economically non-viable and would leave substantial Muslim minorities in Hindu-majority provinces. Instead, it grouped provinces into three sections: Section A (Madras, Bombay, UP, Bihar, Central Provinces, Orissa), Section B (Punjab, NWFP, Sind), and Section C (Bengal, Assam). Each section could frame its own constitution, and after ten years any province could opt out of its group by a simple majority vote in its legislature.

The Mission's electoral formula for the Constituent Assembly allocated 296 seats to British India (roughly one seat per million population) distributed among the three communities—General, Muslim, and Sikh—in proportion to their population in each province. The 93 seats for Princely States were to be filled by nomination, with the method of representation left to negotiation. Elections held in July–August 1946 returned a Congress majority in the General category and a Muslim League sweep in the Muslim category. The League initially accepted the Plan on 6 June 1946, interpreting the grouping clauses as compulsory, while Congress accepted only the Constituent Assembly portion on 24 June, insisting grouping was voluntary. This interpretive divergence—whether Sections B and C must frame group constitutions before provinces could opt out—became the constitutional fault line that led to the League's withdrawal on 29 July 1946 and the launch of Direct Action Day on 16 August. The Mission's final attempt, the London Conference of December 1946, failed to reconcile the two interpretations. On 20 February 1947, Prime Minister Attlee announced a definitive transfer of power by June 1948, later advanced to 15 August 1947 by Mountbatten. The Cabinet Mission Plan thus died as a political settlement, but its electoral architecture survived: the Constituent Assembly convened on 9 December 1946 under the Mission's rules, and the Indian Independence Act 1947 formally derived its authority from the Mission's recommendation that the Assembly become the sovereign legislature of the new dominion.

The Indian Independence Act 1947: Statutory Foundation of the Sovereign Republic

The Indian Independence Act 1947 (10 & 11 Geo. 6 c. 30), passed by the British Parliament on 18 July 1947 and receiving royal assent the same day, is the legal instrument of sovereignty transfer that bridges the Government of India Act 1935 and the Constitution of India. The Act created two independent dominions—India and Pakistan—from 15 August 1947, each with a Governor-General appointed by the Crown on the advice of the respective dominion cabinet. Crucially, Section 7(1) declared that "the suzerainty of His Majesty over the Indian States lapses", ending paramountcy and leaving the Princely States legally free to accede to either dominion or remain independent—a vacuum filled by the Instruments of Accession negotiated by the States Department under Patel and Menon. Section 8 empowered the Constituent Assembly of each dominion to function as its sovereign legislature with unlimited power to make laws, including laws amending the Act itself. This legislative sovereignty was exercised on 14–15 August 1947 when the Assembly adopted the Independence Act (Amendment) Act, removing the Governor-General's reserve powers and vesting all executive authority in the Council of Ministers.

The Act's repeal and savings provisions (Section 18 and Schedule) abolished the office of Secretary of State for India, transferred his functions to the Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations, and continued the Government of India Act 1935 as the interim constitution of each dominion subject to such omissions, additions, adaptations, and modifications as the Governor-General might by order specify. The India (Provisional Constitution) Order 1947, issued by the Governor-General on 14 August 1947, made 57 such adaptations, notably deleting the federal provisions that required princely state participation (which never materialised) and converting the central legislature into a unicameral sovereign body. The Act also contained the territorial definition of the new dominions by reference to the Radcliffe Award (published 17 August 1947), though the Award itself was not annexed to the Act. Critically, the Act did not confer sovereignty on the Constituent Assembly; it recognised the Assembly's inherent sovereign character derived from the political fact of the transfer of power. This distinction—statutory recognition versus statutory grant—was central to the Supreme Court's reasoning in Re: Berubari Union (1960) and Kesavananda Bharati (1973), where the Court held that the Constitution's authority rests on the political sovereignty of the people exercised through the Assembly, not on the British Parliament's enactment. The Act itself was repealed by Article 395 of the Constitution on 26 January 1950, completing the legal autochthony of the Indian Republic.

Examiner's Trap: Source of Constitutional Authority
A question asks: "The Indian Independence Act 1947 is the legal source of the Constitution of India." True or False? Explain with reference to the concept of constitutional autochthony.
False. The Indian Independence Act 1947 provided the external legal recognition of the transfer of power and enabled the Constituent Assembly to function as a sovereign legislature, but it did not confer sovereignty on the Assembly or the Constitution. The Constitution derives its authority from the political sovereignty of "We the People of India" exercised through the Constituent Assembly, as declared in the Preamble. This is the doctrine of constitutional autochthony (self-originated legitimacy): the Constitution is not a gift of the British Parliament but an autochthonous document whose legal validity rests on its own acceptance by the people, not on the statute that preceded it. The Supreme Court affirmed this in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), holding that the basic structure doctrine flows from the Constitution's intrinsic supremacy, not from the Independence Act. The Independence Act was itself repealed by Article 395, severing the last formal legal link to British sovereignty.
Exam-Day Strategy: Distinguishing Legal Continuity from Political Sovereignty
When a question contrasts the Government of India Act 1935, the Indian Independence Act 1947, and the Constitution of India, map them on two axes: (1) Legal continuity (what statutes remained in force, what was repealed, what was adapted via the Provisional Constitution Order) and (2) Political sovereignty (where ultimate authority resided). The 1935 Act provided the administrative machinery (75% of constitutional provisions); the 1947 Act provided the international legal personality and legislative sovereignty to the Assembly; the Constitution provided the autochthonous grundnorm. Examiners often test whether you conflate the 1947 Act's recognition of sovereignty with the grant of sovereignty. Remember: the Constituent Assembly declared itself sovereign on 9 December 1946 (before the 1947 Act), and the 1947 Act merely recognised that fact for international law purposes.

The Constituent Assembly's Dual Role: Constitution-Making Body and Provisional Parliament

From 9 December 1946 to 26 January 1950, the Constituent Assembly performed a historically unique dual function: it drafted the Constitution while simultaneously serving as the sovereign legislature of the Dominion of India. This duality was formalised by the Indian Independence Act 1947, Section 8, which declared that the Assembly "shall have power to make laws for the Dominion... including laws amending this Act." The Assembly's first sitting as a legislative body occurred on 14 August 1947, when it passed the Independence Act (Amendment) Act and the Government of India (Amendment) Act, stripping the Governor-General of his special responsibilities and reserve powers under the 1935 Act. Between August 1947 and January 1950, the Assembly enacted over 100 statutes, including the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, the Minimum Wages Act 1948, the Factories (Amendment) Act 1948, and the Representation of the People Act 1950 (which provided the electoral framework for the first general elections). The legislative business was conducted under the Provisional Standing Orders adopted on 20 July 1947, which provided for a Speaker (G. V. Mavalankar), a Deputy Speaker, and a Business Advisory Committee.

The procedural separation of the two roles was managed through a convention: the Assembly sat as a constitution-making body in the morning (10 am–1 pm) and as the Dominion Legislature in the afternoon (2 pm–6 pm). However, this separation was not rigid; constitutional debates often spilled into legislative sessions, and the same members voted in both capacities. The Drafting Committee, appointed on 29 August 1947, worked alongside the Assembly's legislative committees. The dual role created a unique constitutional moment: the body that was writing the fundamental law was simultaneously making ordinary law under the very framework it was replacing. This meant that statutes passed by the Assembly as Dominion Legislature—such as the Preventive Detention Act 1950 (passed 26 January 1950, hours before the Constitution commenced)—became the first laws of the Republic, subject to the fundamental rights they had just enacted. The Assembly's final session as a legislature was on 24 January 1950; two days later, it transformed into the Provisional Parliament of India under Article 379, continuing until the first elected Lok Sabha was constituted in April 1952. This seamless transition—Constituent Assembly → Dominion Legislature → Provisional Parliament → Elected Parliament—ensured legislative continuity without a single day of governance vacuum, a feat unmatched in comparative constitutional history.

Constitutional Autochthony and the Break from Legal Continuity

The concept of constitutional autochthony—a constitution's legitimacy deriving from its own soil rather than an external sovereign—was the theoretical achievement of the Indian Constitution's commencement on 26 January 1950. The Government of India Act 1935 derived its authority from the British Parliament; the Indian Independence Act 1947 derived its authority from the same source. The Constitution of India, by contrast, was enacted by the Constituent Assembly in the name of "We the People of India" and contained its own commencement and repeal clause (Article 395) that abolished the Independence Act and the 1935 Act ab initio for the territory of India. This was not mere repeal; it was a legal revolution in Kelsenian terms: the grundnorm shifted from "the British Parliament's will is supreme" to "the Constitution of India is supreme." The Assembly achieved this through three deliberate textual strategies. First, the Preamble declares the Constitution is "adopted, enacted, and given to ourselves"—a performative utterance that constitutes the people as the sovereign author. Second, Article 395 repeals the Independence Act and the 1935 Act without a savings clause preserving their validity for past actions; instead, Article 394 and the Repealing and Amending Act 1950 validated all laws made under the repealed Acts, grounding their validity in the new Constitution's transitional provisions, not in the old Acts' continuing force. Third, the Constitution contains its own amendment formula (Article 368) that does not require royal assent or British parliamentary approval—a complete break from the 1935 Act's amendment procedure which required His Majesty's assent.

The Supreme Court crystallised this autochthony in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), where Chief Justice Sikri observed that the Constitution "owes its validity to the sovereign will of the people" and not to the Indian Independence Act. In State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977), the Court held that the Constitution is "the source of all legal authority in India" and that the Independence Act "was only a formal recognition by the British Parliament of the accomplished fact of the transfer of power." The practical consequence is that no Indian court can question the Constitution's validity on the ground that the Constituent Assembly lacked competence under the Independence Act; the Assembly's competence was political and inherent, not statutory and delegated. This distinguishes India from Pakistan, where the 1956 Constitution was enacted by the Constituent Assembly under the Independence Act and the Objectives Resolution, and where the Supreme Court in State v. Dosso (1958) applied Kelsen's revolution theory to validate a military coup—precisely because Pakistan's constitutional chain retained a link to the British Crown until 1956. India severed that link on 26 January 1950.

The Citizenship Debates in the Constituent Assembly: Partition, Migration, and the Definition of the Political Community

The Constitution's citizenship provisions (Articles 5–11, Part II) were drafted under the shadow of Partition, the largest forced migration in history, and the Constituent Assembly's citizenship debates reveal a deliberate choice of jus soli tempered by temporal cut-offs rather than a pure jus sanguinis or religious criterion. Article 5 conferred citizenship at commencement (26 January 1950) on every person who had domicile in the territory of India and fulfilled one of three conditions: (a) born in India; (b) either parent born in India; (c) ordinarily resident in India for five years immediately preceding commencement. The domicile requirement—a common law concept requiring both residence and intention to remain permanently—was inserted on the Drafting Committee's recommendation to prevent "citizenship by accident of birth" for those with no real connection to India. Articles 6 and 7 addressed the Partition migrants: Article 6 granted citizenship to persons who migrated from Pakistan before 19 July 1948 (the permit system date) if they or their parents/grandparents were born in undivided India, provided they had resided in India since migration; those migrating after 19 July 1948 required a permit for resettlement or permanent return issued by the Dominion Government. Article 7 denied citizenship to those who migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947, unless they returned under a permit for resettlement—a provision reflecting the political judgment that migration to Pakistan constituted a voluntary choice of allegiance.

The most contentious debate centred on Article 8 (overseas Indians) and Article 9 (voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship). Article 8 allowed persons of Indian origin residing abroad to register as citizens at Indian consulates, a provision championed by Nehru to maintain ties with the diaspora in East Africa, Southeast Asia, and the Caribbean. Article 9 provided that no person shall be a citizen of India if he has voluntarily acquired the citizenship of any foreign state—a strict single-citizenship rule that contrasted with the Commonwealth citizenship model. The Citizenship Act 1955, enacted under Article 11 (Parliament's plenary power over citizenship), operationalised these provisions and introduced citizenship by descent, registration, and naturalisation. The 1955 Act has been amended six times (1986, 1992, 2003, 2005, 2015, 2019), each amendment reflecting shifting political conceptions of the national community: the 1986 Amendment restricted jus soli by requiring one parent to be an Indian citizen; the 2003 Amendment introduced Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) as a form of dual nationality without political rights; the 2019 Amendment (CAA) created a religion-based fast-track for persecuted minorities from three neighbouring countries, sparking the first direct constitutional challenge to the secular basis of citizenship. The Constituent Assembly's original design—secular, domicile-based, with temporal Partition cut-offs—thus remains the baseline against which every subsequent amendment is measured for conformity with the basic structure of the political community envisioned in 1949.

  • Trap: Confusing the Cabinet Mission Plan's grouping formula (Sections A, B, C) with the final federal structure; the Plan's compulsory grouping was rejected, and the Constitution adopted a Union of States with no group tier.
  • Trap: Stating the Indian Independence Act 1947 "granted" independence or sovereignty; it recognised the transfer of power and enabled the Constituent Assembly's legislative sovereignty, but sovereignty originated from the political fact of the Assembly's constituent authority.
  • Trap: Believing the Constituent Assembly ceased to exist on 26 January 1950; it continued as the Provisional Parliament under Article 379 until the first Lok Sabha was constituted in April 1952.
  • Trap: Assuming constitutional autochthony means the Constitution has no historical antecedents; it means the legal validity of the Constitution rests on its own authority, not on a prior imperial statute, even though 75% of its provisions were borrowed from the 1935 Act.
  • Trap: Treating Article 5 citizenship as pure jus soli; it requires domicile (residence + intention to remain), not mere birth on soil, and the five-year residence alternative applies only to those not born in India and whose parents were not born in India.
  • Trap: Thinking Article 9's bar on dual citizenship applies to OCI cardholders; OCI is a statutory category created by the 2003 Amendment to the Citizenship Act 1955, not constitutional citizenship, and OCI holders are explicitly not citizens under Article 9.
  • Trap: Conflating the Radcliffe Award (boundary demarcation) with the Indian Independence Act (legal transfer); the Award was published two days after independence and was not annexed to the Act, leading to the anomalous situation where the Act defined the new dominions by reference to boundaries not yet known.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee on the Distribution of Legislative Powers and Its Impact on the Seventh Schedule

The Union Powers Committee, chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru, and the Provincial Constitution Committee, chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, were the two principal bodies that shaped the division of legislative subjects between the Centre and the States. Their reports, submitted in 1947 and 1948 respectively, recommended a three‑fold classification — Union List, State List, and Concurrent List — that was largely adopted in the Seventh Schedule. The Union Powers Committee favoured a strong Centre, arguing that defence, foreign affairs, currency, and communications required exclusive central control to preserve national unity. The Provincial Constitution Committee, while accepting a dominant Union, insisted on a robust State List covering police, public health, agriculture, and local government to protect regional autonomy.

The Drafting Committee, under B. R. Ambedkar, refined these recommendations by adding residuary powers to the Union (Article 248) and by inserting a Concurrent List that allowed both Parliament and State Legislatures to legislate on subjects such as criminal law, marriage, and bankruptcy. The Committee also introduced the doctrine of repugnancy (Article 254) to resolve conflicts, stipulating that central law prevails unless the State law receives Presidential assent. The final Schedule contained 97 Union entries, 66 State entries, and 47 Concurrent entries, a configuration that has been amended only a handful of times — notably the 42nd Amendment (1976) which transferred five subjects from State to Concurrent List, and the 101st Amendment (2016) which inserted Goods and Services Tax entries.

Judicial interpretation has further calibrated the balance. In State of West Bengal v. Union of India (1963) the Supreme Court held that the Union’s residuary power is not unlimited; it cannot be used to encroach on matters expressly assigned to the States. Later, in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Court emphasized that the federal structure is a basic feature, limiting the Centre’s ability to reorganise State boundaries without constitutional amendment. These rulings illustrate how the original committee recommendations continue to be mediated through constitutional jurisprudence.

The practical impact of the Seventh Schedule is evident in everyday governance: the Union’s exclusive control over inter‑state trade (Entry 33, Union List) enables a common market, while the State’s authority over police (Entry 1, State List) preserves law‑and‑order autonomy. The Concurrent List’s shared jurisdiction over education (Entry 25) has produced a layered policy framework where central schemes like the Right to Education Act coexist with State‑level curricula. Understanding the committee deliberations therefore provides the historical lens through which current Centre‑State legislative disputes are analysed.

The Constitutional Design of the Electoral College for the President and Vice‑President

Articles 54 to 58 of the Constitution establish an indirect election for the President and Vice‑President through an Electoral College composed of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the Legislative Assemblies of the States (including the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the Union Territory of Puducherry). The value of each vote is calculated to ensure parity between the Union and the States: the total value of votes of all elected MPs equals the total value of votes of all elected MLAs. The formula for an MLA’s vote value is the State’s population (as per the 1971 Census) divided by the number of elected MLAs, further divided by 1,000; an MP’s vote value is the total value of all MLA votes divided by the total number of elected MPs.

The system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote (STV) is mandated for both elections (Article 55). This method allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference, ensuring that the winner secures a quota of votes rather than a simple majority. The quota is determined by the Droop formula: total valid votes divided by (number of seats + 1) plus one. For the President, the seat count is one, so the quota is half the total valid votes plus one. The Vice‑President’s election follows the same STV principle but the Electoral College consists only of MPs (both elected and nominated), reflecting the Vice‑President’s role as ex‑officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

Key judicial pronouncements have clarified procedural aspects. In N. P. Ponnuswami v. Returning Officer (1952) the Supreme Court held that the Election Commission’s decision on the validity of a nomination is final and not subject to judicial review except on grounds of mala fides. In K. K. Verma v. Union of India (1972) the Court ruled that the President’s election cannot be challenged on the ground that a member of the Electoral College was disqualified after the poll, reinforcing the finality of the electoral process. The 70th Amendment (1992) extended the Electoral College to include the Legislative Assemblies of the Union Territories of Delhi and Puducherry, aligning their representation with the principle of federal parity.

Political dynamics often influence the composition of the Electoral College. Since the President is elected by a body dominated by the ruling party at the Centre and in major States, the outcome frequently reflects the executive’s preference. However, the STV system and the requirement of a quota have occasionally produced consensus candidates, as seen in the elections of Dr. A. P. J. Abdul Kalam (2002) and Ram Nath Kovind (2017). The Vice‑President’s election, being confined to Parliament, has historically been less contentious, with most incumbents elected unopposed or with overwhelming majorities.

Worked Example: Calculating Vote Value
A State has a population of 8,00,00,000 (1971 Census) and 200 elected MLAs. The total number of elected MPs is 776. Compute the vote value of an MLA and an MP.
MLA vote value = (8,00,00,000 ÷ 200) ÷ 1,000 = 4,000. Total MLA vote value = 4,000 × 200 = 8,00,000. MP vote value = 8,00,000 ÷ 776 ≈ 1,031 (rounded to nearest integer).
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the two‑step vote‑value formula and the Droop quota; they appear in both polity and quantitative aptitude sections. Practice one numerical example each for MLA and MP values to avoid arithmetic errors under time pressure.

The Role of the Preamble in Judicial Interpretation: From Berubari to Kesavananda

The Preamble’s legal status has evolved through a series of landmark judgments. In the Berubari Union Case (1960), the Supreme Court held that the Preamble is not a source of substantive power nor a limitation on legislative competence; it merely indicates the general purposes of the Constitution. The Court treated it as a “key to open the mind of the makers” but not enforceable in itself. This position shifted dramatically in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), where a 13‑judge bench declared that the Preamble forms part of the basic structure of the Constitution. The majority reasoned that the Preamble embodies the sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic ideals that cannot be amended out of existence.

Subsequent jurisprudence has used the Preamble as an interpretive aid. In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Court invoked the Preamble’s “secular” character to strike down the dismissal of State governments on religious grounds. In Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980), the Preamble’s “socialist” and “democratic” objectives were cited to limit Parliament’s amending power under Article 368. The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted the words “Socialist”, “Secular”, and “Integrity” into the Preamble, a move that the Court later treated as declaratory of the existing basic structure rather than a substantive alteration.

The Preamble also guides the construction of Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles. In Unni Krishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993), the Court read the right to education into Article 21 by referencing the Preamble’s promise of “justice, social, economic and political”. Similarly, the “fraternity” clause has been employed in cases concerning affirmative action and minority rights, reinforcing the Constitution’s transformative vision. The Preamble’s enforceability remains limited — it cannot be directly invoked to invalidate a statute — but its normative force shapes the doctrinal contours of constitutional review.

For aspirants, the trajectory from Berubari to Kesavananda illustrates a core exam theme: the shift from a textualist to a purposive approach in constitutional interpretation. Questions often ask whether the Preamble can be amended; the correct answer is that while the Preamble can be formally amended (as in 1976), its basic features are immune under the basic structure doctrine. Understanding this nuance distinguishes a high‑scoring answer from a superficial one.

The Procedure and Political Dynamics of Constitutional Amendments under Article 368

Article 368 prescribes three tiers of amendment procedures. A simple majority of each House of Parliament suffices for amendments that do not affect the federal structure — such as changes to the composition of the Supreme Court or the creation of new States (Article 3). Most amendments, however, require a special majority: a majority of the total membership of each House and a two‑thirds majority of members present and voting. This tier covers alterations to Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles, and the distribution of legislative powers.

The third tier adds a ratification requirement: if an amendment modifies provisions relating to the federal scheme — specifically the election of the President (Articles 54, 55), the extent of executive power of the Union and States (Articles 73, 162), the Supreme Court and High Courts (Articles 124‑147, 214‑231), the distribution of legislative powers (Seventh Schedule), or representation of States in Parliament (Articles 80, 81) — it must be ratified by the Legislatures of not less than one‑half of the States. The 42nd Amendment (1976) and the 101st Amendment (2016) both passed through this rigorous route.

Judicial review of the amendment process itself was affirmed in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and reinforced in Minerva Mills (1980), where the Court held that Parliament cannot use its constituent power to destroy the Constitution’s basic structure. The 42nd Amendment attempted to curtail judicial review by inserting Articles 31C and 368(4)‑(5), but the Supreme Court struck down those clauses in Minerva Mills, reasserting that the basic structure doctrine applies to the amendment power. The 44th Amendment (1978) subsequently restored several pre‑42nd Amendment provisions, illustrating the political pendulum between executive dominance and judicial guardianship.

Political dynamics heavily influence amendment outcomes. The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) achieved broad consensus because they empowered local self‑government, a goal supported across party lines. Conversely, the 42nd Amendment was pushed through during Emergency, reflecting a concentration of power. The 101st Amendment (GST) required extensive negotiation with States, culminating in a constitutional guarantee of compensation for revenue loss — a rare instance where fiscal federalism was constitutionally entrenched. Aspirants should note that the amendment procedure is not merely mechanical; it reflects the interplay of federal bargaining, judicial oversight, and political will.

The Concept of Constitutional Autochthony and Its Relevance to Indian Sovereignty

Constitutional autochthony denotes that a Constitution derives its legal validity from its own authority rather than from an antecedent imperial statute. In the Indian context, the Indian Independence Act 1947 transferred legislative sovereignty to the Constituent Assembly, but the Assembly’s own resolution of 26 November 1949 declared the Constitution “adopted, enacted and given to ourselves”. This self‑referential enactment severed the chain of legal continuity with the British Parliament, establishing the Constitution as the ultimate source of law.

Scholars such as Granville Austin and H. M. Seervai have emphasized that autochthony is a political fact as much as a legal one. The Constituent Assembly functioned as a sovereign body after 15 August 1947, drafting the Constitution without external approval. The absence of a “royal assent” clause and the inclusion of Article 395, which repeals the Indian Independence Act and the Government of India Act 1935, symbolise this break. The Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati acknowledged autochthony implicitly by treating the Constitution’s basic structure as beyond the reach of any amendment, reinforcing the idea that the Constitution’s authority is intrinsic.

The practical relevance of autochthony surfaces in debates on constitutional supremacy versus parliamentary supremacy. Because the Constitution is autochthonous, no ordinary legislation — including a constitutional amendment — can claim legitimacy if it violates the basic structure. This principle underpins the Court’s power to strike down amendments that alter the federal balance, secular character, or democratic framework. It also informs the interpretation of Article 368: the amending power is a constituted power, not a constituent one, and therefore cannot be exercised to destroy the Constitution’s identity.

For examination purposes, autochthony is often tested through comparative questions: “How does the Indian Constitution’s autochthony differ from the Canadian Constitution’s patriation?” The answer lies in the fact that India’s Constitution was drafted and adopted by an elected Constituent Assembly before independence, whereas Canada’s Constitution Act 1982 patriated an existing British statute. Recognising this distinction demonstrates a deeper grasp of constitutional theory beyond rote memorisation of articles.

  • Confusing the Union Powers Committee’s recommendations with the final Seventh Schedule entries; the Schedule was further modified by the Drafting Committee.
  • Assuming the President’s Electoral College includes nominated members of State Legislative Assemblies; only elected MLAs participate.
  • Believing the Preamble is directly enforceable as a justiciable provision; it is an interpretive guide, not a source of independent rights.
  • Thinking any constitutional amendment requires State ratification; only amendments affecting the federal scheme need ratification by half the States.
  • Equating constitutional autochthony with the mere fact of independence; autochthony specifically means the Constitution’s legal validity rests on its own enactment, not on a prior imperial statute.
  • Overlooking that the 42nd Amendment’s insertion of “Socialist”, “Secular”, “Integrity” into the Preamble was declaratory of the basic structure, not a substantive creation of new enforceable rights.
  • Understanding these nuances prevents common misstatements in both descriptive and analytical answers.

The President’s Legislative Role: Assent, Pocket Veto, and the Constitutional Requirement of Parliamentary Approval for Ordinances

Article 111 of the Constitution governs the President’s assent to Bills passed by Parliament. The President may give assent, withhold assent, or return a Bill (other than a Money Bill) for reconsideration. If Parliament passes the Bill again, with or without amendments, the President is constitutionally bound to give assent. This mandatory assent after reconsideration eliminates any effective pocket veto; the President cannot indefinitely withhold assent once the legislature has reaffirmed its will. The 24th Amendment (1971) made it explicit that the President shall give assent to Constitution Amendment Bills, removing any discretionary power in that category.

Ordinance‑making power under Article 123 enables the President to legislate when either House of Parliament is not in session and immediate action is necessary. The ordinance has the same force as an Act of Parliament but must be laid before both Houses within six weeks of their reassembly. If not approved, it ceases to operate. The Supreme Court in R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) held that an ordinance is subject to judicial review on the same grounds as an Act. In D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987) the Court struck down the practice of repromulgating ordinances without legislative approval, calling it a “fraud on the Constitution.” The 2017 judgment in Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar reiterated that ordinance‑making is an emergency power, not a parallel legislative authority, and that the executive must place the ordinance before the legislature at the earliest opportunity.

The 44th Amendment (1978) inserted a proviso to Article 123 requiring that an ordinance shall cease to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament unless a resolution disapproving it is passed by both Houses. This provision was intended to curb executive overreach during the Emergency period. The President’s role in the legislative process is therefore circumscribed by both textual mandates and judicial doctrine: assent is largely ceremonial for ordinary Bills, mandatory for Constitution Amendment Bills, and the ordinance route is hedged with strict temporal and procedural safeguards.

The Constitutional Position of the Attorney General and Solicitor General: Powers, Duties, and Judicial Interpretation

Article 76 establishes the office of the Attorney General for India. The President appoints a person qualified to be a Supreme Court judge; the Attorney General holds office during the pleasure of the President and receives such remuneration as Parliament may determine. The Attorney General’s duties include giving advice to the Government of India on legal matters, performing other legal duties assigned by the President, and discharging functions conferred by the Constitution or any law. The Attorney General has the right of audience in all courts in India and may participate in the proceedings of either House of Parliament without a vote.

The Solicitor General is not a constitutional functionary. The post is created under the Law Officers (Conditions of Service) Act, 1972, and the appointment is made by the President on the advice of the Council of Ministers. The Solicitor General assists the Attorney General and represents the Union in courts, but lacks the constitutional tenure and the right to address Parliament. The distinction is significant: the Attorney General’s advice is protected by the doctrine of legal professional privilege, whereas the Solicitor General’s opinions do not enjoy the same constitutional shield.

Judicial pronouncements have clarified the scope of the Attorney General’s role. In In re: Attorney General (1975) the Supreme Court held that the Attorney General is not a member of the Cabinet and must maintain independence while advising the executive. In State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) the Court affirmed that the Attorney General’s opinion is not binding on the President but carries persuasive weight. More recently, the controversy surrounding the Attorney General’s advice on the 2020 farm‑law ordinances highlighted the tension between political accountability and constitutional duty. The Court in K. K. Venugopal v. Union of India (2019) emphasized that the Attorney General must not act as a mere mouthpiece of the ruling party.

Technique: Identifying Constitutional vs Statutory Offices
Question: “Which of the following statements about the Attorney General and the Solicitor General is correct? (a) Both are constitutional authorities under Article 76. (b) The Solicitor General enjoys the right of audience in all courts by virtue of the Constitution. (c) The Attorney General holds office during the pleasure of the President; the Solicitor General is appointed under a statute. (d) The Attorney General can vote in Parliament.”
Solution: Statement (c) is correct. Article 76 creates the Attorney General as a constitutional office, tenure during the President’s pleasure. The Solicitor General is appointed under the Law Officers (Conditions of Service) Act, 1972, a statutory provision. The Attorney General has the right of audience in all courts (Art. 76(3)) but cannot vote in Parliament (Art. 88). The Solicitor General’s right of audience derives from the same Act, not the Constitution. Therefore, (c) alone is accurate.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question contrasts constitutional and statutory law officers, first locate the constitutional article (Art. 76 for Attorney General, Art. 165 for Advocate General). Any office not mentioned in the Constitution is statutory. Remember the Attorney General’s unique right to speak in Parliament without voting; this is a frequent distractor.

The Uniform Civil Code Debate in the Constituent Assembly: Historical Context and Constitutional Provisions

Article 44 of the Directive Principles of State Policy directs the State to endeavour to secure a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) throughout the territory of India. The debate in the Constituent Assembly reflected deep divisions. Members such as K.M. Munshi and Rajkumari Amrit Kaur argued that a common civil code was essential for national integration and gender justice. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, while personally favouring a UCC, cautioned that the time was not ripe because of the strong opposition from Muslim members like Mohammad Ismail and B. Pocker Bahadur, who viewed personal law as an integral part of religious identity protected by Article 25.

The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities, chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, recommended that the UCC be placed in the Directive Principles rather than the Fundamental Rights chapter, making it non‑justiciable. The Assembly adopted this recommendation, and Article 44 was inserted as a aspirational goal. The Hindu Code Bills (1951‑1956) enacted by Parliament under Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru and Law Minister Ambedkar reformed Hindu personal law on marriage, succession, adoption and maintenance, but left Muslim, Christian, Parsi and Jewish personal laws untouched.

Judicial nudges toward a UCC began with Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985), where the Supreme Court held that a divorced Muslim woman was entitled to maintenance under Section 125 CrPC, and urged Parliament to enact a UCC. The political backlash led to the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, which diluted the judgment. In Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) and John Vallamattom v. Union of India (2003), the Court reiterated the need for a UCC to prevent conflict of laws. The 2019 Shayara Bano v. Union of India judgment struck down instant triple talaq but stopped short of mandating a UCC. The 22nd Law Commission (2023) recommended a phased approach, beginning with optional uniform provisions in marriage and divorce.

Environmental Protection in the Constitution: Articles 48A, 51A(g), and Judicial Expansion of the Right to a Healthy Environment

The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted Article 48A, obligating the State to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard forests and wildlife. Simultaneously, Article 51A(g) was added as a fundamental duty of every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment. Though Directive Principles and fundamental duties are non‑justiciable, the Supreme Court has read them into the fundamental right to life under Article 21.

In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) (the Oleum gas leak case), the Court evolved the doctrine of absolute liability for hazardous industries, holding that enterprises engaged in inherently dangerous activities are strictly liable for any harm. In Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) the Court recognised the principle of sustainable development and the precautionary principle as part of Indian environmental jurisprudence. Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991) declared that the right to clean water is a facet of Article 21. Virender Gaur v. State of Haryana (1995) extended this to a right to a healthy environment. The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, created a specialised forum for expeditious disposal of environmental cases, giving statutory teeth to the constitutional mandate.

The Doctrine of Judicial Review of Ordinances: Constitutional Limits and Landmark Judgments

Article 123 (President) and Article 213 (Governor) empower the executive to promulgate ordinances when the legislature is not in session and immediate action is required. The Constitution imposes three core limits: (1) the ordinance must be necessitated by circumstances requiring immediate action; (2) it must be laid before the legislature within six weeks of reassembly; (3) it ceases to operate if disapproved by both Houses or if not replaced by an Act within the prescribed period.

The Supreme Court in R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) held that the satisfaction of the President is justiciable and that an ordinance can be challenged on grounds of mala fide or colourable exercise of power. In D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987) the Court condemned the practice of repromulgating ordinances without legislative approval, stating that it subverts the legislative process. The 2017 judgment in Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar reinforced that ordinance‑making is an emergency power, not a parallel legislative authority, and that the executive must present the ordinance for legislative scrutiny at the earliest. In T. Venkata Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1985) the Court applied the same principles to Governor’s ordinances under Article 213. The 44th Amendment (1978) added the six‑week laying requirement explicitly, aiming to prevent executive overreach during the Emergency.

  • Confusing the President’s mandatory assent to Constitution Amendment Bills (Art. 368 post‑24th Amendment) with discretionary assent to ordinary Bills.
  • Assuming the Solicitor General is a constitutional authority; the office is purely statutory under the Law Officers Act, 1972.
  • Treating Article 44 (UCC) as a justiciable right; it remains a Directive Principle and cannot be enforced by courts.
  • Believing that Articles 48A and 51A(g) directly create enforceable environmental rights; they are non‑justiciable but have been read into Article 21 by the Supreme Court.
  • Thinking that an ordinance automatically lapses after six weeks regardless of legislative action; it lapses only if not approved or if a disapproval resolution is passed.
  • Overlooking that the Attorney General’s advice is protected by legal professional privilege, whereas the Solicitor General’s opinions lack constitutional privilege.
  • Misreading the 44th Amendment as removing the President’s power to return a Bill for reconsideration; it only removed discretion over Constitution Amendment Bills.

The Constituent Assembly's Steering Committee and the Finalisation of the Constitutional Text

Composition and Mandate

The Steering Committee was constituted on 11 December 1946, a day after the Constituent Assembly's first sitting. It was chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad in his capacity as President of the Assembly and comprised the chairmen of all principal committees — including the Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar), the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights (Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel), the Union Powers Committee (Jawaharlal Nehru), the Provincial Constitution Committee (Sardar Patel), and the Rules of Procedure Committee (Dr. Rajendra Prasad). The Committee's mandate was to coordinate the work of the various sub‑committees, set the Assembly's agenda, allocate time for debates, and ensure that the drafting process adhered to the timetable adopted on 20 July 1947.

Operational Role

The Steering Committee met 23 times between December 1946 and November 1949. Its minutes reveal that it resolved procedural deadlocks — such as the dispute over the representation of princely states in the Union Powers Committee — and approved the final schedule for the clause‑by‑clause consideration of the Draft Constitution. On 14 November 1949, the Committee recommended that the Assembly adopt the Constitution on 26 November 1949, a date chosen to coincide with the anniversary of the 1929 Lahore Session of the Indian National Congress where the demand for Purna Swaraj was made.

Impact on the Final Text

Because the Steering Committee controlled the flow of amendments, it indirectly shaped the constitutional text. For instance, it limited the number of amendments to the Draft Constitution's federal provisions to 120, forcing members to consolidate their proposals. This discipline contributed to the relatively concise final document of 395 articles and 8 schedules. The Committee also ensured that the Preamble, as amended by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, would be placed before the operative parts, reinforcing its interpretive primacy.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee on the Rules of Procedure and Its Impact on Drafting Discipline

Formation and Leadership

The Rules of Procedure Committee was constituted on 13 December 1946 under the chairmanship of Dr. Rajendra Prasad. Its members included H.V. Kamath, K.M. Munshi, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, and B.N. Rau (as Constitutional Adviser). The Committee's task was to draft the standing orders that would govern the Assembly's debates, voting procedures, committee references, and the handling of amendments.

Key Rules Adopted

The Committee produced the Constituent Assembly Rules of Procedure, adopted on 20 January 1947. Notable rules included: (1) Rule 38 — requiring a minimum of 30 members to constitute a quorum; (2) Rule 45 — limiting each member to two speeches on any clause unless the Chair permitted otherwise; (3) Rule 57 — mandating that amendments be submitted in writing 48 hours before the clause was taken up; and (4) Rule 62 — providing for a "guillotine" motion to cut off debate after a prescribed number of sittings. These rules were modelled on the Government of India Act 1935's legislative procedure but tightened to suit a constitution‑making body.

Effect on Drafting Efficiency

The 48‑hour notice rule forced members to prepare amendments in advance, reducing last‑minute surprises. The guillotine provision was invoked only once — on 16 October 1949 — to conclude the debate on the federal structure after 12 sittings. The two‑speech limit prevented filibustering; the Assembly completed the clause‑by‑clause reading of 395 articles in 165 sittings, a pace unmatched by any other constituent assembly of the era. The Rules Committee also introduced a system of "starred" and "unstarred" questions for the President, ensuring executive accountability even before the Constitution came into force.

Technique: Tracing Committee Influence on Constitutional Provisions
A question asks: "Which committee's procedural rule directly limited the number of speeches per member during the clause‑by‑clause stage, and how did this affect the final constitutional text?"
The Rules of Procedure Committee, through Rule 45, capped each member at two speeches per clause unless the Chair allowed more. This restriction curbed prolonged debates, enabling the Assembly to process 395 articles in 165 sittings. The resulting discipline meant that contentious provisions — such as the emergency articles (352, 356, 360) — were debated within a fixed timeframe, producing a more compact text with fewer qualifying clauses than originally proposed.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question references a specific rule number (e.g., Rule 45, Rule 57), immediately associate it with the Rules of Procedure Committee. Memorise the four key rules (quorum, speech limit, amendment notice, guillotine) and their practical outcomes. This allows you to answer both factual and analytical parts without re‑reading the entire procedural history.

The Debate on Fundamental Duties: The 42nd Amendment, Judicial Reception, and Contemporary Relevance

Origins and Legislative History

The idea of fundamental duties was first mooted by the Swaran Singh Committee (1976), which recommended a set of ten duties to balance the expansive fundamental rights. The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted Part IVA (Article 51A) containing ten duties, including respect for the Constitution, the national flag, and the national anthem; promotion of harmony; protection of public property; and the duty to develop scientific temper. The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 added an eleventh duty — to provide opportunities for education to children between six and fourteen years — linking it to the newly inserted Article 21A (Right to Education).

Parliamentary Debate

During the debate on the 42nd Amendment, members such as Hiren Mukherjee and Piloo Mody warned that duties could be used to curtail rights. The government, led by Law Minister H.R. Gokhale, argued that duties were moral exhortations, not legally enforceable obligations. The amendment passed with a two‑thirds majority in both Houses, reflecting the Emergency‑era political consensus.

Judicial Reception

The Supreme Court has consistently held that fundamental duties are non‑justiciable. In Chandra Bhavan Boarding & Lodging v. State of Mysore (1970) — a pre‑duties case — the Court stated that directives and duties are not enforceable. Post‑1976, in AIIMS Students Union v. AIIMS (2001), the Court observed that Article 51A can be used as an interpretive tool to resolve ambiguities in fundamental rights. In Javed v. State of Haryana (2003), the Court upheld a service rule disqualifying candidates with more than two children, citing the duty to promote family welfare under Article 51A(j). The Court clarified that duties do not create a cause of action but inform the scope of rights.

Contemporary Relevance

Recent jurisprudence, such as Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) (decriminalising adultery), referenced the duty to renounce practices derogatory to women's dignity (Article 51A(e)). The 2020 National Education Policy explicitly links curriculum design to the duty to develop scientific temper (Article 51A(h)). While still non‑justiciable, fundamental duties now function as a constitutional benchmark for legislative and executive action.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on Emergency Provisions: Articles 352, 356, and 360

Background and Drafting

The emergency provisions were debated in the Union Powers Committee (chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru) and later in the full Assembly between July and October 1949. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar presented the draft articles, emphasising that emergency powers were borrowed from the Government of India Act 1935 (Sections 93 and 102) and the Weimar Constitution. The three categories — National Emergency (Art. 352), President's Rule in States (Art. 356), and Financial Emergency (Art. 360) — were designed to address distinct crises.

Key Speeches and Concerns

Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar warned that Article 356 could become a tool for central domination over states. K.M. Munshi proposed a requirement that the President's proclamation under Article 356 be approved by Parliament within two months, a safeguard later incorporated. H.V. Kamath moved an amendment to subject Article 352 proclamations to judicial review, but it was negatived; the Assembly relied on the political check of parliamentary approval. Dr. Ambedkar defended the breadth of Article 360, arguing that financial stability of the Union justified central control over state finances during a crisis.

Voting Outcomes

Article 352 was adopted with 173 votes in favour, 12 against. Article 356 passed 165 to 18 after the two‑month parliamentary approval clause was accepted. Article 360 was adopted without a division, reflecting broad consensus on the need for a financial emergency mechanism. The debates reveal a deliberate choice to keep emergency powers broad but subject to legislative oversight, a balance later tested in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) where the Supreme Court imposed strict judicial scrutiny on Article 356 proclamations.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee on the Judiciary and the Architecture of Judicial Independence

Composition and Terms of Reference

The Committee on the Judiciary was constituted on 24 January 1947 under the chairmanship of Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar. Its members included B.N. Rau, K.M. Munshi, M.R. Jayakar, and T.T. Krishnamachari. The Committee was tasked with designing the structure, jurisdiction, appointment process, and conditions of service for the Supreme Court and High Courts, ensuring independence from executive influence.

Major Recommendations

The Committee recommended: (1) a Supreme Court with a Chief Justice and up to seven puisne judges (later increased to 30 by the 2008 amendment); (2) appointment of judges by the President after consultation with the Chief Justice of India — a formulation that evolved into the collegium system; (3) security of tenure until age 65 for Supreme Court judges and 62 for High Court judges; (4) removal only by impeachment on proved misbehaviour or incapacity; (5) salaries and allowances charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, not subject to annual vote. These recommendations were incorporated almost verbatim into Articles 124–147.

Debates on Appointment and Transfer

During the Assembly debates, K.T. Shah advocated for a judicial appointments commission comprising the Chief Justice, the Law Minister, and two eminent jurists. The Assembly rejected this, preferring the executive‑judicial consultation model. The Committee also recommended that High Court judges could be transferred only with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of India, a principle later affirmed in Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (1993).

Legacy

The Committee's blueprint established a judiciary that is structurally independent, financially autonomous, and insulated from political pressure. Its design has withstood multiple amendment attempts — notably the 42nd Amendment's attempt to curtail judicial review, which was struck down in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980). The collegium system, though not explicitly in the original text, traces its constitutional legitimacy to the Committee's emphasis on "consultation" as a substantive check.
