  • Confusing the Steering Committee's coordinating role with the Drafting Committee's textual authorship.
  • Attributing the guillotine rule to the Drafting Committee instead of the Rules of Procedure Committee.
  • Assuming fundamental duties are justiciable because they appear in Part IVA; they remain non‑justiciable per consistent Supreme Court rulings.
  • Believing Article 356 was adopted without any parliamentary approval safeguard; the two‑month approval clause was inserted on K.M. Munshi's motion.
  • Thinking the Judiciary Committee recommended a judicial appointments commission; it favoured executive‑judicial consultation, a model later interpreted as the collegium.
  • Overlooking that the 42nd Amendment added fundamental duties during the Emergency, not as a product of the Constituent Assembly.
  • Misreading the financial emergency provision (Article 360) as having been invoked; it has never been proclaimed in Indian history.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on Citizenship and the Partition Legacy

The citizenship provisions (Articles 5‑11) were among the most contested parts of the Constitution because they had to address the massive population exchange triggered by Partition. The Assembly debated three distinct categories: persons domiciled in the territory of India on 26 January 1950 (Art. 5), persons who migrated from Pakistan before 19 July 1948 (Art. 6), and persons who migrated after that date but returned under a permit (Art. 7). B.R. Ambedkar, moving the draft, emphasised that citizenship should be based on domicile rather than religion, a principle that contrasted sharply with the communal basis of the Partition plan. Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar warned that a rigid cut‑off date would render many genuine residents stateless, while K.M. Munshi argued for a flexible “permit” system to accommodate refugees who had left after the cut‑off but wished to return. The Assembly ultimately adopted a compromise: Article 6 granted citizenship to those who migrated before 19 July 1948 and had since resided in India, while Article 7 required a permit for post‑cut‑off returnees. The debates also touched on the status of the princely states’ subjects; the Instrument of Accession was deemed sufficient to extend Indian citizenship to their populations. The Citizenship Act 1955 later operationalised these constitutional provisions, introducing acquisition by registration, naturalisation, and the controversial provision for termination of citizenship upon voluntary acquisition of a foreign nationality (Section 9). The 1986 amendment tightened the naturalisation residency requirement from five to ten years, reflecting security concerns after the Assam agitation. The 2003 amendment introduced overseas citizenship of India (OCI), a non‑voting status for the diaspora. These legislative layers illustrate how the Constituent Assembly’s original framework was designed to be adaptable, yet the core principle — domicile‑based citizenship irrespective of religion — has survived every amendment.

The Constitutional Design of the Finance Commission: Original Provisions, Amendments, and Fiscal Federalism

Article 280 mandates the President to constitute a Finance Commission every five years, or earlier if deemed necessary. The original Constitution prescribed that the Commission consist of a Chairman and four other members appointed by the President, with qualifications defined by Parliament (the Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1951). The first Commission, chaired by K.C. Neogy (1951‑56), established the template for vertical distribution (Centre‑State share) and horizontal distribution (inter‑state equity) based on population, income distance, and fiscal effort. The 7th Finance Commission (1978‑83) introduced the “income distance” criterion, giving weight to per‑capita income disparities. The 10th Commission (1995‑2000) added a “tax effort” parameter to reward states improving their own revenue mobilisation. The 14th Finance Commission (2015‑20), chaired by Y.V. Reddy, dramatically increased the States’ share of the divisible pool from 32 % to 42 %, citing the need for greater fiscal autonomy after the GST rollout. The 15th Commission (2020‑25), under N.K. Singh, retained the 41 % share but introduced performance‑based grants for health, education, and agricultural reforms. The Constitution (Eighty‑third Amendment) Act 2000 empowered Parliament to determine the qualifications of members, leading to the inclusion of experts in public finance and economics. The Finance Commission’s recommendations are advisory; however, the President’s acceptance has become a constitutional convention, and the Union Budget routinely incorporates them. The interplay with the GST Council (Article 279A) creates a dual fiscal architecture: the Council decides tax rates and exemptions, while the Commission determines the revenue‑sharing formula. This division has sparked debates on whether the Commission’s horizontal formula should account for GST compensation cess collections, a question the 15th Commission addressed by recommending a separate “GST compensation” grant until 2026.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which Finance Commission first recommended a 42 % share for States in the divisible pool, and what constitutional provision empowers the President to constitute the Commission?”
The 14th Finance Commission (2015‑20) recommended the 42 % share. Article 280 of the Constitution empowers the President to constitute the Finance Commission every five years.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the chronological order of Finance Commissions and their key recommendations (vertical share, horizontal criteria). Link each major shift (e.g., 14th Commission’s 42 % share) to the contemporaneous fiscal reform (GST). This enables quick elimination of distractors in multiple‑choice questions.

The Preamble as an Interpretive Lens: Judicial Construction of Constitutional Identity

The Preamble, though non‑justiciable in the Berubari Union case (1960), has evolved into a “key to the mind of the makers” and a guiding star for constitutional interpretation. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Supreme Court held that the Preamble forms part of the basic structure, making its objectives — justice, liberty, equality, fraternity — immune to amendment. The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted the words “Socialist”, “Secular”, and “Integrity”, and the Court in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) used the secular character of the Preamble to strike down the dismissal of a state government on religious grounds. In Union of India v. R. Gandhi (2010), the Court read the Preamble’s “fraternity” alongside Article 21 to expand the right to dignity for transgender persons. The Preamble also informs the “constitutional morality” doctrine articulated in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018), where the Court held that the Preamble’s promise of liberty and equality obliges the state to decriminalise consensual same‑sex relations. Importantly, the Preamble’s enforceability remains limited: it cannot independently ground a cause of action, but it serves as an interpretive aid for ambiguous statutory or constitutional provisions. The Court’s consistent reliance on the Preamble demonstrates its role as a constitutional identity marker, shaping the trajectory of fundamental rights, directive principles, and the basic structure doctrine.

The Constitutional Safeguards for the Anglo‑Indian Community: Articles 331, 333 and Their Repeal

Articles 331 and 333 provided for the nomination of two Anglo‑Indians to the Lok Sabha and one to each State Legislative Assembly where the community was not adequately represented. The provisions originated from the Constituent Assembly’s Advisory Committee on Minorities, chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, which recognised the community’s distinct cultural identity and its historical service in railways, telegraphs, and the armed forces. The nominations were made by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister (for Lok Sabha) and the Governor on the advice of the Chief Minister (for State Assemblies). The 104th Constitution Amendment Act 2019, passed with near‑unanimous support, omitted both Articles, ending the nomination scheme from the 2020 elections onward. The Statement of Objects and Reasons cited the community’s population decline (from roughly 300,000 in 1951 to under 150,000 in 2011) and the principle of universal adult suffrage as justification. Critics argued that the repeal removed a symbolic guarantee of minority representation without substituting an alternative mechanism. The amendment also deleted Article 334, which had provided for reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in legislatures, extending that reservation until 2030. The Anglo‑Indian repeal thus illustrates how constitutional provisions designed for specific historical contexts can be removed through the ordinary amendment process (Article 368) when the underlying demographic rationale ceases to exist.

The Role of the Constituent Assembly's Committee on the Rules of Procedure and Its Impact on Legislative Drafting

The Rules of Procedure Committee, constituted on 14 August 1947 under the chairmanship of Dr. Rajendra Prasad (President of the Assembly), drafted the procedural framework that governed the Assembly’s debates, voting, and committee system. Its report, adopted on 20 January 1948, introduced the “guillotine” rule — a time‑limit on discussion of each clause — to prevent filibustering and ensure the Constitution’s timely completion. The Committee also prescribed the formation of functional committees (e.g., Drafting Committee, Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights) and defined quorum, voting thresholds, and the procedure for amendment motions. These rules were later transplanted, with minor modifications, into the Rules of Procedure of the Provisional Parliament (1950) and subsequently into the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha rulebooks. The guillotine mechanism, in particular, has been invoked in Parliament to curtail debate on contentious bills, most notably during the passage of the Constitution (Forty‑second Amendment) Bill 1976. The Committee’s emphasis on structured debate and committee‑stage scrutiny shaped the Indian legislative tradition of detailed clause‑by‑clause examination, a practice that distinguishes Indian law‑making from the Westminster model’s more expedited readings. The procedural legacy endures: the current Lok Sabha Rules (Rule 331) still empower the Speaker to apply the guillotine, and the committee system remains the primary vehicle for legislative scrutiny.

  • Confusing the citizenship cut‑off dates (19 July 1948 vs. 26 January 1950) and misattributing the permit requirement to Article 6 instead of Article 7.
  • Assuming the Finance Commission’s recommendations are binding; they are advisory, though conventionally accepted by the President.
  • Treating the Preamble as an independent source of justiciable rights; it remains a non‑justiciable interpretive aid per Berubari and subsequent jurisprudence.
  • Believing the Anglo‑Indian nomination provisions were part of the basic structure; they were ordinary constitutional provisions repealed by the 104th Amendment.
  • Attributing the guillotine rule to the Drafting Committee rather than the Rules of Procedure Committee chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad.
  • Overlooking that the 14th Finance Commission’s 42 % vertical share was a recommendation, not a constitutional mandate, and that the 15th Commission reverted to 41 %.
  • Misreading the 42nd Amendment’s insertion of “Socialist”, “Secular”, “Integrity” as altering the Preamble’s legal enforceability; the amendment changed the text but the Preamble’s interpretive role was already established by Kesavananda.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on the Uniform Civil Code and Article 44

The Uniform Civil Code (UCC) was one of the most contested subjects in the Constituent Assembly. Article 44, placed in Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy), reads: “The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.” The phrase “endeavour to secure” signals its non‑justiciable character, a compromise reached after intense debate between members who favoured immediate codification and those who warned of communal backlash.

The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities, chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, set up a Sub‑Committee on Minority Rights (chaired by H.C. Mookherjee) which examined personal laws. Simultaneously, the Drafting Committee, under Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, prepared a clause for a UCC in the Fundamental Rights chapter. Ambedkar argued that a common civil code was essential for gender justice and national integration, citing the disparate marriage, divorce, inheritance and adoption rules governing Hindus, Muslims, Christians and Parsis.

Opposition came chiefly from Muslim members such as Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, B. Pocker Bahadur and Mohammad Ismail, who contended that personal law was an integral part of religious identity protected by Article 25. They warned that a mandatory UCC would violate the freedom of religion guarantee and alienate minorities. The Hindu members, including K.M. Munshi and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, supported a UCC but accepted a directive‑principle placement to avoid a constitutional clash.

The Assembly voted on 23 November 1948 to move the UCC from the Fundamental Rights chapter to the Directive Principles. The final text of Article 44 was adopted on 24 January 1950. The decision reflected a pragmatic “gradualist” approach: the State was obliged to endeavour, but no timeline or enforcement mechanism was prescribed. Subsequent legislative attempts — the Hindu Code Bills (1955‑56), the Special Marriage Act (1954), and the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act (1986) — illustrate the incremental path the Parliament has taken, while the Supreme Court in Shah Bano (1985) and Sarla Mudgal (1995) repeatedly urged the legislature to fulfil the Article 44 mandate.

The Constitutional Architecture of the Election Commission: Appointment, Tenure, and Removal

Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections in an Election Commission (EC) consisting of a Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and such number of other Election Commissioners as the President may fix. The original Constitution provided for a single‑member CEC; the Election Commission (Conditions of Service of Election Commissioners and Transaction of Business) Act, 1991, later amended in 1993, enabled a multi‑member body. The President appoints the CEC and other Commissioners on the advice of the Council of Ministers, but the Supreme Court in Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (2023) held that the appointment process must be insulated from executive dominance, directing Parliament to enact a law providing for a collegium comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and the Chief Justice of India.

Tenure is fixed at six years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier (Section 4 of the 1991 Act). This mirrors the tenure of a Supreme Court judge, reinforcing functional independence. Removal follows the same procedure as a Supreme Court judge: a motion of impeachment passed by a special majority in each House of Parliament on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity (Article 324(5) read with Article 124(4)). No Election Commissioner has ever been removed; the only instance of a CEC resigning under political pressure was T.N. Seshan’s voluntary resignation in 1996, which underscored the office’s moral authority.

Conditions of service — salary, allowances, pension — are determined by Parliament and cannot be varied to the disadvantage of the incumbent during tenure (Section 5 of the 1991 Act). The EC’s financial autonomy is secured by charging its expenditure on the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 324(3)). The Commission’s decision‑making is by majority vote; the CEC has no casting vote, a design intended to prevent unilateral control. The 2003 amendment (Act 21 of 2003) formalised the three‑member structure, and the 2021 amendment (Act 13 of 2021) clarified that the CEC and other Commissioners shall have equal status, pay and removal safeguards.

Judicial review of EC decisions is available under Article 32 and 226, but courts have consistently deferred to the Commission’s expertise on electoral matters, as seen in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) and Election Commission of India v. State of Tamil Nadu (2020). The institutional design thus balances executive appointment with judicial‑style tenure and removal protections, aiming to preserve electoral integrity in a politically charged environment.

Examiner's Technique: Comparative Constitutional Design
Question: Compare the appointment and removal safeguards of the Indian Election Commission with those of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG). Identify two structural similarities and one key difference.
Similarities: (1) Both are appointed by the President on the advice of the Council of Ministers. (2) Both enjoy security of tenure — removal only by impeachment (special majority in Parliament) on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. Difference: The CAG is a single‑member authority with a fixed six‑year term or age 65, whereas the Election Commission is a multi‑member body (CEC plus two Election Commissioners) where each member has the same tenure and removal protection, and decisions are taken by majority vote.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “constitutional safeguards” of an independent body, list appointment mode, tenure, removal procedure, financial autonomy, and conditions of service. Use a two‑column table (Body vs Safeguard) for quick revision; it scores high on clarity and completeness.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee on the Drafting of the Directive Principles: Socialist and Gandhian Influences

The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) in Part IV owe their shape to a dedicated Committee on the Directive Principles of State Policy, constituted on 27 April 1947 under the chairmanship of Jawaharlal Nehru. The committee comprised B.N. Rau (Constitutional Adviser), K.M. Munshi, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, and several other members representing diverse ideological strands. Its mandate was to translate the socio‑economic aspirations of the freedom movement into constitutional directives.

The committee’s report, submitted in July 1948, drew heavily on the Irish Constitution (1937) which enumerated “Directive Principles of Social Policy” as non‑justiciable guidelines. The Irish model itself was inspired by the Spanish Constitution of 1931. Indian members, however, infused two indigenous ideological currents: Gandhian and socialist. Gandhian influence appears in Articles 40 (organisation of village panchayats), 43 (living wage for workers), 46 (promotion of educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes and Tribes), and 47 (prohibition of intoxicating drinks). These reflect Gandhi’s vision of self‑sufficient village republics, trusteeship, and moral regeneration.

Socialist influence, championed by Nehru and members like K.T. Shah, is evident in Articles 38 (state to secure a social order for the promotion of welfare), 39 (certain principles of policy to be followed by the State — adequate means of livelihood, equal pay for equal work, protection of workers’ health), 41 (right to work, education and public assistance), and 42 (just and humane conditions of work). The committee explicitly rejected a justiciable “Bill of Rights” for socio‑economic claims, opting for moral suasion on the legislature and executive. The Drafting Committee, led by Ambedkar, refined the language, ensuring that the DPSP remained “fundamental in the governance of the country” (Article 37) but not enforceable by courts.

The interplay of these influences produced a hybrid charter: a set of aspirational goals that could guide legislative agendas without exposing the State to judicial compulsion. The Supreme Court in State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) affirmed the non‑justiciable nature, while later judgments such as Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) and Unni Krishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993) read certain DPSP into Fundamental Rights through the doctrine of harmonious construction, demonstrating the enduring interpretive potency of the committee’s work.

The Constituent Assembly's Debate on the Composition and Powers of the Rajya Sabha

The Council of States (Rajya Sabha) was designed as the federal chamber representing the States and Union Territories. The Constituent Assembly debated its composition, election method, and legislative powers extensively between July and October 1949. The final design, enshrined in Articles 80‑84, reflects a compromise between a pure federal council (like the US Senate) and a revising chamber (like the Canadian Senate).

Composition: The Rajya Sabha consists of not more than 250 members — 238 representatives of States and Union Territories elected by the elected members of the respective Legislative Assemblies through proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, and 12 members nominated by the President for expertise in literature, science, art and social service (Article 80). The allocation of seats among States is based on population (Fourth Schedule), giving larger States more representation, unlike the US Senate’s equal representation.

Tenure and continuity: Members serve six‑year terms, with one‑third retiring every two years (Article 83). This staggered retirement ensures continuity and prevents the Upper House from being dissolved, a feature borrowed from the British House of Lords but without hereditary membership. The Vice‑President of India serves as ex officio Chairman (Article 89), presiding over proceedings but voting only in case of a tie.

Legislative powers: The Rajya Sabha enjoys co‑equal legislative authority with the Lok Sabha on all Bills except Money Bills (Article 109). It can initiate legislation, amend or reject non‑Money Bills, and its concurrence is required for constitutional amendment Bills (Article 368). However, in case of a deadlock on a non‑Money Bill, a joint sitting can be summoned by the President (Article 108), where the Lok Sabha’s numerical superiority usually prevails. The Rajya Sabha also has exclusive powers: authorising Parliament to legislate on State List subjects in national interest (Article 249) and creating All‑India Services (Article 312).

The debates reveal that members like N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar and K.M. Munshi favoured a strong revising chamber to check hasty legislation, while others like H.V. Kamath warned against a “second chamber” that could become a tool of party politics. The adopted model sought to balance federal representation with legislative efficiency, a balance that continues to shape Centre‑State legislative dynamics.

  • Confusing the non‑justiciable nature of Article 44 with a justiciable Fundamental Right; the UCC remains a directive, not an enforceable right.
  • Assuming the Election Commission’s appointment is purely executive; the 2023 Supreme Court ruling mandates a collegium‑based law, altering the constitutional practice.
  • Attributing the Directive Principles solely to the Irish Constitution; the Gandhian and socialist inputs were equally decisive in shaping Articles 38‑48.
  • Believing the Rajya Sabha has equal power over Money Bills; it can only make recommendations, which the Lok Sabha may accept or reject.
  • Overlooking that the nominated members of the Rajya Sabha cannot vote in the election of the President (Article 55), a frequent trap in electoral‑college questions.
  • Treating the staggered retirement of Rajya Sabha members as a dissolution mechanism; the House is never dissolved, only its composition changes gradually.
  • Misstating the removal process of the CEC as a simple majority vote; it requires the same impeachment procedure as a Supreme Court judge.

These advanced sections deepen the aspirant’s grasp of the constitutional framework by linking historical deliberations to present‑day institutional operation.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on Emergency Provisions and the Balance of Power

The emergency provisions (Articles 352, 356 and 360) were among the most contested parts of the draft Constitution. The Assembly debated whether the Union should possess the authority to proclaim a national emergency on grounds of war, external aggression or armed rebellion, and whether the President could assume the executive and legislative powers of a State under Article 356. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, while defending the provisions, argued that a federal polity required a “safety valve” to preserve the integrity of the Union in extraordinary circumstances. He cited the experience of the Government of India Act 1935, where the Governor‑General could issue a proclamation of emergency, and the Canadian model of federal emergency powers. Critics such as H.V. Kamath and K.T. Shah warned that the language “if the President is satisfied” conferred unchecked discretion and could be misused to dismiss elected State governments. The Assembly adopted a compromise: the proclamation must be laid before each House of Parliament and approved by a special majority within one month (Article 352(4)), and a similar parliamentary check was inserted for President’s Rule under Article 356(3). The 44th Amendment (1978) later tightened these safeguards by replacing “internal disturbance” with “armed rebellion” and requiring the Cabinet’s written advice before a proclamation. Judicial interpretation in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) further limited the scope of Article 356, holding that the President’s satisfaction is subject to judicial review and that the proclamation cannot be used for political purposes. The financial emergency under Article 360 has never been invoked, reflecting the Assembly’s intent to keep it as a theoretical safeguard rather than an operational tool.

The Constituent Assembly's Design of the Amendment Procedure under Article 368 and Its Judicial Interpretation

Article 368 as originally enacted provided a single amendment procedure: a Bill passed by each House of Parliament by a majority of the total membership and by a two‑thirds majority of members present and voting, followed by Presidential assent. The Assembly deliberately avoided a rigid “entrenched” clause, believing that a written Constitution should be amendable by the representative legislature. However, the Supreme Court in Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951) and Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan (1965) held that Parliament’s amending power under Article 368 was plenary and could abridge Fundamental Rights. This position was reversed in Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967), where a six‑judge bench ruled that Fundamental Rights were beyond the reach of amendment. Parliament responded with the 24th Amendment (1971), expressly stating that Article 368 includes the power to amend Fundamental Rights, and the 25th Amendment (1971), which introduced Article 31C to protect laws giving effect to Directive Principles. The landmark Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) decision then crafted the “basic structure” doctrine, holding that while Parliament may amend any part of the Constitution, it cannot alter its basic features — supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secularism, separation of powers, federal character, and the rule of law. Subsequent amendments such as the 42nd (1976) attempted to curtail judicial review, but the Court in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) struck down clauses that destroyed the basic structure. The 44th Amendment (1978) restored the pre‑1976 position on judicial review and added the requirement that a proclamation of emergency under Article 352 must be based on “armed rebellion”. The evolution of Article 368 thus illustrates a dynamic tension between parliamentary sovereignty and constitutional supremacy, a tension that continues to shape amendment politics.

Technique: Mapping Emergency Safeguards to Constitutional Text
A question asks: “Which constitutional amendments introduced the requirement that a proclamation of emergency under Article 352 must be based on ‘armed rebellion’ and that the Cabinet’s written advice is mandatory?” Identify the amendments and the specific articles they modified.
The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 substituted “internal disturbance” with “armed rebellion” in Article 352(1) and inserted Article 352(3) requiring the President to act on the written advice of the Cabinet. The 42nd Amendment had earlier expanded the grounds to “internal disturbance” and removed the Cabinet advice requirement; the 44th Amendment reversed those changes. Therefore, the correct answer is the 44th Amendment (1978) amending Article 352.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question tests emergency provisions, first locate the article (352, 356, 360), then recall the chronological amendments: 42nd (expansion), 44th (restriction). Pair each amendment with the precise textual change. This two‑step mapping eliminates confusion between “internal disturbance” and “armed rebellion” and between “President’s satisfaction” and “Cabinet advice”.

The Constituent Assembly's Approach to the Representation of Anglo‑Indians and Nominated Members in Parliament

The Assembly recognised the Anglo‑Indian community as a distinct minority and provided for its representation through nomination. Article 331 empowered the President to nominate up to two Anglo‑Indians to the Lok Sabha if the community was not adequately represented, while Article 333 allowed the Governor of a State to nominate one Anglo‑Indian to the Legislative Assembly. The debates reveal that members such as Frank Anthony advocated for nomination as a protective measure, arguing that the community’s small numbers would otherwise render it voiceless. Conversely, some members questioned whether nomination violated the principle of universal adult suffrage. The Assembly ultimately retained the nomination route, viewing it as a transitional safeguard. The 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019 (effective 2020) abolished the nomination of Anglo‑Indians to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies, citing the community’s improved socio‑economic status and the principle of equality. The amendment also removed the provision for nomination of two members to the Lok Sabha under Article 331 and the corresponding State provision under Article 333. The removal reflects a shift from protective representation to a uniform electoral framework, a development that examiners often test by asking whether the nomination power still exists after 2020.

The Constituent Assembly's Debate on the Uniform Civil Code and Article 44: Aspiration vs Enforceability

Article 44, placed in the Directive Principles of State Policy, directs the State to “endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India”. The Assembly’s discussion on this provision was brief but revealing. Dr. Ambedkar, while supporting the ideal, cautioned that a uniform code could not be imposed without the consent of the communities concerned, especially given the diversity of personal laws governing marriage, divorce, inheritance and adoption. He suggested that the State should first codify and reform personal laws on a voluntary basis. Members such as K.M. Munshi and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar echoed the view that the directive was aspirational, not justiciable. The Supreme Court in Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985) and later in Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) urged the legislature to enact a uniform civil code, but consistently held that Article 44 does not confer a legally enforceable right. The 42nd Amendment (1976) added the word “secular” to the Preamble, reinforcing the constitutional commitment to a common civil framework, yet no comprehensive code has been enacted. The debate illustrates the tension between the transformative vision of the Constitution and the pragmatic accommodation of pluralism, a theme that recurs in questions on the interplay between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.

The Constituent Assembly's Design of the Election Commission: Independence, Appointment, and Tenure

Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections in an Election Commission consisting of a Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and such number of other Election Commissioners as the President may fix. The Assembly debated whether the Commission should be a single‑member body or a multi‑member body. Dr. Ambedkar favoured a multi‑member Commission to prevent concentration of power, and the final text allowed the President to appoint additional Commissioners. The original Constitution did not prescribe a fixed tenure; the CEC and Commissioners held office during the pleasure of the President, subject to removal only on the same grounds and in the same manner as a Supreme Court judge (Article 324(5)). The 1993 amendment (the Election Commission (Conditions of Service of Election Commissioners and Transaction of Business) Act) provided a six‑year term or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier, and equated the status of the CEC with that of a Supreme Court judge. The Supreme Court in Election Commission of India v. State of Tamil Nadu (1993) affirmed the Commission’s autonomy, holding that the executive cannot interfere with its functional independence. In 2023, a Constitution Bench ruled that the appointment of the CEC and Election Commissioners must be made by a collegium comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and the Chief Justice of India, thereby institutionalising a transparent selection process. This evolution from executive pleasure to collegium‑based appointment underscores the Constitution’s living character and is a frequent focus of analytical questions on institutional integrity.

  • Confusing the 42nd Amendment’s expansion of emergency grounds with the 44th Amendment’s restriction; the 44th Amendment replaced “internal disturbance” with “armed rebellion” and reinstated Cabinet advice.
  • Assuming Article 368’s amendment power is unlimited after Kesavananda; the basic structure doctrine expressly limits amendments that alter the Constitution’s core features.
  • Believing Anglo‑Indian nomination to Parliament still exists; the 104th Amendment (2019) abolished Articles 331 and 333 nomination provisions effective 2020.
  • Treating Article 44 as a justiciable Fundamental Right; it remains a non‑enforceable Directive Principle despite judicial exhortations.
  • Thinking the Election Commission’s composition has always been a three‑member body; the original Constitution allowed the President to determine the number, and the multi‑member structure was formalised only in 1993.
  • Overlooking that the 2023 Supreme Court collegium ruling applies prospectively and does not invalidate appointments made before the judgment.
  • Misstating the removal procedure for the CEC as a simple majority vote; it requires the same impeachment process as a Supreme Court judge under Article 324(5).

Constituent Assembly Debates on Citizenship and the Partition Legacy

The Constituent Assembly devoted several sessions between 1947 and 1949 to the citizenship provisions that became Articles 5 to 11 of the Constitution. The central tension was between a jus soli principle (citizenship by birth on Indian soil) and a jus sanguinis principle (citizenship by descent), complicated by the massive population exchange following Partition. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, as Chairman of the Drafting Committee, argued that citizenship at commencement (26 January 1950) should be conferred on every person domiciled in the territory of India who was born in India, or whose parents were born in India, or who had been ordinarily resident for five years immediately preceding the commencement. This formulation aimed to include migrants from Pakistan who had entered India before 19 July 1948, while excluding those who arrived later without a permit.

The Assembly also debated the status of persons who had migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 but returned to India. Article 7 provided that such persons would be deemed citizens if they returned under a permit for resettlement. The phrase “ordinarily resident” was deliberately left undefined, leaving its interpretation to the courts. The Citizenship Act, 1955, later operationalised these constitutional provisions, introducing acquisition by registration, naturalisation, and incorporation of territory. Subsequent amendments in 1986, 1992, 2003, 2015 and 2019 progressively tightened the regime, notably the 2003 amendment which introduced the concept of “illegal migrant” and the 2019 amendment which provided a fast‑track path for non‑Muslim minorities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan.

Judicial interpretation has shaped the constitutional meaning of citizenship. In State of Assam v. Union of India (1972), the Supreme Court upheld the validity of the Assam Accord’s cut‑off date (24 March 1971) for detecting foreigners, linking it to Article 6’s “migrated before 19 July 1948” benchmark. The Court in Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India (2005) struck down the Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act, 1983, for violating the equality guarantee under Article 14, reinforcing that citizenship determination must be fair and non‑arbitrary. These rulings illustrate how the Assembly’s open‑textured language continues to generate constitutional litigation.

The Constituent Assembly's Design of the Amendment Procedure under Article 368

Article 368, as originally enacted, embodied a calibrated amendment architecture. The Assembly distinguished three tiers: (i) amendments requiring a simple majority of Parliament (e.g., admission of new States), (ii) amendments requiring a special majority of two‑thirds of members present and voting in each House and a majority of the total membership (most provisions), and (iii) amendments affecting the federal structure — such as the representation of States in Parliament, the extent of executive power of the Union and States, and the provisions of Article 368 itself — which additionally required ratification by the Legislatures of not less than one‑half of the States. This tiered design reflected a compromise between Jawaharlal Nehru’s preference for a flexible Constitution and Dr. Ambedkar’s insistence on rigidity to protect federal balance and minority safeguards.

The first major stress test came with the Golaknath decision (1967), where the Supreme Court held that Parliament could not amend Fundamental Rights. Parliament responded with the 24th Amendment (1971), expressly adding a clause to Article 368 that “nothing in Article 13 shall apply to any amendment made under this article”. The 25th Amendment (1971) further curtailed judicial review of laws giving effect to Directive Principles. The 42nd Amendment (1976), enacted during the Emergency, attempted to make the amendment power virtually unlimited by inserting clauses that barred judicial review of any amendment and expanded the grounds for emergency proclamation.

The Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) introduced the basic structure doctrine, holding that while Parliament’s amending power is wide, it cannot destroy the Constitution’s “basic features” — supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secularism, separation of powers, federalism, and the rule of law. The 44th Amendment (1978) restored judicial review of amendments and reinstated the requirement that a proclamation of emergency under Article 352 be based on “armed rebellion” rather than “internal disturbance”. Subsequent cases — Minerva Mills (1980), Waman Rao (1981), Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) — refined the doctrine, establishing that the basic structure includes the power of judicial review itself and the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles. The Assembly’s original tiered scheme thus survives, but now operates under an unwritten judicial ceiling that the Assembly did not anticipate.

Examiner's Twist: Amendment Power vs Basic Structure
A question asks: “The 42nd Amendment made the amendment power of Parliament absolute. Explain why this statement is constitutionally incorrect.”
The 42nd Amendment inserted clauses in Article 368 purporting to oust judicial review of constitutional amendments. However, in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) the Supreme Court had already declared that the amending power under Article 368 does not extend to altering the basic structure of the Constitution. The 42nd Amendment could not override this judicial limitation because the basic structure doctrine is a constitutional constraint derived from the Constitution’s own architecture, not a mere statutory rule. The 44th Amendment (1978) expressly repealed the 42nd Amendment’s ouster clauses, reaffirming that judicial review of amendments remains intact. Therefore, the amendment power was never absolute; it remains subject to the basic structure limitation.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes amendment history with the basic structure, first identify the specific amendment (24th, 42nd, 44th) and then state the judicial response (Golaknath, Kesavananda, Minerva Mills). Use a two‑column mental table: Amendment → Change → Judicial Check. This prevents conflating the 42nd Amendment’s textual overreach with the Court’s enduring doctrinal ceiling.

Constituent Assembly Deliberations on Emergency Provisions and the 44th Amendment Safeguards

The Assembly incorporated three distinct emergency powers in the Constitution: National Emergency under Article 352 (originally on grounds of “war, external aggression or internal disturbance”), President’s Rule in States under Article 356 (failure of constitutional machinery), and Financial Emergency under Article 360. The debates reveal a deep anxiety about executive overreach. Dr. Ambedkar warned that the emergency provisions were “a necessary evil” and insisted on parliamentary oversight. The original Article 352 required the President to act on the advice of the Cabinet, but the proclamation could be issued on the ground of “internal disturbance”, a term the Assembly left undefined.

The 38th Amendment (1975) rendered the satisfaction of the President non‑justiciable, and the 39th Amendment (1975) placed the election of the Prime Minister beyond judicial scrutiny. The 42nd Amendment (1976) extended the maximum duration of a National Emergency from six months to one year without parliamentary approval and made the proclamation immune from judicial review. These changes were enacted during the 1975‑77 Emergency and were widely criticised for concentrating power in the executive.

The 44th Amendment (1978) reversed the most dangerous alterations. It replaced “internal disturbance” with “armed rebellion”, required the Cabinet’s advice to be communicated in writing, mandated that a proclamation be approved by both Houses of Parliament within one month by a special majority, and limited the duration to six months unless extended by Parliament. Crucially, it restored judicial review of the proclamation’s validity. The Supreme Court in ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976) had held that during an Emergency the right to move courts for habeas corpus stood suspended; the 44th Amendment and subsequent jurisprudence, especially S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), established that the President’s satisfaction under Article 356 is subject to judicial review on grounds of mala fides or irrelevance. The Court also held that the imposition of President’s Rule must be based on objective material and not on political whim. These safeguards reflect the Assembly’s original intent to keep emergency powers exceptional, temporary, and accountable.

The Constituent Assembly's Vision for Judicial Independence: Appointment, Tenure, and Removal

The Assembly’s design for an independent judiciary centred on three pillars: security of tenure, insulation of appointments from executive patronage, and a rigorous removal process. Article 124(2) provided that Supreme Court judges would be appointed by the President after consultation with such judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts as the President may deem necessary. The word “consultation” became the focal point of a decades‑long interpretive battle. In the First Judges Case (S.P. Gupta v. Union of India, 1981), the Supreme Court held that “consultation” did not mean “concurrence”, giving the executive primacy. This was overturned in the Second Judges Case (Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India, 1993), where a nine‑judge Bench ruled that the Chief Justice of India’s opinion, formed in consultation with the two senior‑most judges, would have primacy, effectively creating the Collegium system. The Third Judges Case (1998) expanded the Collegium to the Chief Justice and four senior‑most judges for Supreme Court appointments, and the Chief Justice and two senior‑most judges for High Court appointments.

Tenure was fixed at age 65 for Supreme Court judges (Article 124(2)) and 62 for High Court judges (Article 217(1)), with removal only by an address of each House of Parliament supported by a two‑thirds majority of members present and voting and a majority of the total membership, on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity (Article 124(4)). The Assembly deliberately made removal cumbersome to protect judicial independence from legislative pressure. The 99th Constitutional Amendment (2014) sought to replace the Collegium with the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC), comprising the Chief Justice, two senior judges, the Law Minister, and two eminent persons. The Supreme Court struck down the NJAC in Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (2015), holding that the inclusion of the executive and politicians violated the basic structure’s guarantee of judicial independence. The Court re‑affirmed the Collegium, while directing the government to finalise a Memorandum of Procedure for greater transparency.

These developments illustrate how the Assembly’s sparse textual framework — “consultation”, fixed retirement age, and a high threshold for removal — has been fleshed out by judicial interpretation into a robust institutional architecture that continues to evolve.

  • Confusing the 42nd Amendment’s ouster of judicial review with the 44th Amendment’s restoration; the 44th Amendment expressly repealed the 42nd’s non‑justiciability clauses.
  • Assuming the original Article 368 allowed unlimited amendment of Fundamental Rights; the basic structure doctrine, declared in 1973, limits that power.
  • Treating “consultation” in Article 124 as mere formal advice; the Second Judges Case converted it into binding primacy of the Chief Justice.
  • Believing the President’s emergency satisfaction under Article 352 is immune from review after the 38th Amendment; the 44th Amendment and S.R. Bommai restored judicial scrutiny.
  • Overlooking that the Citizenship Act, 1955, not the Constitution, defines “illegal migrant”; the constitutional text only sets the commencement criteria.
  • Thinking the NJAC judgment abolished the Collegium; the Court struck down the NJAC but retained the Collegium with a directive for a transparent MoP.
  • Misstating the ratification requirement for federal amendments as a simple majority of States; it requires ratification by Legislatures of not less than one‑half of the States.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on Citizenship, Partition, and the Original Citizenship Provisions

The Constitution's citizenship scheme (Articles 5‑11) was crafted against the backdrop of Partition, mass migration, and the need to define the political community of the new Republic. Article 5 conferred citizenship at commencement on every person domiciled in the territory of India who was born in India, or either of whose parents was born in India, or who had been ordinarily resident for five years immediately preceding the commencement. Articles 6 and 7 addressed migrants from Pakistan: those who migrated before 19 July 1948 became citizens if they or their ancestors were born in undivided India and they had resided since migration; those who migrated after that date required registration. Article 8 extended citizenship to persons of Indian origin residing abroad who registered with Indian diplomatic missions. Article 9 provided that voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship entailed loss of Indian citizenship. Article 10 preserved citizenship subject to parliamentary law, and Article 11 empowered Parliament to regulate citizenship by legislation, leading to the Citizenship Act, 1955.

The debates reveal a tension between an inclusive, jus soli‑oriented approach and a restrictive, jus sanguinis‑oriented stance. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar argued for a broad definition to accommodate refugees, while Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel emphasised security concerns and the need to prevent influx from Pakistan. The Assembly rejected a pure jus soli model, fearing it would grant citizenship to large numbers of non‑residents. The compromise embedded a domicile requirement and a cut‑off date for migrants, reflecting the pragmatic politics of 1947‑49. The 1955 Act later codified acquisition by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, and incorporation of territory, and introduced the concept of "illegal migrant" — a term absent from the constitutional text. Judicial interpretation, notably in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rehan (1975) and Assam Sanmilita Mahasangha v. Union of India (2014), has clarified that the constitutional provisions operate only at commencement; subsequent acquisition and loss are governed exclusively by statute.

The Influence of the American Bill of Rights and the Japanese Constitution on the Fundamental Rights Chapter

The Fundamental Rights chapter (Part III) bears the imprint of multiple constitutional traditions. The American Bill of Rights supplied the catalogue of civil liberties — freedom of speech (Art. 19(1)(a)), protection against self‑incrimination (Art. 20(3)), and the guarantee of due process — but the Indian drafters replaced the open‑ended "due process of law" with the narrower "procedure established by law" in Article 21, a phrase borrowed from the post‑war Japanese Constitution (Article 31). This deliberate textual choice was intended to limit judicial review of legislative policy while retaining a procedural safeguard. The Japanese influence is also evident in Article 22's protection against arbitrary arrest and detention, which mirrors the Japanese emphasis on procedural regularity.

Despite the textual restriction, the Supreme Court progressively expanded Article 21 through a "due process" reading. In A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) the Court held that "procedure established by law" meant any procedure enacted by a competent legislature, rejecting substantive due process. This formalist stance was overturned in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), where a seven‑judge Bench ruled that the procedure must be "fair, just and reasonable", effectively importing substantive due process. The American influence resurfaced in the "reasonable classification" test under Article 14, derived from the Equal Protection Clause, and in the "clear and present danger" standard for speech restrictions, adapted from Schenck v. United States (1919) but tempered by Article 19(2)'s enumerated grounds. The Japanese model's procedural minimalism thus became a springboard for a uniquely Indian jurisprudence that blends textual fidelity with purposive expansion.

Worked Answer Technique
Question: "Explain how the Japanese Constitution influenced Article 21 of the Indian Constitution and how the Supreme Court transformed that influence."
The Japanese Constitution (1947) used the phrase "procedure established by law" in Article 31 to guarantee that deprivation of life or liberty must follow a legislated procedure, without importing substantive due process. The Indian Constituent Assembly adopted the same wording in Article 21 to avoid the expansive American "due process of law" and to preserve legislative supremacy. Initially, in A.K. Gopalan (1950), the Supreme Court interpreted the phrase literally, holding that any procedure enacted by a competent legislature satisfied Article 21. In Maneka Gandhi (1978), the Court read "procedure established by law" as requiring a procedure that is fair, just, and reasonable, thereby importing substantive due process through judicial interpretation. The answer should cite the textual borrowing, the Gopalan formalist phase, the Maneka Gandhi purposive turn, and the resulting jurisprudential synthesis.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for foreign influence, first identify the exact textual borrowing, then trace the judicial trajectory: literal reading → purposive expansion → current test. Use the Gopalan‑Maneka Gandhi arc as the template for Article 21; the same pattern appears in Article 14 (reasonable classification) and Article 19 (clear and present danger).

The Constituent Assembly's Debate on the Uniform Civil Code and Article 44: From Directive to Judicial Discourse

Article 44, placed in Part IV (Directive Principles), enjoins the State to "endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India". The debate in the Assembly was sharply polarised. Dr. Ambedkar, as Law Minister, championed a uniform code as essential for national integration and gender justice, arguing that personal laws based on religion perpetuated inequality, especially for women. Muslim members, notably Mohammad Ismail and B. Pocker Bahadur, opposed the directive, viewing it as an infringement on religious autonomy guaranteed by Article 25. The compromise was to locate the provision in the non‑justiciable Directive Principles, signalling aspirational intent rather than enforceable mandate.

Post‑independence, the Supreme Court repeatedly highlighted the Directive's dormant status. In Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985), the Court urged Parliament to enact a uniform civil code while granting maintenance under Section 125 CrPC, sparking political controversy. The Parliament responded with the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, which limited the maintenance period. In Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) and John Vallamattom v. Union of India (2003), the Court reiterated the need for a uniform code, linking it to Article 44 and the constitutional goal of secularism. However, the Court has consistently refused to issue a mandamus, respecting the separation of powers. The Law Commission's 21st Report (2008) and 22nd Report (2018) recommended a gradual, consultative approach, but political consensus remains elusive. The trajectory illustrates how a non‑justiciable directive can shape judicial reasoning and public discourse without compelling legislative action.

The Constituent Assembly's Design of the Amendment Procedure: Balancing Rigidity and Flexibility

Article 368 provides the exclusive constitutional amendment procedure, a deliberate departure from the British model of parliamentary sovereignty and the American model of entrenched rigidity. The original text required a special majority of two‑thirds of members present and voting in each House, and a majority of the total membership of each House. For amendments affecting the federal structure — election of the President, extent of executive power, Supreme Court and High Court jurisdiction, distribution of legislative powers, any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule, representation of States in Parliament, or Article 368 itself — ratification by the Legislatures of not less than one‑half of the States was added.

The 24th Amendment (1971) clarified that Article 368 applies to all amendments, including those to Fundamental Rights, overturning Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967). The 42nd Amendment (1976) attempted to make amendments immune from judicial review by inserting clauses (4) and (5) in Article 368, but the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) struck them down as violating the basic structure. The 44th Amendment (1978) restored the pre‑42nd position and added a requirement that the President's assent to amendment bills cannot be withheld. The basic structure doctrine, articulated in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), operates as an unwritten constraint: Parliament cannot amend the Constitution so as to destroy its essential features — supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form, secularism, federalism, separation of powers, and judicial review. This layered design — textual special majority, state ratification for federal provisions, and judicial basic‑structure review — creates a calibrated rigidity that prevents both facile majoritarian change and absolute immobility.

  • Confusing the original citizenship cut‑off dates (19 July 1948) with the later Citizenship Act amendments.
  • Attributing the "due process" phrase to the Indian Constitution; the text uses "procedure established by law".
  • Assuming Article 44 is justiciable; it remains a Directive Principle and cannot be enforced by courts.
  • Believing the 42nd Amendment's ouster clauses survive; they were invalidated in Minerva Mills.
  • Overlooking that state ratification under Article 368 requires legislatures of at least half the States, not a simple majority of States.
  • Treating the basic structure as a textual provision; it is a judicial construct limiting amendment power.
  • Misstating that the Japanese Constitution contributed "due process of law"; it contributed "procedure established by law".

These advanced themes illustrate how the Constituent Assembly's choices continue to shape constitutional adjudication today.

The Constituent Assembly's Debate on the Uniform Civil Code and Article 44

The Uniform Civil Code (UCC) was one of the most contentious issues in the Constituent Assembly, reflecting the tension between the aspiration for a common civil law and the protection of religious personal laws. The debate centred on Article 44 of the Directive Principles of State Policy, which reads: “The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.” The provision was placed in Part IV, making it non‑justiciable, a deliberate compromise that signalled aspirational intent rather than an enforceable mandate.

Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, as Law Minister, championed the UCC as essential for national integration and gender justice. He argued that personal laws based on religion perpetuated inequality, especially for women, and that a common code would reinforce the secular character of the Constitution. In the Assembly debates of November 1948, Ambedkar stated that the UCC would “remove the disparities which exist in the personal laws of different communities.” Muslim members, notably Mohammad Ismail, B. Pocker Bahadur, and Hussain Imam, opposed the directive, viewing it as an infringement on the religious autonomy guaranteed by Article 25. They contended that personal law was an integral part of religious practice and that the state should not interfere.

The compromise was to locate the provision in the Directive Principles, thereby avoiding a justiciable right. The Assembly adopted Article 44 on 23 November 1948 with a clear understanding that its implementation would depend on political consensus. Post‑independence, the Supreme Court repeatedly highlighted the Directive’s dormant status. In Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985), the Court urged Parliament to enact a UCC while granting maintenance under Section 125 CrPC, sparking political controversy. Parliament responded with the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, which limited the maintenance period. In Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) and John Vallamattom v. Union of India (2003), the Court reiterated the need for a UCC, linking it to Article 44 and the constitutional goal of secularism. However, the Court has consistently refused to issue a mandamus, respecting the separation of powers. The Law Commission’s 21st Report (2008) and 22nd Report (2018) recommended a gradual, consultative approach, but political consensus remains elusive. The trajectory illustrates how a non‑justiciable directive can shape judicial reasoning and public discourse without compelling legislative action.

The Constituent Assembly's Design of the Amendment Procedure: Balancing Rigidity and Flexibility

Article 368 provides the exclusive constitutional amendment procedure, a deliberate departure from the British model of parliamentary sovereignty and the American model of entrenched rigidity. The original text required a special majority of two‑thirds of members present and voting in each House, and a majority of the total membership of each House. For amendments affecting the federal structure — election of the President, extent of executive power, Supreme Court and High Court jurisdiction, distribution of legislative powers, any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule, representation of States in Parliament, or Article 368 itself — ratification by the Legislatures of not less than one‑half of the States was added.

The 24th Amendment (1971) clarified that Article 368 applies to all amendments, including those to Fundamental Rights, overturning Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967). The 42nd Amendment (1976) attempted to make amendments immune from judicial review by inserting clauses (4) and (5) in Article 368, but the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) struck them down as violating the basic structure. The 44th Amendment (1978) restored the pre‑42nd position and added a requirement that the President's assent to amendment bills cannot be withheld. The basic structure doctrine, articulated in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), operates as an unwritten constraint: Parliament cannot amend the Constitution so as to destroy its essential features — supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form, secularism, federalism, separation of powers, and judicial review. This layered design — textual special majority, state ratification for federal provisions, and judicial basic‑structure review — creates a calibrated rigidity that prevents both facile majoritarian change and absolute immobility.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which of the following statements about the amendment procedure under Article 368 is correct? (a) A simple majority in Parliament suffices for all amendments. (b) State ratification is required for any amendment to Fundamental Rights. (c) The basic structure doctrine was introduced by the 42nd Amendment. (d) The special majority requires two‑thirds of members present and voting and a majority of the total membership of each House.”
The correct answer is (d). Article 368 mandates a special majority of two‑thirds of members present and voting in each House together with a majority of the total membership of that House. State ratification is required only for amendments affecting the federal provisions listed in the proviso to Article 368, not for all Fundamental Rights amendments. The basic structure doctrine was judicially evolved in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), not introduced by the 42nd Amendment. The 42nd Amendment attempted to oust judicial review but was invalidated in Minerva Mills (1980).
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the three‑tier amendment framework: (1) ordinary special majority for most provisions, (2) special majority plus ratification by half the State Legislatures for federal provisions, (3) judicial basic‑structure review as an unwritten ceiling. In MCQs, eliminate options that conflate the 42nd Amendment with the basic structure or that treat state ratification as universal. For descriptive answers, cite Kesavananda, Minerva Mills, and the 44th Amendment to show the evolution of the constraint.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on the Emergency Provisions: Articles 352, 356, 360

The emergency provisions were crafted against the backdrop of Partition, communal violence, and the experience of the Government of India Act 1935, which contained a “Governor’s Rule” akin to President’s Rule. The Assembly debated three distinct emergencies: National Emergency (Article 352), State Emergency or President’s Rule (Article 356), and Financial Emergency (Article 360). The overarching concern was to balance the need for swift executive action with safeguards against authoritarian misuse.

Article 352 originally allowed the President to proclaim a national emergency on grounds of “war, external aggression or internal disturbance.” The term “internal disturbance” was criticised for its vagueness. The 44th Amendment (1978) replaced it with “armed rebellion” and introduced procedural safeguards: the proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within one month by a special majority, and it must be renewed every six months. The amendment also restricted the suspension of Fundamental Rights: Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even during an emergency.

Article 356, enabling President’s Rule in a state, was modelled on Section 93 of the 1935 Act. The Assembly debated whether the Governor’s report should be binding on the President. Dr. Ambedkar argued that the President must act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, but the final text left the President’s satisfaction as the trigger. The 44th Amendment added a requirement that the proclamation be approved by Parliament within two months and limited its duration to three years, with periodic parliamentary approval. The Supreme Court in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) laid down judicial review standards, holding that the proclamation is subject to judicial scrutiny on grounds of mala fide or irrelevance.

Article 360, the Financial Emergency, has never been invoked. The Assembly included it to empower the Centre to direct states to observe canons of financial propriety during a threat to financial stability. The provision requires parliamentary approval within two months and remains in force until revoked. The debates reveal a cautious approach: the Assembly wanted a tool for extreme fiscal crises but feared its misuse to undermine federal fiscal autonomy. The 44th Amendment did not alter Article 360, reflecting the view that its dormancy was a feature, not a defect.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on Judicial Review and Constitutional Supremacy

The place of judicial review in the constitutional scheme was a subject of intense discussion in the Constituent Assembly. The Drafting Committee, led by Dr. Ambedkar, incorporated Article 13, which declares that laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void, and Articles 32 and 226, empowering the Supreme Court and High Courts to issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. These provisions established constitutional supremacy over parliamentary legislation, a departure from the British doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty.

During the debates, members such as K. T. Shah and H. V. Kamath argued for an explicit “due process” clause akin to the American Fifth Amendment, but the Assembly adopted the phrase “procedure established by law” in Article 21, reflecting a preference for legislative primacy subject to judicial review of procedural fairness. The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, chaired by Sardar Patel, recommended a strong judicial review mechanism, and the Assembly accepted it with the understanding that the judiciary would act as the guardian of the Constitution.

The early jurisprudence, notably A. K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950), interpreted “procedure established by law” narrowly, limiting judicial review to procedural compliance. This changed with Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), where the Court read “procedure established by law” as requiring fairness, reasonableness, and non‑arbitrariness, effectively importing a due‑process standard. The basic structure doctrine in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) cemented judicial review as an essential feature that cannot be amended away. Subsequent cases — Minerva Mills (1980), Waman Rao (1981), I. R. Coelho (2007) — reinforced that constitutional amendments violating the basic structure are subject to judicial invalidation. The Assembly’s design thus created a dynamic equilibrium: Parliament enjoys wide amendment power under Article 368, but the judiciary retains the final say on whether an amendment destroys the Constitution’s identity.

  • Confusing the original citizenship cut‑off dates (19 July 1948) with the later Citizenship Act amendments.
  • Attributing the “due process” phrase to the Indian Constitution; the text uses “procedure established by law”.
  • Assuming Article 44 is justiciable; it remains a Directive Principle and cannot be enforced by courts.
  • Believing the 42nd Amendment's ouster clauses survive; they were invalidated in Minerva Mills.
  • Overlooking that state ratification under Article 368 requires legislatures of at least half the States, not a simple majority of States.
  • Treating the basic structure as a textual provision; it is a judicial construct limiting amendment power.
  • Misstating that the Japanese Constitution contributed “due process of law”; it contributed “procedure established by law”.

The Constituent Assembly's Steering Committee and the Drafting Committee's Working Procedure

The Constituent Assembly constituted a Steering Committee on 11 December 1946 to coordinate the work of various sub‑committees and to set the agenda for plenary sessions. The committee comprised the President of the Assembly, Dr. Rajendra Prasad, the Chairman of the Drafting Committee, Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, and the chairmen of the major functional committees such as the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights (Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel), the Union Powers Committee (Jawaharlal Nehru), and the Provincial Constitution Committee (Sardar Patel again). This composition ensured that the Steering Committee reflected the principal political and legal currents within the Assembly.

The Drafting Committee, appointed on 29 August 1947, was tasked with preparing a draft constitution based on the reports of the sub‑committees and the decisions of the Assembly. It consisted of seven members: Dr. Ambedkar (Chairman), N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, K. M. Munshi, Mohammad Saadullah, B. L. Mitter (later replaced by N. Madhava Rao), and D. P. Khaitan (later replaced by T. T. Krishnamachari). The committee met for 141 days between 1947 and 1949, producing a draft that ran to 395 articles and 8 schedules. Its working procedure involved circulating a preliminary draft to all members, inviting written comments, holding clause‑by‑clause discussions, and then incorporating approved amendments into a revised draft.

A distinctive feature of the Drafting Committee’s method was the use of “comparative constitutional analysis”. Members systematically examined the Government of India Act 1935, the constitutions of the United States, Canada, Australia, Ireland, and the United Kingdom, and the constitutional documents of the French Republic. For each provision, the committee prepared a comparative note indicating the source, the rationale for adoption or rejection, and the modifications required to suit Indian conditions. This documentary discipline is evident in the extensive footnotes appended to the Draft Constitution submitted to the Assembly on 21 February 1948.

The Assembly debated the draft over 114 sittings between November 1948 and November 1949. The Steering Committee scheduled the debates in thematic blocks — citizenship, fundamental rights, directive principles, federal structure, emergency provisions, and amendment procedure — allowing focused deliberation. Amendments moved by members were first examined by the Drafting Committee, which could accept, modify, or reject them. Accepted amendments were incorporated into the “final draft” that was adopted on 26 November 1949. The procedural rigor of the Steering and Drafting Committees ensured that the final text reflected a negotiated consensus rather than a unilateral imposition.

The Debate on Fundamental Duties: From the 42nd Amendment to Judicial Enforcement

The concept of fundamental duties was absent from the original Constitution. It entered the constitutional text through the Constitution (Forty‑second Amendment) Act, 1976, which inserted Part IVA containing a single Article 51A listing ten duties of citizens. The amendment was moved during the Emergency, and the government argued that duties would balance the expansive fundamental rights and promote a sense of civic responsibility. Critics in the Assembly’s successor Parliament contended that duties imposed by an executive‑dominated legislature lacked democratic legitimacy and could be used to curtail dissent.

The original ten duties included respect for the Constitution, the national flag and the national anthem; cherishing the noble ideals of the freedom struggle; upholding sovereignty, unity and integrity; defending the country; promoting harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood; preserving the rich heritage of composite culture; protecting the natural environment; developing scientific temper and humanism; safeguarding public property; and striving towards excellence in all spheres. The 86th Amendment (2002) added an eleventh duty: providing opportunities for education to children between six and fourteen years.

Judicial enforcement of fundamental duties has remained limited because Article 51A is placed in Part IVA, which is explicitly non‑justiciable under Article 37. However, the Supreme Court has used duties as interpretive aids. In Ranganath Misra v. Union of India (1996), the Court held that while duties are not directly enforceable, they can guide the construction of statutes and the exercise of discretionary powers. In M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (2004), the Court linked the duty to protect the environment (Article 51A(g)) with the right to life under Article 21, thereby giving the duty indirect enforceability through fundamental rights jurisprudence.

The debate continues on whether fundamental duties should be made justiciable. The Law Commission’s 2009 report recommended a constitutional amendment to enable courts to issue directions for the implementation of duties, but no such amendment has been enacted. The tension between the moral aspiration of duties and their legal non‑enforceability remains a distinctive feature of Indian constitutional design.

Identifying the Constitutional Source of Fundamental Duties
A question asks: “Which constitutional amendment introduced fundamental duties and under which Part are they placed?” Provide the precise answer with article reference.
The Constitution (Forty‑second Amendment) Act, 1976 inserted Part IVA into the Constitution. Article 51A, located in Part IVA, enumerates the fundamental duties of citizens. The 86th Amendment (2002) added a further duty under the same Article.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the amendment that introduced a feature, always cite the amendment number and year. For fundamental duties, remember “42nd Amendment, 1976, Part IVA, Article 51A”. Pair this with the 86th Amendment (2002) for the education duty. This two‑point recall covers both the origin and the later expansion.

Judicial Interpretation of the Preamble's "We, the People of India" and Its Enforceability

The opening words of the Preamble — “We, the people of India” — have been the focal point of judicial discourse on popular sovereignty. In Berubari Union v. Unknown (1960), the Supreme Court held that the Preamble is not a source of substantive power but a key to the interpretation of the Constitution. The Court stated that the Preamble indicates the source of the Constitution’s authority, namely the people, and that it can be used to resolve ambiguities in the enacted provisions.

In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the majority opinion elevated the Preamble to a constitutional provision that reflects the basic structure. Justice Sikri observed that the Preamble embodies the “basic features” of the Constitution — sovereignty, socialism, secularism, democracy, republic, justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity — and that any amendment destroying these features would be ultra vires. This reasoning made the Preamble a benchmark for the basic structure test.

Subsequent cases have reinforced the interpretive role of the Preamble. In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Court used the Preamble’s commitment to secularism to strike down a state government’s dismissal on religious grounds. In Union of India v. R. Gandhi (2010), the Court referred to the Preamble’s promise of “justice — social, economic and political” while interpreting the scope of directive principles. Although the Preamble itself remains non‑justiciable in the sense that no writ can be issued solely for its violation, its language operates as a constitutional compass that guides judicial review of legislation and executive action.

The 42nd Amendment (1976) added the words “socialist”, “secular”, and “integrity” to the Preamble. The Supreme Court in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) held that these additions are part of the basic structure and cannot be removed by a subsequent amendment. Thus, the Preamble’s textual evolution is itself protected by the basic structure doctrine, making the phrase “We, the people of India” a living declaration of popular sovereignty that constrains both legislative and constituent power.

Article 368 Amendment Procedure: Special Majority, State Ratification, and the Basic Structure Check

Article 368 prescribes the procedure for amending the Constitution. An amendment bill must be passed by each House of Parliament by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two‑thirds of the members present and voting — the “special majority”. For amendments affecting the federal structure — specifically those enumerated in the proviso to Article 368(2) such as the election of the President, the extent of executive power of the Union and States, the Supreme Court and High Courts, distribution of legislative powers, any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule, representation of States in Parliament, and the amendment procedure itself — ratification by the legislatures of not less than one‑half of the States is additionally required.

The distinction between “ordinary” amendments and “federal” amendments was clarified in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), where the Court held that the anti‑defection provisions (Tenth Schedule) did not require state ratification because they did not alter the federal distribution of powers. Conversely, the 99th Amendment (National Judicial Appointments Commission) was struck down in Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (2015) partly because it altered the composition of the higher judiciary, a federal feature, without the requisite state ratification.

The basic structure doctrine, articulated in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), imposes an unwritten limitation on the amending power.
