The Court enumerated illustrative basic features: supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secular character, separation of powers, federal character, and the mandate to build a welfare state. In Minerva Mills (1980), the Court invalidated clauses of the 42nd Amendment that sought to oust judicial review of constitutional amendments, affirming that the power to amend does not include the power to destroy the Constitution’s identity.

Procedurally, after Parliament passes the amendment bill, it is presented to the President for assent. The President cannot withhold assent to a constitutional amendment bill (Article 368(2) read with Article 111). However, the Supreme Court in R. C. Poudyal v. Union of India (1993) held that the President’s assent is a formal step and does not confer any substantive veto. The amendment becomes part of the Constitution upon presidential assent, subject to judicial review for compliance with the basic structure.

The Role of the President in Constitutional Amendments: Assent, Certification, and Judicial Review

Although Article 368 vests the constituent power in Parliament, the President performs a ceremonial but constitutionally mandated function. Once a bill has been passed by both Houses with the required special majority and, where applicable, ratified by the requisite number of State legislatures, it is presented to the President. Under Article 111, the President may either give assent or withhold assent. However, the Supreme Court has consistently held that the President’s power to withhold assent does not extend to constitutional amendment bills because the constituent power is exercised by Parliament alone and the President’s role is purely formal.

The Speaker of the Lok Sabha (or the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha) certifies that the bill has been passed in accordance with Article 368. This certification is a procedural safeguard ensuring that the special majority and state ratification requirements have been satisfied. In Kihoto Hollohan, the Court examined the Speaker’s certification of the anti‑defection amendment and held that the certification is subject to judicial review only on the ground of constitutional non‑compliance, not on the merits of the amendment.

Judicial review of the amendment process itself was affirmed in Minerva Mills and later in I. R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007). The Court ruled that while the substance of an amendment is subject to the basic structure test, the procedural compliance with Article 368 is also justiciable. A failure to obtain the required special majority or state ratification renders the amendment void ab initio. The Court has, however, declined to review the political wisdom behind an amendment, limiting its scrutiny to constitutional conformity.

In practice, the President’s assent has never been refused for a constitutional amendment bill. The 24th Amendment (1971) explicitly amended Article 368 to clarify that the President shall give assent to any bill passed under that article, removing any ambiguity. This legislative clarification underscores the principle that the constituent power resides in Parliament and the President’s role is ministerial, reinforcing the doctrine of constitutional sovereignty over parliamentary sovereignty.

  • Confusing the special majority required for ordinary legislation with the two‑thirds majority of total membership needed for constitutional amendments.
  • Assuming that all amendments require state ratification; only those affecting federal provisions listed in the proviso to Article 368(2) do.
  • Treating the Preamble as a justiciable provision that can be directly enforced by a writ petition.
  • Believing that fundamental duties under Article 51A are directly enforceable in courts without linking them to a fundamental right.
  • Overlooking that the President’s assent to an amendment bill is mandatory and cannot be withheld on policy grounds.
  • Misidentifying the 42nd Amendment as the sole source of the words “socialist” and “secular” in the Preamble without noting the basic structure protection affirmed in Minerva Mills.
  • Neglecting the distinction between the Drafting Committee’s comparative notes and the final adopted text when answering source‑based questions.

Citizenship Provisions: Drafting History, Judicial Interpretation, and the Citizenship Act, 1955

The Constitution deals with citizenship in Articles 5 to 11, a compact code that was deliberately left to Parliament for detailed regulation. Article 5 conferred citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution on persons domiciled in the territory of India who were born in India, or either of whose parents was born in India, or who had been ordinarily resident for five years immediately preceding the commencement. Articles 6 and 7 addressed migrants from Pakistan, distinguishing those who migrated before 19 July 1948 (deemed citizens) from those who migrated after that date (required registration). Article 8 extended citizenship to persons of Indian origin residing outside India who registered with an Indian diplomatic mission. Article 9 stipulated that voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship entails loss of Indian citizenship. Article 10 preserved citizenship subject to any law made by Parliament, and Article 11 empowered Parliament to regulate the acquisition and termination of citizenship.

The Constituent Assembly debated these provisions intensely. The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities, chaired by Sardar Patel, recommended a single citizenship for the whole Union, rejecting the idea of state‑level citizenship that existed under the Government of India Act 1935. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, in the Drafting Committee, emphasized that citizenship must be a uniform national status to sustain the unity of the Republic. The final text reflects a compromise: a constitutional core that defines the initial citizenry, coupled with a plenary legislative power to amend the details.

Parliament exercised this power through the Citizenship Act, 1955, which has been amended repeatedly — 1986, 1992, 2003, 2005, 2015, and 2019. The 1986 amendment narrowed citizenship by birth to those born in India between 26 January 1950 and 1 July 1987, and thereafter only if at least one parent was a citizen. The 2003 amendment introduced the concept of “illegal migrant” and barred such persons from acquiring citizenship by registration or naturalisation. The 2019 Citizenship (Amendment) Act (CAA) created a fast‑track for non‑Muslim migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan who entered India before 31 December 2014, sparking extensive litigation.

Judicial interpretation has clarified several ambiguities. In State of Assam v. Union of India (1971), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of Section 6A of the Citizenship Act, inserted by the Assam Accord, which fixed 24 March 1971 as the cut‑off date for detection of foreigners in Assam. In Assam Sanmilita Mahasangha v. Union of India (2014), the Court referred the constitutional validity of Section 6A to a larger bench, highlighting the tension between parliamentary power under Article 11 and the cultural rights of indigenous communities under Article 29. The Court has consistently held that Article 11 is a plenary power, but it cannot be exercised in a manner that violates the basic structure, particularly the secular character of the Constitution (see Minerva Mills v. Union of India, 1980). The CAA challenge (pending as of 2024) tests whether a religion‑based classification for citizenship violates Article 14 and the basic structure.

Termination of citizenship occurs through renunciation (Section 8 of the 1955 Act), termination by operation of law upon acquiring foreign citizenship (Section 9), and deprivation by the Central Government on grounds such as fraud, disloyalty, or assisting an enemy (Section 10). The Supreme Court in Louis De Raedt v. Union of India (1991) ruled that deprivation under Section 10 must follow principles of natural justice, including a hearing. The interplay between Articles 5‑11 and the 1955 Act illustrates the Constitution’s design: a rigid constitutional core for the initial citizenry, and a flexible statutory regime for subsequent acquisition and loss, subject to judicial review for constitutional conformity.

The Constitutional Position of the Vice President and the Chairman of Rajya Sabha: Election, Powers, and Judicial Pronouncements

Articles 63 to 71 establish the office of the Vice President, who is ex officio Chairman of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha). The Vice President is elected by an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament, in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote (Article 66). The term is five years, and the Vice President may resign by writing to the President or be removed by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a majority of its then members and agreed to by the Lok Sabha (Article 67). The Constitution does not prescribe any qualification beyond being a citizen of India, aged thirty‑five years, and qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha (Article 66).

As Chairman, the Vice President presides over the Rajya Sabha, maintains order, decides points of order, and exercises a casting vote in the event of a tie (Article 91). The Chairman also authenticates the passage of bills, certifies Money Bills (Article 110), and summons and prorogues the House on the advice of the Council of Ministers. The Vice President acts as President when a vacancy occurs in the office of the President, or when the President is unable to discharge functions (Article 65). In this capacity, the Vice President enjoys all the powers and immunities of the President.

Judicial pronouncements have shaped the contours of the office. In K. K. Venugopal v. Union of India (1995), the Supreme Court held that the election of the Vice President cannot be challenged on the ground of alleged irregularities in the electoral college once the election is complete, emphasizing the finality of the electoral process. In R. C. Poudyal v. Union of India (1993), while primarily concerning the President’s assent, the Court affirmed that the Vice President’s role in certifying constitutional amendment bills is ministerial and not subject to judicial review on merits. The Court in S. R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001) clarified that the Chairman’s decision on disqualification under the Tenth Schedule is subject to judicial review only on grounds of constitutional non‑compliance, not on the merits of the decision, aligning with the principle enunciated in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) for the Speaker.

The Vice President’s casting vote has been exercised sparingly; notable instances include the 1991 vote on the Constitution (Seventy‑Third Amendment) Bill and the 2002 vote on the Prevention of Terrorism Bill. The office has also been pivotal during presidential vacancies: Vice President B. D. Jatti acted as President in 1977, and Vice President K. R. Narayanan acted in 1997. The Constitution’s design — an indirectly elected Vice President who presides over the federal chamber — reflects the framers’ intent to balance parliamentary accountability with federal representation.

Worked Example: Vice President’s Removal
A resolution for removal of the Vice President is moved in the Rajya Sabha. It is passed by a majority of the total membership of the Rajya Sabha but the Lok Sabha does not take up the resolution within the session. Is the Vice President removed?
No. Under Article 67(b), removal requires a resolution passed by a majority of the then members of the Rajya Sabha and agreed to by the Lok Sabha. Mere passage in the Rajya Sabha is insufficient; the Lok Sabha must also agree. If the Lok Sabha does not act, the resolution lapses and the Vice President continues in office.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about the Vice President’s powers, distinguish between functions as Chairman of Rajya Sabha (Articles 89‑91) and functions as Acting President (Article 65). Remember that the Vice President’s election disputes are governed by Article 71 and the Presidential and Vice‑Presidential Elections Act, 1952, not by the ordinary election petition route.

The Constitutional Framework for the Office of the Speaker of Lok Sabha: Election, Powers, and Judicial Review

Articles 93 to 97 provide for the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People. The Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha from amongst its members (Article 93). The term coincides with the life of the House, unless the Speaker resigns, ceases to be a member, or is removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the House (Article 94). The Deputy Speaker is elected similarly and performs the Speaker’s duties when the office is vacant or the Speaker is absent (Article 95).

The Speaker’s powers are extensive. The Speaker presides over sittings, maintains order, interprets and applies the Rules of Procedure, decides points of order, and certifies Money Bills (Article 110). The Speaker also decides questions of disqualification under the Tenth Schedule (Article 102 read with Para 6 of the Tenth Schedule). The Speaker’s certification of a bill as a Money Bill is final and cannot be questioned in any court (Article 110(3)), though the Supreme Court in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) held that the Speaker’s decision on disqualification is subject to judicial review on grounds of constitutional non‑compliance, mala fide, or perversity. The Speaker also has a casting vote in the event of a tie (Article 100).

The Speaker’s role in the legislative process includes referring bills to parliamentary committees, allocating time for discussion, and deciding on the admissibility of motions, resolutions, and questions. The Speaker’s decisions on procedural matters are generally not amenable to judicial review, but the Court has intervened where the Speaker acted beyond constitutional authority. In R. C. Poudyal v. Union of India (1993), the Court examined the Speaker’s certification of a constitutional amendment bill and held that such certification is a procedural safeguard subject to judicial review only for constitutional non‑compliance. In State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977), the Court upheld the Speaker’s power to recognise the Leader of the Opposition, emphasizing that the Speaker’s discretion in parliamentary matters is wide but not unfettered.

The Speaker’s removal mechanism is deliberately rigorous: a resolution requires a 14‑day notice and must be passed by a majority of the total membership of the House, not merely those present and voting. This high threshold protects the Speaker’s independence from executive pressure. The Speaker also enjoys immunity from civil and criminal proceedings for acts done in the discharge of duties (Article 105). The office thus combines procedural authority with constitutional safeguards, ensuring that the Lok Sabha functions as a deliberative body while remaining accountable to the Constitution.

The Constitutional Provisions for Parliamentary Committees: Composition, Powers, and Role in Legislative Scrutiny

Although the Constitution does not enumerate parliamentary committees in detail, Articles 105 and 118 empower each House to regulate its own procedure and to constitute committees for the transaction of its business. The Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha provide for three broad categories: Standing Committees, Ad hoc Committees, and Joint Committees of both Houses.

Standing Committees are permanent bodies reconstituted annually. The most important are the Departmentally Related Standing Committees (DRSCs), twenty‑four in number, each shadowing a ministry or group of ministries. They examine the demand for grants, scrutinise bills referred by the House, and review annual reports and policy documents. Financial Committees — the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), the Estimates Committee, and the Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU) — are constituted under the Rules and have a long tradition of executive accountability. The PAC, chaired by a member of the opposition by convention, examines the Comptroller and Auditor General’s reports and ensures that public expenditure conforms to parliamentary authorisation.

Ad hoc Committees are appointed for a specific purpose, such as the Joint Committee on the Personal Data Protection Bill (2019) or the Select Committee on the Surrogacy (Regulation) Bill (2019). They cease to exist after submitting their report. Joint Committees, with members from both Houses, are formed for bills of significant national importance or for investigating matters of public concern.

Committees possess the power to summon witnesses, call for documents, and examine officials under oath. Their proceedings are confidential, and their reports are presented to the House. While committee recommendations are not binding, they carry substantial moral and political weight; governments often accept amendments suggested by committees. The Supreme Court in K. K. Venugopal v. Union of India (1995) recognised the committees’ role as an extension of parliamentary sovereignty, holding that their power to summon is derived from the House’s collective privileges under Article 105. In State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977), the Court affirmed that committee proceedings are part of parliamentary proceedings and enjoy the same immunities.

The committee system enhances legislative scrutiny by enabling detailed examination that is impractical on the floor of the House. It also provides a platform for opposition members to influence policy. The 1993 restructuring that created the DRSCs marked a shift from ad hoc scrutiny to systematic, ministry‑wise oversight, strengthening the accountability of the executive to Parliament.

  • Confusing the constitutional core of citizenship (Articles 5‑11) with the statutory regime of the Citizenship Act, 1955, and treating amendments to the Act as constitutional amendments.
  • Assuming the Vice President’s removal requires only a Rajya Sabha resolution; forgetting the Lok Sabha’s concurrence under Article 67(b).
  • Believing the Speaker’s certification of a Money Bill is immune from all judicial scrutiny; the Court reviews only constitutional compliance, not the merits of the classification.
  • Overlooking that the Speaker’s disqualification decisions under the Tenth Schedule are subject to judicial review for mala fide or perversity (Kihoto Hollohan).
  • Treating parliamentary committee recommendations as legally binding on the executive; they are advisory but politically influential.
  • Misidentifying the electoral college for the Vice President as the same as that for the President; the Vice President’s college comprises only members of Parliament, not state legislators.
  • Neglecting the distinction between Standing Committees (permanent, ministry‑specific) and Ad hoc Committees (temporary, task‑specific) when answering questions on committee jurisdiction.

The advanced sections above integrate constitutional text, legislative evolution, and judicial doctrine to equip aspirants for analytical questions on citizenship, the Vice Presidency, the Speakership, and parliamentary committees.

Doctrine of Eclipse and Pre‑Constitutional Laws

The doctrine of eclipse addresses the fate of laws enacted before the commencement of the Constitution that are inconsistent with the fundamental rights guaranteed in Part III. Article 13(1) declares that all laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of the Constitution, in so far as they are inconsistent with the provisions of Part III, shall be void to the extent of such inconsistency. The Supreme Court in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955) held that such laws are not dead but merely eclipsed; they remain dormant until the constitutional impediment is removed, either by amendment of the fundamental right or by a subsequent constitutional provision that validates the law. The eclipse is lifted when the inconsistency ceases, and the law revives automatically without the need for fresh legislation.

Key features of the doctrine include:

  • It applies only to pre‑constitutional laws (laws made before 26 January 1950).
  • The law is not void ab initio; it is merely unenforceable while the fundamental right exists.
  • If the fundamental right is amended or the law is saved by a constitutional amendment (e.g., Article 31A, 31B, 31C), the eclipse disappears and the law becomes fully operative.
  • The doctrine does not extend to post‑constitutional laws; those are governed by Article 13(2) and are void ab initio if they contravene fundamental rights.

In State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974), the Court clarified that the doctrine of eclipse does not apply to a law that was void from its inception because it exceeded legislative competence, as distinct from a law that is merely inconsistent with a fundamental right. The distinction is crucial for determining whether a law can be revived by a later constitutional amendment.

Practical implication: when examining a pre‑1950 statute, the examiner expects the candidate to identify whether the statute is eclipsed or void, and to explain the conditions for its revival. The doctrine also interacts with the Ninth Schedule; laws placed in the Ninth Schedule by constitutional amendments are immune from judicial review on fundamental rights grounds, effectively removing the eclipse permanently.

Doctrine of Severability and Article 13

The doctrine of severability (or separability) operates under Article 13(2), which provides that the State shall not make any law that takes away or abridges the rights conferred by Part III, and any law made in contravention shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void. The Supreme Court in R.M.D.C. (Mysore) Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (1957) laid down the test: if the valid and invalid portions of a statute are so inextricably mixed that they cannot be separated, the whole statute falls; if they are distinct, only the offending part is struck down. The Court emphasized that the intention of the legislature is the guiding factor — whether the legislature would have enacted the valid part independently of the invalid part.

Elements of the severability test:

  1. Legislative intent: ascertained from the statute’s preamble, scheme, and language.
  2. Functional independence: the remaining provisions must be capable of operating independently without the severed portion.
  3. Substantial alteration: severance must not change the essential nature or purpose of the legislation.

In A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950), the Court applied severability to the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, holding that Section 14 (which denied the detenu the right to be informed of grounds) was severable from the rest of the Act. Conversely, in State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), the Court refused to sever the offending provisions of the Bombay Prohibition Act because the Act’s scheme was an integrated whole.

The doctrine also interacts with the basic structure limitation: a constitutional amendment that violates the basic structure cannot be saved by severing the offending clause, because the amendment as a whole is ultra vires the constituent power. This was affirmed in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) and reiterated in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980).

For examination purposes, candidates should be able to distinguish between eclipse (pre‑constitutional laws) and severability (post‑constitutional laws), and to apply the three‑pronged severability test to hypothetical statutes.

Worked Example: Severability Analysis
A State enacts the “Public Order Maintenance Act, 2023”. Section 3 authorises preventive detention without judicial review. Section 4 provides for compensation to persons wrongfully detained. Section 5 establishes a review board. The Act’s preamble states that the legislation aims to “maintain public order while safeguarding individual liberty”. The High Court strikes down Section 3 as violative of Article 21. The State argues that Sections 4 and 5 should survive. Apply the severability test.
Step 1 – Legislative intent: The preamble explicitly balances public order with individual liberty, indicating that the compensation and review mechanisms were meant to operate alongside a lawful detention power. Step 2 – Functional independence: Sections 4 and 5 presuppose a valid detention order; without Section 3 there is no detention to compensate or review. They cannot function independently. Step 3 – Substantial alteration: Retaining only Sections 4 and 5 would transform the Act from a preventive detention law into a compensation scheme with no underlying detention authority, altering its essential character. Conclusion: The invalid Section 3 is not severable; the entire Act falls. The State must enact a fresh law with a constitutionally compliant detention provision.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks whether a provision is “saved by severability”, first locate the legislative intent (preamble, long title, scheme). Then test functional independence: can the remaining provisions operate without the struck‑down part? Finally, ask whether the legislature would have passed the remainder alone. If any answer is negative, the whole statute fails. Practice with past year questions on the Preventive Detention Act and the Bombay Prohibition Act to internalise the three‑prong test.

Doctrine of Waiver of Fundamental Rights

The doctrine of waiver concerns whether a person can voluntarily relinquish a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution. The Supreme Court in Basheshar Nath v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1959) held that fundamental rights are not merely personal privileges but are conferred in the public interest; therefore, they cannot be waived by an individual. The Court reasoned that the Constitution embodies a social contract and the rights are part of the basic structure of the constitutional order, making them non‑derogable by private agreement.

Subsequent jurisprudence refined the position:

  • In Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985), the Court reiterated that fundamental rights cannot be waived, but distinguished between waiver and estoppel — a person may be estopped from asserting a right if their conduct has induced the State to act to its detriment.
  • In Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Subhagwanti (1966), the Court allowed a waiver of a statutory right (not a fundamental right) where the statute expressly permitted it.
  • The National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (2014) (NALSA) judgment, while recognising transgender persons’ rights, affirmed that constitutional rights cannot be contracted away.

Exceptions are extremely narrow. A waiver may be recognised only where the Constitution itself provides for a voluntary relinquishment (e.g., Article 31A’s saving of certain agrarian reform laws, or the voluntary acceptance of a benefit under a statutory scheme that expressly conditions the benefit on foregoing a specific right). Even then, the Court scrutinises whether the waiver is informed, voluntary, and not contrary to public policy.

For the aspirant, the key takeaway is that fundamental rights are generally non‑waivable. Any contractual clause or administrative action that purports to make a citizen give up a fundamental right (such as the right to equality, freedom of speech, or life and personal liberty) is void under Article 13(2). The distinction between waiver and estoppel is a frequent examiner’s trap.

The Preamble’s Role in Basic Structure Jurisprudence

The Preamble, though not enforceable by itself, has been elevated by the Supreme Court to a guiding star for interpreting the Constitution’s basic structure. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the majority held that the Preamble reflects the “basic features” of the Constitution — sovereignty, socialism, secularism, democracy, republic, justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity — and that these features cannot be amended out of existence. The Court treated the Preamble as a key to unlock the meaning of the basic structure doctrine.

Subsequent cases have reinforced this role:

  • Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980): The Court used the Preamble’s promise of “socialist” and “secular” to strike down clauses of the 42nd Amendment that sought to curtail judicial review, holding that the amendment destroyed the basic structure.
  • S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994): The Court read “secularism” from the Preamble into the basic structure, ruling that a state government’s dismissal on grounds of religious bias violated the Constitution’s secular character.
  • Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975): The Court referred to the Preamble’s “democratic republic” to invalidate the 39th Amendment’s clause that immunised the Prime Minister’s election from judicial scrutiny.

The Preamble also serves as an interpretive aid for ambiguous provisions. In Berubari Union v. Unknown (1960), the Court held that the Preamble is not a source of power but a key to the minds of the framers. Later, in Kesavananda, the Court reversed this view, declaring the Preamble part of the Constitution and amendable only subject to the basic structure limitation.

Practical tip: When a question asks whether a particular amendment violates the basic structure, check whether the amendment alters any of the Preamble’s declared objectives. The Preamble’s words — “Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity” — are the constitutional lodestars for basic structure analysis.

The Constitutional Position of the Vice President

The Vice President of India occupies a unique dual role under Articles 63 to 71. He is elected by an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament (Article 66), not by state legislatures, distinguishing his election from that of the President. The Vice President serves as the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 64), presiding over its proceedings, casting a vote in case of a tie, and exercising procedural powers under the Rules of Procedure.

Key constitutional features:

  • Term and removal: The Vice President holds office for five years (Article 67). He may resign by writing to the President. Removal requires a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a majority of its total membership and agreed to by the Lok Sabha (Article 67(b)). This dual‑house requirement is a frequent examination point.
  • Acting President: When the President’s office falls vacant due to death, resignation, or removal, the Vice President acts as President until a new President is elected (Article 65). During such period, he enjoys all powers and immunities of the President.
  • Immunity and privileges: The Vice President enjoys the same immunities as the President under Article 361, including immunity from criminal proceedings during tenure.
  • No executive functions: Unlike the President, the Vice President has no executive authority except when acting as President. His role is largely legislative and ceremonial.

Judicial pronouncements have clarified his position. In Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006), the Supreme Court held that the Vice President’s casting vote in the Rajya Sabha is a constitutional function, not a political one, and is subject to judicial review only for constitutional compliance. In K. K. Venugopal v. Union of India (1995), the Court affirmed that the Vice President’s procedural rulings as Chairman are protected by parliamentary privileges under Article 105.

For the aspirant, the critical distinctions are: (1) electoral college composition (Parliament only), (2) removal procedure (Rajya Sabha resolution + Lok Sabha concurrence), (3) acting President role, and (4) absence of executive powers. Confusing the Vice President’s removal with that of the President (which requires impeachment by both Houses with a two‑thirds majority) is a common error.

  • Assuming the doctrine of eclipse applies to post‑constitutional laws; it is limited to pre‑1950 statutes.
  • Treating severability as a mechanical excision without testing legislative intent, functional independence, and substantial alteration.
  • Believing fundamental rights can be waived by contract; they are non‑waivable except where the Constitution expressly permits.
  • Confusing the Vice President’s removal procedure with presidential impeachment; the Vice President requires only a Rajya Sabha resolution plus Lok Sabha concurrence.
  • Overlooking that the Preamble’s “socialist”, “secular”, and “integrity” were inserted by the 42nd Amendment and are now part of the basic structure.
  • Misapplying the basic structure test by ignoring the Preamble’s declared objectives as interpretive guides.
  • Neglecting the distinction between waiver and estoppel in fundamental rights jurisprudence.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee on the Rules of Procedure and Its Legacy for Parliamentary Conduct

The Constituent Assembly constituted a Committee on Rules of Procedure on 14 August 1947 under the chairmanship of Dr. Rajendra Prasad, with members including B. N. Rau, H. V. Kamath, and K. M. Munshi. The committee’s mandate was to draft standing orders that would govern the Assembly’s debates, voting, and committee work. Its report, presented on 22 July 1948, was adopted with minor amendments and became the procedural backbone for the Assembly’s final sessions.

The rules introduced several innovations that survive in the present Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha rule‑books: (1) a structured order of business distinguishing legislative, financial, and deliberative items; (2) a formal mechanism for the introduction of private members’ bills; (3) detailed provisions for the formation and functioning of select committees, joint committees, and the Committee on Petitions; (4) a clear code for maintaining decorum, including the power of the Chair to name a member for disorderly conduct. The committee also prescribed the quorum (one‑tenth of the total membership) and the method for recording divisions, which later informed Article 100 of the Constitution.

After the Constitution came into force, the Rules of Procedure of the Constituent Assembly were adapted by the Provisional Parliament (1950‑1952) and subsequently by the first Lok Sabha (1952). The Speaker’s authority to interpret the rules, the concept of a “half‑hour discussion” on matters of urgent public importance, and the practice of “Zero Hour” all trace their lineage to the 1948 rules. The committee’s emphasis on transparency — requiring that all debates be recorded verbatim — established the precedent for the official parliamentary debates (Lok Sabha Debates, Rajya Sabha Debates) that are now primary sources for constitutional interpretation.

Judicial recognition of this legacy appears in Keshav Singh v. Speaker, Legislative Assembly (1965), where the Supreme Court held that the procedural rules framed by the Constituent Assembly constitute “law” within the meaning of Article 13, and any amendment to them must conform to the constitutional amendment procedure if they affect substantive rights. The Court also noted that the rules embody the principle of parliamentary sovereignty exercised within constitutional limits, reinforcing the basic structure doctrine.

For the aspirant, the key take‑aways are: the committee’s composition, the date of adoption (22 July 1948), the specific procedural innovations that migrated into the current parliamentary rule‑books, and the judicial pronouncement that these rules have the force of law. Questions often test the distinction between rules made by the Assembly (which are “law”) and ordinary standing orders made later by each House (which are “internal regulations”).

The Constitutional Status of National Symbols: Flag, Anthem, Emblem, and Judicial Pronouncements

The Indian Constitution does not enumerate the national flag, anthem, or emblem in its text. Their legal status derives from a combination of statutes, executive orders, and judicial interpretation. The Flag Code of India, 2002 (superseding the 1968 code) regulates the display of the tricolour; the Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950 protects the state emblem (the Lion Capital of Ashoka) and the name “India”; the national anthem, “Jana Gana Mana”, is governed by the Ministry of Home Affairs’ 1971 order prescribing the occasions and manner of its rendition.

In Union of India v. Naveen Jindal (2004), the Supreme Court declared that the right to fly the national flag is a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(a), subject to reasonable restrictions under the Flag Code. The Court struck down the provision that prohibited private citizens from hoisting the flag on non‑governmental premises, holding that the Flag Code, being an executive instruction, could not curtail a fundamental right without legislative backing.

The anthem’s constitutional dimension was examined in Shyam Narayan Chouksey v. Union of India (2018). The Court upheld the 1971 order mandating the playing of the anthem in cinema halls before feature films, reasoning that the order promoted “constitutional patriotism” and did not violate Article 19(1)(a) because it was a reasonable restriction in the interest of public order. However, the Court clarified that the order could not be enforced through criminal sanctions beyond the prescribed fine.

Regarding the emblem, the Supreme Court in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2005) held that unauthorised use of the Lion Capital on private stationery constitutes an offence under the 1950 Act, and that the Act’s penal provisions are compatible with Article 19(2) as they protect the dignity of a state symbol.

These judgments collectively illustrate that while the symbols themselves are not constitutional provisions, the Courts treat them as extensions of the constitutional values enshrined in the Preamble — sovereignty, unity, and fraternity. The executive may regulate their use, but any restriction must satisfy the test of reasonableness under Article 19(2). Aspirants should remember the hierarchy: Constitution → Statute (Flag Code, Emblems Act) → Executive Order (Anthem) → Judicial Review.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “Which of the following statements is correct regarding the legal status of the national anthem in India?” Options: (a) It is a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(a). (b) It is protected by a statutory provision enacted by Parliament. (c) It is regulated by an executive order of the Ministry of Home Affairs, and the Supreme Court has upheld its mandatory playing in cinema halls as a reasonable restriction. (d) It is part of the Constitution under Article 51A.
Correct answer: (c). The national anthem is not mentioned in the Constitution nor in any parliamentary statute. Its rendition is governed by the 1971 executive order of the Ministry of Home Affairs. In Shyam Narayan Chouksey v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court upheld the order requiring the anthem to be played in cinema halls, holding it a reasonable restriction under Article 19(2). Options (a), (b), and (d) are factually incorrect.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes national symbols with fundamental rights, first identify the source of the rule (statute, executive order, or judicial order). Then apply the Article 19(2) reasonableness test. Remember that the Flag Code is an executive instruction, not a statute, so it cannot override a fundamental right without legislative sanction — this is the precise reasoning in Naveen Jindal. For the anthem, the executive order has been upheld because it serves a “constitutional patriotism” objective and imposes only a minor penalty. Keep a mental table: Symbol → Governing Instrument → Key Case → Constitutional Test.

The Evolution of the Basic Structure Doctrine After Kesavananda: Key Expansions and Limits

Following the landmark Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) decision, the Supreme Court progressively enumerated the “basic features” that cannot be amended under Article 368. In Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), the Court added “free and fair elections” to the basic structure, striking down the 39th Amendment’s clause that insulated the Prime Minister’s election from judicial scrutiny. The Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) judgment reinforced two pillars: (i) the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, and (ii) the power of judicial review itself, declaring that any amendment that destroys this balance violates the basic structure.

Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) introduced the doctrine of prospective overruling for amendments placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973, holding that such laws are open to challenge if they damage the basic structure. S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) elevated “secularism” — read from the Preamble — to a basic feature, ruling that the dismissal of a state government on religious grounds is unconstitutional. In I. R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), the Court held that all Ninth Schedule laws enacted after the Kesavananda date are subject to the basic structure test, effectively nullifying the protective shield of the Schedule for post‑1973 enactments.

The National Judicial Appointments Commission case (Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India, 2015) added “independence of the judiciary” and “primacy of the Chief Justice of India in judicial appointments” to the basic structure, striking down the 99th Amendment. More recently, Justice K. S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) recognized “right to privacy” as an intrinsic part of the basic structure, linking it to the Preamble’s guarantee of “liberty”.

Limits have also been delineated. The Court has refused to treat “socialist” or “secular” as immutable in a way that precludes policy shifts, provided the core democratic framework remains intact (R. C. Poudyal v. Union of India, 1993). The doctrine does not extend to ordinary legislation; only constitutional amendments are scrutinised. Moreover, the Court has held that the basic structure test is not a “blank cheque” for judicial activism — it applies only when an amendment alters the Constitution’s identity.

For examination purposes, memorise the chronological chain: Kesavananda (1973) → Indira Gandhi (1975) → Minerva Mills (1980) → Waman Rao (1981) → Bommai (1994) → Coelho (2007) → NJAC (2015) → Puttaswamy (2017). Each case added a specific feature; questions often ask to match the feature with the case or to identify the latest addition.

The Interplay Between the Preamble and Fundamental Duties under Article 51A

The Preamble’s ideals — justice, liberty, equality, fraternity — were supplemented by the 42nd Amendment (1976) which inserted Part IVA containing ten Fundamental Duties (Article 51A). The 86th Amendment (2002) added the eleventh duty: “to provide opportunities for education to his child or ward between the age of six and fourteen years”. Although duties are non‑justiciable, the Supreme Court has repeatedly used them as interpretive aids to ascertain the scope of Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.

In Ranganath Misra v. Union of India (1996), the Court observed that the duty “to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood” (Article 51A(e)) illuminates the meaning of “fraternity” in the Preamble and can guide the State in framing laws under Article 19(2). In M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1997), the Court linked the duty “to protect and improve the natural environment” (Article 51A(g)) with the Directive Principle under Article 48A, holding that the State’s obligation to enforce environmental standards derives strength from the citizens’ corresponding duty.

Javed v. State of Haryana (2003) dealt with a law disqualifying persons with more than two children from contesting panchayat elections. The Court upheld the law, reasoning that the duty “to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women” (Article 51A(e)) and the Preamble’s commitment to “social justice” justify reasonable restrictions on the right to contest elections under Article 243D.

The 2018 judgment in Joseph Shine v. Union of India (decriminalising adultery) referenced Article 51A(e) and the Preamble’s “dignity of the individual” to strike down a gender‑discriminatory provision, illustrating how duties can reinforce constitutional morality. Conversely, the Court has refused to enforce duties directly; in State of Karnataka v. Umadevi (2006) it held that a citizen cannot claim a writ for non‑performance of a duty by another citizen.

Key points for the aspirant: (1) Duties were added by the 42nd and 86th Amendments; (2) They are non‑justiciable but serve as interpretive tools; (3) The Preamble’s “fraternity”, “justice”, and “liberty” are frequently read together with specific duties; (4) Landmark cases — Ranganath Misra, M. C. Mehta, Javed, Joseph Shine — demonstrate this interplay; (5) The Court never creates a direct cause of action from a duty alone.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on Emergency Provisions: Design, Safeguards, and Judicial Review

The emergency provisions (Articles 352, 356, 360) were among the most debated sections of the Constitution. The Drafting Committee, chaired by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, presented the emergency clauses on 4 November 1948. Members such as K. M. Munshi, H. V. Kamath, and Maulana Abul Kalam Azad expressed apprehension that a broad “internal disturbance” ground could be misused to suspend federalism. Ambedkar defended the provisions, arguing that a sovereign state must possess the power to protect its integrity, but he accepted the insertion of parliamentary approval and a six‑month time limit as safeguards.

The original Article 352 allowed proclamation on grounds of “war, external aggression or internal disturbance”. The 44th Amendment (1978), enacted after the 1975‑77 Emergency, replaced “internal disturbance” with “armed rebellion”, required the President to act on the written advice of the Cabinet, and mandated that both Houses approve the proclamation within one month by a special majority. Article 356 (President’s Rule) was similarly tightened: the proclamation must be laid before each House, and if not approved within two months it lapses; the 44th Amendment also introduced the requirement that the President’s satisfaction be based on “objective material” — a phrase later interpreted by the Supreme Court in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) as subject to judicial review.

Article 360 (Financial Emergency) has never been invoked. The Assembly debated whether a financial crisis should trigger a suspension of financial autonomy of states. The final text requires a proclamation by the President, approval by Parliament within two months, and empowers the Union to give directions to states regarding financial propriety. The safeguard of parliamentary oversight mirrors that of Articles 352 and 356.

Judicial review of emergency proclamations was affirmed in Minerva Mills (1980) and concretised in Bommai, where the Court laid down the “objective test”: the President’s satisfaction must be based on relevant material, not on political whim. The Court also held that the proclamation under Article 356 is justiciable and can be struck down if mala fide or based on irrelevant grounds. The 44th Amendment’s requirement of written Cabinet advice was upheld as a constitutional check on executive arbitrariness.

For the aspirant, the essential chronology is: Drafting Committee report (Nov 1948) → Original Articles 352/356/360 (1950) → 44th Amendment (1978) → Minerva Mills (1980) → Bommai (1994). Typical exam questions ask to identify the amendment that substituted “armed rebellion” for “internal disturbance”, the majority required for parliamentary approval, or the judicial test for reviewing President’s Rule. Remember that Article 360 remains a dead letter but its procedural safeguards are identical to the other two emergency articles.

Common Traps

  • Confusing the 42nd Amendment’s insertion of “socialist”, “secular”, “integrity” with the original Preamble text; the original Preamble (1950) did not contain these words.
  • Assuming the Flag Code of India is a statute; it is an executive instruction and cannot override fundamental rights without legislative backing.
  • Treating Fundamental Duties as justiciable rights; they are non‑justiciable and only serve as interpretive aids.
  • Believing the basic structure doctrine applies to ordinary legislation; it restricts only constitutional amendments under Article 368.
  • Thinking the President’s satisfaction under Article 356 is immune from judicial review; Bommai established the objective test.
  • Mixing up the removal procedure of the Vice President (Rajya Sabha resolution + Lok Sabha concurrence) with presidential impeachment (two‑thirds majority in both Houses).
  • Overlooking that the 44th Amendment introduced the requirement of written Cabinet advice for emergency proclamations, a frequent factual question.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee System: Steering, Drafting, and the Architecture of Consensus

The Constituent Assembly's work was channelled through a network of committees that performed the granular labour of constitutional design. The Steering Committee, chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad, coordinated the work of all other committees and set the Assembly's agenda. The Drafting Committee, chaired by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar with members N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, K. M. Munshi, Mohammad Saadullah, B. L. Mitter (later replaced by N. Madhava Rao), and D. P. Khaitan (died 1948, replaced by T. T. Krishnamachari), produced the final text after processing reports from functional committees. The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities, chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, had five sub‑committees: the Sub‑Committee on Fundamental Rights (J. B. Kripalani), the Sub‑Committee on Minorities (H. C. Mookerjee), the Sub‑Committee on North‑East Frontier Tribal Areas (Gopinath Bordoloi), the Sub‑Committee on Excluded and Partially Excluded Areas (A. V. Thakkar), and the Sub‑Committee on the North‑West Frontier (Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan). The Union Powers Committee and Union Constitution Committee (both chaired by Nehru) defined the Centre's legislative, executive, and financial architecture. The Provincial Constitution Committee (Patel) drafted the state‑level framework. The Rules of Procedure Committee (Prasad) governed Assembly proceedings. The Committee on the Functions of the Constituent Assembly (G. V. Mavalankar) clarified its dual role as constitution‑making body and provisional legislature. The House Committee (B. Pattabhi Sitaramayya) managed logistics. The Credentials Committee (Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar) verified membership. The Order of Business Committee (K. M. Munshi) scheduled debates. The Ad Hoc Committee on the National Flag (Rajendra Prasad) finalised the tricolour design. The Ad Hoc Committee on the Supreme Court (S. Varadachari) shaped judicial provisions. The Committee on Chief Commissioners' Provinces (B. N. Rau) administered centrally governed territories. The Expert Committee on Financial Provisions (N. R. Pillai) advised on fiscal federalism. The Linguistic Provinces Commission (S. K. Dhar, later J. V. P. Committee) informed the States Reorganisation debate. This committee system allowed parallel processing of complex issues, ensured specialist input, and produced the reports that the Drafting Committee harmonised into a coherent text. The Assembly debated each committee report clause‑by‑clause, a process that generated the Constituent Assembly Debates — the primary interpretive resource for original intent.

Article 1 and the 'Union of States' Formulation: Drafting History and Federal Implications

Article 1 declares: "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States." The phrase "Union of States" was a deliberate choice by the Drafting Committee to distinguish the Indian federation from the American "Federation of States." Dr. Ambedkar explained on 4 November 1948 that the Union was not the result of an agreement among states and no state had the right to secede. The states had no independent existence before the Constitution; they were created by it. The Union Constitution Committee (Nehru) had recommended a strong Centre with residuary powers vested in the Union (unlike the US, Canada, or Australia where residuary powers rest with states). The Provincial Constitution Committee (Patel) designed the state executive and legislature on the Westminster model. The Government of India Act 1935 provided the structural template: a federal scheme with a powerful Centre, Governor's special responsibilities, and a three‑list distribution (Federal, Provincial, Concurrent). The Drafting Committee retained this architecture but replaced the Crown's paramountcy with popular sovereignty. The expression "Union of States" appears in Article 1; "territory of India" in Article 1(3) includes states, union territories, and any acquired territories. The States Reorganisation Act 1956 and subsequent state‑creation laws (e.g., Gujarat and Maharashtra 1960, Punjab Reorganisation 1966, Uttarakhand 2000, Jharkhand 2000, Chhattisgarh 2000, Telangana 2014, Jammu & Kashmir Reorganisation 2019) demonstrate Parliament's unilateral power under Article 3 to alter state boundaries, names, and areas — a power inconsistent with a compact‑based federation. The Supreme Court in State of West Bengal v. Union of India (1963) held that the Constitution is not a league of states; the Union is indestructible. In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Court reiterated that federalism is a basic feature but the Union's overriding powers (Articles 3, 249, 250, 252, 256, 257, 352, 356, 360) make it quasi‑federal or federal with a unitary bias. The Preamble's "Union of States" thus signals a constitutional design where the Centre holds the constituent power over state boundaries, a feature examined in questions on Article 3, the basic structure, and the distinction between coming together and holding together federations.

Examiner's Twist: Article 1 vs Article 3
A question states: "Article 1 describes India as a 'Union of States'. Article 3 empowers Parliament to form new states, alter boundaries, and change names by a simple majority. Does Article 3 violate the federal principle implicit in Article 1?"
No. The Constituent Assembly deliberately chose "Union of States" to indicate that the Union is indestructible while states are reorganisable. Ambedkar clarified that the Union was not formed by an agreement among states; therefore, no state possesses a right to territorial integrity against Parliament's will. Article 3 requires the President to refer the bill to the affected state legislature for its views, but Parliament is not bound by those views (the 1956 States Reorganisation Act proceeded despite opposition from several states). The Supreme Court in Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay (1960) and State of West Bengal v. Union of India (1963) upheld this architecture. Federalism in India is a basic feature (Bommai), but it is a federalism with a strong Centre, not a compact federalism. The "federal principle" in India accommodates unilateral reorganisation; the basic structure doctrine protects the existence of states as federal units, not their specific boundaries.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question contrasts Article 1's "Union of States" with Article 3's unilateral reorganisation power, do not call it a contradiction. Frame the answer as: "The Constitution adopts a holding‑together federation where the Union possesses constituent power over state boundaries. Article 1 describes the nature of the polity; Article 3 provides the mechanism for its territorial adaptation. The basic structure protects federalism as a principle of power‑sharing, not as a guarantee of immutable state borders." Cite Ambedkar's 4 November 1948 speech and Bommai for authority.

The Citizenship Debates: Partition, Migration, and the Transitional Provisions of Part II

Part II (Articles 5–11) was drafted against the backdrop of Partition, mass migration, and the problem of determining who belonged to the new polity. The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities (Patel) and its Sub‑Committee on Fundamental Rights (Kripalani) initially considered citizenship, but the matter was referred to a separate Citizenship Committee chaired by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar. The Drafting Committee presented the citizenship clauses on 10 August 1949. Article 5 conferred citizenship at commencement (26 January 1950) on persons domiciled in the territory of India who were born in India, or either parent was born in India, or who had been ordinarily resident for five years immediately preceding commencement. Article 6 addressed migrants from Pakistan: those who migrated before 19 July 1948 became citizens if ordinarily resident since migration; those migrating after that date needed registration after six months' residence. Article 7 dealt with migrants to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 — they lost Indian citizenship unless they returned under a permit for resettlement. Article 8 covered persons of Indian origin residing outside India who could register as citizens through Indian diplomatic missions. Article 9 provided that voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship terminated Indian citizenship. Article 10 continued citizenship subject to parliamentary law. Article 11 empowered Parliament to regulate citizenship by law, leading to the Citizenship Act 1955. The debates reveal a tension between jus soli (birth on soil) and jus sanguinis (descent). The 19 July 1948 cut‑off in Article 6 corresponded to the permit system introduced by the Government of India to regulate migration. The phrase "ordinarily resident" was interpreted in Louis De Raedt v. Union of India (1991) as requiring a settled purpose, not mere physical presence. The Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2003 introduced the concept of "illegal migrant" and barred citizenship by birth if either parent was an illegal migrant. The Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2019 provided a fast‑track for non‑Muslim migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan who entered before 31 December 2014, reigniting debate on the secular character of citizenship law and its consistency with Article 14. The Constituent Assembly rejected a purely religious test for citizenship (proposed by some members for Hindu migrants) but accepted the temporal and territorial conditions in Articles 6 and 7 as pragmatic responses to Partition. For the aspirant, the key distinctions are: Article 5 (commencement citizenship), Article 6 (Pakistan migrants), Article 7 (migrants to Pakistan), Article 8 (overseas Indians), Article 9 (voluntary foreign citizenship), Article 11 (parliamentary plenary power). Questions often test the cut‑off dates, the distinction between "domicile" and "residence", and the scope of Article 11 vis‑à‑vis fundamental rights.

The Rajya Sabha's Constitutional Design: Federal Representation, Legislative Powers, and Deadlock Resolution

The Council of States (Rajya Sabha) was modelled on the Council of State under the Government of India Act 1919 and the Canadian Senate (appointed, not elected by popular vote), but with critical modifications. The Union Constitution Committee (Nehru) recommended a second chamber to provide sober second thought, represent federal units, and accommodate talent not suited to electoral politics. Article 80 provides for 238 representatives of states and union territories elected by the legislative assemblies of states and union territories through proportional representation by single transferable vote, plus 12 members nominated by the President for literature, science, art, and social service. The allocation of seats (Fourth Schedule) is based on population, giving larger states more representation — unlike the US Senate's equality of states. The Rajya Sabha is a permanent body not subject to dissolution; one‑third of its members retire every two years (Article 83). Its legislative powers are co‑equal with the Lok Sabha except for Money Bills (Article 110), which can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha may recommend amendments within 14 days, which the Lok Sabha may accept or reject. For ordinary bills, a deadlock is resolved by a joint sitting (Article 108) summoned by the President, where the Lok Sabha's numerical superiority prevails. For Constitution Amendment Bills (Article 368), no joint sitting exists; each House must pass the bill by the prescribed special majority, and the Rajya Sabha has an absolute veto. The Rajya Sabha has exclusive powers under Article 249 (Parliament may legislate on State List subjects in national interest by a two‑thirds Rajya Sabha resolution) and Article 312 (creation of All India Services by a two‑thirds Rajya Sabha resolution). The Vice President is the ex‑officio Chairman (Article 64). The Supreme Court in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) held that the Chairman's decision on disqualification under the Tenth Schedule is subject to judicial review. In State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977), the Court recognised the Rajya Sabha's federal role but upheld Parliament's power to reorganise states. The Delimitation Commission adjusts territorial constituencies for Lok Sabha, but Rajya Sabha representation changes only when state boundaries change or the Fourth Schedule is amended. The Rajya Sabha's design reflects a weighted federalism: states are represented proportionally, not equally; the Centre can create All India Services; and the Lok Sabha dominates financial and confidence matters. This asymmetry is frequently tested in questions on federalism, Money Bill certification (e.g., Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank, 2019), and the basic structure.

The Uniform Civil Code Debate in the Constituent Assembly: Gender, Minority Rights, and Directive Principle 44

Article 44 (originally Article 35 of the Draft Constitution) directs the State to "endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India." The debate in the Constituent Assembly (23 November 1948) exposed deep fissures. K. M. Munshi argued that a common civil code was essential for national integration and gender justice, citing the Hindu law reforms he had piloted in Bombay. Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar supported it as a secularising measure. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar favoured a voluntary code initially, stating that the State should not impose it on unwilling communities but should make it available as an option. Mohammad Ismail, B. Pocker Bahadur, Hussain Imam, and Naziruddin Ahmad opposed inclusion, arguing that personal law was integral to religious identity protected by Article 25 (then Article 19). Maulana Abul Kalam Azad warned that compulsion would alienate minorities. The compromise was to place it in the Directive Principles (Part IV), making it non‑justiciable but a governance directive. The Hindu Code Bill (1951–56), enacted as four separate Acts (Marriage, Succession, Minority and Guardianship, Adoption and Maintenance), reformed Hindu personal law but left Muslim, Christian, Parsi, and Jewish personal laws untouched. The Special Marriage Act 1954 provided a secular marriage option. The Supreme Court in Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985) urged a UCC while granting maintenance under Section 125 CrPC. In Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) and John Vallamattom v. Union of India (2003), the Court reiterated the Article 44 directive. The Law Commission's 21st Report (2018) recommended a gradual, piecemeal approach rather than a single omnibus code, focusing on gender‑just reforms within each community's law. The Uttarakhand Uniform Civil Code Act 2024 is the first state‑level enactment, though its constitutional validity under the Concurrent List (Entry 5: marriage, divorce, infants, adoption) and Article 44's directive remains subject to judicial scrutiny. The debate illustrates the tension between Article 25 (freedom of religion), Article 26 (religious denominations' autonomy), Article 29 (cultural rights), and Article 44 (directive for uniformity). The Constituent Assembly's decision to make it a Directive Principle reflects a sequentialist approach: reform Hindu law first (as the majority community), build consensus, then extend. This history is essential for questions on secularism, gender justice, federalism (personal law is Concurrent), and the enforceability of Directive Principles.

  • Confusing the Steering Committee (chaired by Rajendra Prasad, agenda‑setting) with the Drafting Committee (chaired by Ambedkar, text‑production); they had distinct mandates and memberships.
  • Assuming "Union of States" in Article 1 implies a coming‑together federation like the USA; Ambedkar explicitly rejected this, and Article 3 confirms the Union's constituent power over state boundaries.
  • Treating Articles 5–11 as a complete citizenship code; they are transitional provisions for commencement only, with Article 11 delegating comprehensive legislation to Parliament (Citizenship Act 1955).
  • Believing the Rajya Sabha represents states equally; seat allocation follows population (Fourth Schedule), and its federal role is weighted, not symmetric.
  • Thinking a joint sitting under Article 108 applies to Constitution Amendment Bills; Article 368 requires each House to pass separately by special majority — the Rajya Sabha has an absolute veto on amendments.
  • Assuming Article 44 (UCC) is justiciable or that the Constituent Assembly mandated immediate enactment; it is a Directive Principle, and the Assembly deliberately chose a voluntary, phased approach.
  • Overlooking that the Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2019 introduces a religious criterion for the first time in statutory citizenship law, raising distinct Article 14 and secularism questions separate from the original Part II framework.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee on the Union Judiciary and the Architecture of Judicial Review

The Constituent Assembly constituted a dedicated Union Judiciary Committee in July 1947 under the chairmanship of Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar. Its mandate was to design the judicial hierarchy, define the scope of judicial review, and settle the mode of appointment and removal of judges. The committee submitted its report in February 1948, recommending a single integrated judiciary with the Supreme Court at the apex, High Courts for each state, and a uniform system of subordinate courts. It expressly endorsed judicial review as a constitutional necessity, drawing on the American model but limiting the language to “procedure established by law” (Article 21) rather than the broader “due process” clause, a choice influenced by the Japanese Constitution of 1946 (Article 31). The committee also proposed that the President appoint Supreme Court judges after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, a formulation that later evolved into the collegium system through judicial interpretation (Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India, 1993). The report’s emphasis on the independence of the judiciary — security of tenure until age 65, salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund, and removal only by impeachment — was incorporated almost verbatim into Articles 124‑147 and 214‑231. The committee’s deliberations also recorded a minority view favouring a “due process” guarantee, which was rejected on the ground that it would unduly restrict legislative policy space. This historical choice resurfaced in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), where the Court read “procedure established by law” as requiring fairness, reasonableness, and non‑arbitrariness, effectively importing a due‑process standard through interpretive expansion.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on the Citizenship Provisions: Transitional Articles 5‑11 and the Citizenship Act 1955

Articles 5‑11 of the Constitution were drafted as transitional provisions to determine the citizenship status of persons at the commencement of the Constitution on 26 January 1950. The Assembly’s Citizenship Committee, chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, examined three competing models: the British common‑law allegiance model, the American jus soli model, and a hybrid model based on domicile and descent. The debates (November‑December 1948) revealed a consensus on single citizenship for the whole Union, rejecting any notion of state‑level citizenship that could fragment national unity. Article 5 conferred citizenship on persons domiciled in India who were born in India, or whose parents were born in India, or who had been ordinarily resident for five years. Articles 6‑10 addressed migrants from Pakistan, persons of Indian origin residing abroad, and voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship. Article 11 expressly empowered Parliament to regulate citizenship by law, making the constitutional scheme open‑ended. The Citizenship Act, 1955 operationalised this mandate, providing for acquisition by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, and incorporation of territory. Subsequent amendments — 1986 (restricting birth‑right citizenship), 1992 (gender‑neutral descent), 2003 (overseas citizenship), 2005 (dual citizenship for Persons of Indian Origin), 2015 (merging OCI and PIO), and the controversial 2019 amendment introducing a religious criterion for persecuted minorities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan — illustrate the legislative flexibility envisaged by Article 11. The 2019 amendment has been challenged on the touchstone of Article 14 (equality) and the basic structure doctrine, with the Supreme Court yet to deliver a final verdict as of 2024.

Examiner's Twist: Transitional vs Permanent Citizenship Provisions
A question asks: “Which of the following statements is correct? (a) Articles 5‑11 constitute a complete and exhaustive code of citizenship for all time. (b) Article 11 empowers Parliament to make any law on citizenship, including laws that violate fundamental rights. (c) The Citizenship Act, 1955, was enacted under Article 11 and can be amended only by a constitutional amendment. (d) Articles 5‑10 determine citizenship at commencement; Article 11 delegates future legislation to Parliament.”
Correct answer: (d). Articles 5‑10 are expressly transitional, fixing citizenship status only at the commencement of the Constitution. Article 11 is a plenary legislative delegation, not a constitutional entrenchment; the Citizenship Act, 1955, is ordinary legislation amendable by simple majority. Statement (a) is false because the Constitution envisages future laws. Statement (b) is false — Parliament’s power under Article 11 remains subject to fundamental rights and basic structure. Statement (c) is false because the Act is not a constitutional provision.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question cites Articles 5‑11, first identify whether it concerns the commencement stage (Articles 5‑10) or the ongoing legislative power (Article 11). Remember that the 2019 amendment is the only one to introduce a religious classification; treat it as a separate constitutional‑law issue involving Article 14 and secularism, not as a routine amendment of the 1955 Act.

The Constituent Assembly's Debate on the Abolition of Untouchability and the Drafting of Article 17

The abolition of untouchability was one of the few social‑reform provisions that attracted near‑unanimous support in the Constituent Assembly. The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities formed a sub‑committee on untouchability, chaired by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, which submitted its report in October 1947. The draft article (originally Article 11 of the Draft Constitution) read: “Untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. The enforcement of any disability arising out of untouchability shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law.” The Assembly debated the clause on 29 November 1948. Members such as K. M. Munshi and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar emphasised that the provision must be self‑executing and not merely declaratory. Ambedkar argued that the word “practice” should cover both overt acts and systemic discrimination. The final text, adopted as Article 17, is concise: “Untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. The enforcement of any disability arising out of untouchability shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law.” The Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955 (later renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955) gave teeth to the article, prescribing penalties for enforcing disabilities. The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 further strengthened protection. Judicial interpretation has expanded the scope: in State of Karnataka v. Appa Balu Ingale (1993) the Supreme Court held that Article 17 imposes a positive obligation on the State to eradicate untouchability, and in Kumar Padmaja v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2020) the Court ruled that social boycott of Dalits constitutes a “practice” of untouchability. The provision is also cited as a facet of the basic structure (S. R. Bommai v. Union of India, 1994) because it embodies the constitutional commitment to human dignity and equality.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee on the Election Commission and the Constitutional Design of Electoral Provisions

The Committee on the Election Commission, chaired by K. M. Munshi, was tasked with designing an independent electoral machinery. Its report (March 1948) recommended a single, permanent Election Commission for both Union and State elections, vested with the power of superintendence, direction, and control over the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of elections (Article 324). The Committee rejected the alternative of separate State Election Commissions, arguing that a unified body would ensure uniformity and prevent partisan manipulation. The Constitution originally provided for a single Chief Election Commissioner; the Election Commission (Amendment) Act, 1993 (effective 1 October 1993) transformed it into a multi‑member body with two additional Election Commissioners, a change upheld in T. N. Seshan v. Union of India (1995), where the Supreme Court affirmed the Commission’s independence and its authority to enforce the Model Code of Conduct. The Representation of the People Acts, 1950 and 1951 were enacted under Article 327 to flesh out qualifications, disqualifications, and election procedures. The Committee also debated the inclusion of a “right to vote” as a fundamental right; the Assembly decided against it, placing the franchise under statutory law (Article 326) to allow reasonable restrictions such as age, residence, and disqualification for corrupt practices. The 61st Amendment (1988) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18, demonstrating the flexibility of the statutory framework. Recent controversies — such as the 2021 amendment to the Representation of the People Act allowing postal ballots for senior citizens and persons with disabilities — illustrate the ongoing evolution of the electoral architecture envisaged by the Constituent Assembly.

The Constituent Assembly's Approach to the Protection of Religious Freedom: Articles 25‑28 and the Secularism Debate

The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities drafted the religious‑freedom clauses (originally Articles 19‑22 of the Draft Constitution) after extensive consultations with religious leaders, legal experts, and minority representatives. The debates (December 1948‑January 1949) centred on three tensions: (1) the scope of “propagation” versus “conversion”, (2) the permissible grounds for State regulation (public order, morality, health), and (3) the relationship between individual freedom and denominational autonomy (Article 26). K. M. Munshi and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar advocated a broad “propagation” right but accepted State regulation to prevent forced conversions. Muslim members, including Maulana Abul Kalam Azad and B. Pocker Bahadur, insisted that Article 25 protect the right to manage religious institutions without State interference, leading to the distinct guarantee in Article 26 for religious denominations. The final text — Articles 25‑28 — balances positive secularism (State may regulate secular activities associated with religion) with negative secularism (State shall not favour any religion). The phrase “subject to public order, morality and health” in Article 25(1) was borrowed from the Irish Constitution (Article 44.2.1°). Judicial interpretation has shaped the doctrine: Shirur Mutt v. Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments (1954) defined “essential religious practices” test; Ratilal Panachand Gandhi v. State of Bombay (1954) held that regulation must not destroy the core of the right; S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) declared secularism a basic structure feature, linking Articles 25‑28 to the Preamble’s “secular” (inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976). The 42nd Amendment also added “socialist” and “integrity”, but the secularism jurisprudence remains rooted in the original Constituent Assembly design, which deliberately avoided establishing a State religion while permitting reform of religious practices (e.g., the Hindu Code Bills, 1955‑56). Contemporary disputes — such as the Sabarimala temple entry case (Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala, 2018) and the hijab ban in Karnataka (Resham v. State of Karnataka, 2022) — continue to test the “essential practices” test and the limits of State regulation under Article 25(2).

  • Confusing the Union Judiciary Committee’s recommendation of “procedure established by law” with the American “due process” clause; the former was a deliberate textual choice, not an oversight.
  • Treating Articles 5‑11 as a permanent citizenship code; they are expressly transitional, with Article 11 delegating all future citizenship law to Parliament.
  • Assuming Article 17 is merely declaratory; the Supreme Court has read it as imposing a positive duty on the State to eradicate untouchability, enforceable through legislation and judicial review.
  • Believing the Election Commission was always a multi‑member body; the original Constitution provided for a single Chief Election Commissioner, the multi‑member structure came only in 1993.
  • Equating “secularism” in the Preamble (added 1976) with the original religious‑freedom articles; the Constituent Assembly’s secularism was embedded in Articles 25‑28 long before the Preamble amendment.
  • Overlooking that the “essential religious practices” test was a judicial innovation (Shirur Mutt, 1954), not a textual requirement in Articles 25‑26.

The Doctrine of Eclipse and Severability under Article 13: Judicial Treatment of Pre‑Constitutional and Post‑Constitutional Laws

Article 13 of the Constitution establishes the supremacy of fundamental rights over inconsistent laws. Clause (1) declares that all laws in force immediately before the commencement of the Constitution shall be void to the extent of their inconsistency with Part III. Clause (2) prohibits the State from making any law that takes away or abridges fundamental rights. The Supreme Court has developed two distinct doctrines to operationalise these clauses: the doctrine of eclipse and the doctrine of severability.
