The doctrine of eclipse applies exclusively to pre‑constitutional laws. In Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955) the Court held that a law which was valid when enacted but becomes inconsistent with a fundamental right after the Constitution’s commencement does not die; it merely falls into a state of dormancy — an “eclipse”. The law revives automatically if the constitutional impediment is removed, for instance by a constitutional amendment. This principle was reaffirmed in State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974), where the Court clarified that the eclipse doctrine does not extend to post‑constitutional laws; a law enacted after 26 January 1950 that contravenes a fundamental right is void ab initio under Article 13(2).

The doctrine of severability, by contrast, governs the fate of a statute when only a part of it is unconstitutional. In R.M.D.C. (Mysore) Ltd. v. Union of India (1957) the Court laid down the test: if the valid and invalid portions are so inextricably mixed that the legislature would not have enacted the valid part alone, the whole statute falls; otherwise the valid portion survives. The Court applied this test in A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) to uphold the preventive detention provisions of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, while striking down the procedural safeguards that violated Article 21. Later, in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980), the Court used severability to preserve the basic structure of the Constitution while invalidating the clauses that sought to amend it beyond the permissible limits.

Both doctrines illustrate the Court’s effort to balance legislative continuity with constitutional supremacy. Eclipse preserves the legislative intent of pre‑Constitution enactments, allowing them to spring back to life when the constitutional barrier disappears. Severability respects the legislature’s modular drafting, excising only the offending fragment. Together they ensure that Article 13 operates as a scalpel rather than a sledgehammer.

The Constituent Assembly’s Debate on the Uniform Civil Code and Its Reflection in Article 44

The question of a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) provoked intense discussion in the Constituent Assembly between 1948 and 1949. The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities, chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, examined whether personal laws governing marriage, divorce, inheritance and adoption should be replaced by a common code. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, as Law Minister, argued that a UCC was essential for national integration and gender justice, but he also recognised the political sensitivity of imposing a single code on diverse religious communities. K.M. Munshi and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar supported a directive principle rather than a justiciable right, fearing that a mandatory UCC would exacerbate communal tensions.

Muslim members, notably Maulana Abul Kalam Azad and B. Pocker Bahadur, contended that personal law was an integral part of religious freedom guaranteed under Articles 25‑28. They warned that a compulsory UCC would violate the secular compact the Assembly was forging. The debate culminated in the placement of the UCC in Part IV as Article 44: “The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.” The word “endeavour” signalled a non‑justiciable, aspirational obligation, leaving the timing and manner of implementation to future legislatures.

Judicial pronouncements have repeatedly urged the legislature to fulfil this directive. In Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985) the Supreme Court held that a Muslim woman was entitled to maintenance under Section 125 of the CrPC, and observed that a UCC would help remove contradictions in personal laws. The Parliament responded with the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, which limited the maintenance period. In Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) the Court again called for a UCC, linking it to the prevention of fraudulent conversions for bigamy. The 21st Law Commission (2018) recommended a gradual, consultative approach, emphasising gender justice within each community before a common code.

The UCC debate thus illustrates the Constituent Assembly’s deliberate choice to embed a transformative goal in the Directive Principles, allowing democratic politics to negotiate the pace of reform while keeping the constitutional vision alive.

Technique: Applying Eclipse vs. Severability
A pre‑Constitution statute, the XYZ Act, 1948, contains a provision that conflicts with Article 19(1)(a). After the Constitution’s commencement, the Parliament amends the Constitution to remove that conflict. Simultaneously, a post‑Constitution statute, the ABC Act, 1960, contains two sections: Section 3 violates Article 21, while Section 4 is perfectly valid. The legislature would have enacted Section 4 independently. Determine the constitutional status of the XYZ Act provision and the two sections of the ABC Act.
The XYZ Act provision, being a pre‑Constitution law, falls under the doctrine of eclipse. It became dormant when the Constitution commenced but revives automatically once the constitutional amendment removes the inconsistency; therefore it is now fully operative. For the ABC Act, Section 3 is a post‑Constitution law that violates a fundamental right; under Article 13(2) it is void ab initio and cannot be saved by eclipse. Section 4, being severable and independently enactable, survives the invalidation of Section 3 under the doctrine of severability laid down in R.M.D.C. v. Union of India (1957). Hence, the XYZ Act provision is revived, Section 3 of the ABC Act is void, and Section 4 remains valid.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes pre‑ and post‑Constitution statutes, first classify each law by its enactment date. Apply eclipse only to pre‑Constitution laws; apply void‑ab‑initio rule to post‑Constitution laws. Then test severability on the remaining valid portions. A quick two‑step checklist (date → doctrine) prevents the common error of extending eclipse to post‑Constitution enactments.

The Constitutional Scheme for the Creation of All‑India Services under Article 312 and Its Impact on Federal Balance

Article 312 empowers Parliament to create All‑India Services (AIS) common to the Union and the States, provided the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) passes a resolution supported by not less than two‑thirds of the members present and voting. The first such services were the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) and the Indian Police Service (IPS), constituted under the All‑India Services Act, 1951. The Indian Forest Service (IFoS) was added in 1966 through a similar resolution. Recruitment to these services is conducted by the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC), and members serve under the ultimate control of the Union government while being posted to State cadres.

The design reflects a deliberate centralising tendency in the federal architecture. By entrusting the Union with the recruitment, cadre allocation, and disciplinary authority over senior civil servants, the Constitution ensures a unified administrative standards and a pool of officers loyal to the national perspective. However, this arrangement has been criticised for eroding State autonomy. States argue that they have limited say in the selection, transfer, and promotion of officers who implement State policies, leading to friction documented in the Sarkaria Commission (1988) and the Punchhi Commission (2010). Both commissions recommended greater State participation in cadre management and a more consultative transfer policy.

Judicially, the Supreme Court in State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) upheld the validity of the All‑India Services Act, emphasising that Article 312 is an enabling provision that does not violate the federal structure because it requires a special majority in the Rajya Sabha, representing the States. The Court also noted that the services facilitate the integration of the country and the maintenance of essential services across State boundaries. Nevertheless, the tension persists: the 2019 amendment to the All‑India Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules sought to give States a larger role in disciplinary proceedings, signalling an ongoing negotiation between central efficiency and State accountability.

The Constitutional Framework for the Office of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker: Powers, Impartiality, and Judicial Pronouncements

Articles 93 to 96 (Lok Sabha) and Articles 178 to 181 (State Legislative Assemblies) establish the offices of Speaker and Deputy Speaker. The Speaker presides over the House, certifies Money Bills under Article 110, decides on disqualification petitions under the Tenth Schedule, and exercises a casting vote in case of a tie. The Deputy Speaker performs the Speaker’s functions during vacancy or absence. Although the Constitution does not require the Speaker to resign from his political party, convention and the need for impartiality have led most Speakers to sever formal party ties upon election.

The Speaker’s power to adjudicate disqualification under the Tenth Schedule was subjected to judicial scrutiny in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992). The Supreme Court held that the Speaker’s decision is subject to judicial review on grounds of mala fides, perversity, or violation of natural justice, but not on the merits of the political defection itself. This ruling balanced the need for an internal legislative mechanism with constitutional safeguards. In Ravi S. Naik v. Union of India (1994) the Court clarified that the Speaker’s certification of a Money Bill is final and not justiciable, reinforcing the institutional primacy of the Lok Sabha in financial matters.

State-level Speakers enjoy analogous powers. The 1992 amendment to the Tenth Schedule (by the 52nd Amendment) extended the anti‑defection framework to State legislatures, making the Speaker’s role pivotal in maintaining party discipline. However, controversies such as the 2016 Arunachal Pradesh Assembly crisis, where the Speaker’s disqualification orders were challenged, illustrate the political sensitivity of the office. The Supreme Court’s intervention in Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker, Arunachal Pradesh Legislative Assembly (2016) reiterated that the Speaker cannot act in a manner that undermines the democratic mandate, and that judicial review remains available for constitutional violations.

The Doctrine of Parliamentary Privileges and Their Judicial Review

Articles 105 (Parliament) and 194 (State Legislatures) confer two broad categories of privileges: freedom of speech in the House and immunity from court proceedings for anything said or any vote given; and the power to punish for contempt or breach of privilege. These privileges are derived from the British parliamentary tradition but are constitutionally entrenched in India. The scope of “freedom of speech” was examined in Keshav Singh v. Speaker, Legislative Assembly, Uttar Pradesh (1965), where the Supreme Court held that parliamentary privileges are not absolute and must yield to fundamental rights, particularly Article 21. The Court asserted that a legislator’s arrest for a speech made in the House would violate the privilege only if the speech pertains to legislative business.

The power to punish for contempt was tested in Raja Ram Pal v. Hon’ble Speaker, Lok Sabha (2007). The Court upheld the expulsion of members for accepting money to ask questions (“cash‑for‑query” scandal), ruling that the House’s disciplinary authority extends to acts that undermine the dignity of the institution, even if they also constitute criminal offences. However, in State of Kerala v. K. Ajith (2021) the Court clarified that legislative privilege cannot shield a member from prosecution for a criminal act committed outside the House, such as assault on a public servant.

Judicial review of privilege matters is thus a nuanced exercise: the courts respect the House’s exclusive jurisdiction over its internal proceedings but intervene when fundamental rights are infringed or when the privilege claim is used to obstruct ordinary criminal justice. This balance preserves legislative autonomy while preventing the misuse of privilege as a cloak for illegality.

  • Confusing the doctrine of eclipse with the doctrine of severability; eclipse revives pre‑Constitution laws only after the constitutional impediment is removed, whereas severability excises the offending part of any statute.
  • Assuming Article 44 makes the Uniform Civil Code justiciable; it remains a directive principle, enforceable only through political will, not judicial mandate.
  • Believing All‑India Services can be created by a simple parliamentary majority; Article 312 requires a two‑thirds majority in the Rajya Sabha, reflecting the federal consensus requirement.
  • Thinking the Speaker’s disqualification decisions under the Tenth Schedule are immune from judicial review; Kihoto Hollohan (1992) established limited review on mala fides and perversity.
  • Treating parliamentary privilege as a blanket immunity from all criminal prosecution; the Supreme Court has repeatedly held that privilege does not cover acts unrelated to legislative functions.
  • Overlooking that the Deputy Speaker’s powers are derivative and activate only during the Speaker’s vacancy or absence, not as a parallel authority.
  • Misreading Article 13(2) as applying eclipse to post‑Constitution laws; the Court has consistently held that post‑Constitution laws inconsistent with fundamental rights are void ab initio.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on Emergency Provisions and the Scope of Article 352

The Constituent Assembly devoted three full sittings between 1947 and 1949 to the emergency clauses that would become Articles 352, 356 and 360. The Drafting Committee, chaired by B. R. Ambedkar, presented a draft that distinguished three situations: war or external aggression (Article 352), failure of constitutional machinery in a State (Article 356) and financial emergency (Article 360). Members such as K. M. Munshi, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar and H. V. Kamble argued for stringent parliamentary oversight, fearing that a broad “war” definition could be abused to suspend fundamental rights indefinitely. The Assembly adopted a compromise: a proclamation under Article 352 must be laid before each House of Parliament and ceases to operate unless approved by both Houses within one month (later reduced to two months by the 44th Amendment, 1978). The debate also clarified that “external aggression” includes armed attack by a foreign power but not mere diplomatic pressure, a reading later affirmed in State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977). The 44th Amendment further inserted the requirement that the President act on the written advice of the Cabinet, and that the proclamation be revoked if the Lok Sabha passes a disapproval resolution. These safeguards were a direct response to the Assembly’s fear of executive overreach, a fear that resurfaced during the 1975‑77 Emergency and prompted the judicial pronouncement in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) that the power to amend the Constitution does not include the power to destroy its basic structure, including the emergency safeguards.

The Design of the Finance Commission in the Constituent Assembly and Its Constitutional Mandate

Article 280, which creates the Finance Commission, was drafted by the Union Finance Sub‑Committee under the chairmanship of K. Santhanam. The original text mandated a Commission every five years, consisting of a Chairman and four members appointed by the President, with qualifications ranging from experience in public finance to expertise in economics. The first Finance Commission, constituted in 1951 under K. C. Neogy, set the template for vertical devolution (the share of Union taxes to States) and horizontal distribution (the inter‑se shares among States) based on population, income distance and fiscal effort. The 1971 amendment (the 7th Amendment) expanded the Commission’s terms of reference to include grants‑in‑aid under Article 275. The 1992 amendment (the 73rd and 74th Amendments) required the Commission to recommend measures to augment the Consolidated Fund of States for Panchayats and Municipalities. The 2000 amendment (the 84th Amendment) froze the inter‑se shares until the first Commission after the 2026 census, a move intended to protect States that had successfully controlled population growth. The 2017 Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council, created under Article 279A, introduced a parallel fiscal federal body; the Finance Commission’s 15th report (2020‑25) explicitly recognised the GST Council’s revenue‑sharing mechanism and recommended a “compensation cess” to offset revenue loss for States. The Commission’s recommendations are advisory, yet the Union government has historically accepted them in full, a practice that underscores the constitutional convention of fiscal federalism.

Worked Example: Inter‑State Distribution Formula
A question asks: “Explain how the 15th Finance Commission balanced the criteria of population (2011 Census) and demographic performance in its horizontal devolution formula.”
The 15th Finance Commission assigned a weight of 15 % to the 2011 population figure and 12.5 % to demographic performance (measured by the total fertility rate). The remaining weights were: income distance 45 %, area 15 %, forest and ecology 10 %, and tax effort 2.5 %. By giving a modest weight to the 2011 population, the Commission rewarded States with larger current populations while the demographic performance weight incentivised States that had achieved lower fertility rates. The combined effect reduced the share of high‑population, high‑fertility States (e.g., Uttar Pradesh, Bihar) relative to the 14th Commission, and increased the share of States like Kerala and Tamil Nadu. The answer should cite the specific percentages and explain the policy rationale: balancing equity (population) with efficiency (demographic performance).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “the constitutional mandate” of a body, quote the exact Article number and the original wording (e.g., “Article 280(1) – ‘The President shall, within two years from the commencement of this Constitution and thereafter at the expiration of every fifth year…’”). Then add the key amendments (7th, 73rd, 84th) and the latest Commission’s term of reference. This two‑step citation (text + evolution) scores full marks for both knowledge and analytical depth.

The Debate on Fundamental Duties in the Constituent Assembly and the 42nd Amendment

The original Constitution of 1950 contained no chapter on duties; the framers believed that rights in Part III were sufficient to nurture civic responsibility. The idea of fundamental duties entered the constitutional discourse only during the Emergency, when the Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended a set of ten duties to “strengthen the spirit of patriotism and national integration.” The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted Part IVA, Article 51A, listing duties such as respecting the Constitution, the national flag and the national anthem; cherishing the noble ideals of the freedom struggle; protecting the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India; and promoting scientific temper. The amendment was passed with a two‑thirds majority in both Houses and ratified by more than half the States, satisfying Article 368(2). Critics, including H. M. Seervai, argued that duties without enforceability were mere hortatory exhortations. The Supreme Court in Ranganath Misra v. Union of India (1992) held that while Article 51A is not justiciable, it can be used as an interpretative aid to ascertain the scope of fundamental rights. The 86th Amendment (2002) added a duty to provide opportunities for education to children aged 6‑14, linking it to the newly inserted Article 21A. The 97th Amendment (2011) inserted a duty to promote cooperative societies. These incremental additions illustrate how the Constitution’s “living tree” character allows duties to evolve without altering the basic structure.

The Evolution of Judicial Review of Constitutional Amendments: From Shankari Prasad to Kesavananda Bharati

The first major confrontation between Parliament’s amending power and judicial review arose in Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951), where the Supreme Court upheld the First Amendment (which curtailed the right to property) on the ground that Article 368 conferred plenary amending power, including over fundamental rights. In Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan (1965) the Court reaffirmed this view, though Justice Hidayatullah dissented, warning that unlimited amendment could destroy the Constitution’s identity. The turning point came in Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967), where a 6‑5 majority held that Parliament could not amend Part III, invoking the doctrine of “prospective overruling” to protect past amendments. Parliament responded with the 24th Amendment (1971), explicitly stating that Article 368 includes power to amend fundamental rights and that such amendments are not subject to Article 13. The Supreme Court then delivered its landmark judgment in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), a 7‑6 decision that Parliament’s amending power is wide but cannot alter the “basic structure” of the Constitution. The Court enumerated illustrative basic features: supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secularism, separation of powers, federalism, and the dignity of the individual. Subsequent cases — Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980), Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) — refined the doctrine, holding that judicial review itself is a basic feature and that amendments placed in the Ninth Schedule after 1973 are subject to scrutiny. The 42nd Amendment attempted to curtail judicial review by inserting Articles 31C and 368(4)‑(5), but the Court struck down those clauses in Minerva Mills, reaffirming that the basic structure doctrine is an unwritten limitation on Article 368.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee on the Union Judiciary and the Establishment of the Supreme Court's Jurisdiction

The Union Judiciary Committee, chaired by Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, met between July and October 1947 to design the highest court of the new republic. Its report recommended a Supreme Court with a Chief Justice and seven puisne judges (later increased to 30 by the 2008 amendment), appointed by the President after consultation with the Chief Justice of India — a formulation that sowed the seeds of the collegium system. The Committee also drafted Articles 124‑147, establishing the Court’s original jurisdiction (disputes between the Union and States, and between States), appellate jurisdiction (civil, criminal and constitutional matters), and advisory jurisdiction under Article 143. A crucial debate centred on whether the Court should have the power to review constitutional amendments; the Committee left the question open, leading to the later judicial creation of the basic structure doctrine. The Committee also provided for a “judicial review” of legislative and executive action through Articles 32 and 226, embedding the power of the Supreme Court and High Courts to issue writs for enforcement of fundamental rights. The original provision for a “Supreme Court of India” replaced the Federal Court of India, which had functioned under the Government of India Act 1935. The first Chief Justice, H. J. Kania, took office on 28 January 1950. The Committee’s design has endured, though the appointment process was altered by the 99th Amendment (2014) creating the National Judicial Appointments Commission, which the Supreme Court struck down in Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (2015) as violating judicial independence, a basic feature.

  • Confusing the 44th Amendment’s emergency safeguards with the original Article 352 text; the 44th Amendment added Cabinet advice and Lok Sabha disapproval, which were absent in 1950.
  • Assuming the Finance Commission’s recommendations are binding; they are advisory, though convention treats them as mandatory.
  • Treating Fundamental Duties as justiciable rights; Article 51A is non‑justiciable and serves only as an interpretative aid.
  • Believing the basic structure doctrine was explicitly written into the Constitution; it is a judicial construct emerging from Kesavananda Bharati.
  • Thinking the collegium system was part of the original Constitution; it evolved from the “consultation” phrase in Article 124(2) and was formalised only in the 1990s.
  • Overlooking that the 24th Amendment was a direct legislative response to Golaknath, not a pre‑emptive measure.
  • Misreading Article 143 as granting the Supreme Court original jurisdiction over all advisory matters; it is limited to questions of law or fact referred by the President.

The above sections collectively deepen the aspirant’s grasp of the constitutional framework beyond the standard textbook narrative.

The Doctrine of Eclipse and its Application to Pre‑Constitutional Laws

The doctrine of eclipse addresses the fate of laws enacted before the commencement of the Constitution that conflict with the fundamental rights guaranteed in Part III. Article 13(1) declares that all laws in force immediately before the Constitution shall be void to the extent of inconsistency with fundamental rights. However, the Supreme Court in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955) held that such laws are not dead but merely eclipsed — they remain on the statute book in a dormant state and can be revived if the constitutional inconsistency is removed by a subsequent amendment. The rationale is that the pre‑constitutional legislature never intended to violate rights that did not exist at the time of enactment; therefore the law retains a latent validity.

The eclipse operates only while the fundamental right remains in force. When a constitutional amendment alters or removes the offending right, the eclipse lifts and the original law becomes fully operative again without the need for fresh legislation. This was affirmed in State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974), where a pre‑constitutional tax law inconsistent with Article 19(1)(g) was revived after the 4th Amendment curtailed that freedom. Conversely, in Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1959) the Court clarified that the doctrine does not apply to post‑constitutional laws; a law made after 26 January 1950 that contravenes a fundamental right is void ab initio under Article 13(2) and cannot be resurrected by later amendment.

Key procedural consequences follow. Courts may declare the inconsistent provision “eclipsed” rather than struck down, preserving the legislative framework for future revival. The doctrine also prevents a legislative vacuum: the eclipsed law continues to govern matters not touching the fundamental right. However, the revival is automatic only when the constitutional impediment is removed by a formal amendment; a mere judicial interpretation that narrows the right does not revive the law. This distinction was underscored in Keshavan Madhava Menon v. State of Bombay (1951), where the Court refused to revive a pre‑constitutional press law despite a restrictive reading of Article 19(1)(a), because the constitutional text itself had not been amended.

In practice, the doctrine of eclipse is invoked most often in challenges to colonial‑era statutes — such as the Indian Press (Emergency Powers) Act, 1931, or the Defence of India Act, 1939 — when a constitutional amendment expands or contracts the relevant fundamental right. Aspirants should note that the doctrine is a judicial construct, not an explicit textual provision, and its scope is limited to pre‑constitutional legislation.

The Doctrine of Severability in Constitutional Adjudication

Severability determines whether the unconstitutional portion of a statute can be excised while the remainder continues to operate. The Supreme Court in R.M.D.C. (Mysore) Ltd. v. Union of India (1957) laid down the classic test: the valid part must be capable of standing independently, the legislature must have intended the statute to survive even if the offending provision were removed, and the invalid portion must not be so intertwined with the rest that its removal would alter the legislative scheme. This “blue‑pencil” approach permits the Court to strike out only the offending words or sections, leaving a coherent, enforceable statute.

The doctrine was first applied in State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), where the Bombay Prohibition Act contained a provision banning possession of liquor for medicinal purposes. The Court held that the prohibition on medicinal possession was severable; the rest of the Act, which regulated manufacture and sale, remained valid. In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Court examined the Tenth Schedule’s anti‑defection provisions and severed the paragraph that barred judicial review, preserving the remainder of the Schedule. The principle also extends to delegated legislation: in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985), the Court severed an unconstitutional rule under the Press Council Act while upholding the parent statute.

Severability is not automatic. If the invalid provision constitutes the “core” of the legislation, or if the legislature would not have enacted the statute without it, the entire Act falls. The Court examines the legislative history, the preamble, and the scheme of the statute. For instance, in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980), the Court held that the amendment inserting Articles 31C and 368(4)‑(5) was not severable because it formed an integral part of the 42nd Amendment’s basic structure‑altering design. The doctrine thus balances judicial restraint with the need to preserve constitutional supremacy.

Worked Example
A pre‑constitutional law regulating the sale of essential commodities is challenged after a constitutional amendment removes the fundamental right that rendered it inconsistent. Explain the doctrine of eclipse and state the effect of the amendment on the law.
The doctrine of eclipse (Bhikaji Narain Dhakras, 1955) holds that a pre‑constitutional law inconsistent with a fundamental right becomes dormant, not void. It remains on the statute book but is unenforceable while the right exists. When a constitutional amendment removes or alters that right, the eclipse lifts automatically and the original law revives without fresh legislation (State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills, 1974). Therefore, after the amendment the challenged law becomes fully operative again, governing all matters within its original scope.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the eclipse‑versus‑void‑ab‑initio distinction with the mnemonic “Pre‑Con = Eclipse, Post‑Con = Void”. In MCQs, look for the phrase “pre‑constitutional law” and “amendment removes inconsistency” — that signals eclipse. For severability, recall the three‑prong test: independent operation, legislative intent, and non‑intertwining. A question that asks whether the whole Act falls usually hinges on whether the invalid part is the “core” of the legislation.

The Doctrine of Waiver of Fundamental Rights: Scope and Limits

The Supreme Court has consistently held that fundamental rights, being guarantees against the State, cannot be waived by an individual. In Basheshar Nath v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1959) a Constitution Bench ruled that a taxpayer’s voluntary payment of tax under a statute later declared unconstitutional did not constitute a waiver of the right to challenge the statute; the right under Article 14 (equality) and Article 19(1)(g) (freedom of trade) is non‑waivable because it protects the public interest as well as the individual. The Court emphasised that allowing waiver would enable the State to coerce citizens into surrendering constitutional protections.

Nevertheless, certain procedural or derivative rights may be waived if the waiver is voluntary, informed, and not contrary to public policy. In Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) the Court held that the right to livelihood under Article 21 cannot be waived by pavement dwellers who accepted alternative accommodation, because the right is rooted in human dignity. Conversely, in State of Karnataka v. Appa Balu Ingale (1993) the Court accepted a waiver of the right to be heard in a disciplinary proceeding where the employee explicitly and knowingly relinquished the opportunity. The distinction rests on whether the right is a “core” fundamental right (non‑waivable) or a procedural safeguard that can be foregone without undermining the constitutional scheme.

The doctrine also interacts with the principle of estoppel. In Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Subhagwanti (1966) the Court refused to estop a citizen from challenging a law on the ground that he had previously benefited from it, reiterating that fundamental rights are not subject to estoppel. Aspirants should note that the non‑waiver rule applies primarily to rights in Part III; Directive Principles (Part IV) and Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) are not justiciable and therefore the waiver question does not arise.

The Curative Petition and the Evolution of the Supreme Court’s Inherent Review Power

The curative petition is a narrow, extraordinary remedy created by the Supreme Court to prevent a miscarriage of justice after the exhaustion of review proceedings. It originated in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002), where a Constitution Bench held that the Court’s inherent power under Article 142, read with Article 32, permits a second review in exceptional circumstances. The grounds are strictly limited: (i) violation of principles of natural justice such as bias or denial of hearing; (ii) abuse of process of the Court; (iii) a manifest error apparent on the face of the record that results in a gross miscarriage of justice.

Procedurally, a curative petition must be accompanied by a certification from a senior advocate that the petition meets the prescribed grounds. It is first circulated in chambers to the three senior‑most judges (including the Chief Justice if available). If a majority finds merit, the petition is listed for open hearing; otherwise it is dismissed summarily. The Court in Union of India v. R. Gandhi (2010) reiterated that curative petitions are not a substitute for appeal and cannot be used to re‑argue merits. The remedy has been invoked sparingly — notable instances include the 2014 curative petition in the Nirbhaya case (review of death‑sentence confirmation) and the 2020 curative petition concerning the Ayodhya title suit, both dismissed for lack of qualifying grounds.

The curative petition underscores the Court’s commitment to finality while retaining a safety valve for egregious judicial error. It also illustrates the dynamic interpretation of Article 142, which empowers the Court to pass any order necessary for complete justice. Aspirants should distinguish curative petitions from review petitions (Article 137) and special leave petitions (Article 136): review corrects errors apparent on the record; curative addresses fundamental procedural defects that survived review.

The Doctrine of Legitimate Expectation in Administrative Law and Its Constitutional Underpinnings

Legitimate expectation arises when a public authority, by an express promise or a regular practice, leads a person to expect a particular benefit or procedure. Though not a substantive legal right, it can be enforced through judicial review on the ground that denying the expectation would be arbitrary, violating Article 14, or procedurally unfair, violating Article 21. The Supreme Court first recognised the doctrine in State of Kerala v. K. Bhaskaran (1985), where a government circular granting a concession to a class of employees created a legitimate expectation that could not be withdrawn without a fair hearing.

In Union of India v. Hindustan Development Corporation (1993) the Court held that a consistent practice of renewing licences generated a legitimate expectation of renewal, and the authority’s abrupt policy change without notice was arbitrary. The doctrine was further refined in Navjyoti Co‑operative Group Housing Society v. Union of India (1992), where the Court distinguished between a “procedural” expectation (right to be heard before a decision) and a “substantive” expectation (right to the benefit itself). Substantive expectations receive weaker protection; the authority may override them by showing a compelling public interest, provided the decision is reasoned and non‑discriminatory.

Constitutionally, the doctrine derives from the rule of law and the principle of non‑arbitrariness embedded in Article 14 (as expanded in E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu 1974) and the procedural fairness component of Article 21 (as articulated in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India 1978). It does not create a new cause of action but operates as a ground for judicial review of administrative action. The Court has cautioned that legitimate expectation cannot be invoked against a clear statutory provision or where the authority has reserved the right to change policy. Aspirants should be able to identify the three elements: (1) a clear, unambiguous representation or consistent practice; (2) reliance by the claimant; (3) unfairness in frustrating the expectation.

  • Confusing eclipse with void ab initio — eclipse applies only to pre‑constitutional laws; post‑constitutional inconsistent laws are void from inception.
  • Assuming severability is automatic — the Court applies the three‑prong test; if the invalid part is the legislative core, the whole statute falls.
  • Treating all fundamental rights as waivable — core rights (Articles 14, 19, 21) are non‑waivable; only certain procedural safeguards may be waived voluntarily.
  • Equating curative petition with a second appeal — curative petitions are limited to natural‑justice violations and abuse of process, not re‑evaluation of merits.
  • Believing legitimate expectation creates a substantive right — it is a ground for judicial review; the authority can still deny the benefit by demonstrating overriding public interest.
  • Overlooking the certification requirement for curative petitions — a senior advocate’s certificate is mandatory; without it the petition is not entertained.
  • Misapplying the blue‑pencil test to constitutional amendments — severability applies to ordinary legislation; constitutional amendments are judged by the basic structure doctrine, not by severability.

These advanced doctrines illustrate how the Constitution’s text, judicial innovation, and administrative practice interact to shape the living constitutional order.

The Constituent Assembly as Provisional Parliament: Dual Role and Legislative Output (1947–1952)

The Constituent Assembly performed a unique dual function: it served as the constitution‑drafting body and, from 15 August 1947 until the first general elections in 1952, as the provisional legislature of the Dominion of India. This arrangement flowed from the Indian Independence Act 1947, which declared that the Constituent Assembly would exercise all legislative powers formerly vested in the Central Legislative Assembly. The Assembly met in two distinct capacities — constitution‑making sessions (chaired by Dr Rajendra Prasad) and legislative sessions (chaired by G.V. Mavalankar as Speaker). The procedural separation was maintained through separate sittings, separate records, and distinct rules of procedure.

During its legislative avatar, the Assembly enacted 108 Acts, including the Preventive Detention Act 1950, the Representation of the People Act 1950 and 1951 (laying the electoral framework), the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act 1951, and the Essential Commodities Act 1955. Several of these statutes were enacted under the Government of India Act 1935 as adapted, since the Constitution had not yet come into force. The Preventive Detention Act 1950, passed in February 1950, became the first major test of fundamental rights under the new Constitution; its validity was upheld in A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950), establishing the narrow "procedure established by law" reading of Article 21 that persisted until Maneka Gandhi (1978).

The provisional Parliament also passed the Constitution (First Amendment) Act 1951, which inserted Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule to protect land‑reform laws from judicial invalidation. This amendment was moved by Jawaharlal Nehru in response to the Patna High Court striking down the Bihar Land Reforms Act 1950 and the Supreme Court's decision in Kameshwar Singh v. State of Bihar (1952) on compensation. The debates reveal a tension between the Assembly's constituent power (under Article 368) and its ordinary legislative power — a distinction the Supreme Court later clarified in Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951), holding that "law" in Article 13(2) does not include constitutional amendments.

The dual role ended with the constitution of the first Lok Sabha in April 1952. The transition was seamless because the Constitution itself (Article 379) provided that the Constituent Assembly would become the provisional Parliament until the first House of the People was constituted. This institutional continuity ensured legislative stability during the critical formative years. Aspirants should note that the provisional Parliament could not amend the Constitution's federal provisions requiring state ratification, as the states did not yet exist in their reorganised form — a point often tested in questions on the temporal scope of Article 368.

The First Constitutional Amendment (1951): Land Reform, Reasonable Restrictions, and the Ninth Schedule

The Constitution (First Amendment) Act 1951, enacted within fifteen months of the Constitution's commencement, remains the most consequential early amendment. It was driven by three judicial developments: (1) the Supreme Court's striking down of the Bihar Land Reforms Act in Kameshwar Singh (1952) on the ground that the compensation provision violated Article 31(2); (2) the Patna High Court's invalidation of press restrictions in Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi (1950) and Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950), which held that "public order" was not a ground for restricting Article 19(1)(a); and (3) the Punjab High Court's decision in Tara Singh Gopi Chand v. State of Punjab (1951) striking down a law restricting speech that tended to undermine friendly relations with foreign states.

The Amendment made three clusters of changes. First, it inserted Article 31A, saving laws providing for acquisition of estates (defined broadly to include jagirs, inams, muafi grants) from Articles 14, 19, and 31, provided the law received Presidential assent. Article 31B created the Ninth Schedule, placing specified Acts beyond judicial review for fundamental‑rights violations. The original Ninth Schedule contained 13 Acts, mostly land‑reform statutes from Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, and Madras. Second, it amended Article 19(2) to replace "undermines the security of the State" with "in the interests of the security of the State" and added three new grounds: "public order", "incitement to an offence", and "friendly relations with foreign States". The phrase "reasonable restrictions" was retained, but the expanded grounds gave the State wider latitude. Third, it validated the Preventive Detention Act 1950 and certain other laws retrospectively.

The Amendment was challenged in Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951). The Supreme Court, by a 5‑0 majority, upheld it, holding that Article 368 confers constituent power distinct from legislative power, and "law" in Article 13(2) refers only to ordinary legislation. This position was reversed in Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967), where a 6‑5 majority held that amendments are "law" under Article 13(2) and cannot abridge fundamental rights. Parliament responded with the 24th Amendment (1971), explicitly excluding constitutional amendments from Article 13, leading to Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and the basic‑structure doctrine. The Ninth Schedule, originally a shield for land reform, expanded to 284 Acts by the 76th Amendment (1994). In I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a nine‑judge bench held that Acts placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 (the date of Kesavananda) are open to challenge on basic‑structure grounds, establishing the "basic structure filter" for Ninth Schedule inclusions.

The First Amendment illustrates how judicial interpretation, political urgency (land reform was a Congress election promise), and constitutional design interacted. The "public order" ground inserted in Article 19(2) has been the basis for numerous subsequent restrictions, including the sedition law (Section 124A IPC) upheld in Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar (1962). Aspirants must trace the doctrinal arc: Shankari Prasad → Golak Nath → 24th Amendment → Kesavananda → I.R. Coelho — and understand that the Ninth Schedule is not a constitutional "black hole" but a qualified immunity subject to the basic‑structure test.

Examiner's Twist: Ninth Schedule and Basic Structure
A question states: "The Ninth Schedule provides absolute immunity to laws placed under it from judicial review." Identify the error and explain the correct position with reference to the relevant case law and the cut‑off date.
The statement is incorrect. In I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a nine‑judge bench of the Supreme Court held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment) are subject to judicial review on the touchstone of the basic structure of the Constitution. The Court applied the "basic structure filter": if a Ninth Schedule law destroys or damages the basic structure (e.g., judicial review, separation of powers, federalism), it can be struck down. Laws placed before 24 April 1973 enjoy blanket immunity (validated by the 24th Amendment and Kesavananda itself), but post‑1973 inclusions are not immune. The Ninth Schedule is therefore a qualified, not absolute, immunity.
Exam‑Day Strategy: First Amendment as a Pivot Point
Treat the First Amendment as the pivot connecting three high‑yield themes: (1) the amendment‑power jurisprudence (Shankari Prasad → Golak Nath → Kesavananda → I.R. Coelho); (2) the evolution of Article 19(2) grounds ("public order", "friendly relations", "incitement"); (3) the Ninth Schedule as a political‑constitutional instrument. In a 15‑marker, structure the answer chronologically: trigger (judicial decisions) → Amendment provisions → immediate challenge (Shankari Prasad) → long‑term doctrinal consequences. Always cite the cut‑off date (24 April 1973) for Ninth Schedule review — it is a favourite precise‑fact question.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on Emergency Provisions: Original Design and the 44th Amendment Correction

The emergency provisions (Articles 352–360) were among the most intensely debated chapters in the Constituent Assembly. The Drafting Committee, drawing heavily on Section 93 of the Government of India Act 1935 (which allowed the Governor to assume provincial administration) and the Weimar Constitution's Article 48, proposed a three‑tier scheme: National Emergency (Article 352), President's Rule in States (Article 356), and Financial Emergency (Article 360). The Assembly's debates reveal three fault lines: (1) the scope of "internal disturbance" versus "external aggression"; (2) the role of Parliament in approving and reviewing proclamations; (3) the suspension of fundamental rights, particularly Article 19.

H.V. Kamath moved an amendment to replace "internal disturbance" with "internal disturbance threatening the security of the State", fearing misuse. Dr Ambedkar opposed, arguing that the President's satisfaction was subjective but politically accountable. The original Article 352 allowed proclamation on grounds of "war, external aggression, or internal disturbance". Article 358 provided that Article 19 would be automatically suspended during a national emergency (without a separate order), and Article 359 empowered the President to suspend the right to move courts for enforcement of other fundamental rights (except Articles 20 and 21). The approval mechanism required Parliament's ratification within two months by a simple majority, and the proclamation could continue indefinitely with six‑monthly renewals.

The 1975–77 Emergency exposed the design flaws. The proclamation was issued on the ground of "internal disturbance" based on the Prime Minister's advice; Parliament ratified it with a depleted opposition; Article 19 was suspended automatically; and Article 359 orders barred judicial review of detention orders (leading to ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla, 1976). The Janata Government's 44th Amendment (1978) overhauled the framework: (1) "internal disturbance" was replaced by "armed rebellion" (Article 352); (2) the President can proclaim emergency only on the written advice of the Cabinet (not just the Prime Minister); (3) Parliamentary approval now requires a special majority (two‑thirds of members present and voting, and a majority of total membership) within one month; (4) Article 19 is suspended only if the emergency is proclaimed on grounds of war or external aggression — not armed rebellion (Article 358); (5) Article 359 orders cannot suspend Articles 20 and 21, and must be laid before Parliament; (6) the Lok Sabha can disapprove a proclamation by a simple majority resolution, forcing revocation (Article 352(7)).

Article 356 (President's Rule) was also tightened: the 44th Amendment added the requirement that the proclamation must be approved by both Houses within two months (previously no time limit), and the maximum duration was capped at three years (with yearly Parliamentary approval beyond one year), subject to the Election Commission certifying that elections cannot be held. The Sarkaria Commission (1988) and the Supreme Court in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) further constrained Article 356, establishing judicial review of the President's satisfaction, the requirement of "objective material", and the prohibition on dissolving the Assembly before Parliamentary approval. The 44th Amendment thus represents a constitutional correction informed by lived experience — a rare instance where the amendment process responded directly to a constitutional crisis.

The Constitutional Scheme of Citizenship: Partition, Migration, and the Evolution of Citizenship Law

Part II of the Constitution (Articles 5–11) and the Citizenship Act 1955 together constitute India's citizenship framework. The Constituent Assembly drafted these provisions against the backdrop of Partition, which displaced an estimated 14–18 million people. Articles 5–8 were designed as transitional provisions to determine citizenship at commencement (26 January 1950), while Article 11 empowered Parliament to regulate citizenship by law. Article 5 conferred citizenship on persons domiciled in India who were born in India, or whose parents were born in India, or who had been ordinarily resident for five years immediately preceding commencement. Article 6 granted citizenship to migrants from Pakistan who (or whose parents/grandparents) were born in undivided India, provided they migrated before 19 July 1948, or migrated after that date but were registered as citizens by an officer appointed by the Government of India. Article 7 dealt with migrants to Pakistan after 1 March 1947, denying citizenship unless they returned under a permit for resettlement. Article 8 covered persons of Indian origin residing outside India who could register as citizens through Indian diplomatic missions.

The Citizenship Act 1955 provided for acquisition by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, and incorporation of territory. It has been amended multiple times: the 1986 Amendment restricted birthright citizenship (requiring at least one parent to be a citizen); the 1992 Amendment allowed citizenship by descent through the mother; the 2003 Amendment introduced the concept of "illegal migrant" and barred them from citizenship by registration or naturalisation; the 2005 Amendment created Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI); and the Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2019 (CAA) provided a fast‑track path for Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan who entered India before 31 December 2014, excluding Muslims. The CAA's classification has been challenged under Article 14 (equality) and Article 15 (non‑discrimination), with the Supreme Court yet to deliver a final verdict as of 2024.

The Assam Accord (1985) and Section 6A of the Citizenship Act (inserted in 1985) created a special regime for Assam: persons who entered Assam from Bangladesh before 1 January 1966 were deemed citizens; those entering between 1 January 1966 and 25 March 1971 were disenfranchised for ten years; those entering after 25 March 1971 were to be detected and expelled. The Supreme Court in Assam Sanmilita Mahasangha v. Union of India (2014) referred the constitutional validity of Section 6A to a Constitution Bench, which is pending. The National Register of Citizens (NRC) in Assam (final list published 2019) excluded approximately 1.9 million applicants, raising questions of statelessness and due process.

The constitutional scheme thus evolved from a jus soli‑inclined framework at commencement to a progressively restrictive jus sanguinis model, with religion‑based differentiation introduced only in 2019. Aspirants must distinguish between constitutional provisions (Articles 5–11, which are transitional and spent) and statutory provisions (Citizenship Act 1955, which is the operative law), and track the interplay between the two — for instance, Article 11's plenary power is subject to fundamental rights, a point central to the CAA challenge.

The Doctrine of Constitutional Silence, Implied Powers, and Penumbral Reasoning in Indian Jurisprudence

The Indian Constitution, despite its length, contains silences — gaps where the text does not expressly address a question of power, procedure, or right. The Supreme Court has developed three related but distinct tools to navigate these silences: the doctrine of implied powers, the doctrine of incidental/ancillary powers, and penumbral reasoning (deriving unenumerated rights from the "penumbra" of enumerated guarantees). These tools are grounded in the principle that a constitution is a living instrument whose efficacy cannot be defeated by textual omissions.

The doctrine of implied powers was articulated in Rai Sahib Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955), where the Court held that the executive power of the Union and States (Articles 73 and 162) is co‑extensive with legislative power but also includes powers necessary for effective governance that are not purely legislative — such as entering into contracts, engaging in trade, or formulating policy — provided they do not violate statute or fundamental rights. In Union of India v. R. Gandhi (2010), the Court recognised an implied power of the Supreme Court to devise the curative petition procedure under Article 142, even though the Constitution mentions only review (Article 137) and special leave (Article 136). The doctrine of incidental powers, derived from the Canadian "peace, order, and good government" jurisprudence and applied via the Government of India Act 1935, allows a legislature to enact provisions incidental to its express legislative entries. In State of Rajasthan v. G. Chawla (1959), the Court held that the power to legislate on a topic includes the power to enact all incidental and ancillary provisions necessary to make the law effective.

Penumbral reasoning, borrowed from the U.S. Supreme Court's Griswold v. Connecticut (1965), was adopted in Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1962) (minority opinion of Justice Subba Rao) and firmly established in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), where the Court held that Article 21's "personal liberty" encompasses a bundle of rights (fair procedure, right to travel abroad, right to livelihood) that are the "penumbral" emanations of the enumerated guarantee. This reasoning underpinned the recognition of the right to privacy as a fundamental right in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), where the nine‑judge bench held that privacy is the constitutional core of human dignity, flowing from Articles 14, 19, and 21. The Court rejected the "silence means absence" argument, stating that constitutional silences are filled by the "constitutional culture" of the document.

These doctrines interact with the basic‑structure limitation: implied powers cannot be used to alter the Constitution's basic structure. In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Court struck down clauses of the 42nd Amendment that sought to oust judicial review, holding that Parliament's implied constituent power under Article 368 does not extend to destroying the basic structure. Aspirants should distinguish: (1) implied executive power (Articles 73/162) — administrative, subject to statute and fundamental rights; (2) incidental legislative power — necessary for effective exercise of express entries, judged by the "pith and substance" test; (3) penumbral rights — unenumerated fundamental rights derived from the "penumbra" of enumerated rights, now a core part of Article 21 jurisprudence. The common trap is conflating implied legislative power (which does not exist — legislatures have only express or incidental powers) with implied executive power.

  • Confusing the Constituent Assembly's legislative acts (1947–1950) with its constituent acts — the former were under the Government of India Act 1935, the latter under Article 368; only the latter are "constitutional amendments" for basic‑structure purposes.
  • Assuming the First Amendment's Ninth Schedule immunity is absolute — post‑Kesavananda (24 April 1973) inclusions are subject to basic‑structure review (I.R. Coelho).
  • Believing Article 19 is automatically suspended during any national emergency — the 44th Amendment limited automatic suspension to war/external aggression; armed rebellion emergencies do not suspend Article 19.
  • Treating Articles 5–8 as the current citizenship law — they were transitional provisions for commencement; the operative law is the Citizenship Act 1955 as amended.
  • Equating "internal disturbance" (pre‑1978) with "armed rebellion" (post‑44th Amendment) — the latter is a narrower, higher threshold requiring actual armed insurrection.
  • Conflating implied legislative power with incidental legislative power — Indian legislatures have no freestanding implied legislative power; they have only express entries plus incidental/ancillary powers necessary to make the express power effective.
  • Assuming penumbral reasoning allows courts to create any new right — the right must be traceable to the "penumbra" of an enumerated right or the constitutional core of dignity, liberty, or equality; it cannot be a free‑floating judicial preference.

The Constitutional Position of the President: Executive Power, Discretion, and Judicial Review

Article 52 establishes the President as the head of the Union executive, while Article 53 vests the executive power of the Union in the President, to be exercised either directly or through officers subordinate to him in accordance with the Constitution. The President acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister (Art. 74), a principle affirmed in Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974), where the Supreme Court held that the President’s satisfaction under Articles 123, 352, and 356 is the satisfaction of the Council of Ministers. Nevertheless, the Constitution carves out a narrow sphere of personal discretion. Under Article 75(3) the President appoints the Prime Minister, a power exercised when no party commands a clear majority — illustrated by the 1996 and 1998 hung‑parliament situations. Article 85 empowers the President to dissolve the Lok Sabha on the advice of the Prime Minister, but the President may refuse dissolution if the advice is mala fide, a point noted in R. C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) concerning ordinance‑making power. Article 123 authorises the President to promulgate ordinances when Parliament is not in session; the Court in R. C. Cooper ruled that the President’s satisfaction is justiciable and cannot be a mere rubber‑stamp. Article 356 (President’s Rule) was subjected to judicial review in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), where the nine‑judge bench held that the President’s proclamation is subject to judicial scrutiny for mala fides or irrelevance. The pardoning power under Article 72 was examined in Kehar Singh v. Union of India (1988), where the Court held that the President’s decision is open to limited judicial review on grounds of arbitrariness or non‑application of mind. The 44th Amendment (1978) curtailed the President’s emergency powers by requiring written advice of the Cabinet for proclamation under Article 352 and by limiting the suspension of Article 19 to war or external aggression. In practice, the President’s role remains largely ceremonial, but the constitutional text and judicial pronouncements preserve a residual discretionary core that can become decisive during political crises.

The Constitutional Position of the Vice‑President and the Rajya Sabha: Role, Powers, and Precedents

Articles 63 to 71 delineate the office of the Vice‑President, who is elected by an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament (Art. 66). The Vice‑President serves a five‑year term (Art. 67) and can be removed only by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a majority of its total membership and agreed to by the Lok Sabha (Art. 67(b)). As ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Art. 89), the Vice‑President presides over its proceedings, maintains order, and exercises a casting vote in the event of a tie (Art. 100). The Chairman’s rulings on points of order are final, subject only to a motion of no‑confidence under Article 90, which has never been successfully moved. The Vice‑President also acts as President when the latter’s office falls vacant, or when the President is unable to discharge functions (Art. 65). In K. K. Venugopal v. Union of India (1995) the Supreme Court clarified that the Vice‑President’s casting vote is a constitutional duty, not a political discretion, and must be exercised in accordance with parliamentary conventions. The Rajya Sabha’s special powers — such as authorising Parliament to legislate on State List subjects in the national interest (Art. 249) and creating All‑India Services (Art. 312) — are exercised through resolutions moved in the House where the Vice‑President’s procedural control is pivotal. The Vice‑President’s neutrality is reinforced by the convention that the office‑holder resigns from party membership upon election, a practice observed since 1952. Although the Vice‑President lacks independent executive authority, the office constitutes a crucial institutional bridge between the two Houses and a constitutional safeguard for the continuity of the Union executive.

Technique
A question asks: "Explain the constitutional basis and judicial interpretation of the Vice‑President’s casting vote in the Rajya Sabha." Provide a concise answer referencing the relevant Articles and the leading case.
The Vice‑President, as ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha under Article 89, exercises a casting vote when the House is equally divided on any question (Article 100). This power is not discretionary but a constitutional duty to ensure that the legislative process does not stall. In K. K. Venugopal v. Union of India (1995), the Supreme Court held that the casting vote must be exercised in accordance with established parliamentary conventions and cannot be used to advance partisan interests. The Court emphasised that the Chairman’s role is neutral and that the casting vote is a procedural mechanism, not a substantive legislative power. Therefore, the constitutional basis lies in Articles 89 and 100, and judicial interpretation confirms its limited, non‑political character.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the “constitutional position” of an office, structure the answer in three layers: (1) textual provisions (Articles), (2) conventions and practice, (3) key judicial pronouncements. Cite at least one landmark case for each office; the Vice‑President’s casting vote and the President’s ordinance power are favourite examiners’ hooks.

The Doctrine of Public Interest Litigation: Constitutional Basis, Evolution, and Limits

Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in India derives its constitutional foundation from Articles 32 and 226, which empower the Supreme Court and High Courts to issue directions, orders, or writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights. The relaxation of the traditional locus standi requirement began with Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979), where the Court entertained a letter from a journalist on behalf of undertrial prisoners, recognising that “any member of the public” could approach the Court for enforcement of constitutional rights of a disadvantaged group. S. P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981) formalised the “epistolary jurisdiction”, holding that a postcard or letter could be treated as a writ petition when it raises a question of public importance. Subsequent landmark PILs expanded the doctrine: Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984) on bonded labour; M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) on environmental degradation, introducing the principle of absolute liability; Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) on sexual harassment at the workplace, where the Court laid down guidelines later codified in the 2013 Act. The Supreme Court, in State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal (2010), cautioned against frivolous PILs and laid down guidelines requiring the petitioner to demonstrate bona fide interest, absence of personal gain, and that the matter affects a large section of society. The Court also warned that PIL cannot become a substitute for governance or a tool for judicial overreach into policy domains reserved for the executive and legislature. The evolution reflects a dynamic balance between judicial activism — ensuring access to justice for the marginalised — and judicial restraint — preserving separation of powers.

The Constitutional Framework for Citizenship: Articles 5‑11, the Citizenship Act 1955, and Judicial Interpretation

Articles 5 to 11 of the Constitution, operative at commencement (26 January 1950), defined the initial citizenry: domicile‑based citizenship (Art. 5), citizenship for migrants from Pakistan (Art. 6), citizenship for migrants to Pakistan (Art. 7), citizenship for persons of Indian origin residing abroad (Art. 8), and voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship resulting in loss of Indian citizenship (Art. 9). Article 10 preserves citizenship subject to parliamentary law, and Article 11 empowers Parliament to regulate citizenship. The Citizenship Act 1955 (as amended) provides the operative regime. Sections 3‑5 govern citizenship by birth, descent, and registration; Sections 6‑7 cover naturalisation; Section 7A introduces Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) after the 2003 amendment; Section 9 provides for termination upon voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship. Major amendments include the 1986 amendment restricting birth‑right citizenship to children with at least one Indian parent, the 2003 amendment creating OCI and Persons of Indian Origin (PIO) cards, the 2015 amendment merging PIO into OCI, and the 2019 Citizenship (Amendment) Act (CAA) granting expedited naturalisation to non‑Muslim migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan who entered before 31 December 2014. Judicial interpretation has shaped the framework: State of Assam v. Union of India (1971) upheld the Assam Accord’s cut‑off date for detection of illegal migrants; Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India (2005) struck down the Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act as unconstitutional; Assam Sanmilita Mahasangha v. Union of India (2014) directed the updating of the National Register of Citizens (NRC) under statutory authority. The Supreme Court in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) recognised the right to privacy as a fundamental right, influencing debates on data collection for NRC. The constitutional scheme thus combines a transitional constitutional definition with a detailed statutory regime subject to parliamentary amendment and judicial review.

The Fundamental Duties under Article 51A: Enforceability, Judicial Treatment, and Policy Impact

Inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee, Article 51A originally enumerated ten Fundamental Duties, ranging from respecting the Constitution and national symbols to promoting harmony and protecting the environment. The 86th Amendment (2002) added the eleventh duty — to provide opportunities for education to children between six and fourteen years (Art. 51A(k)). Unlike Fundamental Rights, Fundamental Duties are non‑justiciable; Article 51A expressly states that they shall not be enforceable by any court. Nevertheless, the judiciary has used them as interpretive aids. In M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1997), the Supreme Court invoked the duty to protect the environment (Art. 51A(g)) to justify directions for controlling vehicular pollution in Delhi. In AIIMS Students Union v. AIIMS (2001), the Court referred to the duty to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood (Art. 51A(e)) while upholding a reservation policy. The duties also inform legislative policy: the Swachh Bharat Mission (2014) draws on the duty to protect public property and the environment; the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act (2009) operationalises the duty under Art. 51A(k). The Law Commission’s 2015 report recommended making certain duties justiciable, but Parliament has not acted. The constitutional design thus positions Fundamental Duties as moral obligations that guide state policy and judicial reasoning without creating direct legal liability for citizens.

  • Confusing the President’s discretionary powers with the Governor’s — the President’s discretion is narrower and explicitly listed (Art. 75(3), 85, 123, 356), whereas the Governor enjoys broader discretion under Art. 163.
  • Assuming the Vice‑President’s casting vote is a political tool — it is a constitutional duty exercised neutrally, as held in K. K. Venugopal v. Union of India (1995).
  • Treating PIL as an unrestricted right to file any petition — the Supreme Court’s 2010 guidelines require bona fide public interest and prohibit frivolous or motivated filings.
  • Believing the Citizenship Act 1955 is static — it has been amended six times (1986, 1992, 2003, 2005, 2015, 2019), each altering acquisition and termination criteria.
  • Thinking Fundamental Duties are justiciable — Article 51A expressly declares them non‑enforceable, though courts use them as interpretive guides.
  • Equating the President’s ordinance power with legislative power — ordinances lapse unless approved by Parliament within six weeks of reassembly (Art. 123).
  • Assuming the Vice‑President can be removed by a simple majority — removal requires a Rajya Sabha majority of total membership and Lok Sabha agreement (Art. 67(b)).

The Constituent Assembly’s Deliberations on the Uniform Civil Code and Article 44

Article 44 of the Constitution, placed in Part IV as a Directive Principle of State Policy, directs the State to endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India. The provision emerged from intense debates in the Constituent Assembly between November 1948 and January 1949. The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities, chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, initially recommended a uniform civil code as a justiciable right. However, strong opposition from Muslim members such as Mohammad Ismail, B. Pocker Bahadur, and Hussain Imam argued that personal law was an integral part of religious identity protected under Article 25. The Drafting Committee, led by B. R. Ambedkar, ultimately placed the uniform civil code in the non‑justiciable Directive Principles, recording in the debates that the matter was left to the wisdom of future legislatures. Ambedkar himself stated on 23 November 1948 that “the State shall endeavour to secure a uniform civil code” but emphasised that the State could not impose it by force.

The Hindu Code Bills (1955‑56) — covering marriage, succession, adoption and maintenance — were enacted as a partial step towards codification for Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs. Muslim personal law remained largely uncodified, governed by the Shariat Application Act 1937 and the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939. The Supreme Court in Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985) invoked Article 44 while granting maintenance to a divorced Muslim woman, sparking a political controversy that led to the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act 1986. In Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) and John Vallamattom v. Union of India (2003), the Court reiterated the constitutional aspiration for a uniform civil code but stopped short of mandating it. The 21st Law Commission (2018) recommended a “uniform civil code” that respects diversity, while the 22nd Law Commission (2023) called for wider consultation. The constitutional design thus records a deliberate choice: the Directive Principle remains a moral compass, not a legally enforceable mandate, leaving the timeline and content to legislative consensus.

The Constitutional Scheme of the President’s Veto Powers: Pocket Veto, Suspensive Veto, and Judicial Interpretation

Article 111 governs the President’s assent to Bills passed by Parliament. The President may (a) give assent, (b) withhold assent, or (c) return the Bill (if not a Money Bill) for reconsideration. The first two constitute an absolute veto; the third is a suspensive veto because Parliament can override it by passing the Bill again, whereupon the President must give assent. The Constitution does not prescribe a time‑limit for the President to act, but the President acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers under Article 74, making an independent veto practically impossible. The only instance of a President withholding assent was in 1954 when President Rajendra Prasad returned the Hindu Code Bill for reconsideration; Parliament re‑passed it and he assented. In 1986 President Zail Singh did not act on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, effectively employing a pocket veto; the Bill lapsed with the dissolution of the Lok Sabha. The Supreme Court in K. K. Venugopal v. Union of India (1995), though concerning the Vice‑President, affirmed that the President’s discretionary space is “narrow and explicitly listed” (Article 75(3), 85, 123, 356). In Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006) the Court held that the Governor’s assent (analogous to the President’s) is subject to judicial review for mala fides. Consequently, the President’s veto powers are largely ceremonial; the real legislative check lies in the parliamentary majority and the basic structure doctrine.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The President of India can exercise a pocket veto because the Constitution does not fix a time‑limit for assent.” Is this statement correct?
The statement is incorrect. Although Article 111 does not prescribe a deadline, the President is bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74) and cannot act independently. The only historical instance of inaction (President Zail Singh, 1986) was a political act, not a constitutional power. The Supreme Court has held that the President’s discretion is limited to the situations expressly mentioned in the Constitution; a pocket veto is not one of them.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question tests the President’s veto, distinguish between the three constitutional options (assent, withhold, return) and the practical reality of ministerial advice. Remember that a suspensive veto can be overridden by a simple majority re‑passage, while an absolute veto has never been used independently. Cite Article 111, Article 74, and the Zail Singh episode for a complete answer.

The Constitutional Position of the Vice‑President as Ex‑Officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha: Powers, Precedents, and Limits

Article 64 designates the Vice‑President as the ex‑officio Chairman of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha). Article 89 provides for a Deputy Chairman elected by the House, who presides in the Chairman’s absence. The Chairman’s powers include regulating proceedings, deciding points of order, certifying Money Bills (Article 110), and exercising a casting vote when the House is equally divided (Article 100). The casting vote has been used sparingly; Vice‑President S. Radhakrishnan cast a vote in 1962 on a constitutional amendment, and Vice‑President M. Hidayatullah did so in 1979 on a legislative matter. The Supreme Court in K. K. Venugopal v. Union of India (1995) held that the casting vote is a constitutional duty exercised neutrally, not a political tool. The Chairman also appoints members of parliamentary committees and refers Bills to them. However, the Chairman cannot vote in the first instance and has no role in the legislative agenda, which is controlled by the Leader of the House. Removal of the Vice‑President requires a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a majority of its total membership and agreed to by the Lok Sabha (Article 67(b)). The office thus combines a ceremonial presiding role with limited procedural authority, reinforcing the principle that the Upper House is a revising chamber rather than a political rival to the Lok Sabha.

The Doctrine of Legislative Privilege under Articles 105 and 194: Scope, Judicial Review, and Landmark Cases

Articles 105 (Parliament) and 194 (State Legislatures) confer two core privileges: freedom of speech in the House and immunity from court proceedings for anything said or any vote given. They also empower each House to punish for contempt and to regulate its internal procedure. The scope of these privileges is not absolute. In Keshav Singh v. Speaker, Legislative Assembly (1965), the Supreme Court held that legislative privileges are subject to fundamental rights; a member’s detention for contempt could be reviewed under Article 21. In Raja Ram Pal v. Hon’ble Speaker, Lok Sabha (2007), the Court upheld the expulsion of MPs for accepting bribes, ruling that the power to expel is a privilege but must satisfy the test of proportionality and natural justice. In State of Kerala v. K. Ajith (2021), the Court clarified that legislative privilege does not shield a legislator from criminal prosecution for acts outside the House, such as assault. The privileges also extend to publication of reports and proceedings (Article 105(2)), but the Supreme Court in Searchlight v. State of Bihar (1959) held that the privilege does not override the right to fair trial. Thus, while the Constitution grants broad immunities to ensure legislative independence, judicial review ensures that these privileges do not become a cloak for illegality.
