The Constitutional Framework for Delimitation of Parliamentary and Assembly Constituencies: Commissions, Freeze, and Judicial Oversight

Articles 82 and 170 mandate readjustment of territorial constituencies after each census. The Delimitation Commission Acts of 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002 gave effect to this mandate. The 42nd Amendment (1976) froze the total number of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies at the 1971 census figures until the year 2000, to encourage population control. The 84th Amendment (2001) extended the freeze to 2026, while the 87th Amendment (2003) permitted internal readjustment of boundaries without altering the number of seats. The Delimitation Commission, constituted under the Delimitation Act 2002, comprises a retired Supreme Court judge as Chairperson, the Chief Election Commissioner, and State Election Commissioners. Its orders have the force of law and cannot be questioned in any court (Article 329). However, the Supreme Court in R. C. Poudyal v. Union of India (1993) examined the constitutional validity of the Sikkim delimitation, holding that Article 329 does not bar review of the constitutional amendment itself. The 2026 deadline now looms; the next Delimitation Commission will be based on the first census after 2026, likely the 2031 census. The framework thus balances demographic equity with political stability, using a statutory commission insulated from judicial interference but subject to constitutional scrutiny.

  • Confusing the President’s absolute veto with a pocket veto — the Constitution provides no pocket veto; the President must act on ministerial advice.
  • Assuming the Vice‑President’s casting vote is a political discretion — it is a constitutional duty exercised neutrally, as held in K. K. Venugopal v. Union of India (1995).
  • Treating legislative privilege as absolute immunity from criminal law — the Supreme Court has repeatedly subjected privilege to fundamental rights and proportionality tests.
  • Believing the Delimitation Commission’s orders are entirely immune from judicial review — Article 329 bars challenges to the orders, but the constitutional amendment empowering the Commission remains reviewable.
  • Thinking Article 44 obliges the State to enact a uniform civil code immediately — it is a non‑justiciable Directive Principle, leaving the timing to legislative consensus.
  • Overlooking that the President’s suspensive veto can be overridden by a simple majority re‑passage of the Bill — after reconsideration, the President must assent.
  • Neglecting the distinction between the Chairman’s procedural powers and the Deputy Chairman’s role in day‑to‑day conduct of the Rajya Sabha.

The Doctrine of Eclipse and Severability in Indian Constitutional Law

The doctrine of eclipse addresses the fate of pre‑constitutional laws that conflict with the fundamental rights guaranteed in Part III. Under Article 13(1), any law in force before the commencement of the Constitution that is inconsistent with a fundamental right becomes void to the extent of the inconsistency. However, the Supreme Court in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955) held that such a law is not dead; it is merely eclipsed. When the constitutional impediment is removed — for instance, by a constitutional amendment that alters the fundamental right — the law revives automatically without the need for fresh legislation. This principle preserves legislative continuity while respecting the supremacy of the Constitution.

The doctrine of severability, by contrast, operates on post‑constitutional statutes. If a provision of an Act is found to violate a fundamental right, the court may strike down only the offending portion provided the remainder of the statute is capable of standing independently. The test was formulated in State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951) and refined in R.M.D.C. v. Union of India (1957): the valid part must be severable from the invalid part, the legislature must have intended the statute to operate without the invalid portion, and the remaining provisions must not be so intertwined with the struck‑down part that they become unworkable. In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Court applied severability to uphold the bulk of the Tenth Schedule while invalidating the provision that barred judicial review.

Both doctrines interact with Article 13(2), which prohibits the State from making any law that takes away or abridges fundamental rights. Eclipse deals with the temporal dimension — laws existing before the Constitution — while severability deals with the structural dimension — the internal coherence of a statute. Together they ensure that the fundamental rights regime does not render the entire statute book inoperative, allowing the legislature to cure defects through amendment rather than wholesale repeal. The Supreme Court has repeatedly emphasised that the power to declare a law void is a judicial function, but the power to revive an eclipsed law rests on the constitutional amendment process, preserving the separation of powers.

The Concept of Constitutional Identity and Its Judicial Articulation

Constitutional identity refers to the core values and structural principles that define the Constitution’s essential character, beyond the enumerated basic structure. While the basic structure doctrine, crystallised in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), identifies features such as supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secularism, federalism, and separation of powers, constitutional identity encompasses the deeper narrative that binds these features into a coherent whole. The Supreme Court in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) described the Constitution as a “living organism” whose identity is rooted in the vision of the framers as reflected in the Preamble, the Objectives Resolution, and the Directive Principles.

In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Court invoked constitutional identity to strike down the arbitrary dismissal of state governments, holding that federalism and secularism are not merely structural arrangements but constitutive elements of India’s constitutional identity. The I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) decision extended this reasoning to the Ninth Schedule, ruling that laws placed under its protection after 24 April 1973 must conform to the basic structure, because the identity of the Constitution cannot be altered by legislative immunity. Scholarly work by Granville Austin and later by Upendra Baxi has argued that constitutional identity serves as an interpretive lens for judicial review of amendments, ensuring that the Constitution’s transformative promise — social, economic, and political justice — remains intact.

The practical significance of constitutional identity emerges when an amendment seeks to alter a feature that, while not explicitly listed in the basic structure catalogue, is integral to the Constitution’s self‑understanding. For example, the 42nd Amendment’s insertion of “socialist” and “secular” into the Preamble was upheld because it reinforced, rather than altered, the identity articulated in the Objectives Resolution. Conversely, any amendment that sought to replace the parliamentary system with a presidential one would be struck down as violating constitutional identity, even if the basic structure test were formally satisfied. Thus, constitutional identity operates as a higher-order constraint, guiding the Court in discerning the limits of constituent power.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Distinguish between the basic structure doctrine and the concept of constitutional identity. Can a constitutional amendment violate constitutional identity without violating the basic structure?”
The basic structure doctrine enumerates specific inviolable features (supremacy of Constitution, democracy, secularism, federalism, separation of powers, judicial review). Constitutional identity is a broader, narrative concept that captures the Constitution’s core ethos — the transformative vision of justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity articulated in the Preamble and the Objectives Resolution. An amendment may technically preserve each listed basic feature yet still alter the Constitution’s identity; for instance, replacing the parliamentary system with a presidential system while retaining federalism and judicial review would violate constitutional identity because it changes the democratic republican character envisaged by the framers. The Supreme Court in S.R. Bommai and I.R. Coelho has treated identity as a higher-order limit, so the answer is yes — an amendment can breach constitutional identity without breaching the enumerated basic structure.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for “basic structure” versus “constitutional identity”, list the classic Kesavananda features first, then explain identity as the interpretive umbrella. Cite Minerva Mills, S.R. Bommai, and I.R. Coelho to show the evolution. Use a two‑column table in your answer for quick visual contrast.

The Constituent Assembly’s Committee on the National Flag, Anthem, and Emblem: Symbolic Constitutionalism

The Constituent Assembly recognised that a sovereign republic required visible symbols embodying its constitutional values. On 23 June 1947, the Assembly constituted a Flag Committee under the chairmanship of Dr. Rajendra Prasad, with members including Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, Sarojini Naidu, and C. Rajagopalachari. The committee recommended a horizontal tricolour of deep saffron, white, and dark green in equal proportions, with the Ashoka Chakra in navy blue at the centre of the white band. The design was adopted on 22 July 1947, and the Flag Code was later formalised by the Ministry of Home Affairs.

For the national anthem, a separate committee chaired by Maulana Azad examined several compositions, including “Vande Mataram” and “Jana Gana Mana”. On 24 January 1950, the Assembly adopted “Jana Gana Mana” as the national anthem, recognising its inclusive language and its reflection of the pluralistic ethos of the Constitution. The anthem’s adoption was accompanied by a resolution that it would be played on all official occasions, reinforcing the principle of unity in diversity.

The State Emblem, derived from the Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath, was approved on 26 January 1950. A committee chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad oversaw the adaptation of the capital, ensuring that the motto “Satyameva Jayate” (Truth Alone Triumphs) from the Mundaka Upanishad was inscribed below the abacus. The emblem’s four lions symbolise power, courage, confidence, and pride, while the wheel (Dharma Chakra) represents the rule of law. These symbols were not mere decorative choices; they were deliberately linked to the constitutional vision articulated in the Objectives Resolution and the Preamble, making them part of the Constitution’s symbolic architecture.

The Evolution of Fundamental Duties: From the 42nd Amendment to the 86th Amendment

The original Constitution of 1950 contained no chapter on fundamental duties. The Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended their inclusion to balance rights with responsibilities. The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted Part IVA comprising Article 51A, enumerating ten duties: to abide by the Constitution, respect its ideals and institutions, cherish the noble ideals of the freedom struggle, uphold sovereignty and integrity, defend the country, promote harmony, value and preserve the composite culture, protect the natural environment, develop scientific temper, and safeguard public property.

These duties are non‑justiciable; Article 51A expressly states that they shall not be enforceable by any court. Nevertheless, the Supreme Court has used them as interpretive aids. In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987), the Court invoked the duty to protect the environment (Article 51A(g)) to expand the scope of Article 21. In Ranganath Misra Commission reports and later in State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat (2005), the duties were cited to justify reasonable restrictions on fundamental rights.

The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 added a eleventh duty under Article 51A(k): “who is a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child or, as the case may be, ward between the age of six and fourteen years.” This amendment coincided with the insertion of Article 21A (right to education) and reflected a policy shift towards making elementary education a shared constitutional obligation. The duty remains non‑justiciable, but it has been invoked in public interest litigation to compel state action on school infrastructure and enrolment. The evolution from zero duties to eleven illustrates the Constitution’s adaptive capacity to embed civic responsibility without altering the enforceable rights framework.

The Constitutional Framework for the Protection of Minority Educational Institutions under Articles 29 and 30

Article 29(1) guarantees any section of citizens having a distinct language, script, or culture the right to conserve the same. Article 30(1) confers on all minorities, whether based on religion or language, the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. The Supreme Court in St. Stephen’s College v. University of Delhi (1992) held that the right under Article 30(1) includes the autonomy to determine admission criteria, subject to reasonable regulation by the state to maintain academic standards.

In T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002), an eleven‑judge bench clarified that “minority” is to be determined at the state level, and that the right to administer includes the power to appoint staff, manage finances, and design curricula, provided the institution does not become a “minority institution in name only”. The Court also ruled that the state may impose reasonable regulations concerning qualifications of teachers, sanitation, and financial transparency, but cannot interfere with the essential character of minority administration.

The P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005) decision extended the protection to unaided professional colleges, holding that the state cannot enforce reservation policies in minority institutions without violating Article 30(1). However, the 93rd Amendment (2005) inserted Article 15(5), enabling the state to make special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes in private unaided institutions, with an explicit exemption for minority institutions under Article 30(1). This legislative‑judicial interplay demonstrates the Constitution’s attempt to balance minority autonomy with the broader goal of social justice. The framework thus rests on a dual guarantee: cultural preservation under Article 29 and institutional autonomy under Article 30, both subject to the state’s regulatory power only to the extent that it does not erode the minority character of the institution.

  • Confusing the doctrine of eclipse with the doctrine of severability — eclipse applies only to pre‑constitutional laws, severability to post‑constitutional statutes.
  • Assuming constitutional identity is synonymous with the basic structure list — identity is a broader narrative concept that can invalidate amendments even when each enumerated basic feature is formally preserved.
  • Believing the national flag, anthem, and emblem were adopted without any committee deliberation — each symbol emerged from a dedicated Constituent Assembly committee with recorded debates.
  • Treating fundamental duties as justiciable rights — they are expressly non‑justiciable under Article 51A, though courts use them as interpretive tools.
  • Thinking Article 30(1) gives minorities an absolute right to exclude all state regulation — the Supreme Court permits reasonable regulation that does not destroy the minority character of the institution.
  • Overlooking that the 93rd Amendment’s reservation provision expressly exempts minority institutions under Article 30(1) — this exemption is a constitutional safeguard, not a statutory concession.
  • Neglecting the distinction between “establish” and “administer” in Article 30(1) — the right to administer is the core of minority autonomy and has been the focal point of judicial scrutiny.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on Article 21: The 'Due Process' Rejection and Its Long Shadow

The drafting of Article 21 — "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law" — represents the most consequential textual choice in the Fundamental Rights chapter. The Constituent Assembly explicitly rejected the American "due process of law" standard in favour of the Japanese "procedure established by law" formulation, a decision driven by the Advisory Committee's desire to prevent judicial veto over social legislation. B.N. Rau, the Constitutional Adviser, had warned during his 1947 consultations with Justice Frankfurter in Washington that "due process" would empower courts to strike down land reform and labour laws on substantive reasonableness grounds. The Drafting Committee, led by Ambedkar, initially retained "due process" in the February 1948 Draft Constitution (Clause 15), but the Special Committee on Fundamental Rights, chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru, substituted the Japanese phrase in April 1948 after Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar argued that "due process" imported an undefined judicial discretion incompatible with parliamentary democracy.

The debate crystallised on 6 December 1948 when K.M. Munshi moved an amendment to restore "due process", supported by H.V. Kamath and Naziruddin Ahmad, who contended that "procedure established by law" rendered life and liberty hostage to legislative majorities. Ambedkar opposed the amendment, stating that the phrase "procedure established by law" was "wide enough to cover all the requirements of due process" if the procedure was fair, just, and reasonable — a formulation that anticipated the Maneka Gandhi (1978) interpretation by three decades. The Assembly rejected Munshi's amendment by a voice vote. The immediate judicial consequence was A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950), where the Supreme Court held that Article 21 required only a enacted procedure, not a fair one, and that Articles 19 and 21 operated in mutually exclusive spheres. This formalist reading persisted until the 11-judge bench in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) overruled Gopalan, reading "procedure established by law" as necessarily "fair, just and reasonable" — effectively importing substantive due process through the back door of Article 14 and 19. The Constituent Assembly's rejection thus created a 28-year gap in liberty protection that the Court eventually bridged by interpretive expansion, illustrating how textual minimalism can generate prolonged jurisprudential instability.

The Constitutional Architecture of Princely State Integration: Accession, Merger, and the Territorial Definition of India

The Constitution's territorial integrity was not a given at commencement; it was constructed through a dual legal architecture operating between August 1947 and January 1950. The Indian Independence Act 1947 (Section 7) terminated British paramountcy, leaving 562 princely states legally sovereign. The Government of India Act 1935 (Section 6) provided the accession mechanism: a ruler could execute an Instrument of Accession (IoA) accepting Dominion legislature competence over Defence, External Affairs, and Communications. Sardar Patel's States Ministry, led by V.P. Menon, secured IoAs from all but three states (Junagadh, Hyderabad, Kashmir) by 15 August 1947. The Constitution then transformed these political acts into constitutional law. Article 1 declared India a "Union of States"; Article 2 empowered Parliament to admit new states; Article 3 authorised formation of new states and alteration of boundaries; Article 4 mandated that laws under Articles 2 and 3 were not constitutional amendments under Article 368.

The critical innovation was the Merger Agreement (1948–1949), distinct from the IoA. While the IoA surrendered three subjects, the Merger Agreement transferred full administrative control to the Dominion Government, providing for a privy purse, guarantees of personal privileges, and the ruler's continuation as Rajpramukh in merged unions (e.g., PEPSU, Saurashtra, Madhya Bharat). The Constitution recognised this in Article 238 (Part VII) and the original First Schedule, which listed Part A (former provinces), Part B (princely unions), Part C (chief commissioners' provinces), and Part D (Andaman & Nicobar). The 7th Amendment (1956) abolished the Part A/B/C distinction upon linguistic reorganisation, but the constitutional logic — that territory could be integrated by ordinary legislation under Articles 2–4 — remained. The Supreme Court in In re Berubari Union (1960) held that cession of territory required a constitutional amendment under Article 368, but acquisition or integration did not, affirming the asymmetry built into the founding design. This architecture allowed the integration of Hyderabad (police action 1948, merger 1950), Junagadh (plebiscite 1948), and Kashmir (IoA 1947, Article 370) within a single constitutional framework without a single Article 368 amendment.

Examiner's Trap: Distinguishing Accession from Merger
A question asks: "The Instrument of Accession executed by the Ruler of a princely state under the Government of India Act 1935 automatically made the state a part of the territory of India as defined in Article 1 of the Constitution." True or False? Explain the constitutional distinction.
False. The Instrument of Accession (IoA) under Section 6 of the Government of India Act 1935 surrendered only three subjects (Defence, External Affairs, Communications) to the Dominion Legislature. It did not transfer sovereignty or integrate the state into the "territory of India" under Article 1. Full integration required a subsequent Merger Agreement (1948–49) transferring all administrative powers, followed by constitutional recognition under Articles 2–4 and the original First Schedule (Part B States). The IoA was a federal compact; the Merger Agreement was a cession of internal sovereignty. The Supreme Court in In re Berubari Union (1960) clarified that acquisition of territory (by IoA/Merger) does not require Article 368 amendment, but cession does — confirming that accession alone did not alter India's territorial definition.
Exam-Day Strategy: Territorial Integration Timeline
Memorise the three-stage sequence: (1) Paramountcy lapse (15 Aug 1947, Indian Independence Act s.7) → (2) Instrument of Accession (Aug 1947–Oct 1947, GoI Act 1935 s.6) → (3) Merger Agreements (Jan 1948–Jan 1950, executive action recognised by Constitution Arts 2–4). Questions often confuse the legal effect of each stage. Remember: Article 4 explicitly excludes Art 2/3 laws from Art 368 — this is the textual key for "integration by ordinary law" MCQs.

The Cabinet Mission Plan, the Interim Government, and the Constituent Assembly's Derivative Authority

The Constituent Assembly's legal pedigree derives not from a revolutionary rupture but from a negotiated transfer of power encoded in the Cabinet Mission Plan (16 May 1946). The Plan rejected the Muslim League's demand for a separate Constituent Assembly for Pakistan, proposing instead a single Assembly elected by provincial legislatures (via single transferable vote) with 292 seats for British India and 93 for princely states. The Assembly's authority was derivative: it was convened by the Viceroy's executive order (9 December 1946) under the Government of India Act 1935, not by an indigenous sovereign act. The Interim Government, formed on 2 September 1946 with Nehru as Vice-President of the Executive Council, operated under the 1935 Act while the Assembly drafted the Constitution. This created a dual legitimacy tension: the Assembly claimed to represent "We the People" (Preamble), yet its electoral college was the limited franchise of the 1935 Act (roughly 14% adult suffrage), and its proceedings were boycotted by the Muslim League after July 1947.

The Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947) and the Indian Independence Act 1947 resolved this by transforming the Assembly into a sovereign body for the Dominion of India. Section 8 of the Independence Act declared that the Assembly "shall have full power to frame a Constitution for the new Dominion" and that "no Act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom shall extend to the new Dominion". The Assembly's first act as a sovereign body (14 August 1947 midnight session) was to assume legislative powers under the Independence Act, separating its constituent and legislative functions (the latter as the "Constituent Assembly (Legislative)"). The Drafting Committee, appointed 29 August 1947, worked under this sovereign mandate. The constitutional autochthony thesis — that the Constitution derives authority from the Indian people, not British statute — rests on the Assembly's 26 November 1949 adoption resolution ("We the People... adopt, enact and give to ourselves this Constitution") and the deliberate omission of any enacting formula referencing the Crown or Parliament. Yet the legal continuity via the Independence Act remains the formal bridge; the Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) acknowledged this duality, holding that the Constitution's authority is "autochthonous in spirit but derivative in form".

The Original Constitutional Design of the Supreme Court: Article 124, the Federal Court Legacy, and the 'Consultation' Compromise

The Constituent Assembly's design of the Supreme Court (Articles 124–147) was a deliberate departure from both the Federal Court of India (1937–1950) and the American model. The Federal Court, established under the Government of India Act 1935 (Section 200), had limited original jurisdiction (disputes between units), advisory jurisdiction, and appellate jurisdiction subject to Privy Council appeal. Its judges were appointed by the Crown on the advice of the Secretary of State, with tenure during His Majesty's pleasure. The Assembly rejected this executive dominance. The Ad Hoc Committee on the Supreme Court (chaired by S. Varadachariar, 1947) recommended a "collegium-like" mechanism: appointment by the President after consultation with the Chief Justice of India (CJI) and such other judges as the President may deem necessary. The Drafting Committee refined this into Article 124(2): "Every Judge of the Supreme Court shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal after consultation with such of the Judges of the Supreme Court and of the High Courts in the States as the President may deem necessary."

The word "consultation" was a compromise. K.M. Munshi wanted "concurrence" (judicial veto); Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar insisted on executive primacy with consultation as a formality. Ambedkar mediated: "consultation" implied meaningful dialogue but not concurrence. The Federal Court's Chief Justice, Sir H.J. Kania, became the first CJI of the Supreme Court on 28 January 1950, ensuring institutional continuity. The original Article 124(2) did not bind the President to consult the CJI specifically — it said "such of the Judges... as the President may deem necessary". The convention of consulting the CJI emerged from practice, not text. The Supreme Court in S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981) (First Judges Case) held "consultation" did not mean "concurrence", affirming executive primacy. This was reversed in Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (1993) (Second Judges Case), where a 9-judge bench read "consultation" as "concurrence" and invented the Collegium. The Constituent Assembly's deliberate textual ambiguity thus seeded a 40-year jurisprudential contest resolved only by judicial self-empowerment, not constitutional amendment.

The Constituent Assembly's Citizenship Debates: Articles 5–11, the Partition Migration, and the 'Dominion' Transition

Part II of the Constitution (Articles 5–11) was drafted under the shadow of Partition, addressing a crisis the Government of India Act 1935 ignored: the status of millions displaced across new borders. The Drafting Committee's February 1948 text (Articles 5–9) defined citizenship at commencement (26 January 1950) by domicile, birth, descent, and residence. Article 5 covered persons domiciled in India born in India or with a parent born in India, or ordinarily resident for five years. Article 6 granted citizenship to migrants from Pakistan before 19 July 1948 (if resident since migration) or after (if registered after six months' residence). Article 7 denied citizenship to migrants to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 unless returning under a permit for resettlement. Article 8 covered persons of Indian origin abroad. The debates (10–12 August 1949) revealed deep anxiety. Jaspat Roy Kapoor demanded automatic citizenship for Hindu/Sikh refugees; B. Pocker Sahib warned Article 7 penalised Muslims who fled violence. Ambedkar defended the cut-off dates as administrative necessities, noting the 19 July 1948 date marked the permit system's introduction.

Article 11 — "Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law" — was the escape valve. It empowered Parliament to override Part II by ordinary legislation, a unique feature: a Fundamental Right-adjacent provision (citizenship) made fully amendable by simple majority. The Citizenship Act 1955, enacted under Article 11, created acquisition by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, and incorporation of territory, and loss by renunciation, termination, and deprivation. The 1986, 1992, 2003, 2005, and 2019 amendments progressively restricted birthright citizenship (from unconditional jus soli to requiring one citizen parent, then both, then excluding illegal migrants). The Constituent Assembly's decision to constitutionalise only the commencement snapshot (Articles 5–10) while delegating the ongoing regime to Parliament (Article 11) reflected a pragmatic recognition that citizenship law must respond to demographic flux — a flexibility the 2019 Amendment (CAA) tested by introducing religious criteria into naturalisation, prompting challenges under Article 14 that remain pending. The Assembly's design thus created a two-tier citizenship architecture: a rigid constitutional floor for the founding moment, and a permeable statutory superstructure for the future.

  • Confusing the Instrument of Accession (three subjects, GoI Act 1935) with the Merger Agreement (full administration, executive act) — they are legally distinct instruments with different constitutional consequences.
  • Assuming the Constituent Assembly was elected by universal adult franchise — it was elected by provincial legislatures under the limited 1935 Act franchise (~14% adults); the Muslim League boycott further reduced representativeness.
  • Believing Article 21's "procedure established by law" was a drafting error — it was a deliberate rejection of "due process" after B.N. Rau's US consultations and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar's intervention in the Special Committee.
  • Thinking the Supreme Court's Collegium system was mandated by the original Article 124(2) — the text required only presidential "consultation" with judges "as the President may deem necessary"; the Collegium emerged from judicial interpretation in 1993, not the Constituent Assembly.
  • Treating Articles 5–10 as the complete citizenship code — they applied only at commencement (26 Jan 1950); Article 11 explicitly delegated all subsequent citizenship law to Parliament by simple majority.
  • Overlooking that the 7th Amendment (1956) abolished the Part A/Part B/Part C state classification — the original First Schedule's four-part structure reflected the accession-merger integration stages, not a permanent federal design.
  • Assuming the Preamble's "We the People" declaration was legally operative from 26 Nov 1949 — the Constitution commenced on 26 Jan 1950 (Article 394); the Assembly's adoption resolution was a political act, not a legal commencement.

Constitutionalism in India: Principles, Mechanisms, and Challenges

Constitutionalism, distinct from merely having a constitution, refers to the idea that government power is limited by a supreme law, ensuring individual liberty and preventing arbitrary rule. It embodies principles such as limited government, rule of law, fundamental rights, separation of powers, judicial review, and an independent judiciary. India, despite its detailed written Constitution, has continuously evolved its understanding and application of constitutionalism, often through judicial interpretation.

The Indian Constitution establishes several mechanisms to uphold constitutionalism. Firstly, the supremacy of the Constitution itself, enshrined in Article 13, ensures that any law inconsistent with fundamental rights is void. This forms the bedrock of judicial review, allowing courts to scrutinise legislative and executive actions. Secondly, the inclusion of a comprehensive chapter on Fundamental Rights (Part III) acts as a direct check on state power, enforceable through Articles 32 and 226. While Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) guide state action, they are non-justiciable, yet the judiciary has often harmonised them with Fundamental Rights to expand the scope of constitutional protections, reflecting a commitment to both civil-political and socio-economic justice.

Thirdly, the principle of separation of powers, though not rigidly followed as in the US, is maintained through distinct functions assigned to the legislature, executive, and judiciary. An independent judiciary, with security of tenure and powers of judicial review, serves as the ultimate interpreter and guardian of the Constitution. The Basic Structure Doctrine, enunciated in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), further reinforces constitutionalism by placing implied limitations on Parliament's amending power, ensuring that the core values of the Constitution remain inviolable. This doctrine prevents the transformation of the Constitution into a mere legislative document.

However, Indian constitutionalism has faced significant challenges. The period of the National Emergency (1975-77) starkly exposed vulnerabilities, leading to the suspension of fundamental rights and centralisation of power. Subsequent constitutional amendments, particularly the 44th Amendment (1978), introduced safeguards to prevent such abuses. Persistent challenges include executive dominance over the legislature, the erosion of institutional independence (e.g., concerns over appointments to constitutional bodies), and the rise of populism that sometimes seeks to bypass constitutional procedures or values. The tension between parliamentary sovereignty (within constitutional limits) and judicial activism in upholding constitutional principles remains a dynamic feature of Indian constitutionalism. The judiciary's role in expanding the scope of rights (e.g., right to privacy under Article 21) and ensuring accountability of state organs underscores its critical function in maintaining the constitutional framework.

The Dynamic Evolution of Indian Federalism: From Co-operative to Competitive

India's federal structure, often described as 'quasi-federal' or 'federal with a strong unitary bias', has undergone significant transformations since its inception. The Constituent Assembly, influenced by the need for national unity post-Partition and the desire for strong central planning, deliberately opted for a robust Centre. This initial phase (roughly 1950s-1960s) was characterised by 'co-operative federalism', where the Centre and states, largely governed by the same political party (Congress), worked in tandem, often through institutions like the Planning Commission. Centralised planning and resource allocation dominated, with states relying heavily on central grants and schemes.

The post-1967 era witnessed a shift. The decline of the Congress party's dominance and the rise of regional parties led to increased demands for state autonomy and greater fiscal powers. This period saw growing Centre-State tensions, particularly over issues like the Governor's role, deployment of central forces, and financial devolution. Commissions like the Sarkaria Commission (1983) and the Punchhi Commission (2007) were constituted to review Centre-State relations, recommending measures to strengthen co-operative federalism while preserving the Centre's essential powers. Their reports highlighted the need for greater consultation, equitable resource distribution, and restraint in the use of Article 356 (President's Rule).

In the 21st century, Indian federalism has evolved further, exhibiting elements of 'competitive federalism'. States now actively compete for domestic and foreign investment, often through policy innovations, ease of doing business reforms, and infrastructure development. The Goods and Services Tax (GST) regime, with the GST Council acting as a unique federal institution, represents a significant step towards fiscal integration and co-operative decision-making, albeit with its own set of challenges regarding revenue sharing and state autonomy. However, alongside competition, there are also concerns about 'coercive federalism', where the Centre, through its financial muscle, centrally sponsored schemes, and sometimes the use of investigative agencies, exerts significant influence over state policies and administration. The increasing reliance on central schemes, often with specific implementation guidelines, can limit states' flexibility to address local needs.

The role of inter-state councils and regional councils has become more pronounced in facilitating dialogue and resolving disputes. The dynamic interplay between political centralisation (e.g., a single dominant party at the Centre) and the assertion of regional identities continues to shape the contours of Indian federalism. This evolution reflects a constant negotiation between the constitutional design for a strong union and the democratic aspirations for greater decentralisation and regional self-governance, making Indian federalism a continuously adapting system.

Examiner's trap
Consider the statement: "The Indian Constitution explicitly defines the term 'federalism' and outlines a rigid separation of powers between the Centre and states, akin to the American model." Evaluate this statement.
The statement is incorrect on two counts. Firstly, the Indian Constitution does not explicitly use the term 'federalism' anywhere in its text. It refers to India as a "Union of States" (Article 1). While it exhibits federal features, its character is often described as 'quasi-federal' due to a strong unitary bias. Secondly, the Indian Constitution does not outline a rigid separation of powers between the Centre and states. Instead, it provides for a detailed distribution of legislative, executive, and financial powers (Seventh Schedule, Articles 245-293), but with significant centralising tendencies, especially during emergencies or in areas of national interest. The American model, in contrast, features a more distinct and rigid separation of powers between the federal and state governments, with states retaining substantial residual powers. India's system is characterised by a blend of federal and unitary features, with an emphasis on cooperation and interdependence, rather than strict separation.
Mastering Constitutional Dynamics
When analysing constitutional concepts like federalism or constitutionalism, move beyond static definitions. Focus on their *evolution*, the *challenges* they face, the *mechanisms* that uphold them, and the *role of various institutions* (especially the judiciary and political parties) in shaping their practical application. Always link theoretical concepts to landmark judgments, constitutional amendments, and historical events to demonstrate a comprehensive understanding.

The Constitutional Role of the Speaker and Presiding Officers in Parliament and State Legislatures

The Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Chairpersons of the Rajya Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies/Councils are pivotal constitutional functionaries, embodying the dignity and authority of their respective Houses. Their roles, though largely governed by rules of procedure, derive their constitutional sanctity from provisions like Article 93 (Lok Sabha Speaker and Deputy Speaker), Article 178 (State Assembly Speaker and Deputy Speaker), and Article 89 (Rajya Sabha Chairman and Deputy Chairman). The Speaker's primary duty is to preside over the sittings of the House, maintain order, and ensure the smooth conduct of business. They are the final interpreter of the provisions of the Constitution within the House, its Rules of Procedure, and parliamentary precedents.

Beyond maintaining order, the Speaker exercises several crucial constitutional powers. Under Article 100, the Speaker has a casting vote in case of a tie, but does not vote in the first instance. A significant power is the certification of a Money Bill (Article 110), a decision that has profound implications for legislative procedure and the balance of power between the two Houses. The Speaker's decision on whether a Bill is a Money Bill is final and cannot be questioned in a court of law, though the Supreme Court in Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank Ltd. (2019) indicated that judicial review might be possible in cases of clear constitutional transgression or mala fide exercise of power.

Perhaps the most contentious power of the Speaker arises under the Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law). The Speaker acts as the tribunal for deciding disqualification petitions of members on grounds of defection. This quasi-judicial role has often been criticised for potential political bias and delays, leading to calls for transferring this power to an independent body. The Supreme Court, in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), upheld the Speaker's power but made it subject to judicial review on grounds of mala fides or perversity. The Speaker's role in constituting parliamentary committees, admitting questions, and allowing adjournment motions further underscores their influence over legislative proceedings.

The expectation is that the Speaker, once elected, should rise above party politics and act impartially. While in the UK, the Speaker traditionally resigns from their political party and is often re-elected unopposed, in India, the Speaker typically remains a party member, leading to persistent concerns about their neutrality. The constitutional framework thus entrusts immense power and responsibility to the Speaker, making their conduct crucial for upholding parliamentary democracy and the rule of law.

Emergency Provisions: Impact on Fundamental Rights, Federalism, and Judicial Review

The Indian Constitution, designed to be robust yet flexible, incorporates extraordinary provisions to deal with exceptional circumstances, broadly categorised into three types of emergencies: National Emergency (Article 352), State Emergency or President's Rule (Article 356), and Financial Emergency (Article 360). These provisions allow the Union Executive to assume vast powers, significantly altering the normal distribution of powers and impacting fundamental rights.

During a National Emergency, the most profound impact is on Fundamental Rights. Article 358 automatically suspends the freedoms guaranteed by Article 19 (freedom of speech, assembly, etc.). Article 359 empowers the President to suspend the enforcement of other Fundamental Rights (except Articles 20 and 21, which protect against ex post facto laws, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, and right to life and personal liberty). This crucial safeguard for Articles 20 and 21 was introduced by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1978, a direct response to the abuses during the 1975-77 Emergency, where even the right to life was argued to be suspended (ADM Jabalpur v. Shivakant Shukla, 1976, later overturned by K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, 2017).

The federal structure also undergoes a significant transformation. During a National Emergency, the Centre's executive power extends to giving directions to any state regarding the exercise of its executive power, and Parliament gains the power to legislate on any subject in the State List (Article 353). In the case of President's Rule under Article 356, the President can assume all or any of the functions of the state government, declare that the powers of the state legislature shall be exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament, and make provisions for the administration of the state. This effectively converts the federal structure into a unitary one for the duration of the emergency, centralising legislative and executive authority.

The scope of judicial review over emergency proclamations has evolved significantly. Initially, the judiciary adopted a hands-off approach, particularly after the ADM Jabalpur case. However, post-1978, the 44th Amendment mandated parliamentary approval for emergency proclamations within one month and limited their duration, requiring fresh approval every six months. More importantly, the Supreme Court, in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), asserted that the proclamation of President's Rule under Article 356 is subject to judicial review. The Court held that the satisfaction of the President must be based on relevant material, and if the proclamation is found to be mala fide or based on extraneous grounds, it can be struck down, and the dismissed state government can be restored. This landmark judgment significantly curtailed the arbitrary use of Article 356, reinforcing constitutional checks and balances even during emergencies. Financial Emergency (Article 360), though never invoked, also allows the Centre to give directions to states on financial matters, including reduction of salaries of government employees.

The Unwritten Constitutional Role of Political Parties in Indian Democracy

While the Indian Constitution is a meticulously drafted document, it is remarkably silent on the explicit role and structure of political parties. The original text does not mention them, yet they are the indispensable engines of Indian democracy, forming the bedrock upon which the entire parliamentary system operates. Their constitutional role, therefore, is largely 'unwritten', derived from political practice, statutory laws like the Representation of the People Act (RPA), 1951, and judicial interpretations.

Political parties perform several vital functions that underpin the constitutional framework. They are the primary vehicles for contesting elections, mobilising voters, articulating public opinion, and aggregating diverse interests into policy platforms. They form governments, provide the opposition, and facilitate the smooth functioning of parliamentary proceedings. The concept of collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers (Article 75 for Union, Article 164 for states) inherently relies on party discipline and cohesion. Similarly, the role of the Leader of the Opposition, though not explicitly defined in the Constitution, is a crucial constitutional convention that ensures accountability and provides an alternative voice.

Over time, statutory recognition has been granted to parties. The Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law), introduced by the 52nd Amendment in 1985, explicitly acknowledges political parties by penalising legislators who defect from their party. The RPA, 1951, governs the registration of political parties with the Election Commission of India, their funding, and the allocation of election symbols. The Election Commission, under its constitutional mandate (Article 324), plays a significant role in regulating parties, ensuring internal democracy (though its powers here are debated), and enforcing electoral conduct.

However, the unwritten nature of their constitutional role also presents challenges. The lack of explicit constitutional provisions for internal party democracy often leads to dynastic succession, centralised decision-making, and a lack of accountability to party members. Opaque party funding, the criminalisation of politics (where individuals with criminal backgrounds gain electoral success), and the undue influence of party whips on legislative freedom can undermine the spirit of representative democracy and constitutional morality. The tension between a legislator's individual conscience and party directives is a constant feature. Thus, while political parties are the lifeblood of India's constitutional democracy, their functioning and adherence to democratic principles remain a critical area of concern and ongoing reform efforts.

  • Common Traps
  • Confusing 'constitutionalism' with merely having a 'constitution'; remember constitutionalism implies limited government and adherence to higher law.
  • Assuming Indian federalism is static; it's a dynamic system evolving from co-operative to competitive and sometimes coercive.
  • Believing the Speaker's decision on a Money Bill or anti-defection is absolutely final and beyond judicial review; landmark judgments have introduced caveats.
  • Forgetting the 44th Amendment's critical safeguards for Fundamental Rights (Arts. 20 & 21) and parliamentary approval during emergencies.
  • Asserting that political parties are explicitly defined and regulated by the original Constitution; their role is largely unwritten and governed by statutes and conventions.
  • Overlooking the impact of political dynamics (e.g., single-party dominance vs. coalition era) on the practical application of constitutional provisions.
  • Treating the Indian Constitution as a purely federal or purely unitary document; it's a unique blend, often described as 'quasi-federal'.

Doctrine of Eclipse and Its Application to Pre‑Constitutional Laws

The doctrine of eclipse holds that a pre‑constitutional law which is inconsistent with a fundamental right does not become void ab initio; it is merely eclipsed or rendered dormant until the constitutional impediment is removed. The law remains on the statute book and can revive if the fundamental right is amended or the inconsistency is otherwise cured. This principle was first articulated in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955), where the Supreme Court held that the Madhya Pradesh Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 1947, which nationalised motor transport, was not dead but only eclipsed by Article 19(1)(g). When the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, inserted Article 19(6) permitting such nationalisation, the law revived automatically.

The eclipse doctrine applies only to laws enacted before 26 January 1950. Post‑constitutional laws that violate fundamental rights are void under Article 13(2) and cannot be revived by subsequent amendment; they must be re‑enacted. The distinction is crucial: in State of Gujarat v. Shri Ram (1965) the Court clarified that a law made after the commencement of the Constitution cannot claim eclipse. The doctrine also does not extend to laws that are inconsistent with Directive Principles, because those are non‑justiciable. Moreover, the eclipse is not automatic for every fundamental right; it operates only where the fundamental right is a “right” that can be waived or restricted by constitutional amendment, such as the freedoms under Article 19.

Judicial application has refined the scope. In Keshavan Madhava Menon v. State of Bombay (1951) the Court held that a pre‑constitutional law inconsistent with Article 14 (equality) is also eclipsed, not void. However, in Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1959) the Court ruled that a law which violates Article 21 (life and personal liberty) is void, not eclipsed, because Article 21 is a non‑derogable right. The 24th Amendment (1971) and the 25th Amendment (1971) further shaped the doctrine by expanding Parliament’s power to amend fundamental rights, thereby allowing more pre‑constitutional laws to revive. The doctrine remains a vital tool for legislative continuity, ensuring that the statute book is not littered with dead letters while respecting constitutional supremacy.

Doctrine of Severability under Article 13: Judicial Tests and Landmark Cases

Article 13(1) and (2) declare that any law inconsistent with fundamental rights shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void. The doctrine of severability permits a court to strike down only the offending provision while preserving the remainder of the statute, provided the valid part is capable of standing independently. The Supreme Court has laid down a three‑fold test: (i) the invalid portion must be severable without altering the nature or structure of the legislation; (ii) the legislature must not have intended the statute to operate as an indivisible whole; and (iii) the remaining provisions must be workable and enforceable on their own.

The classic formulation appears in R.M.D.C. (Mysore) v. Union of India (1957), where the Court upheld the Prize Competitions Act, 1955, after severing the clause that violated Article 19(1)(g). The Court emphasized that the legislative intent, gathered from the preamble, the scheme, and the language, is the decisive factor. In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951) the Bombay Prohibition Act was partially struck down; the provisions prohibiting possession of liquor for personal consumption were severed because they were not essential to the Act’s primary objective of prohibiting sale.

Later cases refined the test. In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) the Court applied severability to the Tenth Schedule, holding that the paragraph disqualifying a member for voluntary resignation could be severed from the rest of the anti‑defection provisions. In Indian Medical Association v. Union of India (2011) the Court severed the provision of the Clinical Establishments Act that violated Article 19(1)(g) while retaining the regulatory framework. The doctrine does not apply where the invalid provision is the “heart” of the legislation, as in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980), where the Court refused to sever the amendment to Article 31C because it formed the core of the constitutional amendment. Severability thus balances constitutional fidelity with legislative economy, preventing the wholesale invalidation of statutes for isolated constitutional infirmities.

Identifying the Correct Doctrine in a Mixed Question
A pre‑constitutional law regulating the sale of intoxicating liquor is challenged after the Constitution comes into force on the ground that it violates Article 19(1)(g). The State argues that the law is merely eclipsed and will revive if Article 19(6) is amended. The petitioner contends that the law is void under Article 13(1). Which doctrine applies and why?
The doctrine of eclipse applies because the law was enacted before 26 January 1950. Under Article 13(1), pre‑constitutional laws inconsistent with fundamental rights are not void ab initio but only eclipsed. They remain dormant and can revive automatically when the constitutional impediment is removed, as held in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955). The doctrine of severability is irrelevant here because the challenge is to the whole law, not to a severable provision. Therefore, the State’s argument is correct: the law is eclipsed, not void.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes pre‑ and post‑constitutional laws, first identify the enactment date. If pre‑constitutional, think eclipse; if post‑constitutional, think void under Article 13(2). For severability, look for language such as “to the extent of the inconsistency” and check whether the statute contains a severability clause or whether the invalid part is the legislative core. Memorise the three‑fold test (severability, legislative intent, workability) and the landmark cases R.M.D.C., Balsara, and Kihoto Hollohan.

Constitutional Guarantee of the Right to Education: Article 21A, the 86th Amendment, and Judicial Enforcement

The Constitution (Eighty‑sixth Amendment) Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A, making free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen a fundamental right. The amendment also substituted Article 45, converting the original directive for free and compulsory education into a directive for early childhood care and education for children below six. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act) operationalised Article 21A, prescribing neighbourhood schools, 25 % reservation for economically weaker sections in private unaided schools, and minimum infrastructure norms.

The Supreme Court has interpreted Article 21A expansively. In Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2012) the Court upheld the 25 % quota, holding that the State’s obligation under Article 21A extends to ensuring access in private schools, and that the provision does not violate Article 19(1)(g) because it serves a compelling public interest. In Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India (2014) the Court clarified that minority institutions under Article 30(1) are exempt from the RTE Act’s quota requirement, preserving their autonomy. The Court in Avinash Mehrotra v. Union of India (2009) linked Article 21A with Article 21, declaring that the right to education is an integral facet of the right to life.

Implementation challenges persist. The 2019 amendment to the RTE Act extended the deadline for compliance with infrastructure norms and introduced a “no‑detention” policy up to class VIII, later partially rolled back. The Court in Kumar Shyam v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2021) directed states to fill teacher vacancies within a fixed timeline, treating the shortage as a violation of Article 21A. The jurisprudence establishes that Article 21A is justiciable, imposes positive obligations on the State, and requires progressive realisation backed by judicial monitoring.

Environmental Rights in the Constitution: Article 48A, Article 51A(g), and the Expanding Jurisprudence of Article 21

The Constitution (Forty‑second Amendment) Act, 1976 introduced Article 48A, directing the State to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard forests and wildlife. Simultaneously, Article 51A(g) imposed a fundamental duty on every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment. Though Directive Principles and fundamental duties are non‑justiciable, the Supreme Court has read them into Article 21, transforming environmental protection into an enforceable fundamental right.

The landmark M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) (Oleum gas leak) established the principle of absolute liability for hazardous industries and held that the right to a wholesome environment is part of Article 21. In Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) the Court articulated the “precautionary principle” and the “polluter pays principle” as part of the constitutional mandate under Articles 48A and 51A(g). The Court in Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1985) ordered the closure of limestone quarries in the Doon Valley, invoking Article 21 and the Directive Principles.

Subsequent jurisprudence expanded the scope. T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India (1997) led to the creation of the Central Empowered Committee for forest conservation. In Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991) the Court recognised the right to clean water as a facet of Article 21. The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, though statutory, derives its legitimacy from the constitutional framework of Articles 48A, 51A(g), and 21. The Court has also linked climate change obligations to constitutional duties, as seen in M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (2021), where the Court directed the government to formulate a climate action plan consistent with Article 21. This evolving jurisprudence demonstrates how non‑justiciable provisions become enforceable through judicial interpretation, making environmental protection a constitutional imperative.

  • Confusing eclipse (pre‑constitutional) with severability (post‑constitutional) — they operate on different temporal planes.
  • Assuming every pre‑constitutional law revives automatically; revival requires removal of the specific constitutional impediment.
  • Treating severability as a mechanical excision without checking legislative intent and workability of the remainder.
  • Believing Article 21A imposes only a negative obligation; it imposes a positive duty to provide infrastructure and teachers.
  • Overlooking the minority‑institution exemption under Article 30(1) when applying the RTE Act’s 25 % quota.
  • Thinking Articles 48A and 51A(g) are merely hortatory; the Supreme Court has consistently read them into Article 21 to make them justiciable.
  • Ignoring the distinction between absolute liability (M.C. Mehta) and strict liability (Rylands v. Fletcher) in environmental cases.

The Constituent Assembly's Debate on the Uniform Civil Code and Its Constitutional Status

The Uniform Civil Code (UCC) finds its textual anchor in Article 44 of the Directive Principles of State Policy, which directs the State to endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India. During the Constituent Assembly debates (1947‑1949) the provision provoked sharp divisions. Members such as K.M. Munshi and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar argued that a common civil code was essential for national integration and gender justice, while representatives of minority communities, notably Maulana Hasrat Mohani and B. Pocker Bahadur, warned that it would infringe upon the religious freedom guaranteed under Articles 25‑28. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, while personally favouring a UCC, insisted that the article remain a non‑justiciable directive, leaving the timing and manner of implementation to future legislatures. The Assembly ultimately adopted Article 44 without making it enforceable, reflecting a compromise between the aspiration for legal uniformity and the political reality of a plural society.

Post‑independence jurisprudence has repeatedly invoked Article 44 to urge legislative action. In Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985) the Supreme Court held that a Muslim woman was entitled to maintenance under Section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code, and observed that a UCC would help remove contradictions in personal laws. The judgment triggered the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, which diluted the ruling. In Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) the Court reiterated the need for a UCC to prevent fraudulent conversions for bigamy. John Vallamattom v. Union of India (2003) struck down Section 118 of the Indian Succession Act as discriminatory against Christians, again citing Article 44. More recently, the Law Commission’s 2018 consultation paper on family law reform recommended a phased approach, but no comprehensive legislation has been enacted. The UCC thus remains a constitutional aspiration, its realization dependent on political consensus and legislative will.

The Constitutional Scheme for the Protection of the Rights of the Anglo‑Indian Community and Its Repeal

The Constitution originally contained special provisions for the Anglo‑Indian community, a numerically small but historically distinct group. Article 331 empowered the President to nominate two Anglo‑Indians to the Lok Sabha if the community was not adequately represented. Article 333 provided for the nomination of one Anglo‑Indian to each State Legislative Assembly under similar conditions. These provisions were negotiated in the Constituent Assembly by Frank Anthony, the community’s leading spokesperson, who argued that without guaranteed representation the community’s voice would be lost in majoritarian politics. The nominations were intended as a transitional safeguard, reviewed every ten years.

The 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2020, abolished both Articles 331 and 333, ending the nomination scheme. The amendment followed the recommendation of the 2019 report of the National Commission for Minorities, which noted that the Anglo‑Indian population had fallen below 300,000 and that the community’s educational and economic indicators had improved. The repeal was passed with broad parliamentary consensus, reflecting a shift from community‑based representation to universal adult franchise as the sole basis of legislative membership. The removal of these articles illustrates how constitutional provisions designed for specific historical contexts can be formally deleted when their rationale ceases to exist, without affecting the basic structure of the Constitution.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “Which constitutional amendment removed the provision for nomination of Anglo‑Indians to Parliament and State Legislatures, and what was the stated justification?”
The 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2020 repealed Articles 331 and 333. The government justified the repeal on the ground that the Anglo‑Indian population had declined sharply and that the community no longer required special representation, as reflected in the 2019 National Commission for Minorities report.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question cites a specific amendment number, verify the year and the articles affected. Keep a mental table of recent amendments (99th‑105th) with their subject matter; this avoids confusion with similarly numbered amendments dealing with GST, reservations, or judicial appointments.

The Role of the Constituent Assembly's Committee on the Rules of Procedure in Shaping Parliamentary Practice

The Constituent Assembly’s first session in December 1946 established a Rules Committee to draft the procedural framework that would govern its deliberations and, by extension, the future Parliament of India. The committee, composed of senior members such as B.N. Rau, K.M. Munshi, and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, drew heavily on the Government of India Act 1935, the Standing Orders of the British House of Commons, and the procedural rules of the pre‑independence Central Legislative Assembly. Its report, adopted in 1947, introduced innovations such as the “Question Hour”, “Zero Hour” (later formalised), and the mechanism of “Calling Attention” motions, which allowed members to raise urgent matters without a formal motion.

The Rules Committee also devised the system of parliamentary committees — Public Accounts, Estimates, and Committee on Subordinate Legislation — that became the backbone of executive accountability. The Assembly’s decision to adopt a “whip” system, modelled on British practice, ensured party discipline while permitting limited conscience votes on constitutional amendments. Many of these rules were carried over verbatim into the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha (1952) and Rajya Sabha (1952). The continuity underscores the Constituent Assembly’s role not only as a constitution‑making body but also as the architect of India’s parliamentary culture.

The Constitutional Provision for the Establishment of the National Commission for Minorities and Its Evolution

Unlike the commissions for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Article 338) and for Backward Classes (Article 338B), the National Commission for Minorities (NCM) derives its existence from a statutory enactment — the National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992. The Act was passed pursuant to the Directive Principle in Article 38(2) and the assurance in the 1985 Rajiv Gandhi‑Longowal Accord to protect minority interests. The original 1992 Act provided for a Chairperson, a Vice‑Chairperson, and five members, all appointed by the Central Government. The 1995 amendment expanded the Commission’s mandate to monitor the implementation of the Prime Minister’s 15‑Point Programme for the Welfare of Minorities.

The 2004 amendment (Act 41 of 2004) conferred quasi‑judicial powers: the Commission could summon witnesses, require production of documents, and recommend prosecution for offences under the Communal Violence (Prevention) Bill (which lapsed). In National Commission for Minorities v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2015) the Supreme Court held that the Commission’s recommendations, while not binding, carry persuasive weight and must be considered by the government. The Commission’s annual reports are laid before Parliament, providing a constitutional‑style oversight mechanism despite its statutory origin. The evolution from a purely advisory body to one with investigative powers illustrates how legislative design can approximate constitutional accountability without a formal constitutional amendment.

The Doctrine of Constitutional Morality in the Context of Personal Law Reforms

Constitutional morality, a phrase coined by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar in his 1948 speech to the Constituent Assembly, denotes adherence to the core values of the Constitution — liberty, equality, fraternity, and justice — even when they conflict with majoritarian social norms. The Supreme Court has invoked this doctrine to adjudicate contentious personal‑law issues. In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) the Court declared instant triple talaq (talaq‑e‑biddat) unconstitutional, holding that the practice violated Articles 14, 15, and 21 and was contrary to constitutional morality. The majority opinion emphasized that constitutional morality requires the State to reform personal laws that perpetuate gender inequality.

In Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (2018) (Sabarimala), the Court ruled that the exclusion of women of menstruating age from the Sabarimala temple violated constitutional morality, as it subjugated women’s dignity to a patriarchal custom. The judgment clarified that constitutional morality is not synonymous with popular morality; it is anchored in the constitutional text and its transformative potential. Similarly, Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) decriminalised consensual same‑sex relations, asserting that constitutional morality demands protection of sexual orientation as an facet of dignity under Article 21. These rulings demonstrate that constitutional morality serves as a judicial tool to align personal laws with the Constitution’s egalitarian promise, often prompting legislative follow‑up such as the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019.

  • Confusing the non‑justiciable nature of Article 44 with a judicial mandate to enforce a Uniform Civil Code.
  • Assuming the Anglo‑Indian nomination provisions were permanent; they were expressly repealed by the 104th Amendment.
  • Attributing the Rules of Procedure solely to British precedent, ignoring the indigenous adaptations made by the Constituent Assembly’s Rules Committee.
  • Treating the National Commission for Minorities as a constitutional body on par with the NCSC or NCBC; it remains a statutory creation.
  • Equating constitutional morality with majoritarian public opinion; the doctrine expressly prioritises constitutional values over popular sentiment.
  • Overlooking that the 104th Amendment removed both Lok Sabha and State Assembly nominations in a single act.
  • Believing that the Supreme Court’s invocation of constitutional morality automatically nullifies all personal‑law provisions; each case requires a specific rights‑based analysis.

The Doctrine of Eclipse and Severability: Judicial Tools for Pre‑Constitutional and Post‑Constitutional Laws

The Constitution does not automatically invalidate all pre‑existing statutes. Article 13(1) provides that laws in force before the commencement of the Constitution shall continue until altered or repealed, but they are void to the extent of inconsistency with fundamental rights. The Supreme Court developed the doctrine of eclipse to explain the fate of such laws: a pre‑constitutional law that conflicts with a fundamental right is not dead but merely eclipsed; it remains dormant and can revive if the conflicting fundamental right is amended or removed. The landmark illustration is Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955), where a pre‑independence motor vehicles tax law was held eclipsed by Article 19(1)(g) and revived after the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955 modified the right.

Conversely, the doctrine of severability governs post‑constitutional legislation. Under Article 13(2), any law made after 26 January 1950 that contravenes fundamental rights is void to the extent of the contravention. The Court asks whether the offending provision can be severed from the rest of the statute without destroying its legislative intent. In R.M.D.C. v. Union of India (1957), the Court upheld the Prize Competitions Act after severing the unconstitutional section, establishing the test of “legislative intent” and “independent survival”. Later, in State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills (1974), the Court clarified that severability applies only when the valid and invalid parts are not so inextricably mixed that the legislature would not have enacted the valid part alone.

Both doctrines operate as safety valves preserving legislative continuity while respecting constitutional supremacy. Eclipse protects the statute book from wholesale invalidation of colonial enactments; severability prevents the striking down of entire modern statutes for a single unconstitutional clause. Together they illustrate the Court’s pragmatic approach: the Constitution is supreme, but the legal order need not collapse each time a conflict arises.

The Constituent Assembly’s Committee on Rules of Procedure: Drafting Parliamentary Practice

Even before the Constitution was adopted, the Constituent Assembly recognised that a functioning legislature required its own procedural code. In July 1947 the Assembly constituted a Rules Committee under the chairmanship of Dr. Rajendra Prasad, the Assembly’s President, with members including B.R. Ambedkar, K.M. Munshi and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar. The Committee’s mandate was to frame rules for the conduct of business of the Constituent Assembly itself, which would later serve as the template for the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.

The Committee submitted its report on 20 July 1947, and the Assembly adopted the Rules of Procedure on the same day. Key innovations included the question hour, adjournment motions, calling attention notices, and a structured committee system (Public Accounts, Estimates, and later, Department‑Related Standing Committees). The Rules also codified the Speaker’s powers to maintain order, decide points of order, and certify money bills — a direct borrowing from the British House of Commons but adapted to a written constitution.

When the Constitution came into force, Article 118 empowered each House to make its own rules. The Provisional Parliament (the Constituent Assembly acting as Parliament) adopted the Constituent Assembly Rules with minor modifications as the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha (1952) and the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Rajya Sabha (1952). The continuity is evident: the same numbering of motions, the same committee nomenclature, and the same Speaker/Chairman authority. This institutional memory explains why India’s parliamentary practice, despite a written constitution, retains a strong procedural continuity with the Constituent Assembly’s own deliberations.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “The Rules of Procedure of the Lok Sabha were directly borrowed from the British House of Commons without any indigenous adaptation.” Identify the error and give the correct position.
The statement is false. While the Constituent Assembly’s Rules Committee drew heavily on British parliamentary practice, it made deliberate indigenous adaptations: (1) inclusion of a calling attention notice to enable urgent executive accountability, (2) a committee system tailored to a federal polity with a strong centre, and (3) the Speaker’s certification of money bills under Article 110, a constitutional provision absent in the UK. The Rules were adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 20 July 1947 and later carried forward by the Provisional Parliament, demonstrating an indigenous legislative lineage.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question contrasts “borrowed” versus “indigenous” features, always cite the Rules Committee’s 1947 report and the 1952 Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha Rules as evidence of adaptation. Mention the specific procedural devices (calling attention, committee system, money‑bill certification) that have no exact British counterpart.

The Uniform Civil Code Debate in the Constituent Assembly: Article 44 and Its Legacy

Article 44 (originally Draft Article 35) directs the State to endeavour to secure a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) for all citizens. The debate in the Constituent Assembly (November 1948) reveals the tension between the aspiration for legal uniformity and the protection of religious personal laws. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, while supporting the principle, argued that the State should not impose a code until the society was ready, and therefore placed it in the Directive Principles rather than the Fundamental Rights. K.M. Munshi and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar echoed this pragmatic stance, warning that a premature UCC could provoke communal discord.

Opponents such as Maulana Hasrat Mohani and Naziruddin Ahmad contended that personal laws were integral to religious freedom under Article 25 and that the State lacked competence to legislate on them. The Assembly ultimately adopted the compromise language: “The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.” The word “endeavour” and the placement in Part IV rendered the provision non‑justiciable, signalling a legislative rather than judicial mandate.

Post‑independence, the Supreme Court has repeatedly urged Parliament to enact a UCC, notably in Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985) and Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995). Yet, the political consensus envisioned by the Constituent Assembly remains elusive. The debate illustrates how the Assembly’s deliberative record continues to shape contemporary constitutional discourse on secularism, gender justice, and federalism.

Constitutional Identity and the Basic Structure: The Supreme Court’s Emerging Jurisprudence

Beyond the classic “basic structure” doctrine articulated in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Supreme Court has increasingly invoked the notion of constitutional identity to denote those core features that define the Constitution’s very essence and cannot be altered even by a constitutional amendment. In Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980), the Court held that the balance between fundamental rights and directive principles constitutes part of the Constitution’s identity. In I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), the Court extended the basic structure test to laws placed in the Ninth Schedule, affirming that the identity of the Constitution includes judicial review as a non‑derogable feature.

More recently, in NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018), the Court described the “constitutional identity” of Delhi as a “federal unit with a unique status” that cannot be erased by ordinary legislation. In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), the majority linked the right to privacy to the “constitutional identity” of dignity, liberty and equality.
