These judgments suggest a two‑layered protection: the basic structure doctrine guards against amendments that destroy the Constitution’s fundamental framework, while constitutional identity serves as an interpretive lens for statutory and executive action, ensuring that the Constitution’s animating values remain intact.

Scholars argue that constitutional identity, borrowed from German constitutional theory, provides a more flexible yet robust standard than the rigid “essential features” list. It allows the Court to protect emerging rights (e.g., data protection, environmental sustainability) as part of the Constitution’s evolving identity without formally expanding the basic structure catalogue.

The Constituent Assembly’s Committee on the Distribution of Legislative Powers: Federal Design Choices

The federal architecture of the Constitution was not a foregone conclusion. In 1947 the Assembly appointed a Committee on the Distribution of Powers between the Centre and the Provinces chaired by Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, with members including B.R. Ambedkar, K.M. Munshi and Gopalaswami Ayyangar. The Committee’s report (October 1947) recommended a strong centre with residuary powers vested in the Union, a concurrent list for subjects of common interest, and a limited provincial list. It also proposed an Inter‑State Council (later Article 263) to coordinate policy.

The Committee’s rationale was shaped by the Partition experience, the need for economic planning, and the desire to prevent secessionist tendencies. Its recommendations were largely adopted in the Government of India Act 1935‑derived Seventh Schedule, but with crucial modifications: the Union List was expanded (defence, foreign affairs, atomic energy), the State List was trimmed, and the Concurrent List was enlarged to include criminal law, marriage, and education. The Committee also insisted on Article 3 empowering Parliament to reorganise states by simple majority, a provision that has facilitated the creation of new states (e.g., Andhra Pradesh 1953, Chhattisgarh 2000, Telangana 2014).

Critics argue that the Committee’s centralising bias produced a “quasi‑federal” system where the Union can encroach on state autonomy through the Concurrent List and emergency provisions. Supporters contend that the design has preserved national unity and enabled coordinated development. The Committee’s minutes remain a primary source for interpreting the original federal intent, especially in disputes over legislative competence under Articles 246 and 254.

  • Confusing the doctrine of eclipse (pre‑constitutional laws) with severability (post‑constitutional laws); they operate on different constitutional provisions and temporal scopes.
  • Assuming the Constituent Assembly’s Rules Committee was a mere copy of British standing orders; it introduced indigenous devices such as calling attention notices and a federal committee system.
  • Treating Article 44 as a justiciable mandate for a Uniform Civil Code; the Assembly deliberately placed it in the Directive Principles with the word “endeavour”.
  • Equating “basic structure” with “constitutional identity”; the former is a judicial limit on amendment power, the latter an interpretive concept protecting the Constitution’s core values in statutory and executive action.
  • Believing the Committee on Distribution of Powers favoured a loose federation; its report explicitly advocated a strong centre with residuary powers in the Union.
  • Overlooking that the Rules of Procedure adopted by the Provisional Parliament in 1952 were the direct continuation of the Constituent Assembly’s 1947 Rules, not a fresh British import.
  • Ignoring that the doctrine of severability requires the valid portion to be capable of independent operation; courts will not sever if the legislature would not have enacted the remainder alone.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee Architecture: Steering, Rules, and the Management of Constitutional Drafting

The Constituent Assembly functioned through a layered committee system that translated political consensus into constitutional text. At the apex stood the Steering Committee, chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad, which coordinated the work of all other committees, set the agenda for plenary sessions, and resolved inter‑committee jurisdictional disputes. Its decisions determined the sequence in which reports were presented, ensuring that foundational questions — federal structure, fundamental rights, citizenship — were settled before sectoral provisions. The Rules of Procedure Committee, also chaired by the President, drafted the Assembly’s standing orders. Unlike the British model it referenced, the Rules Committee introduced indigenous procedural devices: the calling attention notice for urgent matters, a federal committee system mirroring the Centre‑State division, and a requirement that amendments to the draft Constitution be circulated fourteen days in advance. These rules were adopted by the Provisional Parliament in 1952 without substantive change, making them the direct procedural ancestor of the Lok Sabha’s current rulebook.

The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities, chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, operated through four sub‑committees: Fundamental Rights (J.B. Kripalani), Minorities (H.C. Mookherjee), North‑East Frontier Tribal Areas (Gopinath Bordoloi), and Excluded and Partially Excluded Areas (A.V. Thakkar). The Fundamental Rights Sub‑Committee’s interim report (April 1947) proposed a “due process” clause modelled on the US Fifth Amendment; the full Advisory Committee replaced it with “procedure established by law” after Patel intervened, fearing judicial unpredictability in preventive detention cases. The Committee on the Distribution of Powers (Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar) and the Union Powers Committee (Jawaharlal Nehru) worked in parallel, the former designing the Seventh Schedule lists, the latter defining exclusive Union subjects such as defence, foreign affairs, and atomic energy. The Drafting Committee (B.R. Ambedkar) received these reports, harmonised overlapping recommendations, and produced the first full draft in February 1948. Its seven members — Ambedkar, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, K.M. Munshi, Mohammad Saadullah, B.L. Mitter (later replaced by N. Madhava Rao), and D.P. Khaitan (died 1948, replaced by T.T. Krishnamachari) — met for 141 days, producing a draft of 315 articles and 8 schedules. The Credentials Committee and the House Committee managed membership verification and logistics, while the Finance and Staff Committee controlled the Assembly’s budget, a rare instance of a constituent body exercising financial autonomy. Understanding this architecture explains why certain provisions bear the imprint of specific sub‑committees — for example, the Fifth and Sixth Schedules originated in the North‑East Frontier and Excluded Areas sub‑committees — and why the Drafting Committee’s language often reflects compromise formulae rather than a single philosophical vision.

Citizenship at Commencement: The Partition‑Driven Design of Articles 5‑11 and the Citizenship Act 1955

The citizenship provisions (Articles 5‑11) were drafted under the immediate pressure of Partition, making them unique in the Constitution for their temporal specificity. Article 5 conferred citizenship at commencement (26 January 1950) on three categories: persons domiciled in the territory of India who were born in India, or either of whose parents was born in India, or who had been ordinarily resident in India for not less than five years immediately preceding commencement. Article 6 addressed migrants from Pakistan: those who migrated before 19 July 1948 became citizens if they had been ordinarily resident since migration; those migrating on or after that date needed to register as citizens after six months’ residence, subject to a permit system. Article 7 dealt with migrants to Pakistan after 1 March 1947, deeming them to have lost Indian citizenship unless they returned under a resettlement permit. Article 8 extended citizenship to persons of Indian origin residing outside India who registered with an Indian diplomatic mission. Article 9 provided that voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship terminated Indian citizenship — a provision that remains the sole constitutional ground for involuntary loss. Article 10 preserved citizenship subject to parliamentary law, and Article 11 empowered Parliament to regulate citizenship by legislation, explicitly ousting judicial review of the acquisition or termination of citizenship under the Constitution itself.

The Citizenship Act 1955 operationalised Article 11. It established five modes of acquisition: birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, and incorporation of territory. The Act originally followed jus soli (birth within territory) for persons born after commencement, but the 1986 amendment restricted birth‑based citizenship to those with at least one Indian parent, and the 2003 amendment further required that the other parent not be an illegal migrant. The 1955 Act also created the framework for Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) in 2005, a statutory category distinct from constitutional citizenship that confers lifelong visa‑free travel and parity with Non‑Resident Indians in economic fields but no political rights. The Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2019 introduced a religious criterion for the first time, granting expedited naturalisation to Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan who entered India before 31 December 2014. This amendment is currently under constitutional challenge on grounds of violating Article 14 (equality) and the basic structure’s secular character. The Partition context also explains the Permit System (1948‑1950) administered by the Ministry of Rehabilitation, which regulated cross‑border movement and whose records remain relevant in Assam’s National Register of Citizens (NRC) exercise under the Citizenship (Registration of Citizens and Issue of National Identity Cards) Rules 2003. The Supreme Court in Assam Sanmilita Mahasangha v. Union of India (2014) referred the constitutional validity of Section 6A of the Citizenship Act (inserted by the Assam Accord 1985) to a Constitution Bench; the question — whether a differentiated citizenship cut‑off for Assam violates Article 14 — remains unresolved. The citizenship scheme thus illustrates how a transitional constitutional design became a permanent framework, with Parliament using Article 11 to adapt the law to shifting demographic and political realities while the judiciary polices the equality and basic structure boundaries.

Applied Scenario: Citizenship Cut‑off Dates
A person born in Dhaka in 1945 migrated to India on 15 August 1948. Her parents remained in Dhaka. She has resided continuously in Kolkata since migration. Under the Constitution as originally enacted, is she an Indian citizen at commencement? Explain the relevant Article and the factual test.
Answer: Yes, she is a citizen under Article 6(a). Article 6 applies to persons who migrated to India from the territory now included in Pakistan. Clause (a) covers migration before 19 July 1948. The test is: (i) migration before 19 July 1948; (ii) ordinary residence in India since the date of migration. She migrated on 15 August 1948 — this is after 19 July 1948, so clause (a) does not apply. She falls under clause (b): migration on or after 19 July 1948. For clause (b), she must have been registered as a citizen of India by an officer appointed by the Government of India on an application made before commencement of the Constitution, provided she had resided in India for at least six months immediately preceding the application. Since the question asks about citizenship at commencement (26 January 1950) and does not state she registered, she would not be a citizen automatically at commencement under Article 6(b) without registration. The key distinction: pre‑19 July 1948 migrants acquired citizenship by operation of law (ordinary residence); post‑19 July 1948 migrants required registration. Many aspirants confuse the two cut‑offs; the 19 July 1948 date corresponds to the permit system introduction.
Exam‑Day Strategy: Citizenship Articles
Memorise the three critical dates: 19 July 1948 (Article 6 cut‑off), 1 March 1947 (Article 7 cut‑off for migrants to Pakistan), and 26 January 1950 (commencement). Draw a two‑column table: pre‑19 July 1948 migrants (automatic citizenship via ordinary residence) vs post‑19 July 1948 migrants (registration + six months residence + permit). For Article 7, remember the return permit exception. In MCQs, the trap is often a migrant who arrived on 20 July 1948 but did not register — answer: not a citizen at commencement. In Mains, link the 2019 Amendment’s religious classification to the Article 14/basic structure challenge and the Assam Accord’s Section 6A reference.

The Original Constitutional Architecture for Jammu & Kashmir: Article 370, the 1954 Presidential Order, and the Doctrine of Asymmetric Federalism

Article 370, placed in Part XXI (Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions), was the constitutional instrument that defined the relationship between the Union and the State of Jammu & Kashmir (J&K) from 1950 until its effective abrogation in August 2019. The Article originated from the Instrument of Accession (26 October 1947), whereby Maharaja Hari Singh acceded to India on three subjects — defence, external affairs, and communications — and the subsequent Delhi Agreement (1952) between the Union Government and the J&K Government led by Sheikh Abdullah. Article 370(1) provided that the provisions of Article 238 (which dealt with Part B States) would not apply to J&K, and that the President could apply other constitutional provisions to the State only with the concurrence of the State Government. Crucially, Article 370(1)(d) allowed the President to specify, by order, the matters in the Union List and Concurrent List on which Parliament could legislate for J&K, and to modify the application of other constitutional provisions, subject to the concurrence of the State Government and, where the modification affected the State’s powers, the ratification by the State’s Constituent Assembly. Article 370(3) empowered the President to declare the Article inoperative, but only on the recommendation of the State’s Constituent Assembly.

The Constitution (Application to Jammu & Kashmir) Order 1954 (C.O. 48), issued under Article 370(1), was the primary vehicle for extending the Constitution to J&K. It applied Part III (Fundamental Rights) with modifications — notably, the right to property (Article 31) remained a fundamental right in J&K after its deletion from the rest of India by the 44th Amendment 1978. It extended the Directive Principles, the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction under Article 132, and the Election Commission’s authority. It also inserted Article 35A via the same Order, empowering the J&K Legislature to define “permanent residents” and confer special rights on them regarding public employment, acquisition of immovable property, settlement, and scholarships. Article 35A was not enacted by Parliament under Article 368 but by the President under Article 370(1)(d), a fact central to the 2019 challenge. The J&K Constitution, adopted by the State’s Constituent Assembly in 1956 and effective 26 January 1957, declared J&K an integral part of India (Section 3) but retained residual legislative power (Section 5) — a reversal of the Union’s residuary power under Article 248. The State’s Constituent Assembly dissolved itself in 1957 without recommending the abrogation of Article 370, creating the constitutional puzzle that persisted for six decades: whether Article 370(3) could ever be activated after the Constituent Assembly’s dissolution.

The Supreme Court in Prem Nath Kaul v. State of J&K (1959) held that Article 370(1) required the “concurrence” of the State Government, not merely consultation, and that this concurrence was provisional until ratified by the State Constituent Assembly. In Sampat Prakash v. State of J&K (1969), the Court ruled that Article 370 remained operative even after the Constituent Assembly’s dissolution because the President’s power under Article 370(1) to issue orders with State Government concurrence survived. The Constitution (Application to Jammu & Kashmir) Order 2019 (C.O. 272), issued on 5 August 2019, superseded the 1954 Order and applied all provisions of the Constitution to J&K “notwithstanding anything contained in Article 370”. On the same day, a statutory resolution under Article 370(3) recommended by the President (acting on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, with the State under President’s Rule) declared Article 370 inoperative except for a residual clause stating that all constitutional provisions apply. The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act 2019 bifurcated the State into two Union Territories: J&K (with legislature) and Ladakh (without legislature). A Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in In re: Article 370 (December 2023) upheld the 2019 actions, holding that: (i) Article 370 was a temporary provision; (ii) the President could unilaterally issue C.O. 272 under Article 370(1)(d) because the “State Government” during President’s Rule meant the Governor/Union Executive; (iii) the Constituent Assembly’s recommendation under Article 370(3) was not mandatory after its dissolution — the President could act on the recommendation of Parliament (which passed the statutory resolution); and (iv) the Reorganisation Act was valid under Article 3 (which allows formation of new States/UTs) read with Article 370’s overriding clause. The judgment effectively ended asymmetric federalism for J&K, integrating it fully into the Union’s legislative and executive framework. The episode remains the definitive case study of how a temporary, negotiated constitutional provision can be transformed through executive order, parliamentary resolution, and judicial validation.

Emergency Provisions: Constituent Assembly Debates, the Weimar Influence, and the 44th Amendment Safeguards

The emergency provisions (Articles 352, 356, 360) were among the most contested in the Constituent Assembly. The Weimar Constitution’s Article 48 — which allowed the President to suspend fundamental rights and rule by decree — was the explicit model for Article 352, as acknowledged by Dr. Ambedkar and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar. However, the Assembly introduced critical modifications: the emergency could be proclaimed only on grounds of “war, external aggression, or internal disturbance” (the phrase “internal disturbance” was replaced by “armed rebellion” by the 44th Amendment 1978), and the proclamation required written Cabinet advice (inserted by the 44th Amendment after the 1975 experience). Article 352 originally allowed suspension of all fundamental rights, including Articles 20 and 21; the 44th Amendment prohibited suspension of Articles 20 and 21 even during emergency. The H.V. Kamath amendment proposal to require parliamentary approval within two months (instead of the original one year) was rejected; the 44th Amendment later reduced the period to one month and mandated that the proclamation cease to operate unless approved by both Houses by special majority within that month.

Article 356 (President’s Rule) derived from Section 93 of the Government of India Act 1935, which allowed the Governor to assume provincial powers on the ground of failure of constitutional machinery. The Assembly debated whether “failure of constitutional machinery” should be justiciable. Dr. Ambedkar argued it was a political question; K.T. Shah and H.V. Kamath wanted judicial review. The original Article 356 contained no time limit; the 44th Amendment introduced a maximum period of three years (with parliamentary approval every six months) and required that the proclamation be based on the Governor’s report or otherwise. The S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) judgment later imposed judicial review on the satisfaction of the President, requiring the material to be relevant and not mala fide, and established that the State Legislative Assembly cannot be dissolved until Parliament approves the proclamation.

Article 360 (Financial Emergency) was modelled on the US National Industrial Recovery Act and the Australian financial agreement provisions. It has never been invoked. The 44th Amendment added a requirement that the proclamation be approved by Parliament within two months. The Assembly’s debates reveal a tension between the need for central authority in crises and the fear of authoritarian drift. The 44th Amendment (1978), enacted by the Janata Government after the 1975‑77 Emergency, represents the constitutional settlement: it narrowed grounds, strengthened parliamentary control, protected core rights, and made the President’s satisfaction subject to Cabinet advice. The 42nd Amendment (1976) had earlier extended the emergency period, allowed suspension of Article 19 freedoms even during “armed rebellion”, and curtailed judicial review — changes the 44th Amendment reversed. The emergency framework thus illustrates the Constitution’s capacity for self‑correction through amendment, driven by political experience and judicial interpretation.

From “Procedure Established by Law” to Due Process: The Constituent Assembly’s Rejection of Due Process and the Judicial Reconstruction in Maneka Gandhi

The phrase “procedure established by law” in Article 21 was a deliberate departure from the American “due process of law”. The Fundamental Rights Sub‑Committee (April 1947) initially recommended “no person shall be deprived of his life, liberty or property without due process of law”. The Advisory Committee (Patel) replaced “due process” with “procedure established by law” on the grounds that “due process” imported an undefined judicial veto over legislative policy, particularly in preventive detention and land reform. B.N. Rau, the Constitutional Adviser, had warned during his 1947 consultation with US Justice Felix Frankfurter that “due process” would empower courts to strike down social legislation. The Drafting Committee adopted “procedure established by law” from the Japanese Constitution (Article 31), which itself borrowed from the English “law of the land” tradition but without the substantive due process gloss. The phrase “personal liberty” was chosen over “liberty” to limit the scope to physical freedom, excluding contractual or property rights.

For 28 years, the Supreme Court read Article 21 literally. In A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950), the majority held that “procedure established by law” meant any procedure enacted by a competent legislature; the court would not examine its fairness, reasonableness, or conformity with natural justice. Article 19 (freedoms) and Article 21 (life/liberty) were treated as mutually exclusive — a law affecting personal liberty need not satisfy Article 19. This formalist reading enabled the Preventive Detention Act 1950 and subsequent detention regimes. The turning point came in R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) (Bank Nationalisation case), where the Court held that a law depriving property (Article 31) must also satisfy Article 19(1)(f), beginning the integration of fundamental rights. In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), a seven‑judge Bench overruled Gopalan. Justice Bhagwati, for the majority, held that “procedure established by law” must be “fair, just and reasonable, not fanciful, oppressive or arbitrary” — effectively importing substantive due process. The Court also ruled that Articles 14, 19, and 21 are not mutually exclusive but form a “trinity”; a law depriving personal liberty must satisfy the reasonableness test of Article 14 and the specific freedoms of Article 19. The “procedure established by law” thus became, through judicial construction, a standard equivalent to “due process of law” but with an Indian textual anchor. Subsequent cases expanded this: Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi (1981) read “right to life” to include “right to live with human dignity”; Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) included livelihood; K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) included privacy. The Constituent Assembly’s textual choice, intended to limit judicial power, became the vehicle for the most expansive rights jurisprudence in the Commonwealth — a striking instance of constitutional irony.

  • Confusing the Steering Committee (agenda‑setting) with the Drafting Committee (text‑writing); the former managed process, the latter produced the draft.
  • Assuming Article 6(a) and 6(b) use the same cut‑off date; 19 July 1948 is the dividing line between automatic citizenship and registration‑based citizenship.
  • Believing Article 370 required the State Constituent Assembly’s recommendation for every Presidential order; Article 370(1)(d) required only State Government concurrence for most orders, with Constituent Assembly ratification only for changes affecting State powers.
  • Stating that the 44th Amendment removed “internal disturbance” from Article 352 but not from Article 356; “internal disturbance” was never in Article 356 — the ground there is “failure of constitutional machinery”.
  • Claiming Maneka Gandhi “overruled” Gopalan on Article 21 alone; it also fused Articles 14, 19, and 21 into an integrated rights framework.
  • Thinking Article 35A was a parliamentary amendment under Article 368; it was inserted by Presidential Order under Article 370(1)(d), which was the core of its constitutional vulnerability.
  • Assuming the Citizenship Act 1955 is immune from judicial review because of Article 11; Article 11 ousts review of acquisition/termination provisions, but the Act’s classification criteria (e.g., CAA 2019) remain subject to Article 14 and basic structure scrutiny.

Doctrine of Eclipse: Judicial Treatment of Pre‑Constitutional Laws

The doctrine of eclipse holds that a pre‑Constitutional statute which conflicts with a fundamental right does not become void ab initio; it is merely eclipsed or rendered dormant to the extent of the inconsistency. The law remains on the statute book and can revive if the constitutional impediment is removed, for instance by a constitutional amendment that alters the fundamental right in question. The Supreme Court first articulated this principle in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955), where a pre‑Constitution motor vehicles law imposing a tax on goods carried by road was challenged under Article 19(1)(g). The Court held that the law was not dead but only eclipsed by the fundamental right, and would become operative again if the right were amended. In Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1959) the Court clarified that the doctrine applies only to laws existing before the commencement of the Constitution; post‑Constitutional laws that violate fundamental rights are void under Article 13(2) and cannot be revived by subsequent amendment. The eclipse doctrine thus preserves legislative continuity while respecting constitutional supremacy. It also underscores the distinction between “void” and “voidable” legislation: a pre‑Constitutional law is voidable at the instance of a citizen whose fundamental right is infringed, whereas a post‑Constitutional law is void from inception. The doctrine has been invoked in later cases such as State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills (1974) concerning labour legislation, and Keshavan Madhava Menon v. State of Bombay (1951) where the Court refused to apply eclipse to a law that had been repealed before the Constitution came into force. The practical effect is that legislatures need not re‑enact eclipsed laws once the constitutional barrier is lifted; the original enactment revives automatically. This principle reinforces the idea that the Constitution is a living instrument that can modify the operation of existing statutes without erasing them.

Doctrine of Severability: Scope, Limits, and Landmark Cases

The doctrine of severability (or separability) enables a court to strike down only the offending provision of a statute while preserving the remainder, provided the valid part is capable of standing independently and the legislature would have enacted it without the invalid portion. The Supreme Court laid down the test in R.M.D.C. (Mysore) v. Union of India (1957): the invalid provision must be so inextricably mixed with the valid that separation would change the nature of the legislation, and the legislature’s intention must be discernible from the statute’s scheme. In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), the Court upheld the Bombay Prohibition Act after severing the provision that prohibited possession of liquor for medicinal purposes, finding the rest of the Act workable. Conversely, in A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) the Court refused to sever the preventive detention provisions from the Preventive Detention Act because the Act’s entire scheme centred on detention. The doctrine does not apply where the invalid provision constitutes the essence of the law, or where the statute contains a non‑severability clause (though such clauses are not conclusive). The Court also considers whether the remaining provisions can be enforced without the severed part and whether the legislative purpose survives. In Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980), the Court applied severability to uphold the basic structure doctrine by reading down the 42nd Amendment’s clauses that sought to curtail judicial review, while leaving the rest of the amendment intact. The doctrine thus acts as a surgical instrument, preserving legislative labour and avoiding the wholesale invalidation of statutes. It also reflects the principle of constitutional economy: the judiciary intervenes minimally, excising only the unconstitutional fragment.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “If a pre‑Constitutional law is eclipsed by a fundamental right, and later that fundamental right is amended to remove the inconsistency, does the law revive automatically or does it require fresh legislative enactment?”
The law revives automatically. The doctrine of eclipse (Bhikaji Narain Dhakras, 1955) treats the pre‑Constitutional law as dormant, not dead. Once the constitutional impediment is removed — by amendment of the fundamental right — the eclipse lifts and the original provision becomes operative again without any fresh legislation. This distinguishes eclipse from the voidness of post‑Constitutional laws under Article 13(2), which cannot revive even if the fundamental right is later amended.
Answer‑Writing Strategy
When a question combines eclipse and severability, first identify the temporal character of the law (pre‑ or post‑Constitutional). Cite Bhikaji Narain for eclipse and R.M.D.C. for severability. Use a two‑step structure: (1) state the doctrine, (2) apply the judicial test (legislative intent, workability of the remainder). Mention the non‑severability clause only as a factor, not a bar. This layered approach fetches full marks.

The President’s Pocket Veto and the Constitutional Requirement of Assent under Article 111

Article 111 of the Constitution provides that when a Bill is passed by both Houses of Parliament, it shall be presented to the President, who shall either give assent or withhold assent. Unlike the United States President, the Indian President has no explicit time limit within which to act, nor does the Constitution provide for a “pocket veto” — the automatic failure of a Bill if the President takes no action before the dissolution of the legislature. In practice, the President acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74), making assent a formal, ministerial act. The Supreme Court in R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) observed that the President’s assent is not a personal discretionary power but a constitutional formality; withholding assent without ministerial advice would be unconstitutional. The 1976 amendment to Article 74 (by the 42nd Amendment) made the advice binding, further negating any pocket veto. However, a theoretical pocket veto could arise if the President simply delays indefinitely while the Lok Sabha is dissolved, because the Bill lapses on dissolution (Article 107). This scenario has never occurred; every Bill presented has received assent. The Constitution’s design thus ensures that the executive cannot unilaterally block legislation, preserving parliamentary supremacy within constitutional limits. The absence of a pocket veto also distinguishes the Indian system from the American model, where the President’s inaction after ten days (excluding Sundays) during a congressional adjournment kills the Bill. In India, the President’s role is ceremonial, and any attempt to withhold assent would trigger a constitutional crisis, likely resolved by judicial intervention under Article 143 or a reference to the Supreme Court.

The Constitutional Role of the Vice‑President: Ex Officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha and Succession

The Vice‑President of India occupies a unique dual office under Articles 63 to 71. As the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 64), the Vice‑President presides over the Upper House, maintains order, decides points of order, and certifies Money Bills (Article 110). The Vice‑President does not vote in the first instance but exercises a casting vote in case of a tie. The office is elected by an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament (Article 66), using the system of proportional representation by means of a single transferable vote. The term is five years, and the Vice‑President may resign by writing to the President or be removed by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a majority of its then membership and agreed to by the Lok Sabha (Article 67). Crucially, the Vice‑President acts as President when a vacancy occurs by reason of death, resignation, removal, or otherwise (Article 65), until a new President is elected, which must happen within six months. During such acting period, the Vice‑President discharges all presidential functions but does not assume the office of President. The Vice‑President’s role in the legislative sphere is largely procedural; however, the casting vote can be decisive in a closely divided Rajya Sabha. The office has been held by distinguished parliamentarians, and its design reflects the framers’ intent to provide a stable, non‑partisan presiding officer for the Upper House while ensuring a ready successor to the presidency. The Vice‑President’s independence is safeguarded by the same removal procedure as the President, requiring a special majority, thereby insulating the office from transient political pressures.

The Constitutional Framework for the Finance Commission’s Horizontal Distribution Formula: Evolution and Judicial Scrutiny

Article 280 mandates the constitution of a Finance Commission every five years to recommend the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (vertical distribution) and the allocation among States (horizontal distribution). The horizontal formula has evolved from a simple population‑based criterion in the First Finance Commission (1951) to a multi‑criteria framework in the Fifteenth Finance Commission (2020‑25). Key criteria include: (i) population (1971 Census until the Fourteenth FC, then 2011 Census), (ii) income distance (per capita GSDP gap), (iii) area, (iv) forest cover, (v) tax effort, and (vi) demographic performance. The Fourteenth Finance Commission (2015‑20) increased the States’ share in the divisible pool to 42 % and introduced a “forest cover” weight to reward ecological services. The Fifteenth Finance Commission retained the 41 % vertical share (adjusted for the creation of the Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh) and added a “demographic performance” criterion to incentivise population control. The Commission’s recommendations are advisory; the President lays them before Parliament, and the Union government implements them through a Presidential order. Judicial scrutiny of the formula is extremely limited. In State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court held that the Finance Commission’s recommendations involve policy choices within the domain of the executive and are not justiciable unless they violate a constitutional provision or are mala fide. The Court reiterated that the Constitution entrusts the Commission with “broad discretion” to balance equity, efficiency, and fiscal federalism. Consequently, challenges to the weightage assigned to any criterion have been dismissed. The evolving formula reflects the dynamic nature of fiscal federalism, responding to demographic shifts, developmental disparities, and environmental concerns while remaining within the constitutional architecture of cooperative federalism.

  • Confusing the doctrine of eclipse (pre‑Constitutional laws) with the doctrine of severability (post‑Constitutional statutes) — they operate on different temporal planes and have distinct revival rules.
  • Assuming the President can exercise a pocket veto; the Constitution makes assent a ministerial act on aid and advice, and no Bill has ever been left unassented.
  • Treating the Vice‑President’s casting vote as a regular vote; it is exercised only to break a tie and cannot be used to initiate legislation.
  • Believing the Finance Commission’s horizontal formula is justiciable; the Supreme Court has consistently held it to be a non‑justiciable policy matter absent constitutional violation.
  • Overlooking that the doctrine of severability requires the remainder of the statute to be workable and consistent with legislative intent; a non‑severability clause is not decisive.
  • Thinking the Vice‑President automatically becomes President on a vacancy; the Vice‑President only acts as President until a new election is held within six months.
  • These traps highlight the need for precise conceptual clarity in answer writing.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on the Emergency Provisions: Articles 352, 356, and 360

The emergency provisions were among the most intensely debated sections of the Constitution. The Constituent Assembly drew heavily on the Government of India Act 1935, which contained a single “Proclamation of Emergency” power for the Governor‑General. The Assembly, however, split this into three distinct heads: a National Emergency (Article 352), a State Emergency commonly called President’s Rule (Article 356), and a Financial Emergency (Article 360). The Emergency Provisions Committee, chaired by Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, examined the British wartime experience, the Canadian “War Measures Act”, and the Australian “defence power” to fashion a framework that balanced executive decisiveness with parliamentary oversight.

During the debates of July‑August 1949, B.R. Ambedkar insisted that the President could act only on the written advice of the Council of Ministers, a safeguard later codified in the 44th Amendment (1978) but already implicit in the original draft. K.M. Munshi argued for a strict time‑limit: the proclamation must be laid before each House of Parliament within one month and cease to operate unless approved by a special majority. The Assembly adopted a one‑month initial period for Articles 352 and 356, extendable by six months at a time with parliamentary approval. For Article 360, the Financial Emergency, the same parliamentary control was prescribed, though it has never been invoked.

A critical point of contention was the scope of Article 356. Members from the provinces feared misuse to dismiss elected state governments. The Committee therefore required that the President’s satisfaction be based on a report from the Governor “or otherwise”, a phrase that later became the focal point of judicial scrutiny in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994). The Assembly also debated whether a Financial Emergency could be proclaimed on the ground of a threat to the credit of India; the final text retained the broad wording “financial stability or credit of India or any part thereof”.

The original Article 352 allowed suspension of Fundamental Rights (except Articles 20 and 21) during a National Emergency. This was amended by the 44th Amendment to prohibit suspension of Articles 20 and 21 altogether and to require that the proclamation specify the rights to be suspended. The Constituent Assembly’s records show that the framers intended the emergency powers to be exceptional, not a routine governance tool, a principle the Supreme Court has repeatedly affirmed.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on Citizenship, Partition, and the Original Articles 5‑11

The citizenship provisions were drafted against the backdrop of Partition, which displaced millions and created an urgent need to define who belonged to the new Indian polity. The Citizenship Committee, chaired by Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, presented its report in May 1948. The Assembly adopted Articles 5 to 11 in August 1949, establishing citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950) and empowering Parliament to regulate subsequent acquisition and termination.

Article 5 conferred citizenship on every person domiciled in the territory of India who was born in India, or either of whose parents was born in India, or who had been ordinarily resident for five years immediately preceding the commencement. Article 6 addressed migrants from Pakistan: those who migrated before 19 July 1948 became citizens if they had been ordinarily resident since migration; those who migrated after that date needed to register as citizens after six months of residence. The cut‑off date of 19 July 1948 was chosen because it marked the last day of the “pre‑Partition” migration flow before the formal transfer of power.

Article 7 dealt with persons who had migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 but returned under a permit for resettlement; they could acquire citizenship after six months’ residence. Article 8 extended citizenship to persons of Indian origin residing outside India who registered with an Indian diplomatic mission. Article 9 provided that voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship would terminate Indian citizenship. Article 10 preserved citizenship subject to any law made by Parliament, and Article 11 gave Parliament plenary power to make any provision concerning citizenship.

The debates reveal a tension between a generous, inclusive approach and the practical need to prevent dual allegiance. Sardar Patel, though not a member of the Committee, intervened to ensure that the provisions did not create a “stateless” class. The subsequent Citizenship Act 1955 operationalised these articles, and the 1986 amendment narrowed the birth‑right principle by requiring at least one parent to be an Indian citizen at the time of birth.

Technique: Linking Constitutional Articles to Subsequent Legislation
Question: Explain how the Constituent Assembly determined the cut‑off date for citizenship under Article 6 and its relevance to the 1955 Citizenship Act.
The Assembly fixed 19 July 1948 as the cut‑off because it was the last day before the formal transfer of power when large‑scale migration from Pakistan was still considered “pre‑Partition”. Article 6 distinguishes migrants before and after this date, imposing a registration requirement only on the latter. The Citizenship Act 1955 (Section 5) mirrors this distinction by prescribing different registration procedures for pre‑ and post‑1948 migrants. In answers, cite the Assembly debate (CAD Vol. VII, 12 August 1949) where Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar justified the date, and show how the Act translates the constitutional scheme into administrative rules.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about citizenship provisions, always connect the constitutional articles (5‑11) to the Citizenship Act 1955 and its amendments (1986, 2003, 2019). Note the shift from jus soli to jus sanguinis in the 1986 amendment and the introduction of the Overseas Citizen of India scheme. This linkage demonstrates both historical depth and current relevance.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on the Amendment Procedure (Article 368) and the Role of State Ratification

Article 368 was crafted to reconcile the need for constitutional flexibility with the federal principle that certain core features require broader consensus. The Drafting Committee, led by Ambedkar, proposed three tiers: (i) amendments by simple majority of Parliament for matters not affecting the federal structure; (ii) amendments by a special majority (two‑thirds of members present and voting, and a majority of the total membership of each House) for most provisions; (iii) amendments requiring the special majority plus ratification by the legislatures of not less than one‑half of the States for a defined list of “entrenched” subjects.

The entrenched list originally included: the election of the President (Articles 54‑55), the extent of the executive power of the Union and States (Articles 73, 162), the representation of States in Parliament (Articles 80‑81), the distribution of legislative powers (Seventh Schedule), and the amendment procedure itself (Article 368). The Assembly debated whether the list should be exhaustive or illustrative. K.T. Shah advocated an exhaustive list to prevent central encroachment, while Ambedkar argued for a flexible but clearly defined schedule to avoid litigation. The final text adopted an exhaustive list in the proviso to Article 368.

During the debates of September 1949, members from the princely states expressed concern that the ratification requirement gave larger States disproportionate influence. The Committee responded by requiring ratification by “not less than one‑half of the States” rather than a population‑weighted formula. The 24th Amendment (1971) later clarified that the President’s assent to amendment bills is obligatory, and the 42nd Amendment (1976) attempted to curtail judicial review of amendments, a move struck down in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980). The original design, however, remains the baseline for assessing the constitutional validity of amendment acts.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on the Representation of Anglo‑Indians and Nominated Members in Parliament

The Anglo‑Indian community, numbering roughly 300,000 at independence, lobbied for guaranteed representation. Frank Anthony, the community’s leader, argued that without nomination the community would be politically invisible. The Assembly’s Advisory Committee on Minority Rights, chaired by Sardar Patel, recommended nomination of two Anglo‑Indians to the Lok Sabha (Article 331) and twelve members to the Rajya Sabha (Article 80) with expertise in literature, science, art, and social service. The nomination was initially limited to ten years, reflecting the expectation that the community would integrate into the mainstream.

The debates of October 1949 reveal a division: some members, including B.R. Ambedkar, viewed nomination as a temporary affirmative action measure, while others, like H.V. Kamath, warned it set a precedent for communal representation. The Assembly adopted the ten‑year sunset clause, which was extended by the 8th Amendment (1959), the 23rd Amendment (1969), the 45th Amendment (1980), the 62nd Amendment (1989), and the 79th Amendment (1999). The 104th Constitutional Amendment (2020) finally abolished the Anglo‑Indian nomination, citing the community’s improved socio‑economic indicators.

For the Rajya Sabha, the twelve nominated members were intended to bring non‑political expertise. The Assembly records show that the President’s discretion in nomination is exercised on the advice of the Council of Ministers, a convention upheld in subsequent practice. The nominated members enjoy the same privileges as elected members except they cannot vote in the presidential election (Article 55).

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on the Freedom of Trade, Commerce, and Intercourse (Article 301) and the Judicial Interpretation

Article 301 guarantees that “trade, commerce and intercourse throughout the territory of India shall be free”. The provision was modelled on Section 92 of the Australian Constitution and Section 297 of the Government of India Act 1935. The Constituent Assembly’s Committee on Fundamental Rights, chaired by J.B. Kripalani, debated whether the freedom should be absolute or subject to reasonable restrictions. The final text empowers Parliament to impose restrictions in the public interest (Article 302) and permits States to impose taxes on goods imported from other States if similar goods are taxed locally (Article 304).

During the debates of November 1949, members from commercial provinces such as Bombay and Bengal pressed for a strong free‑trade clause to prevent economic Balkanisation. The Assembly rejected a proposal to make Article 301 justiciable in the same manner as Fundamental Rights, placing it instead in Part XIII (Trade, Commerce and Intercourse). This placement signalled that the freedom was a structural economic guarantee rather than an individual right.

The Supreme Court’s early jurisprudence (Atiabari Tea Co. v. State of Assam, 1961) interpreted Article 301 as prohibiting any law that directly restricts the free flow of trade, while allowing regulatory measures that facilitate trade. The “compensatory tax” doctrine (Automobile Transport v. State of Rajasthan, 1962) permits States to levy taxes that compensate for the cost of providing infrastructure, provided they are non‑discriminatory. Later, in Jindal Stainless Ltd. v. State of Haryana (2017), the Court reaffirmed that Article 301 is not a fundamental right but a constitutional guarantee that can be restricted only by Parliament under Article 302 or by States under Article 304 with Presidential assent.

  • Confusing the three types of emergency and their parliamentary approval timelines.
  • Assuming Article 368 originally required state ratification for all amendments.
  • Overlooking that Anglo‑Indian nomination was a temporary provision for ten years.
  • Treating Article 301 as an absolute guarantee without the restrictive power of Article 302.
  • Ignoring the distinction between citizenship at commencement (Article 5) and citizenship by migration (Article 6).
  • Misattributing the 44th Amendment changes to the original Constituent Assembly design.
  • Believing the Financial Emergency (Article 360) has ever been invoked.

These sections provide a deeper analytical framework for tackling advanced constitutional history questions in the mains examination.

The Doctrine of Parliamentary Privileges and Judicial Review in India

Parliamentary privileges in India derive from Articles 105 and 194 of the Constitution, which replicate the powers, privileges and immunities of the House of Commons as they stood on 26 January 1950. The Constitution does not enumerate these privileges exhaustively; instead it empowers each House to define them by law, and until such law is made, the privileges of the British House of Commons continue to apply. The core privileges include freedom of speech in Parliament (Art. 105(1)), immunity from court proceedings for anything said or any vote given (Art. 105(2)), and the power to punish for contempt or breach of privilege (Art. 105(3)). State legislatures enjoy identical privileges under Article 194.

The Supreme Court has consistently held that parliamentary privileges are not absolute and are subject to judicial review. In Keshav Singh v. Speaker, Legislative Assembly (1965), the Court ruled that the power to punish for contempt is a judicial function and must conform to the principles of natural justice. The Court asserted its jurisdiction to examine whether a privilege claimed by the House exists under the Constitution and whether the procedure adopted for its enforcement violates fundamental rights. Later, in Raja Ram Pal v. Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha (2007), a Constitution Bench held that the expulsion of a member for breach of privilege is justiciable, and the Court may review the decision for mala fides, procedural irregularity or violation of constitutional provisions.

A significant development came in State of Kerala v. K. Ajith (2021), where the Court clarified that the privilege of freedom of speech does not extend to statements made outside the House, and that the power to punish for contempt cannot be used to stifle legitimate criticism of the legislature. The judgment reinforced the principle that privileges must be exercised in harmony with the fundamental rights guaranteed under Part III, especially Article 19(1)(a). The Court also distinguished between breach of privilege — a violation of the collective rights of the House — and contempt of court, which is an offence against the administration of justice. While the former is dealt with by the House itself, the latter falls within the exclusive domain of the judiciary under Articles 129 and 215.

Parliament has enacted the Parliamentary Proceedings (Protection of Publication) Act, 1977, and the Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act, 1959, to codify certain aspects of privilege. However, no comprehensive legislation has been passed to replace the British precedents, leaving considerable scope for judicial interpretation. The tension between legislative autonomy and constitutional supremacy remains a recurring theme in constitutional litigation, and the Supreme Court’s jurisprudence continues to delineate the boundaries of parliamentary privilege in a manner that preserves both the dignity of the legislature and the rule of law.

The Constitutional Position of the Vice‑President as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha

The Vice‑President of India occupies a unique dual role: as the second highest constitutional office under Article 63 and as the ex officio Chairman of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) under Article 64. The Chairman presides over the sittings of the Rajya Sabha, maintains order, decides points of order, and exercises a casting vote in the event of a tie (Art. 89(1)). Unlike the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, the Chairman is not a member of the House and therefore does not participate in debates or vote except to break a deadlock. The Deputy Chairman, elected from among the members of the Rajya Sabha under Article 89(2), performs the Chairman’s functions during the latter’s absence or when the office falls vacant.

The Vice‑President’s tenure as Chairman is co‑terminous with the five‑year term as Vice‑President (Art. 67). Removal from the Vice‑Presidency requires a resolution passed by a majority of the total membership of the Rajya Sabha and agreed to by the Lok Sabha (Art. 67(b)). This procedure mirrors the impeachment process for the President but with a lower threshold, reflecting the Vice‑President’s primarily ceremonial executive role. The Chairman’s rulings on procedural matters are final and not subject to judicial review, a principle affirmed in K. K. Venugopal v. Union of India (1990), where the Court held that the Speaker’s or Chairman’s decisions on points of order are internal to the House and fall within the domain of parliamentary privilege.

In practice, the Chairman’s casting vote has been exercised on rare occasions. The most notable instance occurred in 1991 when Vice‑President K. R. Narayanan cast the deciding vote on the Constitution (Seventy‑Third Amendment) Bill, enabling the passage of the Panchayati Raj legislation. The Chairman also authenticates bills passed by the Rajya Sabha before they are presented to the President for assent (Art. 111). The office carries significant diplomatic and ceremonial duties, including representing India at state functions when the President is unavailable. The constitutional design thus blends a legislative presiding function with an executive standby role, ensuring continuity in the highest offices of the state.

Technique: Mapping Constitutional Provisions to Functional Roles
Question: Explain how the Constitution delineates the Vice‑President’s functions as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and identify the procedural safeguards that protect the independence of this role.
Answer: Article 64 designates the Vice‑President as ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. Article 89(1) empowers the Chairman to preside, maintain order and exercise a casting vote. Article 89(2) provides for a Deputy Chairman elected by the House to act during the Chairman’s absence. The Vice‑President’s term is fixed at five years under Article 67, and removal requires a special majority in the Rajya Sabha and agreement of the Lok Sabha (Art. 67(b)), insulating the office from arbitrary executive action. The Chairman’s rulings on procedural matters are final and not subject to judicial review, as held in K. K. Venugopal v. Union of India (1990). These provisions collectively ensure that the presiding officer can function without external pressure while remaining accountable to the legislature.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about the Vice‑President’s legislative role, cite Articles 64, 89 and 67 together. Remember the casting vote is the only voting power; the Chairman never votes on the merits of a bill. Contrast with the Speaker of Lok Sabha who is an elected member and votes in the first instance.

The Principle of Subsidiarity and Its Reflection in Indian Federal Practice

Subsidiarity, a principle originating in European Union law, holds that decisions should be taken at the lowest level of governance capable of addressing them effectively. Although the Indian Constitution does not mention the term, its federal architecture embodies the spirit of subsidiarity through the distribution of legislative powers in the Seventh Schedule, the creation of local self‑government institutions under the Seventy‑Third and Seventy‑Fourth Amendments (1992), and the fiscal mechanisms of the Finance Commission and the Goods and Services Tax Council. The Union List, State List and Concurrent List allocate subjects in a manner that reserves matters of national importance — defence, foreign affairs, currency — for the Centre, while entrusting public order, health, agriculture and local government to the States.

The Supreme Court has implicitly recognised subsidiarity in several judgments. In State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977), the Court observed that the Constitution envisages a “cooperative federalism” where the Centre and States operate within their respective spheres, and encroachment by either side undermines the federal balance. In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Court emphasised that the proclamation of President’s Rule under Article 356 must be a last resort, thereby reinforcing the principle that State governments should be allowed to function unless constitutional breakdown is proven. The Seventy‑Third and Seventy‑Fourth Amendments institutionalised subsidiarity by mandating the establishment of Panchayats and Municipalities with constitutionally guaranteed powers, finances and elections, making local bodies the primary units for planning and implementation of economic development and social justice.

Fiscal subsidiarity is operationalised through the Finance Commission, constituted under Article 280, which recommends the vertical and horizontal distribution of tax revenues, ensuring that States and local bodies receive resources commensurate with their responsibilities. The GST Council, created by the One Hundred and First Amendment (2016), embodies a collaborative decision‑making model where the Union and States jointly determine tax rates, exemptions and dispute resolution, reflecting a negotiated subsidiarity rather than a hierarchical one. The Inter‑State Council (Art. 263), though underutilised, provides a constitutional forum for discussion of common interests, further institutionalising the principle that governance should be as close to the citizen as possible.

Despite these structures, centralising tendencies — such as the use of Article 256 (directions to States), the deployment of central agencies in State domains, and the predominance of centrally sponsored schemes — often dilute subsidiarity in practice. The challenge for constitutional governance lies in translating the textual distribution of powers into operational autonomy for sub‑national units, a task that continues to engage the judiciary, the legislature and the executive in an ongoing dialogue.

The Constitutional Framework for Environmental Protection: Articles 48A, 51A(g) and Judicial Expansion

The Constitution addresses environmental protection through a Directive Principle and a Fundamental Duty. Article 48A, inserted by the Forty‑Second Amendment (1976), directs the State to “protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country”. Article 51A(g), also added by the same amendment, imposes on every citizen the duty “to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures”. While neither provision is directly enforceable in courts, the Supreme Court has read them into the fundamental right to life under Article 21, thereby giving them justiciable force.

The judicial expansion began with M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987), where the Court held that the right to a wholesome environment is an integral part of Article 21. In Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996), the Court articulated the “precautionary principle” and the “polluter pays principle” as part of the constitutional environmental jurisprudence, linking them to Articles 48A and 51A(g). The Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2000) judgment balanced developmental needs with environmental safeguards, requiring comprehensive impact assessments and rehabilitation plans. More recently, in MC Mehta v. Union of India (Taj Trapezium Case) (2019), the Court ordered the relocation of polluting industries to protect the Taj Mahal, invoking the State’s duty under Article 48A.

Legislative frameworks have been built upon these constitutional foundations. The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, empowers the Central Government to take measures for environmental protection, set standards and restrict industrial activity. The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, established a specialised environmental court with original and appellate jurisdiction, ensuring expeditious disposal of cases. The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, and the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, operationalise the directive to safeguard forests and wildlife. The judiciary has also recognised the principle of inter‑generational equity, holding that the State holds natural resources in trust for future generations.

Despite robust jurisprudence, enforcement gaps persist. The lack of a standalone fundamental right to environment, reliance on executive discretion for clearance processes, and the frequent dilution of environmental impact assessment norms through executive notifications illustrate the tension between developmental imperatives and constitutional mandates. The ongoing challenge is to translate the aspirational language of Articles 48A and 51A(g) into binding, enforceable standards that withstand political and economic pressures.

The Doctrine of Constitutional Amendment and the Role of the President’s Assent under Article 368

Article 368 governs the amendment of the Constitution and vests the constituent power in Parliament, subject to procedural rigours that distinguish ordinary legislation from constitutional change. An amendment bill must be passed by each House of Parliament by a majority of the total membership and by a two‑thirds majority of members present and voting. For amendments affecting the federal structure — such as the election of the President, the extent of executive power, the representation of States in Parliament, or the amendment procedure itself — ratification by the legislatures of not less than one‑half of the States is additionally required (Art. 368 proviso).

Once passed, the bill is presented to the President for assent. The President’s assent is mandatory; the Constitution does not provide for a pocket veto or a suspensive veto in respect of amendment bills. The Twenty‑Fourth Amendment (1971) explicitly inserted the words “and the President shall give his assent” to remove any ambiguity after the Supreme Court’s decision in Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967) had questioned the amendability of fundamental rights. The Forty‑Second Amendment (1976) attempted to curtail judicial review of amendments by inserting Article 368(4) and (5), declaring that no amendment could be called in question in any court. The Supreme Court struck down these clauses in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), reaffirming that the basic structure doctrine applies to amendment acts and that judicial review is an essential feature of the Constitution.

The Forty‑Fourth Amendment (1978) restored the pre‑1976 position, removed the ouster clauses and reinstated the requirement that the President’s assent cannot be withheld. The Court in Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) held that amendments made before 24 April 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda judgment) are immune from basic structure challenge, while subsequent amendments are subject to it. The Ninety‑Ninth Amendment (2014), which established the National Judicial Appointments Commission, was struck down in Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (2015) for violating the basic structure, demonstrating that even amendments duly passed and assented to can be invalidated if they damage the Constitution’s core.

The President’s role is thus ceremonial but constitutionally significant: assent transforms a parliamentary resolution into supreme law. The absence of a veto power underscores the supremacy of the constituent power of Parliament, while the basic structure doctrine, enforced by the judiciary, acts as the ultimate check. This triadic balance — Parliament’s constituent power, the President’s formal assent, and the Court’s substantive review — constitutes the amendment architecture that has enabled the Constitution to evolve without losing its identity.

  • Confusing the scope of parliamentary privilege with absolute immunity from judicial scrutiny.
  • Assuming the Vice‑President votes on bills in the Rajya Sabha like an ordinary member.
  • Treating subsidiarity as an explicit constitutional term rather than an interpretive principle.
  • Believing Articles 48A and 51A(g) are directly enforceable fundamental rights.
  • Thinking the President can withhold assent to a constitutional amendment bill.
  • Overlooking the requirement of state ratification for amendments affecting the federal structure.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee on the Union and State Legislative Lists and the Crafting of the Seventh Schedule

The distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States was entrusted to a dedicated committee of the Constituent Assembly, formally styled the Committee on the Union and State Legislative Lists. Chaired by Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, the committee comprised members such as K. M. Munshi, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, and B. R. Ambedkar in an ex‑officio capacity. Its mandate was to translate the federal scheme envisaged in the Objectives Resolution into a concrete three‑list structure — Union List, State List, and Concurrent List — that would replace the single‑list system of the Government of India Act 1935.

The committee submitted its report on 12 August 1947. It recommended 97 entries for the Union List, 66 for the State List, and 47 for the Concurrent List. The Union List covered defence, foreign affairs, atomic energy, inter‑state trade, and currency; the State List included public order, police, agriculture, and local government; the Concurrent List comprised criminal law, marriage, bankruptcy, and economic planning. The committee also proposed that residuary powers vest with the Union (Article 248), a departure from the Canadian model where residuary powers belong to the provinces. This choice was justified on the grounds of national integrity and the need for a strong centre to manage post‑partition challenges.

During the Assembly debates, members such as H. V. Kamath and K. T. Shah argued for a larger State List to protect regional autonomy, while others like Gopalaswami Ayyangar emphasised that the Concurrent List would allow uniformity in essential areas without depriving States of legislative initiative. The final text of the Seventh Schedule, adopted on 26 November 1949, reflected several amendments: the number of Union entries rose to 99 after the inclusion of “industries” and “regulation of mines”, while the State List was reduced to 61 entries following the transfer of “education” and “forests” to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment (1976). The Concurrent List expanded to 52 entries over time, notably with the addition of “population control” and “environment” through subsequent amendments.

The committee’s work also influenced the doctrine of pith and substance, later articulated by the Supreme Court in State of Bombay v. F. N. Balsara (1951), which holds that a law’s true character determines its legislative competence irrespective of incidental encroachment. The Seventh Schedule remains the primary reference for Centre‑State legislative disputes, and its amendment requires the special majority under Article 368 plus ratification by half the States when the federal balance is altered.

The Debate on the Inclusion of Fundamental Duties: Swaran Singh Committee Recommendations and the 42nd Amendment

The original Constitution of 1950 contained no chapter on fundamental duties. The idea gained traction during the Emergency (1975‑77) when the government appointed the Swaran Singh Committee in 1976 to examine the need for a codified set of citizens’ duties. The committee, chaired by former Home Minister Swaran Singh, submitted its report in August 1976 recommending the insertion of a new Part IVA comprising ten duties, drawing inspiration from the Soviet Constitution and the Japanese model of civic responsibilities.

The committee’s ten duties included: to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions; to cherish and follow the noble ideals that inspired the national struggle for freedom; to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India; to defend the country and render national service when called upon; to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood; to value and preserve the rich heritage of composite culture; to protect and improve the natural environment; to develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry; to safeguard public property and abjure violence; and to strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity.

The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, enacted these recommendations by inserting Article 51A. The amendment also added the words “Socialist”, “Secular” and “Integrity” to the Preamble, signalling a broader ideological shift. In 2002, the 86th Amendment added an eleventh duty — “to provide opportunities for education to his child or, as the case may be, ward between the age of six and fourteen years” — aligning with the newly inserted Article 21A (Right to Education).

Judicial interpretation has consistently held that fundamental duties are non‑justiciable but serve as interpretive aids. In Ranganath Misra v. Union of India (1992), the Supreme Court observed that while duties cannot be enforced by writs, they guide the construction of fundamental rights and directive principles. The Court in M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1998) invoked Article 51A(g) to reinforce the State’s obligation to protect the environment. The duties also feature in the Model Code of Conduct for elections and in the National Curriculum Framework, illustrating their permeation into governance beyond the courtroom.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which committee recommended the inclusion of Fundamental Duties and through which amendment were they incorporated?” Many candidates answer “Swaran Singh Committee – 44th Amendment”. Identify the error and give the correct answer.
The Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended Fundamental Duties, but they were incorporated by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, not the 44th. The 44th Amendment (1978) dealt with reversing Emergency‑era changes and restoring judicial review. The correct pairing is Swaran Singh Committee – 42nd Amendment.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question links a committee to an amendment, first recall the year of the committee report and the year of the amendment. The Swaran Singh Committee reported in 1976; the 42nd Amendment was passed the same year. The 44th Amendment came two years later. Use this chronological anchor to avoid the common swap.

The Constitutional Architecture of Emergency Powers: Articles 352, 356, 360 and Judicial Safeguards

The Constitution provides three distinct emergency provisions, each with a different trigger, scope, and parliamentary oversight mechanism. Article 352 empowers the President to proclaim a National Emergency on grounds of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion. The original 1950 text required only the President’s satisfaction; the 44th Amendment (1978) inserted the requirement that the proclamation be based on a written recommendation of the Union Cabinet and that it be approved by both Houses of Parliament within one month by a special majority. The proclamation can remain in force for six months at a time, extendable indefinitely with parliamentary approval every six months.

Article 356, commonly known as President’s Rule, allows the President to assume the functions of a State government when the constitutional machinery in that State fails. The 44th Amendment added safeguards: the proclamation must be approved by Parliament within two months, and any continuation beyond one year requires a certificate from the Election Commission that elections cannot be held. The landmark judgment in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) established that the President’s satisfaction is subject to judicial review, that the State Legislative Assembly cannot be dissolved before parliamentary approval, and that secularism is a basic feature that cannot be violated even under Article 356.

Article 360 provides for a Financial Emergency when the financial stability or credit of India is threatened. It has never been invoked. The President’s proclamation must be laid before Parliament and ceases to operate after two months unless approved. During a Financial Emergency, the Union can direct States to observe canons of financial propriety and reduce salaries of all government servants, including judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts.

The 42nd Amendment (1976) had attempted to make the President’s satisfaction under Articles 352 and 356 final and conclusive, but the 44th Amendment restored judicial scrutiny. The Supreme Court in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) held that the power to proclaim emergency is not immune from review and that the basic structure doctrine applies to emergency provisions. The interplay of these articles illustrates the Constitution’s attempt to balance executive decisiveness with parliamentary accountability and judicial oversight.

The Design of the Union Judiciary: Original, Appellate, and Advisory Jurisdictions under Articles 131, 132‑136, and 143

The Supreme Court of India exercises a tripartite jurisdiction that reflects its role as the federal court, the highest court of appeal, and a constitutional adviser to the Executive. Article 131 confers exclusive original jurisdiction in disputes between the Government of India and one or more States, or between States themselves, provided the dispute involves a question of law or fact on which the existence or extent of a legal right depends. The Court in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977) clarified that the dispute must be justiciable and not purely political; the mere existence of a policy disagreement does not attract Article 131.

Articles 132 to 136 constitute the appellate jurisdiction. Article 132 covers appeals in constitutional matters where the High Court certifies a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution. Article 133 governs civil appeals where the High Court certifies that the case involves a substantial question of law of general importance. Article 134 provides for criminal appeals, including those where the High Court has reversed an acquittal and sentenced the accused to death. Article 136, the special leave petition (SLP) jurisdiction, grants the Supreme Court discretionary power to hear any judgment, decree, or order from any court or tribunal in India. The SLP docket dominates the Court’s workload; in 2023, over 70 % of the Court’s filings were SLPs.

Article 143 empowers the President to refer a question of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court for its advisory opinion. The opinion is not binding but carries high persuasive value. Notable references include the 1998 Presidential Reference on the Ayodhya dispute, where the Court declined to answer whether a temple existed at the site, stating it was a matter of faith, and the 2002 reference on the Gujarat Assembly dissolution, where the Court held that the Governor’s report must be based on objective material.

The interplay of these jurisdictions ensures that the Supreme Court can resolve federal disputes, maintain uniformity in legal interpretation, and assist the Executive in constitutional dilemmas. The Court’s own rules, framed under Article 145, regulate the procedure for each jurisdiction, including the requirement of a certificate for appeals under Articles 132‑134 and the filing of a concise statement of facts for SLPs.

  • Confusing the Swaran Singh Committee (1976) with the 44th Amendment (1978) as the vehicle for Fundamental Duties.
  • Assuming Article 356 proclamations are immune from judicial review after the 42nd Amendment.
  • Treating the President’s advisory reference under Article 143 as a binding judgment.
  • Believing the Seventh Schedule’s Union List has remained static since 1950.
  • Overlooking the requirement of a written Cabinet recommendation for a National Emergency under Article 352 post‑44th Amendment.
  • Thinking the Supreme Court’s original jurisdiction under Article 131 extends to political questions between the Centre and States.
  • These traps highlight the need for precise constitutional reading and chronological awareness.

The Doctrine of Eclipse and Severability in Pre‑Constitutional and Post‑Constitutional Laws

The doctrine of eclipse holds that a pre‑Constitutional law which is inconsistent with a fundamental right does not become void ab initio; it merely becomes dormant or “eclipsed” until the constitutional impediment is removed. The Supreme Court first articulated this in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955), where a provincial motor vehicles law conflicting with the freedom of trade under Article 19(1)(g) was held to be eclipsed, not dead. When the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955 amended Article 19(6) to permit reasonable restrictions, the law revived automatically.
