The doctrine applies only to laws enacted before 26 January 1950; post‑Constitutional laws that violate fundamental rights are void ab initio under Article 13(2) and cannot be revived by subsequent amendment.

Severability, by contrast, operates when a statute contains both constitutional and unconstitutional provisions. The court excises the offending part if the remainder is capable of standing alone and the legislature would have enacted it independently. The test was laid down in R.M.D.C. v. Union of India (1957): (i) the invalid portion must be separable without altering the nature of the valid portion; (ii) the valid portion must be complete in itself; (iii) the legislature’s intention to enact the valid part independently must be discernible. In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), the Bombay Prohibition Act’s penal clauses were severed from its regulatory clauses, allowing the latter to survive. The two doctrines often intersect: a pre‑Constitutional law may be partially eclipsed and partially severed, as seen in Keshavan Madhava Menon v. State of Bombay (1951), where the Indian Press (Emergency Powers) Act, 1931 was partly eclipsed and partly severed after the Constitution came into force.

Practical significance: when a challenge is mounted against a colonial statute, counsel must first determine whether the law is pre‑ or post‑Constitutional. If pre‑Constitutional, argue eclipse and seek revival through constitutional amendment; if post‑Constitutional, argue voidness and, where possible, severability to preserve the legislative scheme. Courts also examine whether the eclipse has been removed by a constitutional amendment that expressly or impliedly validates the law, as the 42nd Amendment attempted for several preventive detention statutes before being partially struck down in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980).

The Principle of Non‑Arbitrariness under Article 14: From Reasonable Classification to Substantive Due Process

Article 14 guarantees equality before law and equal protection of laws. The classical test, derived from State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952), requires a rational nexus between the classification and the object sought to be achieved. However, the Supreme Court progressively expanded the doctrine to strike down arbitrary state action even where a formal classification exists. In E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974), Justice Bhagwati declared that “equality is a dynamic concept” and that arbitrariness is the antithesis of equality. This shift moved the jurisprudence from a purely classification‑based approach to a substantive due‑process‑like scrutiny.

The landmark Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) fused Article 14 with Article 21, holding that any procedure depriving personal liberty must be “fair, just and reasonable”, not merely procedurally prescribed. The Court in Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) applied the non‑arbitrariness standard to invalidate the practice of instant triple talaq, emphasising that a law manifestly arbitrary fails Article 14 regardless of classification. The test now comprises two prongs: (i) the classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia; (ii) the differentia must have a rational relation to the object; and (iii) the law must not be manifestly arbitrary, i.e., it must not be capricious, irrational, or lacking adequate determining principle.

Recent applications include Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018), where Section 377 IPC was struck down as manifestly arbitrary in criminalising consensual same‑sex relations, and Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018), which decriminalised adultery on the ground that the provision was based on gender stereotypes and lacked a rational nexus. The doctrine also governs administrative discretion: in Delhi Transport Corporation v. DTC Mazdoor Congress (1991), the Court held that unfettered discretion without guidelines is arbitrary. For aspirants, the key is to recognise that the “reasonable classification” test remains the starting point, but the “manifest arbitrariness” standard operates as an independent ground of challenge, especially in cases involving delegated legislation, policy decisions, and personal law.

Worked Example: Identifying the Correct Standard of Review
A state enacts a law granting the Chief Minister discretionary power to allot government contracts above ₹10 crore without any guidelines. A contractor challenges the law under Article 14. Which standard will the Court apply and what is the likely outcome?
The Court will apply the manifest arbitrariness standard under Article 14, as articulated in Shayara Bano and Navtej Singh Johar. The law confers unguided discretion on a single functionary, lacking any intelligible differentia or rational nexus to a legitimate object. Such unfettered discretion is per se arbitrary. The Court will strike down the provision, holding that the absence of guidelines renders the law manifestly arbitrary and violative of Article 14. The “reasonable classification” test is insufficient because the law does not even create a classification; it vests absolute power. Therefore, the challenge succeeds on the ground of manifest arbitrariness.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks “which test applies”, first check whether the impugned provision creates a classification. If yes, start with the twin‑test of intelligible differentia and rational nexus. Then ask whether the provision is also manifestly arbitrary — if the discretion is unguided or the object is irrational, the Court will strike it down on that independent ground. Cite Shayara Bano (2017) and Navtej Singh Johar (2018) for the modern two‑pronged approach.

The Constitutional Safeguards for the Independence of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India

Article 148 establishes the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) as an independent constitutional authority. The CAG is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal and can be removed only in the manner and on the grounds prescribed for a Supreme Court judge — proved misbehaviour or incapacity — by an address of each House of Parliament supported by a special majority (Article 148(1) read with Article 124(4)). This parity with judicial removal insulates the CAG from executive pressure. The salary, allowances, and pension are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 148(3)), ensuring financial independence. The CAG’s term is six years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier (Article 148(2)), and the conditions of service cannot be varied to his disadvantage after appointment (Article 148(4)).

The CAG’s audit mandate extends to all expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India, the Consolidated Fund of each State, and the Contingency Fund and Public Account (Article 149). The reports are submitted to the President or Governor, who causes them to be laid before Parliament or the State Legislature (Article 151). The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) examines these reports, providing legislative oversight. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. Gandhi (1987) held that the CAG’s audit jurisdiction is not limited to financial propriety but includes performance audit, reinforcing the office’s role as a watchdog of public accountability.

Judicial pronouncements have reinforced independence. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raj Narain (1975), the Court observed that the CAG’s constitutional status is “not subordinate to the executive”. The 2019 amendment to the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, which attempted to restrict the CAG’s access to certain records, was challenged; the Court in Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2020) stayed the restrictive provisions, affirming that statutory amendments cannot dilute constitutional safeguards. For aspirants, the key points are the removal procedure mirroring Supreme Court judges, the charged expenditure, the six‑year/65‑year tenure, and the expansive audit mandate covering Union, State, and local bodies.

The Doctrine of Parliamentary Privileges and Its Judicial Review: Balancing Legislative Autonomy and Constitutional Supremacy

Articles 105 and 194 confer on Parliament and State Legislatures, respectively, powers, privileges, and immunities necessary for their functioning. These include freedom of speech in the House (Article 105(1)), immunity from court proceedings for anything said or any vote given (Article 105(2)), and the power to punish for contempt (Article 105(3)). The privileges are not codified; they derive from the House of Commons as at 26 January 1950, subject to constitutional provisions and judicial review. In Keshav Singh v. Speaker, Legislative Assembly (1965), the Supreme Court held that the judiciary can examine whether a privilege claimed is consistent with fundamental rights, especially Article 21. The Court ruled that the legislative assembly’s power to commit for contempt is subject to judicial review for mala fides or violation of natural justice.

The landmark Raja Ram Pal v. Hon’ble Speaker, Lok Sabha (2007) (the “Cash for Query” case) established that the expulsion of a member for breach of privilege is justiciable. The Court held that while the House is the sole judge of its privileges, the exercise of that power must not be arbitrary, must comply with the principles of natural justice, and is subject to judicial review under Article 32/226. The Court also clarified that the privilege of freedom of speech does not extend to bribery; accepting a bribe for a parliamentary act is a criminal offence under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, and not protected by Article 105(2).

In State of Kerala v. K. Ajith (2021), the Supreme Court reiterated that legislative privileges cannot override fundamental rights. The Court held that the Kerala Legislative Assembly’s resolution to withdraw prosecution against its members for alleged violence inside the House was subject to judicial scrutiny and could not shield criminal acts. The doctrine thus balances legislative autonomy — essential for fearless debate — with constitutional supremacy, ensuring that privileges are not a cloak for illegality. Aspirants should remember the three‑fold test: (i) the privilege must be necessary for the House’s functioning; (ii) its exercise must not violate fundamental rights; (iii) the House’s decision is reviewable for procedural fairness and mala fides.

The Constitutional Position of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies

Articles 93 and 178 provide for the election of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies, respectively. The Speaker is elected by the House from among its members; the Deputy Speaker is elected similarly. The Speaker’s tenure continues until the dissolution of the House, unless he resigns, is removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all then members of the House (Article 94), or ceases to be a member. The removal resolution requires a 14‑day notice and cannot be moved while a motion of no‑confidence against the Council of Ministers is pending, protecting the Speaker from partisan pressure.

The Speaker’s powers are extensive: presiding over sittings, maintaining order, interpreting rules, certifying Money Bills (Article 110), deciding disqualification under the Tenth Schedule (Article 102(2) read with Para 6 of the Tenth Schedule), and constituting parliamentary committees. The Supreme Court in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) held that the Speaker’s decision on disqualification is subject to judicial review for mala fides, perversity, or violation of natural justice, but not for mere errors of fact. The Deputy Speaker performs the Speaker’s duties when the office is vacant or the Speaker is absent (Articles 95, 180).

Constitutional conventions reinforce impartiality: the Speaker resigns from his political party upon election, though not constitutionally mandated. In Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016), the Court held that the Speaker cannot disqualify members while a notice for his own removal is pending, preserving the integrity of the process. The 2019 amendment to the Lok Sabha Rules introduced a “Speaker’s Panel” to assist in presiding, but the constitutional position remains unchanged. For examination, focus on the election method, removal procedure, the Money Bill certification power, the disqualification authority under the Tenth Schedule, and the limited but real judicial review established in Kihoto Hollohan and Nabam Rebia.

  • Confusing the doctrine of eclipse (pre‑Constitutional laws) with severability (post‑Constitutional statutes) and applying the wrong revival mechanism.
  • Assuming that the “reasonable classification” test alone governs Article 14 challenges, ignoring the independent “manifest arbitrariness” standard from Shayara Bano.
  • Believing the CAG can be removed by a simple executive order, overlooking the special‑majority parliamentary address requirement identical to Supreme Court judges.
  • Thinking parliamentary privileges are absolute and non‑justiciable, whereas Raja Ram Pal and State of Kerala v. K. Ajith confirm judicial review for fundamental‑rights violations.
  • Treating the Speaker’s disqualification power under the Tenth Schedule as final and unreviewable, while Kihoto Hollohan permits review for mala fides and perversity.
  • Overlooking that the Deputy Speaker assumes the Speaker’s duties only when the office is vacant or the Speaker is absent, not during routine adjournments.
  • Misapplying the eclipse doctrine to post‑Constitutional laws, which are void ab initio under Article 13(2) and cannot be revived by amendment.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on the Uniform Civil Code and Article 44

Article 44 of the Constitution, placed in Part IV as a Directive Principle of State Policy, directs the State to endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India. The Constituent Assembly debated the provision extensively between 1948 and 1949. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, while supporting the ideal, argued that the time was not ripe for immediate enactment because personal laws were deeply intertwined with religious identity and social stability. K. M. Munshi and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar echoed the view that a uniform code would promote national integration but cautioned against imposing it without consensus. The Assembly ultimately retained Article 44 as a non‑justiciable directive, leaving the legislative initiative to future Parliaments.

In the 1950s Parliament enacted the Hindu Code Bills — the Hindu Marriage Act (1955), Hindu Succession Act (1956), Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act (1956) and Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act (1956) — which reformed Hindu personal law but left Muslim, Christian, Parsi and Jewish personal laws untouched. The Supreme Court in Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985) held that a divorced Muslim woman was entitled to maintenance under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and observed that a uniform civil code would help remove contradictions in personal laws. The judgment triggered political controversy and led to the enactment of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, which limited the maintenance period.

Subsequent cases reinforced the judicial nudge toward a uniform code. In Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) the Court declared that a Hindu husband converting to Islam solely to contract a second marriage without dissolving the first was guilty of bigamy, and reiterated the need for a uniform civil code. In John Vallamattom v. Union of India (2003) the Court struck down Section 118 of the Indian Succession Act as discriminatory against Christians, again citing Article 44. The Law Commission of India, in its 21st Report (2008) and again in its 2018 consultation paper, recommended a gradual, consultative approach rather than a sudden imposition. The 22nd Law Commission (2023) submitted a report advising that a uniform civil code should not be pursued at present, emphasising the protection of cultural diversity and the need for wider societal consensus.

Thus, Article 44 remains a constitutional aspiration. Its implementation depends on political will, legislative drafting that respects pluralism, and judicial restraint that avoids substituting legislative function. Aspirants should note the distinction between a directive principle (non‑justiciable) and a fundamental right (justiciable), and the recurring judicial references that keep the debate alive without mandating immediate legislation.

The Constitutional Position of the Vice‑President and Chairman of the Rajya Sabha

Articles 63 to 71 of the Constitution establish the office of the Vice‑President of India. The Vice‑President is elected by an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament, using the system of proportional representation by means of a single transferable vote (Article 66). The term is five years from the date on which he enters office, and he may resign by writing to the President or be removed by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a majority of all the then members of the House and agreed to by the Lok Sabha (Article 67).

As ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 64), the Vice‑President presides over its sittings, maintains order, interprets the Rules of Procedure, and exercises a casting vote in the event of a tie (Article 100). The Chairman does not vote in the first instance. The office carries no executive powers; the Vice‑President acts as President only when a vacancy occurs in the office of the President by reason of death, resignation, removal or otherwise (Article 65). During such periods he performs all the functions of the President but does not assume the office of President.

The Constitution does not confer any discretionary powers on the Vice‑President beyond the casting vote and the procedural authority of the Chair. Judicial review of the removal process is limited; the Supreme Court in K. K. Venugopal v. Union of India (1995) held that the resolution for removal is a political question and the Court will not interfere unless there is a violation of constitutional procedure. The Vice‑President’s election can be challenged only through an election petition before the Supreme Court under Article 71, as clarified in N. P. Ponnuswami v. Returning Officer (1952).

Conventions have evolved to preserve the impartiality of the Chair. The Vice‑President usually resigns from party membership upon election, though this is not constitutionally mandated. The Chairman’s rulings on points of order, admission of motions and certification of Money Bills (the latter under Article 110, where the Speaker of Lok Sabha has the final say) are generally respected, but the Supreme Court in Rajya Sabha Secretariat v. Union of India (2009) affirmed that the Chairman’s procedural decisions are subject to judicial review for mala fides or violation of natural justice.

For examination purposes, focus on the electoral college composition, the removal procedure requiring a special majority in Rajya Sabha and simple majority in Lok Sabha, the casting vote, the acting President role, and the limited judicial review of procedural decisions. Distinguish the Vice‑President’s constitutional position from that of the Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha, who is elected by the House and performs the Chairman’s duties only during a vacancy or absence.

Worked Example
A question asks: "Which of the following statements about the Vice‑President of India is correct? (a) He is elected by the members of the Lok Sabha only. (b) He can be removed by a simple majority resolution of the Rajya Sabha. (c) He acts as President when a vacancy occurs in the office of the President. (d) He has a deliberative vote in the Rajya Sabha."
The correct answer is (c). Article 65 provides that the Vice‑President shall act as President when a vacancy occurs in the office of the President. Statement (a) is incorrect because the electoral college comprises members of both Houses (Article 66). Statement (b) is incorrect; removal requires a majority of all then members of the Rajya Sabha and agreement of the Lok Sabha (Article 67). Statement (d) is incorrect; the Vice‑President, as Chairman, has only a casting vote, not a deliberative vote (Article 100).
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the exact constitutional articles for election (66), term (67), removal (67), acting President (65) and casting vote (100). In MCQs, eliminate options that confuse the Vice‑President’s electoral college with the President’s or that attribute a deliberative vote to the Chairman. For descriptive answers, structure the response around the three constitutional roles: electoral, presiding, and acting President.

Asymmetric Federalism: Special Provisions for States under Articles 371A‑371J

The Constitution contains a series of special provisions (Articles 371A to 371J) that create asymmetric federal arrangements for specific states, reflecting historical, cultural and tribal distinctiveness. Article 371A (Nagaland) provides that no Act of Parliament shall apply to Nagaland in respect of religious or social practices of the Nagas, customary law and procedure, administration of civil and criminal justice involving decisions according to Naga customary law, and ownership and transfer of land and its resources, unless the Legislative Assembly of Nagaland so decides by a resolution. Article 371B (Assam) enables the President to constitute a committee of the Legislative Assembly for the tribal areas of the state.

Article 371C (Manipur) provides for a Hill Areas Committee of the Legislative Assembly and empowers the Governor to ensure its proper functioning. Article 371D (Andhra Pradesh) and Article 371E (Andhra Pradesh) were inserted to safeguard equitable opportunities in public employment and education for different regions of the erstwhile composite state; after the bifurcation in 2014, these provisions continue to apply to the successor states of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. Article 371F (Sikkim) preserves the special status of Sikkim on its merger in 1975, protecting existing laws, the jurisdiction of the High Court, and the legislative assembly’s term.

Article 371G (Mizoram) mirrors the Nagaland provision, shielding Mizo customary law, social practices and land ownership from parliamentary legislation unless the state assembly consents. Article 371H (Arunachal Pradesh) vests the Governor with special responsibility for law and order in the state, requiring him to exercise individual judgment after consulting the Council of Ministers. Article 371I (Goa) provides for a legislative assembly of not less than thirty members. Article 371J (Karnataka) enables the creation of a separate development board for the Hyderabad‑Karnataka region, with reservations in education and public employment.

These provisions are not temporary; they remain in force until amended by Parliament under Article 368, often requiring ratification by the concerned state legislature. The Supreme Court in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) recognised that such asymmetric arrangements are constitutionally permissible as they address historical compulsions and do not violate the basic structure. In State of Nagaland v. Union of India (2005) the Court upheld the validity of Article 371A, emphasising that the consent of the state legislature is a constitutional safeguard against unilateral central legislation.

Aspirants should be able to list each article, the state it applies to, the core subject matter (customary law, land, administration, employment, development boards) and the procedural requirement for parliamentary override. Comparative questions often ask how these provisions differ from the general distribution of legislative powers under the Seventh Schedule.

The Constitutional Framework for the National Human Rights Commission and State Human Rights Commissions

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) gave statutory effect to India’s obligations under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. The Act establishes the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) at the centre and State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) in states that choose to constitute them. The NHRC consists of a Chairperson who has been a Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, one member who is or has been a Judge of the Supreme Court, one member who is or has been a Chief Justice of a High Court, and two members having knowledge of or practical experience in matters relating to human rights (Section 3). The President appoints the Chairperson and members on the recommendation of a committee comprising the Prime Minister, the Speaker of Lok Sabha, the Minister of Home Affairs, the Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha, the Leader of Opposition in Rajya Sabha and the Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha.

The NHRC’s functions include inquiring into violations of human rights by public servants, intervening in court proceedings involving human rights, reviewing safeguards provided by the Constitution and laws, and promoting human rights literacy (Section 12). It can recommend compensation, prosecution or disciplinary action, but its recommendations are not binding. The Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2009) held that the Commission’s recommendations carry persuasive authority and the state must give reasons for non‑compliance. The 2006 amendment expanded the NHRC’s jurisdiction to include armed forces personnel in certain circumstances, and the 2019 amendment allowed the Chairperson to be a former Judge of the Supreme Court or a former Chief Justice of a High Court, broadening the pool.

SHRCs mirror the NHRC’s composition and powers at the state level, with the Governor appointing members on the advice of a similar committee headed by the Chief Minister. The PHRA also provides for Human Rights Courts at the district level for speedy trial of offences arising out of human rights violations. However, the Commissions lack enforcement teeth; they cannot punish contemnors directly and depend on the executive for implementation. The Law Commission’s 273rd Report (2018) recommended granting the NHRC powers to enforce its orders and to initiate suo motu investigations without a complaint.

For examination, remember the statutory (not constitutional) origin, the composition and appointment mechanism, the recommendatory nature of findings, the 2006 and 2019 amendments, and the distinction between NHRC and SHRC jurisdiction. Questions often test whether the NHRC can investigate allegations against the armed forces — the answer is yes, but only after obtaining a report from the Central Government and within the limits of Section 19 of the PHRA.

The Role of the President in the Constitutional Scheme: Discretionary Powers and Judicial Interpretation

The President of India is the constitutional head of the Union executive (Article 53). Under Article 74, the President acts in accordance with the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister. The Supreme Court in Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974) held that the President’s satisfaction required by the Constitution is the satisfaction of the Council of Ministers, not his personal satisfaction, except in a few narrowly defined areas where the Constitution expressly vests discretion.

These discretionary pockets include: (i) the appointment of the Prime Minister when no party commands a clear majority in the Lok Sabha (the President may exercise situational discretion to invite the leader most likely to secure a majority); (ii) the dissolution of the Lok Sabha on the advice of a Prime Minister who has lost majority support, where the President may refuse dissolution and explore alternative governments (as discussed in the Sarkaria Commission report); (iii) the assent to Bills — the President may withhold assent (pocket veto) or return a non‑Money Bill for reconsideration (Article 111); (iv) the promulgation of Ordinances under Article 123 when Parliament is not in session, subject to parliamentary approval within six weeks of reassembly; (v) the proclamation of Emergency under Articles 352, 356 and 360, where the President’s satisfaction is justiciable to the extent of reviewing whether the factual basis exists (the Court in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) held that the proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review for mala fides or irrelevance).

The President also enjoys immunity from criminal proceedings during his term (Article 361) and his official acts cannot be questioned in any court except on the ground of violation of the Constitution. The 44th Amendment (1978) made the advice of the Council of Ministers binding on the President, removing the earlier provision that allowed the President to act in his discretion in certain matters. Nevertheless, the President’s role as a constitutional sentinel remains significant; the Supreme Court in R. C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) examined the validity of an Ordinance and held that the President’s satisfaction must be based on objective circumstances.

In practice, the President’s discretion is exercised sparingly and guided by constitutional conventions. The President’s address to Parliament, the appointment of Governors, the granting of pardons under Article 72, and the referral of Bills to the Supreme Court under Article 143 are performed on ministerial advice. Aspirants should distinguish between the President’s formal powers and the real executive authority vested in the Council of Ministers, and be ready to cite the landmark judgments that delineate the boundary between constitutional form and political reality.

  • Confusing the Vice‑President’s electoral college with the President’s electoral college, which includes state legislative assemblies.
  • Assuming the Vice‑President has a deliberative vote in the Rajya Sabha; he only has a casting vote.
  • Treating Articles 371A‑371J as temporary provisions that lapse automatically; they continue until amended under Article 368.
  • Believing the NHRC’s recommendations are legally binding on the government; they are recommendatory and the state must only give reasons for non‑compliance.
  • Thinking the President can exercise personal discretion in all matters; the 44th Amendment made ministerial advice binding except in the few expressly discretionary areas.
  • Overlooking that the President’s satisfaction for Emergency proclamation is subject to judicial review for mala fides, as held in S. R. Bommai.
  • Mixing up the removal procedure of the Vice‑President (special majority in Rajya Sabha plus Lok Sabha agreement) with the impeachment process for the President (two‑thirds majority in both Houses).

The Constituent Assembly's Debate on Fundamental Duties and Their Constitutional Status

The original Constitution of 1950 contained no chapter on fundamental duties. The idea of correlating rights with duties was discussed in the Constituent Assembly but did not find a place in the final text. The debate resurfaced in the 1970s when the Swaran Singh Committee, appointed in 1975, recommended the insertion of a set of fundamental duties to remind citizens of their obligations towards the nation. The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, acting on this recommendation, introduced Part IVA consisting of a single Article 51A with ten duties. A further duty — to provide opportunities for education to children between six and fourteen years — was added by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002, bringing the total to eleven.

The duties range from respecting the Constitution, the national flag and the national anthem, to promoting harmony, protecting the environment, and developing scientific temper. Unlike fundamental rights, these duties are not enforceable by any court. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that Article 51A creates only moral obligations; however, courts have used the duties as interpretative aids. In Chandra Bhavan Boarding School v. State of Mysore (1970) the Court referred to the duty to promote scientific temper while interpreting educational policy, and in M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) the duty to protect the environment was invoked to strengthen the doctrine of sustainable development.

The non‑justiciable nature of the duties was a deliberate choice. The framers of the 42nd Amendment feared that justiciable duties could be used to curtail fundamental rights. The Sarkaria Commission (1988) and the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (2002) both recommended retaining the non‑enforceable character while encouraging their inclusion in school curricula and public discourse. The 42nd Amendment also added the words “Socialist”, “Secular” and “Integrity” to the Preamble, signalling a broader constitutional philosophy that duties complement rights in a welfare state.

For examination purposes, aspirants should remember the chronological sequence: Swaran Singh Committee (1975) → 42nd Amendment (1976) → 86th Amendment (2002). They should also be able to distinguish between the enforceability of fundamental rights (Articles 12‑35) and the moral suasion of fundamental duties (Article 51A), and cite the leading cases where duties have been used as interpretative tools.

The Influence of the American Bill of Rights on the Indian Fundamental Rights Chapter

The Constituent Assembly drew heavily on the United States Bill of Rights while drafting Part III of the Constitution. The American model provided a catalogue of individual liberties — freedom of speech, press, assembly, religion, and the right to due process — that resonated with the Indian leadership’s commitment to civil liberties after colonial rule. However, the Indian framers made critical departures. The most notable is the replacement of the American “due process of law” with the phrase “procedure established by law” in Article 21. This change was influenced by the British parliamentary tradition and the desire to avoid the expansive judicial review that the US Supreme Court exercised under the due process clause.

The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, examined the US provisions closely. B. N. Rau, the Constitutional Adviser, prepared a comparative memorandum that highlighted the US First Amendment freedoms and the Fourteenth Amendment’s equal protection clause. The Indian Constitution adopted a detailed enumeration of freedoms under Article 19 (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession) and a broad equality guarantee under Articles 14‑18. The right to property, originally a fundamental right under Article 31, mirrored the US Fifth Amendment’s takings clause but was later removed as a fundamental right by the 44th Amendment (1978).

Judicial interpretation initially followed a narrow reading. In A. K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) the Supreme Court held that “procedure established by law” meant any procedure enacted by a competent legislature, rejecting the American substantive due process test. This position shifted dramatically in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), where the Court read “procedure established by law” as requiring fairness, reasonableness and non‑arbitrariness, effectively importing a due process standard. The Court also expanded the scope of Article 21 to include a bundle of unenumerated rights such as the right to privacy, health, education and a clean environment.

The American influence is also evident in the doctrine of judicial review. While the US Supreme Court’s power of review derives from Marbury v. Madison (1803), the Indian Constitution expressly vests this power in the Supreme Court and High Courts under Articles 32 and 226. The basic structure doctrine, articulated in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), functions as a constitutional limitation on amendment power akin to the US concept of unamendable core principles, though the Indian doctrine is judge‑made rather than textually entrenched.

For the examination, candidates should be able to contrast the textual differences — “due process” versus “procedure established by law” — and trace the judicial journey from Gopalan to Maneka Gandhi. They should also note that the Indian Bill of Rights is more detailed and includes group rights (minority cultural and educational rights under Articles 29‑30) which have no direct US counterpart.

Technique
Explain how the Indian Constitution adapts the American due process concept while retaining a distinct constitutional identity.
The Indian Constitution replaces the phrase "due process of law" with "procedure established by law" in Article 21, signalling a deliberate textual departure from the US model. Initially, the Supreme Court in A. K. Gopalan (1950) interpreted this phrase narrowly, equating it with any legislatively enacted procedure. However, in Maneka Gandhi (1978) the Court expanded the meaning to require that the procedure be fair, just and reasonable, effectively importing substantive due process without using the American terminology. This evolution shows that India borrowed the protective intent of due process but embedded it within a parliamentary sovereignty framework, allowing the judiciary to review legislative fairness while respecting the Constitution's own amendment procedure. The basic structure doctrine further insulates core rights from parliamentary override, a feature absent in the US system where constitutional amendments can alter any provision. Thus, the adaptation is both textual and jurisprudential, creating a hybrid model that balances legislative supremacy with judicial guardianship of fundamental liberties.
Strategy
When a question asks for a comparison between Indian and American rights jurisprudence, structure the answer in three layers: textual difference (due process vs procedure established by law), early judicial stance (Gopalan), and transformative shift (Maneka Gandhi and subsequent expansion). Cite the exact Articles (21, 14, 19) and the two landmark cases. This layered approach fetches maximum marks for both knowledge and analytical depth.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee on the Judiciary and the Design of an Independent Supreme Court

The Constituent Assembly constituted a dedicated Judicial Committee under the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities to deliberate on the structure, composition and independence of the higher judiciary. The committee was chaired by Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar and included members such as K. M. Munshi, B. N. Rau and Dr. B. R. Ambedkar. Its report, submitted in 1947, recommended a Supreme Court of India with a Chief Justice and not more than seven other judges, a number that could be increased by Parliament. The committee emphasised security of tenure, providing that judges would hold office until the age of sixty‑five and could be removed only by an address of both Houses of Parliament supported by a two‑thirds majority on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

The committee also addressed the appointment process. It proposed that the President appoint judges after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, a formulation that sought to balance executive authority with judicial primacy. This consultative model was later interpreted by the Supreme Court in the Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (1993) — the Second Judges Case — to mean that the Chief Justice’s opinion would have primacy, leading to the collegium system. The committee’s insistence on a fixed retirement age and a rigorous removal procedure was intended to shield the judiciary from political pressure, a concern rooted in the experience of the Federal Court of India under the Government of India Act 1935, where judges served at the pleasure of the Crown.

Financial independence was another pillar. The committee recommended that the salaries, allowances and pensions of Supreme Court judges be charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and not subject to annual vote of Parliament. This provision appears in Article 125 and mirrors the British practice of securing judicial remuneration. The committee also envisaged a separate secretariat for the Supreme Court, headed by a Secretary‑General appointed by the Chief Justice, to ensure administrative autonomy.

The design of the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction was also debated. The committee recommended original jurisdiction in disputes between the Centre and states (Article 131), appellate jurisdiction in constitutional, civil and criminal matters (Articles 132‑134), and advisory jurisdiction under Article 143. The power to issue writs for enforcement of fundamental rights (Article 32) was modelled on the US Supreme Court’s certiorari and mandamus powers but made explicitly available to any citizen. The committee’s work laid the foundation for an independent apex court that has since evolved into a powerful constitutional court with the authority to review constitutional amendments under the basic structure doctrine.

For examination, remember the key recommendations: (i) a Supreme Court with a Chief Justice and up to seven puisne judges, (ii) appointment by President after consultation with CJI, (iii) tenure until age 65, removal by parliamentary address with two‑thirds majority, (iv) salaries charged on Consolidated Fund, (v) original, appellate and advisory jurisdiction, and (vi) writ jurisdiction under Article 32. The collegium system, though not in the original text, traces its legitimacy to the committee’s consultative formula.

The Constitutional Scheme for the Election of the President and Vice-President: Electoral College, Disputes, and Judicial Pronouncements

Articles 54 and 55 of the Constitution provide for the election of the President by an electoral college consisting of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States, including the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the Union Territory of Puducherry. The value of each vote is calculated to ensure parity between the Union and the States: the value of an MLA’s vote equals the population of the state divided by the number of elected MLAs, multiplied by one thousand; the value of an MP’s vote equals the total value of all MLAs’ votes divided by the total number of elected MPs. This formula, prescribed by the Presidential and Vice‑Presidential Elections Act, 1952, seeks to maintain federal balance.

The Vice‑President is elected by a different electoral college under Article 66: members of both Houses of Parliament (both elected and nominated) but not state legislators. The Vice‑President also serves as the ex‑officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. Disputes arising out of the election of the President or Vice‑President are adjudicated by the Supreme Court under Article 71, whose decision is final. The Supreme Court’s jurisdiction in this regard is original and exclusive; no other court can entertain such disputes.

Landmark judicial pronouncements have clarified the scope of Article 71. In N. P. Ponnuswami v. Returning Officer (1952), the Court held that the election of the President cannot be challenged on the ground of irregularities in the electoral college composition once the election is complete, unless the challenge is filed within the statutory period. In K. K. Verma v. Union of India (1970), the Court ruled that the validity of the electoral college cannot be questioned after the election, reinforcing the finality of the process. The 1974 amendment to the Presidential and Vice‑Presidential Elections Act introduced a time‑bound dispute resolution mechanism, requiring the Supreme Court to dispose of petitions within a specified period.

The 42nd Amendment (1976) briefly altered the composition of the electoral college by including the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of Union Territories, but the 44th Amendment (1978) restored the original scheme. The 70th Amendment (1992) explicitly included the NCT of Delhi and Puducherry in the presidential electoral college, reflecting their legislative assemblies’ creation. The Vice‑President’s election has remained unchanged since 1950, with the only controversy being the casting vote in the Rajya Sabha, which the Vice‑President exercises only in case of a tie.

For the examination, candidates should be able to compute the vote value formula, distinguish the two electoral colleges, and cite the relevant Articles (54, 55, 66, 71) and the Presidential and Vice‑Presidential Elections Act, 1952. They should also note that the Supreme Court’s decision under Article 71 is not appealable and that the election cannot be challenged on grounds of vacancy in the electoral college.

The Doctrine of Parliamentary Privileges: Constitutional Basis, Scope, and Judicial Interpretation

Articles 105 and 194 of the Constitution confer parliamentary privileges on Members of Parliament and State Legislatures respectively. The core privileges include freedom of speech in the House, immunity from court proceedings for anything said or any vote given in the House, and the power of each House to punish for contempt or breach of privilege. These privileges are derived from the British parliamentary tradition but are codified in the Constitution, making them subject to judicial review.

The scope of freedom of speech under Article 105(1) is absolute within the four walls of the House; no civil or criminal proceeding can be instituted against a member for statements made during proceedings. However, this immunity does not extend to publications outside the House. In Keshav Singh v. Speaker, Legislative Assembly (1965), the Supreme Court held that the legislative assembly’s power to punish for contempt is not absolute and must be exercised in accordance with the principles of natural justice. The Court also ruled that fundamental rights under Part III are not suspended by legislative privileges, establishing that privileges are subordinate to the Constitution.

The power to expel a member for breach of privilege was examined in Raja Ram Pal v. Hon'ble Speaker (2007). The Supreme Court upheld the expulsion of MPs involved in the “cash for query” scandal, holding that the House’s power to punish for contempt includes expulsion, but such power must be exercised judiciously and is subject to judicial review for mala fides or violation of constitutional provisions. The Court also clarified that the privilege of freedom of speech does not protect a member from prosecution for bribery under the Prevention of Corruption Act, as the act of taking a bribe is not a legislative function.

Another dimension is the privilege of the House to regulate its internal proceedings. In State of Kerala v. K. Ajith (2021), the Supreme Court reiterated that the validity of proceedings inside the legislature cannot be questioned in court on the ground of procedural irregularity, reinforcing the principle of separation of powers. However, the Court has also held that the privilege of immunity from arrest in civil cases during the session (Article 105(2)) does not extend to criminal cases or preventive detention.

For examination, aspirants should remember the constitutional articles (105, 194), the three main privileges (speech, immunity from legal proceedings for House acts, power to punish contempt), the landmark cases (Keshav Singh, Raja Ram Pal, State of Kerala v. K. Ajith), and the principle that privileges are not above fundamental rights. They should also distinguish between the privilege of a member and the collective privilege of the House, and note that the Constitution does not enumerate an exhaustive list of privileges, leaving room for judicial interpretation.

  • Confusing the non‑justiciable nature of fundamental duties with the justiciability of directive principles; duties are moral obligations only.
  • Assuming the Indian Constitution adopts the American due process clause verbatim; Article 21 uses “procedure established by law”.
  • Believing the collegium system is explicitly mentioned in the original Constitution; it evolved from judicial interpretation of the consultation clause.
  • Thinking the Vice‑President is elected by the same electoral college as the President; the Vice‑President’s college excludes state legislators.
  • Treating parliamentary privileges as absolute and immune from judicial review; the Supreme Court has subjected them to fundamental rights scrutiny.
  • Overlooking that the value of votes in the presidential election is calculated to balance Union and State representation, not a simple one‑person‑one‑vote.
  • Misidentifying the removal procedure for Supreme Court judges as impeachment; it is an address by Parliament with a two‑thirds majority, not the impeachment process used for the President.

The Constituent Assembly's Citizenship Debates: Partition, Migration, and the Making of Articles 5–11

The Constitution's citizenship provisions (Articles 5–11) were drafted under the shadow of Partition, making them unique in constitutional history: they were the only provisions required to take effect immediately on 26 November 1949, a full two months before the Constitution's general commencement. The Drafting Committee, led by B.R. Ambedkar, presented Article 5 as a "transitional" definition linking citizenship to domicile and birth in the territory of India, but the Assembly's debates reveal a deeper contest over whether citizenship should be jus soli (birth-based), jus sanguinis (descent-based), or a hybrid calibrated to the trauma of displacement.

The core tension emerged in the discussion of Article 6 (rights of citizenship of certain persons who migrated from Pakistan) and Article 7 (rights of citizenship of certain migrants to Pakistan). The original Draft Article 5A (later Article 6) granted citizenship to migrants from Pakistan who arrived before 19 July 1948, provided they had resided in India for six months and registered. For those arriving after that date, a permit system was envisaged. Members like Jaspat Roy Kapoor and Mihir Lal Chattopadhyay argued that the cut-off date was arbitrary and penalised Hindus and Sikhs who fled later due to continuing violence. Conversely, Maulana Hasrat Mohani and B. Pocker Sahib warned that a liberal regime would encourage "infiltration" and alter the demographic balance in border states. The Assembly ultimately adopted a two-tier regime: automatic citizenship for pre-July 1948 migrants (Article 6), and a permit-based system for post-July 1948 migrants (Article 7), with the permit authority vested in the Government of India.

Article 8 addressed persons of Indian origin residing outside India (mainly in Southeast Asia, East Africa, and the Caribbean). The Drafting Committee proposed registration at Indian diplomatic missions, but members like K.T. Shah demanded automatic citizenship for all persons of Indian descent, arguing that the diaspora's loyalty was proven by their contributions to the freedom movement. The Assembly rejected this, fearing dual allegiance complications with newly independent Commonwealth nations. Article 9 stipulated that voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship extinguished Indian citizenship — a provision that later became the basis for the Supreme Court's ruling in State Trading Corporation v. Commercial Tax Officer (1963) that a company cannot be a citizen.

Article 10 provided for continuity of citizenship subject to parliamentary law, and Article 11 expressly empowered Parliament to regulate citizenship by law, leading to the Citizenship Act, 1955. The debates reveal that the framers viewed citizenship not as a static status but as a dynamic instrument of state-building in a post-colonial, post-Partition polity. For examination, aspirants must distinguish the three categories of migrants (pre-1948, post-1948, returnees under permit), recall the 19 July 1948 cut-off, and explain why Article 11 was made non-justiciable in its policy dimension but subject to judicial review for constitutional compliance.

The Integration of Princely States: Constitutional Architecture of Merger, Instruments of Accession, and the Privy Purse Guarantees

The constitutional integration of over 560 princely states was achieved not through a single provision but through a layered architecture spanning the Indian Independence Act 1947, the Instruments of Accession, the Merger Agreements, the Constitution (Articles 1–4, 238, 363, 366), and the subsequent Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act 1956. The process unfolded in three constitutional stages: accession (defence, external affairs, communications), merger (full administrative integration), and constitutionalisation (reorganisation into Part A, B, C, D states under the original First Schedule).

The Instrument of Accession, executed under Section 6 of the Government of India Act 1935 as adapted by the Independence Act, was a sovereign act by the Ruler accepting the Dominion Legislature's authority over three subjects. Crucially, it did not cede sovereignty — a distinction the Supreme Court upheld in State of Seraikella v. Union of India (1951), holding that the Ruler's sovereignty persisted in non-acceded areas until merger. The Merger Agreements (1948–1949), negotiated by V.P. Menon and Sardar Patel, transferred "full and exclusive authority, jurisdiction and powers" to the Dominion Government. These agreements guaranteed the Rulers' personal privileges, dignities, and titles (Article 363), and crucially, the Privy Purse — a tax-free, hereditable sum charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 291).

The original Constitution classified states into four Parts: Part A (former British provinces), Part B (merged princely unions like Rajasthan, Patiala and East Punjab States Union), Part C (centrally administered chief commissioners' provinces), and Part D (Andaman and Nicobar Islands). Article 238 applied Part VI provisions (Governor, Legislature, High Court) to Part B states with modifications. The Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act 1956, implementing the States Reorganisation Commission's recommendations, abolished this classification, creating a uniform structure of States and Union Territories under Article 1. The Privy Purse guarantees were abolished by the Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act 1971, which deleted Articles 291 and 362 and inserted Article 363A, derecognising Rulers. The Supreme Court in H.H. Maharajadhiraja Madhav Rao v. Union of India (1971) had earlier struck down the Presidential derecognition order as ultra vires, prompting the amendment. Aspirants must trace the legal continuity from Instrument of Accession → Merger Agreement → Constitutional classification → Reorganisation → Derecognition, and distinguish the justiciability of Merger Agreement terms (enforceable as political compacts) from the non-justiciability of the Ruler's personal privileges under Article 363.

Examiner's Twist: Distinguishing Accession from Merger
A question asks: "The Instrument of Accession signed by the Ruler of Jammu & Kashmir in 1947 was legally identical to the Merger Agreements signed by other princely states." Evaluate this statement with reference to the constitutional provisions and judicial pronouncements.
The statement is false. The Instrument of Accession (executed under Section 6 of the GoI Act 1935 as adapted) ceded only three subjects — Defence, External Affairs, and Communications — and did not transfer internal sovereignty. The Ruler retained legislative and executive authority over all other matters. In contrast, Merger Agreements (e.g., for Travancore, Mysore, Gwalior) transferred "full and exclusive authority, jurisdiction and powers" to the Dominion Government, effectively ending the Ruler's sovereignty. The J&K Instrument of Accession was supplemented by the 1950 Constitutional Order (C.O. 10) and the 1954 Presidential Order (C.O. 48) under Article 370, which extended Union jurisdiction incrementally. The Supreme Court in Prem Nath Kaul v. State of J&K (1959) recognised J&K's special constitutional position derived from the limited accession. Other states were fully integrated via Merger Agreements and later the Seventh Amendment 1956. The distinction is constitutionally significant: accession was a federal compact; merger was a unitary absorption.
Exam-Day Strategy
When a question mentions "princely states integration", first identify the stage: Accession (1947, three subjects), Merger (1948-49, full powers), Constitutional Classification (1950, Parts A-D), Reorganisation (1956, uniform states), or Derecognition (1971, Privy Purse abolition). Each stage has distinct legal instruments and Articles. Do not conflate the Instrument of Accession with the Merger Agreement — this is the most frequent trap in both Prelims and Mains.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on Emergency Provisions: Transplanting Section 93 of the Government of India Act 1935 and the Safeguards Debate

The emergency provisions (Articles 352, 356, 360) were not original inventions but deliberate transplants of Section 93 of the Government of India Act 1935, which allowed the Governor to assume provincial powers if constitutional machinery failed. The Constituent Assembly's debates, particularly in the Sub-Committee on Federal Constitution and the full Assembly sessions of August 1949, reveal a conscious choice to retain this colonial instrument while embedding safeguards absent in the 1935 Act. The key figures — Ambedkar, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, K.M. Munshi, and H.V. Kamath — clashed over three issues: the trigger threshold, parliamentary control, and judicial review.

Article 356 (President's Rule) attracted the fiercest debate. The Draft Article 278 allowed proclamation on the Governor's report or "otherwise". H.V. Kamath moved an amendment requiring the President to be "satisfied" based on the Governor's report alone, arguing that "otherwise" gave the Centre unchecked power. Ambedkar defended the wider phrasing, stating that the President might receive information from sources other than the Governor. The Assembly rejected Kamath's amendment but inserted a crucial safeguard: the proclamation must be laid before both Houses of Parliament and ceases to operate after two months unless approved by both Houses (Article 356(3)). This parliamentary oversight was absent in Section 93, where the Governor's proclamation was final.

On judicial review, the Drafting Committee initially treated the President's satisfaction as non-justiciable. However, members like K.T. Shah and Prof. K.T. Shah argued that "satisfaction" must be based on relevant material and not mala fide. The Assembly did not explicitly resolve this, leaving it to judicial evolution. The Supreme Court in State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) initially held the President's satisfaction non-justiciable, but S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) reversed this, declaring that the proclamation is subject to judicial review on grounds of mala fides, irrelevance, or perversity. Article 352 (National Emergency) originally allowed proclamation on "war, external aggression, or internal disturbance". The 44th Amendment (1978) replaced "internal disturbance" with "armed rebellion" and required written Cabinet advice, directly responding to the 1975 Emergency experience. Article 360 (Financial Emergency) remains the only never-invoked provision; its trigger — threat to financial stability or credit of India — was debated by Naziruddin Ahmad, who warned it could be used to impose central fiscal diktats. Aspirants must compare the 1935 Act's Section 93 (Governor's discretion, no legislative oversight) with Article 356 (President on Governor's report/otherwise, parliamentary approval within two months, judicial review post-Bommai), and explain how the 44th Amendment altered Article 352's trigger and procedural requirements.

The Making of the Seventh Schedule: The Federalism Sub-Committee, the Residuary Power Debate, and the Final Distribution of Legislative Subjects

The Seventh Schedule — the Union List (List I), State List (List II), and Concurrent List (List III) — was the product of the Sub-Committee on Federal Constitution (chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru, with members including Ambedkar, K.M. Munshi, and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar) and the subsequent Expert Committee on Financial Provisions. The distribution was modelled on the Government of India Act 1935's Seventh Schedule but with three critical modifications: the creation of a robust Concurrent List (absent in the 1935 Act's federal scheme), the assignment of residuary powers to the Union (Article 248 + Entry 97, List I) rather than the Governor-General, and the inclusion of specific entries to enable planned development (e.g., Entry 20, List I: economic and social planning; Entry 23, List III: social security and social insurance).

The residuary power debate was sharp. The 1935 Act vested residuary powers in the Governor-General (Section 104), exercisable at his discretion. The Federalism Sub-Committee initially considered the Canadian model (residuary to Centre) and the American model (residuary to States). K.M. Munshi argued for Union residuary power to handle unforeseen matters in a developing economy. The Drafting Committee adopted the Canadian model but with a textual twist: Article 248 grants Parliament exclusive power over "any matter not enumerated in List II or List III", and Entry 97 of List I explicitly includes "any other matter not enumerated in List II or List III including any tax not mentioned in either of those Lists". This double entrenchment (Article + Entry) makes the Union's residuary power textually explicit, unlike Canada's unwritten convention. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon (1971) and State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977) affirmed that the residuary field is not a "dustbin" but a positive legislative domain.

The Concurrent List (List III) was an innovation over the 1935 Act, which had only a Federal and Provincial List with a few "concurrent" subjects governed by federal paramountcy. The Indian Constitution made Concurrent List subjects (originally 36, now 52 after amendments) subject to Article 254's repugnancy resolution: Union law prevails unless the State law was reserved for Presidential assent and received it. The Sub-Committee placed critical welfare subjects — criminal law, marriage, contracts, trusts, electricity, newspapers, population control — in List III to enable uniform minimum standards while permitting state-level variation. The 42nd Amendment (1976) transferred five subjects from State to Concurrent List (education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals, administration of justice) — a move criticised for centralising tendency. Aspirants must be able to map the 1935 Act's Lists to the Constitution's Lists, explain the Canadian-model residuary power with Indian textual reinforcement, and analyse how the Concurrent List's expansion reflects the tension between cooperative federalism and centralised planning.

The Preamble's "We the People" and the Absence of Popular Ratification: The Legitimacy Debate in the Constituent Assembly and Subsequent Jurisprudence

The Preamble's opening words — "We, the people of India, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic..." — assert a popular sovereignty that the Constituent Assembly itself never submitted to a referendum. This "autochthony gap" was debated explicitly in the Assembly. During the Preamble discussion on 17 October 1949, H.V. Kamath moved to insert "In the name of God" and argued that the Constitution derived authority from the people, not the Assembly. Ambedkar replied that the Assembly was elected on a limited franchise (provincial legislatures under the 1935 Act) and represented the people's will through the mandate of the 1946 elections, which were fought on the issue of constitution-making. He invoked the "continuity of sovereignty" theory: the Assembly was the people's agent, and the Constitution's adoption by the Assembly was the people's act.

The legitimacy question resurfaced in jurisprudence. In Re: Berubari Union (1960), the Supreme Court held the Preamble not a part of the Constitution and not a source of power. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the majority reversed this, declaring the Preamble a part of the Constitution and a key to interpreting the "basic structure". Justice Khanna observed that "We the people" signifies that the Constitution is not a gift of the British Parliament but an autochthonous charter. However, the Court has never ruled on the absence of a referendum. The 42nd Amendment's insertion of "Socialist", "Secular", and "Integrity" in 1976 — during Emergency, without fresh electoral mandate — intensified the legitimacy critique. In S.R. Bommai (1994), the Court treated "Secularism" as a basic structure feature derived from the Preamble, effectively constitutionalising a term inserted without popular ratification. Contemporary scholarship (Granville Austin, Arvind Elangovan) argues that the Assembly's legitimacy rested on "representative claim" rather than "direct democracy", a distinction crucial for understanding why the Preamble is amendable (subject to basic structure) but not self-executing. Aspirants must distinguish three legitimacy layers: (1) legal continuity from the Indian Independence Act 1947, (2) representative legitimacy of the 1946 provincial elections, and (3) the symbolic claim of "We the people" — and explain how the Supreme Court uses the Preamble as an interpretive lens without treating it as an independent source of rights.

  • Confusing the Instrument of Accession (three subjects, sovereignty retained) with the Merger Agreement (full powers transferred, sovereignty extinguished) — they are distinct legal instruments with different constitutional consequences.
  • Assuming the 19 July 1948 cut-off in Article 6 applies to all migrants from Pakistan; it applies only to those claiming citizenship under Article 6 (pre-1948 migrants). Post-1948 migrants fall under Article 7's permit system.
  • Believing the President's satisfaction under Article 356 is non-justiciable; S.R. Bommai (1994) made it reviewable for mala fides, irrelevance, and perversity, though the Court does not substitute its own assessment.
  • Thinking the Concurrent List existed in the Government of India Act 1935; it was an Indian innovation. The 1935 Act had a Federal List, Provincial List, and a few concurrent subjects governed by federal paramountcy, not a full Concurrent List with Article 254 repugnancy mechanism.
  • Treating the Preamble's "We the people" as evidence of a referendum; no referendum was held. The phrase reflects the Assembly's representative claim, not direct popular ratification.
  • Overlooking that Article 248 (residuary power) and Entry 97 List I operate together — the double textual entrenchment is unique to India and stronger than the Canadian convention it mimics.
  • Confusing the 42nd Amendment's transfer of subjects to the Concurrent List (education, forests, etc.) with the original Constitution's distribution; the transfer is a major centralising shift often tested in federalism questions.

The Doctrine of Eclipse and the Validation of Pre‑Constitutional Laws

The doctrine of eclipse addresses the fate of laws enacted before the commencement of the Constitution that conflict with the fundamental rights guaranteed in Part III. Such laws are not rendered void ab initio; they become dormant — eclipsed — to the extent of the inconsistency. When the constitutional impediment is removed, either by amendment of the fundamental right or by a judicial declaration that the right does not apply to the particular subject‑matter, the pre‑constitutional provision revives and operates as if it had never been in conflict. The Supreme Court first articulated this principle in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955), holding that a pre‑Constitution law prohibiting the sale of liquor could be enforced again after the relevant fundamental right was amended. The doctrine was refined in State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974), where the Court clarified that eclipse applies only to laws that were valid when made and that the inconsistency must be with a fundamental right that is justiciable. A critical limitation is that the doctrine does not extend to post‑constitutional laws; those are void under Article 13(2) if they contravene fundamental rights. The eclipse principle also interacts with the doctrine of severability: if the offending portion of a pre‑constitutional statute can be severed, the remainder continues to operate without invoking eclipse. Examiners often test the distinction between eclipse and the “void ab initio” rule for post‑constitutional legislation, and they may ask whether a law that was partially eclipsed can be revived by a constitutional amendment that removes the fundamental right altogether. The answer is yes, provided the amendment does not violate the basic structure. The doctrine thus preserves legislative continuity while respecting constitutional supremacy.

The Doctrine of Severability and Its Application in Saving Statutes

Severability allows a court to excise the unconstitutional portion of a statute while preserving the remainder, provided the valid part is capable of standing independently and the legislature would have enacted it without the invalid portion. The test was laid down in R.M.D.C. v. Union of India (1957), where the Court held that the doctrine applies only when the unconstitutional provision is not so intertwined with the rest of the Act that its removal would alter the legislative intent. The Court examines three factors: (1) whether the invalid provision is separable in terms of language and structure; (2) whether the remaining provisions can function coherently; and (3) whether the legislature’s dominant purpose survives the excision. In Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980), the Court applied severability to uphold the bulk of the 42nd Amendment while striking down the clauses that curtailed judicial review, because the amendment’s primary objective — strengthening directive principles — remained intact. A notable exception arises when the statute contains a “non‑severability clause” expressly stating that the invalidity of any part renders the whole Act void; such clauses are respected unless they themselves violate the basic structure. The doctrine also interacts with the principle of reading down: courts may interpret a provision narrowly to avoid unconstitutionality, resorting to severability only when reading down fails. In practice, examiners ask candidates to identify whether a given amendment can be partially upheld, and to explain why the Court refused severability in Keshavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) for the basic‑structure‑violating clauses. Mastery of the three‑factor test and the distinction between severability and reading down is essential for answering applied‑scenario questions.

Applied Scenario
A State legislature enacts the “Public Health (Amendment) Act, 2023” which contains three sections: Section 2 imposes a mandatory vaccination requirement; Section 3 authorises the State to seize private property for quarantine centres without compensation; Section 4 creates a penalty for non‑compliance. The High Court strikes down Section 3 as violative of Article 300A (property right) but upholds Sections 2 and 4. The State appeals, arguing that the Act is a single legislative scheme and that severability is impermissible because the Act lacks a severability clause. Decide.
The High Court’s decision is correct. Under the R.M.D.C. test, Section 3 is linguistically and functionally distinct from Sections 2 and 4; its removal does not impair the operation of the vaccination mandate or the penalty regime. The absence of an express severability clause does not bar judicial severance — the Court may sever unless the legislature has indicated the contrary. Since the dominant purpose of the Act (public health protection through vaccination) survives without the property‑seizure power, severability applies. The appeal fails.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question presents a multi‑section statute, first isolate the challenged provision. Apply the three‑factor R.M.D.C. test mentally: separability, independent workability, legislative intent. If the statute contains a non‑severability clause, note it but remember the clause itself can be struck down if it protects a basic‑structure violation. Practice writing the test in three bullet points; examiners award marks for structured reasoning.

The Principle of Judicial Activism versus Judicial Restraint in Indian Constitutional Jurisprudence

Judicial activism refers to the willingness of courts to interpret the Constitution expansively, often filling legislative gaps or creating new rights, while judicial restraint emphasizes deference to the elected branches and a narrow reading of constitutional text. The Indian Supreme Court has oscillated between these poles. The early phase, exemplified by A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950), displayed restraint by adopting a literal reading of Article 21, refusing to import due‑process concepts. The turning point came with Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), where the Court asserted the power to review constitutional amendments, a quintessentially activist move that established the basic‑structure doctrine. Subsequent decades saw activism in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) — reading “procedure established by law” as “fair, just and reasonable” — and in Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997), where the Court laid down guidelines against sexual harassment in the absence of legislation. The Court’s activism peaked in the 1990s with public‑interest litigation (PIL) expanding locus standi and directing executive action on environmental, bonded‑labour, and custodial‑death issues. However, the late 2000s witnessed a restraint revival: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) limited judicial review of President’s Rule to mala fides, and Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) balanced privacy with state interests, refusing to strike down the Aadhaar Act wholesale. The current jurisprudence stresses “constitutional morality” as a guiding principle, allowing activism only when the Constitution’s core values are threatened. Examiners test the ability to classify a given judgment as activist or restraint‑oriented and to argue whether the Court overstepped its institutional role. A nuanced answer acknowledges that the line is fluid and that the Court often employs “dialogic” reasoning — inviting legislative response while providing interim relief.

The Constitutional Scheme of Environmental Protection: Article 48A, Article 51A(g) and Judicial Expansion

The Constitution originally contained no explicit environmental right. The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted Article 48A, directing the State to protect and improve the environment, and Article 51A(g), imposing a fundamental duty on citizens to protect natural resources. Though non‑justiciable as directive principles and duties, the Supreme Court has transformed them into enforceable obligations through Article 21. In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) (the Oleum gas leak case), the Court held that the right to life includes the right to a wholesome environment, making environmental degradation actionable under Article 32. The “polluter pays” principle and the “precautionary principle” were imported from international law in Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996). The Court further expanded the doctrine of “public trust” in M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997), declaring that natural resources are held in trust for the public. In T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India (1995), the Court assumed continuous monitoring of forest conservation, effectively acting as a “green bench”. The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, later institutionalised specialised environmental adjudication, but the Supreme Court retains suo‑motu jurisdiction. A recurring examiner twist is to ask whether Article 48A can be directly enforced; the correct answer is that it cannot be enforced directly but serves as an interpretive aid for Article 21. Another trap is confusing the fundamental duty under Article 51A(g) with a justiciable right — duties are not enforceable by courts against citizens, though they inform statutory interpretation. Candidates must also distinguish the “polluter pays” principle (cost internalisation) from the “precautionary principle” (preventive action despite scientific uncertainty).

The Constitutional Framework for the Protection of Women’s Rights: Articles 15(3), 39(a), 42 and Legislative Measures

The Constitution contains several provisions aimed at ameliorating gender‑based disadvantage. Article 15(3) empowers the State to make special provisions for women and children, an exception to the non‑discrimination rule. Article 39(a) directs the State to secure equal right to adequate means of livelihood for men and women, while Article 42 mandates just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief. These directive principles have been invoked to uphold protective legislation. In Air India v. Nargesh Meerza (1981), the Court struck down a regulation terminating air‑hostesses on first pregnancy, holding it violated Article 15(3) read with Article 14. The landmark Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) used Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g) and 21 to lay down guidelines against workplace sexual harassment, later codified in the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013. The Court’s activist stance continued in Secretary, Ministry of Defence v. Babita Puniya (2020), granting permanent commission to women officers in the Army, interpreting Article 15(3) as enabling substantive equality. In Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018), the adultery provision (Section 497 IPC) was struck down as violative of Articles 14, 15 and 21, reinforcing women’s autonomy. The 2017 Shayara Bano v. Union of India decision invalidated instant triple talaq, citing Articles 14, 15(1) and 21. Legislative measures such as the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 (amended 2017), the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, and the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013 (post‑Nirbhaya) operationalise constitutional mandates. Examiners often ask whether Article 15(3) permits “reverse discrimination” — the answer is yes, provided the classification is rationally related to the objective of remedying historical disadvantage. Another common trap is to treat Article 42 as justiciable; it remains a directive principle, enforceable only through legislation.

  • Confusing the doctrine of eclipse with the void‑ab‑initio rule for post‑constitutional laws; eclipse applies only to pre‑constitutional statutes.
  • Assuming severability is automatic whenever a statute lacks a non‑severability clause; the three‑factor R.M.D.C. test must be satisfied.
  • Labeling every expansive interpretation as “judicial activism” without distinguishing between dialogic reasoning and outright policy‑making.
  • Treating Article 48A or Article 51A(g) as directly enforceable fundamental rights; they are directive principles and fundamental duties, enforceable only through Article 21.
