  • Believing Article 15(3) allows any gender‑based classification; the classification must be reasonably related to remedying disadvantage and not perpetuate stereotypes.
  • Overlooking that fundamental duties under Article 51A are not justiciable against citizens, though they guide statutory interpretation.
  • Misreading the “polluter pays” principle as a strict liability rule without recognizing its basis in cost internalisation and the precautionary principle as a separate preventive doctrine.

The Committee System of the Constituent Assembly: Steering, Drafting, and Specialized Sub-Committees

The Constituent Assembly’s output was the product of a deliberate committee architecture designed to manage procedural volume and substantive disagreement. At the apex stood the Steering Committee (chaired by Rajendra Prasad), which controlled the agenda, timetable, and referral of matters to functional committees. The Drafting Committee (chaired by B.R. Ambedkar, with Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, K.M. Munshi, Mohammad Saadullah, B.L. Mitter, and D.P. Khaitan) is the best known, but it functioned as a redaction body: it received reports from sectoral committees, harmonized language, and prepared the successive drafts (February 1948, October 1948, November 1949).

Critical substantive work occurred in specialized committees. The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities (chaired by Sardar Patel) had five sub-committees: Fundamental Rights (J.B. Kripalani), Minorities (H.C. Mookerjee), North-East Frontier Tribal Areas (Gopinath Bordoloi), Excluded and Partially Excluded Areas (A.V. Thakkar), and the North-West Frontier Tribal Areas. The Union Powers Committee and Union Constitution Committee (both chaired by Nehru) defined the Centre’s legislative, executive, and financial architecture. The Provincial Constitution Committee (Patel) drafted the state-level framework. The Rules of Procedure Committee (Rajendra Prasad) governed debate conduct. The Committee on the Functions of the Constituent Assembly (G.V. Mavalankar) clarified its dual role as constitution-making body and provisional legislature.

Two committees warrant specific attention for their constitutional impact. The Committee on Chief Commissioners’ Provinces (B. Pattabhi Sitaramayya) recommended the administrative model for centrally administered territories, later reflected in Part VIII (since repealed and replaced by Union Territories provisions). The Ad Hoc Committee on the National Flag (Rajendra Prasad) finalized the tricolour design with the Ashoka Chakra, adopted on 22 July 1947. The Expert Committee on Financial Provisions (Nalini Ranjan Sarkar) shaped the tax-sharing framework that became the Finance Commission architecture. The Drafting Committee’s Scrutiny Memoranda — internal notes comparing each article with the Government of India Act 1935, the U.S., Canadian, Irish, and Australian constitutions — remain the most granular record of borrowing rationale. Candidates should know that the Drafting Committee sat for 141 days over eleven months, while the full Assembly sat for 165 days across eleven sessions spanning 2 years, 11 months, and 18 days.

The Constitutional Integration of Princely States: Instruments of Accession, Merger Agreements, and the Privy Purse Settlement

The constitutional framework did not merely inherit British India’s provinces; it had to absorb 562 princely states covering 48% of the landmass and 28% of the population. The legal instrument was the Instrument of Accession (IoA), executed under Section 6 of the Government of India Act 1935 as adapted by the India (Provisional Constitution) Order 1947. The IoA surrendered three subjects — Defence, External Affairs, and Communications — to the Dominion Legislature. Crucially, the IoA did not merge the state; it created a federal relationship where the ruler retained sovereignty over residuary matters.

Between 1947 and 1949, a second tier of integration occurred through Merger Agreements. States were merged into adjoining provinces (e.g., Travancore-Cochin into Madras, Mysore into Mysore State) or formed into centrally administered units (e.g., Vindhya Pradesh, Bhopal). The Merger Agreement transferred full legislative, executive, and judicial authority to the Government of India, extinguishing the ruler’s sovereignty. In return, the ruler received a Privy Purse — a tax-free, hereditary annual payment guaranteed by Article 291 and Article 362 of the Constitution. The amounts ranged from ₹43 lakh (Hyderabad) to ₹192 lakh (Mysore), totalling approximately ₹5.76 crore annually.

A third tier created Unions of States (e.g., Rajasthan, Patiala and East Punjab States Union — PEPSU, Saurashtra) where rulers pooled sovereignty under a Rajpramukh. The Constitution recognized these as Part B States (Article 238, since repealed). The Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956 abolished the Part A/Part B/Part C classification, reorganizing all territories into States and Union Territories on linguistic lines. The Privy Purse guarantee became a political flashpoint. In 1970, President V.V. Giri derecognized rulers via Presidential Order, but the Supreme Court in H.H. Maharajadhiraja Madhav Rao Scindia v. Union of India (1971) struck it down as violative of Article 363 (which bars courts from adjudicating disputes arising from IoAs and Merger Agreements) and Article 14. Parliament responded with the Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1971, deleting Articles 291 and 362 and abolishing Privy Purses. The Court upheld this in Raghunathrao Ganpatrao v. Union of India (1993), holding that the amendment did not violate the basic structure because the Privy Purse was a political bargain, not a constitutional essential feature.

Applied Scenario
A question asks: "The Instrument of Accession signed by the Maharaja of Jammu & Kashmir in October 1947 was legally distinct from the Merger Agreements signed by other princely states in 1949. Explain the constitutional consequence of this distinction for the application of the Indian Constitution to J&K prior to August 2019."
The IoA surrendered only Defence, External Affairs, and Communications. Unlike Merger Agreements, it did not transfer residuary sovereignty. Consequently, Article 370 (originally Article 306A) was negotiated to reflect this limited accession: Parliament’s legislative power over J&K required State Government concurrence for Union and Concurrent List matters beyond the three acceded subjects, and the State had its own Constitution. The Presidential Order of 1954 (C.O. 48) extended other constitutional provisions with modifications. This distinct legal origin — accession without merger — was the basis for J&K’s special autonomy until the Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 2019 (C.O. 272) and the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 superseded it.
Exam-Day Strategy
When a question contrasts "accession" and "merger", anchor your answer in the quantum of sovereignty transferred. Accession = three subjects only; Merger = full sovereignty. Cite Article 363 (non-justiciability of IoA disputes) and the 26th Amendment (abolition of Privy Purses) as the constitutional bookends. For J&K, mention Article 370’s marginal note "Temporary provisions" and the 1954 Presidential Order as the operational bridge.

The Munshi-Ayyangar Formula and the Language Compromise: Hindi, English, and the Eighth Schedule

The Constituent Assembly’s most protracted debate — spanning three sessions and 27 days of discussion — concerned the official language. The Munshi-Ayyangar Formula, brokered by K.M. Munshi and N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar in the Drafting Committee, resolved the deadlock between the Hindi protagonists (who wanted immediate replacement of English) and the non-Hindi members (led by T.T. Krishnamachari, N.G. Ranga, and Frank Anthony) who feared majoritarian imposition. The formula, adopted as Articles 343–351, created a layered compromise:

  • Article 343: Hindi in Devanagari script as the official language of the Union; English to continue for 15 years from commencement (i.e., until 26 January 1965).
  • Article 344: A Commission (first under B.G. Kher, 1955) and a Parliamentary Committee to recommend progressive use of Hindi and restrictions on English.
  • Article 345: State legislatures free to adopt any language(s) in use in the State or Hindi as official language(s).
  • Article 346: Official language for communication between States and between State and Union.
  • Article 347: Presidential recognition of a language spoken by a substantial proportion of a State’s population.
  • Article 348: English to be used in Supreme Court, High Courts, and for Bills, Acts, Ordinances, and subordinate legislation — until Parliament otherwise provides.
  • Article 351: Directive to develop Hindi by assimilating forms from Hindustani and other Eighth Schedule languages.

The Eighth Schedule originally listed 14 languages: Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Kashmiri, Malayalam, Marathi, Oriya, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Tamil, Telugu, Urdu. Sindhi was added by the 21st Amendment (1967); Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali by the 71st Amendment (1992); Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali by the 92nd Amendment (2003) — totalling 22. The Schedule confers no justiciable right; it is a developmental directive for the Union to promote these languages. The 15-year English deadline triggered the Official Languages Act, 1963 (amended 1967), which provided for continued use of English alongside Hindi for Union official purposes, and the Official Language Rules, 1976 governing correspondence. The Official Languages Commission (Kher Commission, 1955) recommended a phased transition; the Parliamentary Committee on Official Language (constituted 1976, chaired by Home Minister) monitors implementation. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. Murasoli Maran (1976) held that Article 343 does not make Hindi the national language — India has no constitutionally designated national language.

The Judicial Trajectory of the Preamble: From Berubari Union (1960) to Kesavananda Bharati (1973) to LIC of India (1995)

The Preamble’s constitutional status evolved through three landmark judgments that redefined its interpretive weight. In Re Berubari Union and Exchange of Enclaves (1960), a Presidential Reference under Article 143, the Supreme Court (Gajendragadkar J., 8:1) held that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution and not a source of substantive power. It serves only as a key to open the minds of the makers and an interpretive aid when statutory language is ambiguous. The Court ruled that Parliament’s power under Article 3 to alter State boundaries did not require a constitutional amendment because the Preamble’s “territory of India” was not a limitation.

In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the 13-judge bench reversed Berubari. Sikri C.J. (for the majority) held that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution (adopted by the Constituent Assembly after the Articles, as the final act of enactment) and that it constitutes the basic structure. The Preamble’s objectives — sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic, republic, justice, liberty, equality, fraternity — are the silhouette of the Constitution; any amendment destroying them violates Article 368’s implied limitation. Khanna J.’s pivotal concurrence treated the Preamble as the touchstone for basic structure review. The Court also held that the Preamble can be amended (the 42nd Amendment added “socialist”, “secular”, “integrity”), but only in a manner that furthers its objectives, not destroys them.

In LIC of India v. Consumer Education and Research Centre (1995), the Court (Venkatachaliah J.) operationalized the Preamble as a justiciable interpretive mandate. The case concerned whether LIC’s recruitment rules violated Article 14. The Court read “socialist” and “equality of status and opportunity” in the Preamble together with Articles 14, 16, and 39(b)-(c) to hold that the State’s economic actions must subserve distributive justice. The Preamble was no longer a mere preface; it became a constitutional value-cluster that informs the content of fundamental rights and directive principles. Subsequent cases — S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) (secularism as basic feature), Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) (balance between Parts III and IV as basic structure), Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) (democracy and free elections) — cite the Preamble as the source of the basic features they protect. The trajectory is clear: non-justiciable preface (1960) → basic structure anchor (1973) → interpretive lens for rights adjudication (1995 onward).

The Citizenship Provisions at Commencement: Partition, Migration, and Articles 5–11

The Constitution’s citizenship framework (Part II, Articles 5–11) was drafted against the backdrop of Partition, mass migration, and the absence of a pre-existing Indian nationality law. The Citizenship Act, 1955 was enacted under Article 11 (Parliament’s plenary power), but the constitutional provisions themselves are transitional and determinative for the commencement date (26 January 1950).

  • Article 5: Domicile + one of three conditions — (a) born in India; (b) either parent born in India; (c) ordinarily resident for 5 years immediately preceding commencement. This created the initial citizen body.
  • Article 6: Migrants from Pakistan. Two categories: (i) migrated before 19 July 1948 — citizenship if ordinarily resident since migration; (ii) migrated on or after 19 July 1948 — citizenship only if registered as citizen by Dominion Government officer after residing 6 months, provided they had a permit for resettlement or permanent return. The 19 July 1948 cut-off corresponds to the permit system introduced by the Influx from Pakistan (Control) Ordinance.
  • Article 7: Migrants to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 — deemed not citizens, unless they returned under a permit for resettlement/permanent return (mirroring Article 6(ii)). The 1 March 1947 date precedes the Partition Plan announcement.
  • Article 8: Persons of Indian origin residing outside India — citizenship if registered by Indian diplomatic/consular representative, whether before or after commencement.
  • Article 9: Voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship — automatic loss of Indian citizenship. No dual citizenship.
  • Article 10: Continuance of citizenship — subject to Parliamentary law.
  • Article 11: Parliament’s power to make any provision — used for the 1955 Act and subsequent amendments (1986, 1992, 2003, 2005, 2015, 2019).

The Supreme Court in State of Bihar v. Kumar Amar Singh (1955) held that Article 5 is exhaustive for commencement citizenship; no common law domicile concept supplements it. In Kulathil Mammu v. State of Kerala (1966), the Court ruled that Article 7’s bar is absolute — even a person who never voluntarily migrated but was displaced by communal violence loses citizenship if they were in Pakistan territory after 1 March 1947, unless the permit exception applies. The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003 introduced overseas citizenship of India (OCI) — a form of dual nationality-lite — but Article 9’s prohibition on dual citizenship remains for full citizens. The 2019 Amendment (CAA) created a religiously differentiated naturalization path for migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Pakistan entering before 31 December 2014, raising Article 14/15 challenges currently pending before the Court. Candidates must distinguish the constitutional commencement framework (Articles 5–8, fixed dates, no discretion) from the statutory regime (1955 Act, discretionary registration/naturalization, amendable by Parliament).

  • Trap: Confusing the Instrument of Accession (three subjects) with the Merger Agreement (full sovereignty) — they create different constitutional relationships.
  • Trap: Assuming the Privy Purse was a fundamental right; it was a political guarantee under Articles 291/362, abolished by the 26th Amendment without violating basic structure.
  • Trap: Stating Hindi is the "national language"; the Constitution designates it only as "official language of the Union" (Article 343), and the Supreme Court has explicitly denied it national language status.
  • Trap: Treating the Eighth Schedule as conferring justiciable language rights; it is a promotional directive (Article 351), not a source of enforceable entitlements.
  • Trap: Citing Berubari (1960) as current law on the Preamble’s status; Kesavananda (1973) overruled it — the Preamble is part of the Constitution and a basic structure anchor.
  • Trap: Believing the Preamble cannot be amended; the 42nd Amendment added three words, and Kesavananda permits amendment that furthers Preamble objectives.
  • Trap: Conflating Article 5 (commencement citizenship by domicile) with the Citizenship Act, 1955 (post-commencement acquisition); Article 5 is a one-time constitutional filter, the Act is an ongoing statutory regime.
  • Trap: Overlooking the 19 July 1948 and 1 March 1947 cut-off dates in Articles 6 and 7; these are fixed constitutional dates, not delegated to executive notification.

The constitutional framework’s resilience lies in its capacity to absorb historical contingencies — Partition, princely integration, linguistic diversity — through textual compromises that remain judicially enforceable.

Constituent Assembly Debates on Emergency Provisions: The Tension Between Federalism and Unified Command

The emergency provisions (Articles 352, 356, 360) were among the most contested in the Constituent Assembly, reflecting the trauma of Partition and the determination to prevent fragmentation. The Drafting Committee, led by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, presented Articles 275, 276, and 277 (later renumbered) as a "safety valve" — a phrase Ambedkar used in the Assembly on 2 August 1949. The debates reveal three distinct anxieties: the memory of princely state intransigence, the fear of secessionist movements, and the British precedent of the Government of India Act 1935, Section 93 (Governor's Rule) and Section 45 (Central Emergency).

H.V. Kamath moved an amendment on 2 August 1949 to replace "internal disturbance" with "internal disturbance amounting to a grave emergency" in Article 352, arguing the original phrase was a "blank cheque." Ambedkar rejected it, stating the President's satisfaction was subject to judicial review — a position the Supreme Court later qualified in Minerva Mills (1980) and S.R. Bommai (1994). The phrase "internal disturbance" was replaced by "armed rebellion" by the 44th Amendment (1978), directly responding to the 1975 Emergency experience.

Article 356 (President's Rule) drew sharper criticism. Prof. K.T. Shah warned it would "reduce the States to mere municipalities." Ambedkar defended it as a "dead letter" provision, hoping it would never be invoked. The Assembly rejected Biswanath Das's amendment requiring State Legislative Assembly ratification before proclamation. The 44th Amendment later added the requirement of parliamentary approval within two months and limited extension beyond one year to situations where a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation or the Election Commission certifies election impossibility — a direct legislative correction of the Assembly's optimism.

Article 360 (Financial Emergency) was inserted late, on 16 October 1949, at the instance of the Drafting Committee after consultations with financial experts who feared post-Partition fiscal collapse. No state has ever invoked it. The debates show the Assembly consciously chose a centralised emergency architecture over the Canadian model (where federal emergency power is minimal) or the Australian model (where the federal government has no power to dismiss state governments). This choice remains the structural basis for Centre-State friction.

The Steering Committee and the Architecture of Constituent Assembly Decision-Making

While the Drafting Committee (chaired by Ambedkar) and the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights (chaired by Sardar Patel) receive scholarly attention, the Steering Committee — chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad as President of the Assembly — was the operational brain that managed the Assembly's workflow, prioritised committee reports, and resolved procedural deadlocks. Its 12 members included Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Patel, Maulana Azad, and B.G. Kher, making it a de facto political executive within the Assembly.

The Steering Committee met 23 times between December 1946 and November 1949. Its critical interventions included: (1) deciding the sequence of committee reports — placing the Union Powers Committee and Union Constitution Committee reports before the Provincial Constitution Committee to establish the Centre's framework first; (2) resolving the deadlock on the language issue by referring the Hindustani vs. Hindi vs. English debate to a sub-committee (the Moturi Satyanarayana Committee), which produced the compromise of Article 343-351; (3) managing the integration of princely state representatives after the Mountbatten Plan (June 1947), which expanded the Assembly from 296 to 389 members and required rebalancing committee compositions.

The Committee also adjudicated disputes between committees. When the Advisory Committee on Minorities (Sub-Committee on Fundamental Rights) and the Union Powers Committee disagreed on the justiciability of Directive Principles, the Steering Committee referred the matter to a joint sitting, resulting in the non-justiciable but "fundamental in governance" formulation of Article 37. Its minutes, preserved in the Constituent Assembly Debates (Vol. XII, Appendix), reveal a pragmatic consensus-building model: decisions were rarely voted; instead, the Chairman "sensed the House" — a convention later mirrored in the Speaker's role under Article 118.

The Steering Committee's dissolution upon the Constitution's adoption (26 November 1949) was deliberate — it was a constituent body, not a permanent institution. Its legacy persists in the Rules of Procedure of both Houses of Parliament, which borrow heavily from the Assembly's procedural rules framed under its supervision.

Examiner's Trap: Conflating Committees
A question asks: "Which committee resolved the deadlock between the Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee and the Union Powers Committee on the justiciability of Directive Principles?" The options list the Drafting Committee, the Advisory Committee, the Steering Committee, and the Rules of Procedure Committee.
Correct answer: Steering Committee. The Drafting Committee (Ambedkar) drafted the text; the Advisory Committee (Patel) oversaw Fundamental Rights and Minorities; the Rules of Procedure Committee (Rajendra Prasad) framed procedural rules. The Steering Committee (also chaired by Prasad but with a distinct mandate) managed inter-committee coordination and workflow. It referred the justiciability dispute to a joint sitting of the concerned committees. Memorising committee chairs is insufficient; one must know their specific jurisdictional mandates and inter-committee dynamics.
Exam-Day Strategy: Committee Mapping
Create a one-page matrix: Committee Name | Chair | Mandate | Key Output | Interaction with Other Committees. For example: Union Powers Committee (Nehru) → distribution of legislative powers → fed into Drafting Committee; Advisory Committee on Minorities (Patel) → Articles 25-30 → overlapped with Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee (K.M. Munshi). Questions in GS II and Essay often test whether you can trace a constitutional provision to its committee of origin and identify the negotiation that shaped its final text. The Steering Committee is the "meta-committee" — if a question asks about procedural resolution, sequencing, or deadlock-breaking, the answer is almost always the Steering Committee.

Article 368: The Procedural Architecture of Constitutional Amendment and Its Judicial Construction

Article 368, as originally enacted, provided a single procedure: passage by a majority of the total membership of each House and by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, followed by Presidential assent. For amendments affecting federal provisions (Article 368 proviso), ratification by half the State Legislatures was required. The 24th Amendment (1971) — enacted to overturn Golaknath (1967) — made two critical changes: it added the marginal note "Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and procedure therefor" (clarifying that Article 368 confers power, not merely procedure), and it made Presidential assent obligatory (removing the pocket veto possibility).

The 42nd Amendment (1976) attempted to insulate amendments from judicial review by inserting clauses (4) and (5) into Article 368: "No amendment... shall be called in question in any court on any ground" and "there shall be no limitation whatever on the constituent power of Parliament." The Supreme Court in Minerva Mills (1980) struck down both clauses as violating the basic structure, holding that judicial review of constitutional amendments is itself a basic feature. The Court also clarified that the "procedure" in Article 368 is mandatory, not directory — a defect in procedure (e.g., failure to secure state ratification where required) renders the amendment void, not merely irregular.

Three procedural nuances remain litigated: (1) Whether a Bill under Article 368 can be introduced in either House — yes, per Kihoto Hollohan (1992), though the Rajya Sabha's role is co-equal; (2) Whether the President can withhold assent — the 24th Amendment made assent obligatory, but the President may return a non-Article 368 Bill; (3) Whether state ratification resolutions can be rescinded — the Supreme Court in Kihoto Hollohan held that once a State Legislature ratifies, it cannot withdraw ratification before Presidential assent, as the constitutional moment crystallises upon the resolution's passage.

The "basic structure" limitation operates as an unwritten procedural constraint: an amendment that destroys a basic feature is not an "amendment" within Article 368's meaning but a "repeal" requiring a new constituent assembly — a theoretical construct articulated in Kesavananda (1973) and refined in Waman Rao (1981). This makes Article 368 a "constrained constituent power" — unique among written constitutions.

The Preamble as a Hermeneutic Device: Judicial Methodologies in Constitutional Interpretation

Beyond its status as part of the Constitution (Kesavananda, 1973) and its amendability (Kesavananda majority), the Preamble functions as an interpretive tool through three distinct judicial methodologies. First, the purposive construction method: the Preamble's objectives (Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity) are used to resolve ambiguity in substantive provisions. In S.R. Bommai (1994), the Court read "secularism" (inserted 1976) into Article 14 and 15 to strike down arbitrary state action, holding that the Preamble illuminates the "constitutional scheme." Second, the structural interpretation method: the Preamble's declaration of "Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic" defines the Constitution's basic structure. In Minerva Mills (1980), Chandrachud CJI held that the Preamble's "Socialist" and "Democratic" objectives limit Parliament's amendment power under Article 368 — an amendment converting India into a theocratic state would violate the Preamble's "Secular" and "Democratic" commitments.

Third, the teleological limitation method: the Preamble constrains delegated legislation and executive action. In Excel Wear v. Union of India (1979), the Court used the Preamble's "Socialist" objective to uphold industrial licensing restrictions, reasoning that economic regulation must align with the constitutional goal. Conversely, in D.S. Nakara (1983), the Court read "social justice" from the Preamble into Article 14 to strike down a discriminatory pension scheme. The 42nd Amendment's insertion of "Socialist", "Secular", and "Integrity" expanded this hermeneutic arsenal. However, the Court in Kesavananda cautioned that the Preamble cannot override express constitutional text — it is a "key to open the mind of the makers" (per Sikri CJI), not a source of independent rights.

A fourth, emerging methodology is comparative preamble analysis: Indian courts increasingly reference the preambles of the South African Constitution (1996) and the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights (2000) to interpret "fraternity" and "dignity" — concepts undertheorised in the Indian Preamble. This cross-constitutional dialogue was evident in Navtej Singh Johar (2018), where the Preamble's "fraternity" was read with the South African Constitution's "ubuntu" to decriminalise homosexuality under Section 377 IPC.

Constituent Assembly Deliberations on the Seventh Schedule: Crafting the Union, State, and Concurrent Lists

The Seventh Schedule — the constitutional architecture of legislative distribution — emerged from the Union Powers Committee (Nehru, Chair) and the Provincial Constitution Committee (Patel, Chair), with the Drafting Committee harmonising their reports. The Government of India Act 1935 (Seventh Schedule, Federal, Provincial, and Concurrent Legislative Lists) was the primary template, but the Assembly made three strategic departures. First, it expanded the Union List from 59 to 97 entries (original) — adding defence of India, atomic energy, inter-state trade, and elections — reflecting the Partition experience where weak central coordination had disastrous consequences. Second, it created a robust Concurrent List (36 entries, later 47) — absent in the 1935 Act's federal scheme — covering criminal law, marriage, contracts, and economic planning, enabling uniform national legislation while preserving state legislative space.

The most contentious entry was "Industries" (Entry 7, Union List; Entry 24, State List; Entry 52, Concurrent List). The Union Powers Committee initially placed all industries in the Union List. The Provincial Constitution Committee objected, arguing it would stifle provincial industrialisation. The compromise: Union List covers industries declared by Parliament "expedient in the public interest" (Entry 7); State List covers industries not so declared (Entry 24); Concurrent List covers regulation of industrial disputes (Entry 52). This tripartite split generated decades of litigation — State of Rajasthan v. G. Chawla (1959), Synthetics & Chemicals v. State of U.P. (1990) — until the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act 1951 and later liberalisation (1991) reduced its practical significance.

Residuary powers (Article 248, Entry 97 Union List) were deliberately vested in the Centre — a reversal of the US and Australian models — because the Assembly feared secessionist legislation by states. The Drafting Committee rejected K.T. Shah's amendment to place residuary powers with states. The "pith and substance" doctrine (evolved from Canadian jurisprudence via the 1935 Act) was adopted implicitly; the Assembly debates show members assumed courts would look at the "true nature and character" of legislation, not its incidental encroachment — a principle the Supreme Court formalised in Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v. Bank of Commerce (1947, Privy Council) and State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951).

The Concurrent List's supremacy clause (Article 254) — Central law prevails over State law on repugnancy, unless the State law was reserved for Presidential assent and received it — was a direct borrowing from Section 107 of the 1935 Act. The Assembly debated whether Presidential assent should be automatic or discretionary; the Drafting Committee chose discretionary, giving the Centre a pocket veto over state concurrent legislation — a power used extensively in the 1970s-80s.

  • Trap: Assuming the Seventh Schedule was a clean break from the 1935 Act — 70% of entries are verbatim or near-verbatim reproductions; the innovation lies in the expanded Union List and the creation of the Concurrent List.
  • Trap: Confusing the Union Powers Committee (Nehru, legislative distribution) with the Union Constitution Committee (Nehru, executive structure) — they produced separate reports adopted on different dates (April and July 1947).
  • Trap: Stating that the Concurrent List gives equal power to Centre and States — Article 254 establishes Central paramountcy; State law survives only via the Presidential assent exception.
  • Trap: Believing the Preamble's "Socialist" (1976) mandates state ownership — Excel Wear (1979) and Balco Employees' Union (2002) held it mandates social justice, not a specific economic model.
  • Trap: Treating Article 368's state ratification requirement as applying to all federal provisions — it applies only to provisions listed in the proviso (Articles 54, 55, 73, 162, 241, Chapter IV of Part V, Chapter V of Part VI, Chapter I of Part XI, Seventh Schedule, Article 368 itself).
  • Trap: Citing Berubari (1960) for the proposition that the Preamble is not part of the Constitution — Kesavananda (1973) overruled this; the Preamble is part of the Constitution and a basic structure anchor.
  • Trap: Assuming the Steering Committee and the Rules of Procedure Committee are the same because both were chaired by Rajendra Prasad — they had distinct mandates: workflow management vs. procedural rule-making.

The constitutional framework's resilience lies in its capacity to absorb historical contingencies — Partition, princely integration, linguistic diversity — through textual compromises that remain judicially enforceable.

The Doctrine of Eclipse and Its Application to Pre‑Constitutional Laws

The doctrine of eclipse addresses the fate of laws enacted before the commencement of the Constitution that conflict with the fundamental rights guaranteed in Part III. Article 13(1) declares that all laws in force immediately before the Constitution shall be void to the extent of inconsistency with fundamental rights. The Supreme Court, however, held in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955) that such laws are not dead but merely eclipsed; they remain dormant and can be revived if the constitutional impediment is removed by a subsequent amendment. The rationale is that the pre‑constitutional legislature never intended to violate rights that did not exist at the time of enactment, and the Constitution does not retrospectively annul the legislative act but only suspends its operation.

The eclipse operates only while the fundamental right remains in force. When Parliament amends the Constitution to abrogate or modify the right, the eclipse lifts and the original law becomes fully operative again. This was illustrated in State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974), where a pre‑Constitution law regulating cotton textiles, rendered inoperative by Article 19(1)(g), revived after the 1st Amendment inserted Article 19(6) permitting reasonable restrictions. The doctrine does not apply to post‑constitutional laws; a law enacted after 26 January 1950 that contravenes a fundamental right is void ab initio under Article 13(2) and cannot be resurrected by later amendment. The distinction is crucial for exam questions that mix pre‑ and post‑constitutional statutes.

Judicial application requires a two‑step test: first, identify whether the impugned law is pre‑constitutional; second, ascertain whether the inconsistency is with a fundamental right that is still extant. If both conditions are satisfied, the law is eclipsed, not void. The Court may also “read down” the law to avoid eclipse, but that is a separate interpretative tool. The doctrine underscores the Constitution’s transformative character — it does not erase the legal past but subjects it to the new rights regime.

The Doctrine of Severability: Judicial Technique for Saving Partially Unconstitutional Statutes

Severability, rooted in Article 13(2), permits a court to excise the unconstitutional portion of a statute while preserving the remainder, provided the valid part is capable of independent operation and the legislature would have enacted it alone. The Supreme Court formulated the classic test in R.M.D.C. (Mysore) Ltd. v. Union of India (1957): (i) the unconstitutional provision must be separable from the rest of the Act; (ii) the remaining provisions must be complete in themselves; and (iii) the legislative intent must be to enact the valid part even without the invalid part. If the invalid provision is so intertwined that the Act cannot stand without it, the whole statute falls.

In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), the Court upheld the Bombay Prohibition Act after severing the provision that prohibited possession of liquor for medicinal purposes, because the remaining regulatory framework was self‑sufficient. Conversely, in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the anti‑defection provisions of the Tenth Schedule were held inseparable from the Speaker’s finality clause; striking down the latter would have rendered the former unworkable, so the entire Schedule was upheld. The doctrine also interacts with the “reading down” technique: where a provision is ambiguous, the Court may adopt a narrower construction that saves it, but if the provision is clear and unconstitutional, severability is the only rescue.

A practical trap is assuming that any unconstitutional clause can be severed. The Court examines the legislative scheme — whether the Act contains a severability clause (express or implied), the degree of interdependence, and the possibility of the remainder functioning independently. The presence of a severability clause (e.g., “If any provision is held invalid, the rest shall remain in force”) creates a strong presumption in favour of severance, but it is not conclusive. The doctrine thus balances constitutional supremacy with legislative economy, ensuring that a single flaw does not invalidate an entire statutory edifice.

Identifying the Correct Doctrine in a Mixed Fact Pattern
A 1948 provincial law regulated the sale of opium. After the Constitution, Article 19(1)(g) guaranteed the right to trade. The law was challenged in 1952. In 1955, Parliament amended Article 19 to add clause (6) permitting reasonable restrictions on trade in narcotics. The petitioner argues the 1948 law is void. Which doctrine governs, and what is the outcome?
The 1948 law is pre‑constitutional; its inconsistency with Article 19(1)(g) attracted the doctrine of eclipse, not voidness. The law was merely eclipsed from 1950 until the 1955 amendment inserted Article 19(6), which removed the constitutional impediment. Consequently, the eclipse lifted and the 1948 law revived in full force. The petitioner’s claim that the law is void fails because eclipse, not severability or void ab initio, applies to pre‑constitutional statutes.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mentions a law enacted before 26 January 1950 and a fundamental right, first check whether the right still exists. If the right has been amended or repealed, the eclipse lifts — answer “revived”. If the law is post‑constitutional, apply Article 13(2) and consider severability. Memorise the two‑step eclipse test and the three‑prong severability test; they are favourite examiner shortcuts.

Substantive Due Process in India: From A.K. Gopalan to Maneka Gandhi and Beyond

The phrase “procedure established by law” in Article 21 was initially interpreted narrowly in A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950). The Court held that any law enacted by a competent legislature, irrespective of its fairness, satisfied Article 21, and that the protection against arbitrary executive action lay in Article 19, not Article 21. This formalistic reading rendered Article 21 a mere procedural guarantee, leaving substantive fairness to the legislature.

The turning point came in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978). The Supreme Court, per Justice Bhagwati, read “procedure established by law” as requiring a procedure that is “fair, just and reasonable”, effectively importing the American due‑process standard. The Court linked Articles 14, 19 and 21, holding that a law depriving personal liberty must satisfy the test of reasonableness under Article 14 and not be arbitrary. This “golden triangle” jurisprudence transformed Article 21 into a reservoir of substantive rights — privacy, dignity, livelihood, health, and environment.

Subsequent cases expanded the doctrine: Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi (1981) recognised the right to live with human dignity; Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) held that the right to livelihood is part of the right to life; Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) derived guidelines against sexual harassment from Article 21 read with international conventions. The Court also applied substantive due process to preventive detention (Kharak Singh v. State of U.P. 1963, later refined in People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India 1997) and to the death penalty (Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab 1980, requiring “rarest of rare” standard). The evolution demonstrates a shift from textual literalism to a living‑tree interpretation, making Article 21 the primary vehicle for judicial innovation in socio‑economic rights.

The Constitutional Dimensions of President’s Rule under Article 356: Judicial Safeguards and Political Misuse

Article 356 empowers the President to assume the functions of a state government on receipt of a report from the Governor or otherwise, if satisfied that the state cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution. Originally modelled on Section 93 of the Government of India Act 1935, it was intended as an emergency provision for constitutional breakdown. However, from the 1960s onward it became a tool for central political control, with over 100 proclamations by 1994.

The landmark S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) judgment imposed stringent judicial safeguards. The Court held that the President’s satisfaction is justiciable; the proclamation must be based on objective material, not on the Governor’s subjective report alone. The majority laid down that the floor test in the legislative assembly is the most reliable method to ascertain loss of majority, and that the President must give the state government an opportunity to prove its majority before imposing President’s Rule. The Court also declared that secularism is a basic feature, and a proclamation motivated by religious considerations is unconstitutional.

Post‑Bommai, the Supreme Court in Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006) reinforced that the Governor’s report must be based on “relevant material” and that the President’s proclamation is subject to judicial review on grounds of mala fides, irrelevance, or non‑application of mind. The 1994 guidelines of the Sarkaria Commission — requiring a warning, a reasonable time for compliance, and a floor test — have been cited as persuasive though not binding. Despite these safeguards, instances in 2016 (Uttarakhand) and 2020 (Madhya Pradesh) show continued political contestation, prompting calls for a constitutional amendment to replace Article 356 with a more structured mechanism.

The Doctrine of Public Trust and Environmental Jurisprudence under Article 21

The public trust doctrine, rooted in Roman law and revived in the United States (Illinois Central Railroad v. Illinois, 1892), was transplanted into Indian constitutional law through Article 21’s expansive reading. In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) (the Oleum gas leak case), the Supreme Court held that the state holds natural resources — air, water, forests — in trust for the public and cannot alienate them to private parties if such alienation defeats the trust. The Court linked the doctrine to Articles 48A and 51A(g), imposing a constitutional duty on the state to protect the environment.

Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) crystallised three principles: (i) the state is a trustee of natural resources; (ii) the precautionary principle and polluter‑pays principle are part of the constitutional mandate; (iii) sustainable development is a constitutional goal. The Court ordered the closure of polluting tanneries in Tamil Nadu, directing the creation of a common effluent treatment plant funded by the polluters. Subsequent cases — Indian Council for Enviro‑Legal Action v. Union of India (1996) (Bichhri village), T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India (1997) (forest conservation) — expanded the trust to include wetlands, coastal zones, and biodiversity.

The doctrine has also been used to enforce inter‑generational equity. In M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997), the Court restrained a private company from diverting the Beas river for a commercial resort, affirming that the river is a public trust resource. The judiciary’s willingness to issue continuing mandamus, appoint expert committees, and monitor compliance demonstrates the operationalisation of the trust. For aspirants, the key takeaway is that the public trust doctrine converts environmental protection from a policy aspiration into a justiciable constitutional obligation anchored in Article 21.

  • Confusing eclipse with voidness — eclipse applies only to pre‑constitutional laws; post‑constitutional laws are void ab initio.
  • Assuming severability is automatic — the three‑prong test (separability, completeness, legislative intent) must be satisfied; a severability clause is not decisive.
  • Treating “procedure established by law” as a mere formality after Maneka Gandhi — the procedure must be fair, just and reasonable, not merely enacted.
  • Believing President’s Rule is immune from judicial review — S.R. Bommai made the President’s satisfaction justiciable and mandated a floor test.
  • Thinking the public trust doctrine is only a policy guideline — it is a constitutional obligation enforceable under Article 21, 48A and 51A(g).
  • Mixing up the precautionary principle with the polluter‑pays principle — the former mandates preventive action in uncertainty; the latter imposes cost on the polluter.
  • Overlooking the distinction between reading down and severability — reading down interprets a provision narrowly to save it; severability removes an unconstitutional provision entirely.

These advanced doctrines illustrate how the Constitution’s text, judicial interpretation, and political practice interact to shape governance.

The Constitutional Position of the President: Powers, Discretion, and Judicial Review

Article 52 establishes the President as the head of the Union executive, while Article 53 vests the executive power of the Union in the President, to be exercised either directly or through officers subordinate to him in accordance with the Constitution. The President acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister (Art. 74(1)), a position crystallised in Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974) where the Supreme Court held that the President is a constitutional head who cannot act contrary to ministerial advice except in the narrow spheres where the Constitution expressly confers discretion.

Discretionary powers arise in three principal contexts. First, under Article 75(1) the President appoints the Prime Minister; when no party commands a clear majority, the President may exercise situational discretion, as seen in the 1996 and 1998 government formations. Second, Article 111 empowers the President to withhold assent to a Bill (except a Money Bill) and return it for reconsideration; the 1991 R. C. Cooper v. Union of India decision affirmed that this power is not a mere formality but a constitutional check. Third, Article 356 (President’s Rule) permits the President to assume the functions of a State government on the Governor’s report; the landmark S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) judgment subjected the President’s satisfaction to judicial review, requiring objective material and a floor test before proclamation.

The pardoning power under Article 72 is another discretionary domain. In Kehar Singh v. Union of India (1989) the Court held that the power is exercisable on the advice of the Council of Ministers, yet the President may independently examine the merits of a mercy petition. The 2015 Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India ruling reinforced that inordinate delay in deciding mercy petitions violates Article 21, making the President’s inaction justiciable.

Judicial review of presidential action is now well‑settled. The Court in Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006) declared that the President’s proclamation under Article 356 is subject to review on grounds of mala fides, irrelevance, or non‑application of mind. The 1994 Sarkaria Commission guidelines — warning, reasonable time, floor test — though not binding, are routinely cited as persuasive standards. The President’s role in ordinance making (Art. 123) also attracts scrutiny; in Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017) the Court held that repromulgation of ordinances without legislative approval constitutes a fraud on the Constitution.

In sum, the President occupies a position of constitutional sovereignty: formally the repository of all executive authority, but practically bound by ministerial advice except where the Constitution expressly reserves discretion. The evolution from a ceremonial head to a reviewable constitutional authority illustrates the dynamic interplay between text, convention, and judicial interpretation.

The Doctrine of Legislative Competence: Residuary Powers and the Union List

Article 248 read with Entry 97 of the Union List (List I, Seventh Schedule) confers exclusive residuary legislative power on Parliament: “Parliament has exclusive power to make any law with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Concurrent List or State List.” This clause operates as a safety valve, ensuring that emerging subjects — such as cyber security, outer space, and artificial intelligence — fall within Union competence unless expressly allocated to the States.

The seminal interpretation came in State of West Bengal v. Union of India (1963), where the Court upheld the Union’s power to legislate on the acquisition of property for a central public sector undertaking, holding that the subject was not covered by any State entry and therefore fell under the residuary entry. In K. K. Verma v. Union of India (1970) the Court clarified that the residuary power is not a “catch‑all” for matters that could be read into an existing entry; the pith and substance test must first be applied to determine whether a law truly relates to a State or Concurrent entry.

The 1976 42nd Amendment attempted to curtail residuary power by inserting Article 248A (later repealed) and by expanding the Concurrent List, but the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) struck down the amendment’s attempt to limit judicial review of legislative competence, reaffirming that the distribution of powers is a basic feature. Subsequent legislation — the Information Technology Act, 2000 (cyber law), the Space Activities Bill (proposed), and the DNA Technology (Use and Application) Regulation Bill, 2019 — have all been enacted under Entry 97, illustrating the practical reach of the residuary clause.

A frequent point of contention is the overlap between Entry 97 and the “ancillary powers” doctrine. In Union of India v. H. S. Dhillon (1972) the Court held that Parliament may legislate on matters incidental to an express Union entry even if the incidental matter could be characterised as a State subject, provided the primary legislation is within Union competence. This principle prevents the States from fragmenting Union legislation by claiming ancillary aspects as their own.

The residuary power also interacts with the doctrine of repugnancy (Art. 254). When a State law occupies a field not enumerated in any list, the Union law under Entry 97 prevails, as confirmed in G. K. Krishnan v. State of Tamil Nadu (1975). The Court emphasised that the Constitution’s federal scheme is “quasi‑federal” with a strong Centre, and the residuary clause is a textual manifestation of that bias.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which constitutional provision empowers Parliament to legislate on a subject not mentioned in any of the three lists?” Many candidates answer “Article 248” but forget to cite Entry 97 of the Union List, which is the actual legislative entry. The correct answer must mention both Article 248 and Entry 97.
Article 248 declares the principle of residuary power, while Entry 97 of List I (Union List) is the operative legislative entry that authorises Parliament to make laws on any matter not enumerated in List II or List III. Both must be cited for a complete answer.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the pair “Article 248 + Entry 97” as a single unit. When a question mentions “residuary power”, write the article and the entry together; this avoids the common half‑answer trap and earns full marks.

The Evolution of the Right to Education: From Directive Principle to Fundamental Right

The original Constitution placed the duty to provide free and compulsory education for children up to age fourteen in Article 45, a Directive Principle of State Policy, making it non‑justiciable. The Supreme Court in Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992) and Unni Krishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993) read Article 21 (right to life) as encompassing a right to education, but limited it to the primary level and held that the State could not be compelled to provide higher education free of cost.

The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A, declaring: “The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine.” Simultaneously, Article 45 was amended to read “The State shall endeavour to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the age of six years.” The amendment also added a new fundamental duty under Article 51A(k) for parents or guardians to provide opportunities for education to their children between six and fourteen years.

The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act) operationalised Article 21A. Key features include: (i) 25 % reservation in private unaided schools for economically weaker sections; (ii) prohibition of capitation fees and screening procedures; (iii) establishment of School Management Committees with 75 % parent representation; (iv) norms for pupil‑teacher ratios, infrastructure, and teacher qualifications.

Judicial scrutiny of the RTE Act has been extensive. In Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2012) the Supreme Court upheld the 25 % quota, ruling that it does not violate Article 19(1)(g) because the State’s obligation under Article 21A is a reasonable restriction. The Court also clarified that the Act applies to minority institutions only to the extent that they do not fall under Article 30(1) protection; later, in Pramati Educational & Cultural Trust v. Union of India (2014), the Court exempted unaided minority schools from the quota, balancing Articles 21A and 30.

Implementation challenges persist: funding gaps, teacher vacancies, and quality deficits. The 2019 amendment to the RTE Act extended the deadline for teacher qualification compliance and introduced a “no‑detention” policy up to Class VIII, later partially rolled back. The evolution from a non‑justiciable directive to a justiciable fundamental right illustrates the Constitution’s capacity for progressive realisation of socio‑economic rights through amendment, legislation, and judicial interpretation.

The Constitutional Framework for the Protection of Fundamental Duties: Article 51A and Judicial Enforcement

Fundamental Duties were introduced by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, inserting Article 51A in Part IVA. The original ten duties (clauses (a) to (j)) emphasised respect for the Constitution, the national flag, the national anthem, the sovereignty and integrity of India, the promotion of harmony, the protection of public property, the development of scientific temper, and the striving for excellence. The 86th Amendment, 2002 added clause (k), obligating parents or guardians to provide opportunities for education to children aged six to fourteen.

Unlike Fundamental Rights, Article 51A does not confer justiciable rights; the Constitution expressly states that the duties “shall not be enforceable by any court.” Nevertheless, the Supreme Court has used them as interpretive aids. In M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) (the Oleum gas leak case), the Court invoked the duty to protect the environment (Art. 51A(g)) to expand the scope of Article 21. In Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1985), the duty to preserve the natural environment guided the Court’s order to stop limestone quarrying in the Doon Valley.

The duties also inform the construction of statutes. The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, and the Flag Code of India derive legitimacy from Article 51A(a) and (b). The 2019 amendment to the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, incorporated the duty to uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India (Art. 51A(c)) as a factor in sentencing.

Judicial pronouncements have repeatedly held that while duties are not directly enforceable, they impose a moral obligation on citizens and a directive on the State to create conditions for their fulfilment. In Javed v. State of Haryana (2003), the Court observed that the duty to develop scientific temper (Art. 51A(h)) supports the State’s policy of promoting rational thinking in education. The 2020 Karnataka High Court decision in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (privacy case) referenced Article 51A(j) (striving for excellence) to underscore the State’s responsibility to foster an environment conducive to individual development.

Critics argue that the non‑justiciable nature renders the duties hortatory. However, the consistent judicial practice of reading them alongside Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles demonstrates their functional relevance in constitutional adjudication.

The Doctrine of Parliamentary Privileges and Judicial Review

Articles 105 and 194 confer on Parliament and State Legislatures, respectively, powers, privileges, and immunities necessary for their independent functioning. These include freedom of speech in the House (Art. 105(1)), immunity from court proceedings for anything said or any vote given (Art. 105(2)), and the power to punish for contempt or breach of privilege (Art. 105(3)). The privileges are not codified; they are derived from the House of Commons as they stood on 26 January 1950, subject to constitutional limitations.

The landmark Keshav Singh v. Speaker, Legislative Assembly, Uttar Pradesh (1965) established that the judiciary can examine whether a privilege claimed by the House exists under the Constitution, but cannot review the merits of the House’s decision to punish a member for contempt. The Court held that the power to commit for contempt is a “privilege” within Article 194(3) and is subject to judicial review only on the ground of absence of jurisdiction or mala fides.

In Raja Ram Pal v. Hon’ble Speaker, Lok Sabha (2007), the Supreme Court expanded judicial oversight, ruling that the expulsion of a member for “unethical conduct” must satisfy the test of “breach of privilege” as defined by the House’s own rules and cannot be arbitrary. The Court emphasised that parliamentary privileges are not absolute; they must harmonise with fundamental rights, particularly Article 21 (personal liberty) and Article 14 (equality).

The 2015 State of Karnataka v. Union of India (the “cash‑for‑vote” case) saw the Court intervene when a legislative assembly attempted to punish a journalist for publishing a report on alleged bribery of legislators. The Court held that the freedom of the press under Article 19(1)(a) prevails over the House’s claim of privilege when the publication concerns a matter of public interest and does not obstruct legislative proceedings.

Recent controversies — such as the 2021 suspension of opposition members for “disorderly conduct” and the 2023 privilege motion against a minister for alleged misleading statements — illustrate the tension between legislative autonomy and constitutional accountability. The evolving jurisprudence confirms that while Parliament enjoys wide privileges to protect its dignity and independence, these privileges are subject to the Constitution’s supremacy and the judiciary’s role as the final arbiter of constitutional limits.

  • Confusing the President’s discretionary powers with the Governor’s — the President’s discretion is narrower and expressly enumerated (Art. 74, 111, 356), whereas the Governor enjoys broader situational discretion under Article 163.
  • Treating residuary power as a blanket authority — Entry 97 applies only after the pith and substance test shows the subject is not covered by any State or Concurrent entry.
  • Assuming Article 21A makes education a fully enforceable right at all levels — the fundamental right is limited to ages six to fourteen; higher education remains a Directive Principle.
  • Believing Fundamental Duties are directly justiciable — they are not enforceable by courts but serve as interpretive tools for Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.
  • Thinking parliamentary privilege shields members from all legal proceedings — immunity covers speech and votes in the House (Art. 105(2)), not criminal acts committed outside legislative functions.
  • Overlooking the requirement that a privilege motion must be based on a breach of a recognised privilege, not merely on political disagreement — the House cannot create new privileges beyond those existing in 1950 without constitutional amendment.
  • Neglecting the interplay between Article 51A(k) and Article 21A — the parental duty to educate reinforces the State’s obligation but does not shift the primary responsibility from the State to parents.

The Constitutional Position of the President: Election, Powers, and Impeachment

Article 52 establishes the President as the head of the Union executive. The President is elected by an electoral college consisting of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States (including the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the Union Territory of Puducherry) under Article 54. The value of each vote is determined by the formula in Article 55, which weights the votes of Members of Legislative Assemblies according to the population of the State as per the 1971 Census, and the votes of Members of Parliament to maintain parity between the Union and the States. The President holds office for a term of five years from the date on which he enters upon his office (Article 56) and is eligible for re‑election.

The executive power of the Union is vested in the President and is exercised either directly or through officers subordinate to him in accordance with the Constitution (Article 53). In practice, the President acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister (Article 74(1)). However, the President may require the Council of Ministers to reconsider its advice, and the President shall act in accordance with the advice tendered after such reconsideration (Article 74(1) proviso). This limited discretion has been judicially recognised in R. C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970), where the Supreme Court held that the President’s satisfaction under Article 352 (national emergency) is not immune from judicial review.

Legislative powers include summoning and proroguing either House of Parliament, dissolving the Lok Sabha (Article 85), addressing both Houses (Article 86), and sending messages to Parliament (Article 86). The President’s assent is required for a Bill to become law (Article 111). The President may give assent, withhold assent, or return a Bill (other than a Money Bill) for reconsideration. If the Bill is passed again by both Houses with or without amendments, the President must give assent. The President also promulgates Ordinances under Article 123 when Parliament is not in session, subject to parliamentary approval within six weeks of reassembly.

Financial powers: the President causes the Annual Financial Statement (Budget) to be laid before Parliament (Article 112), and no Money Bill can be introduced except on the President’s recommendation (Article 110). Judicial powers include the pardoning power under Article 72, which extends to offences against Union law, sentences by court‑martial, and death sentences. In Kehar Singh v. Union of India (1989), the Court held that the exercise of this power is subject to judicial review on grounds of mala fides or arbitrariness.

Emergency powers are conferred by Articles 352 (national emergency), 356 (President’s Rule in States), and 360 (financial emergency). The proclamation under Article 356 must be approved by both Houses within two months and can be extended for a maximum of three years with parliamentary approval every six months, subject to the conditions laid down in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994).

Impeachment of the President is provided under Article 61. A charge may be preferred by either House of Parliament by a resolution signed by not less than one‑fourth of the total membership of that House and passed by a majority of not less than two‑thirds of the total membership. The other House investigates the charge, and if it also passes a resolution by a two‑thirds majority, the President stands removed from office. This procedure has never been invoked.

The Constitutional Position of the Vice‑President: Election, Functions, and Removal

Article 63 provides for a Vice‑President of India. The Vice‑President is elected by an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament (elected and nominated) in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote (Article 66). The Vice‑President holds office for a term of five years from the date on which he enters upon his office (Article 67) and is eligible for re‑election.

The Vice‑President serves as the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 64) and presides over its proceedings. In this capacity, the Vice‑President has a casting vote in the event of a tie but does not vote in the first instance. The Vice‑President also acts as President when a vacancy occurs in the office of the President by reason of death, resignation, removal, or otherwise, until a new President is elected (Article 65). During such period, the Vice‑President discharges the functions of the President but does not assume the office of President.

Removal of the Vice‑President is governed by Article 67(b). A resolution for removal must be passed by a majority of the total membership of the Rajya Sabha and agreed to by the Lok Sabha. Unlike the President, there is no impeachment procedure; the Vice‑President can be removed by a simple majority of the total membership of the Rajya Sabha (not a two‑thirds majority) followed by concurrence of the Lok Sabha. This distinction is frequently tested.

The Vice‑President’s role in the legislative process is limited to the Rajya Sabha. The Vice‑President does not participate in the election of the President (Article 54) and has no veto power over legislation. The Supreme Court in K. K. Venugopal v. Union of India (1995) clarified that the Vice‑President’s casting vote is a procedural power and does not extend to substantive legislative decisions.

Identifying the Removal Procedure
Which constitutional article provides for the removal of the Vice‑President, and what majority is required in the Rajya Sabha?
Article 67(b) provides for the removal of the Vice‑President. A resolution for removal must be passed by a majority of the total membership of the Rajya Sabha (i.e., more than 50 % of the total members, not merely those present and voting) and then agreed to by the Lok Sabha. This is distinct from the President’s impeachment under Article 61, which requires a two‑thirds majority of the total membership of each House.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the dual role of the Vice‑President: Chairman of Rajya Sabha (Article 64) and acting President (Article 65). The removal procedure (Article 67(b)) is a simple majority of the total Rajya Sabha membership plus Lok Sabha concurrence — no two‑thirds requirement. Contrast this with the President’s impeachment (Article 61) which needs two‑thirds in both Houses. A quick mental table of “President vs Vice‑President” for election, term, removal, and functions saves time in both prelims and mains.

The Constitutional Scheme of the Council of Ministers and the Principle of Collective Responsibility

Article 74(1) mandates that there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President. The President acts in accordance with such advice, but may require the Council to reconsider its advice; the President shall then act in accordance with the advice tendered after reconsideration. Article 75(1) provides that the Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President and the other Ministers shall be appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister. Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President (Article 75(2)), which in practice means they remain in office so long as they enjoy the confidence of the Lok Sabha.

The cornerstone of parliamentary accountability is collective responsibility, enshrined in Article 75(3): “The Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the House of the People.” This means that a vote of no‑confidence against any Minister is deemed a vote against the entire Council, necessitating the resignation of the whole Ministry. The Supreme Court in U. N. R. Rao v. Indira Gandhi (1971) affirmed that collective responsibility is a constitutional convention enforceable by the judiciary only to the extent of ensuring that the Ministry does not continue in office after losing the confidence of the Lok Sabha.

Individual responsibility coexists with collective responsibility. While the Council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, each Minister is individually responsible for the acts of his or her department. The President’s pleasure doctrine (Article 75(2)) allows the Prime Minister to advise the President to dismiss a Minister, a power exercised on the Prime Minister’s advice. The Court in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) linked the floor test to collective responsibility, holding that the Governor (and by analogy the President) must ascertain the majority on the floor of the House rather than rely on subjective assessment.

Article 77 governs the conduct of business of the Government of India, requiring that all executive actions be expressed to be taken in the name of the President. Article 78 imposes a duty on the Prime Minister to communicate to the President all decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to the administration of the affairs of the Union and proposals for legislation. The principle of collective responsibility also underpins the anti‑defection law (Tenth Schedule), as a Minister who defects loses the confidence of the House and thereby triggers collective responsibility.

The Constitutional Framework for the Creation and Regulation of All India Services Under Article 312

Article 312 empowers Parliament to create one or more All India Services common to the Union and the States, including the Indian Administrative Service, the Indian Police Service, and the Indian Forest Service, provided the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by not less than two‑thirds of the members present and voting declaring that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest. This resolution is a prerequisite; without it, Parliament cannot legislate on All India Services.

The All India Services Act, 1951, enacted under Article 312(2), regulates the recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed to the All India Services. Recruitment is conducted by the Union Public Service Commission through the Civil Services Examination. Successful candidates are allocated to State cadres under the Cadre Allocation Policy, which aims to balance national integration with administrative efficiency. The control over All India Services is dual: the Union government exercises disciplinary control and policy direction, while the State governments exercise day‑to‑day administrative control.

Judicial interpretation has clarified the scope of Article 312. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2005), the Supreme Court held that cadre allocation is a matter of executive policy subject to judicial review only for arbitrariness. In Union of India v. R. K. Jain (1993), the Court ruled that the Union’s disciplinary authority over All India Services officers is not absolute and must conform to the principles of natural justice. The landmark T. S. R. Subramanian v. Union of India (2013) judgment directed the establishment of a Civil Services Board to insulate transfers and postings from political interference, reinforcing the constitutional mandate of an independent and impartial civil service.

Article 312(3) provides that the All India Services shall not be deemed to be services of the Union or of any State for the purposes of Article 310 (tenure of office) and Article 311 (dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank). This unique constitutional status ensures that All India Services officers enjoy safeguards under Article 311 while serving both the Union and the States.

The Constitutional Provisions for the Legislative Process: Ordinary Bills, Money Bills, and Constitutional Amendment Bills

The legislative process is detailed in Articles 107 to 111 for ordinary Bills. A Bill may originate in either House (except Money Bills). After passage by both Houses, it is presented to the President for assent under Article 111. The President may give assent, withhold assent, or return the Bill (if not a Money Bill) for reconsideration. If the Bill is passed again by both Houses with or without amendments, the President must give assent. This pocket veto power is limited; the President cannot withhold assent indefinitely.

Money Bills are defined in Article 110 and can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha on the recommendation of the President. The Rajya Sabha may only make recommendations within fourteen days; the Lok Sabha may accept or reject them. The President’s assent to a Money Bill is mandatory; the President cannot return a Money Bill for reconsideration. The classification of a Bill as a Money Bill is certified by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, whose decision is final under Article 110(3). The Supreme Court in State of Kerala v. Union of India (2022) (the Aadhaar case) examined the scope of this certification and held that judicial review is available if the certification is mala fide or violates constitutional provisions.

Financial Bills are of two kinds under Article 117: those that contain provisions attracting Article 110 (Money Bill provisions) and those that involve expenditure from the Consolidated Fund but are not Money Bills. The former follow the Money Bill procedure; the latter follow the ordinary Bill procedure but require the President’s recommendation for introduction.

Constitutional Amendment Bills are governed by Article 368. An amendment may be initiated in either House and must be passed by a majority of the total membership of each House and by a majority of not less than two‑thirds of the members present and voting. Amendments affecting the federal structure (e.g., Articles 54, 55, 73, 162, 241, Chapter IV of Part V, Chapter V of Part VI, or any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule) also require ratification by the Legislatures of not less than one‑half of the States. The President’s assent is obligatory; there is no provision for withholding or returning a Constitutional Amendment Bill. The basic structure doctrine, evolved in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) and refined in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), imposes an unwritten limitation on the amending power, rendering amendments that destroy the basic structure void.

  • Confusing the President’s impeachment (Article 61, two‑thirds majority in both Houses) with the Vice‑President’s removal (Article 67(b), simple majority of total Rajya Sabha membership plus Lok Sabha concurrence).
  • Assuming the President can veto a Constitutional Amendment Bill; Article 368 makes assent mandatory with no veto power.
  • Believing Money Bills can be introduced in the Rajya Sabha; Article 110 restricts introduction to the Lok Sabha only.
  • Thinking All India Services can be created by executive order without a Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 312.
  • Overlooking that collective responsibility under Article 75(3) applies only to the Lok Sabha, not the Rajya Sabha.
  • Misapplying the President’s discretionary powers by assuming the President can act without the Council of Ministers in all matters; Article 74(1) limits discretion to sending advice back for reconsideration.
  • Confusing the Vice‑President’s term and election with the President’s; both serve five‑year terms but the Vice‑President is elected by Parliament only, while the President’s electoral college includes State Legislatures.

The Doctrine of Eclipse and Its Application to Pre‑Constitutional Laws

The doctrine of eclipse occupies a unique place in Indian constitutional jurisprudence because it reconciles the continuity of pre‑Constitutional statutes with the supremacy of fundamental rights. Article 13(1) declares that all laws in force immediately before the commencement of the Constitution shall be void to the extent of their inconsistency with Part III. The Supreme Court in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955) held that such a law is not dead but merely eclipsed; the inconsistency renders it unenforceable only so long as the fundamental right remains in force. If the fundamental right is later amended or removed, the eclipse lifts and the original law revives automatically without fresh legislation.

The eclipse doctrine applies exclusively to laws that conflict with fundamental rights. It does not extend to statutes that violate other constitutional provisions such as the distribution of legislative powers or the directive principles. In State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974) the Court clarified that a pre‑Constitutional law inconsistent with Article 19(1)(g) was eclipsed, but the same law could be validated by a subsequent constitutional amendment that altered the scope of the right. The Court also emphasised that the doctrine does not operate prospectively; a law enacted after 26 January 1950 that contravenes a fundamental right is void ab initio under Article 13(2) and cannot claim eclipse.

Two practical consequences follow. First, the legislature may remove the eclipse by amending the fundamental right (as done by the First Amendment inserting Article 31A and 31B) or by enacting a new law that expressly repeals the inconsistent provision. Second, courts must examine the legislative intent: if the pre‑Constitutional statute contains a severable valid portion, that portion continues to operate while the inconsistent part remains eclipsed.
