This interplay with the doctrine of severability (discussed later) ensures that the statute is not rendered wholly inoperative unless the invalid part is so integral that the remainder cannot stand alone.

Examiners often test the distinction between eclipse and the doctrine of severability. Eclipse concerns the temporary dormancy of an entire law due to a fundamental‑right conflict, whereas severability deals with excising only the offending portion of a law—whether pre‑ or post‑Constitutional—so that the rest survives. A typical trap is to state that eclipse applies to post‑Constitutional laws; the correct answer is that Article 13(2) renders such laws void from inception, leaving no room for eclipse.

The President’s Rule under Article 356: Judicial Safeguards and the S.R. Bommai Test

Article 356 empowers the President to assume the functions of a State government when satisfied that a situation has arisen in which the government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution. The proclamation must be laid before each House of Parliament and ceases to operate unless approved by both Houses within two months; if approved, it may continue for six months and can be extended up to a maximum of three years with periodic parliamentary approval (the 44th Amendment inserted the requirement of parliamentary approval every six months after the first year).

The landmark S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) judgment laid down stringent judicial safeguards. The nine‑judge bench held that the President’s satisfaction is not immune from judicial review; the Court may examine the material on which the Governor’s report and the President’s decision were based. The judgment established several principles: (i) the proclamation must be based on objective material, not on the subjective whim of the central executive; (ii) the State Legislative Assembly should not be dissolved until the proclamation is approved by Parliament; (iii) a floor test in the Assembly is the most reliable method to ascertain the loss of majority; (iv) secularism and federalism are basic features, and any proclamation that undermines them is liable to be struck down; (v) the Court can restore the dismissed government if the proclamation is found mala fide.

Subsequent cases refined the Bommai framework. In Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006) the Court held that the Governor’s report must contain concrete facts, not mere political assessments, and that the President’s proclamation cannot be based on the Governor’s “subjective satisfaction” alone. Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016) extended the floor‑test requirement to situations where the Chief Minister advises dissolution of the Assembly, reinforcing that the Assembly’s democratic mandate cannot be circumvented by executive action. The Court also clarified that Article 356 cannot be used to settle intra‑party disputes or to install a preferred political formation.

Despite these safeguards, the provision remains controversial. The Sarkaria Commission (1988) and the Punchhi Commission (2010) recommended that Article 356 be used sparingly, only as a last resort, and that an independent body be constituted to advise the President. The 44th Amendment’s insertion of the six‑month parliamentary review was intended to curb misuse, but political practice shows frequent resort to President’s Rule in States governed by opposition parties. Aspirants should be able to cite the exact constitutional text, the Bommai guidelines, and the subsequent judicial gloss when answering questions on the limits of executive emergency power.

Applied Scenario
A State Governor sends a report to the President claiming that the Chief Minister has lost majority support because 15 legislators of the ruling party have resigned. The President issues a proclamation under Article 356 without convening the Assembly for a floor test. The proclamation is challenged in the Supreme Court. Decide the validity of the proclamation with reference to the S.R. Bommai principles.
The proclamation is likely invalid. S.R. Bommai mandates that the Assembly not be dissolved before parliamentary approval and that a floor test is the most reliable method to test majority. The Governor’s report based solely on resignations, without a floor test, does not constitute objective material. The Court can strike down the proclamation and order restoration of the State government.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “judicial safeguards” under Article 356, list the Bommai guidelines in bullet form: (1) judicial review of President’s satisfaction, (2) no dissolution before parliamentary approval, (3) floor test as primary test, (4) secularism and federalism as basic features, (5) restoration of government if proclamation mala fide. Cite the case name and year; a single‑line reference to Rameshwar Prasad and Nabam Rebia adds depth.

The Doctrine of Severability and Its Interaction with Article 13

The doctrine of severability enables courts to preserve the constitutional validity of a statute by excising only the offending provision, provided the remainder can stand independently. Article 13(2) declares that any law made after the commencement of the Constitution which contravenes fundamental rights shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void. The Supreme Court in R.M.D.C. (Mysore) v. Union of India (1957) formulated the test: the invalid part must be so inextricably mixed with the valid part that the legislature would not have enacted the valid part alone. If the valid portion is capable of operating independently and the legislative intent indicates severability, the Court will uphold it.

Severability differs from eclipse in two crucial respects. First, severability applies to both pre‑ and post‑Constitutional laws, whereas eclipse is confined to pre‑Constitutional statutes. Second, severability results in the permanent removal of the unconstitutional fragment, while eclipse merely renders the whole law dormant until the fundamental right is altered. In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951) the Court severed the provisions of the Bombay Prohibition Act that violated Article 19(1)(g) but upheld the remaining regulatory framework. The Court also held that the presence of a severability clause in the statute is not decisive; the judicial test focuses on legislative intent discerned from the scheme and object of the Act.

The doctrine also interacts with the principle of reading down. Where a provision is capable of two interpretations, one constitutional and the other not, the Court prefers the constitutional interpretation, effectively “reading down” the provision to save it. This technique was employed in Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1962) regarding the Police Regulations, where the Court read down the surveillance provisions to conform to Article 21. However, reading down cannot be used to rewrite a statute or to supply omissions; it is limited to narrowing the scope of an existing provision.

Examiners frequently test the distinction between severability and eclipse through hypothetical statutes. A typical question presents a pre‑Constitutional law with multiple sections, some violating Article 19 and others not. The correct approach: apply eclipse to the whole law if the violation permeates the entire enactment, but if the offending sections are separable, apply severability to retain the valid sections while the offending ones remain eclipsed. Remember that a post‑Constitutional law cannot claim eclipse; it is either wholly void or saved by severability.

The Supreme Court’s Advisory Jurisdiction under Article 143: Scope, Procedure, and Landmark References

Article 143 empowers the President to refer to the Supreme Court any question of law or fact which he considers of public importance. The Court’s opinion is advisory, not binding, yet it carries immense persuasive authority and has shaped constitutional discourse. The reference may be made under Article 143(1) for questions of law or fact, or under Article 143(2) for disputes arising out of pre‑Constitutional treaties, agreements, or engagements. The Court may decline to answer if the question is purely political, involves policy matters unsuitable for judicial determination, or is premature.

Landmark references illustrate the breadth of this jurisdiction. The Kerala Education Bill Reference (1958) addressed the validity of a State law regulating aided educational institutions and clarified the scope of Article 30(1). The Special Courts Bill Reference (1978) examined the constitutionality of a bill providing for special courts for trial of offences committed during the Emergency, and the Court held that the bill violated the basic structure by undermining judicial independence. The Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal Reference (1992) dealt with the inter‑State water dispute and the Court’s opinion guided the tribunal’s subsequent award. The Ram Janmabhoomi Reference (1993) sought the Court’s opinion on whether a temple existed at the disputed site before the mosque; the Court declined to answer, stating the question was essentially factual and not suitable for advisory opinion.

Procedure-wise, the President forwards the reference to the Supreme Court, which constitutes a Bench (usually of at least five judges) to hear arguments from the Attorney General, the concerned State governments, and any interveners. The Court then delivers its opinion, which is transmitted back to the President. Although advisory, the opinion has been treated as authoritative by the executive and legislature; for instance, the government withdrew the Special Courts Bill after the adverse opinion. The Court has also used the advisory jurisdiction to clarify constitutional ambiguities without waiting for litigation, thereby performing a quasi‑legislative interpretive function.

Critics argue that advisory opinions bypass the adversarial process and may encroach on the political domain. The Supreme Court itself, in Re: Presidential Reference (1998), cautioned that the jurisdiction should not be used to obtain judicial endorsement for executive decisions. Aspirants should be able to distinguish Article 143(1) from 143(2), cite at least three landmark references, and explain why the opinion is not binding yet influential. A common examiner twist is to ask whether the Supreme Court can refuse a reference; the answer is yes, on grounds of political question, prematurity, or lack of public importance.

  • Confusing eclipse with severability: eclipse applies only to pre‑Constitutional laws and renders the whole law dormant; severability excises only the offending part of any law.
  • Assuming Article 356 proclamations are immune from judicial review; S.R. Bommai explicitly subjects the President’s satisfaction to judicial scrutiny.
  • Believing a floor test is optional under Article 356; Bommai and Nabam Rebia make it the primary method to test majority.
  • Thinking the Supreme Court’s advisory opinion under Article 143 is binding on the President or Parliament; it is only persuasive.
  • Stating that the doctrine of severability requires an express severability clause; the Court applies the legislative‑intent test regardless of a clause.
  • Mixing up Article 143(1) (questions of law/fact of public importance) with Article 143(2) (pre‑Constitutional treaty disputes).
  • Claiming that a post‑Constitutional law can be eclipsed; Article 13(2) makes such a law void ab initio, leaving no scope for eclipse.

These advanced doctrines illustrate how the Constitution balances continuity, federal stability, legislative precision, and judicial restraint.

Judicial Standards for President’s Rule under Article 356: The S.R. Bommai Framework and Subsequent Developments

Article 356 empowers the President to assume the functions of a State government on receipt of a report from the Governor or otherwise, if the President is satisfied that a situation has arisen in which the government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution. The scope of judicial review of this satisfaction was authoritatively settled in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) by a nine‑judge Bench. The Court held that the President’s satisfaction is not immune from judicial scrutiny; it is justiciable on the grounds of mala fides, irrelevance, or non‑application of mind. The judgment laid down a set of procedural safeguards that have become the benchmark for every subsequent imposition of President’s Rule.

Core Principles from Bommai

  • Floor test as the primary method: The majority must be tested on the floor of the Legislative Assembly; the Governor cannot rely solely on a subjective assessment.
  • Secularism as a basic feature: A State government pursuing policies that undermine secularism can be dismissed, but the burden of proof lies on the Centre.
  • Material relevance: The report of the Governor must contain material facts; a mere assertion of “breakdown of constitutional machinery” is insufficient.
  • Parliamentary approval: The proclamation must be laid before each House of Parliament within two months; failure to secure approval leads to automatic revocation.

Post‑Bommai Jurisprudence

In Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006), the Court struck down the dissolution of the Bihar Assembly after the Governor’s report was found to be based on extraneous considerations, reinforcing the requirement of relevant material. Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016) extended the floor‑test principle to situations where the Governor advances the date of the Assembly session to pre‑empt a confidence motion, holding that such action violates the constitutional scheme. The 2018 Karnataka and 2020 Madhya Pradesh episodes saw the Supreme Court ordering immediate floor tests within 24‑48 hours, citing Bommai as the controlling precedent.

Constitutional Amendments and Their Impact

The 38th Amendment (1975) had attempted to make the President’s satisfaction final and conclusive, but the 44th Amendment (1978) restored judicial review by deleting the ouster clause. The 94th Amendment (2006) extended the maximum period of President’s Rule in Punjab from three to five years under special circumstances, but the Bommai safeguards continue to apply irrespective of the duration.

Aspirants should be able to articulate the distinction between the subjective satisfaction of the President (which is not reviewable per se) and the objective material on which that satisfaction is based (which is fully reviewable). The examiner often tests this nuance by asking whether the Court can substitute its own judgment for that of the President; the answer is no — the Court only examines whether the satisfaction was formed on relevant material and without mala fides.

The Doctrine of Eclipse and Severability: Distinctive Application to Pre‑Constitutional and Post‑Constitutional Laws

The doctrine of eclipse operates exclusively on pre‑Constitutional statutes that conflict with the fundamental rights enumerated in Part III. In Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955), the Supreme Court held that such a law does not become void ab initio; it remains in a dormant state — eclipsed — and can be revived by a constitutional amendment that removes the inconsistency. The law is not dead; it is merely unenforceable until the constitutional impediment is lifted.

Severability: The Legislative‑Intent Test

Severability, by contrast, applies to any statute — pre‑ or post‑Constitutional — when only a part of it violates the Constitution. The test, crystallised in R.M.D.C. v. Union of India (1957), asks whether the valid and invalid portions are so inextricably mixed that the legislature would not have enacted the valid part alone. If the valid portion can stand independently, it is severed and preserved; the offending provision alone is struck down. The presence or absence of a severability clause is not decisive; the Court examines the legislative intent gathered from the scheme, object, and language of the statute.

Interaction Between the Two Doctrines

A pre‑Constitutional law may contain several sections, some violating Article 19 and others not. The correct approach: apply eclipse to the whole law if the violation permeates the entire enactment, but if the offending sections are separable, apply severability to retain the valid sections while the offending ones remain eclipsed. Remember that a post‑Constitutional law cannot claim eclipse; Article 13(2) renders such a law void ab initio, leaving no scope for dormancy. The Supreme Court in State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills (1974) reiterated that eclipse is a doctrine of temporary suspension, not of validation.

Practical Implications for Legislative Drafting

Drafters often insert express severability clauses to signal legislative intent, but the Court’s inquiry remains substantive. In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Court upheld the Tenth Schedule’s anti‑defection provisions while severing the paragraph that barred judicial review, demonstrating that even constitutional amendments are subject to severability when they infringe basic structure.

Examiner's trap
A pre‑Constitutional statute contains five sections. Sections 2 and 4 violate Article 19(1)(g). The Parliament amends the Constitution to remove the restriction on the right to trade. The State argues that the whole statute revives automatically. Decide.
The amendment removes the constitutional impediment only for the offending sections. Under the doctrine of eclipse, the entire statute was eclipsed only if the violation permeated the whole enactment. Since Sections 1, 3, and 5 were never inconsistent, they remained operative throughout. Sections 2 and 4 revive automatically because the eclipse is lifted; the valid sections never needed revival. The State’s argument that the whole statute revives is partially correct — the eclipsed provisions revive, but the never‑eclipsed provisions were always in force.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes eclipse and severability, first identify whether the law is pre‑ or post‑Constitutional. If pre‑Constitutional, ask: does the inconsistency affect the entire statute or only separable parts? Apply eclipse to the whole only if the violation is pervasive; otherwise sever the valid portions and keep the offending ones eclipsed. For post‑Constitutional laws, eclipse is unavailable — only severability or total invalidation applies.

The Supreme Court’s Advisory Jurisdiction under Article 143: Scope, Procedure, and Landmark References

Article 143 empowers the President to refer to the Supreme Court any question of law or fact which he considers of public importance. The Court’s opinion is advisory, not binding, yet it carries immense persuasive authority and has shaped constitutional discourse. The reference may be made under Article 143(1) for questions of law or fact, or under Article 143(2) for disputes arising out of pre‑Constitutional treaties, agreements, or engagements. The Court may decline to answer if the question is purely political, involves policy matters unsuitable for judicial determination, or is premature.

Landmark References

  • Kerala Education Bill Reference (1958): The Court examined the validity of a State law regulating aided educational institutions and clarified the scope of Article 30(1) on minority rights.
  • Special Courts Bill Reference (1978): The Court held that the bill providing for special courts for trial of offences committed during the Emergency violated the basic structure by undermining judicial independence.
  • Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal Reference (1992): The opinion guided the tribunal’s subsequent award on inter‑State water sharing.
  • Ram Janmabhoomi Reference (1993): The Court declined to answer whether a temple existed at the disputed site before the mosque, stating the question was essentially factual and not suitable for advisory opinion.
  • Presidential Reference (1998): On the consultation process for judicial appointments, the Court laid down the collegium system, cautioning that the advisory jurisdiction should not be used to obtain judicial endorsement for executive decisions.

Procedure

The President forwards the reference to the Supreme Court, which constitutes a Bench (usually of at least five judges) to hear arguments from the Attorney General, the concerned State governments, and any interveners. The Court then delivers its opinion, which is transmitted back to the President. Although advisory, the opinion has been treated as authoritative by the executive and legislature; for instance, the government withdrew the Special Courts Bill after the adverse opinion.

Critical Distinctions

Article 143(1) deals with questions of law or fact of public importance; Article 143(2) is confined to pre‑Constitutional treaty disputes. The Court has refused references under 143(1) when the matter was sub‑judice or when the reference sought to circumvent the normal litigation process. In Re: Presidential Reference (1998), the Court emphasised that the advisory jurisdiction is not a substitute for the adversarial process and must be exercised sparingly.

The Principle of Federal Balance in the Seventh Schedule: Judicial Tests for Legislative Competence

The Seventh Schedule distributes legislative powers between the Union and the States through three lists — Union List (List I), State List (List II), and Concurrent List (List III). The principle of federal balance requires that neither level of government encroaches upon the other’s exclusive domain. The Supreme Court has evolved a battery of tests to determine legislative competence when a law is challenged on the ground of transgression.

Pith and Substance

The foundational test, articulated in State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), directs the Court to ascertain the true nature and character of the legislation. If the pith and substance falls within the competence of the enacting legislature, incidental encroachment on another list does not invalidate the law. This test was refined in State of West Bengal v. Union of India (1963), where the Court upheld a Union law on coal mines despite its impact on State land rights, because the dominant purpose was regulation of mines (Union List Entry 54).

Doctrine of Occupied Field

When Parliament enacts a law on a Concurrent subject with the intention of occupying the entire field, State legislatures are precluded from legislating on the same subject. In Tika Ramji v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1956), the Court held that a comprehensive Central statute on essential commodities left no room for State legislation. The test is whether the Central law exhibits a clear legislative intent to exhaust the field.

Colorable Legislation

A law that appears to be within legislative competence but in reality seeks to achieve an object beyond that competence is struck down as colorable. The classic illustration is K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953), where a State law on religious endowments was held to be a colorable exercise of power because its true purpose was to appropriate temple property.

Harmonious Construction and Residuary Powers

When entries in different lists overlap, the Court applies harmonious construction to give effect to both. If a subject is not enumerated in any list, residuary power vests in the Union under Article 248 and Entry 97 of List I. In Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon (1971), the Court upheld a Union law on taxes on services, a subject not mentioned in any list, by invoking residuary power.

Federal Balance as a Basic Structure Feature

In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Court declared federalism a basic feature of the Constitution. Consequently, any constitutional amendment that destroys the federal balance by transferring State List subjects to the Union List without State consent would be vulnerable to basic structure challenge. This principle underpins the judicial scrutiny of the 42nd Amendment’s attempt to shift several State subjects to the Concurrent List.

The Constitutional Status and Functions of the National Human Rights Commission: Statutory Mandate and Judicial Oversight

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) was established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, and is not a constitutional body. Its composition — a Chairperson who has been a Chief Justice of India, one Supreme Court judge, one Chief Justice of a High Court, and two members with knowledge of human rights — reflects an intent to insulate it from executive control. The Act empowers the NHRC to inquire, suo motu or on petition, into violations of human rights by public servants, to intervene in proceedings involving allegations of human rights violations, and to recommend remedial measures including compensation and prosecution.

Powers and Limitations

The NHRC’s recommendations are not binding on the government; however, the Act requires the concerned authority to report action taken within one month. In practice, compliance is uneven. The Commission lacks suo motu prosecutorial power and cannot enforce its orders. Its jurisdiction excludes the armed forces, where a separate mechanism under the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act operates.

Judicial Oversight and Expansion of Remedies

The Supreme Court has repeatedly treated NHRC reports as credible evidence. In NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2003), the Court directed the Gujarat government to implement the Commission’s recommendations on the 2002 communal violence, holding that the State’s failure to act amounted to a violation of Article 21. In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (1997), the Court used NHRC findings to issue directions on custodial deaths, effectively converting the Commission’s advisory role into a judicial enforcement tool.

Recent Developments

The 2019 amendment to the Protection of Human Rights Act expanded the NHRC’s composition to include a member from the National Commission for Women and the National Commission for Minorities, and extended its jurisdiction to cover human rights violations by private entities performing public functions. The Supreme Court, in Common Cause v. Union of India (2021), emphasised that the NHRC’s independence is essential for the realization of the constitutional guarantee of dignity under Article 21, and directed the Centre to fill vacancies within a fixed timeline.

Comparative Perspective

Unlike the South African Human Rights Commission, which is a Chapter 9 constitutional institution with binding powers, the NHRC remains a statutory body. This distinction is frequently tested: aspirants must be able to explain why the NHRC’s recommendations are persuasive but not mandatory, and how the judiciary has compensated for this structural weakness through proactive interpretation of Article 32 and Article 226.

  • Confusing the doctrine of eclipse (pre‑Constitutional dormancy) with severability (excision of offending provisions) and applying eclipse to post‑Constitutional laws.
  • Assuming the President’s satisfaction under Article 356 is non‑justiciable; Bommai makes the material basis reviewable.
  • Believing the Supreme Court’s advisory opinion under Article 143 is binding on the executive or legislature; it is only persuasive.
  • Thinking the NHRC’s recommendations are legally enforceable without a court order; they are advisory unless adopted by a judicial directive.
  • Overlooking the distinction between Article 143(1) (public importance) and 143(2) (pre‑Constitutional treaty disputes) in reference questions.
  • Misapplying the pith‑and‑substance test by ignoring incidental encroachment; the test permits incidental overlap if the dominant purpose lies within competence.
  • Asserting that a severability clause in a statute automatically saves the valid portions; the Court applies the legislative‑intent test irrespective of such a clause.

These advanced doctrines illustrate how the Constitution balances continuity, federal stability, legislative precision, and judicial restraint.

Parliamentary Sovereignty versus Constitutional Supremacy

The United Kingdom’s constitutional tradition rests on parliamentary sovereignty: Parliament can enact, amend or repeal any law, and no court may question the validity of an Act of Parliament. In India the Constitution itself is the supreme legal authority. Article 13 declares that any law inconsistent with the fundamental rights is void to the extent of the inconsistency, and Article 368 prescribes a special amendment procedure that cannot be bypassed by ordinary legislation. The Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) held that Parliament’s amending power under Article 368 does not extend to altering the basic structure of the Constitution. Consequently, even a constitutional amendment passed by the requisite majorities can be struck down if it destroys features such as the supremacy of the Constitution, the republican and democratic form of government, the secular character of the State, the separation of powers, or the federal balance.

The practical consequence is that Indian courts exercise judicial review over both ordinary statutes and constitutional amendments. In contrast, British courts (prior to the Factortame litigation) could only interpret statutes; they could not invalidate them. The Indian model therefore combines a written, rigid constitution with a powerful judiciary that acts as the guardian of constitutional supremacy. This distinction is frequently tested: aspirants must be able to explain why the Indian Parliament is not sovereign in the British sense, and how the basic‑structure doctrine operates as an unwritten limitation on the formal amendment power.

Another nuance is the role of constitutional conventions. While the UK relies heavily on conventions (e.g., the monarch’s assent is a formality), India’s conventions — such as the President acting on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers — are also recognized but are subordinate to the written text. The Supreme Court has repeatedly affirmed that conventions cannot override express constitutional provisions (e.g., R.C. Poudyal v. Union of India, 1993). Thus, the Indian system is best described as constitutional sovereignty with a parliamentary form of government operating within constitutionally defined limits.

The Doctrine of Eclipse and Severability in Constitutional Adjudication

The doctrine of eclipse applies to pre‑Constitutional laws that conflict with fundamental rights. Such laws are not void ab initio; they become dormant — eclipsed — for so long as the inconsistency persists. When a constitutional amendment removes the conflict (for instance, by inserting a new article that validates the earlier law), the eclipse lifts and the law revives automatically. The Supreme Court has clarified that the doctrine does not apply to post‑Constitutional legislation; a law enacted after 26 January 1950 that contravenes a fundamental right is void from its inception and cannot be revived by a later amendment unless the amendment expressly validates it.

The doctrine of severability governs the fate of a statute that contains both constitutional and unconstitutional provisions. The Court examines whether the valid portions can stand independently after the offending part is excised. The test, formulated in R.M.D.C. v. Union of India (1957), asks whether the legislature would have enacted the remaining provisions had it known the invalid part would be struck down. If the valid and invalid parts are so intertwined that the legislative purpose would be defeated, the entire statute falls. A severability clause in the statute does not bind the Court; the judicial determination of legislative intent remains paramount.

Both doctrines illustrate the Court’s commitment to preserving as much legislation as possible while upholding constitutional supremacy. Eclipse protects the continuity of pre‑Constitutional law, whereas severability prevents the wholesale invalidation of complex statutes. In practice, the two doctrines may intersect: a pre‑Constitutional law partially eclipsed may also be subject to severability if only some of its provisions conflict with fundamental rights.

Distinguishing Eclipse from Severability
A 1948 provincial act regulated money‑lending. After the Constitution came into force, several of its provisions were found to violate Article 19(1)(g). In 1975 Parliament amended the Constitution to insert a new Article 31B placing the act in the Ninth Schedule. Explain the constitutional status of the act before and after the amendment, and whether severability is relevant.
Before 1975 the act was eclipsed: its offending provisions lay dormant because they conflicted with fundamental rights, but the statute as a whole was not dead. The 1975 amendment removed the constitutional obstacle, so the eclipse lifted and the entire act revived — no severability analysis was needed because the amendment validated the whole law. Severability would have been relevant only if the amendment had validated only part of the act, leaving other provisions still inconsistent; then the Court would test whether the validated portions could stand alone.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mentions a pre‑Constitutional law and a later constitutional amendment, first identify whether the doctrine of eclipse applies. If the amendment places the law in the Ninth Schedule, the eclipse lifts entirely. Only invoke severability when a statute contains a mix of valid and invalid provisions and the legislature has not expressly validated the whole enactment.

The Advisory Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 143

Article 143 empowers the President to refer to the Supreme Court any question of law or fact of public importance (clause 1) or any dispute arising out of a pre‑Constitutional treaty, agreement or similar instrument (clause 2). The Court’s opinion is advisory — not binding on the executive or legislature — but it carries considerable persuasive authority. The jurisdiction is discretionary; the Court may decline to answer if the reference is politically motivated or lacks a genuine legal question.

Landmark references include In re: Kerala Education Bill (1958), where the Court outlined the scope of legislative competence over education; In re: Special Courts Bill (1979), which clarified the limits of legislative power to create special courts; and In re: Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal (1992), where the Court interpreted the Inter‑State Water Disputes Act. In each case the opinion guided subsequent legislation and judicial interpretation, demonstrating that advisory opinions, while non‑binding, shape constitutional practice.

Clause 2 references are rare. The only instance was the 1963 reference concerning the Berubari Union agreement with Pakistan, where the Court held that the President’s power to refer such disputes is not fettered by the requirement of a “question of law or fact of public importance”. The advisory jurisdiction thus serves as a constitutional safety valve, allowing the executive to obtain authoritative legal guidance without awaiting litigation.

The Doctrine of Legislative Privilege and Its Judicial Review

Articles 105 and 194 confer on Parliament and State Legislatures, respectively, certain privileges — freedom of speech in the House, immunity from court proceedings for anything said or any vote given, and the power to punish for contempt. These privileges are modelled on the British parliamentary tradition but are subject to the written Constitution. The Supreme Court has held that legislative privilege is not absolute; it is subject to fundamental rights and judicial review.

In Keshav Singh v. Speaker, Legislative Assembly (1965) the Court ruled that the power to punish for contempt cannot be exercised in a manner that violates Article 21 (personal liberty). Later, in Raja Ram Pal v. Hon’ble Speaker (2007), the Court affirmed that judicial review extends to the exercise of privilege, especially when the privilege is claimed to shield corruption or criminal conduct. The Court distinguished between internal matters (e.g., regulation of procedure) which are largely non‑justiciable, and external actions (e.g., expulsion of a member, breach of privilege against a citizen) which are reviewable.

The 2003 amendment to the Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act and the 2018 Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (Fourth Judges case) further clarified that the judiciary can examine whether a legislative body has acted within its constitutional mandate when invoking privilege. Thus, while privileges protect legislative independence, they do not create a zone of immunity from constitutional scrutiny.

Constitutional Safeguards for the Independence of the Judiciary: Appointment, Transfer, and Removal

The independence of the higher judiciary is secured through a cluster of constitutional provisions and judicial pronouncements. Articles 124, 217 and 222 govern the appointment of Supreme Court and High Court judges, their transfer, and the establishment of a collegium system. The First Judges case (S.P. Gupta v. Union of India, 1981) gave the executive primacy in appointments; the Second Judges case (Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India, 1993) reversed this, vesting primacy in the Chief Justice of India and a collegium of senior judges. The Third Judges case (1998) expanded the collegium to five senior-most Supreme Court judges for Supreme Court appointments and to the Chief Justice plus two senior judges for High Court appointments.

The Fourth Judges case (2015) struck down the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) Act and the 99th Constitutional Amendment, reaffirming the collegium as part of the basic structure. The Court held that judicial independence requires insulation from executive influence in appointments and transfers. Article 222 permits transfer of High Court judges only after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, and the Supreme Court has ruled that such consultation must be effective, not merely formal (Union of India v. R. Gandhi, 2010).

Removal of a judge is governed by Article 124(4) and the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968. A judge can be removed only on proved misbehaviour or incapacity, by an address of each House of Parliament supported by a special majority. The procedure is deliberately cumbersome: a three‑member inquiry committee (a Supreme Court judge, a High Court Chief Justice, and a distinguished jurist) must first find the charges substantiated. To date, no judge has been removed under this process, underscoring the high threshold for judicial accountability.

  • Confusing the doctrine of eclipse (pre‑Constitutional dormancy) with severability (excision of offending provisions) and applying eclipse to post‑Constitutional laws.
  • Assuming the President’s advisory opinion under Article 143 is binding on the executive or legislature; it is only persuasive.
  • Believing legislative privilege under Articles 105/194 is absolute; the Supreme Court has subjected external exercises of privilege to judicial review.
  • Overlooking that the collegium system, while not expressly in the Constitution, has been held to be part of the basic structure and cannot be replaced by a statutory commission without a constitutional amendment that survives basic‑structure scrutiny.
  • Thinking that a severability clause in a statute automatically saves the valid portions; the Court applies the legislative‑intent test irrespective of such a clause.
  • Misapplying the pith‑and‑substance test by ignoring incidental encroachment; the test permits incidental overlap if the dominant purpose lies within competence.
  • Assuming that the basic‑structure doctrine only limits amendments that affect fundamental rights; it also protects federalism, secularism, and the separation of powers.

B.N. Rau and the Pre‑Drafting Constitutional Architecture

Before the Drafting Committee convened, the constitutional edifice rested on the solitary labour of Sir Benegal Narsing Rau, appointed Constitutional Advisor on 1 July 1946. A career civil servant with a Cambridge doctorate in law, Rau approached the task as a comparative constitutional engineer rather than a political negotiator. He circulated a detailed questionnaire to provincial governments, princely states, and political parties, eliciting over 200 memoranda on federalism, minority rights, and judicial review. Between October 1946 and February 1948, Rau and his small staff in the Constituent Assembly Secretariat produced a series of working papers analysing the constitutions of the United States, Canada, Australia, Ireland, South Africa, and the Government of India Act 1935. His Notes on Clauses — running to several hundred pages — provided clause‑by‑clause justifications for every provision, citing foreign precedents and flagging policy choices for the Assembly.

Rau’s first full draft, submitted on 21 February 1948, contained 240 articles and 13 schedules. It introduced structural innovations that survived into the final text: the distinction between Union and State legislative lists (derived from the Canadian model but with a stronger Centre), the device of a Concurrent List (borrowed from Australia), and the framework for judicial review of legislative competence (modelled on the US Supreme Court’s commerce clause jurisprudence). Crucially, Rau advocated a due process clause for fundamental rights, drawing on the American Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments. The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, however, replaced “due process of law” with “procedure established by law” (Article 21), a deliberate narrowing that Rau recorded as a dissent in his notes. His draft also included a Bill of Rights for Minorities with explicit representation guarantees — later subsumed into Articles 29–30 after the Partition made separate electorates politically untenable.

Rau’s influence extended beyond the text. He accompanied the Indian delegation to the United Nations in 1947–48, where the Universal Declaration of Human Rights was being drafted, and fed international developments back into the Indian project. His memorandum on the President’s position — arguing for a ceremonial head of state bound by ministerial advice — shaped Article 74(1) before the Drafting Committee formalised it. After the Constitution’s adoption, Rau served as India’s first Permanent Representative to the UN and later as a judge of the International Court of Justice, but his constitutional legacy remains the intellectual scaffolding upon which the Drafting Committee built. The Assembly’s resolution of 26 November 1949 formally acknowledged “the valuable services rendered by Sir B.N. Rau as Constitutional Advisor” — a rare institutional tribute to a bureaucrat‑scholar.

The Constituent Assembly’s Committee System: Architecture of Deliberation

The Constituent Assembly did not debate in plenary alone; it operated through a nested committee system that performed the granular work of constitutional design. Eight principal committees and over a dozen sub‑committees were constituted between August 1947 and January 1948, each chaired by a political heavyweight to ensure legitimacy. The Steering Committee (Chair: Rajendra Prasad) managed the agenda and timetable; the Union Powers Committee (Chair: Jawaharlal Nehru) defined the Centre’s legislative, executive, and financial authority; the Provincial Constitution Committee (Chair: Sardar Patel) drafted the template for State governments; and the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities (Chair: Patel, with sub‑committees chaired by J.B. Kripalani and H.C. Mookherjee) produced the blueprint for Parts III and the minority provisions of Part III/IV.

Two committees deserve particular attention for their structural impact. The Union Constitution Committee (Chair: Nehru) decided that India would be a parliamentary republic with a President elected by an electoral college of federal legislators — rejecting both the American presidential model and the British Crown‑in‑Parliament model. Its report of July 1947 settled the doctrine of ministerial responsibility (Article 75) and the President’s obligation to act on aid and advice (Article 74), though the final text added the proviso allowing the President to require reconsideration (inserted by the 42nd Amendment, partially restored by the 44th). The Committee on the Functions of the Judiciary (Chair: Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar) designed the integrated judiciary: a single Supreme Court with original, appellate, and advisory jurisdiction, and High Courts for each State with superintendence over subordinate courts — a departure from the US dual‑court system and the Government of India Act’s federal court.

The committee reports were not rubber‑stamped. The Advisory Committee’s interim report on fundamental rights (April 1947) sparked a 16‑day debate in the Assembly, leading to the deletion of “due process,” the insertion of “reasonable restrictions” on freedoms (Article 19), and the crafting of Article 32 as the “heart and soul” of the Constitution (Ambedkar’s phrase). The Minorities Sub‑Committee initially recommended reserved seats in legislatures for Muslims, Sikhs, and Christians; after Partition, the Assembly replaced separate electorates with reservation for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes only (Articles 330, 332), a pivot recorded in the Sub‑Committee’s final report of August 1947. The committee system thus converted political compromises into constitutional text before the Drafting Committee — chaired by Ambedkar with Rau as ex‑officio member — harmonised the reports into a coherent draft between February and October 1948.

Examiner's Trap: Committee Reports vs Final Text
A question asks: "Which committee recommended the deletion of 'due process' from the fundamental rights chapter?" The tempting answer is the Drafting Committee. The correct answer is the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights (Sub‑Committee on Fundamental Rights, chaired by J.B. Kripalani), whose interim report of April 1947 proposed "procedure established by law." The Drafting Committee merely formalised this choice. Always trace a provision to the committee that made the policy decision, not the one that polished the language.
The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities, through its Sub‑Committee on Fundamental Rights (Chair: J.B. Kripalani), recommended replacing "due process of law" with "procedure established by law" in its interim report of April 1947. The Drafting Committee (Chair: B.R. Ambedkar) incorporated this into Article 21 of the February 1948 draft. The plenary Assembly debated and retained the phrase in December 1948. Therefore, the policy decision originated in the Advisory Committee, not the Drafting Committee.
Exam‑Day Strategy: Committee Genealogy
Memorise a two‑column table: Committee Name (Chair) → Key Constitutional Output. Example: Union Powers Committee (Nehru) → Union List, Residuary Power (Art. 248), Emergency Provisions (Art. 352–360); Provincial Constitution Committee (Patel) → State Executive (Art. 153–167), State Legislature (Art. 168–212), High Courts (Art. 214–231). UPSC often asks "Who chaired the committee that designed X?" or "Which committee's report led to Article Y?" Knowing the genealogy saves 2–3 marks per paper.

Citizenship at Commencement: Partition, Migration, and Articles 5–11

The Constitution’s citizenship provisions (Articles 5–11, Part II) were drafted in the shadow of the largest forced migration in history. When the Constituent Assembly took up citizenship in August 1949, nearly 14 million people had crossed the new borders, and the legal status of millions more — refugees, returnees, and those stranded in the “wrong” dominion — was unsettled. The Drafting Committee’s February 1948 draft contained a single citizenship clause (Article 5) based on domicile plus one of three conditions: birth in India, parent born in India, or five years’ ordinary residence. The Partition forced a radical rewrite.

Article 5, as adopted, conferred citizenship at commencement (26 January 1950) on every person who had domicile in the territory of India and satisfied one of three tests: (a) born in India; (b) either parent born in India; (c) ordinarily resident in India for five years immediately preceding commencement. The term “domicile” — a common‑law concept implying permanent home with intent to remain — was deliberately chosen over “residence” to exclude temporary sojourners. Article 6 addressed migrants from Pakistan: those who migrated before 19 July 1948 (the date the permit system was introduced) became citizens if they or their parents/grandparents were born in undivided India and they had been ordinarily resident since migration; those migrating after 19 July 1948 required a permit for resettlement or permanent return issued by the Government of India. Article 7 dealt with migrants to Pakistan after 1 March 1947: they lost Indian citizenship unless they returned under a permit for resettlement. Article 8 extended citizenship to persons of Indian origin residing abroad (e.g., in Burma, Ceylon, East Africa) if they or their parents/grandparents were born in undivided India and they registered with an Indian diplomatic mission.

The debates reveal the tension between jus soli (birth‑right) and jus sanguinis (descent). H.V. Kamath moved an amendment to grant citizenship to anyone born in India regardless of parentage — a pure jus soli rule — but it was defeated. B.R. Ambedkar defended the domicile requirement as a safeguard against “citizenship by accident of birth” for children of foreign diplomats or temporary visitors. The Citizenship Act, 1955 (enacted under Article 11’s plenary power) later codified acquisition by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, and incorporation of territory, and has been amended six times (1986, 1992, 2003, 2005, 2015, 2019) — each amendment reflecting shifting political conceptions of belonging. Notably, the 2003 amendment introduced overseas citizenship of India (OCI), a novel status short of full citizenship, and the 2019 amendment (CAA) created a religion‑based fast‑track for migrants from three neighbouring countries — a departure from the Constitution’s religion‑neutral framework at commencement.

The Dual Capacity of the Constituent Assembly: Constitution‑Making Body and Provisional Parliament

From 26 November 1949 (adoption) to 26 January 1950 (commencement), and thereafter until the first general elections of 1951–52, the Constituent Assembly functioned simultaneously as the constitution‑making authority and the provisional legislature of the Dominion of India. This dual role, unique in comparative constitutional history, was mandated by the Indian Independence Act, 1947 (Section 8) and the Government of India Act, 1935 as adapted by the India (Provisional Constitution) Order, 1947. The Assembly’s legislative sittings were distinct from its constitution‑making sittings: the Speaker (G.V. Mavalankar) presided over legislative business, while the President (Rajendra Prasad) chaired constitution‑making sessions. The Rules of Procedure provided separate notice periods, quorum requirements, and voting thresholds for each capacity.

As a legislature, the Assembly enacted 78 laws between January 1950 and March 1952, including the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 (the first preventive detention law under the new Constitution), the Representation of the People Act, 1950 (providing the electoral machinery for the first general elections), and the Contingency Fund of India Act, 1950. These statutes were passed under the Government of India Act, 1935 as modified, because the Constitution’s legislative provisions (Chapter II, Part V) only became operative on 26 January 1950. Crucially, the Assembly’s legislative acts were subject to the Governor‑General’s assent until 26 January 1950, and thereafter to the President’s assent under Article 111 — a transitional arrangement that underscored the continuity of the Dominion’s executive authority.

The dual capacity ended with the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, which was passed by the Provisional Parliament (the Assembly in its legislative avatar) using the amending power under Article 368 — a power that the Constitution itself conferred on “Parliament,” defined in Article 79 as the President and two Houses. The First Amendment inserted Articles 31A, 31B, and the Ninth Schedule to protect land reform laws from judicial review, and amended Article 19(2) to add “public order” and “incitement to an offence” as grounds for restricting free speech. The fact that the same body that drafted the Constitution amended it within 15 months of commencement — using a special majority it had itself prescribed — illustrates the fluid boundary between constituent power and legislative power in India’s founding moment. The Supreme Court in Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951) upheld the First Amendment, ruling that “Parliament” in Article 368 included the Provisional Parliament, and that the amending power was not subject to judicial review on fundamental rights grounds — a position reversed only in Golaknath (1967) and restructured in Kesavananda (1973).

"India, that is Bharat": The Article 1 Debate on the Nation's Name

Article 1 — “India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States” — appears self‑evident today, but its phrasing emerged from a sharp, two‑day debate on 17–18 November 1948. The Drafting Committee’s draft read: “India shall be a Union of States.” H.V. Kamath moved an amendment: “Bharat, or in the English language, India, shall be a Union of States.” He argued that “Bharat” carried the civilisational continuity of the Bharata Varsha of the Puranas and the Mahabharata, while “India” was a Greek derivative (Indoi) imposed by outsiders. Seth Govind Das countered with “Bharat known as India also,” insisting on primacy for the indigenous name. K.M. Munshi proposed “Bharat, or India, shall be a Union of States.” The debate exposed three fault‑lines: historical authenticity (Bharat as the ancient name), international recognition (India as the name in the UN Charter, treaties, and the Government of India Act), and linguistic federalism (non‑Hindi members feared “Bharat” privileged Sanskritised Hindi).

Ambedkar, intervening for the Drafting Committee, rejected both extremes. He noted that the Objectives Resolution (January 1947) had used “India,” and that the Indian Independence Act, 1947 created the “Dominion of India.” Changing the name at the constitutional stage would require renegotiating every international instrument. His formulation — “India, that is Bharat” — was a bilingual equivalence rather than a hierarchy: both names denote the same political entity, usable interchangeably in official communication. The Assembly adopted Ambedkar’s wording by voice vote. The phrase “Union of States” (not “Federation of States”) was equally deliberate: it signalled that the Union was indestructible and the States had no right to secede — a point Ambedkar emphasised by contrasting the Indian Union with the American “Union” (which the Civil War settled as indestructible) and the Soviet “Union of Republics” (which constitutionally permitted secession under Article 17 of the 1936 USSR Constitution).

The Article 1 debate resurfaced in 2004 when a private member’s bill sought to replace “India” with “Bharat” in all official usage, and again in 2023 when the President’s G20 dinner invitations used “President of Bharat.” The Constitution itself uses both names: the Hindi authoritative text (Article 394A) reads “भारत अर्थात् इंडिया” (Bharat arthaat India), while the English text reads “India, that is Bharat.” The Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977) treated the two as synonymous for jurisdictional purposes. The dual nomenclature thus remains a living constitutional compromise — one that encodes the founding moment’s negotiation between civilisational self‑identification and the practicalities of modern statehood.

  • Confusing the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights (Patel/Kripalani) with the Drafting Committee (Ambedkar) on who made the policy choice to replace “due process” with “procedure established by law.”
  • Assuming the Constituent Assembly’s legislative acts before 26 January 1950 were passed under the Constitution; they were passed under the Government of India Act 1935 as adapted, with the Governor‑General’s assent.
  • Believing Article 1’s “Union of States” implies a federation formed by agreement among States; Ambedkar explicitly stated the Union is not the result of an agreement and no State has the right to secede.
  • Overlooking that the Citizenship Act, 1955 was enacted under Article 11 (Parliament’s plenary power over citizenship), not under the Constitution’s original citizenship articles which only governed commencement.
  • Thinking B.N. Rau’s draft was merely a “first draft” without policy content; his Notes on Clauses contain the first articulation of the Concurrent List, the integrated judiciary, and the President’s ceremonial role — all retained in the final Constitution.
  • Misattributing the First Amendment to the “first Parliament” elected in 1952; it was passed by the Provisional Parliament (the Constituent Assembly in legislative session) in June 1951.
  • Confusing the permit system under Articles 6 and 7 (administered by the Government of India for migrants from/to Pakistan) with the later permit/registration regime under the Citizenship Act, 1955 for other categories.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee on Rules of Procedure and the Conduct of Business

The Constituent Assembly functioned both as a constitution‑drafting body and as a provisional legislature. To manage its dual role it established a Committee on Rules of Procedure (often called the Rules Committee) on 14 August 1947, chaired by the Assembly President, Dr Rajendra Prasad. The committee comprised 15 members representing the major parties and communities, including B. N. Rau (Constitutional Adviser), K. M. Munshi, and Maulana Abul Kalam Azad. Its mandate was to draft standing orders that would govern debates, voting, committee references, and the passage of constitutional provisions.

The Rules Committee produced the Constituent Assembly Rules of Procedure, adopted on 20 January 1948. Key features included: a quorum of one‑third of the total membership; a requirement that substantive motions be moved only after a day’s notice; provision for select committees to examine specific clauses (e.g., the Union Powers Committee, the Provincial Constitution Committee); and a three‑reading process for each constitutional article — general discussion, clause‑by‑clause consideration, and final voting. The rules also created a Steering Committee to prioritise the agenda and allocate time, ensuring that the Assembly could meet its self‑imposed deadline of 26 November 1949.

These procedural innovations had lasting constitutional consequences. The three‑reading model was later mirrored in the legislative procedure of Parliament under Articles 107‑108. The select‑committee system became the template for department‑related standing committees in the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. Moreover, the Rules Committee’s decision to allow ‘conscience votes’ on certain moral issues (such as the Uniform Civil Code debate) established a precedent for free votes in Parliament, a practice still invoked today.

Critically, the Rules Committee also resolved the question of language of proceedings. It mandated that debates be conducted in Hindustani (Hindi/Urdu) and English, with simultaneous translation, a compromise that pre‑figured the Official Language provisions of Part XVII. The committee’s minutes, preserved in the Constituent Assembly Debates, remain a primary source for interpreting the original intent behind procedural articles such as Article 118 (rules of procedure for Parliament) and Article 119 (regulation of procedure in state legislatures).

The Doctrine of Eclipse and Severability: Judicial Techniques for Pre‑Constitutional and Post‑Constitutional Laws

When the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, a vast body of pre‑constitutional legislation — enacted under the Government of India Act 1935 — remained on the statute book. Articles 13(1) and 13(2) declared that any law inconsistent with the Fundamental Rights would be void to the extent of the inconsistency. The Supreme Court developed two complementary doctrines to manage this transition: eclipse and severability.

Doctrine of Eclipse. In Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955), the Court held that a pre‑constitutional law which contravened a Fundamental Right did not die but became eclipsed — dormant — until the constitutional impediment was removed. If the offending Fundamental Right was later amended (e.g., the First Amendment’s insertion of Article 31A), the eclipsed law revived automatically. The rationale: the legislature’s original intent remained valid; only the constitutional barrier prevented operation. This doctrine applies exclusively to pre‑constitutional laws; post‑constitutional laws that violate Fundamental Rights are void ab initio under Article 13(2) and cannot be revived by subsequent amendment.

Doctrine of Severability. In R. M. D. C. v. Union of India (1957), the Court articulated that when a statute contains both constitutional and unconstitutional provisions, the valid portions may be severed and enforced if they are independent of the invalid part and the legislature would have enacted them separately. The test involves three questions: (1) Can the valid part stand alone? (2) Is there a legislative intent to enact the valid part irrespective of the invalid part? (3) Does severance alter the statute’s essential nature? If the answers are affirmative, the statute survives in its truncated form. This principle was reinforced in State of Bombay v. F. N. Balsara (1951) and later in K. A. Abbas v. Union of India (1971) concerning the Cinematograph Act.

Together, these doctrines preserve legislative continuity while upholding constitutional supremacy. Eclipse prevents a legislative vacuum by allowing dormant laws to spring back when the constitutional obstacle disappears; severability saves the remainder of a statute from total invalidation, respecting the principle of ut res magis valeat quam pereat (let the thing rather have effect than perish). Both doctrines illustrate the Court’s role as a constitutional surgeon — excising only the diseased tissue while keeping the body of law functional.

Worked Illustration
A 1948 provincial law authorised compulsory acquisition of land for public purposes without compensation. After the Constitution, Article 31 (original) guaranteed compensation. The law is challenged in 1952. In 1951, the First Amendment inserted Article 31A, protecting certain acquisition laws from Fundamental Rights challenge. Explain the fate of the 1948 law under the doctrines of eclipse and severability.
The 1948 law is pre‑constitutional. Under Article 13(1), its provision denying compensation is inconsistent with Article 31 and therefore becomes eclipsed — it is not dead but dormant. When Article 31A is inserted in 1951, the constitutional barrier is removed; the eclipsed provision revives and the law operates fully. Severability is not needed because the entire law is saved by eclipse; however, if the law also contained a separate, unrelated provision (e.g., a procedural rule for land records) that was constitutional, that provision would remain in force throughout, unaffected by eclipse.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks whether a pre‑constitutional law “revives” after a constitutional amendment, always invoke the eclipse doctrine and cite Bhikaji Narain Dhakras. For post‑constitutional laws, remember they are void ab initio and cannot be revived — cite Article 13(2). For severability, apply the three‑fold test from R. M. D. C. and check whether the valid part can function independently. A quick mental checklist: (1) pre‑ or post‑constitutional? (2) Is the inconsistency with a Fundamental Right? (3) Has the Right been amended? (4) Can the rest of the statute stand alone? This structure yields full marks.

The Constitutional Design of All‑India Services under Article 312: Integration of the Civil Service

Article 312 empowers Parliament to create one or more All‑India Services (AIS) common to the Union and the States, provided the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by not less than two‑thirds of the members present and voting. This provision was a deliberate departure from the Government of India Act 1935, which maintained separate provincial and central services. The Constituent Assembly’s Committee on the Services (chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel) recommended an integrated bureaucracy to ensure administrative cohesion, national standards, and a pool of officers transferable across the Union and States.

The first All‑India Service created under Article 312 was the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) in 1951, followed by the Indian Police Service (IPS) (1951) and the Indian Forest Service (IFoS) (1966). The All‑India Services Act, 1951 provides the statutory framework: recruitment through the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC), common training at the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration, and a cadre allocation system that assigns officers to State cadres while retaining their All‑India character. The Act also establishes the All‑India Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, ensuring uniform disciplinary standards.

Constitutionally, AIS officers hold a dual allegiance: they are appointed by the President (Union) but serve under the State government when posted to a State cadre. Article 312(2) clarifies that the conditions of service of AIS officers shall be regulated by Parliament, and until Parliament legislates, by rules made by the President. This arrangement was upheld in Union of India v. S. K. Sharma (1975), where the Court affirmed that the Centre’s control over recruitment and discipline does not violate federalism because the service is a constitutional creation designed for national integration.

The AIS model has been both praised for fostering a meritocratic, mobile civil service and criticised for centralising power. The Sarkaria Commission (1988) recommended greater State participation in cadre management, leading to the Indian Administrative Service (Cadre) Rules amendments in 2008. Nevertheless, Article 312 remains the constitutional bedrock for a unified administrative architecture, distinguishing India’s federal design from classical federations where civil services are exclusively State‑based.

The Preamble's Phrase 'We, the People of India': Popular Sovereignty and Judicial Interpretation

The opening words of the Preamble — “WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA” — were adopted on 26 November 1949 after a brief debate in the Constituent Assembly. The phrase was moved by Dr B. R. Ambedkar on behalf of the Drafting Committee, replacing the earlier formulation “We, the people of the States and territories comprising India”. The change signalled a shift from a compact of princely units to a single sovereign people, echoing the American “We the People” but rooted in the Indian independence movement’s claim that legitimacy derives from the masses, not the Crown.

Judicially, the phrase has been invoked to anchor three core principles. First, popular sovereignty: in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the majority held that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution and that “We, the People” signifies that the Constitution’s authority flows from the people, making the basic structure doctrine a safeguard of the people’s constituent power. Second, interpretive aid: in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Court used the Preamble’s declaration of a “Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic” to read secularism into the basic structure, stating that the people’s resolve to constitute a secular polity cannot be undone by a simple parliamentary majority. Third, justiciability of Directive Principles: in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Court observed that the Preamble’s promise of “social, economic and political justice” informs the harmonious construction of Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, preventing the latter from being rendered mere pious aspirations.

The phrase also underpins the doctrine of constitutional identity. In Justice K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), the plurality opinion referred to “We, the People” as the source of the Constitution’s identity, arguing that any amendment altering the core identity (republican, democratic, secular, federal) would require a constituent assembly, not merely the Article 368 procedure. Thus, the seven words operate as a constitutional compass, guiding interpretation, limiting amendment, and affirming that the Indian State’s legitimacy rests on the continuous consent of its people.

The Constitutional Position of the Vice‑President and the Rajya Sabha Chairman: Dual Role and Functional Significance

Articles 63‑71 establish the office of the Vice‑President of India, who is elected by an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote. The Vice‑President serves a five‑year term, is eligible for re‑election, and may be removed by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a majority of its then membership and agreed to by the Lok Sabha — a higher threshold than the simple majority required for a no‑confidence motion against the Council of Ministers.

The Vice‑President’s most visible constitutional function is the ex officio Chairmanship of the Rajya Sabha (Article 64). In this capacity, the Vice‑President presides over the Upper House, maintains order, decides points of order, and exercises a casting vote in case of a tie (Article 100). Unlike the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, the Vice‑President is not a member of the Rajya Sabha and does not participate in debates or vote except to break a deadlock. This design ensures an impartial presiding officer drawn from a national electoral college rather than a State‑based constituency.

The Vice‑President also acts as President when a vacancy occurs by reason of death, resignation, removal, or otherwise (Article 65). During such periods, the Vice‑President discharges all presidential functions, including the power to promulgate ordinances (Article 123) and to grant pardons (Article 72). The first such instance occurred in 1969 when Vice‑President V. V. Giri assumed the presidency after Dr Zakir Husain’s death. The Constitution does not provide for a Deputy Chairman to act as Vice‑President; the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (elected by the House) presides only in the Vice‑President’s absence from the Chair.

Functionally, the dual role creates a unique institutional bridge: the Vice‑President represents the federal principle (elected by both Houses) while safeguarding the legislative independence of the Rajya Sabha. The Sarkaria Commission (1988) and the Punchhi Commission (2010) both recommended that the Vice‑President’s removal procedure be aligned with that of the President (impeachment) to enhance stability, but the existing framework remains unchanged. The office thus embodies a blend of executive succession, legislative presiding, and federal representation — a constitutional innovation without direct parallel in other parliamentary federations.

  • Confusing the eclipse doctrine (pre‑constitutional laws) with severability (post‑constitutional statutes) and applying the wrong test.
  • Assuming the Vice‑President is a member of the Rajya Sabha and can vote on ordinary legislation.
  • Believing All‑India Services are created by executive order; they require a Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 312.
  • Treating the Preamble’s “We, the People” as merely rhetorical and ignoring its role in basic‑structure jurisprudence.
  • Overlooking that the Constituent Assembly’s Rules Committee also framed the language‑of‑proceedings rule, which later influenced Part XVII.
  • Thinking the Vice‑President’s removal requires the same procedure as the President’s impeachment; it is a simpler parliamentary resolution.
  • Neglecting that severability applies only when the valid part can operate independently and the legislature would have enacted it alone.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on Emergency Provisions and the Balance Between State Security and Civil Liberties

The Constituent Assembly devoted several sittings between 1948 and 1949 to the three emergency articles — 352 (National Emergency), 356 (President's Rule in States) and 360 (Financial Emergency). Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, moving the draft, argued that a sovereign state must possess the power to protect its existence against war, external aggression or armed rebellion, but he also insisted that the exercise of such power be subjected to parliamentary control. K.M. Munshi and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar supported a broad executive discretion, citing the experience of the Government of India Act 1935 where the Governor‑General could proclaim emergency without legislative sanction. H.V. Kamath and Maulana Azad warned that unchecked emergency powers could become instruments of political repression.

The original draft of Article 352 required only a proclamation by the President on the advice of the Council of Ministers, with parliamentary approval within two months. Article 356 allowed the President to assume the functions of a State government on the report of the Governor, again subject to parliamentary ratification. Article 360 empowered the President to declare a financial emergency if the financial stability of India was threatened. The Assembly adopted these provisions with the understanding that the President would act on the binding advice of the Cabinet — a principle later codified by the 44th Amendment (1978), which inserted the requirement that the proclamation under Article 352 be issued only on the written advice of the Cabinet and that both Houses of Parliament approve it within one month.

Judicial interpretation has further trimmed the scope. In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court laid down that the imposition of President's Rule under Article 356 is subject to judicial review; the Court may examine the material on which the Governor's report was based and strike down a proclamation found to be mala fide or based on irrelevant grounds. In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Court held that the power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 cannot be used to destroy the basic structure, and by implication, the emergency provisions cannot be amended to make them immune from judicial scrutiny. The 44th Amendment also removed the provision that allowed the suspension of Fundamental Rights under Article 19 during a national emergency, limiting suspension to Articles 20 and 21 only.

These debates and subsequent amendments illustrate a deliberate constitutional design: the state retains the capacity to respond to existential threats, but the exercise of that capacity is hemmed in by parliamentary oversight, judicial review, and the non‑derogable core of fundamental rights.

The Design of the Amendment Procedure under Article 368: Textual Mechanics, Judicial Gloss, and the Basic Structure Constraint

Article 368, as originally enacted, prescribed three tiers of amendment. First, amendments to provisions affecting the federal structure — such as the representation of States in Parliament, the extent of executive power of the Union and States, and the provisions of Article 368 itself — required a special majority of two‑thirds of the members present and voting in each House, a majority of the total membership of each House, and ratification by the legislatures of not less than one‑half of the States. Second, amendments to other provisions (including Fundamental Rights) required only the special majority in Parliament. Third, a residuary category allowed amendment by simple majority for matters not falling in the first two categories, though this category was rarely invoked.

The 24th Amendment (1971) inserted a new clause (1) in Article 368 declaring that Parliament may amend any provision of the Constitution by way of addition, variation or repeal, and that such amendment shall be effected in accordance with the procedure laid down in the article. This was a direct response to Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967), where the Supreme Court had held that Fundamental Rights were beyond Parliament's amending power. The 42nd Amendment (1976) went further, adding clauses (4) and (5) to Article 368 which purported to oust judicial review of constitutional amendments and to declare that there shall be no limitation on the constituent power.

The Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) upheld the 24th Amendment but struck down the 42nd Amendment's clauses (4) and (5), propounding the basic structure doctrine: Parliament's amending power under Article 368 is wide but cannot alter the Constitution's basic features — supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secularism, federalism, separation of powers, and the rule of law. Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) reinforced this by invalidating the 42nd Amendment's attempt to give primacy to Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights. Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) applied the basic structure test to amendments made after 24 April 1973, establishing a temporal threshold. The 44th Amendment (1978) restored the requirement that amendments to the federal provisions continue to need State ratification and removed the provision that allowed the extension of the term of Lok Sabha beyond five years during emergency.

Thus, the amendment procedure today operates as a layered mechanism: the textual categories in Article 368 determine the parliamentary majority and State ratification required, while the basic structure doctrine, a judicial creation, imposes an unwritten substantive ceiling on the content of any amendment.

Worked Answer Technique
Question: Explain how the basic structure doctrine limits the amending power under Article 368, citing two landmark cases.
The basic structure doctrine, evolved in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), holds that Parliament cannot amend the Constitution so as to destroy its basic features — supremacy of the Constitution, democratic republic, secularism, federalism, separation of powers, and rule of law. In Kesavananda, the Court upheld the 24th Amendment but struck down the 42nd Amendment's clauses (4) and (5) which sought to make amendments immune from judicial review. In Minerva Mills (1980), the Court applied the doctrine to invalidate the 42nd Amendment's attempt to give Directive Principles precedence over Fundamental Rights, ruling that the balance between Parts III and IV is a basic feature. Therefore, any amendment under Article 368, irrespective of the procedural majority achieved, is subject to judicial review for compliance with the basic structure.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about the amendment procedure, first classify the provision to be amended (federal, fundamental rights, or other) to identify the required majority and State ratification.
