Then, irrespective of the category, mention that the amendment must survive the basic structure test — cite Kesavananda and Minerva Mills as the two pillars. This two‑step answer covers both textual mechanics and the judicial constraint.

The Constituent Assembly's Decision on the Parliamentary System: Rejection of the Presidential Model and Its Constitutional Consequences

During the debates of November 1948, Dr. Ambedkar moved the motion for a parliamentary executive, arguing that the British model ensured continuous accountability of the executive to the legislature through the confidence mechanism. He contrasted this with the American presidential system, where the President is elected for a fixed term and cannot be removed except by impeachment, creating a rigidity unsuitable for a diverse, newly independent polity. K.M. Munshi and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar echoed this view, emphasizing that a parliamentary system would facilitate coalition‑building across linguistic, religious and regional lines. A minority, including H.V. Kamath, initially favoured a directly elected executive but withdrew after the Assembly's overwhelming support for the parliamentary model.

The Constitution consequently enshrines the parliamentary system in Articles 74 and 75. Article 74 mandates a Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister to aid and advise the President, who acts in accordance with such advice. Article 75(3) establishes collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the House of the People, making the government's survival contingent on the confidence of the Lok Sabha. The Prime Minister is appointed by the President but must be a member of either House; the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible, and a vote of no‑confidence forces resignation. The President's role is largely ceremonial, with discretionary powers limited to situations where no party commands a clear majority — such as the appointment of a Prime Minister in a hung Parliament or the dissolution of the Lok Sabha on the advice of a defeated government.

The choice has had lasting constitutional consequences. It produced a fused executive‑legislature, enabling swift legislative action but also concentrating power in the Prime Minister's Office. The confidence mechanism has led to frequent floor tests, coalition negotiations, and the phenomenon of "horse‑trading" during trust votes. The Supreme Court, in S.R. Bommai (1994), affirmed that the floor test is the only constitutional method to determine majority, reinforcing the parliamentary principle. Moreover, the parliamentary design influenced the adoption of the anti‑defection law (Tenth Schedule, 1985) to curb instability caused by legislators switching allegiance.

In sum, the Assembly's rejection of the presidential model was a deliberate institutional choice to embed accountability, flexibility, and inclusiveness in the executive, shaping the dynamics of Indian democracy for over seven decades.

The Citizenship Provisions (Articles 5‑11): Partition, Migration, and the Making of a Single Citizenship

The Constitution's citizenship scheme, contained in Articles 5 to 11 of Part II, was crafted against the backdrop of Partition and massive population movements. Article 5 conferred citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950) on every person who had domicile in the territory of India and who was born in India, or either of whose parents was born in India, or who had been ordinarily resident in India for not less than five years immediately preceding the commencement. Article 6 addressed migrants from Pakistan: those who migrated before 19 July 1948 became citizens if they or either parent or grandparent were born in undivided India and they had been ordinarily resident since migration; those migrating after that date required registration as citizens of India.

Article 7 dealt with persons who had migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 but later returned to India under a permit for resettlement; they could acquire citizenship upon fulfilling residence requirements. Article 8 extended citizenship to persons of Indian origin residing outside India who registered with an Indian diplomatic mission. Article 9 stipulated that any person who voluntarily acquired the citizenship of a foreign state would cease to be a citizen of India. Article 10 provided that every person who is a citizen under the foregoing provisions shall continue to be such, subject to any law made by Parliament. Article 11 empowered Parliament to regulate the acquisition and termination of citizenship and all other matters relating thereto.

Parliament exercised this power through the Citizenship Act, 1955, which detailed modes of acquisition (birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, incorporation of territory) and termination (renunciation, termination, deprivation). Subsequent amendments in 1986, 1992, 2003, 2005, 2015 and 2019 modified criteria — for instance, the 1986 amendment restricted citizenship by birth to those born in India only if at least one parent was a citizen; the 2003 amendment introduced overseas citizenship of India (OCI) for persons of Indian origin; the 2019 amendment provided a fast‑track path for persecuted minorities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan.

The Constitution thus establishes a single, uniform citizenship for the whole of India, rejecting the notion of State‑level citizenship that existed under the Government of India Act 1935. This unitary citizenship reinforces national integration, ensures equal rights across States, and enables free movement and residence throughout the territory.

The Linguistic Provinces Committee and the Constitutional Basis for State Reorganisation

The Constituent Assembly recognised the demand for linguistic states but chose to defer the matter to Parliament. In 1948 it constituted a Linguistic Provinces Committee under the chairmanship of S.K. Dar to examine the feasibility of reorganising provinces on linguistic lines. The committee's report, submitted in 1948, recommended postponement on the grounds that linguistic reorganisation might jeopardise national unity and administrative stability in the immediate post‑Partition period. The Assembly accepted this recommendation and left the creation of new States to the ordinary legislative process under Article 3.

Article 3 empowers Parliament by law to form a new State by separation of territory from any State, by uniting two or more States or parts of States, or by uniting any territory to a part of any State. It also authorises Parliament to increase or diminish the area of any State, alter its boundaries or change its name. Article 4 provides that any law made under Article 3 shall contain provisions for the amendment of the First Schedule (list of States) and the Fourth Schedule (allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha) and shall not be deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368.

Following the Dar Committee, the JVP Committee (Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel, Pattabhi Sitaramayya) in 1949 again advised postponement. However, popular movements — notably the Telugu‑speaking agitation for a separate Andhra State culminating in the death of Potti Sriramulu in 1952 — forced the government to act. The States Reorganisation Commission (SRC) was appointed in 1953 under Justice Fazal Ali, with K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru as members. The SRC's 1955 report recommended the creation of linguistic States, leading to the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, which redrew the map of India into 14 States and 6 Union Territories largely on linguistic lines.

Subsequent reorganisations — creation of Gujarat and Maharashtra (1960), Punjab, Haryana and Himachal Pradesh (1966), and the formation of Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand (2000) — have all been effected through ordinary legislation under Article 3, without invoking the constitutional amendment procedure. The Constitution's silence on a linguistic basis for State formation thus gave Parliament the flexibility to respond to democratic demands while preserving the federal balance.

  • Confusing the three categories of amendment under Article 368 and applying the wrong majority or ratification requirement.
  • Assuming the basic structure doctrine applies only to Fundamental Rights amendments; it applies to any amendment that alters a basic feature.
  • Believing the President can proclaim emergency on his own discretion; the 44th Amendment mandates written Cabinet advice.
  • Thinking the parliamentary system was adopted without debate; the Assembly recorded extensive discussions and a formal vote.
  • Treating Articles 5‑11 as exhaustive of citizenship law; Parliament's power under Article 11 and the Citizenship Act, 1955, provide the detailed regime.
  • Assuming linguistic reorganisation required a constitutional amendment; it is effected by ordinary law under Article 3.
  • Overlooking that the 42nd Amendment's attempt to oust judicial review of amendments was struck down in Kesavananda and Minerva Mills.

The advanced sections above integrate textual analysis, historical context, and judicial interpretation to equip aspirants for the nuanced questions that appear in the mains examination.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on the Uniform Civil Code and Article 44

The Uniform Civil Code (UCC) appears in Article 44 of the Directive Principles of State Policy, which reads: “The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.” The placement of the UCC in Part IV, rather than Part III, was the result of intense debate in the Constituent Assembly between 1947 and 1949. The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities, chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, initially recommended a justiciable provision for a common civil code. However, the Sub‑Committee on Minorities, led by H. C. Mookherjee, warned that a mandatory code would alienate religious minorities, especially Muslims, whose personal laws were protected under the Government of India Act 1935.

During the Assembly’s plenary sessions, B. R. Ambedkar argued that a uniform code was essential for national integration and gender justice, citing the disparate treatment of women under Hindu, Muslim, Christian and Parsi personal laws. He proposed that the State be empowered to enact a common code within ten years. K. M. Munshi supported Ambedkar, emphasizing that the Constitution’s secular character required a single civil framework. In contrast, Maulana Abul Kalam Azad and Frank Anthony contended that personal law was a matter of religious freedom guaranteed by Article 25, and that any compulsory unification would violate the minority rights safeguards in Articles 29 and 30.

The Assembly ultimately adopted a compromise: Article 44 was retained as a non‑justiciable directive, and the power to legislate on personal law was left to Parliament under Entry 5 of the Concurrent List. The decision reflected the political reality of 1949 — Partition had just occurred, and the leadership feared that a mandatory UCC would exacerbate communal tensions. The debates were recorded in Volumes VII and VIII of the Constituent Assembly Debates, where the vote on the amendment to make Article 44 enforceable was defeated 68 to 41.

Post‑independence judicial pronouncements have repeatedly invoked Article 44. In Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985), the Supreme Court held that a Muslim husband’s obligation to pay maintenance under Section 125 CrPC could not be overridden by personal law, and urged Parliament to enact a UCC. The judgment triggered the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, which diluted the ruling. In Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995), the Court again called for a UCC to prevent fraudulent conversions for bigamy. The 2003 John Vallamattom v. Union of India case struck down Section 118 of the Indian Succession Act as discriminatory, reinforcing the directive’s relevance. The Law Commission’s 2018 report recommended a phased approach, beginning with optional uniform marriage and divorce laws, while the 2023 Supreme Court observation in Shayara Bano v. Union of India reiterated that Article 44 remains a constitutional goal, not a justiciable right.

The UCC debate illustrates the tension between the Constitution’s transformative ambition and its accommodation of pluralism. The Assembly’s choice to keep the directive non‑justiciable has allowed successive governments to defer legislative action, while courts have used the provision as an interpretive tool to push for gender‑just reforms within existing personal laws.

The Doctrine of Eclipse: Judicial Treatment of Pre‑Constitutional Laws

The doctrine of eclipse is a uniquely Indian constitutional principle that reconciles the supremacy of fundamental rights with the continued existence of pre‑Constitutional statutes. Article 13(1) declares that all laws in force immediately before the commencement of the Constitution shall be void to the extent of inconsistency with Part III. Article 13(2) prohibits the State from making any law that takes away or abridges fundamental rights. The Supreme Court, in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955), held that a pre‑Constitutional law inconsistent with a fundamental right does not become dead; it is merely eclipsed — rendered unenforceable — until the constitutional impediment is removed by amendment.

The rationale is that the legislature’s original intent remains valid, and the law can revive automatically when the conflicting fundamental right is amended or when the inconsistency ceases to exist. In State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974), the Court clarified that the doctrine applies only to pre‑Constitutional laws; post‑Constitutional laws that violate fundamental rights are void ab initio under Article 13(2) and cannot be revived by subsequent amendment. The distinction rests on the premise that the Constitution’s framers could not have intended to nullify the entire pre‑existing statute book, which would create a legislative vacuum.

Key elements of the doctrine include: (1) the law must have been enacted before 26 January 1950; (2) the inconsistency must be with a fundamental right that existed at the commencement of the Constitution; (3) the law remains on the statute book but is unenforceable against citizens; (4) if the fundamental right is amended (e.g., the 1st Amendment 1951 inserting Article 31A‑31C), the eclipsed law revives to the extent the amendment removes the inconsistency. In Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1959), the Court applied the doctrine to the Uttar Pradesh Land Acquisition Act, 1894, holding that the provision for compensation was eclipsed by Article 31 (since repealed) but revived after the 17th Amendment inserted Article 31A.

The doctrine has been invoked in several landmark cases. In Keshavan Madhava Menon v. State of Bombay (1951), the Court held that the Press (Emergency Powers) Act, 1931, was eclipsed by Article 19(1)(a) but could be revived by a constitutional amendment. In Mahendra Lal Jain v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1963), the Court refused to apply eclipse to a post‑Constitutional law, reinforcing the void ab initio rule. The doctrine also interacts with the basic structure limitation: an amendment that seeks to revive an eclipsed law by removing a fundamental right must not violate the basic structure, as held in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980).

Critics argue that eclipse creates uncertainty because the revived law’s scope depends on the precise wording of the amendment. Proponents maintain that it preserves legislative continuity and respects the doctrine of prospective overruling. The doctrine remains a vital tool for courts to balance constitutional supremacy with the pragmatic need to keep pre‑Independence statutes operable.

Technique: Structuring a Doctrine‑of‑Eclipse Answer
Question: “Explain the doctrine of eclipse under Article 13 of the Constitution. How does it differ from the treatment of post‑Constitutional laws? Illustrate with two landmark cases.”
Answer: Begin by defining the doctrine — pre‑Constitutional laws inconsistent with fundamental rights are not void but eclipsed (Bhikaji Narain Dhakras, 1955). State the three conditions: pre‑1950 enactment, inconsistency with a fundamental right existing at commencement, and revival upon removal of the inconsistency (e.g., by constitutional amendment). Contrast with post‑Constitutional laws, which are void ab initio under Article 13(2) and cannot be revived (State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills, 1974). Cite Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1959) for revival after the 17th Amendment, and Keshavan Madhava Menon v. State of Bombay (1951) for eclipse of the Press (Emergency Powers) Act. Conclude with the basic structure check from Minerva Mills (1980) that any amendment reviving an eclipsed law must not destroy the Constitution’s basic features.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “doctrine of eclipse”, allocate the first paragraph to the textual basis (Art. 13(1) and (2)), the second to the three‑step test, the third to the pre‑ vs post‑Constitutional distinction, and the fourth to two cases with year and principle. Use the phrase “eclipsed, not dead” as a mnemonic. Avoid conflating eclipse with the doctrine of severability; they operate on different constitutional provisions.

The President's Power of Reference under Article 143: Scope, Procedure, and Landmark Opinions

Article 143 empowers the President to refer to the Supreme Court any question of law or fact which he considers to be of such a nature and of such public importance that it is expedient to obtain the Court’s opinion. The reference is made on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, as mandated by Article 74(1). The Supreme Court’s opinion is advisory; it does not bind the President or the government, but it carries significant persuasive authority and has shaped constitutional practice.

The procedural requirements are minimal: the President formulates the question, transmits it to the Court, and the Court may hear arguments from the Attorney General, the Solicitor General, and any interested parties granted leave. The Court may decline to answer if the question is purely political or lacks a legal dimension, as observed in the 1998 Special Courts Bill reference. The Court sits in a bench of at least five judges for references, reflecting the gravity of the function.

Landmark references include: (1) In re Delhi Laws Act (1951) — the first reference, where the Court upheld the validity of the Delhi Laws Act, 1912, and clarified that the President could refer questions on the constitutionality of existing legislation. (2) In re Kerala Education Bill (1965) — the Court examined the Bill’s provisions on minority educational institutions and held that the Bill violated Article 30(1); the opinion guided the state to amend the Bill before enactment. (3) In re Special Courts Bill (1998) — the Court refused to answer on the ground that the Bill involved policy choices beyond judicial review, establishing a self‑restraint precedent. (4) In re Gujarat Assembly Dissolution (2002) — the Court opined that the Governor’s report under Article 356 must be based on objective material, reinforcing the S. R. Bommai (1994) principles. (5) In re Presidential Reference on the Constitution (One Hundred and Third Amendment) Act (2019) — the Court upheld the 10% economically weaker sections quota, stating that the amendment did not violate the basic structure.

The advisory jurisdiction has also been used to resolve inter‑state disputes, such as the 1961 reference on the Punjab‑Haryana boundary, and to clarify the scope of legislative competence, as in the 1977 reference on the Constitution (Forty‑second Amendment) Act. Although the opinions are not binding, governments have generally respected them; the 1998 Special Courts Bill was withdrawn after the Court’s refusal to opine, and the 2002 Gujarat dissolution reference influenced the subsequent imposition of President’s Rule.

Critics argue that Article 143 allows the executive to seek judicial cover for politically sensitive decisions, potentially compromising judicial independence. Proponents contend that it provides a mechanism for authoritative constitutional interpretation without the need for adversarial litigation, thereby preventing constitutional crises. The Supreme Court, in In re Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal (1992), emphasized that the advisory opinion should not be used to pre‑empt judicial review in pending cases.

The Introduction and Judicial Interpretation of Fundamental Duties under Article 51A

Fundamental Duties were inserted into the Constitution by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee. Article 51A originally enumerated ten duties, ranging from respecting the Constitution, the national flag and the national anthem, to promoting harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood, protecting the environment, and developing scientific temper. The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 added an eleventh duty: “who is a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child or, as the case may be, ward between the age of six and fourteen years.”

Unlike Fundamental Rights, the duties are non‑justiciable; Article 51A does not confer any legal right or impose any legal obligation enforceable by courts. However, the Supreme Court has repeatedly used them as interpretive aids. In M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1992), the Court held that the duty to protect and improve the natural environment under Article 51A(g) reinforces the State’s obligation under Article 48A and can be invoked to direct governmental action against pollution. In Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1985), the Court linked the duty to safeguard public property (Article 51A(i)) with the principle of sustainable development.

The duties have also been employed to expand the scope of Fundamental Rights. In Chandra Bhavan Boarding School v. State of Mysore (1970), though decided before the 42nd Amendment, the Court’s reasoning anticipated the duty to promote scientific temper. In State of Karnataka v. Praveen Bhai Thogadia (2004), the Court referred to Article 51A(e) (promoting harmony) to uphold restrictions on hate speech. The 2018 judgment in Joseph Shine v. Union of India (decriminalising adultery) cited the duty to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women (Article 51A(e)) as a constitutional value supporting the decision.

Parliament has occasionally attempted to give statutory teeth to the duties. The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, and the Flag Code of India, 2002, operationalise the duty to respect the national flag and anthem. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009, gives effect to the 11th duty. However, the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Naveen Jindal (2004) refused to enforce the duty to sing the national anthem in cinema halls, holding that patriotism cannot be compelled.

Scholars debate whether the duties should be made justiciable. The Verma Committee (1999) recommended against legal enforcement, arguing that duties are moral obligations best promoted through education. The 2020 National Education Policy reiterates the integration of Fundamental Duties into school curricula. The evolving jurisprudence shows that while Article 51A remains hortatory, it serves as a constitutional compass for legislative policy and judicial reasoning, bridging the gap between rights and responsibilities.

Common Traps

  • Confusing the doctrine of eclipse with the doctrine of severability; eclipse applies only to pre‑Constitutional laws, severability to any statute.
  • Assuming Article 44 creates a justiciable right to a Uniform Civil Code; it is a non‑enforceable directive principle.
  • Believing the President’s reference under Article 143 is binding on the government; the opinion is advisory only.
  • Treating Fundamental Duties as legally enforceable obligations; they are moral duties used as interpretive tools.
  • Thinking the 42nd Amendment made the UCC mandatory; it only added the words “socialist”, “secular”, “integrity” to the Preamble.
  • Overlooking that post‑Constitutional laws inconsistent with fundamental rights are void ab initio and cannot be revived by amendment.
  • Misidentifying the Swaran Singh Committee as the body that drafted the Preamble; it recommended Fundamental Duties.

The Doctrine of Eclipse: Scope, Judicial Interpretation, and Its Distinction from Severability

The doctrine of eclipse addresses the fate of pre‑Constitutional laws that conflict with the fundamental rights guaranteed in Part III. Under Article 13(1), any law in force before the commencement of the Constitution that is inconsistent with a fundamental right does not become void ab initio; instead it is rendered dormant or “eclipsed” for the duration of the inconsistency. The law revives automatically if the conflicting fundamental right is amended or removed, because the constitutional impediment disappears. The Supreme Court first articulated this principle in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955), where a pre‑Constitutional motor vehicles tax law was held to be eclipsed by Article 19(1)(g) and later revived when the right was curtailed by the First Amendment.

Key features of the doctrine:

  • Applies only to laws enacted before 26 January 1950; post‑Constitutional laws inconsistent with fundamental rights are void ab initio under Article 13(2) and cannot be revived by subsequent amendment.
  • The eclipsed law remains on the statute book but is unenforceable against citizens whose fundamental rights it violates.
  • Revival occurs automatically upon constitutional amendment that removes the inconsistency; no fresh legislation is required.
  • The doctrine does not extend to constitutional amendments themselves; an amendment that abridges a fundamental right is subject to the basic structure test, not eclipse.

Judicial interpretation has refined the scope. In State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills (1974), the Court held that a pre‑Constitutional law eclipsed by Article 14 could be revived by the 24th Amendment which altered the scope of equality. Conversely, in Keshavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Court clarified that eclipse does not apply to constitutional amendments, reinforcing the distinction between ordinary legislation and constituent power. The doctrine is often confused with severability; however, eclipse concerns the temporal operation of a single law vis‑à‑vis a fundamental right, whereas severability deals with the surgical removal of an unconstitutional provision from a statute that contains both valid and invalid parts.

The Doctrine of Severability: Textual Basis, Judicial Tests, and Landmark Cases

Severability enables a court to preserve the constitutional portion of a statute when an unconstitutional provision can be excised without destroying the legislative scheme. The textual anchor is Article 13(2), which declares that any law made after the Constitution that contravenes a fundamental right shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void. The Supreme Court in R.M.D.C. v. Union of India (1957) formulated a three‑fold test that remains the benchmark:

  1. The unconstitutional provision must be capable of being separated from the rest of the Act, both textually and functionally.
  2. The remaining provisions must be complete in themselves and capable of being enforced independently of the severed part.
  3. The legislature must have intended to enact the valid portion even if the invalid portion had not been included; this is ascertained from the object, scheme, and language of the statute.

Application of the test varies with the degree of interdependence. In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), the Court upheld the regulatory framework of the Bombay Prohibition Act after striking down the total prohibition clause, because the licensing and control provisions could operate independently. In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Court severed Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule, which barred judicial review, while retaining the anti‑defection disqualification mechanism, holding that the core legislative purpose survived. Conversely, in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), the Court refused to sever the clause that validated the Prime Minister’s election, because the amendment was a single, indivisible enactment aimed at a specific political outcome.

Severability also operates in constitutional amendment challenges. In M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006), the Court applied the doctrine to the 77th and 81st Amendments, upholding the reservation‑in‑promotion provisions after severing the consequential seniority rule that violated Article 16(4A). The principle underscores that the Constitution prefers preservation of legislative intent over wholesale invalidation, provided the valid remainder is coherent and self‑sufficient.

Application of Severability Test
A statute contains a provision that is unconstitutional and another that is constitutional. Explain the test the Supreme Court applies to decide whether the constitutional provision can survive.
The Supreme Court in R.M.D.C. v. Union of India (1957) laid down a three‑fold test: (1) the unconstitutional provision must be severable from the rest of the statute; (2) the remaining provisions must be capable of standing independently and giving effect to the legislative intent; (3) the legislature must have intended to enact the valid part even without the invalid part. If the valid and invalid provisions are so intertwined that the legislature would not have passed the valid part alone, the whole statute falls. The Court examines the legislative scheme, the object of the Act, and whether the valid part can operate without the invalid part. In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), the Court severed the unconstitutional prohibition provisions while retaining the regulatory framework. In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Court upheld the anti‑defection law’s core provisions after severing the paragraph that barred judicial review. The test is thus both textual and purposive.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks to distinguish eclipse from severability, remember: eclipse applies only to pre‑Constitutional laws and renders them dormant until the conflicting fundamental right is amended; severability applies to any statute and allows the valid portion to survive if it is independent. Cite R.M.D.C. for severability and Bhikaji Narain for eclipse.

The President’s Pardoning Power under Article 72: Constitutional Limits, Judicial Review, and Comparative Perspective

Article 72 empowers the President to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions, or commutations of sentence in cases where the punishment is for an offence against a Union law, or where the sentence is a death sentence. The power is exercised on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74), but the President may return the advice for reconsideration once. The Supreme Court has consistently held that the pardoning power is not a mere executive grace but a constitutional duty subject to limited judicial review.

In Maru Ram v. Union of India (1980), the Court ruled that the President’s decision can be challenged on grounds of mala fide exercise, non‑application of mind, or arbitrariness. The Court declined to review the merits of the clemency decision but insisted on procedural fairness. Kehar Singh v. Union of India (1989) laid down guidelines: the President must consider the nature of the offence, the circumstances of the convict, and the public interest; the decision must be based on relevant material and not on extraneous considerations. In Epuru Sudhakar v. Government of Andhra Pradesh (2006), the Court extended similar review standards to the Governor’s pardoning power under Article 161, emphasizing that the power is not absolute.

Judicial intervention has increased in death‑penalty cases. In Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India (2014), the Court held that inordinate delay in executing a death sentence could be a ground for commutation under Article 72, linking the pardoning power to the right to life under Article 21. Union of India v. V. Sriharan (2015) reinforced that the President must consider the delay factor and that failure to do so renders the decision reviewable. Comparative practice shows that in the United Kingdom the royal prerogative of mercy is exercised on ministerial advice with no judicial review, whereas in the United States the President’s pardon power is plenary and largely non‑justiciable. The Indian model thus occupies a middle ground: constitutional text grants the power, convention binds it to ministerial advice, and the judiciary polices the boundaries of arbitrariness.

Article 131 and the Supreme Court’s Original Jurisdiction in Inter‑State Disputes: Scope, Procedure, and Key Judgments

Article 131 confers exclusive original jurisdiction on the Supreme Court to adjudicate disputes between the Government of India and one or more States, or between two or more States, provided the dispute involves a question of law or fact on which the existence or extent of a legal right depends. The jurisdiction does not extend to disputes arising out of treaties, agreements, or other instruments that expressly exclude judicial settlement, nor to matters within the exclusive domain of Parliament under Article 131’s proviso.

The Court has interpreted “legal right” broadly. In State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977), the Court entertained a suit by Karnataka challenging the Centre’s directive to allocate river water, holding that the State’s right to equitable water distribution constituted a legal right. In State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977), the Court allowed a suit concerning the Centre’s power to acquire land for a defence project, affirming that a State’s proprietary rights over land are justiciable under Article 131. The landmark State of West Bengal v. Union of India (1963) established that a dispute over the validity of a Central law affecting State powers falls within Article 131, provided the State asserts a legal right.

Procedurally, a State files a plaint as in a civil suit; the Court may appoint commissioners, receive evidence, and issue commissions. The judgment is binding and enforceable as a decree of the Supreme Court. However, the Court has cautioned that Article 131 is not a substitute for judicial review under Article 32; a State cannot invoke Article 131 to challenge the constitutional validity of a Central statute unless it demonstrates a direct infringement of its legal right. In State of Kerala v. Union of India (2020), the Court dismissed a suit challenging the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, holding that the State lacked a legal right distinct from the general constitutional challenge available under Article 32. The jurisprudence thus balances federal comity with the need for a judicial forum to resolve inter‑governmental disputes.

The Constitutional Position of the Advocate General of a State: Appointment, Tenure, and Role in State Governance

Article 165 provides for an Advocate General for each State, appointed by the Governor on the advice of the Council of Ministers. The appointee must be qualified to be a Judge of the High Court — i.e., a citizen of India who has been an advocate of a High Court for at least ten years or a judicial officer of equivalent standing. The Advocate General holds office during the pleasure of the Governor, meaning there is no fixed term and removal does not require a formal impeachment process.

The Advocate General is the highest law officer of the State. Duties include advising the State Government on legal matters, representing the State in the High Court and the Supreme Court, and performing any other legal functions assigned by the Governor. Unlike the Attorney General of India, the Advocate General does not have a right of audience in the Supreme Court as a matter of course; appearance requires specific authorization. The Advocate General may participate in the proceedings of the State Legislature and its committees but cannot vote.

Judicial pronouncements have clarified the office’s independence. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raj Narain (1975), the Supreme Court observed that the Advocate General’s advice must be free from political pressure, though the office is not constitutionally insulated from the executive. The Court in K. Veeraswami v. Union of India (1991) (though concerning a High Court judge) underscored that law officers must maintain professional integrity. The Governor’s pleasure doctrine means the Advocate General can be replaced when a new government assumes office, a practice that has sparked debate about the office’s autonomy. Some States have enacted rules prescribing a minimum tenure or requiring consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court before removal, but these are statutory, not constitutional, safeguards.

  • Confusing the doctrine of eclipse with severability; eclipse applies only to pre‑Constitutional laws, severability to any statute.
  • Assuming the President’s pardoning power is absolute; it is subject to judicial review for mala fide, arbitrariness, and non‑application of mind.
  • Believing Article 131 allows any State to challenge any Central law; the State must demonstrate a specific legal right, not merely a political grievance.
  • Thinking the Advocate General has a fixed tenure like the Attorney General; the office is held during the Governor’s pleasure and can be terminated at will.
  • Overlooking that the doctrine of eclipse revives a law automatically upon amendment of the conflicting fundamental right, without fresh legislation.
  • Misapplying the severability test by ignoring legislative intent; the Court examines whether the legislature would have enacted the valid part alone.
  • Neglecting that the President must act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers in pardoning matters, though the President may return the advice once for reconsideration.

Fundamental Duties: The 42nd Amendment, Judicial Interpretation, and Enforceability

The original Constitution of 1950 contained no chapter on Fundamental Duties. The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 inserted Part IVA consisting of Article 51A, which enumerated ten duties for every citizen of India. These duties were modelled on the Soviet Constitution and reflected the philosophy that rights and duties are correlative. The ten original duties included respect for the Constitution, the national flag and the national anthem; cherishing the noble ideals of the freedom struggle; upholding the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India; defending the country; promoting harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood; preserving the rich heritage of composite culture; protecting the natural environment; developing scientific temper and humanism; safeguarding public property; and striving towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity.

The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 added an eleventh duty under Article 51A(k): “who is a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child or, as the case may be, ward between the age of six and fourteen years.” This addition coincided with the insertion of Article 21A, making free and compulsory education a Fundamental Right.

Judicial interpretation has consistently held that Fundamental Duties are not legally enforceable by courts. In Javed v. State of Haryana (2003), the Supreme Court observed that while Fundamental Duties are not justiciable, they serve as valuable interpretive aids for Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles. The Court in AIIMS Students Union v. AIIMS (2001) reiterated that Article 51A does not create a cause of action but can guide the construction of statutes and constitutional provisions. The duties have been invoked in cases concerning environmental protection, where the duty to protect the natural environment under Article 51A(g) has been read with Article 21 to expand the right to a healthy environment.

Despite their non‑justiciable character, Fundamental Duties have acquired practical significance. They are referenced in the Model Code of Conduct for elections, in the oath administered to public servants, and in judicial reasoning when balancing individual rights against collective interests. The 42nd Amendment also inserted a provision in Article 31C (later modified) that gave primacy to Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights, a move that was partially struck down in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980). The interplay between duties, rights, and directive principles continues to shape constitutional jurisprudence.

Constitutional Provisions for Political Representation of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes: Articles 330, 332, and 334

Articles 330 and 332 provide for reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) in the House of the People (Lok Sabha) and in the Legislative Assemblies of the States respectively. The reservation is proportional to the population of SCs and STs in each State or Union Territory as determined by the Census. Article 334 originally stipulated that this reservation would cease after ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, i.e., 26 January 1960. However, successive constitutional amendments have extended the period: the 8th Amendment (1960), 23rd Amendment (1969), 45th Amendment (1980), 62nd Amendment (1989), 79th Amendment (1999), 95th Amendment (2009), and most recently the 104th Amendment Act, 2020, which extended the reservation until 25 January 2030.

The Delimitation Commission, constituted under the Delimitation Act, 2002, is tasked with readjusting the boundaries of parliamentary and assembly constituencies and determining the seats reserved for SCs and STs based on the 2001 Census. The Commission’s orders have the force of law and cannot be challenged in any court. The 84th Amendment Act, 2001 froze the total number of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies until the first Census after 2026, but allowed the readjustment of reserved seats within that freeze.

Judicial scrutiny has upheld the constitutional validity of these extensions. In K. Krishna Murthy v. Union of India (2010), the Supreme Court held that the power to extend reservation under Article 334 is a constituent power and not subject to the basic structure doctrine, provided the extension does not alter the federal balance. The Court also clarified that the reservation is a temporary special measure aimed at ensuring adequate representation, not a permanent entitlement. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. Pradeep Tandon (1975), the Court emphasized that the determination of SC/ST lists is a presidential function under Articles 341 and 342, and any inclusion or exclusion must be based on objective criteria.

The interplay between Articles 330, 332, and 334 and the Delimitation Commission’s orders ensures that political representation reflects demographic changes while maintaining the constitutional mandate of social justice. The 104th Amendment’s extension to 2030 signals a legislative consensus that the historical disadvantages faced by SCs and STs continue to warrant affirmative action in the political sphere.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “Article 334 originally fixed a ten‑year limit for reservation of seats for SCs/STs in legislatures. Explain how this limit has been extended and whether the Supreme Court has treated such extensions as amendments to the basic structure.”
The ten‑year limit in Article 334 has been extended seven times through constitutional amendment acts (8th, 23rd, 45th, 62nd, 79th, 95th, and 104th). Each extension was passed under Article 368 with the requisite special majority and, where required, ratification by half the States. In K. Krishna Murthy v. Union of India (2010), the Supreme Court held that these extensions are exercises of constituent power and do not violate the basic structure because they do not alter the federal distribution of powers or the essential features of the Constitution. The Court distinguished between the constituent power to amend Article 334 and ordinary legislative power, affirming that the extensions are constitutionally valid.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question combines Articles 330, 332, and 334, first identify the specific article referenced. Remember that Article 330 deals with Lok Sabha, Article 332 with State Assemblies, and Article 334 with the duration of reservation. Memorise the sequence of amendment acts (8th, 23rd, 45th, 62nd, 79th, 95th, 104th) and the current expiry date (25 January 2030). Cite K. Krishna Murthy for the judicial view on basic structure.

The Doctrine of Eclipse and the Doctrine of Severability: Judicial Tests and Landmark Cases

The Doctrine of Eclipse applies exclusively to pre‑Constitutional laws that are inconsistent with the Fundamental Rights conferred by Part III. Such laws are not void ab initio; they become dormant or eclipsed to the extent of the inconsistency. If the constitutional impediment is removed — for instance, by an amendment to the Fundamental Right — the law revives automatically without the need for fresh legislation. The Supreme Court first articulated this doctrine in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955), where a pre‑Constitution motor vehicles law was held to be eclipsed by Article 19(1)(g) but revived after the 1st Amendment modified Article 19(6). In State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills (1974), the Court clarified that the doctrine does not apply to post‑Constitutional laws, which are void under Article 13(2) if they contravene Fundamental Rights.

The Doctrine of Severability, by contrast, governs the fate of a statute when only a part of it is unconstitutional. The test is whether the valid portion can stand independently of the invalid portion, both in terms of legislative intent and functional separability. The Supreme Court in R.M.D.C. (Mysore) v. State of Mysore (1962) laid down the classic test: if the valid and invalid parts are so inextricably mixed that the legislature would not have enacted the valid part alone, the whole statute falls. In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), the Court severed the unconstitutional provisions of the Bombay Prohibition Act, allowing the remainder to operate. The principle was reiterated in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), where the Court upheld the Tenth Schedule’s anti‑defection provisions while striking down the bar on judicial review in paragraph 7.

A critical distinction is that eclipse concerns the temporal operation of a law vis‑à‑vis constitutional change, whereas severability concerns the structural integrity of a statute at the moment of judicial review. Both doctrines reflect the Court’s effort to preserve legislative enactments to the maximum extent compatible with the Constitution. In practice, the Court first determines whether the law is pre‑ or post‑Constitutional; if pre‑Constitutional, eclipse may apply; if post‑Constitutional, the law is void to the extent of inconsistency, and severability is then examined to save the remainder.

The Constitutional Position of the President: Election, Powers, and the Doctrine of Aid and Advice

The President of India is the constitutional head of the Union Executive. Article 54 provides for an indirect election by an electoral college consisting of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States (including the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the Union Territory of Puducherry). The system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote ensures that the President reflects the federal character of the polity. The President holds office for a term of five years from the date on which he enters upon office (Article 56) and is eligible for re‑election.

The executive power of the Union is vested in the President and is exercised either directly or through officers subordinate to him (Article 53). However, Article 74(1) mandates that there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President, and the President shall act in accordance with such advice. The 42nd Amendment (1976) made this advice expressly binding. The 44th Amendment (1978) added a proviso allowing the President to require the Council of Ministers to reconsider its advice, but the President must ultimately act on the advice tendered after such reconsideration.

The Supreme Court in Samsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974) held that the President is a constitutional head who acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, and that the satisfaction required under various articles (e.g., Article 123 for ordinances, Article 356 for President’s Rule) is the satisfaction of the Council of Ministers, not the President’s personal satisfaction. In U.N.R. Rao v. Indira Gandhi (1971), the Court ruled that the President cannot act without the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers even when the Lok Sabha is dissolved. The President’s discretionary space is thus extremely limited, confined essentially to the appointment of the Prime Minister when no party has a clear majority, the dismissal of a Council of Ministers that has lost the confidence of the House but refuses to resign, and the return of advice for reconsideration under the 44th Amendment proviso.

The President also possesses legislative powers (summoning, prorogation, dissolution, assent to bills, promulgation of ordinances), financial powers (causing the budget to be laid, recommending money bills), judicial powers (granting pardons, reprieves, respites under Article 72), and military and diplomatic powers. In each sphere, the doctrine of aid and advice operates, making the President a ceremonial head in the Westminster model adopted by the Constitution.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee on the Drafting of the Schedules: Design and Significance

While the Drafting Committee under Dr. B.R. Ambedkar is widely recognised for preparing the constitutional text, the Constituent Assembly also constituted a specialised Committee on the Drafting of the Schedules to handle the twelve (later expanded to twelve) schedules that form an integral part of the Constitution. The schedules contain detailed provisions that are too extensive for the main articles, such as the list of States and Union Territories (First Schedule), forms of oaths and affirmations (Third Schedule), allocation of seats in the Council of States (Fourth Schedule), administration of Scheduled Areas and Tribal Areas (Fifth and Sixth Schedules), the Union, State and Concurrent Lists (Seventh Schedule), the list of official languages (Eighth Schedule), validation of certain acts and regulations (Ninth Schedule), anti‑defection provisions (Tenth Schedule), and the powers of Panchayats and Municipalities (Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules).

The Committee on the Drafting of the Schedules worked in close coordination with the Drafting Committee and the various sub‑committees (e.g., the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, the Committee on Minority Rights, the Committee on Tribal Areas). Its mandate was to ensure that each schedule was internally consistent, aligned with the corresponding articles, and reflected the decisions taken in the Assembly debates. For instance, the Fifth and Sixth Schedules were shaped by the reports of the Sub‑Committee on Excluded and Partially Excluded Areas, which recommended special administrative mechanisms for tribal regions. The Seventh Schedule’s three‑fold distribution of legislative powers was the product of intense negotiation between the Union and Provincial representatives, and the Committee on the Drafting of the Schedules refined the entries to avoid overlap.

The Ninth Schedule, introduced by the 1st Amendment (1951), was later expanded by subsequent amendments to shield land reform laws from judicial review. The Committee’s design allowed Parliament to add entries to the Ninth Schedule by amendment, a feature that has been central to the basic structure jurisprudence (e.g., I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu, 2007). The Tenth Schedule, added by the 52nd Amendment (1985), and the Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules, added by the 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992), demonstrate the Constitution’s capacity for institutional innovation through the schedule mechanism.

The significance of the schedules lies in their ability to accommodate detailed administrative, fiscal, and cultural arrangements without cluttering the main text. They also provide a flexible framework for future amendments, as new schedules can be added (as happened with the Eleventh and Twelfth) and existing schedules can be amended by ordinary constitutional amendment procedures. The Committee’s work thus exemplifies the Constituent Assembly’s foresight in creating a modular constitutional architecture.

  • Confusing the doctrine of eclipse with severability; eclipse applies only to pre‑Constitutional laws, severability to any statute.
  • Assuming Fundamental Duties are justiciable; they are non‑justiciable but serve as interpretive aids.
  • Believing Article 334’s original ten‑year limit is still operative; it has been extended seven times, most recently to 2030.
  • Thinking the President can act on personal discretion in all matters; the President is bound by the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers except in narrow situations.
  • Overlooking that the Ninth Schedule’s immunity from judicial review is not absolute; laws placed after 24 April 1973 are subject to basic structure review.
  • Neglecting that the Delimitation Commission’s orders on reserved seats cannot be challenged in any court.
  • Misapplying the severability test by ignoring legislative intent; the Court examines whether the legislature would have enacted the valid part alone.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee on the Rules of Procedure and Its Impact on Constitutional Drafting

The Constituent Assembly constituted a Rules of Procedure Committee in December 1946, shortly after its inaugural sitting on 9 December 1946. The committee was chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad, who also served as the President of the Assembly. Its mandate was to frame the procedural rules that would govern the conduct of debates, the moving of motions, the handling of amendments, and the voting mechanisms for the adoption of constitutional provisions. The committee presented its report on 20 January 1947, and the Assembly adopted the rules the same day.

The rules established a quorum of one‑third of the total membership, required a two‑thirds majority for substantive amendments, and introduced a system of “division” for recorded votes. They also provided for the formation of functional committees — such as the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, the Committee on Minority Rights, and the Drafting Committee — and defined the relationship between these committees and the plenary Assembly. By institutionalising a clear amendment procedure, the rules prevented procedural deadlocks during the intense deliberations on the Objectives Resolution, the federal scheme, and the language provisions.

The procedural framework influenced the drafting timeline in two concrete ways. First, the requirement that any amendment to a clause be circulated at least 48 hours before debate forced the Drafting Committee to finalise its drafts well in advance, contributing to the relatively swift completion of the first draft by February 1948. Second, the rule that a motion for reconsideration could be moved only once per clause limited repetitive debates, allowing the Assembly to move through the 395 articles and 8 schedules within the stipulated period.

Scholars such as Granville Austin have noted that the Rules of Procedure Committee’s design reflected a deliberate choice to balance thorough deliberation with the urgency of producing a constitution before the transfer of power. The committee’s decisions on voting thresholds, for instance, ensured that the federal provisions — which required broad consensus — were not easily overridden by a simple majority, thereby embedding a structural bias toward consensus‑building that persists in the amendment process under Article 368.

In retrospect, the Rules of Procedure Committee’s work exemplifies how procedural design can shape substantive constitutional outcomes. The Assembly’s ability to adopt a lengthy, detailed constitution within two years owes much to the procedural discipline imposed by this often‑overlooked committee.

The Debate on the Uniform Civil Code in the Constituent Assembly and Its Reflection in Article 44

The question of a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) provoked some of the most impassioned exchanges in the Constituent Assembly. The debate centred on whether personal laws governing marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption should be unified under a single secular code or left to religious communities. Key protagonists included Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, who argued that a common civil code was essential for gender justice and national integration; K.M. Munshi, who warned that imposing a uniform code would alienate minorities; and Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, who emphasised the plight of women under discriminatory personal laws.

The discussion unfolded over several sittings in 1948, notably during the consideration of the Draft Constitution’s Directive Principles. Ambedkar moved an amendment to place the UCC in the chapter on Fundamental Rights, but the Assembly rejected it, fearing that a justiciable right would provoke communal tension. Instead, the Assembly adopted a compromise: Article 44 was placed in Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy), stating, “The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.” The word “endeavour” signalled a non‑justiciable, aspirational obligation.

The compromise reflected the political reality of 1949: the Partition had heightened communal sensitivities, and the leadership prioritised constitutional stability over immediate legal uniformity. Nevertheless, the Directive Principle has served as a constitutional lodestar for subsequent judicial and legislative action. The Supreme Court, in Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985), invoked Article 44 to urge Parliament to enact a UCC, while in Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) it reiterated the directive’s relevance to gender justice.

Legislatively, the Hindu Code Bills (1955‑56) reformed Hindu personal law, but Muslim, Christian, and Parsi personal laws remained largely untouched. The 2019 Supreme Court judgment in Shayara Bano v. Union of India (triple talaq) again highlighted the tension between personal law reform and the UCC directive. The debate thus continues to illustrate the interplay between constitutional aspiration, judicial interpretation, and legislative politics.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “Article 44 is a justiciable provision.” True or False? Explain the constitutional basis for your answer.
False. Article 44 resides in Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy). Article 37 expressly declares that the provisions in Part IV shall not be enforceable by any court. The word “endeavour” further indicates a moral, not legal, obligation. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that Directive Principles are non‑justiciable, though they guide legislative policy (e.g., State of Tamil Nadu v. L. Abu Kavur Bai, 1984).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question cites Article 44, immediately locate it in Part IV and recall Article 37’s non‑justiciability clause. Pair this with the Shah Bano and Sarla Mudgal references to show awareness of judicial nudges toward a UCC without converting the directive into a right.

The Constitutional Design of the Inter‑State Water Disputes Mechanism under Article 262

Article 262 empowers Parliament to provide for the adjudication of disputes relating to the use, distribution, or control of waters of inter‑state rivers and river valleys. It also expressly bars the Supreme Court and any other court from exercising jurisdiction over such disputes. Pursuant to this article, Parliament enacted the Inter‑State Water Disputes Act, 1956, which establishes a tribunal mechanism: a dispute is referred to a tribunal constituted by the Central Government, whose decision is final and binding on the parties.

The 1956 Act has been invoked in several high‑profile disputes. The Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal (constituted 1990) delivered its final award in 2007, later modified by the Supreme Court in 2018. The Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal (1969) and the Godavari Water Disputes Tribunal (1969) similarly produced awards that shaped inter‑state water sharing agreements. The Ravi‑Beas Tribunal (1986) and the Mahanadi Tribunal (2018) illustrate the continuing relevance of the mechanism.

Critics argue that the exclusion of judicial review under Article 262(2) creates a democratic deficit, as tribunal awards cannot be challenged on grounds of legal error. The Supreme Court, in State of Karnataka v. State of Tamil Nadu (2018), clarified that while it cannot review the merits of a tribunal award, it retains jurisdiction to examine whether the tribunal acted within its statutory powers or violated principles of natural justice. This limited supervisory role preserves a constitutional check without undermining the finality intended by Article 262.

The 2002 amendment to the Inter‑State Water Disputes Act introduced a time‑bound framework for tribunal constitution and award delivery, aiming to reduce delays that had plagued earlier tribunals. The 2019 amendment further streamlined the process by allowing the Central Government to notify a “single tribunal” for multiple disputes in a river basin, promoting integrated basin management.

In practice, the mechanism reflects a federal compromise: states retain control over water resources (Entry 17, State List), while the Centre facilitates dispute resolution through a quasi‑judicial body. The design underscores the Constitution’s preference for negotiated settlement backed by a binding adjudicatory forum, rather than protracted litigation.

The Evolution of the Right to Education as a Fundamental Right under Article 21A

The right to education traversed a long constitutional journey before becoming a justiciable fundamental right. The original Constitution placed education in the Directive Principles (Article 45), directing the State to provide free and compulsory education for children up to age fourteen within ten years. The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A, stating: “The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine.” Simultaneously, Article 45 was amended to refer to early childhood care and education for children below six.

The amendment was a response to persistent advocacy, the Supreme Court’s interpretation in Unni Krishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993) that the right to education flows from Article 21 (right to life), and international commitments under the Convention on the Rights of the Child. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act) operationalised Article 21A, mandating 25% reservation in private unaided schools for economically weaker sections, prescribing pupil‑teacher ratios, and establishing School Management Committees.

Judicial scrutiny followed. In Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2012), the Supreme Court upheld the 25% quota, ruling that it did not violate Article 19(1)(g) (freedom of occupation) because the State’s obligation under Article 21A justified reasonable restrictions. The Court also clarified that the RTE Act applies to minority institutions only to the extent consistent with Article 30(1).

Implementation challenges remain: infrastructure gaps, teacher vacancies, and monitoring of learning outcomes. The 2019 amendment to the RTE Act extended the deadline for compliance with certain norms and introduced provisions for learning assessments. The evolution from a non‑justiciable directive to a enforceable right illustrates the dynamic interplay between Directive Principles, judicial activism, and legislative action in expanding the constitutional guarantee of social justice.

The Doctrine of Eclipse and Its Application to Pre‑Constitutional Laws

The doctrine of eclipse holds that a pre‑Constitutional law which is inconsistent with a fundamental right does not become void ab initio; rather, it is “eclipsed” or rendered dormant to the extent of the inconsistency. The law revives if the constitutional impediment is removed, for instance by a constitutional amendment that alters the fundamental right. The Supreme Court first articulated this doctrine in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955), where a pre‑independence motor vehicles law was held eclipsed by Article 19(1)(g) but revived after the 1st Amendment modified the freedom of trade clause.

The doctrine applies exclusively to laws enacted before 26 January 1950. Post‑Constitutional laws that contravene fundamental rights are void under Article 13(2) and cannot be revived by subsequent amendments — a distinction the Court emphasised in State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974). In that case, a 1956 labour law was struck down as void, not eclipsed, because it was enacted after the Constitution’s commencement.

The eclipse doctrine interacts with the doctrine of severability. While severability allows a court to excise the unconstitutional portion of a statute and preserve the remainder, eclipse preserves the entire pre‑Constitutional statute in a dormant state. The Court in Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1959) clarified that if a pre‑Constitutional law is wholly inconsistent with a fundamental right, the whole law is eclipsed; if only a part is inconsistent, only that part is eclipsed, and the rest remains operative.

Practical significance arises when a constitutional amendment expands or contracts a fundamental right. For example, the 44th Amendment (1978) removed the right to property from Part III, converting it into a constitutional right under Article 300A. Pre‑Constitutional land acquisition laws that had been eclipsed by Article 31 (original right to property) revived fully, as the constitutional impediment ceased to exist. This revival mechanism underscores the doctrine’s role in maintaining legislative continuity while respecting constitutional supremacy.

Common Traps

  • Confusing the doctrine of eclipse with severability; eclipse applies only to pre‑Constitutional laws, severability to any statute.
  • Assuming Article 44 creates a justiciable right to a Uniform Civil Code; it is a non‑justiciable Directive Principle under Article 37.
  • Believing the Inter‑State Water Disputes Tribunal’s award is immune from all judicial scrutiny; the Supreme Court can review jurisdictional errors and natural justice violations.
  • Thinking the Right to Education under Article 21A applies to minority institutions without qualification; the Supreme Court limited its application consistent with Article 30(1).
  • Overlooking that the Rules of Procedure Committee’s quorum and amendment thresholds shaped the federal consensus required for the Constitution’s adoption.
  • Misapplying the eclipse doctrine to post‑Constitutional laws; such laws are void under Article 13(2), not eclipsed.
  • Neglecting the 86th Amendment’s simultaneous amendment of Article 45, which shifted early childhood care to a directive while making elementary education a fundamental right.

These advanced sections equip aspirants with the nuanced understanding of procedural history, directive‑principle dynamics, federal water governance, educational rights evolution, and the eclipse doctrine that examiners frequently test through comparative and application‑based questions.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee System: Steering Committee, Rules of Procedure, and the Mechanics of Consensus-Building

The Constituent Assembly functioned through a sophisticated committee architecture that translated political consensus into constitutional text. While the Drafting Committee (chaired by B.R. Ambedkar) receives the most attention, the Steering Committee (chaired by Rajendra Prasad) acted as the Assembly's executive brain, coordinating the work of over twenty committees and sub-committees, setting agendas, and resolving jurisdictional overlaps. The Rules of Procedure Committee (chaired by Rajendra Prasad, with Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar as a key member) designed the procedural framework: it mandated a two-thirds majority for substantive motions, required a quorum of one-third of the total membership (later relaxed), and established the practice of circulating draft provisions for written comments before oral debate — a procedural innovation that forced members to articulate positions on paper, creating a documented legislative history.

Critical committees included the Union Powers Committee (Nehru), which defined the Union List and residuary powers; the Provincial Constitution Committee (Patel), which drafted the state-level framework; the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities (Patel), with its sub-committees on Fundamental Rights (Munshi), Minorities (H.C. Mookherjee), and North-East Frontier Tribal Areas (Gopinath Bordoloi); and the Committee on the Functions of the Constitution (Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar), which examined the relationship between the three organs. The Order of Business Committee managed the daily schedule, while the House Committee handled logistics. The Credentials Committee vetted the representation of princely states, a politically sensitive task after the Mountbatten Plan.

The mechanics of consensus-building were deliberate. The Steering Committee often referred contentious issues to smaller "informal committees" or "conciliation committees" — for instance, the deadlock on the national language was broken by a sub-committee (Munshi-Ayyangar formula) that produced the Hindi-English compromise (Articles 343-351). The Rules of Procedure Committee's decision to allow "amendments to amendments" enabled granular negotiation; over 7,000 amendments were moved, of which roughly 2,500 were discussed and 300 adopted. The Assembly's secretariat, led by B.N. Rau as Constitutional Adviser and S.N. Mukherjee as Chief Draftsman, provided technical continuity. Rau's preparatory memoranda — comparative surveys of 60 constitutions — were circulated to all committees, ensuring a common factual baseline. This institutional design, more than any single personality, explains the Constitution's coherence despite ideological diversity.

The "Due Process" Debate in the Constituent Assembly: From "Procedure Established by Law" to Maneka Gandhi

The choice of the phrase "procedure established by law" in Article 21 — instead of the American "due process of law" — was a deliberate, contested decision recorded in the Constituent Assembly debates of December 1948. B.N. Rau, returning from consultations with U.S. Justice Felix Frankfurter, advised against "due process" because it empowered unelected judges to strike down economic legislation on substantive grounds, as the U.S. Supreme Court had done during the Lochner era (1905-1937). Rau warned that in a nascent democracy with a socialist directive (Article 39), judicial veto over land reform and labour laws would paralyse the social revolution. The Drafting Committee accepted this; Ambedkar moved the phrase "procedure established by law" on 6 December 1948, arguing that the Japanese Constitution (1947) used identical language (Article 31) and that "due process" was a "vague" term inviting judicial subjectivity.

Dissent came from K.T. Shah, who moved an amendment to insert "due process," supported by H.V. Kamath and Thakur Das Bhargava, who feared that "procedure established by law" would legitimise any legislative process, however arbitrary. Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar countered that Article 19(1)(a)-(g) and Article 22 (protection against arrest) provided sufficient substantive safeguards. The Assembly rejected "due process" by a voice vote. For 28 years, the Supreme Court interpreted Article 21 narrowly: in A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950), a six-judge bench held that "procedure established by law" meant any procedure enacted by a competent legislature, rejecting the argument that it must be "fair, just, and reasonable." The Court read Articles 19, 21, and 22 as mutually exclusive codes.

The reversal came in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978). A seven-judge bench, led by Chief Justice Beg, overruled Gopalan by holding that the procedure under Article 21 must be "fair, just, and reasonable" — effectively importing substantive due process through the back door. The Court read Article 21 in conjunction with Article 14 (equality) and Article 19 (freedoms), establishing the "golden triangle" of fundamental rights. Justice Bhagwati's concurrence explicitly invoked the Constituent Assembly debates, noting that the framers' fear of Lochner-style judicial activism was addressed by the basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973), which constrained judicial overreach while allowing rights-expansive interpretation. The Maneka Gandhi judgment transformed Article 21 into the fountainhead of unenumerated rights: privacy (K.S. Puttaswamy, 2017), speedy trial (Hussainara Khatoon, 1979), legal aid (M.H. Hoskot, 1978), and dignity in custodial settings (D.K. Basu, 1997). The Constituent Assembly's textual compromise thus became, through judicial construction, a broader guarantee than the American model it had deliberately rejected.

Examiner's Twist: Comparative Textual Analysis
A question asks: "The Indian Constitution's Article 21 uses the phrase 'procedure established by law' while the Japanese Constitution's Article 31 uses identical wording. Yet the Indian Supreme Court in Maneka Gandhi (1978) read substantive due process into Article 21, whereas the Japanese Supreme Court has consistently refused to do so. Explain the institutional reasons for this divergence."
The divergence stems from three institutional factors. First, the Japanese Constitution (1947) was imposed under Allied occupation; its Article 98 makes treaties supreme, and the Japanese Supreme Court lacks the power of concrete judicial review over legislation in the same robust sense — it exercises only abstract review in limited contexts. Second, India's basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda, 1973) gave the Supreme Court a self-created constraint against legislative overreach, which paradoxically legitimised rights-expansive interpretation because the Court could not be accused of unchecked activism — the basic structure acted as a meta-limit. Third, the Indian Constituent Assembly debates show the framers rejected "due process" to avoid Lochner-era economic substantive due process, not procedural fairness. Maneka Gandhi exploited this distinction: the Court held that "procedure" must be fair, not that the legislature's substantive policy choice was reviewable. The Japanese Court, lacking a basic structure doctrine and operating under a pacifist constitution with limited review jurisdiction, had neither the institutional incentive nor the doctrinal tool to expand Article 31. The Indian Court's "golden triangle" (Articles 14, 19, 21) provided a textual hook absent in the Japanese scheme where Article 31 stands alone.
Exam-Day Strategy: Article 21 Genealogy
Memorise the three-stage evolution: (1) Constituent Assembly rejection of "due process" (Dec 1948) citing Frankfurter/Lochner fear; (2) Gopalan (1950) narrow reading — procedure = legislative enactment; (3) Maneka Gandhi (1978) overruling — procedure = fair, just, reasonable + golden triangle linkage. For Mains, quote Justice Bhagwati's Maneka Gandhi observation: "The expression 'procedure established by law' means a procedure which is fair, just and reasonable, not fanciful, oppressive or arbitrary." This single sentence captures the doctrinal pivot and is frequently asked as a "comment" question.

The Citizenship Debates in the Constituent Assembly: Partition, Migration, and Articles 5-11

The citizenship provisions (Articles 5-11) were drafted under the shadow of Partition, making them the most politically volatile part of the Constitution. The Citizenship Committee (chaired by Sardar Patel, with B.N. Rau as adviser) produced a report in April 1947 that was overtaken by events: the Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947), the Indian Independence Act (18 July 1947), and the mass migration of 14-18 million people. The Assembly debated citizenship over five days in August 1949. Article 5 conferred citizenship at commencement (26 January 1950) on persons domiciled in India who were born in India, or either parent born in India, or ordinarily resident for five years. Article 6 granted citizenship to migrants from Pakistan who arrived before 19 July 1948 (the "permit system" date) and had resided since; those arriving after needed registration. Article 7 denied citizenship to migrants to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 unless they returned under a resettlement permit. Article 8 covered persons of Indian origin residing abroad.

The core tension was between jus soli (birth-based) and jus sanguinis (descent-based) principles. The Drafting Committee favoured jus soli modified by domicile, but Partition forced a hybrid. B.R. Ambedkar admitted on 10 August 1949: "There is no provision in the Constitution which has given so much headache to the Drafting Committee as this one." The Muslim League members (before withdrawal) and some Congress members like Maulana Hasrat Mohani argued that Article 7 penalised Muslims who fled to Pakistan in fear but intended to return. The permit system (Article 7) was a Patel-Nehru compromise: it allowed return of "genuine" refugees while screening "undesirables." The Influx from Pakistan (Control) Ordinance, 1949 and the subsequent Citizenship Act, 1955 operationalised these provisions. The 1955 Act introduced citizenship by registration, naturalisation, and incorporation of territory, and crucially, Section 6A (inserted 1985) created a special regime for Assam following the Assam Accord — a direct legislative descendant of the Partition-era compromise.

Judicial interpretation has centred on "domicile" and "migration." In State of Bihar v. Kumar Amar Singh (1955), the Supreme Court held that domicile requires both residence and intention to remain permanently. In Kulathil Mammu v. State of Kerala (1966), the Court ruled that a person who migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 but returned before 26 January 1950 on a valid permit became a citizen under Article 7. The National Register of Citizens (NRC) exercise in Assam (2019) and the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 (CAA) — which grants expedited citizenship to non-Muslim migrants from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan who entered before 31 December 2014 — represent the contemporary collision of the 1949 framework with demographic politics.
