The CAA's classification based on religion and country of origin is currently under constitutional challenge (Article 14, 15, 21, 25), with the Supreme Court yet to rule on whether it violates the basic structure by making religion a criterion for citizenship — a question the Constituent Assembly explicitly avoided by not defining citizenship on religious lines.

The Linguistic Reorganisation of States: From the Dar Commission to the States Reorganisation Act, 1956

The Constitution as adopted in 1950 did not reorganise states on linguistic lines; it retained the British provincial structure (Part A, B, C, D states) and empowered Parliament to alter boundaries by simple majority under Article 3. The Linguistic Provinces Commission (Dar Commission), appointed in June 1948 under S.K. Dar, recommended against linguistic reorganisation, citing administrative efficiency and national unity. Its report (December 1948) triggered widespread protests, especially in Telugu-speaking areas of Madras Presidency. The death of Potti Sriramulu on 15 December 1952 after a 56-day fast unto death for a separate Andhra state forced the government's hand. Prime Minister Nehru announced the formation of Andhra State on 19 December 1952 (effective 1 October 1953), the first linguistic state.

The States Reorganisation Commission (SRC) was appointed in December 1953 under Fazl Ali (with H.N. Kunzru and K.M. Panikkar). Its report (September 1955) recommended 16 states and 3 centrally administered territories based on language, with safeguards for minorities. The Commission rejected the "one language, one state" principle where it conflicted with economic viability (e.g., Vidarbha, Marathwada) or strategic considerations (e.g., Punjab's trifurcation was deferred). The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (7th Constitutional Amendment) implemented the SRC recommendations with modifications: it created 14 states and 6 Union Territories, abolished the Part A/B/C/D classification, and introduced Articles 350A (mother-tongue instruction) and 350B (Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities). The Act also amended the Seventh Schedule to adjust legislative entries.

Subsequent reorganisations followed political demands rather than the SRC framework: Gujarat and Maharashtra (1960, Bombay Reorganisation Act); Punjab's trifurcation into Punjab, Haryana, and Himachal Pradesh (1966, Punjab Reorganisation Act); Meghalaya, Manipur, Tripura (1971-72); Sikkim's integration (1975, 36th Amendment); Goa, Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram (1987); Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand (2000); Telangana (2014, Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act). The Article 3 procedure — President's recommendation, State Legislature's views (not consent), Parliament's simple majority — has been upheld as valid (Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay, 1960). The Supreme Court in Pradeep Chaudhary v. State of Haryana (2011) clarified that Article 3 does not require a fresh Presidential recommendation for every amendment to a reorganisation Bill. The linguistic principle, once feared as separatist, became the primary instrument of federal accommodation, though demands for new states (Vidarbha, Bodoland, Gorkhaland) persist, testing the Constitution's flexibility.

The Uniform Civil Code Debates in the Constituent Assembly: Article 44 and the Hindu Code Bill Controversy

Article 44 — "The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India" — was drafted as a Directive Principle, not a fundamental right, after intense debate in the Constituent Assembly. The Sub-Committee on Fundamental Rights (chaired by J.B. Kripalani, with K.M. Munshi, Hansa Mehta, and Amrit Kaur) initially included a justiciable right to a uniform civil code in its interim report (April 1947). Muslim members — B. Pocker Sahib, Mohammad Ismail, Naziruddin Ahmad — opposed it vehemently, arguing that personal law (marriage, divorce, inheritance) was integral to religious identity protected by Article 25 (then Draft Article 19). K.M. Munshi countered that a common civil code was essential for national integration and gender justice, citing the Hindu Code Bill (then under preparation) as a precedent for reforming majority personal law first.

The compromise, brokered by Patel in the Advisory Committee on Minorities (August 1947), moved the provision to the Directive Principles (Part IV) as Article 35 (later renumbered 44). The debates of 23 November 1948 reveal the fault lines: Naziruddin Ahmad moved an amendment to delete Article 35, warning it would "create discontent among Muslims." K.M. Munshi replied that the article imposed no obligation, only an "endeavour," and that the Hindu Code Bill — which reformed Hindu marriage, succession, and adoption — demonstrated the State's willingness to touch majority personal law. Dr. Ambedkar, as Law Minister, defended the Hindu Code Bill in Parliament (1951-54) against orthodox Hindu opposition, arguing that Article 44's "endeavour" applied equally to all communities. The Bill was split into four Acts (Hindu Marriage Act, 1955; Hindu Succession Act, 1956; Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956; Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956) after Ambedkar's resignation in protest over its dilution.

Judicial engagement with Article 44 has been episodic. In Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985), the Supreme Court granted maintenance to a divorced Muslim woman under Section 125 CrPC, urging Parliament to enact a UCC. The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 overturned the judgment legislatively. In Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995), the Court directed the government to file an affidavit on steps taken towards UCC. In John Vallamattom v. Union of India (2003), the Court struck down Section 118 of the Indian Succession Act (discriminating against Christians) but declined to mandate UCC. The Law Commission's 21st Report (2008) and 22nd Report (2018) recommended a piecemeal approach — reforming personal laws community by community — rather than a single code. The Uttarakhand Uniform Civil Code Act, 2024 (passed February 2024) is the first state-level UCC legislation, governing marriage, divorce, inheritance, and live-in relationships for all residents regardless of religion. Its constitutional validity under Article 44 read with Entry 5 of the Concurrent List (marriage, divorce, infants) and Article 25 (religious freedom) is likely to be tested, reviving the Constituent Assembly's unresolved tension between uniformity and pluralism.

  • Confusing the Dar Commission (1948, opposed linguistic states) with the SRC/Fazl Ali Commission (1953-55, recommended linguistic states with caveats).
  • Assuming Article 21's "procedure established by law" was a drafting error; it was a deliberate choice documented in the Constituent Assembly debates (6 December 1948) to avoid Lochner-era judicial activism.
  • Believing the Citizenship Act, 1955 reproduced the Constitution's citizenship provisions verbatim; the Act created new modes (registration, naturalisation) and the 1985 Assam Accord amendment (Section 6A) has no constitutional counterpart.
  • Thinking the Hindu Code Bill was enacted as a single statute; it was split into four Acts (1955-56) after Ambedkar's resignation, and the UCC directive (Article 44) remains unfulfilled.
  • Overlooking that the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 implemented the SRC report with modifications — e.g., Bombay State was kept bilingual (Gujarati-Marathi) until 1960, and Punjab's trifurcation was deferred until 1966.
  • Misreading Maneka Gandhi (1978) as importing American "substantive due process"; the Court imported "procedural due process" (fair, just, reasonable procedure) while keeping substantive policy review constrained by the basic structure doctrine.
  • Assuming the Constituent Assembly adopted the citizenship provisions without dissent; the debates (August 1949) saw sharp exchanges on Articles 6 and 7, with Muslim members warning of statelessness for returnees.
The Constituent Assembly's institutional design, textual compromises, and unresolved tensions continue to shape constitutional adjudication and political contestation in contemporary India.

The Constituent Assembly's Union Powers Committee and the Architecture of Centre‑State Legislative Relations

The Union Powers Committee, chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru and constituted in January 1947, was tasked with delineating the legislative competence of the Centre and the provinces. Its twelve members included B. R. Ambedkar, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, K. M. Munshi, and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar. The committee submitted its report on 16 April 1947, recommending a three‑fold distribution of subjects — Union List, State List, and Concurrent List — modelled on the Government of India Act 1935 but with a deliberately stronger Centre. The report proposed 97 entries for the Union List, 66 for the State List, and 47 for the Concurrent List; these numbers were adopted almost unchanged in the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution.

A pivotal recommendation was the vesting of residuary legislative power in Parliament (Article 248), a departure from the 1935 Act where residuary powers rested with the Governor‑General. The committee also endorsed the Centre's power to legislate on State List subjects during a Proclamation of Emergency (Article 250) and the Parliament's authority to create new all‑India services (Article 312). Debates in the Assembly saw members such as K. T. Shah and H. V. Kamath argue for a more balanced federation, but the committee's vision of a "Union of States" with a dominant Centre prevailed. The final constitutional text reflects these choices, establishing a quasi‑federal structure that has shaped Centre‑State relations for over seven decades.

The Drafting of the Citizenship Provisions: Partition, Migration, and the Debate on Articles 5‑11

The citizenship clauses (Articles 5 to 11) were drafted against the backdrop of Partition and the massive population exchange between India and Pakistan. The Drafting Committee, under Ambedkar's stewardship, presented the provisions in July 1949, and the Assembly debated them intensively on 10‑12 August 1949. Article 5 conferred citizenship at commencement on persons domiciled in India who were born in India, or whose parents were born in India, or who had been ordinarily resident for five years. Articles 6 and 7 addressed migrants: Article 6 granted citizenship to those who migrated from Pakistan before 19 July 1948, while Article 7 dealt with those who migrated after that date but returned under a permit for resettlement. Article 8 extended citizenship to persons of Indian origin residing abroad, and Article 9 stipulated that voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship terminated Indian citizenship. Article 10 ensured continuity of citizenship subject to parliamentary law, and Article 11 gave Parliament plenary power to regulate all matters of citizenship.

Muslim members such as B. Pocker Sahib and Mohammad Ismail warned that the cut‑off dates would render many returnees stateless, while Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar defended the scheme as a pragmatic response to unprecedented demographic upheaval. The Citizenship Act, 1955, enacted under Article 11, elaborated modes of acquisition (birth, descent, registration, naturalisation) and termination. The 1985 Assam Accord introduced Section 6A into the Act, creating a special regime for migrants entering Assam between 1966 and 1971; its constitutional validity under Article 11 read with Article 14 remains a live issue before the Supreme Court (Assam Sanmilita Mahasangha v. Union of India, 2014). The original debates thus continue to resonate in contemporary citizenship jurisprudence.

Technique: Locating the Constitutional Source of a Statute
Question: The Citizenship Act, 1955 was enacted under which constitutional provision?
Answer: Article 11 of the Constitution expressly confers on Parliament the power to make any provision with respect to the acquisition and termination of citizenship and all other matters relating to citizenship. The Act was passed pursuant to this plenary power.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about the constitutional basis of a law, first locate the enabling article (e.g., Article 11 for citizenship, Article 246 for legislative lists). Then verify whether the law falls within the legislative competence (Union/State/Concurrent). This two‑step check avoids the trap of citing the wrong list.

The Inclusion of Fundamental Duties: The 42nd Amendment, the Swaran Singh Committee, and Judicial Reception

Fundamental Duties were inserted into the Constitution by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, during the Emergency, as Article 51A in a new Part IVA. The immediate impetus came from the Swaran Singh Committee, constituted by the Union Government in early 1976 under the chairmanship of Sardar Swaran Singh. The committee, which included jurists such as P. N. Bhagwati and administrators like L. P. Singh, submitted its report in August 1976 recommending ten duties modelled partly on the Soviet Constitution's emphasis on civic obligations and the Japanese Constitution's duty to work. The Amendment incorporated these ten duties — ranging from respect for the Constitution and national symbols to the promotion of harmony and the protection of the environment.

The 86th Amendment, 2002 added an eleventh duty (Article 51A(k)) obligating parents to provide opportunities for education to children between six and fourteen years. Although the duties are expressly non‑justiciable, the Supreme Court has repeatedly used them as interpretive tools. In Ranganath Misra v. Union of India (1992) the Court held that duties cannot be enforced by writs but may guide statutory construction. In AIIMS Students Union v. AIIMS (2001) the Court invoked the duty to promote scientific temper to uphold reservation policies. Environmental jurisprudence, notably M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1996), has relied on the duty to protect the natural environment (Article 51A(g)) to expand the scope of Article 21. Thus, while not directly enforceable, Fundamental Duties have become a significant normative resource in constitutional adjudication.

The Preamble's Word 'Fraternity': Drafting History, Ambedkar's Vision, and Its Use in Social Justice Jurisprudence

The term "Fraternity" appears in the Preamble as one of the four pillars — Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity — and its inclusion traces back to the Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru on 13 December 1946. The Resolution declared that the future Constitution would secure "fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity of the nation." During the Preamble debates in October 1949, B. R. Ambedkar emphasised that political democracy cannot survive without social democracy, and that fraternity is the emotional bond that transforms a collection of individuals into a cohesive community. He argued that the caste system had historically denied fraternity, making its constitutional affirmation essential for the eradication of untouchability (Article 17) and the prohibition of discrimination (Article 15).

Judicial engagement with fraternity has been profound. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the majority identified fraternity as part of the basic structure, linking it to the dignity of the individual. In Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992), the Court invoked fraternity to justify reservations for Other Backward Classes, stating that substantive equality requires a sense of common brotherhood. More recently, Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) and Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) employed fraternity to strike down colonial-era provisions criminalising consensual same‑sex relations and adultery, respectively, holding that a constitutional order founded on fraternity cannot tolerate laws that stigmatise identity. The word thus operates as a bridge between the Preamble's aspirational language and the enforceable guarantees of Part III.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee on the Judiciary: Designing the Supreme Court's Original and Appellate Jurisdiction

The Advisory Committee on the Judiciary, chaired by Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar and assisted by Constitutional Adviser B. N. Rau, was constituted in March 1947 to design the higher judiciary. Its report, submitted in August 1947, recommended a Supreme Court of India with a Chief Justice and seven puisne judges (later increased), appointed by the President after consultation with the Chief Justice of India. The committee envisaged security of tenure until age 65, removal only by impeachment, and salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund — provisions that appear verbatim in Articles 124, 125, and 126.

On jurisdiction, the committee proposed three distinct heads: original jurisdiction under Article 131 for disputes between the Government of India and one or more States, or between States inter se; appellate jurisdiction under Articles 132‑134 covering constitutional, civil, and criminal appeals from High Courts; and advisory jurisdiction under Article 143 enabling the President to seek the Court's opinion on questions of law or fact of public importance. The committee also recommended the power of judicial review over legislative and executive action, a principle later cemented in Article 13. The Assembly adopted these recommendations with minor modifications, notably expanding the original jurisdiction to include disputes arising under the Constitution (Article 131). The collegium system for appointments, however, was not part of the committee's design; it evolved through the Supreme Court's own decisions in the 1990s (Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India, 1993). The Judiciary Committee's blueprint thus remains the structural backbone of India's apex court.

  • Confusing the Union Powers Committee with the Union Constitution Committee; they had distinct mandates.
  • Assuming Article 6 and 7 of the citizenship provisions apply identically to all migrants; the cut‑off dates differ.
  • Treating Fundamental Duties as justiciable rights; they are non‑justiciable but used as interpretive aids.
  • Overlooking that the word 'Fraternity' was present in the Objectives Resolution before the Preamble; it was not a 1976 insertion.
  • Believing the Judiciary Committee recommended a collegium system; the collegium evolved later through judicial decisions.
  • Misreading the residuary powers clause (Article 248) as a State power; it vests in Parliament.
  • Ignoring that the 42nd Amendment added both Fundamental Duties and the words 'Socialist', 'Secular', 'Integrity' simultaneously; they are distinct amendments.

The Constituent Assembly’s Steering Committee and the Architecture of the Constitution

The Steering Committee, constituted on 11 December 1946 and chaired by Dr Rajendra Prasad, was the principal managerial body that orchestrated the Assembly’s workflow. Its mandate covered the preparation of the agenda, allocation of time to various committees, and the sequencing of debates so that the Drafting Committee could receive reports in a logical order. The committee comprised the President of the Assembly, the Chairmen of all major sub‑committees (including the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, the Union Powers Committee, the Provincial Constitution Committee, and the Committee on the Rules of Procedure), and a few nominated members. By controlling the calendar, the Steering Committee ensured that the most contentious issues — federal distribution of powers, minority safeguards, and the language question — were debated after the foundational reports on the Objectives Resolution and the Union Constitution had been adopted.

Operationally, the Steering Committee met 23 times between December 1946 and November 1949. Its decisions were recorded in the Assembly’s proceedings and later reproduced in the “Constituent Assembly Debates” volumes. A notable intervention occurred in July 1947 when the committee postponed the discussion on the Uniform Civil Code to allow the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights to finalise its report on Articles 25‑28. This sequencing prevented a premature clash between personal law reform and the broader fundamental‑rights framework. The committee also recommended the creation of a “Committee on the Functions of the President” to clarify the executive’s constitutional position, a suggestion that shaped Article 53 and the subsequent presidential oath.

The Steering Committee’s influence extended to the final revision stage. In October 1949 it directed the Drafting Committee to incorporate the “Preamble” as a separate part, rather than as a mere preface, after the Objectives Resolution had been formally adopted on 22 January 1947. This procedural decision gave the Preamble its distinct constitutional status, later affirmed in Kesavananda Bharati (1973). The committee’s minutes reveal a deliberate effort to keep the Assembly’s work transparent: every major report was circulated to members at least ten days before debate, a practice that reduced last‑minute amendments and contributed to the relatively smooth adoption of the Constitution on 26 November 1949.

The Uniform Civil Code Debate in the Constituent Assembly: Articles 44 and 25‑28

The demand for a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) originated in the Objectives Resolution’s promise of “justice, social, economic and political” and was crystallised in Article 44 of the Directive Principles, which directs the State to “endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.” The debate unfolded primarily in the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities (chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel) and later on the floor of the Assembly between November 1948 and January 1949. Two distinct camps emerged: proponents led by K. M. Munshi, B. R. Ambedkar, and Hansa Mehta argued that a common code was essential for gender justice and national integration; opponents, notably Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, Frank Anthony, and members representing Muslim, Christian, and Parsi communities, contended that personal laws were protected under Articles 25‑28 (freedom of religion, management of religious affairs, and freedom from taxation for religious purposes).

Ambedkar’s speech on 23 November 1948 is frequently cited: he acknowledged the sensitivity of the issue but insisted that the Directive Principle was not justiciable and therefore left the timing to future legislatures. He proposed a “gradual” approach, suggesting that the State could first codify Hindu law (which materialised as the Hindu Code Bills of the 1950s) before addressing minority personal laws. The Assembly ultimately adopted Article 44 without amendment, but the accompanying debates were recorded in Volume VII of the Constituent Assembly Debates, preserving the nuanced positions. The compromise was reflected in the inclusion of Article 25(2)(b), which permits the State to regulate “secular activity” associated with religious practice, thereby leaving a constitutional opening for future reform.

Post‑independence, the Supreme Court has repeatedly invoked the UCC debate. In Shah Bano (1985) the Court urged Parliament to enact a uniform code, citing the Directive Principle. In Sarla Mudgal (1995) and John Vallamattom (2003) the Court reiterated that Article 44 remains a constitutional directive, not a justiciable right. The 42nd Amendment (1976) added the word “secular” to the Preamble, which scholars argue strengthens the moral case for a UCC, yet no comprehensive legislation has been enacted. The debate therefore illustrates how a non‑justiciable Directive Principle can shape judicial discourse and legislative agenda over decades.

Technique: Mapping Directive Principles to Judicial Reasoning
Explain how the Constituent Assembly’s treatment of Article 44 illustrates the relationship between a non‑justiciable Directive Principle and subsequent judicial interpretation.
The Assembly placed the Uniform Civil Code in Part IV (Directive Principles), explicitly rendering it non‑justiciable (Article 37). However, the recorded debates show that members intended the provision to guide future legislation. The Supreme Court, while refusing to enforce Article 44 directly, has used it as an interpretive aid: in Shah Bano the Court urged Parliament to act, in Sarla Mudgal it held that the absence of a UCC does not invalidate personal laws but underscores a constitutional aspiration, and in John Vallamattom it cited Article 44 to support a purposive reading of secularism. Thus, the Assembly’s decision to keep the UCC as a directive, coupled with the detailed debate, gave the judiciary a textual and historical basis to invoke the principle without overstepping the separation of powers.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about the “legal status” of a Directive Principle, first state its non‑justiciable nature (Art. 37), then cite the specific Assembly debate or amendment that shows legislative intent, and finally note any Supreme Court cases that have used it as an interpretive tool. This three‑step structure scores full marks for both factual accuracy and analytical depth.

The Constitutional Design of Emergency Provisions and the 44th Amendment Safeguards

The Constitution envisages three distinct emergencies: National Emergency under Article 352 (war, external aggression, or armed rebellion), State Emergency (President’s Rule) under Article 356 (failure of constitutional machinery in a State), and Financial Emergency under Article 360. The original 1950 text granted the Executive wide discretion: a proclamation under Article 352 could be issued on the “satisfaction” of the President, and Parliament’s approval was required only within two months. The 42nd Amendment (1976) further expanded executive power by allowing the President to suspend fundamental rights (except Articles 20 and 21) during a National Emergency and by extending the maximum duration of President’s Rule to three years.

The 44th Amendment (1978), enacted after the 1975‑77 Emergency, introduced critical checks. For Article 352, it mandated that the President act only on the written advice of the Cabinet, that the proclamation be laid before each House of Parliament within one month, and that it cease to operate unless approved by a special majority (two‑thirds of members present and voting) within that period. It also restored the pre‑1976 position that Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended. For Article 356, the amendment required that the proclamation be approved by both Houses within two months and limited the total duration to three years, with a mandatory parliamentary review every six months. Article 360 was left largely untouched but now also requires parliamentary approval within two months.

Judicial review of emergency proclamations was affirmed in Minerva Mills (1980), where the Court held that the satisfaction of the President is justiciable to the extent of examining whether the advice of the Cabinet was bona fide. The landmark S. R. Bommai (1994) judgment established that the imposition of President’s Rule is subject to judicial scrutiny on grounds of mala fide, irrelevance, or constitutional impropriety, and that the floor test in the State Assembly is the ultimate test of majority. These rulings, together with the 44th Amendment’s procedural safeguards, transformed emergency powers from a near‑absolute executive tool into a constitutionally constrained mechanism.

The Doctrine of Eclipse: Pre‑Constitutional Laws, Article 13(1), and Judicial Evolution

Article 13(1) declares that all laws in force immediately before the commencement of the Constitution, to the extent of inconsistency with the fundamental rights, shall be void. The Supreme Court, however, developed the “doctrine of eclipse” to avoid a wholesale invalidation of pre‑constitutional statutes. In Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955), the Court held that a pre‑constitutional law inconsistent with a fundamental right does not become dead; it is merely eclipsed — rendered unenforceable — and can be revived by a subsequent constitutional amendment that removes the inconsistency. The rationale is that the legislature’s original intent remains valid and the law merely awaits constitutional compatibility.

The doctrine was refined in Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1959), where the Court clarified that eclipse applies only to laws that were valid when enacted but later became inconsistent due to the Constitution. It does not apply to post‑constitutional laws, which are void ab initio under Article 13(2). In State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills (1974), the Court extended the doctrine to statutory provisions that were partially inconsistent, allowing the valid portions to survive. The 24th Amendment (1971), which inserted Article 13(4) to protect amendment acts from judicial review, was later struck down in Kesavananda Bharati, reaffirming that the doctrine of eclipse cannot be used to shield constitutional amendments from basic‑structure scrutiny.

Practical significance: when a pre‑1950 law (e.g., the Press (Emergency Powers) Act, 1931) conflicts with Article 19(1)(a), courts treat it as eclipsed. If Parliament later amends the Constitution to permit reasonable restrictions on press freedom, the law revives without fresh legislation. This mechanism preserves legislative continuity while respecting the supremacy of fundamental rights.

The Preamble as an Interpretive Tool in Statutory Construction and Constitutional Amendments

Although the Preamble was declared non‑justiciable in the Berubari Union (1960) advisory opinion, the Supreme Court has consistently used it as a “key to the mind of the makers” for interpreting ambiguous constitutional provisions and statutes. In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the majority held that the Preamble forms part of the basic structure, thereby limiting the amending power under Article 368. The Court reasoned that the words “Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic” and the objectives of justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity embody the Constitution’s identity.

In statutory interpretation, the Preamble aids the “purposive construction” method. For instance, in the interpretation of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, the Court in Kihoto Hollohan (1992) referred to the Preamble’s commitment to “democratic republic” to uphold the anti‑defection provisions as essential to preserving democratic integrity. Similarly, in the Navtej Singh Johar (2018) decision decriminalising consensual same‑sex relations, the Court invoked the Preamble’s promise of “liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship” and “fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual” to read down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code.

The 42nd Amendment’s insertion of “Socialist”, “Secular”, and “Integrity” into the Preamble (1976) expanded its interpretive reach. Subsequent cases — such as S. R. Bommai (1994) on secularism and the 2017 Right to Privacy judgment — have treated these words as constitutional values that inform the scope of fundamental rights. The Preamble thus functions as a living interpretive lens: it does not confer independent rights but shapes the meaning of enforceable provisions, guides the doctrine of basic structure, and informs the judicial review of constitutional amendments.

  • Confusing the Steering Committee’s procedural role with the Drafting Committee’s substantive drafting function.
  • Assuming Article 44 creates a justiciable right to a Uniform Civil Code; it remains a Directive Principle.
  • Believing the 44th Amendment removed the President’s power to proclaim Emergency; it only added procedural safeguards.
  • Thinking the doctrine of eclipse applies to post‑constitutional laws; it is limited to pre‑1950 statutes.
  • Treating the Preamble as an independent source of enforceable rights; it is interpretive, not justiciable.
  • Overlooking that the 42nd Amendment’s Preamble changes were part of a broader amendment package that also introduced Fundamental Duties.
  • Misreading the basic‑structure limitation as applying only to amendments after Kesavananda; it applies to any amendment that alters the Constitution’s identity.

The Constituent Assembly's Rules of Procedure Committee and Its Impact on Constitutional Drafting

The Rules of Procedure Committee was constituted at the very first session of the Constituent Assembly in December 1946 to frame the procedural framework that would govern the Assembly's functioning. Its mandate included drafting rules for the conduct of debates, the formation and operation of sub‑committees, the procedure for moving and voting on amendments, and the timeline for the various stages of constitution‑making. By establishing a clear order of business — general discussion, clause‑by‑clause consideration, and final voting — the committee ensured that the Assembly could process over 2,000 amendments and adopt the Constitution within a period of less than three years.

The rules also institutionalised the committee system. Apart from the Drafting Committee, the Assembly created over a dozen functional committees (e.g., Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Committee on Minority Rights, Committee on the Judiciary). The Rules of Procedure Committee defined the composition, quorum, and reporting mechanisms for each, which allowed parallel work streams and prevented procedural bottlenecks. The committee's decision to require a two‑thirds majority for substantive amendments to the draft Constitution mirrored the rigidity that would later be embedded in Article 368.

Another critical contribution was the recording and publication of debates. The rules mandated verbatim transcripts, which became the primary source for later judicial interpretation of constitutional intent. The Supreme Court has repeatedly relied on these proceedings (e.g., in Kesavananda Bharati and S. R. Bommai) to discern the framers' understanding of key concepts such as "secularism" and "federalism". Thus, the procedural architecture designed by the Rules of Procedure Committee not only facilitated the timely completion of the Constitution but also created an enduring interpretive record.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on the Union Judiciary and the Establishment of the Supreme Court

The design of the Union Judiciary was one of the most intensely debated aspects of the Constitution. The Drafting Committee, drawing on the Government of India Act 1935, the United States model of a supreme court, and the British principle of judicial independence, proposed a unified judicial hierarchy with the Supreme Court at its apex. A dedicated Sub‑Committee on the Judiciary examined issues such as the mode of appointment, tenure, removal, and the scope of jurisdiction.

On appointments, the Assembly rejected a purely executive appointment in favour of a consultative process: the President appoints judges after consultation with the Chief Justice of India and such other judges as the President may deem necessary (Article 124(2)). This formulation was intended to balance executive accountability with judicial independence. Tenure was fixed at 65 years, and removal was made possible only through a rigorous impeachment process requiring a two‑thirds majority in each House of Parliament (Article 124(4)).

Jurisdictional design combined original, appellate, and advisory functions. Original jurisdiction covered disputes between the Centre and states or among states (Article 131). Appellate jurisdiction extended to civil, criminal, and constitutional matters from High Courts (Articles 132‑134). The advisory jurisdiction (Article 143) allowed the President to seek the Court's opinion on questions of law or fact of public importance — a feature borrowed from the Government of India Act 1935 but retained to enable executive reference without litigation.

The debates also addressed the power of judicial review. While the Constitution does not expressly confer judicial review, Article 13 (laws inconsistent with fundamental rights are void) and Article 32 (right to constitutional remedies) together established the Court's authority to strike down legislation. The Assembly's records show a conscious decision to embed this power in the text rather than leave it to implication, distinguishing the Indian model from the British parliamentary sovereignty tradition.

Examiner's Trap: Confusing the Constituent Assembly's Judicial Committee with the Post‑Independence Collegium
A question asks: "Which body in the Constituent Assembly was responsible for finalising the provisions relating to the appointment of Supreme Court judges?" The options include the Drafting Committee, the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, the Rules of Procedure Committee, and the Collegium.
The correct answer is the Drafting Committee. Based on the recommendations of the Sub‑Committee on the Judiciary, the Drafting Committee formulated Article 124(2), which prescribes appointment by the President after consultation with the Chief Justice of India. The Collegium system evolved decades later through judicial interpretation in the Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association cases (1993, 1998) and was not part of the Constituent Assembly's design.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When answering questions on the Constituent Assembly's judicial design, focus on the textual provisions (Articles 124‑147) and the debates recorded in the Assembly proceedings. Avoid conflating the original appointment mechanism with the later collegium system; the latter is a judicial innovation, not a constitutional provision.

The Constituent Assembly's Treatment of Princely States and the Constitutional Provisions for Integration

The integration of over 500 princely states posed a unique constitutional challenge. The Constituent Assembly addressed this through a combination of political negotiation and constitutional provisions. A Committee on the Representation of Princely States was formed to determine how these entities would be represented in the provisional legislature and in the future Rajya Sabha. Simultaneously, the Ministry of States, under Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, negotiated Instruments of Accession and subsequent Merger Agreements.

The Constitution itself contains enabling provisions that facilitated integration. Article 2 empowers Parliament to admit new states into the Union or establish new states on such terms as it thinks fit. Article 3 authorises Parliament to form new states, alter boundaries, or change names by a simple majority. Article 4 provides that laws made under Articles 2 and 3 are not deemed amendments under Article 368, thereby bypassing the stringent amendment procedure. These articles were deliberately drafted with flexibility to allow swift territorial reorganisation.

The Assembly also debated the status of the rulers' privy purses and guarantees. Article 291 and Article 362 (later repealed by the 26th Amendment in 1971) provided constitutional recognition to the privy purses and the rulers' rights. The debates reveal a tension between honouring the commitments made during accession and the republican ethos of equality. The eventual abolition of privy purses demonstrated the Constitution's capacity to override transitional arrangements through the amendment process.

The States Reorganisation Act 1956, enacted under Article 3, gave effect to the linguistic reorganisation of states, redrawing the map of India. This legislative exercise was made possible because the Constituent Assembly had vested Parliament with plenary power over state boundaries, a departure from the rigid federal models of the United States or Australia.

The Constitutional Significance of the Preamble's Phrase 'We, the People of India' and Popular Sovereignty

The opening words of the Preamble — "We, the people of India" — were the result of deliberate drafting choices. Early drafts of the Objectives Resolution used the phrase "We, the people of the States", reflecting a confederal conception. The final version, adopted on 22 January 1947, replaced "States" with "India", signalling that the Constitution derives its authority from the collective citizenry rather than from constituent units.

This phrase has been invoked by the Supreme Court to underscore the republican character of the polity. In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the majority observed that the Preamble's declaration of popular sovereignty forms part of the basic structure, limiting the amending power under Article 368. In Union of India v. R. Gandhi (2010), the Court held that the phrase reinforces the principle that all public power is a trust exercised on behalf of the people.

The phrase also informs the interpretation of the Preamble's four objectives — justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity. Courts have treated these as constitutional values that the state is obligated to pursue, using the Preamble as a guide for statutory construction and for testing the validity of legislative and executive action. For instance, in the Right to Information jurisprudence, the Court linked the citizens' right to know to the Preamble's promise of "liberty of thought and expression" rooted in popular sovereignty.

Thus, "We, the people of India" is not a mere rhetorical flourish; it is a constitutional anchor that establishes the source of legitimacy, shapes the basic structure doctrine, and serves as an interpretive lens for the entire constitutional scheme.

The 42nd Amendment's Introduction of Fundamental Duties and Their Interpretive Link to the Preamble

The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted Part IVA, comprising Article 51A, which enumerates ten fundamental duties of citizens. Although non‑justiciable, the duties were intended to balance the fundamental rights in Part III with civic responsibilities. The duties include respect for the Constitution, the national flag and anthem, the promotion of harmony, the protection of public property, and the development of scientific temper.

The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the 42nd Amendment explicitly linked the duties to the Preamble's ideals — "socialist, secular, democratic republic" — and to the goals of justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity. The amendment's architects argued that a charter of rights without a corresponding charter of duties would be incomplete in a participatory democracy.

Judicial decisions have used Article 51A as an interpretive aid. In AIIMS Students' Union v. AIIMS (2001), the Supreme Court referred to the duty to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood to uphold restrictions on student protests that threatened public order. In Chandra Bhavan Boarding School v. State of Mysore (1970), though decided before the duties' insertion, the Court later cited Article 51A in subsequent cases to justify reasonable restrictions on fundamental rights in the interest of the duties.

The 86th Amendment (2002) added a further duty — to provide opportunities for education to children between six and fourteen years (Article 51A(k)) — reinforcing the link between the Preamble's promise of "justice, social, economic and political" and the state's obligation to enable citizens to fulfil their duties. The interplay between fundamental duties and the Preamble remains a dynamic area of constitutional jurisprudence, illustrating how non‑justiciable provisions can shape the enforcement of justiciable rights.

  • Confusing the Rules of Procedure Committee with the Steering Committee or the Drafting Committee.
  • Attributing the collegium system to the Constituent Assembly's original design.
  • Assuming the princely states were integrated solely through the Constitution without the role of the Ministry of States and Instruments of Accession.
  • Treating the phrase "We, the people of India" as a mere rhetorical flourish without constitutional significance.
  • Believing fundamental duties are justiciable or that they were part of the original Constitution.
  • Overlooking that the 42nd Amendment's fundamental duties were added alongside the Preamble changes and are used as interpretive tools rather than enforceable obligations.

The Doctrine of Eclipse and Severability: Judicial Techniques for Pre‑Constitutional and Post‑Constitutional Laws

The Constitution did not wipe the slate clean; hundreds of statutes enacted before 26 January 1950 continued to operate. Article 13(1) declares that any pre‑Constitutional law inconsistent with the fundamental rights shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void. The Supreme Court developed two complementary doctrines to manage this transition: the doctrine of eclipse and the doctrine of severability.

Doctrine of Eclipse. In Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955) the Court held that a pre‑Constitutional law which violates a fundamental right does not die permanently; it is merely eclipsed. The law remains on the statute book but is unenforceable so long as the fundamental right exists. If the right is later amended or removed, the eclipse lifts and the law revives automatically. The rationale is that the legislature never intended to repeal the statute; the Constitution merely suspends its operation. The doctrine applies only to pre‑Constitutional laws; post‑Constitutional laws that contravene fundamental rights are void ab initio under Article 13(2) and cannot be resurrected by later amendment.

Doctrine of Severability. When a statute contains both constitutional and unconstitutional provisions, the Court may excise the offending part and preserve the remainder, provided the valid portion is capable of standing alone. The test, crystallised in R.M.D.C. v. Union of India (1957), asks whether the legislature would have enacted the valid part independently of the invalid part. If the answer is yes, the statute survives in its severed form. The Court also examines whether the severed provisions are so intertwined that removal would alter the legislative scheme. In State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974) the Court applied severability to a taxing statute, upholding the valid rates while striking down the discriminatory exemption.

Interaction of the Two Doctrines. Eclipse deals with the temporal dimension — a law’s enforceability before and after the Constitution — while severability addresses the structural dimension — the internal coherence of a statute. A pre‑Constitutional law may be partially eclipsed; the unconstitutional sections are eclipsed, the rest continues. If the eclipsed sections are later removed by amendment, the doctrine of severability determines whether the remaining provisions can function independently. The Supreme Court in Keshavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) implicitly recognised this interplay when it held that the basic structure doctrine limits the amending power, thereby preventing a constitutional amendment from reviving an eclipsed law that would violate the basic structure.

Practical Significance. These doctrines prevent legislative vacuum and preserve legislative intent. They also guide lower courts: when confronted with an old statute, the judge first checks for eclipse, then applies severability if only part of the statute is problematic. The doctrines have been invoked in diverse contexts — labour laws, land reform enactments, and criminal procedure codes — ensuring continuity while respecting fundamental rights.

The Constituent Assembly's Debate on the Uniform Civil Code and Article 44: From Directive to Judicial Discourse

Article 44, placed in Part IV (Directive Principles), enjoins the State to “endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India”. The provision emerged from intense deliberations in the Constituent Assembly between 1947 and 1949. The debate reflected competing visions of nation‑building: a common civil law as a tool for national integration versus respect for personal laws rooted in religion.

Key Participants and Positions. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, as Chairman of the Drafting Committee, supported a uniform code but recognised the political sensitivity; he argued that the State should have the power to enact it when conditions were ripe. K.M. Munshi and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar echoed this, viewing a common code as essential for gender justice and secular citizenship. Conversely, members such as Maulana Hasrat Mohani and Naziruddin Ahmad warned that imposing a uniform code would alienate minorities and violate the cultural autonomy guaranteed by Articles 25‑28. The Assembly ultimately adopted a compromise: the directive was made non‑justiciable, leaving implementation to future legislatures.

Textual Evolution. The original draft of the Directive Principles (Article 35 in the Draft Constitution) read “The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code”. The word “endeavour” was deliberately chosen to signal a moral obligation rather than a legally enforceable duty. The final text in Article 44 retained this language, and the Assembly rejected amendments that would have made the provision justiciable or set a time‑frame.

Judicial Engagement. Although non‑justiciable, Article 44 has been invoked by the Supreme Court to highlight legislative inaction. In Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985) the Court, while granting maintenance under Section 125 CrPC, observed that a uniform civil code would help remove disparities in personal law. In Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) the Court reiterated the directive, urging Parliament to enact a common code to prevent fraudulent conversions for bigamy. More recently, in John Vallamattom v. Union of India (2003) the Court struck down a discriminatory provision in the Indian Succession Act, citing Article 44 as a constitutional aspiration for uniformity.

Contemporary Relevance. The debate continues to shape law‑reform commissions, the Law Commission’s 2018 consultation paper on a uniform civil code, and political discourse. The Constituent Assembly’s decision to keep the directive aspirational reflects a pragmatic federal bargain: the Constitution sets the goal, but the path remains a legislative choice, subject to the constraints of fundamental rights and the basic structure.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “Article 44 is a justiciable provision that empowers the Supreme Court to direct Parliament to enact a uniform civil code.” Identify the error and explain the correct constitutional position.
The statement is false. Article 44 is a Directive Principle of State Policy under Part IV and is expressly non‑justiciable (Article 37). The Supreme Court cannot issue a mandamus to Parliament to legislate; it can only urge or highlight the constitutional aspiration. The Court’s references to Article 44 in Shah Bano, Sarla Mudgal, and John Vallamattom are obiter dicta, not enforceable directions.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes Directive Principles with Fundamental Rights, first classify the provision (Part III vs Part IV). Remember: only Part III rights are justiciable. Article 44 is a classic trap — mark it non‑justiciable, note the judicial “urge” language, and cite Shah Bano or Sarla Mudgal as examples of judicial persuasion, not compulsion.

The Doctrine of Parliamentary Privileges: Articles 105 and 194, Judicial Interpretation, and the Balance with Fundamental Rights

Parliamentary privileges are the special rights, immunities, and powers enjoyed by each House of Parliament and its members, essential for the legislature to function without external interference. Articles 105 (for Parliament) and 194 (for State Legislatures) enumerate two core privileges: freedom of speech in the House and immunity from court proceedings for anything said or any vote given. The Constitution also empowers each House to define its other privileges, powers, and immunities by law; until such law is made, the privileges are those of the British House of Commons as on 26 January 1950.

Freedom of Speech. Article 105(1) guarantees that no member shall be liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said or any vote given in Parliament. This immunity is absolute and cannot be curtailed by any law, including the law of defamation. In Keshav Singh v. Speaker, Legislative Assembly (1965) the Supreme Court upheld the absolute nature of this privilege, holding that a member’s speech cannot be questioned in any court, even for contempt of court.

Immunity from Arrest. Article 105(2) provides that members cannot be arrested in civil cases during the session and 40 days before and after. Criminal arrest is permissible, but the House must be informed. The privilege aims to ensure attendance and prevent executive harassment.

Power to Punish for Contempt. Each House may punish any person — member or outsider — for breach of privilege or contempt. The landmark Raja Ram Pal v. Hon’ble Speaker, Lok Sabha (2007) case examined the expulsion of MPs for “cash‑for‑questions”. The Court held that the power to expel is a privilege derived from Article 105(3) and is subject to judicial review only on grounds of mala fides, violation of natural justice, or excess of jurisdiction. The Court refused to interfere with the merits of the expulsion, affirming the House’s autonomy.

Conflict with Fundamental Rights. The tension between parliamentary privileges and fundamental rights, especially Article 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech) and Article 21 (personal liberty), has been adjudicated repeatedly. In M.S.M. Sharma v. Sri Krishna Sinha (1959) the Court ruled that privileges under Article 194 prevail over the fundamental right to freedom of speech of a non‑member (the press). However, in Keshav Singh the Court balanced the privilege against the right to personal liberty, holding that the House cannot detain a person indefinitely without judicial scrutiny. The later State of Kerala v. K. Ajith (2021) reiterated that privileges are not absolute and must be exercised consistently with the Constitution’s basic structure.

Codification and Reform. Despite the constitutional mandate, Parliament has not enacted a comprehensive law defining its privileges. The Privileges Committee periodically reviews the matter, but the reliance on the British House of Commons precedent creates uncertainty. The Law Commission’s 2015 report recommended codification to align privileges with democratic accountability and fundamental rights.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee on Rules of Procedure: Drafting the Legislative Process and Its Constitutional Legacy

The Constituent Assembly’s Rules of Procedure Committee, constituted on 14 December 1946 and chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad (the Assembly’s President), was tasked with framing the rules that would govern the Assembly’s own deliberations. Its work laid the procedural foundation for India’s parliamentary democracy and influenced the subsequent Rules of Procedure of both Houses of Parliament.

Composition and Mandate. The Committee comprised 15 members representing major parties and communities, including B.R. Ambedkar, K.M. Munshi, and Maulana Abul Kalam Azad. Its mandate covered quorum, voting procedures, committee system, amendment of bills, and the conduct of debates. The Committee submitted its report on 23 April 1947, which the Assembly adopted with minor modifications.

Key Innovations. The Committee introduced the concept of a “Committee of the Whole” for clause‑by‑clause consideration of the Constitution, a practice later mirrored in the Lok Sabha’s consideration stage. It also devised the “Select Committee” and “Joint Committee” mechanisms for detailed scrutiny of bills, establishing a precedent for the modern department‑related standing committees. The rules provided for a “Question Hour” and “Zero Hour” equivalents, ensuring executive accountability from the outset.

Impact on Parliamentary Practice. When the first Lok Sabha convened in 1952, its Rules of Procedure were largely modelled on the Assembly’s rules. The Speaker’s powers to regulate debate, admit motions, and refer matters to committees trace directly to the Committee’s design. The anti‑defection provisions (Tenth Schedule) later inserted in 1985 also drew on the Assembly’s experience of party discipline and floor‑crossing.

Constitutional Significance. Although the Rules of Procedure are not part of the Constitution’s text, they acquire constitutional status through Article 118 (for Parliament) and Article 208 (for State Legislatures), which empower each House to make its own rules subject to the Constitution. The Committee’s work thus represents a rare instance where a constituent body’s procedural choices became a living constitutional convention, shaping legislative behaviour for decades.

  • Confusing the doctrine of eclipse (temporary suspension of pre‑Constitutional laws) with the doctrine of severability (excising unconstitutional portions of any statute).
  • Treating Article 44 as a justiciable mandate rather than a non‑justiciable directive principle.
  • Assuming parliamentary privileges are absolute and immune from any judicial review; the Supreme Court reviews them for mala fides and basic‑structure compliance.
  • Believing the Constituent Assembly’s Rules of Procedure Committee was a post‑Constitution body; it operated before the Constitution’s adoption and its rules were adopted by the Assembly itself.
  • Overlooking that the doctrine of eclipse applies only to pre‑Constitutional laws; post‑Constitutional laws violating fundamental rights are void ab initio.
  • Misattributing the power to expel members to the Speaker alone; expulsion is a collective privilege of the House exercised through a resolution.
  • Ignoring the distinction between freedom of speech in the House (Article 105) and the fundamental right to free speech (Article 19(1)(a)); the former is absolute, the latter is subject to reasonable restrictions.

The advanced sections above equip aspirants with the nuanced doctrinal tools and historical insights that examiners expect in high‑difficulty polity questions.

The Constituent Assembly's Committee on the Union Judiciary and the Architecture of the Supreme Court

The Union Judiciary Committee, constituted on 21 July 1947 and chaired by Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, was tasked with designing the highest court of the new republic. Its members included B.R. Ambedkar, K.M. Munshi, Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, and N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar. The Committee submitted its report on 21 August 1947, recommending a Supreme Court with three distinct jurisdictions: original (Article 131), appellate (Articles 132‑134), and advisory (Article 143). It also fixed the initial strength at a Chief Justice and seven other judges, with provision for Parliament to increase the number by law.

Appointment and Tenure Safeguards

The Committee insisted that judicial independence required a collegial appointment mechanism. It proposed that the President appoint judges after consultation with the Chief Justice of India and such other judges as the President may deem necessary. This formulation became Article 124(2). Tenure was secured until the age of 65, with removal only by impeachment on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity (Article 124(4)). The Committee rejected a mandatory retirement age of 60, arguing that a higher age would attract eminent jurists.

Original Jurisdiction and Federal Disputes

Original jurisdiction was confined to disputes between the Government of India and one or more States, or between States inter se, involving a question of law or fact on which the existence of a legal right depends. The Committee deliberately excluded disputes arising out of treaties or agreements entered into before the Constitution, leaving them to the political process. This design reflected the federal bias of the Constitution while preserving the Centre’s supremacy in inter‑governmental conflicts.

Advisory Jurisdiction and Its Limits

Article 143, modelled on Section 213 of the Government of India Act 1935, empowers the President to refer a question of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court. The Committee clarified that the Court’s opinion is advisory, not binding, but carries high persuasive value. The first reference, In re Kerala Education Bill (1958), established that the Court may decline to answer if the question is purely political or lacks a legal character.

Legacy and Subsequent Amendments

The 99th Amendment (2014) attempted to replace the collegium with the National Judicial Appointments Commission, but the Supreme Court struck it down in Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (2015), reaffirming the Committee’s original vision of judicial primacy in appointments. The current strength stands at 34 judges (including the Chief Justice) after the 2019 amendment.

The Inclusion of Fundamental Duties: Constituent Assembly Debates, the 42nd Amendment, and Judicial Interpretation

The original Constitution contained no chapter on citizens’ duties. During the Constituent Assembly debates, members such as K.T. Shah and H.V. Kamath argued for a reciprocal obligation clause, but the Drafting Committee, led by B.R. Ambedkar, considered duties as moral exhortations rather than legally enforceable norms. The idea resurfaced in the 1970s when the Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended a set of fundamental duties to balance the expansive fundamental rights. The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted Part IVA, Article 51A, listing ten duties (later eleven by the 86th Amendment, 2002).

Text and Scope of Article 51A

Article 51A enumerates duties such as abiding by the Constitution, cherishing the ideals of the freedom struggle, defending the country, promoting harmony, preserving the composite culture, protecting the environment, developing scientific temper, safeguarding public property, and striving for excellence. The 86th Amendment added the duty of parents to provide education to children aged six to fourteen. The duties are addressed to “every citizen of India”, making them inapplicable to non‑citizens and corporate entities.

Non‑Justiciability and Judicial Use

The Constitution does not provide for direct enforcement of these duties. In Chandra Bhavan Boarding and Lodging v. State of Mysore (1970) the Court held that directives in Part IV are non‑justiciable; the same reasoning extends to Part IVA. However, courts have used fundamental duties as interpretive aids. In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1988) the Supreme Court invoked the duty to protect the environment (Article 51A(g)) to justify stringent pollution control orders. In Ranganath Mishra v. Union of India (1995) the Court observed that duties serve as a “moral compass” for legislative and executive action.

Legislative Attempts at Enforcement

Several private member bills have sought to make duties enforceable, but none have succeeded. The 2002 National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution recommended retaining the non‑justiciable character while encouraging civic education. The 2019 Fundamental Duties (Enforcement) Bill lapsed with the dissolution of the Lok Sabha.

Comparative Perspective

Unlike the Indian model, the Japanese Constitution (Article 27) imposes a duty to work, and the German Basic Law (Article 20) binds all state authority to the constitutional order. India’s approach remains aspirational, reflecting the Constituent Assembly’s preference for moral suasion over coercion.

Examiner's Trap
A question asks: “Fundamental Duties under Article 51A are justiciable because they are placed in the Constitution.” Choose the correct response and explain why the statement is flawed.
The statement is false. Article 51A does not contain any enforcement mechanism, and the Supreme Court has consistently held that fundamental duties are non‑justiciable (e.g., M.C. Mehta v. Union of India). They function as interpretive guides, not as independent causes of action. The placement in the Constitution does not automatically confer justiciability; Part IV (Directive Principles) suffers the same limitation.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question links fundamental duties to judicial review, recall that courts use them only as aids to interpretation, never as standalone grounds for striking down legislation. Mention the key cases (M.C. Mehta, Ranganath Mishra) to score full marks.

Article 143: The President's Advisory Jurisdiction and Its Role in Constitutional Interpretation

Article 143 empowers the President to refer to the Supreme Court any question of law or fact which he considers of public importance. The provision mirrors Section 213 of the Government of India Act 1935, which allowed the Governor‑General to seek the Federal Court’s opinion. The Constituent Assembly retained it to enable the executive to obtain authoritative judicial guidance on contentious constitutional issues without awaiting litigation.

Procedural Requirements

The reference must be made by the President on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74). The Supreme Court may hear the reference in open court, receive written submissions, and deliver its opinion. The opinion is advisory; the President is not bound to follow it, but the Court’s reasoning carries significant weight in subsequent judicial and legislative action.

Landmark References

  1. In re Kerala Education Bill (1958): The Court declined to answer whether the Bill violated Article 30(1), stating the question was premature and political.
  2. In re Special Courts Bill (1979): The Court upheld the constitutionality of special courts for trial of offences during the Emergency, but warned against misuse.
  3. In re Presidential Poll (1974): The Court clarified that the election of the President cannot be challenged except through an election petition under Article 71.
  4. In re Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal (1992): The Court opined that the Tribunal’s award was binding, reinforcing the principle of finality in inter‑state water disputes.

Judicial Reluctance and Doctrinal Limits

The Supreme Court has occasionally refused to entertain references that are purely political, hypothetical, or involve matters pending before a court. In In re Gujarat Assembly Election (2002) the Court held that the reference sought to bypass the electoral dispute resolution mechanism, violating the basic structure principle of separation of powers.

Comparative Note

Canada’s Supreme Court Act allows the Governor in Council to refer questions; the Canadian Court’s opinions are similarly advisory but have shaped constitutional law (e.g., Reference re Secession of Quebec, 1998). India’s Article 143 has been used sparingly, reflecting a preference for adversarial adjudication.

The Distribution of Legislative Powers: The Union, State, and Concurrent Lists in the Constituent Assembly's Deliberations

The Seventh Schedule, comprising the Union List (List I), State List (List II), and Concurrent List (List III), is the constitutional blueprint for legislative competence. Its architecture was hammered out by the Union Powers Committee (chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru) and the Committee on the Distribution of Legislative Powers (chaired by Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar). Both committees drew heavily on the Government of India Act 1935, which had a Federal Legislative List and a Provincial Legislative List, but introduced a Concurrent List to accommodate subjects requiring uniform yet flexible regulation.

Union List – Exclusive Central Domain

The Union List originally contained 97 entries (now 100 after amendments). Key entries include defence, foreign affairs, atomic energy, currency, banking, inter‑state trade, and railways. The Committee deliberately placed residuary powers (Entry 97) with the Centre, a departure from the Canadian model where residuary powers rest with the provinces. This choice reflected the Assembly’s fear of fragmentation and the need for a strong Centre to preserve unity.

State List – Exclusive State Domain

The State List comprised 66 entries (now 61). Subjects such as public order, police, agriculture, land, water, and local government were assigned to the States. The Committee rejected proposals to move “police” to the Concurrent List, arguing that law‑and‑order is a core state function. However, the 42nd Amendment transferred five subjects (education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals, and administration of justice) to the Concurrent List, a move partially reversed by the 44th Amendment.

Concurrent List – Shared Legislative Space

The Concurrent List initially had 47 entries (now 52). It includes criminal law, marriage and divorce, bankruptcy, trusts, trade unions, and economic and social planning. The doctrine of repugnancy (Article 254) resolves conflicts: a State law repugnant to a Central law on a concurrent subject is void unless reserved for the President’s assent and approved. The Committee envisaged the Concurrent List as a laboratory for cooperative federalism, allowing States to experiment while the Centre sets minimum standards.

Judicial Interpretation of Legislative Competence

The Supreme Court developed the “pith and substance” test (State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, 1951) to determine the true character of a law when its incidental encroachment on another list is challenged. The “colourable legislation” doctrine prevents legislatures from achieving indirectly what they cannot do directly (K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa, 1953). The “doctrine of occupied field” holds that if Parliament has exhaustively legislated on a concurrent subject, State legislation is impliedly excluded.

Recent Developments

The 101st Amendment (2016) introduced the Goods and Services Tax, inserting Article 246A and a new GST Council, effectively creating a fiscal concurrent domain that overrides the traditional lists for indirect taxation. The 103rd Amendment (2019) added economic reservation, prompting debates on whether the Centre can legislate on “education” (a concurrent subject) without State consent. These amendments illustrate the dynamic tension between the constitutional design and evolving governance needs.

  • Confusing the advisory opinion under Article 143 with a binding judgment; the President is not constitutionally obliged to follow it.
  • Assuming fundamental duties are enforceable through writ petitions; they are non‑justiciable and serve only as interpretive aids.
  • Treating the Union Judiciary Committee’s recommendations as the final text; several provisions (e.g., judge strength) were later altered by constitutional amendments.
  • Believing the Concurrent List gives States equal legislative power; Central law prevails in case of repugnancy unless the State law receives Presidential assent.
  • Overlooking that the residuary powers belong to the Centre (Entry 97, Union List), not to the States, a point frequently tested in federalism questions.
  • Misreading the 42nd Amendment’s transfer of subjects as permanent; the 44th Amendment restored several to the State List.
  • Ignoring the distinction between “pith and substance” (determining legislative competence) and “colourable legislation” (testing mala fide exercise of power).

These advanced sections equip aspirants with the doctrinal depth and historical context required for high‑difficulty polity questions.

Doctrine of Eclipse: Application to Pre‑Constitutional Laws and the Shadow of Fundamental Rights

The doctrine of eclipse holds that a pre‑constitutional statute which conflicts with a fundamental right does not become void ab initio; it merely becomes dormant — eclipsed — for the period during which the fundamental right operates. When the constitutional inconsistency is removed, either by amendment of the Constitution or by the expiry of the fundamental right, the statute revives and regains full force. The Supreme Court first articulated this principle in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (AIR 1955 SC 781), where a pre‑1950 law imposing a tax on motor vehicles was held to be eclipsed by Article 19(1)(g) but revived after the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955 placed the subject in the Ninth Schedule. The Court reiterated the doctrine in State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974) 4 SCC 656, emphasizing that eclipse applies only to laws existing before the commencement of the Constitution; post‑constitutional laws that contravene fundamental rights are void under Article 13(2) and cannot be revived by subsequent amendment. A critical nuance is that the eclipsed law remains on the statute book and can be enforced against non‑citizens or in respect of matters not covered by the fundamental right, as clarified in Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1959) Supp (1) SCR 8. The doctrine thus preserves legislative continuity while respecting the supremacy of Part III.

Doctrine of Severability: Judicial Technique for Saving Partially Unconstitutional Statutes

Article 13(1) and (2) mandate that any law inconsistent with fundamental rights shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void. The doctrine of severability permits courts to excise only the offending provision if the remainder of the statute is capable of standing independently and reflects the legislative intent. The Supreme Court laid down a two‑step test in R.M.D.C. (Mysore) Ltd. v. Union of India (1957) SCR 930: first, determine whether the invalid portion is so intertwined with the valid portion that the legislature would not have enacted the latter alone; second, apply the “blue‑pencil” rule — if the invalid words can be removed without altering the sense of the remaining text, the statute survives. In State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977) 2 SCC 241, the Court refused to sever a provision because the legislative scheme would be fundamentally altered. Conversely, in K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) SCR 88, the preventive detention act was upheld after severing the procedural safeguards that violated Article 21. The doctrine does not empower courts to rewrite legislation; it only permits removal of the unconstitutional fragment when the residual law is complete, coherent, and consistent with the legislature’s purpose.

Worked Illustration
A state enacts the “Public Health Act, 2020” containing three sections: (1) compulsory vaccination, (2) mandatory disclosure of medical records to the police, and (3) penalty for non‑compliance. Section 2 is challenged as violating Article 21. Explain how the court would apply the doctrine of severability.
Step 1 – Identify the constitutional provision: Article 13(2) read with Article 21. Step 2 – Apply the two‑step test: (a) Is Section 2 so integral that the legislature would not have enacted Sections 1 and 3 without it? The Act’s primary aim is disease control; disclosure to police is ancillary. (b) Can Section 2 be struck out without rewriting the remaining text? Yes — removing Section 2 leaves a coherent scheme of vaccination and penalties. Conclusion: The court would sever Section 2, uphold Sections 1 and 3, citing R.M.D.C. v. Union of India (1957) and the blue‑pencil rule.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “severability”, first quote Article 13, then state the two‑step test (legislative intent + blue‑pencil). Cite R.M.D.C. as the leading authority and mention the limitation that courts cannot rewrite the statute. A one‑sentence summary of the test earns full marks.

Waiver of Fundamental Rights: Judicial Limits on Voluntary Relinquishment

The Supreme Court has consistently held that fundamental rights under Part III are not subject to waiver by the individual. In Basheshar Nath v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1959) Supp (1) SCR 528, the Court declared that a citizen cannot waive the protection of Article 14 or Article 19, because these rights are conferred in the public interest and form part of the basic structure of the Constitution. The principle was reinforced in Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) 3 SCC 545, where the right to livelihood under Article 21 was held non‑waivable even if a slum dweller signed an undertaking to vacate. The rationale is twofold: (i) fundamental rights are enforceable against the State, not merely private bargains, and (ii) allowing waiver would enable the State to coerce citizens into surrendering constitutional guarantees. However, the Court has distinguished procedural rights — such as the right to be heard under Article 311(2) — which may be waived if the waiver is voluntary, informed, and not contrary to public policy (State of Punjab v. Salil Sabhlok (2003) 5 SCC 1). The right to property, after the 44th Amendment, became a constitutional right under Article 300A and can be waived by contract, but this does not extend to the original fundamental rights. Thus, any contractual clause purporting to waive a Part III right is void ab initio.

The Principle of Constitutional Supremacy versus Parliamentary Sovereignty: Indian Context and Comparative Perspective

India adopts constitutional supremacy: the Constitution is the supreme law, and every organ of the State, including Parliament, derives its authority from it. Article 13 establishes that laws inconsistent with fundamental rights are void, and Article 368 prescribes a rigid amendment procedure requiring special majorities and, for federal provisions, ratification by half the States. The basic structure doctrine, crystallised in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) 4 SCC 225, places substantive limits on Parliament’s amending power, preventing the destruction of essential features such as democracy, secularism, judicial review, and federalism. In contrast, the United Kingdom follows parliamentary sovereignty — Parliament can make or unmake any law, and no court can strike down an Act of Parliament (pre‑Factortame [1990] 2 AC 85). The Indian model therefore combines a written, rigid constitution with judicial review, whereas the British model relies on an uncodified constitution and political accountability. The table below summarises the key differences.

Constitutional Supremacy vs Parliamentary Sovereignty
FeatureIndia (Constitutional Supremacy)United Kingdom (Parliamentary Sovereignty)
Source of legal authorityWritten Constitution (Art. 368 amendment)Parliament (statute + convention)
Judicial review of legislationFull (Art. 13, 32, 226)None (courts interpret, cannot invalidate)
Amendment rigiditySpecial majority + state ratification for federal provisionsOrdinary legislative majority
Basic structure limitationYes (Kesavananda 1973)Not applicable

The Indian Supreme Court has repeatedly affirmed that Parliament’s power under Article 368 is not plenary; it cannot alter the “basic framework” (Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) 3 SCC 625) and cannot immunise constitutional amendments from judicial review (I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) 2 SCC 1). This constitutional supremacy is the bedrock of Indian federalism and rights jurisprudence.

Doctrine of Legitimate Expectation in Administrative Action: Constitutional Underpinnings and Judicial Tests

Although not enumerated in Part III, the doctrine of legitimate expectation has been read into Articles 14 and 21 as a facet of fairness and non‑arbitrariness. It arises when a public authority, by representation or consistent practice, creates an expectation in a person that a particular benefit or procedure will be continued, and the authority then departs from it without reasonable cause. The Supreme Court recognised the doctrine in State of Kerala v. K.
