Bhaskaran (1985) 1 SCC 521, holding that a government circular granting dearness allowance to a class of employees generated a legitimate expectation that could not be withdrawn arbitrarily. In Union of India v. Hindustan Development Corporation (1993) 3 SCC 499, the Court laid down a three‑prong test: (i) a clear and unambiguous representation or consistent practice; (ii) reliance by the claimant to his detriment; and (iii) the decision to frustrate the expectation must be unreasonable, disproportionate, or in breach of procedural fairness. The doctrine does not confer a substantive right; it only entitles the aggrieved party to a fair hearing before the expectation is defeated (Navjot Singh Sidhu v. State of Punjab (2005) 8 SCC 674). Courts balance the public interest against the individual’s expectation, and a change in policy justified by compelling public interest may override the expectation. The doctrine thus operationalises the constitutional guarantee of equality and due process in administrative law.

  • Confusing eclipse with severability — eclipse revives pre‑constitutional laws; severability saves post‑constitutional statutes by excising the bad part.
  • Assuming fundamental rights can be waived by contract — Basheshar Nath and Olga Tellis make waiver impermissible for Part III rights.
  • Treating legitimate expectation as a substantive right enforceable by writ — it only mandates procedural fairness before withdrawal.
  • Overlooking the blue‑pencil requirement in severability — courts cannot rewrite or add words to save a statute.
  • Equating Indian constitutional supremacy with UK parliamentary sovereignty — India has a rigid written constitution and basic structure limits.
  • Forgetting that the 44th Amendment converted the right to property into a constitutional right under Article 300A, which unlike Part III rights can be waived.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on the Term 'Republic' and Its Constitutional Consequences

The word Republic appears in the Preamble as the first descriptor of the Indian State: “Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic”. In the Constituent Assembly the choice of this term was not automatic; it followed a series of debates between members who favoured a monarchical or dominion model and those who insisted on an elected head of state. The decisive intervention came from Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, who argued that a republic signifies that the head of state is elected, directly or indirectly, by the people, and that the office is not hereditary. He cited the French and American precedents where the term denoted a government “of the people, by the people, for the people”.

The Assembly’s Sub‑Committee on the Preamble, chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru, examined the draft prepared by the Drafting Committee. The original draft used “Sovereign Democratic Republic”. The adjective “Socialist” and “Secular” were added later by the 42nd Amendment, but the word “Republic” remained unchanged from the 1949 adoption. During the debates of November 1949, members such as K. T. Shah and H. V. Kamath questioned whether a republic could coexist with a ceremonial President who exercised limited powers. Ambedkar clarified that the President’s role under Articles 52‑62 is constitutional, not monarchical, and that the President is elected by an electoral college comprising Parliament and State Legislatures, satisfying the republican criterion.

The constitutional consequences of adopting “Republic” are threefold. First, it precludes any hereditary claim to the head‑of‑state office; the President must be elected every five years under Article 56. Second, it reinforces the principle of popular sovereignty: the ultimate source of authority is the electorate, not a dynasty. Third, it informs judicial interpretation of Articles 74 and 75, where the Council of Ministers aids and advises the President, ensuring that executive power flows from the elected legislature. The Supreme Court in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) 2 SCC 179 referred to the republican character to strike down arbitrary dismissal of State governments, holding that the Centre’s power under Article 356 must respect the federal republican structure.

In comparative perspective, the Indian republic differs from the British constitutional monarchy where the Crown is hereditary. The Indian model aligns with the Irish Constitution of 1937, which also declares a “Republic” and provides for an elected President. The Constituent Assembly’s deliberate choice thus entrenched a constitutional guarantee that the head of state remains accountable to the people through their representatives, a guarantee that continues to shape the interpretation of executive power and federal balance.

The Preamble's 'We, the People of India' and the Doctrine of Popular Sovereignty in Indian Jurisprudence

The opening phrase “We, the People of India” is more than a rhetorical flourish; it operationalises the doctrine of popular sovereignty within a written constitution. The Constituent Assembly adopted this language from the Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru on 13 December 1946, which declared that “the sovereignty of India resides in the people”. The Drafting Committee retained the phrase verbatim, signalling that the Constitution derives its legitimacy directly from the citizenry, not from the Crown or any external authority.

Judicial recognition of this principle began with the Berubari Union case (1960) 3 SCR 250, where the Supreme Court held that the Preamble is not a source of substantive power but a key to the Constitution’s purpose. Later, in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) 4 SCC 225, the majority opinion treated the Preamble as part of the basic structure, affirming that the people’s sovereign will cannot be amended away. The Court observed that “the Preamble embodies the fundamental values of the Constitution and reflects the sovereign will of the people”.

The doctrine has practical implications for constitutional amendment under Article 368. In Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) 3 SCC 625, the Court struck down clauses that sought to immunise amendments from judicial review, reasoning that such clauses would nullify the people’s sovereign authority to have their fundamental rights protected. Similarly, in S. R. Bommai, the Court invoked “We, the People” to emphasise that the federal compact is a pact among the people of the States, limiting the Centre’s power to impose President’s Rule arbitrarily.

Popular sovereignty also underpins the Court’s approach to electoral reforms. In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) 2 SCC 321, the majority linked the anti‑defection law to the people’s mandate, stating that legislators owe allegiance to the electorate, not to party whips. More recently, the K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1 judgment on privacy cited the Preamble’s promise of “liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship” as an expression of the people’s sovereign claim to dignity.

Thus, “We, the People of India” functions as a constitutional touchstone: it legitimises the text, guides interpretation of amendment limits, and informs the balance between state power and individual rights. The phrase transforms the Constitution from a mere legal instrument into a social contract continuously ratified by the electorate.

Application of Popular Sovereignty in a Hypothetical Amendment Challenge
A constitutional amendment seeks to replace the phrase “We, the People of India” with “We, the Parliament of India” in the Preamble, arguing that Parliament represents the people. The amendment is passed with the required special majority and ratified by half the States. A public interest litigation challenges the amendment on the ground that it violates the basic structure. How should the Court decide?
The Court would hold the amendment unconstitutional. In Kesavananda Bharati the Supreme Court ruled that the Preamble forms part of the basic structure and that the sovereign will of the people cannot be substituted by a parliamentary declaration. The phrase “We, the People of India” embodies popular sovereignty, a core feature that Parliament cannot amend away under Article 368. Even with procedural compliance, the amendment destroys an essential feature — popular sovereignty — and therefore fails the basic structure test laid down in Kesavananda and reaffirmed in Minerva Mills. The Court would strike down the amendment, preserving the original Preamble text.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks whether a Preamble amendment is permissible, first identify the feature being altered (e.g., popular sovereignty, secularism, republican character). Then recall the basic structure test: if the feature is an “essential feature” identified in Kesavananda or subsequent cases, the amendment is invalid regardless of procedural compliance. Cite the specific case (Kesavananda, Minerva Mills, S. R. Bommai) that recognised that feature as part of the basic structure. This two‑step approach — feature identification + basic‑structure precedent — earns full marks.

The Relationship Between the Preamble and the Basic Structure Doctrine: Kesavananda Bharati and Subsequent Jurisprudence

The basic structure doctrine, crystallised in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) 4 SCC 225, holds that Parliament’s amending power under Article 368 cannot destroy the Constitution’s essential features. The Preamble was central to the majority’s reasoning. Chief Justice Sikri, writing for the majority, listed the “supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secular character, separation of powers, and federalism” as basic features, all of which find textual expression in the Preamble. The Court explicitly stated that the Preamble “contains the basic structure of the Constitution” and that any amendment abrogating its declared objectives would be ultra vires.

Subsequent jurisprudence refined this link. In Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) 2 SCC 159, the Court applied the basic structure test to strike down the 39th Amendment’s clause that insulated the Prime Minister’s election from judicial scrutiny, holding that free and fair elections — a democratic republican promise of the Preamble — constitute a basic feature. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) 3 SCC 625 further cemented the Preamble’s role by invalidating the 42nd Amendment’s attempt to curtail judicial review, reasoning that the Preamble’s guarantee of “justice, liberty, equality and fraternity” requires an independent judiciary.

The 1994 S. R. Bommai judgment extended the doctrine to federalism. The Court read the Preamble’s “Union of States” language (though not verbatim) together with Article 1 to conclude that the federal balance is a basic feature. The dismissal of State governments under Article 356 was subjected to strict judicial review, with the Court warning that the Centre cannot “destroy the federal structure which is a basic feature of the Constitution”.

In I. R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) 2 SCC 1, the Court held that even constitutional amendments placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are subject to basic structure scrutiny. The judgment reiterated that the Preamble’s objectives — sovereignty, socialism, secularism, democracy, republic — are the yardstick for testing any amendment’s constitutionality.

Thus, the Preamble operates as both a textual repository and an interpretive lens for the basic structure doctrine. It supplies the “essential features” that the Court protects from majoritarian amendment, ensuring that the Constitution’s founding compact with the people remains inviolate.

The Use of the Preamble in Interpreting Fundamental Duties under Article 51A and Directive Principles

Article 51A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976), enumerates ten Fundamental Duties. Though non‑justiciable, courts have increasingly invoked the Preamble to give these duties normative weight. The Preamble’s promise of “fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation” resonates with duties such as “to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood” (Article 51A(e)) and “to safeguard public property and to abjure violence” (Article 51A(i)).

In M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) 1 SCC 395, the Supreme Court linked the duty to protect the environment (Article 51A(g)) with the Preamble’s “socialist” and “secular” objectives, holding that the State’s obligation to preserve ecology flows from the constitutional vision of a just society. The Court observed that “the Preamble’s commitment to a socialist pattern of society imposes a duty on citizens to protect natural resources”.

Similarly, in Ranganath Misra Commission Report (2007) and subsequent judgments like National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (2014) 5 SCC 438, the Preamble’s “fraternity” clause was used to interpret the duty to “renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women” (Article 51A(j)). The Court held that the Preamble’s assurance of dignity obliges both State and citizens to eliminate gender‑based discrimination.

The interaction with Directive Principles (Part IV) is equally significant. Article 38 directs the State to secure a social order “in which justice, social, economic and political, shall inform all the institutions of the national life”. The Preamble’s “justice, liberty, equality, fraternity” provides the moral compass for this directive. In State of Kerala v. N. M. Thomas (1976) 2 SCC 310, the Court read Article 38 together with the Preamble to uphold reservations in public employment, stating that the Preamble’s egalitarian promise justifies affirmative action as a means to achieve substantive equality.

Moreover, the Preamble assists in resolving conflicts between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles. The “harmonious construction” principle, articulated in Kesavananda and refined in Minerva Mills, uses the Preamble’s overarching goals to balance individual liberty (Article 19) with socio‑economic directives (Article 39). The Court has held that neither set of provisions can be read to destroy the other because both emanate from the same sovereign will expressed in the Preamble.

In sum, the Preamble functions as a hermeneutic key that elevates Fundamental Duties from hortatory statements to enforceable constitutional expectations and aligns Directive Principles with the Constitution’s foundational values. This interpretive role reinforces the Constitution’s transformative character, ensuring that duties and directives are not merely aspirational but integral to the governance framework.

Common Traps

  • Confusing the Preamble’s declaratory nature with justiciability — the Preamble itself is not directly enforceable, but its values inform judicial review of amendments and statutes.
  • Assuming the 42nd Amendment’s insertion of “Socialist” and “Secular” altered the basic structure — the Court in Kesavananda had already recognised these as implicit in the original Preamble.
  • Treating “Republic” as merely ceremonial — the term imposes a constitutional requirement that the head of state be elected, a point repeatedly affirmed in S. R. Bommai.
  • Overlooking that Fundamental Duties, though non‑justiciable, can be read into Part III through the Preamble’s “fraternity” and “dignity” clauses, as done in M. C. Mehta and NALSA.
  • Believing the basic structure doctrine applies only to amendments — it also constrains ordinary legislation that seeks to undermine Preamble values, per Minerva Mills.
  • Neglecting the distinction between “We, the People of India” and “We, the Parliament of India” — the former embodies popular sovereignty, the latter would constitute a basic‑structure violation.
  • Failing to cite the specific case that identified a Preamble value as a basic feature — examiners expect precise references such as Kesavananda (republican, democratic), S. R. Bommai (federalism), Minerva Mills (judicial review).

The Phrase ‘We, the People of India’: Popular Sovereignty and Its Judicial Construction

The opening words of the Preamble — “We, the people of India” — embody the principle that the Constitution derives its authority from the citizenry, not from the Crown or the legislature. The Constituent Assembly deliberately chose this formulation to reject the colonial doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty and to affirm that the Constitution is a social contract enacted by the sovereign people. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) 4 SCC 225, the Supreme Court held that the Preamble’s declaration of popular sovereignty is a basic feature of the Constitution, immune from amendment under Article 368. The Court reasoned that any amendment that seeks to replace “We, the people” with “We, the Parliament” would destroy the republican character guaranteed by the Preamble and therefore violate the basic structure.

The phrase also informs the interpretation of Article 32, the right to constitutional remedies. In Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) 3 SCC 625, the Court observed that the power of judicial review flows from the people’s sovereign will expressed in the Preamble, and that Parliament cannot curtail this power through a constitutional amendment. The Court linked the Preamble’s “justice, liberty, equality, fraternity” to the enforceability of fundamental rights, stating that the people’s mandate requires an independent judiciary to guard those rights.

Subsequent jurisprudence has used the phrase to strike down attempts to dilute democratic accountability. In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) 3 SCC 1, the Court held that the dismissal of a state government under Article 356 must be subject to judicial scrutiny because the Preamble’s commitment to a “democratic republic” obliges the Centre to respect the federal balance ordained by the people. The Court emphasized that “We, the people” includes the peoples of the states, and any unilateral central action undermines the federal compact.

The phrase also underpins the doctrine of constitutional morality. In Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) 10 SCC 1, the Court invoked “We, the people” to argue that constitutional morality demands protection of minority rights against majoritarian impulses, because the sovereign people encompass all citizens, not merely the majority. This reading reinforces the transformative potential of the Preamble as a living charter of popular sovereignty.

The 44th Amendment and the Restoration of Judicial Review over Constitutional Amendments

The 44th Amendment Act, 1978, enacted after the Emergency, reversed several provisions of the 42nd Amendment that had curtailed judicial review. Notably, it restored the power of the Supreme Court and High Courts to review constitutional amendments under Article 13(2) by deleting Article 31C’s blanket protection for laws implementing Directive Principles. The amendment also re‑inserted the word “judicial review” in Article 32 and Article 226, affirming that the courts could examine the constitutional validity of any law, including amendment acts.

In Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) 2 SCC 362, the Supreme Court upheld the 44th Amendment’s restoration of judicial review, holding that the basic structure doctrine, articulated in Kesavananda, remains the touchstone for testing amendments. The Court clarified that the 44th Amendment did not create a new basic feature but reinstated the pre‑Emergency constitutional equilibrium. The judgment emphasized that the Preamble’s “sovereign democratic republic” requires an independent judiciary to prevent legislative overreach.

The amendment also altered Article 368 by inserting a proviso that any amendment affecting the federal structure, the representation of states in Parliament, or the powers of the Supreme Court and High Courts must be ratified by at least half of the state legislatures. This procedural safeguard reflects the Preamble’s federal and democratic commitments. In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) 2 SCC 321, the Court held that the ratification requirement is mandatory and non‑compliance renders the amendment void, reinforcing the Preamble’s federal character.

Furthermore, the 44th Amendment removed the provision that allowed the President to promulgate ordinances during a recess of Parliament without any time limit, thereby curbing the “ordinance raj”. The Court in D. C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987) 1 SCC 378 linked this change to the Preamble’s promise of “liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship”, reasoning that unchecked executive ordinance‑making threatens the democratic accountability envisaged by the people.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The 44th Amendment restored judicial review of constitutional amendments. Which article was amended to achieve this, and what was the key judicial precedent that confirmed the restoration?”
The 44th Amendment amended Article 368 (by adding the ratification proviso) and deleted Article 31C’s protective clause, thereby reviving Article 13(2) judicial review. The key precedent is Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) 2 SCC 362, where the Supreme Court held that the basic structure doctrine survived the Emergency amendments and that the 44th Amendment reinstated the pre‑Emergency position of judicial review over constitutional amendments.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question links an amendment to the restoration of a constitutional feature, identify the specific article altered, the provision removed, and the landmark case that interpreted the change. Use the Preamble’s key words (sovereign, democratic, republic) as the doctrinal anchor for why the restoration was necessary.

Judicial Interpretation of ‘Secular’ in the Preamble after the 42nd Amendment

The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted the word “secular” into the Preamble, making explicit a principle that the Supreme Court had already recognised as implicit in the constitutional scheme. In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) 3 SCC 1, the Court held that secularism is a basic feature of the Constitution, deriving from the Preamble’s declaration of a “secular democratic republic”. The Court defined secularism as the State’s equal treatment of all religions and its neutrality in religious matters, not merely the absence of a state religion.

Subsequent cases have expanded this interpretation. In Ismail Faruqui v. Union of India (1994) 6 SCC 360, the Court ruled that the acquisition of religious property for a secular purpose does not violate secularism, provided the State does not favour any religion. The judgment stressed that the Preamble’s “secular” obliges the State to maintain a principled distance from religious institutions while allowing regulation in the public interest.

In Aruna Roy v. Union of India (2002) 7 SCC 368, the Court upheld the inclusion of religious education in a secular curriculum, stating that secularism does not require a strict separation of religion and education but demands that no religion be given preferential treatment. The Court linked this to the Preamble’s “fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual”, arguing that exposure to diverse religious traditions fosters mutual respect.

The most recent articulation appears in Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (2019) 11 SCC 1 (Sabarimala), where the Court held that the exclusion of women of a certain age from a Hindu temple violated the Preamble’s secular and equality guarantees. The majority observed that secularism, as a basic feature, requires the State to ensure that religious practices do not infringe fundamental rights, and that the Preamble’s “secular” mandates a constitutional morality that transcends majoritarian religious norms.

The Preamble as an Interpretive Lens for Article 21: Expanding the Right to Life

Article 21 — “No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law” — has been read expansively through the Preamble’s promises of “justice, liberty, equality, fraternity”. In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) 1 SCC 248, the Court held that the procedure must be “fair, just and reasonable”, invoking the Preamble’s “liberty” and “equality” to reject a purely formalistic reading. The judgment established that the Preamble supplies the substantive content of “procedure established by law”.

The Preamble’s “fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual” has been pivotal in recognizing derivative rights. In Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi (1981) 1 SCC 608, the Court declared that the right to life includes the right to live with human dignity, citing the Preamble’s fraternity clause. This reasoning underpinned later recognitions of the right to health (Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity v. State of West Bengal (1996) 4 SCC 37), right to shelter (Chameli Singh v. State of U.P. (1996) 2 SCC 549), and right to a clean environment (Vellore Citizens’ Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) 5 SCC 647).

In Justice K. S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1, the nine‑judge bench held that privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21, grounding the decision in the Preamble’s “liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship” and “dignity of the individual”. The Court stated that the Preamble’s transformative vision requires the Constitution to adapt to evolving conceptions of personal autonomy.

The Preamble also guides the balancing of Article 21 against state interests. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Court used the Preamble’s “justice, liberty, equality, fraternity” to assess the proportionality of internet shutdowns in Jammu & Kashmir, holding that restrictions must be necessary, proportionate, and subject to judicial review, lest they undermine the democratic republic promised by the people.

The Doctrine of Basic Structure Applied to Preamble Amendments: Key Cases and Limits

The basic structure doctrine, crystallised in Kesavananda Bharati, extends to the Preamble because the Preamble encapsulates the Constitution’s identity. The Court in Kesavananda listed “sovereign democratic republic”, “secular”, “socialist”, “unity and integrity of the Nation” as essential features that cannot be abrogated. Any amendment that seeks to delete or alter these words would be ultra vires.

In Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) 2 SCC 159, the Court struck down the 39th Amendment’s clause that insulated the Prime Minister’s election from judicial scrutiny, holding that it violated the Preamble’s “democratic republic” and the basic structure of free and fair elections. The judgment affirmed that the Preamble’s democratic character is non‑negotiable.

The 42nd Amendment attempted to entrench “socialist” and “secular” in the Preamble while simultaneously curtailing judicial review. In Minerva Mills, the Court held that the amendment’s attempt to remove judicial review destroyed the basic structure, even though the Preamble’s new words were permissible. The Court clarified that adding words to the Preamble is allowed only if the amendment does not damage the Constitution’s core identity.

In S. R. Bommai, the Court reiterated that the Preamble’s “secular” and “federal” character are basic features. The judgment established that a constitutional amendment converting India into a theocratic state or a unitary state would be invalid, because it would alter the Preamble’s essential declaration.

Recent jurisprudence in K. S. Puttaswamy and Navtej Singh Johar confirms that the Preamble’s “dignity”, “liberty”, and “fraternity” are integral to the basic structure. The Court has held that any amendment seeking to dilute these values — for instance, by removing “fraternity” or “dignity” — would be struck down. The limit, therefore, is not textual immutability but substantive preservation of the constitutional vision articulated in the Preamble.

  • Confusing the Preamble’s declaratory language with justiciability — the Preamble itself is not directly enforceable, but its values inform judicial review of amendments and statutes.
  • Assuming the 42nd Amendment’s insertion of “Socialist” and “Secular” created new basic features — the Court in Kesavananda had already recognised these as implicit in the original Preamble.
  • Treating “Republic” as merely ceremonial — the term imposes a constitutional requirement that the head of state be elected, a point repeatedly affirmed in S. R. Bommai.
  • Overlooking that the 44th Amendment restored judicial review by deleting Article 31C’s protective clause, not by amending Article 13 directly.
  • Believing the basic structure doctrine applies only to constitutional amendments — it also constrains ordinary legislation that seeks to undermine Preamble values, per Minerva Mills.
  • Neglecting the distinction between “We, the People of India” and “We, the Parliament of India” — the former embodies popular sovereignty, the latter would constitute a basic‑structure violation.
  • Failing to cite the specific case that identified a Preamble value as a basic feature — examiners expect precise references such as Kesavananda (republican, democratic), S. R. Bommai (federalism, secularism), Minerva Mills (judicial review).

These advanced sections equip the aspirant to handle nuanced questions on the Preamble’s interpretive reach, the interplay of amendments with the basic structure, and the judicial construction of popular sovereignty.

The Constitutional Position of the President: Powers, Discretion, and Judicial Pronouncements

The President of India occupies a unique place in the constitutional architecture: the executive power of the Union is formally vested in the President under Article 53, yet the real exercise of that power is conditioned by the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister (Article 74). The Constitution delineates three broad categories of presidential authority — powers exercised on ministerial advice, powers exercised in discretion, and powers that are subject to parliamentary oversight. The most significant discretionary powers arise in situations where the constitutional text does not prescribe a binding advice, notably the appointment of the Prime Minister when no party commands a clear majority in the Lok Sabha (as witnessed in 1996, 1998 and 2004), the dissolution of the Lok Sabha on the advice of a Prime Minister who has lost majority support, the assent to or return of non‑money bills (Article 111), the promulgation of ordinances when Parliament is not in session (Article 123), and the grant of pardons, reprieves and commutations (Article 72).

The Supreme Court has repeatedly clarified the boundaries of these powers. In Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974) the Court held that the President acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers in all matters except those where the Constitution expressly confers discretion. The 42nd Amendment (1976) attempted to make the advice binding by inserting the words “shall act in accordance with such advice” in Article 74(1), but the 44th Amendment (1978) restored the President’s power to require the Council of Ministers to reconsider its advice, thereby preserving a narrow window of discretion. In Kehar Singh v. Union of India (1988) the Court ruled that the pardoning power under Article 72 is subject to limited judicial review — only on grounds of mala fides, arbitrariness or non‑application of mind. The ordinance‑making power under Article 123 was examined in R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) and later in Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017), where the Court emphasised that ordinances cannot be a parallel legislative track and must be laid before Parliament within six weeks of reassembly.

Emergency powers constitute another domain where presidential satisfaction is justiciable. Article 352 (national emergency), Article 356 (President’s rule in states) and Article 360 (financial emergency) all require a presidential proclamation. In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) the nine‑judge bench held that the President’s satisfaction under Article 356 is subject to judicial review and that the proclamation must be based on objective material, not on the subjective whim of the central executive. The Court also laid down the floor‑test mechanism to ascertain the majority in the state assembly. The President’s role in constitutional amendments under Article 368 is formal — the President must give assent to a bill passed by the requisite special majorities, but cannot withhold assent. The President also possesses the power to refer a question of law or fact to the Supreme Court under Article 143, a consultative jurisdiction that has been used sparingly (e.g., the Special Reference No. 1 of 1998 on the appointment of judges).

In sum, the President is a constitutional head whose discretionary space is deliberately narrow, confined to situations of political uncertainty or where the Constitution expressly reserves a decision to the President. The jurisprudence underscores that any exercise of discretion must be grounded in constitutional morality, transparent reasoning and, where applicable, the advice of the Council of Ministers after reconsideration.

The Constituent Assembly's Debates on Secularism and the Guarantees of Religious Freedom (Articles 25‑28)

The word “secular” did not appear in the original Preamble; it was inserted by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. Nevertheless, the Constituent Assembly engaged in extensive deliberations on the relationship between the state and religion, shaping Articles 25 to 28 of Part III. The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, recommended a robust guarantee of religious freedom while empowering the state to regulate secular activities associated with religious practice. Members such as K.T. Shah, H.V. Kamath and B.R. Ambedkar debated the scope of “propagation” in Article 25(1), fearing that unrestricted proselytisation could disturb public order. The Assembly ultimately adopted the phrase “subject to public order, morality and health” as a limiting clause, and added Article 25(2)(b) allowing the state to make laws for social welfare and reform, including the opening of Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus.

Article 26 guarantees every religious denomination the right to manage its own affairs in matters of religion, subject to public order, morality and health. The Assembly rejected a proposal to give the state sweeping control over religious endowments, opting instead for a balance that protects denominational autonomy while permitting legislative intervention for administration of property. Article 27 prohibits the state from compelling any person to pay taxes for the promotion or maintenance of any particular religion, embodying the principle of non‑preferentialism. Article 28 bars religious instruction in wholly state‑funded educational institutions, but permits it in institutions administered by the state but established under an endowment or trust requiring such instruction.

The debates also touched on the concept of a Uniform Civil Code. While the Directive Principles (Article 44) urge the state to endeavour to secure a uniform civil code, the Assembly deliberately refrained from making it a justiciable fundamental right, recognising the sensitivity of personal laws among minorities. The Sub‑Committee on Minorities, headed by H.C. Mookherjee, ensured that Articles 29 and 30 protect the cultural and educational rights of minorities, reinforcing the secular fabric by guaranteeing that the state would not impose a majoritarian cultural norm.

Judicial interpretation later elevated secularism to a basic feature of the Constitution. In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) the Court declared that secularism is part of the basic structure, and any amendment seeking to establish a theocratic state would be invalid. The essential‑practices test formulated in Shirur Mutt v. Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments (1954) and refined in Ratilal Panachand Gandhi v. State of Bombay (1954) owes its origin to the Assembly’s textual choice of “matters of religion” in Article 26. The Court in Stanislaus v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1977) upheld anti‑conversion laws, interpreting “propagation” as not including a right to convert. These judgments demonstrate how the Assembly’s careful wording continues to shape the contours of religious freedom in India.

Technique: Mapping Constitutional Text to Judicial Tests
Question: Explain how the Constituent Assembly’s wording of Articles 25 and 26 provided the foundation for the Supreme Court’s “essential practices” test and the “secularism as basic structure” doctrine. Cite the relevant Articles and at least two landmark cases.
Answer: Article 25(1) guarantees freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion “subject to public order, morality and health”. Article 26(b) protects the right of every religious denomination to manage its own affairs in matters of religion. In Shirur Mutt (1954), the Court held that the phrase “matters of religion” in Article 26(b) requires the judiciary to determine which practices are essential to a religion, thereby creating the essential‑practices test. The Court relied on the Assembly’s deliberate inclusion of “matters of religion” as a term of art, distinct from secular activities that the state may regulate under Article 25(2)(a). In S.R. Bommai (1994), the nine‑judge bench declared secularism a basic feature, reasoning that the Preamble’s declaration of a “Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic” (as amended) reflects the Assembly’s original intent to keep the state equidistant from all religions, an intent evident from the non‑establishment clauses in Articles 27 and 28. The Court linked the textual guarantees of religious freedom and non‑discrimination to the structural principle that the Constitution’s identity cannot be altered to favour a single religion. Thus, the Assembly’s precise language in Articles 25‑28 directly underpins both the essential‑practices jurisprudence and the basic‑structure protection of secularism.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the constitutional basis of a judicial doctrine, first locate the exact Article(s) the Court interpreted. Quote the operative phrase (e.g., “matters of religion” in Art. 26(b)). Then name the case that first articulated the test and the case that elevated the principle to basic structure. This two‑step mapping — text → first interpretation → constitutional entrenchment — scores full marks.

The Constituent Assembly's Design of the Parliamentary Executive: Collective Responsibility, the Prime Minister, and the Council of Ministers

The Constituent Assembly consciously adopted the British parliamentary model but embedded it within a written constitution that distributes authority between a ceremonial President and a responsible Council of Ministers. Article 74(1) mandates that there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President, and Article 74(2) provides that the President may require the Council to reconsider its advice, but shall act in accordance with the advice tendered after such reconsideration. This formulation, restored by the 44th Amendment after the 42nd Amendment had made the advice binding, preserves a thin layer of presidential discretion while affirming the principle of responsible government.

Article 75(1) vests the appointment of the Prime Minister in the President, and the other ministers are appointed on the Prime Minister’s advice. The Prime Minister must be a member of either House of Parliament (Article 75(5)), and a minister who is not a member of Parliament ceases to hold office after six months unless elected. The Assembly debated whether the Prime Minister should be directly elected by the people; the proposal was rejected in favour of the parliamentary convention that the leader of the majority party in the Lok Sabha becomes Prime Minister. The principle of collective responsibility is enshrined in Article 75(3): the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. This means that a vote of no‑confidence against any minister is deemed a vote against the entire Council, compelling resignation or dissolution.

The Assembly also provided for individual responsibility under Article 75(2): ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President, which in practice translates to the pleasure of the Prime Minister. The size of the Council of Ministers was left unrestricted in the original Constitution; the 91st Amendment (2003) inserted Article 75(1A) limiting the total number of ministers, including the Prime Minister, to fifteen per cent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha. The Prime Minister’s power to advise dissolution of the Lok Sabha (Article 85) is a critical executive lever; the President may refuse dissolution only in exceptional circumstances, as discussed in U.N.R. Rao v. Indira Gandhi (1971) where the Court upheld the Prime Minister’s advice to dissolve despite a pending no‑confidence motion.

Judicial pronouncements have reinforced the parliamentary character. In S.R. Bommai (1994) the Court mandated a floor test to prove majority, underscoring that the executive’s legitimacy derives from the confidence of the elected house. In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) the Court examined the anti‑defection law in the context of collective responsibility, holding that a legislator’s disqualification for defection does not violate the basic structure. The Assembly’s design thus creates a fused executive‑legislative relationship where the Prime Minister is the keystone, the Council of Ministers operates as a collective, and the President’s role remains largely ceremonial, activated only when constitutional conventions break down.

The Constituent Assembly's Deliberations on Citizenship (Articles 5‑11) and the Impact of Partition

The Partition of 1947 created an unprecedented humanitarian crisis and forced the Constituent Assembly to craft citizenship provisions that could accommodate millions of displaced persons while defining the political community of the new Republic. Articles 5 to 11, placed in Part II, were designed as transitional provisions to determine citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution on 26 January 1950, leaving the detailed law to Parliament (Article 11). Article 5 conferred citizenship on every person who had domicile in the territory of India and who was born in India, or either of whose parents was born in India, or who had been ordinarily resident in India for not less than five years immediately preceding the commencement. Article 6 addressed migrants from Pakistan: persons who migrated before 19 July 1948 became citizens if they had been ordinarily resident since migration; those migrating after that date required registration. Article 7 dealt with persons who migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 but returned under a permit for resettlement, granting them citizenship upon fulfilment of residence conditions. Article 8 extended citizenship to persons of Indian origin residing outside India who registered with an Indian diplomatic mission. Article 9 stipulated that voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship entails loss of Indian citizenship. Article 10 ensured continuity of citizenship rights subject to any law made by Parliament. Article 11 empowered Parliament to regulate the acquisition and termination of citizenship by law, leading to the Citizenship Act, 1955.

The Assembly’s debates reveal a tension between a generous, inclusive approach and the need for administrative certainty. B.R. Ambedkar, as Chairman of the Drafting Committee, argued for a clear domicile‑based criterion to avoid statelessness, while members like Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar emphasised the need to prevent dual allegiance. The Partition’s violence meant that records were often lost; the Assembly therefore allowed proof of domicile through oral testimony and community certificates. The provision for registration of overseas Indians (Article 8) anticipated the diaspora’s future role. The decision to not embed a comprehensive citizenship code in the Constitution but to delegate it to Parliament reflected a pragmatic recognition that citizenship law would need to evolve with changing geopolitical realities.

Judicial interpretation has clarified several ambiguities. In State Trading Corporation of India v. Commercial Tax Officer (1963) the Supreme Court held that a company cannot be a citizen under Article 5, restricting citizenship to natural persons. In Louis De Raedt v. Union of India (1991) the Court ruled that the right to reside in India under Article 19(1)(e) is available only to citizens, reinforcing the link between citizenship and fundamental rights. The 1986 amendment to the Citizenship Act introduced the concept of “illegal migrants” and the 2003 amendment provided for Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI), a form of limited dual citizenship not envisaged by the Assembly but enabled by Article 11’s broad legislative power. The Assembly’s transitional framework thus proved durable, allowing Parliament to adapt citizenship law while preserving the core principle that citizenship derives from a connection to the territory and the people of India.

  • Confusing the President’s ceremonial role with the Governor’s discretionary powers — the President’s discretion is far narrower and explicitly conditioned by Article 74(2).
  • Assuming the word “secular” in the Preamble originated in the Constituent Assembly — it was inserted by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, though the Assembly’s debates on Articles 25‑28 laid the substantive foundation.
  • Treating collective responsibility as merely a political convention — Article 75(3) gives it constitutional force, and the Supreme Court has enforced it through floor‑test mandates.
  • Overlooking that Article 11 empowers Parliament to make any law on citizenship, including provisions that may appear to contradict the transitional Articles 5‑10.
  • Believing the Prime Minister must be a member of the Lok Sabha — Article 75(5) only requires membership of either House, and several Prime Ministers have been Rajya Sabha members.
  • Neglecting the distinction between the essential‑practices test (Article 26) and the public‑order limitation (Article 25) — the former protects denominational autonomy, the latter permits state regulation of secular activities linked to religion.
  • Failing to cite the specific amendment that restored the President’s power to send back ministerial advice — the 44th Amendment (1978) reversed the 42nd Amendment’s binding‑advice clause.

The Doctrine of Eclipse and the Validation of Pre‑Constitutional Laws

The doctrine of eclipse holds that a pre‑Constitutional law which is inconsistent with a fundamental right does not become void ab initio; it merely becomes dormant or “eclipsed” to the extent of the inconsistency. When the constitutional impediment is removed — either by a constitutional amendment or by a judicial declaration that the fundamental right no longer applies — the law revives automatically without the need for fresh legislation. The Supreme Court first articulated this principle in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955), where a pre‑independence motor vehicles tax law was held to be eclipsed by Article 19(1)(g) but revived after the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, modified the relevant fundamental right. The Court emphasised that the law was not dead but only unenforceable during the period of conflict.

A critical nuance is that eclipse applies only to laws that were valid when enacted and became inconsistent solely because of the commencement of the Constitution. It does not apply to post‑Constitutional laws that violate fundamental rights from their inception; such laws are void under Article 13(2). In State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974) the Court clarified that a law enacted after 26 January 1950 which contravenes a fundamental right is stillborn and cannot be revived by a later amendment — the doctrine of eclipse is inapplicable. The distinction turns on the temporal origin of the statute.

The practical effect of eclipse is significant for legislative continuity. When Parliament amends a fundamental right (for example, the 25th Amendment curtailing the right to property), a host of pre‑1950 land‑reform and tenancy statutes that had been eclipsed spring back to life. Courts have repeatedly refused to strike down such revived laws on the ground that they were “re‑enacted” by the amendment; the revival is automatic. However, the revived law must still conform to the amended constitutional provision. If the amendment itself is later held to violate the basic structure, the eclipse may be re‑imposed, as seen in the aftermath of Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) where the 25th Amendment’s attempt to insulate land‑reform laws from judicial review was partially invalidated.

An examiner may test the distinction between eclipse and the doctrine of severability. While eclipse concerns the temporary suspension of an otherwise valid law, severability deals with the excision of an unconstitutional portion from a statute that contains both valid and invalid provisions. The two doctrines operate at different stages: eclipse is a temporal suspension; severability is a structural surgery. Confusing them leads to the erroneous conclusion that a post‑Constitutional law can be “eclipsed” and later revived, which the Court has expressly rejected.

The Principle of Constitutionalism and the Limits of Parliamentary Power

Constitutionalism denotes the idea that government authority is derived from and limited by a supreme constitutional text. In the Indian context, this principle is embodied in the supremacy of the Constitution (Article 13), the doctrine of basic structure (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973), and the judicial power to review constitutional amendments. The Constituent Assembly deliberately chose a written, rigid constitution over the British model of parliamentary sovereignty, thereby placing the Constitution above ordinary legislative majorities.

The basic structure doctrine, evolved through a series of landmark judgments — Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967), Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), and I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) — operates as an unwritten limitation on the amending power under Article 368. The Court has identified several “essential features” that cannot be abrogated: supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secularism, separation of powers, federalism, judicial review, and the rule of law. Any amendment that destroys or damages these features is ultra vires.

Parliament’s constituent power is thus not plenary. The 42nd Amendment (1976) attempted to curtail judicial review by inserting Articles 31C and 368(4)–(5), but the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills struck down those clauses as violating the basic structure. The 44th Amendment (1978) restored judicial review of amendments, reinforcing that the Constitution’s identity cannot be altered by a simple parliamentary majority. The doctrine also extends to the “essential features of federalism” — the Court in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) held that the federal balance is a basic feature, limiting the Centre’s power to dismiss state governments under Article 356.

A subtle but exam‑relevant point is the distinction between “amendment” and “repeal”. The basic structure doctrine applies to amendments; a total repeal of the Constitution and enactment of a new one would be a revolutionary act outside the constitutional framework, not an exercise of Article 368. The Court has never ruled on such a scenario, but constitutional theorists argue that the basic structure doctrine presupposes the continued existence of the Constitution as a living document.

Examiner's Twist: Eclipse vs. Severability
A pre‑1950 statute regulating trade was eclipsed by Article 19(1)(g). In 1976, Parliament amended Article 19(6) to permit reasonable restrictions. The statute revived. Later, the Supreme Court held that the amendment violated the basic structure and struck it down. What is the status of the pre‑1950 statute now?
The statute becomes eclipsed again. The revival was contingent on the constitutional amendment remaining valid. Once the amendment is declared unconstitutional, the fundamental right regains its original force, and the pre‑Constitutional law is once more inconsistent with that right. The doctrine of eclipse operates dynamically: the law is enforceable only while the constitutional impediment is removed. Since the impediment has been restored, the law is again dormant. No fresh legislative action is required for the eclipse to re‑attach.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about the “revival” of a pre‑Constitutional law, first identify whether the law is pre‑ or post‑Constitutional. Only pre‑Constitutional laws can be eclipsed. Then trace the constitutional amendment that removed the inconsistency; if that amendment is later invalidated, the eclipse returns automatically. Do not confuse this with severability, which deals with cutting out an offending provision from a single statute.

The Doctrine of Severability and Reading Down in Fundamental Rights Adjudication

Severability (or the “blue‑pencil” rule) permits a court to strike down only the unconstitutional portion of a statute while preserving the remainder, provided the valid part is capable of standing independently and the legislature would have enacted it without the invalid portion. The Supreme Court formulated the test in R.M.D.C. v. Union of India (1957): (i) the unconstitutional provision must be severable without altering the nature of the statute; (ii) the remaining provisions must be workable; and (iii) the legislative intent must not be defeated. If the invalid part is so intertwined with the rest that the statute becomes a “mere skeleton”, the whole Act falls.

Reading down is a complementary technique where the court interprets a provision narrowly to bring it within constitutional limits, rather than striking it down. In Chintaman Rao v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1950), the Court read down a broad licensing power under the Madhya Pradesh Bharat Sewak Samaj Act to exclude arbitrary discretion, thereby saving the statute. The distinction is procedural: severability excises; reading down constricts meaning. Both aim to preserve legislative effort but operate at different interpretive stages.

A landmark illustration of severability is State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), where the Bombay Prohibition Act’s provisions banning possession of liquor were upheld, but the provision criminalising mere possession for personal consumption was severed as violating Article 21. The Court held the remainder of the Act could function without the severed section. Conversely, in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Court refused to sever the “disqualification on voluntary giving up of membership” clause from the Tenth Schedule because it was integral to the anti‑defection scheme; the entire paragraph was struck down.

Examiners often test the “legislative intent” prong. If the statute contains a severability clause (e.g., “If any provision is held invalid, the rest shall remain in force”), the Court presumes intent to sever, but this presumption is rebuttable. In Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel (1985), the Court ignored a severability clause because the invalid provision was the “heart” of the legislation. Candidates must articulate the three‑fold test and apply it to the factual matrix rather than merely quoting the clause.

The Constitutional Position of the Vice‑President: Election, Tenure, and Role as Rajya Sabha Chairperson

The Vice‑President occupies a unique dual office under Articles 63–71. Elected by an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament (Article 66), the Vice‑President serves a five‑year term (Article 67) and is eligible for re‑election. The election follows the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, ensuring a broad consensus. The Vice‑President is ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 64), presiding over its proceedings, maintaining order, and exercising a casting vote in case of a tie (Article 100).

Unlike the President, the Vice‑President does not enjoy immunity from criminal proceedings during tenure; Article 71(2) only bars challenges to the election after the term has commenced. The Vice‑President can be removed by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a majority of its total membership and agreed to by the Lok Sabha (Article 67(b)). This removal procedure mirrors that for the President but requires only a simple majority in the Rajya Sabha, reflecting the Vice‑President’s primarily legislative role.

The Vice‑President’s casting vote has been exercised on rare but consequential occasions. In 1991, Vice‑President K.R. Narayanan cast the deciding vote on the Constitution (Seventy‑Third Amendment) Bill, enabling its passage. The Chairperson’s rulings on points of order, admission of motions, and certification of Money Bills (Article 110) are final and not subject to judicial review, though the Supreme Court in R.C. Poudyal v. Union of India (1993) held that the Speaker’s (and by analogy the Chairman’s) certification of a Money Bill is justiciable if it violates constitutional provisions.

A common misconception is that the Vice‑President acts as President during a vacancy. Article 65 provides that the Vice‑President discharges the President’s functions until a new President is elected, but does not assume the office of President. The Vice‑President continues to chair the Rajya Sabha during this period, leading to a temporary dual function. The 1977 election of Vice‑President B.D. Jatti, who later acted as President after Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed’s death, illustrates this constitutional arrangement.

The Residuary Legislative Power under Article 248 and Its Judicial Interpretation

Article 248 vests Parliament with exclusive power to make laws with respect to any matter not enumerated in the State List or the Concurrent List. Entry 97 of the Union List (List I) mirrors this residuary authority, empowering Parliament to legislate on “any other matter not enumerated in List II or List III including any tax not mentioned in either of those Lists.” The scheme reflects the framers’ intent to give the Centre a broad legislative catch‑all, ensuring that no governance vacuum exists.

The Supreme Court has consistently upheld a wide interpretation of residuary power. In Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon (1972), the Court held that the power to enact the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, fell within residuary authority because coal mining was not explicitly mentioned in any list. The Court emphasised that the residuary entry is not a “dead letter” but a functional tool for emerging subjects such as space technology, cyber law, and environmental regulation.

However, the residuary power is not unlimited. In State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977), the Court struck down a central law on “industrial disputes concerning banks” on the ground that the subject fell under Entry 22 of the State List (trade and commerce within the state) and Entry 23 of the Concurrent List (social security), leaving no room for residuary legislation. The principle is that if a matter can be reasonably accommodated in an existing entry, the residuary entry cannot be invoked to circumvent the federal distribution.

The Goods and Services Tax (GST) regime illustrates the dynamic interplay. The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, inserted Article 246A, granting concurrent power to Parliament and State Legislatures over GST. This amendment effectively removed a vast swathe of indirect taxation from the residuary domain, demonstrating that the residuary power yields to explicit constitutional redistribution. Candidates should note that the residuary power is a default, not a primary, legislative source; its invocation signals the absence of a specific entry, and courts scrutinise such claims closely.

  • Confusing the doctrine of eclipse (temporary suspension of pre‑Constitutional laws) with severability (excising an unconstitutional portion of a single statute).
  • Assuming that a post‑Constitutional law can be “eclipsed” and later revived by an amendment — the Court has held such laws are void ab initio under Article 13(2).
  • Treating the basic structure doctrine as a mere judicial invention without textual anchor; it is rooted in the Constitution’s supremacy (Article 13) and the limited amending power (Article 368).
  • Believing the Vice‑President becomes President on a vacancy; Article 65 only authorises the Vice‑President to discharge the President’s functions, not to assume the office.
  • Overlooking that the Vice‑President’s casting vote in the Rajya Sabha is a constitutional power (Article 100) and not a mere procedural convention.
  • Invoking residuary power under Article 248 for subjects that can be fitted into an existing Union, State, or Concurrent entry — courts reject such overreach.
  • Neglecting the three‑fold severability test (severability, workability, legislative intent) and relying solely on a statutory severability clause.

These advanced concepts — eclipse, constitutionalism, severability, the Vice‑President’s dual role, and residuary power — are frequently tested through comparative scenarios and require precise doctrinal articulation rather than rote memorisation.
